title: Supporting Craig Hickman for state Senate
text:
What I love about the Maine Legislature are the local characters who serve — lobstermen, waitresses, carpenters, landscapers — all with distinctive accents and big hearts.
Craig Hickman, our state senator from Gardiner, Winthrop, Manchester, Hallowell and eight other southern Kennebec County towns, is one of this breed. He’s a businessman, an organic farmer, a poet and someone who gives away free food to those who show up hungry at his door. Craig is a leader in promoting child health and rural job development.
Vote Craig Hickman for the Maine Senate this November.
Frank O’Hara
Hallowell

title: Former University of Kentucky student sentenced for baby’s death
text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT/Gray News) - The former University of Kentucky student who pleaded guilty to killing her newborn baby was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
Laken Snelling, 22, pleaded guilty in August to manslaughter, abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence, and concealing the birth of an infant. In court, she told the judge, “Instead of helping him, I ended his life.”
Fayette County Circuit Court Judge Diane Minnifield told Snelling that she made a decision and that comes with consequences.
“And sometimes those choices and consequences affect our future for the rest of our lives, and you’ve made a decision that has affected not only your future but the future of all of [the baby’s] biological paternal side,” Minnifield said.
Baby found in closet
The charges stem from an August 2025 discovery by Lexington police. Officers were called to a home on Park Avenue for an unresponsive infant. Inside a closet, police say they found a baby boy wrapped in a towel, inside a trash bag. He was pronounced dead at the scene, and Snelling was arrested four days later.
Snelling said in court Friday that she had named the baby McCoy Cade Hall.
Court records obtained by WKYT say Snelling’s roommates discussed hearing unusual noises on the morning of Aug. 27 in a Snapchat group chat that Snelling was part of.
According to a search warrant filed for Snelling’s Snapchat account, around 4 a.m. that day, one roommate sent a message saying she heard a loud noise that sounded like something had fallen. A second roommate said she heard it too and that whatever caused it had been forceful enough to knock a picture off the wall. One roommate said the noises lasted about an hour.
Just before 9 a.m. that morning, Snelling sent a message in the group chat saying the noise was her passing out. She added that she had not been feeling well and had not eaten, and said she was going to get checked out by a doctor.
The court documents say the roommates told police they were “curious” about Snelling’s story and later went into her room to investigate, which is when they found the baby. The officer who requested the warrant wrote that all of the roommates told police they had suspicions that Snelling could be pregnant but had never confirmed them with her.
The Kentucky Medical Examiner’s Office said the baby was born alive and ruled his cause of death asphyxia by undetermined means.
Baby’s father’s family speaks in court
Baby Hall’s biological father, Izaiah Hall, and his family members addressed the court and Snelling.
“He was not garbage; he was the most beautiful, perfect, innocent, full-term baby boy,” Izaiah Hall’s sister said.
Although the baby’s life was limited, the family made it known in court that their grief is not.
“You imagine birthdays, holidays, first steps, first words, laughter, hugs, kisses, and all the little moments that become lifelong memories. For Cade, those possibilities were taken away before he ever had the chance to [experience them],” said a family member identified as Izaiah Hall’s mother or aunt.
Sentencing details
Prosecutors recommended the court sentence Snelling to 10 years for the manslaughter charge, and one year each for the other three charges. Judge Minnifield said she considered Snelling’s age, education, and clean prior record before fulfilling the state’s request for a concurrent sentence.
Fayette County Commonwealth’s Attorney Kimberly Baird said the baby’s family still has questions about why this happened.
“They are so raw right now and so emotional right now, still have questions about why, so I think they are okay with the fact that she got sent to prison. I’m not sure there’s a number big enough that that was going to make this okay for them,” Baird said.
Snelling will receive 415 days of credit for time served while on bond. She is not eligible for probation, but qualifies for parole after serving 85% of her 10-year sentence.

title: NBA, sportsbooks to ban and restrict certain wagers
text:
NBA, sportsbooks to ban and restrict certain wagers
The NBA has agreed with multiple prominent sportsbooks to ban and restrict specific wagers this season, including parlays involving the under on some players' stats.
According to multiple reports citing league memos, the NBA instructed its authorized gaming operators -- including DraftKings and FanDuel -- to not allow bets that the league has deemed problematic in the wake of recent betting scandals.
Related video above | Carnegie Mellon professor discusses what bet to avoid and why
The prohibited wagers include parlays that combine bets on the same player’s statistics going under, “first of” bets such as who wins the opening tip or records a player’s first rebound, and under bets on players expected to play fewer than 12 minutes.
The changes add to earlier restrictions on bets involving players on 10-day or two-way contracts, turnovers, fouls and missed free throws, according to the report.
DraftKings has released a statement on the decision, saying in part, "The NBA’s guidance formalizes many of the market restrictions already reflected in DraftKings Sportsbook’s practices. DraftKings supports the NBA’s efforts and is committed to continued collaboration with the league to maintain game integrity, including through appropriate limits on betting markets. DraftKings’ Code of Responsible."
Engagement is fully aligned with the league’s stance on the harassment of athletes, coaches or officials.”
The NBA has pushed to limit some player-performance bets amid concerns that a player could influence a narrow statistic more easily than the outcome of a game.
The scrutiny has grown after a series of gambling investigations, including cases involving former Toronto Raptors player Jontay Porter and Miami Heat guard Terry Rozier.
The league has said it wants to reduce opportunities to manipulate player performances and protect players from harassment tied to wagers.

title: Brother-in-law recounts man’s final moments on Goliath coaster at Six Flags
text:
COBB COUNTY, Ga. (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — A birthday celebration at Six Flags Over Georgia ended in tragedy Monday when a father was ejected from the Goliath roller coaster and fell to his death, investigators said.
Hassan Kariem had gone to the park with his wife, daughter and niece to celebrate a birthday.
Joshua Nelson is Kariem’s brother-in-law. Nelson said Kariem sat next to his daughter on the ride.
“His last words were to my daughter and they were, ‘This is my favorite ride, I’m so excited to be here,’” Nelson said.
Daughter described seeing restraint come undone
Nelson said his daughter described seeing Kariem lift from his seat as the ride moved before the restraint came undone.
Nelson said his daughter called him crying after she got off the ride.
“She was like, ‘I don’t know where he went,’” he said.
Ride passed inspection in March
The Georgia Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner said the Goliath was last inspected in March and showed no warning signs.
Nelson said the family is awaiting the results of the investigation.
“We’re banding together and once the investigation is done, give him the proper send off,” he said.
Family remembers Kariem as teacher and father
Family members remembered Kariem as a dedicated teacher and father.
“He loved everything about Atlanta. He loved kids. He loved technology,” Nelson said.
Six Flags Over Georgia will reopen Friday. The park said Goliath will remain closed until further notice.

title: How to discuss firearm safety as older loved ones’ abilities change
text:
(Aging Untold) — Firearms are part of the home for some families. But as parents and grandparents age, changes in vision, memory or mood can affect how safely those firearms are handled and stored. It’s about checking in to make sure the safeguards in place still fit the person today.
What to watch for
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the signals families should watch for go beyond the firearm itself.
“You’re looking at the firearms itself, but what about missed medications and balance, and falling and financial judgments being off? These are all signs that maybe cognitively there’s something that has changed,” Rogers said.
She added that the stakes are different when a firearm is involved.
“It’s just that when you’re dealing with a firearm, that error is irreversible,” Rogers said.
It’s about the whole picture, not just the firearm
Rogers said families shouldn’t focus only on removing a firearm, but on reading all the signals together.
“It’s really not about removing things. You have to look at all the different signals that are going on, and that makes your assessment. And then look at how safe you can keep the environment if these things are happening,” Rogers said.
Use a diagnosis as a natural checkpoint
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said a new medical diagnosis can be a practical moment to raise the subject.
“Has there been a medical diagnosis of something like Parkinson’s or congestive heart failure, or something that would cause weakness and instability, that you would question the safety of the firearm in the home?” O’Rourke said.
She also encouraged families to plan ahead, before any problems appear.
“If they own a firearm and they’re fine, have the conversation then,” O’Rourke said. “If you run into trouble, Dad, Mom, how are we going to approach this? Or I am going to approach this, or can we talk about this now so we’re kind of ready if this happens.”
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the timing of the discussion matters.
“These are rational, thought-provoking discussions, and they have to be made when you have two cognitively whole humans,” Cradduck said.
Dementia raises the urgency
Cradduck said the changes in the brain associated with dementia are reasons to have the conversation early.
“We know that there is a rise of dementia diagnosis and with that comes poor judgment, oftentimes, and misjudgment, and sometimes hallucinations,” Cradduck said. “And God forbid, if grandpa’s having hallucinations and he pulls the gun out, now we have a family tragedy. Let’s have the conversation when the diagnosis happens.”
Cradduck said the conversation doesn’t need to wait for a diagnosis at all.
“Even before, as you’re aging,” she said. “This isn’t rights. This is safety. This is human safety.”
A home care story that shows the stakes
Cradduck shared an experience from her time running a home care agency involving a legally blind client who kept a firearm in her home.
“She thought there was somebody outside, and so she called the police. And the police come rolling up, and she walked out the door with her gun in hand. And unfortunately, they saw a gun, and we lost her to that,” Cradduck said. “So this isn’t just protecting the other person. It could be protecting them.”
Rogers said the story reflects the broader point.
“I think you have to look at all the signs that say where’s the brain headed,” Rogers said.
How home care agencies handle firearms in the house
O’Rourke said her own policy as a home care agency owner was not to go into homes where there were firearms or ammunition for the safety of her employees.
“That was my policy,” O’Rourke said. “Other people have different ways of running their businesses, but I would say, are there firearms in the home? They would say no or yes, if they were telling the truth, or if they even remembered. And then if they did, I would want the plan to get them removed, because I didn’t want to have a conversation with a caregiver and say, I’m sorry.”
Ambrose asked O’Rourke to clarify the reasoning behind the policy.
“So as an employer, you felt responsibility for your employees to be safe in the house? Sometimes maybe the patient or the client might not be thinking straight, and so you had to protect the employees that worked for you. So that’s what that was about. It’s not judgment about guns,” Ambrose said.
Cradduck said many home care agencies take a similar approach, though not all handle it the same way.
“So when you’re looking for home care, you may be met with that. Lots of agencies have that,” Cradduck said. “Mine was different. My policy was different, and it was: do you have guns in the home? I’m not going to ask you to do anything. Do you have them? I want to know where they’re at. I want to be able to be informed. I didn’t want you to have to lie to me and then find out something later on the down low. I wanted the open, honest conversation. But I get why, because we’re sending people into these homes, and we are responsible.”
Letting the doctor be the one to say no
O’Rourke also described a client who asked for outside help delivering the message.
“I had one client that went to her doctor and said, ‘Would you tell him he can’t have his guns anymore?’” O’Rourke said. “And when the doctor said it, it took all the responsibility from her and gave it to the doctor, and the doctor supported her. I thought that was brilliant.”

title: Letter: Dakota Dupuis is the future of the Hancock County Sheriff’s Office
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I support Dakota Dupuis for Hancock County Sheriff. I recognized the spark in Dakota from the outset. Prepared, even-tempered, and thoughtful, it was refreshing having him represent the Sheriff’s Office at county commissioners’ meetings. Dakota came to the forefront for me when the animosity between Commissioner William Clark and Sheriff Scott Kane hindered any constructive dialogue.
Over my tenure as a county commissioner, I’ve seen a good amount of bad behavior during our meetings. It seems ego must go hand in hand in some positions, but l’ve never sensed that in Dakota. He advocates for his people and for the citizens of the county.
When I expressed the necessity to extend the working life of cruisers, he listened and complied. He wins some battles and loses some too, but his character never changes.
He doesn’t yell or belittle — it’s not some personal vendetta — he moves on like a mature adult.
I see Dakota Dupuis as the future of the sheriff’s office. Yes, he’s younger than the past sheriffs but not a kid and not inexperienced both in the field and administratively. In a time when so many in leadership seem mired in past transgressions and ill will, I believe Dakota has the energy, enthusiasm and leadership Hancock County needs as we restore humility and integrity to the office.
John Wombacher
Bucksport

title: New England's having an 'elite' year, but there's fall foliage elsewhere, too
text:
CONCORD, N.H. (AP) — Kyle Cotner knew nothing about fall foliage when he trolled his White House colleagues in 2007, telling them he was an expert despite having grown up in Florida.
When autumn rolled around, he kept up the bit, sending out weekly newsletters with foliage statistics and information to a handful of co-workers. Today, he has mastered complex mapping systems, calls himself “Leaf Daddy” and owns The Foliage Report, a website that tracks fall color from coast to coast.
Thus, he was speaking with actual authority last week when he said 2026 has been a spectacular year for foliage in New England.
“I’ve been doing this for almost 20 years, and this is the best I’ve seen of New England in that time,” he said. “2020 was a very good year, but this one seems elite to me.”
New England had adequate rain through the spring and summer, plus warm days and cool nights heading into fall, but that wasn’t the case elsewhere, he said.
Extreme drought conditions stressed trees in Colorado, for example, leading to a quick and lackluster foliage season. Aspens in Wyoming, Montana and Idaho aren’t as golden this year, he said. But Utah is a bright spot.
“They got enough rainfall in that area,” he said. “You basically want an average amount of precipitation to really bring out the most majestic and colorful leaves.”
Fall foliage: The last supper for trees
Fall foliage is all about trees preparing for winter, according to experts at the University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension.
Leaves exist to provide food for the tree. They absorb sunlight through a green pigment called chlorophyll, and that energy is used to convert water and carbon dioxide from the air into glucose, a type of sugar. As days shorten, the tree stops making food, allowing orange and yellow pigments that have been there all along to be unmasked. When sunny days are followed by cold nights, sugars get trapped in leaves, producing red pigments.
Eventually, the layer of cells between a twig and a leaf weakens, allowing leaves to be blown down during wind and rain. The timing varies widely by location. According to Cotner’s research, foliage season starts in Alaska in mid-August and ends in Florida in late December. Hawaii is the only U.S. state without fall foliage, he said.
Leaf peepers share their perspective
For Kirk Giglio, leaf peeping provides an escape from his day job as a nurse in a cardiac and stroke unit of a Connecticut hospital. A photographer who frequently chases storms as well, he is used to studying maps and forecasts, and was hopeful by early September that this would be a good year. A recent trip to Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont with his fiancee confirmed it.
“I was just really kind of blown away,” he said, describing sunrise hikes and fog lifting to reveal vibrant colors in New Hampshire’s Crawford Notch and elsewhere. Though some spots were packed with tourists, he still found plenty of secluded and stunning scenery.
“The more I travel, the more I realize how much we take for granted up here,” he said. “In a world that is so modern and gray with these corporate, soulless colors that we see everywhere, the trees are one of the last things that make color anymore, so it’s nice to just observe, especially in a good year like this.”

title: Multiple Southern California homes are ablaze in a fast-moving wildfire fueled by hot, windy weather
text:
SANTA ANA, Calif. (AP) — A fast-moving fire fueled by high winds burned at least six homes in Southern California on Friday, engulfing expensive coastal properties and prompting thousands to evacuate.
Black smoke — visible from miles away — billowed over tennis courts and swimming pools while firefighters doused blazing homes in San Juan Capistrano in Orange County. Some homeowners sprayed water on their properties before heeding evacuation orders.
Two firefighters were taken to the hospital with heat-related injuries, officials said. Authorities have not said how the blaze, which was less than a square mile as of Friday evening, started.
“Had these winds been a little bit stronger, a little bit different direction, this could have been a whole lot worse,” said San Clemente Mayor Rick Loeffler.
Howard Hart, a councilmember for San Juan Capistrano, said he and his wife doused their roof with water and moved propane tanks away from their home before they evacuated Friday with a to-go bag.
Laura Hart hasn’t had to evacuate due to fire in the more than five decades she’s lived in the community, she said.
“This doesn’t usually happen to us, we usually see it on the news,” she said. “We always pray to God it’s not us, but yeah, it was today.”
The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente, and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano. An evacuation shelter has opened in each city. By Friday night, about 16,000 residents had been ordered to evacuate, said Fire Chief TJ McGovern, of the Orange County Fire Authority.
It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast. The strongest winds were expected through Friday afternoon, but conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night, with a heat advisory in effect until 8 p.m. Saturday on the Orange County and San Diego County coast, the National Weather Service said.
Tens of thousands of people in the state are without power after their electricity was turned off. A separate fire by the Marine Corps base Camp Pendleton shut down for hours a section of Interstate 5 that is a major artery connecting Orange County to San Diego. That added hours to commutes throughout Southern California.
The coastal cities are surrounded by hillsides. San Juan Capistrano, a city of 35,000, is known for horse trails and the historic Mission San Juan Capistrano. San Clemente, which is home to 62,000 people, is known as a “Spanish village by the sea” and popular with beachgoers and surfers.
“The fire is right up on the city,” said Victor Cabral, a San Clemente Council member. “It’s on the perimeter of our homes on the north end.”
Nine schools were also closed Friday in San Juan Capistrano, the Capistrano Unified School District said.
Nearby residents were also on edge as smoke darkened the sky.
Wyoming resident Shannon Needham was visiting her mother at her assisted living facility in Dana Point just north of San Clemente when she learned about the fire.
The facility director told her that two buses would be on standby in case they needed to evacuate, Needham said.
“You could hear the fire trucks, you could hear the helicopters and everything above. And it was so smoky, it was just dark smoke,” Needham said.
Some of California’s worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power in dry winds. More than 200,000 customers in California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.
The weather service also issued a red flag warning for parts of central and Northern California through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.
___
Rodriguez reported from San Francisco. Associated Press writer Jaimie Ding contributed from Los Angeles.

title: Jackson tells Collins to 'shut up' during heated Senate debate
text:
Troy Jackson tells Susan Collins to 'shut up' during heated Maine Senate debate
Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson told Republican Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during a heated final Maine U.S. Senate debate that also included an interruption from a data center protester.
Thursday night's debate in a Bangor theater was the last of four meetings between Collins and Jackson, who are running for a seat that's considered crucial in the fight for a Senate majority. The debate, like those that preceded it, included several testy exchanges over issues including the national debt, Collins' relationship with President Donald Trump's administration, and the candidates' respective roles in worsening partisan divisions.
The scene became briefly chaotic when a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. As moderators asked for the protester to be removed, Collins said the shouting demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy's supporters.”
Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don't even know that kid.”
Maine GOP said in a social media post after the debate that Jackson's “shut up” comment was “unacceptable behavior.” Jackson's campaign declined to comment on the exchange.
The issue of party loyalty came up during the debate, with one question posed to Collins asking her to cite a time she has defied the Republican Party. She referenced her push to oppose Pete Hegseth's nomination as defense secretary, saying she organized Republicans to vote no. But Collins acknowledged he was confirmed despite her effort.
Collins accused Jackson of being a guaranteed vote for the Democratic Party while she has a track record of independence. Jackson disputed that characterization and said Collins is loyal to Trump when he needs key votes.
“What I know is that 100% of the time when Donald Trump goes to Susan Collins for a vote, he gets it,” Jackson said.
Collins, who is seeking her sixth term, has sought to distance herself from Trump during the debates, including using the phrase “Gulf of Mexico” instead of Trump's preferred “Gulf of America.” Jackson described Collins' votes against Trump as “managed votes” when she already knows the outcome is decided.
Jackson's campaign also said Thursday that it raised $20.4 million in the third quarter as it seeks to close a funding gap with Collins. Jackson was a late entry into the race and the third quarter was his first quarter of fundraising.
Collins’ campaign said she raised $5.2 million in the same time period. Collins began the race with a considerable fundraising advantage over Jackson, as she had raised more than $18 million by the end of June and Jackson did not become the Democrats’ nominee until late July.

title: Reports: Trump considers using 'Mother of All Bombs' against Iran
text:
Reports: Trump considers using 'Mother of All Bombs' against Iran
Reports say President Donald Trump is weighing the use of the Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, bomb. Here's what that is.
Reports: Trump considers using 'Mother of All Bombs' against Iran
Reports say President Donald Trump is weighing the use of the Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, bomb. Here's what that is.
New reports say President Donald Trump may be considering using the Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, also known as the MOAB or "Mother of All Bombs," against Iranian forces and energy infrastructure.
The MOAB has only been used once before. In 2017, Trump authorized the U.S. military to deploy the bomb, targeting an ISIS-linked cave and tunnel in Afghanistan.
The bomb, considered the most powerful non-nuclear weapon in the U.S. arsenal, weighs about 11 tons, contains nearly 19,000 pounds of explosives, and has a blast radius of approximately one mile, according to Just Security.org.
Experts say the MOAB is massive by conventional bomb standards, but even the smallest nuclear bombs are at least 900 times more powerful, according to a former defense official.
The cost of the MOAB is estimated at around $16 million each, according to experts.

title: Popular indie music festival returns to Belfast for fall event
text:
BELFAST, Maine (WABI) - A popular stage for local indie music made its return to Belfast. All Roads Music Festival is in its 11th year. While the event is usually held every May, organizers decided to bring it back for the fall.
The festival invited musical artists from across Maine, blending genres including country, folk, indie rock and singer-songwriters.
For the founders, giving independent artists the chance to show their talents to concert-goers is what makes the festival unique.
“So All Roads was created off this genesis of celebrating Maine music and all of the talent that’s here. I mean, it’s immense. All different genres, all different ages. So I think for Mainers, they’re adventurous. They love to support creativity and art and music. So this festival is kind of on brand for that type of community member who wants to just come out, see 30 bands for $40 over the course of two days and really take it in,” said Meg Shorette, festival booker and creative director.
The festival shifts between different venues in Belfast: Marshall Wharf Brewing Company, The Bazz, The First Church, American Legion Hall and Opera House Video.
There is enough time between each performance for attendees to get from one venue to the other.
Performances kick off tomorrow at 1:30 p.m. and continue until 1 a.m.
Tickets and schedule information are available at allroadsmusicfest.com.

title: Is Maine’s foliage peaking later as falls get warmer?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
While satellite models show New England’s foliage arriving a week later than it did 70 years ago, Maine’s weekly forest ranger maps reveal a climate system in flux, with peak dates swung wildly between early drought-induced leaf drops and warm, delayed autumns.
This shifting schedule is watched closely by Maine residents, for whom the vibrant crimson and gold canopy is cherished, and by leaf peepers who pump nearly a half-billion dollars in economic activity into Maine’s tourism economy each fall.
How leaves change color every autumn is dictated by plant biology.
As the days grow shorter and cool temperatures arrive, deciduous trees stop pumping out green chlorophyll, allowing underlying yellow, gold and red pigments to finally be revealed. However, chlorophyll breakdown is slowed by rising fall temperatures, keeping leaves green into October.
But ecologists say temperature is only one piece of the puzzle. Seasonal foliage timing and color brilliance are also heavily influenced by rainfall, soil moisture and pest outbreaks, which is why year-to-year ranger reports can mask the long-term trends in Maine’s changing foliage.
Comparing weather and climate is akin to mood versus personality. Daily moods can be easily swayed by immediate events, much like short-term weather anomalies. In contrast, a person’s underlying personality is formed gradually over decades, much like long-term climate baselines.
A review of the state forest rangers’ weekly foliage progression reports underscores the year-to-year variability. In 2020, after a severe summer drought, more than half the state’s seven foliage zones peaked in late September. It would be another six years before any zone peaked so early.
Tree stress caused by severe summer droughts often triggers premature browning and leaf drop, creating the appearance of an early peak. Conversely, fungal blights promoted by heavy fall rain and sudden windstorms can denude entire canopies before peak vibrancy.
How can the long-term delay in fall color be confirmed when the ranger reports look so chaotic?
The underlying shift was uncovered by geographer Stephanie Spera through research at Acadia National Park. She used decades of satellite imagery alongside historical diaries and park photos to strip away annual weather noise.
She identified a distinct pattern: Peak foliage at Acadia, which would fall into Maine’s Zone 2 in the statewide fall foliage map, was arriving nine to 10 days later than it did in the 1950s, or about one day later with each passing decade.
Acadia has warmed by 3.4 degrees Fahrenheit over the last century. One out of five plant species documented in the park a century ago are gone. Seven of the park’s 10 most common tree species are expected to decline or possibly even disappear by 2100.
Climate change is driving not just rising temperatures, but several of the other variables that play a role in Maine’s annual foliage show. The future climate will likely see more more droughts and deluges play out in the same calendar year, according to the Maine Climate Council.
Because fall nights are warming across Maine, trees are staying active later in the season. Thus, while year-to-year peak foliage dates remain at the mercy of the fickle weather moods, Maine’s climate personality is predicted to push peak colors deeper into the calendar over time.
Maine’s modern foliage tracking traces back to 1959, when then Forestry Commissioner Austin Wilkins ordered weekly foliage updates from state forest rangers. These early assessments were radioed to state headquarters and manually distributed to local reporters by phone.
In 1996, Maine became the first state to post weekly leaf conditions on the web. Over time, these reports have established a baseline for seasonal environmental tracking and created a marketing tool for the state’s growing leaf-peeping economy.

title: Some Franklin Towers residents pleased with results of relocation meeting
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Some Franklin Towers residents pleased with results of relocation meeting
Residents in Franklin Towers were told they would all have to relocate and then said they were left in the dark. But a meeting on Thursday with the Portland Housing Authority is leaving some of them with hope and more details.
Some Franklin Towers residents pleased with results of relocation meeting
Residents in Franklin Towers were told they would all have to relocate and then said they were left in the dark. But a meeting on Thursday with the Portland Housing Authority is leaving some of them with hope and more details.
Franklin Towers residents have been told they will need to relocate during extensive renovations to the 16-story building.
Franklin Towers has been plagued by bedbugs, cockroaches, mold, asbestos and other toxins, so the Portland Housing Authority is conducting a multi-million-dollar renovation project. Some residents have previously expressed that they were left in the dark; after initially being told the renovation would be in phases, residents were later told they would all need to move out of the building.
On Thursday, the Portland Housing Authority held a meeting with residents. That meeting was limited to residents only, but Maine's Total Coverage spoke with three residents afterward who said they felt satisfied with the results.
"They have been working around the clock for us. It was a safety issue. That is it, they want us to be safe," said one resident.
Samantha Hashey, who has lived in the Franklin Towers since 2017, just finished relocating in the building when she thought renovations would be phased. Now, she will need to move again, but said she had a lot of questions answered on Thursday.
"It seems like it is going to be something good," Hashey said.
Hashey said she was told their security and pet deposits would be returned and would be usable at other buildings. She said she was told in the meeting that Portland Housing Authority was securing buildings in Portland, South Portland and Westbrook, and that residents would not have to return to Franklin Towers once renovations are complete. She said residents could start moving in as soon as three months, but had no timeline on when all residents would be out so renovations can begin.
"A lot of us are like, this really sucks, but if it is good for our health and stuff, it is worth the aggravation," Hashey said.
We reached out to the Portland Housing Authority. A spokesman said additional details will be released on Friday.

title: Northern Maine rail improvements tagged for federal funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than $37 million in federal funding has been awarded to the rail system in Aroostook County.
The Northern Aroostook Rail Gateway Modernization and Safety Project funding will support the rehabilitation of 90 miles of railroad tracks in Fort Kent, Madawaska and Van Buren. The Maine Department of Transportation is the recipient of the federal money.
The funding comes through the U.S. Department of Transportation Federal Railroad Administration’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements Program and was announced by U.S. Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Angus King, I-Maine.
Freight rail ‘essential’
In July, Collins and King sent a letter to the Federal Railroad Administration in support of MaineDOT’s application for the funding, highlighting the importance of the rail corridor to northern Maine’s forest products and agricultural industries.
“Freight rail is essential to northern Maine’s economy, connecting our forest products and agricultural industries to markets across the country and around the world,” Maine’s two senators said in a joint statement.
“This $37 million investment will help modernize aging rail infrastructure and increase railcar capacity, making it easier and safer for Maine businesses to move their products,” they added. “By strengthening this critical rail corridor, this funding will support local jobs and help keep Aroostook County’s forest products and agricultural industries competitive for years to come.”
Improvements will include replacing aging rail, cross-ties and ballast, as well as rehabilitating a key railroad bridge.
Collins, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, is running for a sixth term this November.

title: Bar Harbor-Canada ferry saw 10% increase in passengers this year
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR, Maine — The CAT ferry, which brings passengers between Bar Harbor, Maine, and Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, saw its ridership increase 10% over last year.
The news was announced Friday.
“The Nova Scotia-Maine ferry service recorded the second highest passenger numbers of the last ﬁve years,” the operator said in a press release.
The last trip of the 2026 season was Wednesday.
“A total of 44,032 passengers and 18,124 vehicles used The CAT ferry between Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and Bar Harbor, Maine,” the release stated.
In 2025, the cat had carried 39,745 passengers and 16,233 vehicles.
“We had a signiﬁcant bounce back year despite many issues beyond our control as a company,” President and Chief Executive Oﬃcer of Bay Ferries Limited Mark Wilson said. “The vessel and our teams performed well on all accounts and we were able to grow the service bringing tens of thousands of high value visitors into Nova Scotia.”
Bay Ferries Limited operates the Maine-Nova Scotia ferry service, which leases land from the Town of Bar Harbor for the ferry’s operations.
“Approximately 85% of the total passengers using the service were Americans with Canadians making up the remaining 15%,” Wilson said. “Americans using the service grew year over year making up the majority of the growth.”
This season The CAT ferried 120 round trips. Twelve round trips had to be canceled because of weather.
It costs approximately $350,000 to the Province of Nova Scotia for pilot service into Bar Harbor’s waters during the season. The pilots execute a 180-degree turn when docking it at the Bay Ferries Terminal at the town-owned site on Route 3. Pilots move it through a roughly 600-foot-wide channel between lobster buoys and gear and back to its port, which is farther than where cruise ships dock.
The CAT is 8,127 tons with a 12-foot draft and it can have more than 800 people onboard.
In the press release, President of the Tourism Industry Association of Nova Scotia Darlene Grant Fiander stressed the CAT’s importance to bringing people to the province.
“It is great to see growth over last year which is very positive considering the geo-political climate,” Grant Fiander said. “This continues to be one of several very important tourist conduits into our province and our tourism operators depend on predictability and stability as they work hard to attract visitors to Nova Scotia.”
The ferry’s fees do not cover its $21 million operating costs, and it has been subsidized by the Canadian government.
“We are excited to welcome passengers on The CAT next year and look forward to continuing to grow this important service to the maximum benefit of Nova Scotians,” Wilson said.
The ferry did not run during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021. It had existed in Bar Harbor from 1956 through 2009, stopping when Nova Scotia ended subsidies. From 2014 through 2018, it ran from Portland to Nova Scotia instead, returning to Bar Harbor at a fully operational status in 2022.
The 2027 schedule is expected to be released in the next two weeks.
The company has a contract with the Canadian province. That contract runs through mid October. An economic analysis has shown the ferry’s impact on Nova Scotia is positive.

title: More roller coasters shut down as authorities investigate fatal fall at Georgia amusement park
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — A growing number of amusement parks have shut down roller coasters as police and state regulators investigate what caused a man to fall out of his seat and plummet to his death at a Georgia park.
SeaWorld Orlando in Florida and La Ronde theme park in Montreal, Canada, confirmed on Thursday they had temporarily closed rides, bringing the total number of roller coasters halted to 11.
Police and a state regulatory agency are investigating what caused Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, to fall from the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. Witnesses described seeing him ejected from the coaster; some people who rode the Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints.
Nine of the roller coasters taken out of service have the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system as the Goliath at Six Flags.
Mom says her son’s restraint didn’t work properly
Erica Billups said her son and daughter rode Goliath about an hour before Kariem’s death and encountered a problem with the restraint on one seat. Her son initially sat in that seat and tried to lock it, but then moved when it repeatedly became unlocked. The roller coaster embarked with the seat empty and the harness up, she said in a post on X.
She confirmed the post in a text message to The Associated Press on Thursday.
She said staff did not tell her kids there was a problem.
Summer Bates, who was at the Georgia park with her husband and three children and saw Kariem fall, told the AP previously that her older two children kept trying to push their restraints down tighter while on the ride. She understood why they were doing that later when she was on the coaster, she said, because the restraints didn’t feel secure.
Six Flags did not immediately respond to an email for comment on any issues with restraints.
At least one of the other closures is for safety
La Ronde in Montreal said one of its coasters — also named Goliath — is offline “while we conduct a thorough safety review in collaboration with the ride’s manufacturer.” Sea World Orlando said that it closed its Mako roller coaster with no set date to reopen.
Neither La Ronde nor SeaWorld Orlando said why those specific rides were closed. Both were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, which also built the Goliath ride in Georgia and eight of the other coasters that Six Flags closed. Bolliger & Mabillard declined Thursday to answer questions about the shutdowns.
In an updated list of ride closures provided Thursday, Six Flags no longer included the Goliath coaster at its Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California. The coaster has a different manufacturer and restraint system from the others. Six Flags had listed it as closed earlier in the week.
Online photos and videos of most of the closed coasters show each equipped with so-called “clamshell” restraints, mounted in front of each seat on a vertical bar that sits between the rider’s knees. The bar locks the padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.
Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group, said the similar restraint systems are almost certainly why most of the coasters were closed.
Speigel said they’re likely to remain shut down until investigators have determined what went wrong on the Georgia coaster, but he said that “obviously it was something with the restraint.”
Roller coaster manufacturers decide what type of restraints to use after considering speed, force and the track’s transitions, said Brian D. Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert.
He advocates the use of a backup restraint for riders, but there is a long-running debate in the industry over whether that would increase wait times, Avery said.
Bolliger & Mabillard says it is investigating
The company said in an email it would have no further comment until it had a “better understanding of what transpired” on Monday.
Kariem was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Goliath, one of Six Flags Over Georgia’s headline attractions, towers above the park’s entrance. It opened in 2006 and features a series of hills and turns. It doesn’t take riders upside down, but its first hill rises to 200 feet (61 meters) and it has a top speed of 70 miles per hour (112 kilometers).
Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars passing overhead, said it looked like Kariem was hovering because the car was moving underneath him. He fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mendenhall said, and then was ejected from the ride on its final turn.
Six Flags has faced legal trouble before
A class-action lawsuit filed by investors in 2025 alleges that Six Flags concealed the poor state of its amusement parks — including long-neglected maintenance — ahead of its merger with major amusement park operator Cedar Fair.
“Prior to the Merger, Legacy Six Flags had for years deferred or foregone basic park maintenance, operational improvements, infrastructure repairs, and ride design and development updates,” the complaint said. The company also cut staffing to reduce costs, it alleges.
Timothy Loranger, a California attorney who sued Six Flags in a fatal case, said it’s a positive step that the theme park chain closed down rides at other parks as a precaution. Loranger represented the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 roller coaster in 2022 at Six Flags Magic Mountain.
“In all instances, X2 had many reports of injury in the past, and instead of doing a deep dive investigation into the ride, they did things like blame the passengers, the injured person for not sitting properly or holding their head against the headrest or they blamed an imaginary pre-existing condition,” Loranger said.
Six Flags permanently closed the X2 ride last month.
Georgia park to reopen
Six Flags Over Georgia is set to reopen on Friday. The Goliath, however, is not expected to be running.
The park, which has about a dozen roller coasters, is in Mableton, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta.

title: Jake Bauers was ready to retire. Now, he's the 2026 NLCS MVP
text:
Jake Bauers was ready to retire. Now, he's the Brewers' 2026 NLCS MVP
Jake Bauers was named the 2026 NLCS Most Valuable Player after the Brewers swept the Dodgers.
Two seasons after he nearly quit baseball, Bauers has become a big hitter in the middle of the Milwaukee Brewers' lineup — and he put his renewed focus on display in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series.
Bauers’ two-run homer on the 11th pitch of a seventh-inning at-bat against Los Angeles Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell gave Milwaukee the lead for good in a 6-2 victory Wednesday, putting the Brewers on the cusp of their first World Series since 1982.
“Incredible at-bat,” manager Pat Murphy said.
Bauers fouled off five two-strike pitches before turning on a 97 mph fastball and launching it 412 feet to right field.
“Super sick,” teammate Garrett Mitchell said. “I think that more just goes to show the type of player he is. It’s a selfless at-bat. He’s just trying to put the ball in play. He’s trying to move the guy over, and put an incredible swing on that. For me, being able to watch that on deck was awesome.”
Mitchell followed with a home run of his own to chase Snell and make it 4-2. Milwaukee has a 3-0 lead in the best-of-seven NLCS, with Game 4 at Los Angeles on Thursday.
Bauers was drafted in 2013 by the San Diego Padres out of Marina High School in Huntington Beach, located about 40 miles south of Dodger Stadium. After batting .202 for the New York Yankees in 2023, he was traded that November to Milwaukee — where he hit .199 in 2024.
Ready to hang up his spikes, Bauer changed his mind when his wife told him she was pregnant. Wanting to be a provider for his growing family, he put off retirement and maintained their health insurance.
Earlier this week, Bauers spoke eloquently about his wife and her sacrifice while raising two rambunctious children while he is away playing baseball.
Video below: Brewers fans buying World Series and NLCS champion merchandise
Now, he's making fans all over Milwaukee feel like little kids again.
“There’s a lot of people to credit, man,” Bauers said after Wednesday's game. “I’ve played a lot of places. I’ve picked up knowledge from a lot of different people.
“I think what changed for me this year was I stopped caring about results. I started caring about competing. I started caring about being in the moment and getting out of my own way.”
All that showed up in Game 2 of the series when he worked a two-out walk to load the bases on the 12th pitch he saw from Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto in the third inning. Christian Yelich followed with a two-run single for a 3-2 lead in a 7-4 victory, ending Yamamoto's outing.
Bauers, who turned 31 last week, is in his third year with Milwaukee — his fifth team in seven major league seasons. The first baseman and corner outfielder led the Brewers with 26 home runs and an .874 OPS during the regular season.
“Jake got an opportunity, that’s what he got,” Murphy said. “He got an opportunity to contribute, and he kind of found his offensive approach. And he kind of found, like, I’m really talented, but this is what serves me best. It’s a growth in the game. He’s continued to grow.”
Video below: Inside the Brewers' clubhouse during the champagne celebration
Patient and disciplined with a sharp eye at the plate, Bauers drew 94 walks and compiled a .389 on-base percentage this season. He also had 86 RBIs in 144 games, shattering his previous career highs across the board.
“I came into this year feeling like there was really only one person holding me back, and that was myself,” Bauers said. “So I think I just gave myself the space to believe that I could play — I could play in this league.”

title: Aging Untold: Where to find senior discounts and why you should ask
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we look into senior discounts to see which perks are actually worth asking for and how to maximize your savings.
Then we examine tinnitus, the constant ringing or buzzing in the ears, and share practical ways to manage symptoms and protect your hearing.
Finally, we take you inside an imaginative, coloring-book-style coworking space near Nashville designed to spark creativity and build connections.
Many restaurants and museums offer senior discounts, and you might be surprised by other places you could find them.
You just have to ask — and bring your identification with you to prove you are eligible.
“I think the baseline should be the assumption that everybody’s going to give a discount,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “So no matter where you go, I’m going to get a discount. And I’d be brave enough to ask it.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said some seniors feel uncomfortable requesting a discount, but they shouldn’t feel that way — they should accept it.
“You earned it,” she said.
Tinnitus is a constant ringing, hissing or humming in the ears.
Millions of Americans experience the condition. Goutham Gosu, a doctor of audiology, said tinnitus is difficult to measure because it relies on a patient’s description.
As family members age and their abilities change, it might be time to make sure the safeguards that are in place still fit the person today. That includes safety plans for firearms if they are present in the home.
Cradduck said the timing of the discussion matters.
“These are rational, thought-provoking discussions, and they have to be made when you have two cognitively whole humans,” Cradduck said.
The walls of the Creativity Bar just outside Nashville look like a coloring book. Shapes outlined in black are designed to help imagination and ideas flow.
Stephanie Pruitt-Gaines founded the space where members can drop in and work toward their next great idea.
It is part playroom, part art studio and part office.

title: Flamingo recovers with custom brace from orthopedist
text:
TYLER, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A Chilean flamingo at Tyler’s Caldwell Zoo is recovering from a soft tissue injury to his ankle joint with the help of a custom-built brace.
Queenie, 9, got spooked and ran while on exhibit, tearing ligaments in his ankle. Bird Department Supervisor Nichole Moore said keepers noticed him lagging behind.
“He sustained this injury on exhibit. We saw him lagging behind his flock. And then we decided since he’s so tactile, we’d be able to get him in hand and really help him,” Moore said.
Injury first appeared years ago
The injury first showed up in 2021. Medicine did not fully fix the problem, so the zoo worked with Ben Guenther, an orthopedist who typically builds braces and prosthetics for people. Guenther designed a brace for Queenie.
“This was the best opportunity for him because we would be able to put a brace on him and work with him and make sure it would really work so he would be able to live a really long life,” Moore said.
Why leg function matters
Flamingos use their legs for more than walking. They also use their feet to stir up food so they can filter through it.
“It is really important for us to be quick when assessing injuries, especially on long-legged birds like this, they utilize their feet quite a bit when they’re moving around,” Moore said. “They also use their feet to kind of stir up the the food, to really like move things around for them to filter through. So it’s just such a really important thing for them to have function in both legs. So yeah, it’s really important for us to really make sure that we’re able to take care of them as quick as we can.”
Chilean flamingos can live into their 60s.
Brace is a lifelong fit
Moore said the brace provides joint support Queenie’s leg cannot provide on its own. He will wear it for life, and it will be checked weekly for swelling or irritation.
“Now that he’s quite used to it, we see such a change in him. He puts full weight on that leg. He’s around with the rest of the flock. He’s taking baths with the flock and running around,” Moore said.
There is no timeline yet for when Queenie will fully rejoin the rest of the flock.

title: Planting Hope in Limestone
text:
LIMESTONE, Maine (WAGM) - Limestone will look a little different next spring thanks to 500 yellow tulips planted in honor of a Rotary leader’s fight against suicide.
The Limestone Rotary Club sponsored the town’s Yellow Tulip Project in honor of Suicide Prevention Month and in memory of Aroostook County’s Rotary District Governor Serge Poulin (Sur-j Poo-lin), a strong advocate for suicide prevention, who died in a traffic accident on August 3rd. The Rotary bought 500 tulip bulbs for the community to plant throughout town. Over the last several weeks, Rotary members, community members, and students worked together to plant the tulips. One hundred bulbs were planted at Limestone Community School. 300 more were planted across town at places like the town office, post office, park, local churches, and even under the town welcome sign. The last 100 bulbs were sent to Dawn F. Barnes Elementary in Caswell, where students planted them.
The Limestone Rotary says it was a meaningful project that brought community members out for a good cause, saying quote: “Yellow tulips represent happiness, hope, and a reminder that even in dark times, support is available. Together we can plant hope and make a difference. We are grateful for the support from the community towards this project and look forward to seeing these bursts of yellow this spring as a reminder of this project and what the tulips represent.”
Now, the Rotary and community are waiting for spring, when the tulips will bloom throughout town as a lasting, colorful reminder that hope and support are always within reach for anyone struggling.

title: Trump casts doubt on press secretary Zacharia's future

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump signaled Friday that his embattled new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, may be on her way out — a mere week after he picked her for the post.
Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia, Trump said he’d spoken to Zacharia and that he felt she didn’t deserve what he called negative media coverage.
Recounting what was said in that conversation, the president added, “I told her, ‘I think you’re better off being happy,’” Trump said.
“We’re talking about — I want her to have a good life. I don’t want her to have a life like she’s led the last three days,” Trump said.
He added, ”I said, Katie, do you need this? i don’t think you need this.’”
The president said he’d make a final determination later perhaps after his campaign travel, adding, “When I get back we’re gonna talk”
He also said, “I told Katie, in my opinion, she was treated very unfairly,” Trump said, noting that Zacharia has been “brutalized by the media.”

title: Does a Russian lab worker's death carry pandemic risk? Not based on what we know now, experts say
text:
Does a Russian lab worker’s death carry pandemic risk? Not based on what we know now, experts say
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
It sounded familiar: Pneumonia reported near a lab studying infectious pathogens in a country where the government is known to conceal unfavorable information.
Conflicting reports and unanswered questions about a potential pneumonic plague death in Russia on Oct. 2 brought back memories of COVID-19's early days.
A laboratory worker at an anti-plague research lab in Siberia died of an illness, and a local official initially reported the woman had died "possibly from the plague." The earliest reports sounded like the death followed an accidental lab exposure to pneumonic plague, the World Health Organization reported. Dozens of people had been quarantined or isolated.
The WHO confirmed the woman’s death followed her hospitalization with "severe pneumonia," but the exact pathogen that caused her illness has not been announced or independently verified.
Adding to the confusion: Russian authorities reported no recent case of plague in Irkutsk Oblast, an administrative region in east-central Russia, where all this was said to have happened.
Despite some of the situation's parallels to the coronavirus news of late 2019 and early 2020, virology and health security experts told PolitiFact's Well Informed they don't see signals that this is a precursor to another pandemic crisis.
The caveat, however, could be significant: Russian authorities' actions didn't align with their public statements.
Although the government's official statement was that the lab worker had pneumonia of undetermined origin, Russia responded by putting 200 contacts under observation, quarantining a hospital and flying its top disease control leader to Irkutsk.
"That is not how you respond to garden-variety pneumonia — and it isn't really how you'd respond to ordinary plague either, which has been curable with cheap antibiotics for decades," Dr. Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, said.
Even without confirmation of the pathogen, however, the shape of spread is the most important factor to watch.
"Pandemic potential shows up as a growing chain of human-to-human transmission, and that is not what we're seeing," Adalja said.
Adalja said no cluster of severe illness had developed among nearly 200 people who The Moscow Times reported were placed under medical observation.
Hayley Anne Severance, deputy vice president for the Nuclear Threat Initiative's global biological policy and programs, said she needed more information before providing a global health risk assessment.
"I am still in 'wait-and-see' mode," Severance said. "We need to know more about laboratory test findings, the treatments provided and her reaction to them, and any other potential exposure factors. We do not have confirmation of the causative agent, or if there even is an infectious agent involved, so we are flying in the dark here."
Experts are watching Russian authorities, local media for reports of more cases
Currently, about 10 days after the researcher's death, there have been no secondary cases confirmed in connection with the lab worker’s death.
"If this were a fast-spreading cluster, the window in which we'd expect to see it has basically passed," Adalja told Well Informed on Oct. 8.
Other concerns would include expanding quarantine measures and Russian authorities refusing outside investigators or blocking a WHO team, Adalja said.
Local media reports could also offer clues, Severance said.
"I would be concerned if I begin to see reports from independent news outlets in Russia that there are unreported cases or deaths ongoing in the region that are not being acknowledged or confirmed by official Russian sources," she said.
Standard pneumonic plague isn't a significant pandemic threat
Pneumonic plague occurs when someone inhales respiratory droplets that contain the bacteria Yersinia pestis — or when the bacteria causing bubonic or septicemic plague spreads to the lungs.
It can be treated with antibiotics. Without prompt treatment, pneumonic plague has "a nearly 100% case-fatality rate," according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
It is the only plague that can spread person to person, usually with prolonged contact.
Measures such as masking could decrease disease spread. Pneumonic plague's incubation period is short — about one to four days — so it's less likely infected people would spread disease unknowingly, Severance said.
"In past pneumonic plague outbreaks, on average, each infected person spread to between one and two others," and that dropped quickly with isolation measures, Severance said.
Experts worry about information obstruction
WHO officials said the illness that caused a lab worker’s death in Russia presents a "very low" risk to people outside of Russia, based on available information. But more answers are needed.
"A trained worker inside a plague research institute died of something still unexplained, and we're relying on the word of a government with a documented history of concealment on biosecurity," Adalja said.
Ian Jones, a virology professor at the University of Reading in the United Kingdom, said it was "almost unbelievable" that scientists hadn't identified the cause of the lab worker's pneumonia given modern testing capabilities.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged timely and transparent information sharing.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Cause of deadly Bangor fire still unknown
text:
The cause of Wednesday’s deadly blaze in Bangor is still unknown.
The fire broke out at the two-unit apartment building at the intersection of Cedar and Second streets at 6:36 a.m., according to Shannon Moss, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
It took two minutes for firefighters to arrive on scene, because it’s near the Bangor Fire Department’s Central Station on Main Street.

title: Katie Zacharia is out as Trump's White House press secretary, advisers say
text:
Katie Zacharia is out as Trump's White House press secretary, advisers say
Katie Zacharia is out as press secretary, advisers to the president said, ending her turbulent week-long stint as the White House’s top spokesperson.
President Donald Trump told reporters earlier he had asked Zacharia to reconsider her role, all but declaring her brief tenure in the job over.
“Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” Trump said he told Zacharia on Friday morning.
He said they would speak when he returned to the White House after a trip to Georgia and he would leave the decision to her. But he did not sound particularly encouraging of his embattled press secretary.
“Katie, do you need this?” he said he told her. “I don’t think you need this.”
It was a remarkable vote of no confidence in Zacharia, who entered the job a week ago. Her shaky debut in the briefing room on Tuesday and persistent questions about her background had led to immense scrutiny from the media and fellow Trump aides.
Speaking as he was leaving the White House for a political rally in Georgia, Trump said Zacharia had been mistreated by the media and praised her as a loyal supporter.
But he made clear he did not believe Zacharia was suited to speak on his behalf as the government’s top spokesperson.
“Maybe it’s not for her,” he conceded.
Zacharia had captured Trump’s attention as a conservative commentator on television, and her hiring occurred quickly after other candidates were deemed ineligible because of critical comments they made about Trump.
Her inexperience was revealed quickly, however. At the White House lectern on Tuesday, she appeared nervous and only took three questions.
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

title: He didn’t know he had Lyme disease. How cases are rising in the Midwest
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Richard Dolnik spent much of his free time running on trails, training for marathons. Now he avoids the woods and tall grass because of his fear of a disease that can be transmitted by ticks.
Dolnik is recovering from Lyme disease, an infection that early on can include fever, headache, joint and muscle pain and a rash. That’s how it started for him.
“I went to take a shower, I noticed there was a giant rash right here,” Dolnik said. “And then the next day I wake up and I have a chainsaw headache.”
For a month, Dolnik didn’t know what was wrong with him.
Because he didn’t know what was wrong, Dolnik didn’t get treatment, and his condition worsened. He developed Lyme carditis, a condition that attacks electrical signals in the heart.
“That first night in the hospital, it was bad,” he told us. “I had a code blue where the entire emergency team had to come in because my heart paused for like 15 seconds.”
When Dolnik got the disease, he said “not a single person” aside from his infectious diseases doctor knew it “could cause a 21-year-old who’d been training for a marathon to go into cardiac arrest in only four weeks.”
Nearly half of Michigan is forest, and ticks primarily live in wooded and grassy areas. In the 1990s and 2010s, Lyme disease was not a major health concern in the state.
“My family and the people I know in my community were kind of ignorant to Lyme disease and what it is,” Dolnik said.
Cases rising sharply in Michigan
Michigan health leaders say everyone needs to think about Lyme disease now.
“Our state’s Lyme disease rates have been increasing over the past 10 years pretty dramatically. And we are actually now a high incidence state based on CDC’s definition of Lyme disease incidence,” said Rachel Burkholder, with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.
Burkholder said the state has seen a more than 350% increase in Lyme disease cases in five years, from 471 cases in 2020 to more than 2,000 in 2025.
Michigan Lyme disease cases by year:
- 2020: 471
- 2021: 860
- 2022: 553
- 2023: 1,146
- 2024: 1,215
- 2025: 2,167
The increase is not unique to Michigan. CDC data shows that while Lyme disease incidence has historically been high on the East Coast, the Midwest is catching up.
“It’s scary because, you know, we’re following the same trends that you saw, you would have seen in the East Coast states. And also like Wisconsin 20 years ago,” Burkholder said.
Experts say warmer weather and shorter cold winters are contributing to the increase in tick populations and the spread of the disease.
Burkholder said neighboring states like Ohio will be “high incidence” by next year.
Experts warn against dismissing symptoms
Health experts say people need to know rates are growing so they don’t dismiss warning signs.
“It’s a problematic disease if it’s not caught early enough and treated early enough, it can cause lifelong debilitating symptoms,” Burkholder said when asked why Lyme disease is problematic.
Carrie Nielsen said she has never fully recovered from Lyme disease and still has symptoms.
Nielsen said she went undiagnosed for decades because Lyme disease was not widely recognized at the time. Treatment has helped, but her family recently received another diagnosis.
“Unfortunately, my sister was just diagnosed a week ago. It was a complete gut punch and we were devastated,” Nielsen said.
Nielsen said her sister, like Dolnik, never saw a tick and never developed the bullseye rash that is often associated with the illness, which delayed her treatment.
“She has had tingling, like pins and needle feelings in her legs, joint pain. But most importantly, she’s had a lot of heart issues,” Nielsen said.
Nielsen is part of the Michigan Lyme Disease Association, which works to raise awareness and help people get diagnosed quickly.
“Absolutely. We know when it’s like getting bad, the calls are nonstop,” Nielsen said when asked if more people have been reaching out to the group for help.
Prevention recommended
There is no cure for Lyme disease, so health officials say prevention is the best option.
The CDC recommends avoiding grassy and bushy areas, using insect repellent with DEET or oil of lemon eucalyptus, wearing light, long-sleeve clothing, and tucking pants into socks when hiking in the woods. The CDC also recommends removing any attached tick as quickly as possible with tweezers, noting that the longer a tick is attached, the higher the risk for Lyme disease.
Dolnik now takes those steps seriously.
“My nervous system is still hypersensitive. Anytime I feel, I can feel skip beats now. I can feel flutters,” Dolnik said.
Dolnik is now an ambassador with the Global Lyme Alliance, sharing his story and raising awareness.
“The knowledge in my community for how dangerous this disease is, it’s subpar,” Dolnik said. “People really need to take more preventative action and really get a lot more knowledge on Lyme disease.”
Not all species of ticks carry Lyme disease. Different species of the parasite can cause other diseases in people.
The lone star tick can trigger alpha-gal syndrome, which can bring a severe allergy to red meat and dairy. The brown dog, American dog and Rocky Mountain wood ticks can spread Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which left untreated can be deadly.
The CDC warns of 16 tick-borne diseases in all, many of which have no vaccines.

title: Steven Soderbergh to Help Finish ‘The Batman Part II’
text:
Steven Soderbergh to Help Finish ‘The Batman Part II’ While Matt Reeves Deals With Family Issue
With director Matt Reeves dealing with a “family matter” and the clock ticking down toward a release date for The Batman Part II, we now know how Warner Bros. plans to finish the film: Director Steven Soderbergh will step in for Reeves, overseeing the shoot in London. while Reeves remains in Los Angeles.
In a statement about his joining work on the film, Soderbergh said...
I thought Matt Reeves’ work on The Batman was stunning; it was intentional, specific, and rigorously coherent. The goal here is to work with Matt and his team to generate footage that will integrate seamlessly with what’s already been shot so Matt can properly finish his film.
Warner Bros. announced production on The Batman Part II was pausing for Reeves to attend to his family issue two weeks ago. But the film has been delayed numerous times already; it’s been four years and counting since The Batman first introduced Robert Pattinson’s new interpretation of the Dark Knight. Waiting longer for Reeves runs the risk of forcing Warners to push the film back yet again.
On social media, Reeves clarified that he was “not leaving The Batman Part II” and that he was “profoundly grateful to Steven for coming to my aid during this challenging time to help me finish principal photography.”
READ MORE: Every Batman Actor Ranked From Worst to Best
Soderbergh’s involvement is interesting. He’s made big movies in the past — most famously his trilogy of Ocean’s movies — but in recent years he’s focused on smaller-scale projects like Presence, The Christophers, Kimi, and Black Bag. But Soderbergh also tried to convince Disney to greenlight a Star Wars movie he wanted to make with Adam Driver, an effort that ultimately proved unsuccessful. In some way, this gives Soderbergh the chance to scratch that itch to take charge of a massive Hollywood production.
On the DC side, the situation recalls what happened behind the scenes of Justice League, when Zack Snyder stepped down from the middle in the middle of production and Joss Whedon was hired to finish principal photography. The results in that case weren’t ideal; they didn’t really feel like a Zack Snyder movie or a Joss Whedon movie. Hopefully this time, with Reeves still involved (albeit remotely), the finished film will still capture his vision for his Batman sequel.
The Batman Part II is currently scheduled to open in theaters on February 18, 2028.

title: As heating costs rise, officials urge caution with alternative heat sources
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CARIBOU, Maine (WAGM) - As heating costs remain a concern this winter, some homeowners may turn to alternative ways to stay warm. Those changes can come with safety risks.
Darren Woods, director of Aroostook County’s Emergency Management Agency and a local homeowner, said he changes his heating source multiple times each season to save money.
“So in a typical heating season, I will change my heating source two or three times just to save money in my own budget. So I totally understand what people are facing,” Woods said.
This month the statewide average for heating oil was nearly six dollars a gallon, while kerosene was nearly seven dollars. Propane averaged the cheapest at about three dollars and 46 cents a gallon, according to data published by the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
Space heater safety
Alternative heating might help manage costs, but changing how you heat your home can also mean changing how you keep it safe. For anyone using an electric space heater, Woods said placement and power cords are especially important.
“Make sure you follow the manufacturer’s recommendations. If you’re going to use like an electric heater, make sure you have good spacing around it, that it’s got adequate cords preferably plugged directly into the wall,” Woods said.
Wood stove preparation
If homeowners are turning to a wood stove for heat, Woods said it’s important to make sure the system is ready before use.
“Prior to every heating season that you have your stove serviced by a professional. So that means having your chimney cleaned, having your stovepipes clean,” Woods said.
Detectors and preparedness
No matter how residents choose to heat their homes this winter, Woods said to be prepared. Smoke alarms should be newer than 10 years old with fresh batteries. Woods also recommends carbon monoxide and propane detectors. Those devices can be especially important in rural areas, where help may take longer to arrive.
“A couple of minutes, you know, is all it takes. And the fire department won’t be there that fast, so you’re better off to be prepared and get yourself out,” Woods said.
With heating costs adding another challenge this winter, Woods said finding ways to save is important, but so is making sure those savings don’t come at the expense of safety.

title: Billy Joel says he can no longer perform or drive due to health condition
text:
(Gray News) — Billy Joel said his health is keeping him from being able to perform or drive, he revealed in a new interview with The Hollywood Reporter.
Joel, 77, said he has a condition called hydrocephalus that has affected his balance.
He wants nothing more than to get back onstage, but he said he must take a series of tests before he knows if he can.
“I can’t do performances because what the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion,” Joel told The Hollywood Reporter.
He said the extremely loud volume, lighting, stress and energy it takes to perform are all concerns and stressors on his health.
Joel also said he is not allowed to drive.
Joel said hydrocephalus affects his balance, memory, vision and hearing.
“But I’m OK. They call it a brain disorder, but it’s not that serious. It’s just something that affects your balance mostly,” he said.
According to The Mayo Clinic, hydrocephalus is the buildup of cerebrospinal fluid in spaces called ventricles deep within the brain. This buildup can make the ventricles larger and put pressure on the brain.
Symptoms can vary by age group. Among adults 60 and older, common symptoms of hydrocephalus include memory loss, trouble walking, poor coordination or balance and progressive loss of other reasoning skills.
