title: Portland needs a plan to arrest its further decline
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Michael Todd Chretien is a candidate for Portland City Council District 5. He taught Spanish at Deering High School and now works as an interpreter for the Multilingual Center.
Portland’s in trouble: runaway housing costs, declining public school enrollment, ballooning property taxes, traffic fatalities and a disturbing spike in violence on our streets. I’ve knocked on over 3,000 doors in District 5 in the last three months and this is what I hear. Worse, President Trump’s Iran war gas tax, federal healthcare cuts and ICE raids have no end in sight. If you feel like these problems are snowballing out of control, you’re not alone.
We need a plan to turn Portland around.
First, Portland must grow. We need 5,000 units of new housing in the next five years. Maine is growing faster than at any time since the 1970s. Climate chaos will accelerate that trend. Yet, Portland has added just over 5,000 residents in the last 25 years. It’s hard to believe but Portland’s population was bigger in 1950. Back then, Portland accounted for 8.4% of Maine’s population. Today that’s down to 5%, which means we’re losing representational power in Augusta.
Constructing 5,000 units will start rebuilding Portland’s political clout, expand our tax base, grow our workforce and enroll hundreds of new students in our schools. We need rent control and an “all of the above” approach to construction: market rate, social, workforce, senior and low-income.
Second, we must fix the school funding formula. Maine provides 55% of public school funding for our towns. However, in 2026-27, Portland received just 16% of our public school funding from the state. Each percentage point represents $1.8 million. If Portland got just 25% of our rightful state allocation, that would mean an additional $16 million, more than covering the impact of inflation in the school district and allowing us to control property taxes.
Third, Portland must be safe for everyone. Roughly 12% of Portland residents are new Mainers. Portland has spoken out and organized against ICE, but we must do more to stop the terror.
Safety means doing everything we can to keep pedestrians safe. We’ve lost three lives just this year. We must put Portland’s Vision Zero into effect by slowing traffic and reducing congestion, making it easier to bike and walk, improving public transportation and designing new housing with off-street parking and sidewalks in mind.
Safety means continuing our commitment to people experiencing homelessness, substance use disorder and mental health crises. Thanks to these services, thousands of people have entered recovery, 400 families have transitioned from shelters to permanent homes and countless teens, women and LGTBQ people have escaped domestic violence. We should maintain our needle exchange program, stand up a winter shelter and provide more beds for families and smaller low-barrier shelters. District 5 does our part by hosting the Homelessness Services Center; all districts have to pitch in.
But safety also means eliminating needle waste on our streets, near our schools and in our parks. It means growing programs like the downtown ambassadors and organizing community cleanups and investing in addiction and mental health services so more of our neighbors can heal in their communities, instead of behind bars, which is the costliest of all outcomes. And, it means using Maine’s involuntary commitment authority for the very small percentage of people who constitute a danger to themselves or others while expanding adult treatment and recovery courts.
These mutually reinforcing initiatives will put a lid on property taxes while maintaining critical services. More housing brings union construction jobs, funds for our schools, a larger workforce, and increases city revenue.
Fixing Maine’s school funding formula provides resources to pay educators so they can live in Portland, expands equity and access for our diverse student body, and incentivizes families to move here. Expelling ICE puts out the welcome sign for our immigrant neighbors and their families. And guaranteeing that our streets and schools are safe for everyone gives us the chance to breathe.
City Council needs a plan to build a better Portland.

title: K-9 officer seen jumping off highway overpass, survives fall
text:
PARK CITY, Utah (CNN) - A Utah police dog is on the mend after a terrifying fall from an overpass that was caught on camera.
Newly released video shows the moment a police K-9 jumped off a highway overpass, seriously injuring itself.
It happened when Park City police officers responded to a suspicious object spotted on a highway overpass.
As the officer and his K-9, Bruno, began investigating, Bruno suddenly leaped over the edge and fell to the roadway below.
His handler hurries back to his patrol unit and quickly drives down to find Bruno seriously injured on the road below.
The handler then lays down to comfort the injured K-9 and to prevent it from trying to stand.
The department said Bruno later underwent surgery for serious injuries to his front legs and jaw and is now recovering at home.
The department later posted on Facebook that Bruno is more than a police K-9; he’s a partner, a companion and part of the police family.

title: He didn’t know he had Lyme disease. How cases are rising in the Midwest
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Richard Dolnik spent much of his free time running on trails, training for marathons. Now he avoids the woods and tall grass because of his fear of a disease that can be transmitted by ticks.
Dolnik is recovering from Lyme disease, an infection that early on can include fever, headache, joint and muscle pain and a rash. That’s how it started for him.
“I went to take a shower, I noticed there was a giant rash right here,” Dolnik said. “And then the next day I wake up and I have a chainsaw headache.”
For a month, Dolnik didn’t know what was wrong with him.
Because he didn’t know what was wrong, Dolnik didn’t get treatment, and his condition worsened. He developed Lyme carditis, a condition that attacks electrical signals in the heart.
“That first night in the hospital, it was bad,” he told us. “I had a code blue where the entire emergency team had to come in because my heart paused for like 15 seconds.”
When Dolnik got the disease, he said “not a single person” aside from his infectious diseases doctor knew it “could cause a 21-year-old who’d been training for a marathon to go into cardiac arrest in only four weeks.”
Nearly half of Michigan is forest, and ticks primarily live in wooded and grassy areas. In the 1990s and 2010s, Lyme disease was not a major health concern in the state.
“My family and the people I know in my community were kind of ignorant to Lyme disease and what it is,” Dolnik said.
Cases rising sharply in Michigan
Michigan health leaders say everyone needs to think about Lyme disease now.
“Our state’s Lyme disease rates have been increasing over the past 10 years pretty dramatically. And we are actually now a high incidence state based on CDC’s definition of Lyme disease incidence,” said Rachel Burkholder, with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.
Burkholder said the state has seen a more than 350% increase in Lyme disease cases in five years, from 471 cases in 2020 to more than 2,000 in 2025.
Michigan Lyme disease cases by year:
- 2020: 471
- 2021: 860
- 2022: 553
- 2023: 1,146
- 2024: 1,215
- 2025: 2,167
The increase is not unique to Michigan. CDC data shows that while Lyme disease incidence has historically been high on the East Coast, the Midwest is catching up.
“It’s scary because, you know, we’re following the same trends that you saw, you would have seen in the East Coast states. And also like Wisconsin 20 years ago,” Burkholder said.
Experts say warmer weather and shorter cold winters are contributing to the increase in tick populations and the spread of the disease.
Burkholder said neighboring states like Ohio will be “high incidence” by next year.
Experts warn against dismissing symptoms
Health experts say people need to know rates are growing so they don’t dismiss warning signs.
“It’s a problematic disease if it’s not caught early enough and treated early enough, it can cause lifelong debilitating symptoms,” Burkholder said when asked why Lyme disease is problematic.
Carrie Nielsen said she has never fully recovered from Lyme disease and still has symptoms.
Nielsen said she went undiagnosed for decades because Lyme disease was not widely recognized at the time. Treatment has helped, but her family recently received another diagnosis.
“Unfortunately, my sister was just diagnosed a week ago. It was a complete gut punch and we were devastated,” Nielsen said.
Nielsen said her sister, like Dolnik, never saw a tick and never developed the bullseye rash that is often associated with the illness, which delayed her treatment.
“She has had tingling, like pins and needle feelings in her legs, joint pain. But most importantly, she’s had a lot of heart issues,” Nielsen said.
Nielsen is part of the Michigan Lyme Disease Association, which works to raise awareness and help people get diagnosed quickly.
“Absolutely. We know when it’s like getting bad, the calls are nonstop,” Nielsen said when asked if more people have been reaching out to the group for help.
Prevention recommended
There is no cure for Lyme disease, so health officials say prevention is the best option.
The CDC recommends avoiding grassy and bushy areas, using insect repellent with DEET or oil of lemon eucalyptus, wearing light, long-sleeve clothing, and tucking pants into socks when hiking in the woods. The CDC also recommends removing any attached tick as quickly as possible with tweezers, noting that the longer a tick is attached, the higher the risk for Lyme disease.
Dolnik now takes those steps seriously.
“My nervous system is still hypersensitive. Anytime I feel, I can feel skip beats now. I can feel flutters,” Dolnik said.
Dolnik is now an ambassador with the Global Lyme Alliance, sharing his story and raising awareness.
“The knowledge in my community for how dangerous this disease is, it’s subpar,” Dolnik said. “People really need to take more preventative action and really get a lot more knowledge on Lyme disease.”
Not all species of ticks carry Lyme disease. Different species of the parasite can cause other diseases in people.
The lone star tick can trigger alpha-gal syndrome, which can bring a severe allergy to red meat and dairy. The brown dog, American dog and Rocky Mountain wood ticks can spread Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which left untreated can be deadly.
The CDC warns of 16 tick-borne diseases in all, many of which have no vaccines.

title: New Hampshire’s DJ Shaw caps memorable auto racing season with BHBT win
text:
It is 158 miles one-way from Center Conway, New Hampshire, to Hermon, Maine.
But the trip was well worth it for Center Conway native D.J. Shaw, whose six trips to Hermon’s Ricky Craven Speedway presented by Bar Harbor Bank and Trust this season produced four victories, including the inaugural Bar Harbor Bank and Trust 200 pro stock race on Sunday.
Shaw, who said he has always enjoyed the track, earned a PASS Super Late Model North Series win in 2018.
But after a 2019 race, the PASS SLM North Series never returned.
Former NASCAR Cup Series driver and two-time winner Craven from Newburgh bought the track from long-time owner Del Merritt 14 months ago and reinstituted the Pro Stock class, which represents the fastest and most expensive stock cars at this level.
The Late Model class had been the top class at the speedway for the last several years but it is a notch below the pro stocks.
Craven established a seven-race series on six dates. There were twin 50-lap races on July 12.
Shaw, who had two seconds and a third in the other three races, captured the series championship followed closely by Gray’s Austin Teras, who won the other three races and also posted a second, two fourths and a ninth.
Craven made several improvements to the track as part of a $5 million renovation he will oversee over several years.
“It’s a good atmosphere. The buzz is good. People are excited about Ricky reviving a place that didn’t look like it had much of a future a year ago,” said the 36-year-old Shaw, son of New England Auto Racers Hall of Famer Dale Shaw. “He has the fan support, he has the car support. Everything is on the up-and-up.”
Shaw turned in an impressive performance on Sunday.
He won the pole but they made one mistake before the race by not getting the right front tire tight enough, which meant he had to make an unscheduled pit stop just 15 laps into the race.
Following the pit stop, Shaw and his Ford were hovering around 25th place.
“That changed the complexion of the race for us,” Shaw said. “It became more of a come-from-behind kind of deal.”
There was a mandatory caution scheduled for lap 80. But a natural caution occurred on lap 77 so that served as the mandatory caution.
“We were able to climb from the mid-20s to fifth by the break and that enabled us to stick to the plan as far as not having to make anything happen. We had recovered at that point,” said Shaw, who took the lead for good with 46 laps to go.
Craven said Shaw is a very gifted racer.
“He is a generational talent in New England,” said Craven, who added that Teras is also a top-notch driver.
Durham’s Evan Beaulieu was second and Stetson’s Mathew Bourgoine finished third with Teras and Windham’s Cole Robie completing the top five in the 28-car field.
Casey Call of Pembroke, New Hampshire, wound up sixth and rounding out the top 10 were Joey Doiron from Berwick, Lonnie Somerville from Barnesville, New Hampshire, Ryan Deane from Winterport and Jamie Wright from Woolwich.
There were several other races during the three days of racing that concluded Craven’s first year as the owner.
The Crown Vic class involved three 33-lap races and the driver with the best results in the three races earned the championship.
Frankfort’s Joey Doyon posted finishes of second, third and fourth to claim the title.
Wiscasset’s Kevin Sherman was second with finishes of second, fifth and eighth, and third was Lily Smith of Hermon, who had two thirds and an 11th.
Smith is the granddaughter of Bangor’s Gary Smith, who won pro stock races at all of the state’s tracks, including Scarborough’s Beech Ridge Motor Speedway, which closed in 2021.
Completing the top 10 were Hermon’s Steve Kimball, Detroit’s Chandler Myrick, Corinth’s Lloyd Nickerson, Liberty’s Josh St. Clair, Hudson’s Donny Silva, Winterport’s Fred Brown and Glenburn’s Talon Blanchard.
In the 100-lap Super Street-Street Stock Open, Jimmy Renfrew Jr. of Candia, New Hampshire, took the checkered flag with Max Dolliver of Londonderry, New Hampshire, and Ryan Robinson of Clinton joining him on the podium.
Finishing fourth and fifth were Isaac Rollins of Hudson and Corey Fanning of Mapleville, Rhode Island, respectively.
The sixth through 10th-place finishers were Keith Drost from Stetson, Shane Tatro from Levant, Scott Modery from Hermon, Jeff Alley from Machias and Andrew Turbovsky from Albion.
In the 25-lap Super-Street-Street Stock Open, Robinson captured the win followed by Thorndike’s Jordan Pearson, Renfrew Jr., Drost, Wiscasset’s Tiger Colby, Gorham’s Dan McKeage Sr., Modery, Sanford’s Adam Lovejoy and Hollis’ Mike St. Pierre.
None of the other cars in the 16-car field finished the race.
Lincoln’s Brock Worster collected the win in the 50-lap Road Runners race followed by Etna’s Nick Bickford, Newburgh’s Mark Sawyer, Hampden’s Erik Worster, Etna’s Waylon Giguere, Bangor’s Derek Smith, Hermon’s Andrew Crosby, Appleton’s Karigan Glasier, Bucksport’s David Boulier and Newcastle’s James Grover Jr.
Kyle Robinson won the 50-lap Sport 4’s race and seven others finished the race with Nick Miller of Berlin, New Hampshire, in second place followed by Brownville’s Roy Hathorn, Hudson’s Mason Silva, Rome’s Wyatt Dipietro, Norridgewock’s Ricky Austin, Milo’s Josh Dillon and Vassalboro’s Kalib Bernatchez.
The 20-lap Vintage race had Woolwich’s James Osmond and Adam Chadbourne taking the top two spots followed by Tim Reynolds of Milford, Donnie Young of Fredericton, New Brunswick, Kris Watson of Kenduskeag, Jamie Young of Hancock, Keith Smalley of Warren, Nick Overlock of Warren and Barrett Ayer of LaGrange.
Just three finished the 20-lap Northeast Pro Sprint Series feature with Lamoine’s Aaron Carter, Hancock’s Gary Dow and Milford’s Mike Headd placing in that order.

title: Maine doesn’t need Jonathan Bush’s interference in local races
text:
Jonathan Bush doesn’t seem to take defeat lying down.
After coming in a distant third in the Republican gubernatorial primary in June, Bush is now angling to win grassroots support around the state in the future, launching “Maine for Keeps,” a new initiative to get Republicans elected in our larger cities.
By doing this, Bush is injecting even more partisan politics into the cities’ municipal campaigns — exposing, once again, how foolish it is for us to go on pretending these races are nonpartisan.
Bush told WVOM radio this week that he’s using $50,000 of his own money to target races in Lewiston, Bangor and Waterville in a bid “to make it easy for the candidates that kind of come from the land of sanity to win and to take back those city councils.”
Translation for those who have yet to master the tricky language of politics: He is promoting GOP candidates to oust officials aligned with the Democrats.
This isn’t a strategy pioneered by Bush. The Maine Republican Party didn’t hesitate, quite openly, to block Democrat Ben Chin from winning Lewiston’s mayoral races in 2015 and 2017. Maine Democrats angle to win municipal races, too, if only by the practice of calling attention to their candidates.
To his credit, Bush isn’t hiding what he’s doing. As he explained, “I’m fighting where I think we’ve got Republicans and unenrolled folks” with enough business sense to overcome opponents aligned with the Democrats.
As far as I can see, Bush backs a GOP agenda that consists mostly of trashing the cities its champions hope to represent. Following the misbegotten lead of the Maine Wire and other agitators, this involves slamming these communities’ safety and cleanliness and insisting that everything has gone downhill for years. What malarkey.
Not that I’m a fan of most city councilors or mayors; it’s at best a mixed bag. Yet for Bush to come in and say that sitting councilors in these cities don’t have “a basic sense of right and wrong” or “basic sanity” is ridiculous.
Perhaps, though, it’s no more silly than the notion that Bush is somehow going to be the savior whose unexpected cash can turn Maine’s municipalities into Republican strongholds. With President Donald Trump at the helm of the party, that’s not about to happen.
What does strike me about Bush’s foray into city politics across the state is that it could become a turning point for the handling of municipal elections. It’s time we dropped the pretense that they are somehow above politics.
I looked at a few sample ballots in Lewiston this week, trying to get it straight in my head who’s running for what, and was appalled to see that beneath each candidate’s name was not his or her party affiliation, which would help the average voter decide. Instead, the ballots listed their home addresses, which seems both useless to voters as well as risky in this bitter age.
Take Lewiston’s mayoral race. The ballot lists the names of five candidates and where each of them lives (three on the same street!). But it provides nothing to help a voter distinguish among them, as party affiliations do in state and federal races.
I don’t believe Bush has any career prospects in Maine politics. The money resulting from his Maine for Keeps effort, though, could perhaps be remembered as the push needed to toss out nonpartisan elections, and stop hiding what’s most important about candidates from voters who lack the information only party insiders possess.
Meanwhile, instead of trying to buy far-flung city councilors, Bush should consider running for municipal office in his own town. There’s a good chance sanity is needed in Cape Elizabeth, too.

title: Decline in baby Maine lobsters is warning to the fishery, study finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A sharp decline in baby lobsters offered an early warning of substantial losses in Maine’s Midcoast lobster population, according to a new University of Maine study that connects falling numbers across successive stages of the crustaceans’ lives.
Researchers found that an 80% decline in baby lobsters sampled between 2010 and 2022 preceded declines farther along in the population: a 70% decrease in young lobsters since 2015 and a 50% decrease in adults large enough for fishermen to catch.
The findings show how a shortage of the smallest lobsters can work its way through the population, eventually reducing the number reaching harvestable size. They also underscore the importance of monitoring lobsters years before they enter the commercial fishery.
The study’s midcoast region, extending from Brunswick to the Schoodic Peninsula, recorded the steepest declines in the Gulf of Maine. That broad study area encompasses the waters off Waldo County and much of Maine’s central coast.
The losses followed a substantial boom. From the 2000s to the 2010s, the number of lobsters sampled in the region doubled before the trend reversed.
The research adds to evidence that the Gulf of Maine’s lobster population has declined since the mid-2010s, raising questions about the future of a fishery that generated more than $461 million in Maine landings in 2025.
Published in the journal Marine Ecology Progress Series, the study brought together UMaine researchers and the Maine Department of Marine Resources. Scientists analyzed state surveys that used scuba divers, traps and trawls to sample lobsters at different depths and stages of development.
Comparing those surveys allowed researchers to trace changes from baby lobsters to adolescents and, eventually, adults. The study classified adolescent lobsters as those with shell lengths of 45 to 83 millimeters.
Lead researcher Robert Jarrett II, a recent doctoral graduate who began the work at UMaine, said central Maine provided the clearest evidence connecting changes across life stages. Researchers linked the region’s boom and subsequent decline to warmer water temperatures.
Growth rates also affected how readily those connections emerged. Faster growth in central Maine produced a more consistent pattern, while slower and more variable growth in eastern Maine likely made the relationship harder to detect.
Down East Maine experienced a similar decline in baby lobsters sampled since 2010, but a smaller decline among adults. Findings for adolescent lobsters differed among surveys.
Researchers said fewer sampling efforts in Down East Maine could help explain some of those differences, highlighting a central challenge in interpreting the results: surveys provide valuable evidence, but their coverage and methods influence what scientists can see.
Warming water further complicates that picture by changing where lobsters can live.
In midcoast and Down East Maine, deeper habitats have become more suitable for lobsters as temperatures rise. Lobsters spreading into those areas can become harder to track through surveys that cover limited locations, depths and habitat types.
Previous UMaine research found that lobster population density declined as the animals became more dispersed and shifted the habitats they occupied. The new study reinforces the need to consider those movements when interpreting changes in survey counts.
For fishermen and coastal communities, that distinction matters. A decline in lobsters sampled can reflect changes in abundance, distribution or both. By comparing multiple surveys across life stages, researchers sought a clearer understanding of the broader population trend.
Kathleen Reardon, a study co-author and the department’s senior lobster fishery scientist, said Maine’s monitoring program follows lobsters throughout their life cycle. Partnerships with the fishing industry make the surveys possible, while collaboration with UMaine helps researchers interpret extensive datasets and supplement stock assessment findings.
Southern Maine presented a different pattern. There, the number of lobsters sampled across all life stages has remained relatively stable since 2010, according to the study.
Researchers attributed the regional contrast partly to differences in water circulation. Southern Maine lacks the circulation pattern that brings cold, deep water toward the surface in other regions. Its deeper waters remain too cold for lobsters even as temperatures rise, leaving the area of suitable habitat relatively unchanged.
Those differences caution against treating Maine’s coast as a single, uniform lobster habitat. Temperature, growth, circulation and survey coverage all influence the patterns researchers observe.
Still, the study’s central finding was consistent: declines in baby lobsters preceded decreases in adolescent populations in Midcoast and Downeast Maine, affirming the smallest lobsters’ value as an early indicator for the fishery.
The work follows another recent UMaine study examining a preferred plankton food source for baby lobsters amid concerns about declining food availability and young lobster survival.
Together, the research efforts are helping scientists examine both what happens to lobsters early in life and how those changes may shape the fishery years later.
Even with extensive monitoring, researchers said, differences in survey methods and lobster behavior can make population changes difficult to interpret. Expanding sampling will remain important as environmental conditions shift.
For midcoast communities, the findings give the decline in baby lobsters a consequence extending well beyond the nursery habitat: fewer young lobsters surviving and growing through the population can ultimately mean fewer adults available to the fishing fleet.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Bangor Fire Department shares winter heating safety tips
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Bangor Fire Department is sharing tips to prevent fires as winter approaches and the cost of heating oil remains near a record high, prompting some Mainers to consider other ways to heat their homes.
The number one tip is to make sure smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are working, and to change the batteries with daylight saving time.
Assistant Chief Chandler Corriveau said getting a heating system checked by a professional can prevent fires as well.
He said making sure extension cords are being used properly is also important. Personal or space heaters should never be plugged into an extension cord and should only be used directly in an outlet.
Corriveau said ensuring a household has a plan in case a home catches fire is paramount.
“Obviously, make sure you have working smoke detectors, make sure you have working carbon monoxide detectors. Believe it or not, make sure you have a home escape plan. Make sure you have pre-planned with your family members, your children, that if your house catches on fire, God forbid you have a plan on where you’re going to meet. Have a meeting place where the fire department can come and we can talk to them. Make sure, is everybody out of the building? That is always the first question we always ask when we talk to homeowners. If that’s a yes, great. If that’s a no, if they can provide us where people may be staying,” Corriveau said.
Corriveau said once you get out, stay out and allow first responders to work once they arrive.

title: Former University of Kentucky student sentenced for baby’s death
text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT/Gray News) - The former University of Kentucky student who pleaded guilty to killing her newborn baby was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
Laken Snelling, 22, pleaded guilty in August to manslaughter, abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence, and concealing the birth of an infant. In court, she told the judge, “Instead of helping him, I ended his life.”
Fayette County Circuit Court Judge Diane Minnifield told Snelling that she made a decision and that comes with consequences.
“And sometimes those choices and consequences affect our future for the rest of our lives, and you’ve made a decision that has affected not only your future but the future of all of [the baby’s] biological paternal side,” Minnifield said.
Baby found in closet
The charges stem from an August 2025 discovery by Lexington police. Officers were called to a home on Park Avenue for an unresponsive infant. Inside a closet, police say they found a baby boy wrapped in a towel, inside a trash bag. He was pronounced dead at the scene, and Snelling was arrested four days later.
Snelling said in court Friday that she had named the baby McCoy Cade Hall.
Court records obtained by WKYT say Snelling’s roommates discussed hearing unusual noises on the morning of Aug. 27 in a Snapchat group chat that Snelling was part of.
According to a search warrant filed for Snelling’s Snapchat account, around 4 a.m. that day, one roommate sent a message saying she heard a loud noise that sounded like something had fallen. A second roommate said she heard it too and that whatever caused it had been forceful enough to knock a picture off the wall. One roommate said the noises lasted about an hour.
Just before 9 a.m. that morning, Snelling sent a message in the group chat saying the noise was her passing out. She added that she had not been feeling well and had not eaten, and said she was going to get checked out by a doctor.
The court documents say the roommates told police they were “curious” about Snelling’s story and later went into her room to investigate, which is when they found the baby. The officer who requested the warrant wrote that all of the roommates told police they had suspicions that Snelling could be pregnant but had never confirmed them with her.
The Kentucky Medical Examiner’s Office said the baby was born alive and ruled his cause of death asphyxia by undetermined means.
Baby’s father’s family speaks in court
Baby Hall’s biological father, Izaiah Hall, and his family members addressed the court and Snelling.
“He was not garbage; he was the most beautiful, perfect, innocent, full-term baby boy,” Izaiah Hall’s sister said.
Although the baby’s life was limited, the family made it known in court that their grief is not.
“You imagine birthdays, holidays, first steps, first words, laughter, hugs, kisses, and all the little moments that become lifelong memories. For Cade, those possibilities were taken away before he ever had the chance to [experience them],” said a family member identified as Izaiah Hall’s mother or aunt.
Sentencing details
Prosecutors recommended the court sentence Snelling to 10 years for the manslaughter charge, and one year each for the other three charges. Judge Minnifield said she considered Snelling’s age, education, and clean prior record before fulfilling the state’s request for a concurrent sentence.
Fayette County Commonwealth’s Attorney Kimberly Baird said the baby’s family still has questions about why this happened.
“They are so raw right now and so emotional right now, still have questions about why, so I think they are okay with the fact that she got sent to prison. I’m not sure there’s a number big enough that that was going to make this okay for them,” Baird said.
Snelling will receive 415 days of credit for time served while on bond. She is not eligible for probation, but qualifies for parole after serving 85% of her 10-year sentence.

title: How to discuss firearm safety as older loved ones’ abilities change
text:
(Aging Untold) — Firearms are part of the home for some families. But as parents and grandparents age, changes in vision, memory or mood can affect how safely those firearms are handled and stored. It’s about checking in to make sure the safeguards in place still fit the person today.
What to watch for
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the signals families should watch for go beyond the firearm itself.
“You’re looking at the firearms itself, but what about missed medications and balance, and falling and financial judgments being off? These are all signs that maybe cognitively there’s something that has changed,” Rogers said.
She added that the stakes are different when a firearm is involved.
“It’s just that when you’re dealing with a firearm, that error is irreversible,” Rogers said.
It’s about the whole picture, not just the firearm
Rogers said families shouldn’t focus only on removing a firearm, but on reading all the signals together.
“It’s really not about removing things. You have to look at all the different signals that are going on, and that makes your assessment. And then look at how safe you can keep the environment if these things are happening,” Rogers said.
Use a diagnosis as a natural checkpoint
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said a new medical diagnosis can be a practical moment to raise the subject.
“Has there been a medical diagnosis of something like Parkinson’s or congestive heart failure, or something that would cause weakness and instability, that you would question the safety of the firearm in the home?” O’Rourke said.
She also encouraged families to plan ahead, before any problems appear.
“If they own a firearm and they’re fine, have the conversation then,” O’Rourke said. “If you run into trouble, Dad, Mom, how are we going to approach this? Or I am going to approach this, or can we talk about this now so we’re kind of ready if this happens.”
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the timing of the discussion matters.
“These are rational, thought-provoking discussions, and they have to be made when you have two cognitively whole humans,” Cradduck said.
Dementia raises the urgency
Cradduck said the changes in the brain associated with dementia are reasons to have the conversation early.
“We know that there is a rise of dementia diagnosis and with that comes poor judgment, oftentimes, and misjudgment, and sometimes hallucinations,” Cradduck said. “And God forbid, if grandpa’s having hallucinations and he pulls the gun out, now we have a family tragedy. Let’s have the conversation when the diagnosis happens.”
Cradduck said the conversation doesn’t need to wait for a diagnosis at all.
“Even before, as you’re aging,” she said. “This isn’t rights. This is safety. This is human safety.”
A home care story that shows the stakes
Cradduck shared an experience from her time running a home care agency involving a legally blind client who kept a firearm in her home.
“She thought there was somebody outside, and so she called the police. And the police come rolling up, and she walked out the door with her gun in hand. And unfortunately, they saw a gun, and we lost her to that,” Cradduck said. “So this isn’t just protecting the other person. It could be protecting them.”
Rogers said the story reflects the broader point.
“I think you have to look at all the signs that say where’s the brain headed,” Rogers said.
How home care agencies handle firearms in the house
O’Rourke said her own policy as a home care agency owner was not to go into homes where there were firearms or ammunition for the safety of her employees.
“That was my policy,” O’Rourke said. “Other people have different ways of running their businesses, but I would say, are there firearms in the home? They would say no or yes, if they were telling the truth, or if they even remembered. And then if they did, I would want the plan to get them removed, because I didn’t want to have a conversation with a caregiver and say, I’m sorry.”
Ambrose asked O’Rourke to clarify the reasoning behind the policy.
“So as an employer, you felt responsibility for your employees to be safe in the house? Sometimes maybe the patient or the client might not be thinking straight, and so you had to protect the employees that worked for you. So that’s what that was about. It’s not judgment about guns,” Ambrose said.
Cradduck said many home care agencies take a similar approach, though not all handle it the same way.
“So when you’re looking for home care, you may be met with that. Lots of agencies have that,” Cradduck said. “Mine was different. My policy was different, and it was: do you have guns in the home? I’m not going to ask you to do anything. Do you have them? I want to know where they’re at. I want to be able to be informed. I didn’t want you to have to lie to me and then find out something later on the down low. I wanted the open, honest conversation. But I get why, because we’re sending people into these homes, and we are responsible.”
Letting the doctor be the one to say no
O’Rourke also described a client who asked for outside help delivering the message.
“I had one client that went to her doctor and said, ‘Would you tell him he can’t have his guns anymore?’” O’Rourke said. “And when the doctor said it, it took all the responsibility from her and gave it to the doctor, and the doctor supported her. I thought that was brilliant.”

title: Woman says ‘something felt off’ during first date with man accused of posing as 49ers player
text:
PORTLAND (KPTV/Gray News) - An Oregon woman said she went on a date with a man accused of posing as an NFL player to defraud at least 26 women of more than $1 million.
Daejon Labrayae Delenar Love, 35, appeared in federal court Tuesday before a U.S. magistrate judge.
He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Portland on one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
News of his indictment shocked many people, including Rachel Anderson, who briefly went on a date with Love.
In 2024, Anderson said she met Love on the dating app Bumble. He told her his name was John Prince and that he was a Swiss real estate developer.
But during their first date, Anderson said something felt off.
“He said I’m very intentional and efficient when it comes to dating, and if I pursue you, you will be the only one I pursue you I need someone who has been around money, who understands these things aren’t luxuries to me this is just my normal life,” Anderson said. “Within five minutes I knew I wasn’t going to see him again.”
Investigators said he also worked with alleged accomplice Taylor Chan, 18. Both are charged with wire fraud and conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
The indictment also alleges Love used online dating and social media profiles with false personal and financial information, built romantic relationships with victims and showed signs of wealth to persuade them to send cash or wire money. Instead of investing the money, Love is accused of spending it on travel, hotels, luxury cars, clothes, jewelry and other buys.
“When I saw that, I almost fell out of bed, I could not believe it,” Anderson said. “It’s just awful, I can’t imagine how those women feel, I really can’t.”
Anderson said that, although her time with Love was brief, he falsely portrayed himself to be wealthy and having close friendships with celebrities and NFL players.
“He did say I have $5 million sitting in this account, and he said the home that I just mentioned in Vancouver was $3 million the entire time it was just that, this cost this, this cost this, I had never seen or heard anything like it before and I was just totally blown away,” Anderson said.
Recently, Netflix announced a new documentary titled “Untold: Wide Deceiver” about Love.
Netflix didn’t reveal when the documentary will be released.
Love was arraigned, pleaded not guilty and was ordered held in jail pending a jury trial set to start Dec. 15, 2026.

title: Heal points are the standard in Maine, but what do other New England states do?
text:
In the 1949-50 season, Maine high schools turned to a new system invented by a local principal to seed teams not just by their record, but by the quality of the teams they played and beat, in the hopes of more fairly ranking the best teams in a playoff region
More than 70 years later, the Heal points, named after Durward Heal, remain Maine’s weighted formula of choice. But across New England, other states have found their own systems to try to solve the seeding dilemma and create the most fair, accurate matchups.
Here is how other states go about it:
VERMONT
Vermont uses an index system that since the 2015-16 season has reflected strength of schedule. Like in Maine, teams get points based on the level of the opponent they’re defeating, but Vermont schools also get more points for winning on the road. Home and away doesn’t factor into Maine’s Heals.
Teams beating higher division teams get five points for home wins and six points for road wins, four and five for home and road wins against teams in the same division, 3.5 and 4.5 for wins against teams a division below, and two and three against teams two divisions below. Teams get half those points for ties.
The total amount of points, divided by the amount of games played, is the team’s point index.
MASSACHUSETTS
Massachusetts split its state tournaments into sectionals — the equivalent of regions — until 2021, and seeded its teams by winning percentage. This led to numerous instances of lower seeds that played in tougher conferences beating higher seeds, and even reaching state finals.
Since the fall of 2021, however, Massachusetts has ditched sectionals for statewide tournaments, and instituted a weighted formula to seed teams within a division.
Teams are rewarded for margin of victory (capped at a specific amount); their average margin added to their average opponent’s rating results in their overall rating, with teams slotted according to that overall number.
RHODE ISLAND
Rhode Island used win-loss records to seed teams until 2024, when it opened up scheduling to allow teams to play out of division.
The state then instituted a rating percentage index formula similar to the one used in college basketball. A team’s winning percentage (multiplied by 10) makes up 60% of the number, and its opponents’ winning percentage makes up 40%.
CONNECTICUT
Connecticut handles its seeding systems on a sport-by-sport basis.
Soccer just this fall moved to a formula that factors in multipliers for interdivision games, strength of schedule and winning percentage.
Volleyball, meanwhile, gives teams points for every win an opponent has, then divides that total by the number of games for a final point value.
Not all rankings are done in house. Lacrosse, for instance, uses calculations from LaxNumbers.com to put together its playoff fields.
NEW HAMPSHIRE
New Hampshire, which adopted Maine’s Heal points formula on a trial basis in 2009, now uses a modified version that assigns a point figure for each win (more points for beating a team in a higher division).
All points are added up, then divided by the number of games played, and teams are sorted based on those ratings.

title: Norridgewock voters to weigh in on noise moratorium, ordinance updates
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NORRIDGEWOCK — Voters have the opportunity Wednesday to weigh in on a 180-day moratorium on certain new commercial developments that create noise, a measure officials proposed to develop more specific regulations.
If approved, the moratorium includes a provision that pending applications for developments that fall under its scope would be put on hold until voters have their say on new proposed rules.
Among those likely subject to the stay include a tire burnout pit off Ward Hill Road and a gun shop with shooting ranges on Skowhegan Road. Both have sparked concerns from neighbors about potential noise and other environmental impacts.
The Norridgewock Planning Board is continuing to review the site plan applications for both projects and has requested noise impact studies for each.
Along with the moratorium proposal, Wednesday’s special town meeting is slated to include votes on updates to the town’s Subdivision Ordinance, Board of Appeals Ordinance and Street Naming and House Numbering Ordinance.
Voters are also being asked to approve a $2,500 purchase of a parcel in downtown Norridgewock and to repeal a requirement that the town put notices in the Morning Sentinel for special town meetings.
All articles are set to be voted on by show of hands in an open-floor style town meeting. The special town meeting is set for 6:30 p.m. Wednesday at Mill Stream Elementary School, 26 Mercer Road.
NOISE MORATORIUM
The Select Board drafted the moratorium proposal after hearing concerns from residents over the proposed shooting ranges, which include one of up to 1,000 yards, at 255 Skowhegan Road, Town Manager Richard LaBelle said in an interview by telephone Friday.
If approved, the moratorium would prohibit certain kinds of new developments and the town’s processing of applications for such projects.
The moratorium would apply to developments deemed a new nonresidential use or change in existing nonresidential use that requires a formal site plan review by the planning board, and have one of the following primary uses:
• Shooting ranges.
• Facilities used for testing and demonstration of firearms, ammunition, explosives, or pyrotechnic devices.
• Facilities used for motorsport activities such as racing, pulling, demolition or testing.
• Outdoor entertainment venues using amplification systems on a regular basis.
• Outdoor industrial operations such as rock crushing, pile driving, forging, impact-based metal fabrication, sawmilling and log processing.
The moratorium would not apply to construction activity for a development that does not fall under those categories. It also would not apply to temporary events on the same parcel of no more than three consecutive days and no more than four times in a 12-month period, provided the activity has obtained all other necessary approvals.
It also would not apply to developments the town already approved.
The goal of the halt on developments is to give town officials time to draft new proposed regulations for voters to review by the annual town meeting in March, the moratorium states.
It includes a provision that the select board may extend it an additional 180 days, after notice and hearing, provided the problem that prompted the moratorium still exists and reasonable progress is being made to alleviate it.
“If the moratorium passes and the voters decline to accept proposed changes (in March), we would stay status quo,” LaBelle said. “If the moratorium passes and proposed regulations are approved by voters, then the applications that were stayed will be reviewed under the revised guidelines.”
ORDINANCE REVISIONS
The proposed amendments to the Subdivision Ordinance may look familiar to the discerning voter: Officials presented the changes to voters at the annual town meeting in March, and voters rejected them.
The revisions are largely to comply with state law, and where the planning board was able to make choices, the regulations are the least strict possible, according to LaBelle.
“It was a lack of understanding by voters who just assumed that, when an ordinance was being … amended, it was going to mean stricter regulations,” LaBelle said.
He noted that even some new planning board members elected this spring admitted they did not fully understand the March vote.
Town officials decided to propose changes to the Board of Appeals Ordinance to change meeting notice requirements, LaBelle said. If approved, appellants would no longer have to pay for legal notices of hearings to be published in a newspaper, which LaBelle said can be a burden. Instead, the ordinance would be amended to require notices to be posted at the town office and online and sent to relevant property owner, abutters and town officials.
Other minor proposed modifications include a few additional types of matters the appeals board may hear, a change to the procedure for determining conflicts of interest of board members that complies with state law and cleaning up of language.
The Street Naming and Housing Numbering Ordinance outlines a new process for reviewing requests to change road names.
It is rare people ask the town to make changes to road names, LaBelle said, but recently, the town received a request from someone building a new home.
“When we brought it to the select board to request the name change, there was conflict amongst the select board about the process and the appropriateness of allowing for a name change,” LaBelle said. “So, that’s what precipitated the review to kind of formalize the process.”
A proposed medical marijuana growing facility on Waterville Road, which was recently approved by the planning board, as part of its application requested a new road name and provided options that were puns using the word “high,” LaBelle said. The select board said no to the suggestions, and the updated ordinance aims to clarify the board’s authority moving forward.
PROPERTY ACQUISITION
Town officials are asking for approval to buy a small parcel at the corner of Mechanic and Main streets. The 0.21-acre parcel sits along Mill Stream.
The agreed-upon sale price is $2,500, and officials are asking voters to authorize appropriating up to $3,500 from tax increment financing funds to complete the acquisition.
Town officials want the property to maintain and enhance the appearance of the downtown area. They are not planning any development there.
LaBelle said the town approached the owner, Wayne Rogers, about a decade ago about buying the property, and he was not interested then. Recently, Rogers, now living out of state, indicated he would be open to an offer, according to LaBelle.
The deal includes a condition that the town call the property “Wade’s Landing,” after Rogers’ late son.
NEWSPAPER NOTICES
The last item on the meeting warrant is to repeal a requirement voters enacted in 1983 that the town place notices of special town meetings in the Morning Sentinel for three days, one week before the meeting.
Readership of print newspapers has been declining, as people turn online to get information, LaBelle said.
For Wednesday’s special town meeting, the town paid $820 to run the three notices in the Sentinel, LaBelle said.
“Is that really the best use of your money, with the widest reach?” LaBelle said. “I’m not sure that it is.”

title: Obituary: Frank W. Sheldon
text:
YARMOUTH – Dr. Frank W. Sheldon, 80, died peacefully on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. Frank was born on Sept. 28, 1946, in Philadelphia, Pa. to Warner Sheldon and Margaret McKay Sheldon.
Growing up, Frank spent summers with his family on Mount Desert Island, Maine, where his father served as director of the Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory in the 1950s. These summers instilled in Frank both a deep love of science and a deep love of Maine. After graduating from college at St. Lawrence University in 1969 and medical school at McGill University in 1974, Frank established his family medicine practice in Wiscasset and Bath, serving families throughout midcoast Maine.
Frank will be remembered for his curiosity and his child-like sense of fun. He loved to tinker, to take things apart, and to start do-it-yourself projects. An excellent cook and adventurous eater, Frank introduced his children and their friends to a wide variety of global cuisines while teaching them to savor and delight in the pleasures of food. Frank loved to sail and for many years had his J/24, Fancy, at the Wiscasset Yacht Club. An animal lover, Frank had pets throughout his life and is survived by his dog, Blueberry.
Frank was married to Barbara Wessinger (deceased) and later to Cynthia Williams. In his later years, Frank lived with his long-term partner, Belva Horn, splitting their time between Wiscasset, Freeport, Deer Isle; Montreal, Canada; and Apollo Beach, Fla.
In addition to his parents, Frank was predeceased by his older sister, Margo Ross of Pitlochry, Scotland.
Frank is survived by his long-term partner, Belva Horn; his three children, Maxwell Sheldon, Winthrop Sheldon, and Abigail Sheldon Jeck; his eight grandchildren, Wyatt Sheldon, Sage Sheldon, Reed Sheldon, Warner Sheldon, Adelaide Sheldon, Georgina Sheldon, Linus Jeck and Peter Jeck; his siblings, Wendy Wood, Lura Clark, and W. Richard Sheldon; and many nieces and nephews.
A funeral service will be held on Oct. 24, at 2 p.m. at St. Philip’s Episcopal Church, 12 Hodge St., Wiscasset.

the family suggests
a donation to:
Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory

title: Bath Rotary grants available
text:
The Rotary Club of Bath is once again encouraging nonprofit charitable organizations to submit applications for Community Service Grants. It’s often a juggling act for nonprofits to direct limited funds in a way that benefits those who need it most. Many times a few thousand dollars can be enough to expand a critically needed service. For that reason, the club distributes money every year to several nonprofit organizations who reach out to make lives better for people who need a helping hand.
Up to $10,000 has been designated for grants this year. Beginning in 1919, the Bath Rotary Club in its earliest days raised money for basic needs like food, clothing, and education. While continuing to meet those needs, the club continued to expand its mission over the next 100-plus years to meet new challenges from Bath and surrounding communities. In the last few years Rotary members have awarded volunteer time and grants to the Backpack Program, Best Buddies at Morse High School, the Midcoast Youth Center, Bath Parks & Recreation, the Bath Area YMCA, Woolwich Odyssey of the Mind, and Salvation Army Bell Ringing.
The deadline for submitting applications is Dec. 31, 2027. Application forms are available on the Bath Rotary website, bathrotary.org. For more information, email bathrotary@gmail.com.

title: Before Maine Wildness had a name, it was an inspiration
text:
Zoe Durrant waited. Standing dead center, in front of the stage, next to her father, Colin, the 12-year-old was all eager anticipation. This team is potential personified. It can show his daughter and other girls around Maine a pathway to the possible, Colin Durrant said.
This soccer team, the Maine Wildness, is for Zoe.
“I’m really excited,” she said. “I think it will be an inspiration.”
On Thursday evening, the Maine Wildness name was revealed in front of hundreds of fans crammed into Live at Madrid’s for the announcement. The women’s soccer team, which will play in the USL W League beginning next spring, didn’t have a name or a roster, but it already had an enthusiastic fan base.
In June, the team needed just an hour to sell 5,000 season ticket deposits, with 4,400 of those now Wildness season ticket holders.
Jessica Mayhew of Saco is one of those season ticket holders. She arrived at the party early, wearing her Hearts of Pine scarf. As she waited for the announcement, she chatted with Sarah Robble of Kennebunk.
“It’s great to have the ladies represented,” Robble said.
Robble wasn’t able to get in on season tickets. They sold so fast. Don’t worry, Mayhew said. We’ll get you to some games.
“I grew up playing soccer. We’ve got some young girls who play here. This gives them something to strive for,” Mayhew said.
The Maine Wildness is for Mayhew and Robble.
According to data from the National Federation of State High School Associations, close to 3,000 girls played high school soccer in Maine last fall. There are a dozen women’s college soccer teams in Maine, including the University of Maine, which has won three America East titles to advance to the NCAA Division I tournament.
The Maine Wildness is for them.
The Wildness had two supprt groups before it had a name. The Halyard takes its name from the line that raises a ship’s sail so it can catch wind and go. The Lightkeepers strive to illuminate and promote girls and women’s soccer across Maine.
BrynWynne, 13, and her father, Patrick, were among the first in line for Wildness merch when the pop-up store opened shortly after the team name and crest were revealed. Bryn wore a Lightkeepers T-shirt that states succinctly what the group is about.
“Women’s soccer makes Maine better,” the shirt reads. Throughout the crowd at Live at Madrid’s on Thursday, it was a popular wardrobe choice. Bryn doesn’t play soccer, but she has a lot of friends who do. When she supports Maine Wildness, she supports them.
“(Soccer) has really grown on me,” Bryn said.
The Maine Wildness is for Bryn and all her friends who play the game.
Teila Norris-Julien of Biddeford wore a Halyard T-shirt and talked up the new team to everyone she met. This team is something both her daughter, Gabbi, 11, and son, Hayden, 10, can cheer on and draw inspiration from.
“It’s something they can look up to. These people are in our community. Kids can watch them play and think, they did this, maybe I can,” Norris-Julien said.
The Maine Wildness is for Gabbi and Hayden, and their mom.
The Wildness name evokes the underlying hardscrabbleness of Maine. The coast is rocky. The mountains aren’t the highest peaks, but they’re daunting. The name implies fighting for every scrap you can get against an environment not inclined to hand over anything easily.
It doesn’t immediately roll off the tongue, but it fits. Remember, Hearts of Pine had to grow on a lot of fans, too.
When the Maine Wildness plays, it will be in front of a packed Fitzpatrick Stadium, in front of a loyal fan base that knew it was waiting for something, and that something now has a name.
The Maine Wildness is for all of us.

title: A widow sold her home to care for her husband with Alzheimer’s. She’s not alone.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (InvestigateTV) - Family caregivers are considered the backbone of America’s long-term care system and experts say that backbone is breaking.
About one in four adults in the country provide ongoing care for a loved one, sometimes at the expense of their own well-being.
Caregiving costs can add up fast, forcing caregivers to take on debt and in some cases making it hard to cover basic necessities. This is often driven by fixed budgets, high out of pocket medical costs, and the immense time constraints of caregiving.
When police in Floyd County, Georgia arrived to search for a missing 74-year-old man last year, they found him army crawling through the woods, believing he was back in Vietnam.
Lamar Jones had escaped his memory care facility. His wife, Sue Jones, described the scene.
“They found him belly crawling, just like army crawling through the woods,” Sue Jones said. “He crawled under a log, just like you would if you were in the war and at some point in time, he found a pipe in the woods. He was pretending like it was a gun.”
Lamar Jones’ behavior — a symptom of his Alzheimer’s disease — repeated itself for years. He would wander away from facilities, and staff would call police. The facilities would refuse to take him back.
Then Sue Jones would search for another care home, pay another entry fee, pay monthly bills, and begin the cycle again.
“The part that was not manageable was probably the last three years,” Sue Jones said.
Months after the police incident in the woods, Lamar Jones died peacefully. Sue Jones held onto his memory and the life they built together: 44 years of marriage. He was a father and grandfather.
“Sometimes the grief that I have is because I loved him so much,” Sue Jones said. “That’s the price for paying for love: it’s a very long hard grief.”
An Atlanta News First investigation found memory care facilities in Georgia average $3,849 per month. Georgia State University (GSU) recently conducted the research which shows based on that monthly payment, in one year alone a family would spend more than $46,000 for bed at a specialized memory facility.
According to the GSU study, dementia patients in Georgia spent nearly 83% of their monthly income on long-term care.
To afford her husband’s care, Sue Jones sold everything she owned, including her home. She moved into her daughter’s basement.
“We had dementia,” Sue Jones said when asked about the burden. “My husband did not have dementia; he and I had dementia, because it takes over your life.”
Data from the Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reveals unpaid caregivers across the country like Sue Jones provide the equivalent of nearly $470 billion a year in free care.
But the greatest cost, Sue Jones argued, is isolation. Without enough support groups, she navigated the emotional toll, insurance decisions and facility placements alone.
“I just kept trying to find a solution,” she said. “I just wanted to fix it. I was never able to fix it.”
That isolation is why the Georgia chapter of the Alzheimer’s Association went to the state capitol for advocacy day during the current legislative session. They were urging lawmakers to appropriate an extra $2 million in the state’s dementia support program for respite care, which is short-term relief and services for overwhelmed primary caregivers.
Nancy Pitra, the association’s director of government affairs, said such services are needed “so that caregivers don’t get burnt out or have their own crisis. If you are caring for someone, chances are, you’re not taking care of your own health.”
The $2 million appropriation passed through the Georgia legislature, but was removed from the budget by Governor Brian Kemp.
The Alzheimer’s Association called the veto a “setback” and said: “...we are deeply encouraged by the strong, bipartisan support this initiative received in both the Georgia House and Senate. This widespread legislative alignment highlights a growing, shared recognition of the essential role caregivers play in our communities.”
In the room where Lamar Jones spent his final months, Sue Jones showed a whiteboard where her husband — a man whose memory had largely faded — wrote a message that never wavered: “I love you.”
Sue Jones has since started her own support group in Cobb County for other dementia caregivers.

- Alzheimer’s Foundation of America - helpline: 866-232-8484

title: Susan Collins’ Portland office receives letter containing ‘unknown substance’
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ office in Portland received a letter containing an “unknown substance” on Friday as the FBI investigates a slew of such incidents reported across the country.
A spokesperson for the Republican confirmed in an email that the letter at the Portland office was intercepted and no injuries were reported. She also said Collins’ Washington, D.C., office received such a letter Thursday.
“Thank you to the Portland police, the Portland fire department, the hazmat team, and the FBI (for) their quick and courageous response,” Katie Brown, Collins’ chief of staff, said in a written statement.
Last month, Collins’ Biddeford office was vandalized by someone who spray-painted a vulgar message on the office’s outer doors.
The FBI has been investigating “a series of suspicious mailings” across the country, including to secretary of state and election offices.
“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the FBI said in a written statement.
A spokesperson for the FBI’s Boston field office said the agency is “not confirming specific instances of letters” when asked about the incident in Portland on Friday.
A spokesperson for the Portland Fire Department did not immediately respond to a request for information on the department’s involvement in the response at Collins’ office. A Portland police spokesperson deferred inquiries on the incident to the FBI.
Collins is currently seeking her sixth term in the U.S. Senate, facing Democrat Troy Jackson.

title: Man raises awareness about rare cancer with soccer-themed prosthetic eye
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — Ryan Gibson faced an unexpected choice after losing his right eye to ocular melanoma: blend in with a normal-looking prosthetic or make a statement.
Gibson chose to make a statement.
After getting official clearance from the professional soccer team Bayern Munich, Gibson unveiled a prosthetic eye featuring his favorite team’s logo.
“I could go back to normality and get the same eye, nobody will really know — or I can go big or go home,” Gibson said.
Extremely rare diagnosis
Ocular melanoma affects only five or six out of every million people each year. The cancer starts in specialized cells that make melanin, the pigment that gives color to eyes and skin.
Most eye melanomas form in parts of the eye that cannot be seen when looking in a mirror.
The cancer may not cause symptoms, but when they occur, signs can include flashes of light that look like specks of dust, a growing dark spot in the colored part of the eye, poor or blurry vision in one eye and loss of peripheral vision.
“In 2016, I started seeing spots everywhere,” Gibson said.
After weeks of blurry vision and spots in his right eye, Gibson went to a doctor and received a rare diagnosis.
“The 30 years she’s been an eye doctor she’s never seen that before,” Gibson said. “It was like the yeti or bigfoot. Heard of it, never seen it.”
Treatment and recovery
Treatment for large ocular melanomas typically leads to vision loss, and in some cases, loss of the entire eye. Gibson faced a choice of radiation treatment or amputation.
“I went ahead and made the decision, pop it out,” Gibson said.
Gibson, who lives outside Charlotte, said his love of Bayern Munich has been a family tradition that has remained constant through his most difficult chapter.
“Family tradition-type thing. Over the years it’s just gotten more ingrained and more personal for me,” Gibson said. “It’s always there, it’s the constant.”
Raising awareness
Gibson uses his prosthetic eye as a conversation starter to raise awareness about ocular melanoma.
“I want to use it as a tool, not just an eye,” Gibson said. “At some point in that conversation, they’ll get up the nerve to go ‘What happened?’ And when they get to that point, then you have the opening for awareness for ocular melanoma.”
His love of Bayern Munich has taken him to games around the world.
“I have to sit extremely close so I can at least see what’s going on,” Gibson said. “For some people it’s not just a game. Some people don’t quite grasp that.”
Gibson encourages anyone having issues with their eyes to get regular dilated eye exams to catch any potential cancer early.

title: Out-of-state police agency searched a university’s Flock camera network more than 183K times in 3 months
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - Records obtained from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte show that out-of-state police departments are searching the college’s network of Automatic License Plate Recognition cameras far more than local law enforcement.
The agency that searched the UNC Charlotte network the most between March and May 2026 was the Houston Police Department. The law enforcement agency conducted searches that included the UNC Charlotte network more than 183,000 times from March through May 2026.
Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police ranked 30th in total searches of the UNC Charlotte network. UNC Charlotte Police Department ranked 1,491st, with 229 searches over the three-month period.
Cameras feed a nationwide database
As cars drive by the Flock cameras on the UNC Charlotte campus, the cameras capture license plate numbers and add them to a nationwide database that law enforcement agencies across the country can search. Searching the data and the license plates they capture is limited to law enforcement, but there are also cameras owned by private companies and HOA’s that are included in the network.
Records from UNC Charlotte show that when Houston officers searched a license plate in the Flock system, they often searched more than 6,000 networks across the country, while many other departments appeared to limit their searches to fewer networks.
Students approached on campus were unable to guess which agencies searched the network most.
“Houston, Texas?!? Wow. OK. Interesting!!” said Verity Morgan, a student who recently hosted a campus debate on Flock cameras.
“Houston??? Why is Houston looking at Charlotte?” said Radhika Chaudha, a student.
“I mean what rights do people have now? You’re losing your right to privacy and you don’t have a choice,” Chaudha said.
“In my personal opinion, I don’t see why they’re necessary for our campus,” Morgan said.
“Money could definitely go to different things, I would say. And then it’s kind of creepy that people in Houston are trying to figure out what we got going on over here,” said Peyton Marshall, a student.
In an email statement sent to WBTV, the Houston Police Department said, “The use of automated license plate recognition systems by Houston Police Department personnel is regularly reviewed. The department has identified usage that is being investigated further.”
Attorney tracking flock camera use statewide
Mark Williams, an attorney in Wilmington, North Carolina, runs a website dedicated to opposing Flock cameras and other license plate reading technology. His records requests have helped reveal which police agencies are searching Flock networks on college campuses across the state.
“This is a mass government surveillance system that has been built throughout the state of North Carolina,” Williams said.
Williams warned that while there are rules in North Carolina limiting what law enforcement can use the data for, other agencies in other states lack some of the same guidelines. Meaning UNC Charlotte can’t control how the data their cameras capture is used.
“Under North Carolina law, you can’t sell the data. Texas has no guardrails. Most of those places don’t have rules against selling the data, how it’s used, and who has access to it. That’s a problem,” Williams said.
University responds
UNC Charlotte denied WBTV’s request for an interview with Police Chief Jeffrey Baker.
The university’s Director of Media Relations wrote in an email: “UNC Charlotte participates in a shared law enforcement network that includes approximately 1,600 agencies. When a law enforcement agency searches the network for a specific license plate, UNC Charlotte cameras may be included in that query. If the plate has been detected, the system returns the location, date and time of the detection.”
The university said the technology has helped University police in a wide variety of cases, including the arrest of a suspect in a larceny investigation involving more than $100,000 in equipment stolen from an on-campus construction site. The university has not provided the arrest record nearly a month after it was first requested by WBTV.
UNC Charlotte said it does not share network access with non-law enforcement entities such as homeowner associations and private businesses. Records show some other police agencies that searched the network include CSX railroad police and the parks department in Toledo, Ohio.
UNC Charlotte is not required to share its network with other law enforcement agencies. Appalachian State University turned off national sharing of its Flock network, and UNC Chapel Hill made the same decision last week.
There have been no accusations of misuse of the Flock network at UNC Charlotte. The university says it regularly reviews the system, and officers are required to use specific case numbers any time they search the network.
North Carolina does not require reporting of misuse of the Flock system. Past cases of misuse have come to light when officers were arrested for misusing the system, including at the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department and Mooresville Police Department, or when a department voluntarily reported misuse.
