title: Maine’s Heal points is a time-tested formula, but many coaches want improvements
text:
In 2025, the Bonny Eagle High School boys basketball team caught a break. The Scots were 6-11 and headed for the last playoff spot in Class AA South, until a victory in the regular season finale over Noble High School allowed them to jump from seventh to fourth, and from a road to a home playoff game.
The 16-1 Noble Knights were without four starters for much of the game, but as far as the Heal point standings were concerned, it didn’t matter. In the tournament, Bonny Eagle parlayed its good fortune into a quarterfinal win over Sanford, and then a shocking semifinal win over No. 1 Thornton Academy.
“It was kind of a gift for us,” Scots coach John Trull said. “If I were another coach, I’d probably be upset. … But it motivated us. We had to prove that we deserved to be in that spot.”
The scenario showed both the strengths and flaws of the Heal point formula, the system the Maine Principals’ Association has used to seed most high school sports (football excluded) for postseason play. Developed by Durward Heal, a former principal of Schenck High in East Millinocket, and implemented in the 1949-50 season, Heal points rank teams according to their strength by factoring in not just their record but the quality of their victories.
And for over 75 years, while sometimes challenged, no one has found a better, more fair way to do it.
“It’s as equitable a system as there is,” Cheverus girls hockey coach Scott Rousseau said. “I don’t think it’s the perfect system, but generally speaking, it gets it right.”
MPA executive director Mike Bisson noted the objectivity of the Heal points formula, which separates itself from more opinion-based rankings and polls used in some other states.
“While it’s not a perfect system, it’s a mathematical formula,” he said. “And any type of power ranking based on a mathematical formula is going to have some weird things in it.”
While most of the coaches interviewed approve of the structure, there are dissidents whose arguments include that the system can punish victories over weaker opponents, lead to scheduling difficulties and reward victories over opponents with good records, rather than opponents tested by better competition.
A Varsity Maine email survey sent to more than 200 coaches asking if they think Heal points are an effective system, an effective system that could be improved, or not effective received 55 responses. Twenty said it’s effective as is, while 35 said either that the system should be improved or that it just doesn’t work.
“Heal points are no longer effective as currently constructed,” Rob Sullivan, the girls basketball coach at Kennebunk for 30 years, wrote in an email. “It is an outdated system that could easily be replaced for a much simpler system.”
‘ONE OF THE BEST SYSTEMS YOU CAN HAVE’
Heal points work by awarding a point value to a team based on how often it wins and the quality of the teams that it beats.
Here’s how the formula works:
- A team is assigned a preliminary index based on their wins — everyone gets 40 points for a win over a Class A team, 38 for Class B, 36 for Class C, 34 for Class D and 32 for eight-man or Class S. Classes are determined by enrollment.
- That number is then divided by the number of scheduled games. The preliminary index grows as the season goes on.
- Next, you add up all of the preliminary indices for the teams you defeated, and divide that by the number of scheduled games.
- That number is then multiplied by 10, which gives you a team’s tournament index.
- The teams are then ranked by their tournament index to form the Heal point standings. Teams at the top, are the top teams of the year.
Debate surrounding Heals and their effectiveness has gone on for decades. Proponents of the system like that it goes beyond just win-loss record, paints a more accurate hierarchy by factoring in who teams have beaten, and aim to provide balance in classes where teams don’t all share common opponents.
Lucas McNelly, who runs the Maine Basketball Rankings website, developed his own formula that ranks teams and predicts outcomes based on a variety of factors, including point differential and home and road performance. He said, though, that Heal points are “one of the best methods you can have.”
“I think the bones of Heal points are so good that I built the entire ranking system on them,” he said. “Every game in the state matters, and it’s hard to find a system that does that. … It can swing a seeding in C North on the last day of the season. I think that level of chaos is awesome.”
McNelly said the ideal system would include every team in a region playing each other twice, but Maine’s geography prohibits that.
“Let’s say Caribou and Gardiner are in the same (region). … You can’t do that on a Tuesday night for a game,” he said. “The state’s too big. The state’s never going to not be big.”
South Portland boys basketball coach Kevin Millington said a big strength of Heal points is that they reward strength of victory (beating good teams) rather than strength of schedule (simply playing them). Craig Roberts, Scarborough’s girls soccer coach, said tournament results have validated the formula.
“The system has gotten it right,” he said. “If you look at the last four teams standing in the regional semis and regional finals, typically it’s the teams that are at the top (or) near the top of the Heal points.”
Brunswick girls basketball coach Sam Farrell likes that Heal points can give a team that would otherwise be out of the playoff race something to play for late in the season.
“I like being rewarded for big wins,” he said. “It keeps the kids motivated: ‘Hey, I know what our record is, but this game matters.’ You can shock the world, and now you get to play in the (Augusta) Civic Center.”
HEAL POINT HICCUPS
Opponents, however, say the system often doesn’t churn out the best representation within a region. A frequent criticism from the coaches’ survey was that Heal points favor teams that beat opponents with many wins, without taking into consideration whether those wins came against strong opponents.
Conversely, a team wouldn’t get as many points for beating a good team that plays strong competition, but has an inferior record as a result.
Boothbay boys basketball coach Dan Hallinan’s Class D team, which plays in the Mountain Valley Conference with several Class C schools, missed the tournament last year despite playing 10 Class C teams and beating two, while three of the teams that qualified played a combined two C teams and beat none.
“We have been penalized for playing a much harder schedule,” he said. “We are rewarding teams for playing weaker schedules. The best (or) better teams aren’t being placed appropriately seeding-wise, or not making the tournament at all.”
Freeport field hockey and girls lacrosse coach Marcia Wood said she sees a similar dynamic in lacrosse, where teams that play in tougher conferences get seeded lower because they don’t get the number of wins that teams that play weaker schedules do.
Because of that, she said, the two strongest teams can meet up in earlier rounds of the tournament, and “the game before states is the big game.”
Some conferences allow schools the ability to schedule a fixed number of out-of-conference games, but the process of determining which teams to compete against also becomes complicated under the Heal points system.
“Now you have the decision to make of, ‘OK … (who) makes the most sense to play against?'” Dirigo boys basketball coach Cody St. Germain said. “The team that’s geographically close and also gives you a challenge? Or a lot of teams are saying, ‘I’m going to go play a 16-win team that stinks that I know I’m going to beat because I know I get 16 guaranteed Heal points out of going and beating that team.
“And we’re starting to see now there are teams that are really utilizing that to their advantage, and I can’t really blame them. I’ve considered it myself at times.”
How Heal points factor into scheduling can also raise issues from an administrative perspective.
Leavitt Athletic Director Ryan LaRoche said it can be difficult to find games for different sports, as well as for girls programs versus boys programs, given different classifications and talent levels.
“There are definitely teams in the state where the boys team is not competitive at all and the girls team is in the state championship every year,” he said. “So when the conference is making a schedule and they’re looking at crossovers that are appropriate, they’re trying to keep those the same for the boys and the girls, it’s sometimes a challenge to make that work where you don’t want a team that’s bad to just have to play good teams every week.
“But if you have a team that’s very competitive and historically successful, you want them to be able to play the best teams and have those opportunities for the Heal points.”
Mt. Blue baseball coach Steve Porter and Deering boys soccer coach Joel Costigan shared another qualm with the structure: wins over bad teams in-conference earn too few points, and teams can be passed in the standings despite winning games they are obigated to play.
“The Heal points are a way to address the scheduling disparities, but they also create disparities in the points,” Costigan said. “You (can) have a team with more wins, but those wins don’t matter because they still finished behind a team that had fewer wins. I see that every year.”
NO ‘REAL TRACTION’ FOR CHANGE
Several soccer coaches said they’d like to see a more straightforward system of awarding three points for wins and one for ties, while Sullivan at Kennebunk said he’d like to see Heals eliminated in favor of an open tournament.
Farrell at Brunswick said he’d prefer a return to the former difference of five points for a win in each class, rather than the current two, in order to discourage teams looking for wins against teams in lower classes.
Bisson at the MPA said he hasn’t had people come forward “with any proposals that have gained any real traction to change.”
“We would certainly listen if people had an alternative that they felt was a better option and gained some support from the schools,” Bisson said.
For over 70 years, no one’s developed a better one.

title: Governor praises local who 'heroically' helped end the mass shooting at an Oregon elementary school
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — Officials are lauding the actions of a local who they say chased down and shot a teenage gunman who killed three children and a teacher at an Oregon elementary school.
At a news conference hours after Thursday’s attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Gov. Tina Kotek praised the person’s response as police arrived at the scene, saying they helped end the rampage and likely saved lives.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” said Kotek.
Like police, the Democratic governor didn’t provide any details about the person who intervened, including whether they have a link to the school and whether it was a shot they fired that killed the attacker.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartener at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that a member of the public pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. “I’m feeling very grateful.”
The shooter used a gun bought by his mom
The 16-year-old suspect, identified only as a Bend resident, was found dead inside the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Mike Krantz said. Police said he got into the school by shooting through locked doors.
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Authorities didn’t give details about the teacher who was killed. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded in the attack and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Police said they didn’t know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended it.
Police respond within minutes
The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education.
Children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home.
A community grieves
Shaken residents held a vigil Thursday night, where children drew hearts in chalk on the sidewalk and held candles side-by-side with adults.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for the area’s 32 schools.
Bend, which has about 100,000 residents, is the biggest city in central Oregon. Ringed by mountains, it has ballooned in population over the past three decades and is a tourism and outdoor recreation hub, about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland.
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.
Just four years ago in Bend, a grocery store employee who had served in the U.S. Army attacked a gunman who was spraying shots inside the supermarket. Both the employee, whom police hailed as a hero, and a customer were killed, and the gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
___
Durkin and Tucker reported from Washington. Associated Press reporters Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City, Gene Johnson in Seattle, Ed White in Detroit and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

title: Why dementia makes it so hard to eat — and what caregivers can do
text:
(Aging Untold) — As dementia progresses, eating can become one of the hardest daily tasks. The brain can lose its ability to recognize hunger, identify food or remember how to use a fork.
We are breaking down why eating becomes so complicated and what caregivers can do to help.
The brain’s signals get disrupted
Dementia can disrupt the part of the brain that controls hunger, thirst and appetite signaling — the hypothalamus — Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. And the process of getting food to the mouth is complex, requiring motor skills and sensory response.
“It’s not that they don’t want to eat. They may not know, because now you have mixed signals, or they may have the senses but it’s not working, so it’s a disconnect,” Rogers said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said that disconnect means a loved one isn’t choosing to skip meals. Their brain has changed and we are expecting them to perform as they always have.
“Maybe my brain hasn’t told my stomach it’s hungry and it’s been 24 hours,” Cradduck said. “Or maybe it told it it’s hungry, but I don’t know what that feeling is anymore. And oh, I figured out what the feeling is, but I sure as heck don’t know what this is for. And you gave me a fork. Why would you give me a fork?”
Rogers compared the experience to a familiar daily drive suddenly filled with detours.
“You go the same route every day, right? And you know where you’re going,” Rogers said. “But one day you go and there’s a whole bunch of detours.”
Watch, observe and simplify the setting
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke described working with a client in a memory care unit who had lost 15 pounds. The woman had macular degeneration, was hard of hearing and had memory impairment, yet staff were placing a plate, fork and knife in front of her and expecting her to eat.
“I think the first thing I would want people to do is just watch, observe and see how are they doing?” O’Rourke said. “Look at the contrast between the plate and the placemat. How much clutter is around the table? ... How many flower tablecloths have I seen in communities and it can be very confusing.”
O’Rourke said what works can also change by stage.
“You have the early, middle and late stage. ... Maybe the contrast plates work in the first stage early on, and then the next day it’s not working,” O’Rourke said. “They look at that special utensil, and they don’t know what to do.”
Abilities can come and go — and that’s not manipulation
Cradduck said families often misread a loved one’s inconsistent ability to eat independently as intentional behavior.
“People think that if I did it yesterday, I should be able to do it today,” Cradduck said. “Well maybe I did it yesterday, I don’t know how to do it today, but tomorrow those neural pathways hit again and I can do it tomorrow.”
That inconsistency is frequently misunderstood, Cradduck said.
“Too many families and too many people oftentimes see that as, they’re manipulating me. They did it yesterday — watch, they’ll be able to do it tomorrow,” Cradduck said. “That goes with so many things with dementia.”
She said families need to figure out what changed that is keeping the loved one from eating.
O’Rourke described a strategy once used in a memory care unit, known as “the drive-by,” for a resident who couldn’t tolerate sitting at a table.
“You’d just walk down the hall and you’d just hand him a sandwich and then keep walking,” O’Rourke said. “We stopped having him sit at the table because it just didn’t work for him. You have to figure out creatively what’s going to work.”
O’Rourke added that caregivers should stay open to sudden changes in taste as well.
“If they used to like a ham sandwich, and then all of a sudden they don’t, and they never would eat roast beef, and now they want to eat roast beef — don’t be opposed to any change in their taste,” she said.
Watch for swallowing problems
Rogers said swallowing difficulty is one of the most serious concerns during mealtimes.
“Make sure that you’re watching the swallowing, because a lot of times that’s a big thing,” Rogers said. “They’re not eating, or they’re eating but they can’t swallow.”
Swallowing trouble carries serious risk, including aspiration, Rogers said.
She also suggested getting ahead of the issue early with a baseline swallowing study, which a physician would order.
“I think it’s not a bad idea, as a baseline, because we know how the progression is, to go out and have maybe a baseline swallowing study,” Rogers said.
Practical strategies that can help
Cradduck said finger foods, texture changes and flexibility can make meals easier.
“Finger foods are great. You can try different utensils,” Cradduck said.
“Stop worrying so much about the perfect diet. This is about nutrition and hydration. It doesn’t mean that we’ve got to have a salad and a three- or four-course meal. This means I’m getting nutrition into your system,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said options that tend to work well include finger foods, fruit with high water content, pudding, smoothies, milkshakes and smaller, more frequent meals
She said caregivers should avoid judging a loved one’s eating behavior.
“Just know that they really can’t help it. It is brain damage,” Ambrose said. “It’s not like you’re going to instruct them. So just give them a break. Have some grace. Don’t harass them to eat.”
Cradduck said sitting beside — not across from — a loved one can encourage eating through mimicry.
“If you’re sitting next to someone and we’re going to share a meal... I’m going to set the same plate beside you,” Cradduck said. “You know what you see me do, you’re going to mimic, right? That is one of the greatest ways for a caregiver to get someone to start to eat.”
Ambrose also pointed to speech pathologists as a resource as well.
“I love the work they do, but their title is so confusing,” she said. “They can really help with swallowing and figuring things out.”
Key takeaways
- Dementia disrupts appetite signals and motor planning, making it harder for the brain to recognize hunger, identify food or remember how to use utensils.
- Simplify the table setting. High-contrast plates, reduced clutter and fewer distracting patterns can help, especially in early stages.
- Try finger foods and sensory favorites like ice cream and water-rich fruit.
- Adapt as they progress. Use high-contrast plates early, then switch to bowls and spoons in the mid-stage. Focus on softer foods and hydration in later stages.

title: Fryeburg football edges Mt. Blue in B North battle
text:
FARMINGTON — Fryeburg Academy quarterback Marcus Sutton and his brother, Darryl, acknowledge they have a special connection. It helped the Raiders earn a key victory on Friday night.
Marcus threw two touchdown passes to Darryl, and Fryeburg held on for a 14-13 victory in a Class B North game when Mt. Blue failed on a 2-point conversion attempt with 1:45 left.
“I just trust (Darryl),” said Marcus. “I just put all my faith into him and he’s down there somewhere.”
Added Darryl: “He’s my brother, we got great chemistry. We’ve been playing sports with each other for a long time, so I’m not surprised, and just can’t wait for the rest of the season.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
The Cougars (2-5) made a defensive stop early when Jakob Corey recovered a Fryeburg fumble. Karter Meader also recovered a fumble on the Raiders’ third drive.
Mt. Blue took the lead with just over five minutes left in the second quarter. A long punt return by Cannon Smith and a couple penalties against Fryeburg (3-4) set up a 5-yard touchdown run by Dillon Gray.
The Sutton brothers connected with just over two minutes left in the first half, but the extra point was blocked.
In the third quarter, Darryl Sutton caught a 24-yard TD pass, and Conner Keaten caught a 2-point conversion pass to give the Raiders the lead.
Gray scored on a 2-yard run in the fourth quarter, but the Cougars threw an incomplete pass on the conversion attempt.
Mt. Blue forced Fryeburg to punt, and when the snap went awry, the Cougars had the ball at the Fryeburg 7 with 28 seconds to play, but they were out of timeouts and were unable to score.
UNSUNG HERO
Buk Awe’s rushing was paramount in Fryeburg’s second touchdown drive. He carried the ball seven straight times to start the possession. Two plays later, Darryl Sutton caught his second touchdown pass.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “I think we both tried to give it away. Their team battled, we battled. We both, I think, (have) been struggling in the same (areas) throughout the year, finding ways to lose games, both us and Mt. Blue, and we just were the ones that were lucky enough to win tonight. It wasn’t anything special … we made enough mistakes to lose, but fortunately, we came out with a win.” — Fryeburg coach David Turner
• “What you see is our season. That’s our season. We’ve been in every game besides one, and we just, right now, can’t find the right one … (Fryeburg) played hard. Neither team deserved to lose tonight. I’m sad for my seniors, because they’ve given me everything I ask.” — Mt. Blue coach Craig Collins
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Fryeburg: Marcus Sutton (4 of 9 passing, 75 yards, two touchdowns), Darryl Sutton (two receptions, 53 yards, two touchdowns)
• Mt. Blue: Dillon Gray (two rushing touchdowns)

title: Jury awards $33 million to man hit by falling tree limb while jogging in park
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (KCRA) — A jury awarded a University of California, Davis graduate more than $33 million after a falling tree limb caused a brain injury, finding the city of Sacramento liable.
“It was a nice spring day and I decided to go for a run in McKinley Park,” Michael Flynn said.
Flynn was running in Sacramento’s McKinley Park in April 2020 when a dead tree limb fell 26 feet and struck him.
“I woke up in the hospital about three days later. I was hit on the head so hard that part of my skull had to be removed,” Flynn said.
Flynn, an MIT graduate, was six months away from completing his Ph.D. at UC Davis. He had planned to work in quantum computing. He was left with a traumatic brain injury.
Attorney describes impact on Flynn’s career
“He’s never going to be able to be employed in the same field in the same way that he would have been had this not happened to him,” attorney Jason Sigel said.
Sigel’s law firm filed a lawsuit against the city of Sacramento on Flynn’s behalf.
“The jury returned a verdict finding the city of Sacramento 100% liable for what happened. They found that that limb had been dead long enough for a city to see it and remove it, had they had a reasonable inspection practice,” Sigel said.
A judge awarded Flynn $33.3 million.
“I’m going to face serious limitations the rest of my life. All the things that I had wanted for myself, or many of them at least, are out of reach,” Flynn said.
Flynn said he will be financially stable but will always wonder what he could have achieved.
“It’s unrealistic to imagine that I’ll be able to achieve what I had hoped to before the accident,” Flynn said.
Flynn said he hopes the city takes new measures to maintain its public parks.

title: Brother-in-law recounts man’s final moments on Goliath coaster at Six Flags
text:
COBB COUNTY, Ga. (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — A birthday celebration at Six Flags Over Georgia ended in tragedy Monday when a father was ejected from the Goliath roller coaster and fell to his death, investigators said.
Hassan Kariem had gone to the park with his wife, daughter and niece to celebrate a birthday.
Joshua Nelson is Kariem’s brother-in-law. Nelson said Kariem sat next to his daughter on the ride.
“His last words were to my daughter and they were, ‘This is my favorite ride, I’m so excited to be here,’” Nelson said.
Daughter described seeing restraint come undone
Nelson said his daughter described seeing Kariem lift from his seat as the ride moved before the restraint came undone.
Nelson said his daughter called him crying after she got off the ride.
“She was like, ‘I don’t know where he went,’” he said.
Ride passed inspection in March
The Georgia Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner said the Goliath was last inspected in March and showed no warning signs.
Nelson said the family is awaiting the results of the investigation.
“We’re banding together and once the investigation is done, give him the proper send off,” he said.
Family remembers Kariem as teacher and father
Family members remembered Kariem as a dedicated teacher and father.
“He loved everything about Atlanta. He loved kids. He loved technology,” Nelson said.
Six Flags Over Georgia will reopen Friday. The park said Goliath will remain closed until further notice.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Colder and Breezy Saturday, Sunshine Returns Sunday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Friday. Our latest storm system is beginning to pull away from northern Maine tonight, with lingering rain gradually coming to an end. Colder air will rush back into the region overnight, setting us up for a chilly and breezy Saturday before sunshine and quieter weather return Sunday.
Friday morning brought the first real measurable snow of the season to portions of northern Aroostook County. Madawaska picked up 2.3 inches of snow, while Grand Isle reported 2.1 inches. Farther south, Caribou measured 0.3 inches before warmer air arrived and changed the snow over to rain. Temperatures climbed above freezing across the region during the day Friday, allowing the remaining precipitation to fall primarily as rain.
Rain will continue to taper off this evening as a cold front crosses northern Maine. Behind that front, winds will shift to the northwest and colder air will quickly return. Temperatures will fall into the upper 20s across northwestern Aroostook County, with lower 30s expected around Presque Isle, Caribou and Houlton. Patchy fog will also be possible tonight, especially where rain has recently fallen.
Saturday will feel much different. High temperatures will only reach the mid to upper 30s across northern Aroostook County, including around 39 degrees in Caribou. Presque Isle should reach around 41, with Houlton also near 41. Northwest winds will remain noticeable through the day, generally around 15 to 20 mph across northeastern Aroostook County with gusts approaching 30 mph. Some gusts could reach around 35 mph, which may be enough for a few isolated power outages. A few isolated snow showers will also be possible across northern areas Saturday morning, especially across the North Woods, but widespread precipitation is not expected.
Conditions improve considerably Sunday as high pressure takes control of the region. Sunshine returns, winds become much lighter and temperatures recover slightly. Highs should reach the lower 40s across northern Aroostook County, with mid 40s expected farther south toward Houlton. Sunday night will remain clear and cold, with temperatures falling back into the 20s.
A noticeable warmup arrives Monday. Plenty of sunshine is expected, with temperatures climbing into the mid 50s across much of Aroostook County. Caribou, Presque Isle and Houlton are all forecast to reach around 55 degrees, with a few spots farther north and east approaching the upper 50s. Tuesday looks similarly mild, with highs again reaching the mid to upper 50s.
After Saturday’s chilly high near 39 degrees in Caribou, temperatures rebound to around 43 Sunday, 55 Monday and 57 Tuesday. Another cooler push arrives by the middle of next week, bringing highs back closer to 50 degrees Wednesday and Thursday. The larger story beyond this weekend is the lack of additional storm systems. High pressure is expected to dominate through much of next week, and while a few weak fronts may cross the region, moisture will be limited enough that the National Weather Service expects generally dry weather to continue.
For the latest details on Saturday’s colder temperatures, gusty winds and the stretch of quieter weather ahead, check out the First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Dunlap, LePage clash over health care, costs in final CD2 debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - For the second and final time, Democrat Matt Dunlap met Republican Paul LePage on the debate stage Thursday night.
Hosted by WABI in partnership with WAGM, the candidates for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District went head-to-head on affordability, energy, health care and immigration.
Questions ranged from close-to-home topics like keeping heating affordable and hospital closures to global issues like the Iran War.
Heating costs lead off
As Mainers brace for an incoming winter, candidates were asked what action they would take to provide immediate heating assistance.
Both candidates agreed on fully funding LIHEAP, but discussion quickly pivoted to the Iran War and its impact on fuel affordability.
“I want the war to end as quickly as possible. However, I do not want Iran to get a nuclear weapon. I do not support having any boots on the ground,” LePage said.
Dunlap countered, “We had the nuclear weapon issue well in hand. President Obama negotiated an agreement with the Iranians. President Trump tore it up, and that’s how we got to where we are today. Can we get back to a negotiated settlement? I would hope so.”
Health care clash
Tensions rose when debating health care, as LePage campaigned against Medicaid expansion and Dunlap called for Medicare for All.
“What he’s talking about with PL90 and some of these other issues, if you read it, it’s an all-you-can-eat buffet for the insurance companies. They get to insure who they want to insure, they don’t have to, and they have incredibly expensive rates for people with pre-existing conditions,” Dunlap said.
LePage fired back, “What are you reading? PL90 lowered the premiums by 76%. Matt, you’ve been lying a lot at this campaign.”
When pressed to respond, LePage added, “It’s outrageous. He’s lying.”
Cost of living & fraud accusations
On the topic of cost of living, LePage criticized Dunlap’s efficacy as state auditor for catching fraud.
“He said that there’s no fraud in Maine. Until recently,” LePage said.
Dunlap responded, “Just this year, we prosecuted the largest embezzlement case in Maine history, a procurement card fraud that an individual stole between $2.5 and $4 million, which we caught.”
Social Security sparks spirited exchange
While they found common ground in wanting to raise the income cap for Social Security but not the rates, a spirited debate soon broke out regarding LePage’s verbiage in a press release.
“You said that Social Security was welfare,” Dunlap said.
“I did not say that. I said transfer payments were welfare,” LePage said.
Dunlap pressed, “And you also said that Social Security payments were part of transfer payments.”
“No, I did not say that,” LePage said. “You know, instead of criticizing, why don’t you create some good policy?”
Homelessness & immigration
Afterwards, candidates differed on Maine’s leading cause of homelessness.
“One of the problems we can address is affordable housing,” Dunlap said.
LePage said, “Drug addiction is a big part of it, of homelessness, and mental illness is a big part of homelessness. And to deny that, you’re just not being realistic.”
When asked about whether Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be reformed, abolished, or kept the same, Dunlap and LePage called for strengthening training, transparency and accountability for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Candidates diverged in how to deal with illegal immigration.
“Ending welfare to illegals is really a big deal here in Maine because Maine has become a sanctuary for illegals,” LePage said.
Dunlap said, “We need more immigration judges to move some of these cases along so that people don’t languish for years and years in sort of an unsettled status about whether or not they’re gonna be allowed to stay or not.”
Residency question, closing messages
Later, Dunlap levied LePage’s second residence in Florida as an argument against his commitment to Mainers.
LePage responded, “In the winter months, we go to Florida. I have never been in Florida a whole year. And secondly,” before adding, “And I pay my taxes in Maine.”
To close out the debate, candidates left voters with final messages.
“I will listen to people, I will hold town halls. I’ll always be accountable to you, and I’ll be here for you,” Dunlap said.
LePage closed, “In Congress, I will fight first for lowering taxes, secure borders, protect Social Security and Medicaid despite what my opponent likes to tax, keep men out of women’s sport, and find fraud and corruption, and prosecute all those that we get.”

title: Police officer crashes patrol car into school bus stopped picking up children; 4 sent to hospital
text:
OCALA, Fla. (WCJB/Gray News) - A police officer in Florida has been sent to the hospital after crashing his patrol car into a Marion County school bus Friday morning.
According to the Florida Highway Patrol, troopers responded to a reported crash on Southwest 49th Avenue involving a Gainesville police officer in a marked patrol car that collided with the school bus.
Troopers investigating the crash say the bus was stopped in the southbound lane with lights flashing and the stop sign extended as it prepared to pick up children at a bus stop.
The off-duty officer driving behind the bus failed to stop and crashed into the back of it, authorities said.
Thirteen children were on the bus, and one student was taken to the hospital as a precaution. The bus driver and the bus aide were also taken to the hospital as a precaution.
The Gainesville police officer was taken to the hospital, and troopers say his injuries were “very serious,” but not life-threatening.

title: Goaded on Maine residency, Paul LePage says, 'I'm a snowbird'
text:
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate Paul LePage responded to questions about his Maine residency on the debate stage Thursday.
Democratic challenger Matt Dunlap has questioned whether LePage actually lives in a small apartment above a car rental business in Augusta.
Dunlap raised the subject again during a debate hosted by WABI, prompting an animated response from LePage.
“Yes, I’m a snowbird. At my age I don’t like snow anymore. I don’t ski anymore. I’ve got knee problems, so I don’t ski and I don’t play hockey anymore. So yes, in the winter months, we got to Florida,” he said.
LePage went on to say that he’s never lived in Florida an entire year.
Questions about LePage’s residency have followed him ever since the former two-term governor left office in 2019. He was registered to vote in Florida in 2018 and 2023, a year after he attempted a failed bid for a third term against Democratic Gov. Janet Mills. Last year the Augusta city clerk confirmed that he voted in Maine during the 2024 election.
LePage and Dunlap are locked in an important race that could play a role in determining which party controls the U.S. House next year. Some election prognosticators give LePage the edge in the contest, citing the 2nd District’s right-leaning electorate and because it’s voted three times decisively for President Donald Trump.
However, Democrats have been competitive there. Dunlap hopes to replace retiring U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, who has held the seat since 2018.

title: Trump heads to Kansas to stump for Sen. Marshall ahead of midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is campaigning across the country ahead of the midterms, with stops planned in several states, including one notable visit to a longtime Republican stronghold.
Trump will travel to Wichita, Kan., on Monday. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and Trump won the state in three previous elections.
Trump is campaigning on behalf of incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.). Polling shows Marshall trailing Democrat Adam Hamilton. A recent YouGov poll shows Hamilton leading by three points.
Democrats need to flip four seats to regain control of the Senate. According to CIVIQS polling, Kansas is one of only 10 states where Trump’s approval rating remains above water, at 46%.
After Wichita, Trump will travel to North Carolina and South Carolina on Tuesday and Wednesday, followed by Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday.

title: Maine’s new women’s soccer team unveils name, logo ahead of 2027 debut
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - Maine’s newest women’s soccer team officially has a name.
Maine Wildness was unveiled Thursday as the identity of the state’s new USL W League team, which is scheduled to begin play in May 2027 at Fitzpatrick Stadium.
The team, which is affiliated with the Portland Hearts of Pine, revealed its name and crest during an event at Live at Madrid’s in Portland’s Old Port, where approximately 500 community members got their first looks.
According to the club, the name emerged after months of discussions with supporters and community members. Staff considered more than 300 potential names before selecting Maine Wildness to reflect the state’s natural landscape and the characteristics of Maine women.
“We asked people across Maine what they wanted for this team, and we kept hearing the same response: a love for what we’ve created with Hearts, and a deep desire for something distinct to the women of Maine,” said Gabe Hoffman-Johnson, the club’s founder and chief community officer.
The crest was designed by Portland-based artist Pame Chevez and features imagery inspired by Katahdin, Maine’s waterways and wildflowers. The red Dirigo Heart is also featured, which is a prominent symbol of the men’s team.
Two-time World Cup champion and Olympic gold medalist Michelle Akers has also joined the club as a founding adviser, helping shape the team’s identity and long-term vision.
Gov. Janet Mills proclaimed Thursday as the second-ever “Maine Day of Soccer” in celebration of the new women’s franchise.
“The Hearts of Pine have brought a tremendous amount of pride and energy to Maine during their first two seasons, and I can’t wait to welcome their new women’s team to Portland,” Mills said in a statement Wednesday.
The first “Maine Day of Soccer” came in April 2024 when the men’s Hearts of Pine team launched its name, crest and brand identity.
According to Hoffman-Johnson, the addition of the women’s team has been a vision since the beginning.
“This is a moment we’ve imagined for a long time, and to see it become real with so much support from people across the state is incredibly meaningful,” said Hoffman-Johnson.
Maine Wildness will compete in the USL W League’s Northeast Division. Additional information about coaching staff, players and opponents is expected to be announced in the coming months.

title: This Maine town will vote on a spending cap it can't enforce
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Voters in Shapleigh will weigh whether to impose a cap on local budget increases via an ordinance that will likely lack force.
Petitioners managed to push the town to hold a vote on tying future budget increases to the consumer price index, a federal measure of inflation.
The rural York County town is taking up a version of an old debate in Maine. Two decades ago, anti-tax activists forced three statewide votes on capping taxes, and the Legislature put its own soft limit on towns. These discussions are coming back up at the local level amid growing frustrations in communities of all sizes.
If Shapleigh voters pass the spending cap, it may be largely symbolic. Only charter amendments can force a town council or select board to heed a spending cap, according to Kate Dufour, a lobbyist for the Maine Municipal Association. Shapleigh lacks a formal charter, instead relying on a list of ordinances.
“Just as one Legislature cannot bind a future Legislature, absent a charter provision, one town meeting cannot bind another,” she said. “If a town enacted a spending cap via an ordinance or warrant article, a future town meeting could simply ignore it.”
A handful of towns have passed charter provisions to bind their budget increases to the cost of living, including Bradley and Bath. Bradley, which has used the cap since 1996, explicitly allows its council to override the limit, which it has occasionally done over the years.
“It’s a great tool,” Bradley Town Manager Melissa Doane said, adding she believes it’s important “to have the flexibility to override it when there’s situations that occur that you can’t really control.”
Shapleigh’s proposed ordinance lacks an override clause. Even if the voluntary cap is followed, it might have limited effect in Shapleigh. Just like all other Maine cities and towns, it must pay the county and school taxes that are assessed by other elected bodies.
“We can only cap ourselves,” Town Administrator Michelle Rumney said.
Rumney said local costs began rising quickly after the pandemic. To ease the burden of rising school costs on taxpayers, the town delayed capital expenditures. Now, those projects are increasingly urgent.
“This past year, we had a significant increase because of a bridge that needs to be repaired, and the town of Shapleigh is not a fan of taking out loans, so that increase came all at once,” she said. “We held back to kind of compensate when the school was going up. It’s a catch-up game now.”
The idea of limiting local tax increases is not new. For nearly three decades, Maine’s property tax fights have swung between the ballot boxes and the State House. They run from anti-tax activist Carol Palesky’s first petition drive in 1996 to the Legislature’s recent repeal of a soft local cap.
Voters rejected the Palesky limit on property taxes in a statewide referendum in 2004. They also turned down a Colorado-style Taxpayer Bill of Rights in 2006 and again in 2009. In between, former Gov. John Baldacci’s 2005 tax reform package created a limit tied to the state’s average personal income growth and a local property value growth factor.
The 2005 cap limited growth only in the share of each town’s tax levy that paid for municipal services, and towns could exceed it if voters approved a separate override. At first, it seemed to work. In its first year, property taxes in towns it covered grew 1.2%, compared with 5.1% and 4.9% in the two years before, according to a state-commissioned University of Maine analysis.
But school and county taxes fell outside the cap, and school costs kept climbing. By the 2009-10 school year, 87% of school districts were over a separate state spending target. Gov. Janet Mills signed a bill repealing the cap in 2024, with opposition from Republicans but support from local officials who said it had become more trouble than it was worth.
“In practice this has created a significant burden on towns like Gray, needlessly requiring excessive amounts of staff time each year and [confusing] voters,” Gray Town Councilor Anne Gass wrote in 2024 testimony.
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: Police officer fired for sharing Flock login with husband, who works for ICE
text:
SAVANNAH, Ga. (WJCL) - Records show a former police officer in Georgia shared her Flock camera login with her husband, who works as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent.
He used the account for nearly 1,000 license plate searches across six states, which mostly involved vehicles registered to Hispanic owners.
Former Savannah police officer Amber Harpe admitted she gave her husband access to the Savannah Police Department’s Flock surveillance system.
“Did you run these flocks?” an investigator asks Harpe in a recording obtained by WJCL.
“I didn’t,” she responded, later confirming it was her husband who did.
Harpe was fired in August, along with five other Savannah Police Department employees, after an internal investigation uncovered Flock misuse.
Four of those employees were later arrested and charged by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation.
Harpe was not among them, and until now, her name had not been publicly identified as one of the employees fired.
Now WJCL has obtained internal records and interviews in which Harpe and her husband, identified in the interviews as Tyler Harpe, acknowledged that her account was used for ICE-related searches.
“Every name that I ever ran was an ICE target,” Tyler Harpe said in an interview.
An internal investigation found that between January and July, Amber Harpe’s account was used to conduct 983 searches involving 97 license plates.
The searches spanned six states, including Florida, Georgia, New Jersey, Maryland, North Carolina and South Carolina, with South Carolina accounting for 788 of those Flock searches.
Investigators found that most of the registered owners of the vehicles searched were Hispanic.
“I asked her if I could have her Flock login, and she asked what I was going to be using it for,” Tyler Harpe said. “And I told her that once we had already developed target packages for people that had arrest warrants, it would be easier while we’re out on the street to be able to locate them.”
Amber Harpe confirmed that her husband, an ICE agent, did not have access to Flock.
“They don’t have flock. That’s surprising. They don’t have access to Flock,” an investigator said.
“No one really wants to work with them, sir,” Amber Harpe responded.
Further records obtained by WJCL show Savannah police share their Flock data with more than 1,700 agencies, but ICE is not listed as one.
“I’m hoping that, you know, nothing too bad comes out on this as far as it just being a policy violation. But, I mean, the tool actually helped our agency, like, get people off the street,” Tyler Harpe said.
Amber Harpe initially appealed her termination, but later apparently withdrew her appeal.

title: 24th annual Cans for a Cure raises $60.9K for Maine Cancer Foundation
text:
24th annual Cans for a Cure raises $60,932 for Maine Cancer Foundation
The 24th annual Cans for a Cure raised $60,932.60 for the Maine Cancer Foundation. The collection drive was held Wednesday through Friday outside the Maine Mall in South Portland.
Donations were dropped off at the collection site on Gorham Road near Jordan's Furniture, where WHOM and WBLM were broadcasting live inside a tent. WBLM joined WHOM as a first-time partner for this year's event.
Following their live radio broadcasts, WHOM's morning hosts, Lizzy Snyder and Chris Sedenka, spent time driving around Maine to collect donations in what they have dubbed "the can van." Sedenka said, "We've been on the road the last couple of days meeting folks, going to businesses, going to residences, and you hear so many stories. You really understand why this is so important to keep going."
And when Snyder was asked why she wanted to bring the event back, she said, "Because we still need more money. Because there's still a fight to fight. Because our neighbors and our moms and our cousins and our sisters and the people we love closest are still fighting cancer. Sadly, it costs a lot of money just for one person to go and get treatment."
The Maine Cancer Foundation's executive director, Ray Ruby, spoke about that cost too. MCF has seen a high demand for requests for assistance with transportation and lodging on top of the work it does to promote cancer screenings and prevention.
Ruby said, "The money raised here today will go to help support Mainers all across Maine and all 16 counties. ... It's everywhere in this state."
With this year's Cans for a Cure now complete, MCF is looking ahead to other fundraising projects, including the 20th annual Tri for a Cure coming up in July 2027.

title: Farmington superintendent says private employers drawing some staff away

FARMINGTON — Regional School Unit 9 has lost about 10 employees to private-sector jobs over the past year and continues to face staffing shortages, particularly in special education, Superintendent Christian Elkington said.
In his October report to the school board, Elkington said private employers offering more attractive hourly wages are most often what draws employees away. In an Oct. 14 email, he said the district typically has 10 to 15 vacant positions, representing about 2% to 3% of its workforce.
“We have lost about ten staff in the last year to the private sector,” Elkington said.
He identified special education as the hardest area to staff, affecting both professional and support positions.
Despite the vacancies, Elkington said all student programs remain operational, with existing staff and administrators taking on additional responsibilities.
“All programs are servicing students through the sharing of responsibilities by current program staff or admin filling in where they can,” he said. “Our staff are working incredibly hard to overcome openings while we work to advertise and fill them.”
The RSU 9 board approved hiring additional support staff in special education and regular education to address increased needs in district schools and programs.
Elkington said the number of vacancies fluctuates throughout the school year as the district continues recruiting employees.

title: New England's having an 'elite' year, but there's fall foliage elsewhere, too
text:
CONCORD, N.H. (AP) — Kyle Cotner knew nothing about fall foliage when he trolled his White House colleagues in 2007, telling them he was an expert despite having grown up in Florida.
When autumn rolled around, he kept up the bit, sending out weekly newsletters with foliage statistics and information to a handful of co-workers. Today, he has mastered complex mapping systems, calls himself “Leaf Daddy” and owns The Foliage Report, a website that tracks fall color from coast to coast.
Thus, he was speaking with actual authority last week when he said 2026 has been a spectacular year for foliage in New England.
“I’ve been doing this for almost 20 years, and this is the best I’ve seen of New England in that time,” he said. “2020 was a very good year, but this one seems elite to me.”
New England had adequate rain through the spring and summer, plus warm days and cool nights heading into fall, but that wasn’t the case elsewhere, he said.
Extreme drought conditions stressed trees in Colorado, for example, leading to a quick and lackluster foliage season. Aspens in Wyoming, Montana and Idaho aren’t as golden this year, he said. But Utah is a bright spot.
“They got enough rainfall in that area,” he said. “You basically want an average amount of precipitation to really bring out the most majestic and colorful leaves.”
Fall foliage: The last supper for trees
Fall foliage is all about trees preparing for winter, according to experts at the University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension.
Leaves exist to provide food for the tree. They absorb sunlight through a green pigment called chlorophyll, and that energy is used to convert water and carbon dioxide from the air into glucose, a type of sugar. As days shorten, the tree stops making food, allowing orange and yellow pigments that have been there all along to be unmasked. When sunny days are followed by cold nights, sugars get trapped in leaves, producing red pigments.
Eventually, the layer of cells between a twig and a leaf weakens, allowing leaves to be blown down during wind and rain. The timing varies widely by location. According to Cotner’s research, foliage season starts in Alaska in mid-August and ends in Florida in late December. Hawaii is the only U.S. state without fall foliage, he said.
Leaf peepers share their perspective
For Kirk Giglio, leaf peeping provides an escape from his day job as a nurse in a cardiac and stroke unit of a Connecticut hospital. A photographer who frequently chases storms as well, he is used to studying maps and forecasts, and was hopeful by early September that this would be a good year. A recent trip to Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont with his fiancee confirmed it.
“I was just really kind of blown away,” he said, describing sunrise hikes and fog lifting to reveal vibrant colors in New Hampshire’s Crawford Notch and elsewhere. Though some spots were packed with tourists, he still found plenty of secluded and stunning scenery.
“The more I travel, the more I realize how much we take for granted up here,” he said. “In a world that is so modern and gray with these corporate, soulless colors that we see everywhere, the trees are one of the last things that make color anymore, so it’s nice to just observe, especially in a good year like this.”

title: Letter with suspicious substance sent to Sen. Collins' office in Portland
text:
Letter with suspicious substance sent to Sen. Susan Collins' office in Portland
Spokesperson for the Senate Appropriations Committee, which Collins chairs, says a note was also sent to the senator's D.C. office
Letter with suspicious substance sent to Sen. Susan Collins' office in Portland
Spokesperson for the Senate Appropriations Committee, which Collins chairs, says a note was also sent to the senator's D.C. office
A spokesperson for the Senate Appropriations Committee, which is chaired by Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), informed Maine's Total Coverage that the senator's office in Portland received a letter with a suspicious substance on Friday.
The spokesperson said the letter was intercepted and that no one was injured. According to the spokesperson, law enforcement is investigating the incident.
WMTW's sky cam in Portland captured video Friday afternoon showing a fire engine and an ambulance stopped on Middle Street near Fidelity Investments, which is located at 190 Middle St. The address for Collins' Portland office is 200 Middle St.
"Thank you to the Portland police, the Portland Fire Department, the hazmat team, and the FBI for their quick and courageous response," Katie Brown, Collins' chief of staff, said in a statement to Maine's Total Coverage. "This was the fourth attack targeting Sen. Collins' office or home in the past two months. Despite escalating political rhetoric and harassment, we will continue our work for the people of Maine."
The Appropriations Committee spokesperson also said that a note was sent to Collins' office in Washington, D.C.
On Thursday, The Associated Press received a statement from the FBI that said the bureau and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service were "investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices."
"Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the FBI said in its statement to the AP. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters."
The office of Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, a Delaware Democrat, said in a statement that it was sent a letter with a "suspicious substance" that was intercepted by Capitol Police. Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California said the Postal Service intercepted a suspicious package before it reached his office. And Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said postal inspectors intercepted a suspicious piece of mail addressed to her New York City office.
Mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation this week of election offices in at least two states, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder intended for its office and noted that similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said their election offices either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said in a statement that it received a letter and the white powder enclosed in it was not hazardous, according to tests. "Let this be very clear: this incident will not shake us," Wisconsin elections administrator Meagan Wolfe said.
Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.
