title: Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya reportedly set to star in ‘Fourth Wing’ TV series
text:
Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya reportedly set to star in ‘Fourth Wing’ TV series
Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya are set to star in the small-screen adaptation of Rebecca Yarros’ hit romantasy novel “Fourth Wing” when it lands on Prime Video, industry outlets reported Thursday.
According to Deadline, Variety and The Hollywood Reporter, McGregor, who is the daughter of Scottish actor Ewan McGregor and appears in Prime Video’s mystery drama “We Were Liars,” will play protagonist Violet Sorrengail — an unassuming scholar who hopes to graduate as a historian but is forced to become a dragon rider by her ruthless army general mother.
German actor Sakraya, who starred alongside Anthony Hopkins in Peacock’s Roman gladiator saga “Those About to Die,” will reportedly take on the role of Xaden Riorson. As fearsome as he is ambitious, Xaden is determined to join the ranks as an elite dragon rider.
In Yarros’ novel, the pair are the antithesis of one another, making for a classic enemies-to-lovers arc as they battle their way through the tyrannous Basgiath War College, where there are only two ways to leave: graduate or die.
CNN has reached out to Amazon MGM Studios, which has yet to confirm the rumored casting.
Published in 2023, “Fourth Wing” is the first of Yarros’ Empyrean series, which is set to run to five books. So far, three volumes have been published — selling millions of copies worldwide.
Book lovers took to the internet Friday to have their say on the rumored castings.
“I’m squinting and I can kind of see the vision,” widely followed social media book reviewer Kaila Anttila, who posts as Kaila Books, said in an Instagram video. “Prime … they never let us down,” she added.
Actor and creator Joel Wood also weighed in: “Violet’s not blonde,” Wood said, pointing at an image of McGregor sporting a short blonde cut.
“But I know we can fix that,” he added, before explaining, “I’m not loving it, but I’m not hating it.”
Others expressed greater excitement at the prospect of McGregor and Sakraya stepping into the roles.
“I know I speak for many people when I say: The biggest congratulations to these two,” Nicole Holleman, one of the hosts of the Fantasy Fangirls Podcast, said in a video — before squealing excitedly.
She followed up with another short video encouraging fans to be “open-minded” about casting.

title: The Latest: Trump will rally Georgia Republicans despite party divisions in the battleground state
text:
President Donald Trump’s midterm campaign blitz arrives in Georgia on Friday for a rally with top Republican candidates in a state that has long been the epicenter of the president’s false claims about election fraud.
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia defended her legal background and justified her truncated inaugural briefing on Thursday as she navigates a rocky first week as the president’s chief spokeswoman. Zacharia said she did not have time to prepare for her first briefing on Tuesday fully and that keeping it short was always the plan because Trump would field questions from journalists later that morning.
Alaska’s major U.S. Senate candidates clashed over the Iran war, soaring consumer prices and personal credibility Thursday during a high-stakes debate in a contest that will play into control of the closely divided chamber.
The Latest:
Trump wants the midterms to be all about himself. Judging by the ads, Democrats are happy to oblige
President Donald Trump says he wants voters to pretend that he’s on the ballot in this year’s midterm elections.
His rivals are doing their best to help his case.
Democratic candidates and their allies have spent more than $163 million since Sept. 1 on television advertising that mentions the Republican president, according to an Associated Press analysis of data from AdImpact, which charts media spending.
That includes airing ads that reference Trump on broadcast, cable and streaming nearly 180,000 times, the data shows. Republicans, meanwhile, have run ads that talk about the president just 16,000 times, at an estimated cost of $11 million, over the same period.
It’s a noticeable silence about the party’s dominant yet unpopular leader.
Many of the Democrats’ ads accuse Republican opponents of siding with the president over voters, particularly on issues like tariffs and the Iran war, which they blame for jacking up costs.
Alaska Senate candidates express support for Ukraine, disagree with Russian diesel deal
Democrat Mary Peltola said the U.S. should be doing all it can to help support Ukraine and not bolster Russia. The Alaska U.S. Senate candidate said a Trump administration plan to buy diesel from Russia was “foolish.”
“I do not think there’s any way, shape or form the U.S. should be buying anything from Russia,” she said.
Peltola made the comments during a late Thursday debate with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Sullivan said he’s been “one of the strongest supporters of Ukraine” before pivoting to national security and saying Democrats were always “cutting our military, undermining readiness.”
He said he opposed buying diesel from Russia.
Alaska US Senate candidates agree a third term for Trump isn’t allowed
The two major candidates in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race agreed Thursday that President Donald Trump is not allowed to seek a third term.
The question arose in a debate between Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman. Some people were wearing or selling T-shirts and sweatshirts emblazoned with “Trump 2028 (Rewrite the Rules)” at Trump’s rally for Sullivan in Wasilla.
The candidates were asked if they’d support a third term. Both said no.
Peltola said the law calls for two terms. Sullivan, a former state attorney general and Trump ally, said a third term would be unconstitutional.
Sullivan swipes at Peltola’s use of notes in Alaska US Senate debate
Alaska Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan questioned the use of notes during a debate late Thursday by his main opponent in his reelection bid.
Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, referred numerous times to a stack of notes during the one-hour debate, seemingly reading from them at times. At one point, Sullivan asked: “We weren’t supposed to get these questions beforehand, were we?”
The moderator said neither had received any questions in advance. Peltola said she was prepared.
After the debate, Sullivan brought the issue up again. “You can’t cue card your way to the U.S. Senate,” he told reporters.
Sullivan has tried to characterize Peltola as ineffective during her time in the U.S. House.
The Peltola campaign released a statement saying Sullivan had “copied” answers from Peltola in a prior meeting, but “this debate he got mad that she was too prepared.”
Talarico compares his campaign to the biblical David after GOP invests over $158M against him
At a packed rally in Texas on Thursday, James Talarico compared his U.S. Senate campaign to David — who fought Goliath — as the Democrat faces more than $158 million in outside spending by Republican leadership and the world’s richest man, Elon Musk.
Talarico told rallygoers under bright lights that David may not have had Goliath’s strength, but he had a slingshot.
“You are my slingshot,” he continued, without mentioning Musk or the other spending against him. “We are going up against our own Goliaths.”
The description falls in line with Talarico’s past rhetoric painting politics not as right versus left, but the ultrawealthy versus everyone else, as he tries to become the first Democrat to win statewide in over 30 years. Talarico’s own campaign has raised record amounts of money in one of the nation’s more expensive and competitive Senate races.
The national conversation around Talarico’s campaign has evolved over the past months. Initially, the state lawmaker was considered just the latest of several Democratic candidates over the past years who gave the party hope of flipping Texas, only for that hope to deflate come Election Day.
Alaska’s Sullivan and Peltola clash over Iran and high prices in testy Senate debate
Alaska’s major U.S. Senate candidates clashed over the Iran war, soaring consumer prices and personal credibility Thursday during a high-stakes debate in a contest that will play into control of the closely divided chamber.
Two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan said the war needs to end soon, and he wants the Strait of Hormuz to open and a deal to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, said an agreement is “so far out of sight” and lamented the deaths of 20 military personnel.
“This war is driving up our energy bills and hurting Alaskans with no end in sight,” she said.
Sullivan said the best way to bring down energy costs “is to produce more Alaskan energy by and for Alaskans.”
The debate followed contours of Senate contests around the country, with Peltola blaming the Trump administration for rising gas and consumer prices and pulling back from traditional alliances around the globe, while Sullivan warned that Democratic leadership in Congress would undercut the military and curb domestic energy production.
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia defends her legal background and short first briefing
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia on Thursday defended her legal background and justified her truncated inaugural briefing as she navigates a rocky first week as the president’s chief spokeswoman.
Zacharia sat down for an interview with conservative media. She told the conservative Human Events outlet that she did not have time to get fully prepared ahead of her first briefing on Tuesday and that it was always the plan to keep it short because President Donald Trump would field questions from journalists later that morning.
“It was absolutely my goal to keep it short, considering he is his own best spokesperson, and he would love — and does love — gaggling with the media as he goes to Marine One,” Zacharia said. “So I wanted to give ample deference and not barge into his time.”
The initial briefing materials were given to Zacharia on Monday evening, then completed Tuesday at 8 a.m., less than two hours before she would appear before the White House press corps. She had been up since 3 a.m. preparing, Zacharia said.
Trump will rally Georgia Republicans despite party divisions in battleground state
Donald Trump’s midterm campaign blitz arrives in Georgia on Friday for a rally with top Republican candidates in a state that has long been the epicenter of the president’s false claims about election fraud.
In Dalton, the population center of conservative northwest Georgia, Trump will appear with Senate candidate Mike Collins and gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson as part of the White House effort to boost Republican enthusiasm in an election that could reshape the final years of Trump’s second presidency.
“President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party,” said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle.
Yet unlike some of Trump’s recent trips to solidly Republican states — Alabama, Montana, Tennessee — Georgia is a critical battleground. That means Jackson, a billionaire businessman, and Collins, a two-term congressman, need more than Trump stalwarts to defeat their respective Democratic opponents, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Sen. Jon Ossoff.

title: Greely football slams door on Hermon’s unbeaten start
text:
CUMBERLAND — Unbeaten Hermon High had gaudy defensive statistics and a lopsided scoring margin going into a Class C showdown against Greely.
By the end of Friday’s game, it was Greely’s defense that proved superior, shutting out the Hawks in the second half.
Meanwhile, Greely senior quarterback Luke Piper made enough big plays to offset three poor-decision interceptions. It added up to a decisive 28-14 win for Greely on Senior Night, leaving both two teams with 6-1 records.
In its first six games, Hermon allowed 5.3 points per game and had an overall scoring advantage of 258-32.
“We know we’re a better team than them. We’re better conditioned than them. Things hadn’t been going our way and we just had to prove it to them,” said Greely defensive tackle/right guard Luke Cline.
Defensive linemen Cline, Jackson Justice (two sacks) and James Tyll (one sack) applied heavy pressure on Hermon quarterback Ethan Curtis after clogging the running lanes for standout back Sam Hopkins.
Curtis went into the game completing 63.9% of his passes. He was held to 6 of 18 passing for 62 yards. Hopkins, who now has 995 rushing yards on the season, gained 72 yards on 18 carries after averaging 14.9 yards per carry through the first six games.
BIG STOP
Cline, a junior, may have made the play of the game in the third quarter. On the first two plays of the second half, Piper ran off left tackle for 34 yards and off right tackle for a 23-yard touchdown to put Greely ahead 21-14 after the third of Jack Carthy’s four point-after kicks.
Hermon had responded and moved 55 yards to the Greely 10, where it faced fourth-and-1.
Cline got free and was right in the hole, where he stuffed Hopkins for a 1-yard loss.
“To be honest, they just didn’t block me,” Cline said. “I was expecting a block to come and I was there, and I could see the guy coming right at me and it was like, thank you very much, you know?”
Hermon coach Kyle Gallant said that missed assignment was indicative of what hurt his team in the second half and where the Hawks will have to improve, especially next week against league-leader Leavitt (7-0).
“Second half, we had some missed rules, some missed assignments,” Gallant said. “When you’re playing a Greely, playing a Leavitt, playing … Wells, the predominant southern teams that have been powerhouses for years, you can’t do that stuff. That’s the learning curve we’re in right now.”
CONVERTING
Greely made the defensive stand even better by going 89 yards in 12 plays. Justice capped it with a 1-yard run for a two-score lead. A Piper-to-Justice jump pass off a rollout to the right went for 37 yards on third-and-9.
Piper’s throwing set up every score except for his 23-yard touchdown run — three TDs for Greely and both of Hermon’s scores.
In the first half, Rocky Axelsen turned a wide receiver screen into a 46-yard gain, setting up a Noah Allen 1-yard run. Later, an 18-yard slant pass to Tyll as time was running down in the first half got the ball to the 1, and Piper ran it in from there.
Hermon’s Hopkins and Dunton each had second-quarter interceptions — thrown basically right to them — and turned into long returns. Hopkins went 48 yards to the 2 and scored two plays later. Dunton’s interception return was 49 yards to the Rangers 16. Curtis connected with Tyler Corson from the 10 for a 14-7 lead.
UNSUNG HEROES
Several of Greely’s 13 seniors are playing football for the first time. Two made big plays. Ethan Kittredge had an interception, the first Curtis has thrown this season.
Axelsen’s catch-and-run to set up Greely’s first score was impressive. So, too, was the job he did at cornerback, blanketing Hermon’s top target, Dunton, and holding him to one catch for 11 yards.
STATISTICS
• Hermon: Sam Hopkins (18 carries, 72 yards, 1 TD; one interception), Ethan Curtis (6 of 18 passing, 62 yards, 1 TD, 1 interception)
• Greely: Luke Piper (18 carries, 145 yards, 2 TDs; 6 of 12 passing, 136 yards, 3 interceptions), Jackson Justice (2 sacks; 3 catches, 69 yards; 8 carries, 27 yards, 1 TD), Noah Allen (11 carries, 61 yards, 1 TD)

title: Why dementia makes it so hard to eat — and what caregivers can do
text:
(Aging Untold) — As dementia progresses, eating can become one of the hardest daily tasks. The brain can lose its ability to recognize hunger, identify food or remember how to use a fork.
We are breaking down why eating becomes so complicated and what caregivers can do to help.
The brain’s signals get disrupted
Dementia can disrupt the part of the brain that controls hunger, thirst and appetite signaling — the hypothalamus — Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. And the process of getting food to the mouth is complex, requiring motor skills and sensory response.
“It’s not that they don’t want to eat. They may not know, because now you have mixed signals, or they may have the senses but it’s not working, so it’s a disconnect,” Rogers said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said that disconnect means a loved one isn’t choosing to skip meals. Their brain has changed and we are expecting them to perform as they always have.
“Maybe my brain hasn’t told my stomach it’s hungry and it’s been 24 hours,” Cradduck said. “Or maybe it told it it’s hungry, but I don’t know what that feeling is anymore. And oh, I figured out what the feeling is, but I sure as heck don’t know what this is for. And you gave me a fork. Why would you give me a fork?”
Rogers compared the experience to a familiar daily drive suddenly filled with detours.
“You go the same route every day, right? And you know where you’re going,” Rogers said. “But one day you go and there’s a whole bunch of detours.”
Watch, observe and simplify the setting
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke described working with a client in a memory care unit who had lost 15 pounds. The woman had macular degeneration, was hard of hearing and had memory impairment, yet staff were placing a plate, fork and knife in front of her and expecting her to eat.
“I think the first thing I would want people to do is just watch, observe and see how are they doing?” O’Rourke said. “Look at the contrast between the plate and the placemat. How much clutter is around the table? ... How many flower tablecloths have I seen in communities and it can be very confusing.”
O’Rourke said what works can also change by stage.
“You have the early, middle and late stage. ... Maybe the contrast plates work in the first stage early on, and then the next day it’s not working,” O’Rourke said. “They look at that special utensil, and they don’t know what to do.”
Abilities can come and go — and that’s not manipulation
Cradduck said families often misread a loved one’s inconsistent ability to eat independently as intentional behavior.
“People think that if I did it yesterday, I should be able to do it today,” Cradduck said. “Well maybe I did it yesterday, I don’t know how to do it today, but tomorrow those neural pathways hit again and I can do it tomorrow.”
That inconsistency is frequently misunderstood, Cradduck said.
“Too many families and too many people oftentimes see that as, they’re manipulating me. They did it yesterday — watch, they’ll be able to do it tomorrow,” Cradduck said. “That goes with so many things with dementia.”
She said families need to figure out what changed that is keeping the loved one from eating.
O’Rourke described a strategy once used in a memory care unit, known as “the drive-by,” for a resident who couldn’t tolerate sitting at a table.
“You’d just walk down the hall and you’d just hand him a sandwich and then keep walking,” O’Rourke said. “We stopped having him sit at the table because it just didn’t work for him. You have to figure out creatively what’s going to work.”
O’Rourke added that caregivers should stay open to sudden changes in taste as well.
“If they used to like a ham sandwich, and then all of a sudden they don’t, and they never would eat roast beef, and now they want to eat roast beef — don’t be opposed to any change in their taste,” she said.
Watch for swallowing problems
Rogers said swallowing difficulty is one of the most serious concerns during mealtimes.
“Make sure that you’re watching the swallowing, because a lot of times that’s a big thing,” Rogers said. “They’re not eating, or they’re eating but they can’t swallow.”
Swallowing trouble carries serious risk, including aspiration, Rogers said.
She also suggested getting ahead of the issue early with a baseline swallowing study, which a physician would order.
“I think it’s not a bad idea, as a baseline, because we know how the progression is, to go out and have maybe a baseline swallowing study,” Rogers said.
Practical strategies that can help
Cradduck said finger foods, texture changes and flexibility can make meals easier.
“Finger foods are great. You can try different utensils,” Cradduck said.
“Stop worrying so much about the perfect diet. This is about nutrition and hydration. It doesn’t mean that we’ve got to have a salad and a three- or four-course meal. This means I’m getting nutrition into your system,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said options that tend to work well include finger foods, fruit with high water content, pudding, smoothies, milkshakes and smaller, more frequent meals
She said caregivers should avoid judging a loved one’s eating behavior.
“Just know that they really can’t help it. It is brain damage,” Ambrose said. “It’s not like you’re going to instruct them. So just give them a break. Have some grace. Don’t harass them to eat.”
Cradduck said sitting beside — not across from — a loved one can encourage eating through mimicry.
“If you’re sitting next to someone and we’re going to share a meal... I’m going to set the same plate beside you,” Cradduck said. “You know what you see me do, you’re going to mimic, right? That is one of the greatest ways for a caregiver to get someone to start to eat.”
Ambrose also pointed to speech pathologists as a resource as well.
“I love the work they do, but their title is so confusing,” she said. “They can really help with swallowing and figuring things out.”
Key takeaways
- Dementia disrupts appetite signals and motor planning, making it harder for the brain to recognize hunger, identify food or remember how to use utensils.
- Simplify the table setting. High-contrast plates, reduced clutter and fewer distracting patterns can help, especially in early stages.
- Try finger foods and sensory favorites like ice cream and water-rich fruit.
- Adapt as they progress. Use high-contrast plates early, then switch to bowls and spoons in the mid-stage. Focus on softer foods and hydration in later stages.

title: High school QB dismissed from team after calling audible, 12 teammates suspended for supporting him
text:
MESA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A football player in Arizona says his high school playing career is over after being dismissed from the team following a dispute over a play call.
Gunner Brewer, a senior at Desert Ridge High School, said the situation unfolded on the final play of the game two weeks ago when he was quarterbacking the team.
“Basically called the play, trusted my running back behind me who scored a touchdown, definitely was rolling with him,” Brewer said. “The play was originally called for me, but I definitely wanted him to run the ball and get us the first down to basically seal the game.”
Brewer said changing the play at the line was something he had been allowed to do under his previous offensive coordinator, who was fired at the end of September.
The senior quarterback said after the game, head coach Miles Smith asked to speak with him.
Brewer said Smith told him he had disrespected him, and Brewer was cut from the team.
The following Monday, Brewer said 12 other players told coaches they disagreed with the decision. Those players were suspended for the rest of the season, Brewer said.
“They definitely had my back, and I have theirs 100 percent,” Brewer said. “When they did that, I stood right by them.”
Brewer said earlier this season he was late to a meeting because of car trouble and sat out a quarter, but he felt the dismissal was extreme.
“It’s definitely sad,” Brewer said. “Obviously wanted to come off this field with a win on my senior night, but just want to stay humble. And I know that God’s got a plan for me in the future.”
Since his dismissal, Brewer said Smith has only communicated with his mother, except for last week’s game against Ramon, when Brewer said he was told not to be around the team.
“The only word he said to me was when I tried to go help out last week’s game … [he] told me to get out … Don’t go near the field house. Don’t go near the players," Brewer said.
It wasn’t made clear whether there were any other disciplinary issues leading up to the dismissal.
Officials with Desert Ridge High School did not immediately return a request for comment regarding the situation.

title: Before Maine Wildness had a name, it was an inspiration
text:
Zoe Durrant waited. Standing dead center, in front of the stage, next to her father, Colin, the 12-year-old was all eager anticipation. This team is potential personified. It can show his daughter and other girls around Maine a pathway to the possible, Colin Durrant said.
This soccer team, the Maine Wildness, is for Zoe.
“I’m really excited,” she said. “I think it will be an inspiration.”
On Thursday evening, the Maine Wildness name was revealed in front of hundreds of fans crammed into Live at Madrid’s for the announcement. The women’s soccer team, which will play in the USL W League beginning next spring, didn’t have a name or a roster, but it already had an enthusiastic fan base.
In June, the team needed just an hour to sell 5,000 season ticket deposits, with 4,400 of those now Wildness season ticket holders.
Jessica Mayhew of Saco is one of those season ticket holders. She arrived at the party early, wearing her Hearts of Pine scarf. As she waited for the announcement, she chatted with Sarah Robble of Kennebunk.
“It’s great to have the ladies represented,” Robble said.
Robble wasn’t able to get in on season tickets. They sold so fast. Don’t worry, Mayhew said. We’ll get you to some games.
“I grew up playing soccer. We’ve got some young girls who play here. This gives them something to strive for,” Mayhew said.
The Maine Wildness is for Mayhew and Robble.
According to data from the National Federation of State High School Associations, close to 3,000 girls played high school soccer in Maine last fall. There are a dozen women’s college soccer teams in Maine, including the University of Maine, which has won three America East titles to advance to the NCAA Division I tournament.
The Maine Wildness is for them.
The Wildness had two supprt groups before it had a name. The Halyard takes its name from the line that raises a ship’s sail so it can catch wind and go. The Lightkeepers strive to illuminate and promote girls and women’s soccer across Maine.
BrynWynne, 13, and her father, Patrick, were among the first in line for Wildness merch when the pop-up store opened shortly after the team name and crest were revealed. Bryn wore a Lightkeepers T-shirt that states succinctly what the group is about.
“Women’s soccer makes Maine better,” the shirt reads. Throughout the crowd at Live at Madrid’s on Thursday, it was a popular wardrobe choice. Bryn doesn’t play soccer, but she has a lot of friends who do. When she supports Maine Wildness, she supports them.
“(Soccer) has really grown on me,” Bryn said.
The Maine Wildness is for Bryn and all her friends who play the game.
Teila Norris-Julien of Biddeford wore a Halyard T-shirt and talked up the new team to everyone she met. This team is something both her daughter, Gabbi, 11, and son, Hayden, 10, can cheer on and draw inspiration from.
“It’s something they can look up to. These people are in our community. Kids can watch them play and think, they did this, maybe I can,” Norris-Julien said.
The Maine Wildness is for Gabbi and Hayden, and their mom.
The Wildness name evokes the underlying hardscrabbleness of Maine. The coast is rocky. The mountains aren’t the highest peaks, but they’re daunting. The name implies fighting for every scrap you can get against an environment not inclined to hand over anything easily.
It doesn’t immediately roll off the tongue, but it fits. Remember, Hearts of Pine had to grow on a lot of fans, too.
When the Maine Wildness plays, it will be in front of a packed Fitzpatrick Stadium, in front of a loyal fan base that knew it was waiting for something, and that something now has a name.
The Maine Wildness is for all of us.

title: Is Maine’s foliage peaking later as falls get warmer?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
While satellite models show New England’s foliage arriving a week later than it did 70 years ago, Maine’s weekly forest ranger maps reveal a climate system in flux, with peak dates swung wildly between early drought-induced leaf drops and warm, delayed autumns.
This shifting schedule is watched closely by Maine residents, for whom the vibrant crimson and gold canopy is cherished, and by leaf peepers who pump nearly a half-billion dollars in economic activity into Maine’s tourism economy each fall.
How leaves change color every autumn is dictated by plant biology.
As the days grow shorter and cool temperatures arrive, deciduous trees stop pumping out green chlorophyll, allowing underlying yellow, gold and red pigments to finally be revealed. However, chlorophyll breakdown is slowed by rising fall temperatures, keeping leaves green into October.
But ecologists say temperature is only one piece of the puzzle. Seasonal foliage timing and color brilliance are also heavily influenced by rainfall, soil moisture and pest outbreaks, which is why year-to-year ranger reports can mask the long-term trends in Maine’s changing foliage.
Comparing weather and climate is akin to mood versus personality. Daily moods can be easily swayed by immediate events, much like short-term weather anomalies. In contrast, a person’s underlying personality is formed gradually over decades, much like long-term climate baselines.
A review of the state forest rangers’ weekly foliage progression reports underscores the year-to-year variability. In 2020, after a severe summer drought, more than half the state’s seven foliage zones peaked in late September. It would be another six years before any zone peaked so early.
Tree stress caused by severe summer droughts often triggers premature browning and leaf drop, creating the appearance of an early peak. Conversely, fungal blights promoted by heavy fall rain and sudden windstorms can denude entire canopies before peak vibrancy.
How can the long-term delay in fall color be confirmed when the ranger reports look so chaotic?
The underlying shift was uncovered by geographer Stephanie Spera through research at Acadia National Park. She used decades of satellite imagery alongside historical diaries and park photos to strip away annual weather noise.
She identified a distinct pattern: Peak foliage at Acadia, which would fall into Maine’s Zone 2 in the statewide fall foliage map, was arriving nine to 10 days later than it did in the 1950s, or about one day later with each passing decade.
Acadia has warmed by 3.4 degrees Fahrenheit over the last century. One out of five plant species documented in the park a century ago are gone. Seven of the park’s 10 most common tree species are expected to decline or possibly even disappear by 2100.
Climate change is driving not just rising temperatures, but several of the other variables that play a role in Maine’s annual foliage show. The future climate will likely see more more droughts and deluges play out in the same calendar year, according to the Maine Climate Council.
Because fall nights are warming across Maine, trees are staying active later in the season. Thus, while year-to-year peak foliage dates remain at the mercy of the fickle weather moods, Maine’s climate personality is predicted to push peak colors deeper into the calendar over time.
Maine’s modern foliage tracking traces back to 1959, when then Forestry Commissioner Austin Wilkins ordered weekly foliage updates from state forest rangers. These early assessments were radioed to state headquarters and manually distributed to local reporters by phone.
In 1996, Maine became the first state to post weekly leaf conditions on the web. Over time, these reports have established a baseline for seasonal environmental tracking and created a marketing tool for the state’s growing leaf-peeping economy.

title: Beers Criteria: The medication list every senior should know about
text:
(Aging Untold) — As we age, our bodies process medicine differently — and a drug that felt fine at 40 can cause problems at 70. Even small details, like whether a pill can be cut, chewed or dissolved, can carry serious consequences for older adults.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down the Beers List, or “Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults,” a tool every family should know about before the next doctor’s visit.
What is the Beers List?
“We’re talking about the geriatric list of medications and their adverse effects on our aging population,” “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “It doesn’t mean that just because that medication’s on there that you can’t take it — it means that it could affect you differently because of the way you metabolize after you age.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said the list, published by the American Geriatrics Society, includes about 100 medications and is updated every three years to reflect new research.
The danger of cutting, crushing or chewing pills
One of the biggest risks families overlook has nothing to do with the medication itself — it’s how it’s taken.
“Can’t tell you how many times I’ve heard, ‘We’ll just crush it and put it in applesauce, it’s easier,’” Cradduck said. “Well, you just gave them a lethal dose of a blood pressure med because that was a time release.”
Cradduck offered a simple rule of thumb: “If a pill is scored, it usually means that you can cut it. But if it’s not scored, I don’t care how good that pill cutter is — you shouldn’t be cutting it, because it’s not distributed equally.”
Even physicians can be caught off guard
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said that this information isn’t always top of mind for doctors outside of geriatric specialties.
“I think that information is not known to a lot of physicians,” Rogers said. “As a surgeon, and seeing people in the office, I really did not know that.”
So ongoing education is essential, she said.
“So when we’re doing all this continuing education, these are some basic things that we need to know, especially since we’re taking care of people of all ages,” she said.
Rogers added that time-release medications deserve extra scrutiny as patients get older.
“Understanding as the aging process, the same way that we treat everybody as they’re aging, we look at all their metabolism — that they do metabolize different,” she said. “And then we haven’t even begun to look at their own genetics, what’s going on there to interfere. So it could be a lot of risk for falling and memory and everything else.”
Don’t let social media cause fear over the Beers List
Cradduck warned that misinformation about the list is causing some older adults to stop taking medications they actually need.
“Don’t listen to the fearmongers that are on social media,” Cradduck said. “They’ll start reading from this and say if your loved one, age 65 or older, is on this medication, they can’t take it. This is causing harm, because we’re seeing a lot of people that aren’t taking the medications that they need.”
Cradduck pointed out that the list isn’t new.
“It’s been out there forever,” she said, and it’s revamped every three years.
Rogers said that the fact that a medication is on the list does not mean you can’t take it.
“It just means it’s a higher risk associated with a certain age,” she said.
How to use the Beers List with your doctor
O’Rourke said lifestyle changes are a good reason to revisit the list with a doctor.
“If you’ve changed your lifestyle, you’re more active, or something’s changed, you really want to make sure that that doctor’s looking at your medicine, looking at the Beers List and adjusting it as you grow older,” she said.
O’Rourke recommends bringing a copy of the list straight to an appointment.
“I like to tell people to make a copy of the list and bring it in to your doctor and just ask your doctor, do you know about this list? Is there anything on here? Look at my medicine and compare the two and see how I’m doing,” she said. “Be a really proactive patient with the list with your physician, especially when you’re older.”
Resource
Key takeaways
- Older bodies process meds more slowly: Bodies change with age and process medications more slowly, so drugs stay in the system longer.
- Ask your doctor. Ask your doctor if they use the Beers List of high-risk medications for seniors to help prevent falls and confusion.
- Review and simplify. Advocate for regular reviews of your medications.

title: Wet Friday in Maine with ice cold winds Saturday
text:
Wet Friday in Maine with ice cold winds Saturday
Rain tapers by afternoon and picks back up this evening, with a cold blast arriving Saturday
Wet Friday in Maine with ice cold winds Saturday
Rain tapers by afternoon and picks back up this evening, with a cold blast arriving Saturday
Rain will spread across Maine early today as a fast-moving storm system tracks through Quebec. The steadiest rain is expected from about 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., with more scattered showers during the afternoon. Rainfall amounts should stay manageable, though clogged storm drains and leaf-covered roads could lead to minor ponding in a few spots.
A warm front lifting through the state may produce fog and scattered showers through mid-afternoon. As a cold front arrives later, winds will shift sharply from the northwest, bringing sudden gusts. A brief rumble of thunder cannot be ruled out in far southwestern areas, but the main change will be the much colder air moving in behind the front.
Saturday turns raw across Maine as northwest winds gust 25 to 35 mph. Coastal highs may struggle to reach the 40s, while many inland and mountain areas stay in the 30s and 40s. Wind chills could hold in the 30s for much of the state. Higher terrain should prepare for winter-like conditions, including snow, strong winds and dangerous wind chills. Anyone heading above 2,500 feet should plan for full winter conditions.
Saturday night brings the coldest air so far this season, with widespread lows in the 20s and freezing temperatures possible even near the coast. Sunshine and milder weather return Sunday, with highs in the low to mid-50s. Dry conditions and highs in the upper 50s and 60s are expected through much of next week, though clear, calm nights could turn quite chilly.

title: Teacher says she thought she was ‘going to die saving my kids’ in deadly elementary school shooting
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — A teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Oregon said she was prepared to die to save her students during a mass shooting that left multiple people dead.
From her classroom window, Kathy Smith said she witnessed the 16-year-old shooter walking into the elementary school with a long gun.
“I just figured today, OK, today is the day that I’m sure every teacher at the school thought, today is the day that I’m going to die saving my kids,” Smith said.
Smith said she immediately called the main office to warn them an active shooter was on school grounds, then hid her students in a corner, hoping the shooter wouldn’t come inside.
“They were so afraid, the looks on their faces, it was really hard to see. I was just trying to calm them down. Some kids were praying, some kids were consoling other kids, but they were doing it quietly because they know you don’t make any noise,” she said.
Bend police said the shooter shot at a person in a vehicle before forcing his way into the school by shooting at locked doors.
The shooting killed a 5-year-old, an 8-year-old, an 11-year-old and one teacher. Another child and a teacher were wounded and taken to a hospital in critical condition.
The 16-year-old shooter was killed by a bystander who police said followed the gunman into the building.
Smith said that person saved countless lives, including her own.
“That person saw something, they did something, and that took its own courage,” Smith said.
Smith said the tragedy is constantly replaying in her head, and she can’t imagine how the close-knit school family will ever be the same.
“I don’t see how, but also in my head I refuse to let somebody tear apart our family even more, because if we don’t return and if we don’t come together, then that person wins,” she said.

title: College football player dies days after being critically injured during game
text:
Oklahoma college football player dies days after being critically injured during game
Southern Nazarene University football player Tyler Ulrich has died after suffering a traumatic injury during a game on Oct. 10, the university announced.
Ulrich, a safety for the team, was injured during an away game and had been hospitalized since the incident.
SNU President Keith Newman said in a statement, “Tyler sustained a traumatic injury during last Saturday's football game. Since that time, he has been in the hospital, continually surrounded by the love, prayers, and presence of his family, teammates, and dear friends.”
Ulrich, from Azle, Texas, was remembered by his community.
"It’s heart-wrenching. And my thoughts and prayers are with that family," Renee Frasier, a resident of Azle and a worker at a local café, said. "It definitely hit home, I have three kids of my own."
Southwestern Oklahoma State University Athletics expressed its condolences in a statement, saying, “Our thoughts & prayers are with the Southern Nazarene football program and university community during this difficult time.”
Ulrich’s high school football coach, Jason Vines, reflected on his former player’s talent and character. "Tyler is built. He is. He looks like a professional football player to me," Vines said. "When I think of good, I think of Tyler Ulrich. One of the sweetest young men I’ve ever been around, and ever known."
Southern Nazarene University canceled its game against Southwestern Oklahoma State University, which was scheduled for Saturday.

title: 7-year-old who battled cancer three times back home after 10 months in hospital
text:
7-year-old who battled cancer three times back home after 10 months in hospital
A 7-year-old girl is back home after facing cancer for the third time.
Nova Stafford spent 10 months at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, where she underwent chemotherapy and surgery for a rare bone cancer.
Now, she and her family are celebrating her homecoming and enjoying life one moment at a time.
“You beat cancer again, how do you feel?” Nova was asked.
“Good. Very good,” she said.
Nova’s journey through life has been filled with ups and downs, including finishing chemotherapy.
At such a young age, she has already battled cancer three times — twice in the eye and, more recently, in her thigh bone with osteosarcoma.
One of the side effects of treatment is hair loss, something that has been difficult for Nova.
“A little bit sad,” she said. “I’ve been crying yesterday about it.”
Nova’s mother, Matisha, said her daughter started complaining of leg pain in December of last year.
“Picking her up from school, the teacher would carry her out of school. It happened fairly fast. I said, 'let’s go to St. Jude and see what’s going on,'” Matisha said.
Tests confirmed a third cancer diagnosis, something the Stafford family was not ready to hear.
“We left with a week of clothing because we thought we would just be there for our annual appointments, and we ended up staying there longer for 10 months,” Matisha said.
Matisha said she was overwhelmed and found it hard to have positive thoughts. The cancer battle was physically difficult for Nova and emotionally difficult for her family.
“She has a prosthetic femur and a prosthetic knee, devices inside of her leg,” Matisha said.
When it became too much for Nova, her mother would use her favorite artists to motivate her to push through.
“I love Beyoncé. She’s my favorite singer,” Nova said.
When asked about her favorite Beyoncé song, Nova said, “Yaya, because I got a yaya,” she said, referring to her grandmother.
The Staffords had been home from St. Jude in Memphis for 18 hours when they began planning what comes next.
“I think right now we’re not going to worry about getting back into a routine. We’re just going to live life and find things to do. We’re going to travel a little bit before we get back into the swing of school, because we’ve been confined to a hospital for 10 months with her,” Matisha said.
For the Stafford family, the moments are too precious to let slip away.

title: Kim Yesis releases third book in Mayenne Bay Novels Trilogy
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Author Kim Yesis has released “Not for Profit,” the third installment in her Mayenne Bay Novels Trilogy.
Yesis joined WABI in 2025 with “Artifice,” followed by “Brush with Fire” in August. “Not for Profit” is the latest release in the series.
About the series
The Mayenne Bay Novels are set in contemporary Midcoast Maine. Yesis describes the books as light mysteries involving art, romance and psychology, along with small town characters and drama.
“I wanted to highlight the lives of everyday people (fascinating—no capes or superpowers required) and to write substantive but humorous stories to remind people why reading is fun. The series is meant as a respite from, an antidote to, all the heavy literature we read and the troubling news we hear daily,” Yesis said.
Yesis says her stories are “realistic” fiction with settings, characters and events that could happen in the real world.
About the Author
Yesis is a New Jersey native now living in Searsport, Maine. She describes herself as “a serious Maine enthusiast” who can’t wait to get up each morning to write.

title: I support Lead Maine’s scrutiny of MaineCare
text:
MaineCare, at its finest, provides vital healthcare services to vulnerable Maine citizens. Or it should. However, disturbing allegations of fraud have made it clear that stricter methods for accountability need to be implemented in our state.
In addition, grossly inadequate living conditions for autistic individuals under MaineCare have been uncovered by the Maine Wire. As a wife, mother and grandmother who raised my family in Maine, I am finding it difficult to understand why our state government does not do more to protect these individuals.
As a concerned Maine citizen, I want to know that my tax dollars are being used responsibly by our elected officials. I want to know that those who truly need help are getting it the best way possible.
That is why the rules Lead Maine is proposing for MaineCare to adopt are essential in protecting the most vulnerable people in our state (“Amid fraud concerns, conservative group pushes for new MaineCare oversight rules,” June 23). These two rules require on-site inspections of MaineCare providers and pausing payment to providers if improper billing for services is detected by onsite inspections.
These rules are not onerous or overreaching. They are a commonsense approach to beginning the task of making MaineCare truly accountable to the people of Maine.
Wendy Munsell
Livermore Falls

title: Aging Untold: Where to find senior discounts and why you should ask
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we look into senior discounts to see which perks are actually worth asking for and how to maximize your savings.
Then we examine tinnitus, the constant ringing or buzzing in the ears, and share practical ways to manage symptoms and protect your hearing.
Finally, we take you inside an imaginative, coloring-book-style coworking space near Nashville designed to spark creativity and build connections.
Many restaurants and museums offer senior discounts, and you might be surprised by other places you could find them.
You just have to ask — and bring your identification with you to prove you are eligible.
“I think the baseline should be the assumption that everybody’s going to give a discount,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “So no matter where you go, I’m going to get a discount. And I’d be brave enough to ask it.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said some seniors feel uncomfortable requesting a discount, but they shouldn’t feel that way — they should accept it.
“You earned it,” she said.
Tinnitus is a constant ringing, hissing or humming in the ears.
Millions of Americans experience the condition. Goutham Gosu, a doctor of audiology, said tinnitus is difficult to measure because it relies on a patient’s description.
As family members age and their abilities change, it might be time to make sure the safeguards that are in place still fit the person today. That includes safety plans for firearms if they are present in the home.
Cradduck said the timing of the discussion matters.
The walls of the Creativity Bar just outside Nashville look like a coloring book. Shapes outlined in black are designed to help imagination and ideas flow.
Stephanie Pruitt-Gaines founded the space where members can drop in and work toward their next great idea.
It is part playroom, part art studio and part office.

title: Cumberland County needs Stephanie Anderson as its next DA
text:
Tammy Walter lives in Cape Elizabeth.
I am supporting Stephanie Anderson for Cumberland County district attorney. This isn’t about party politics. It’s personal.
I met Philip Walter — Pip — in 1995. We married in 1999 and shared 30 years together. Around 2016 he started drinking, and eventually escalated to crack cocaine. His addiction turned our lives upside down, and we divorced in 2023. But a piece of paper never ended our bond. We talked or texted almost every day. I took care of him, made sure he was fed, drove him to appointments and never gave up on him.
What destroyed him wasn’t just addiction — it was a justice system that refused to do its job.
In 2022 alone, he was arrested at least six times in just a few months for drunk driving, hit-and-run crashes, drug possession and resisting arrest. Despite these repeated arrests, he kept returning to the streets, drinking, using drugs and driving.
Under our current district attorney, Jacqueline Sartoris, the cycle continued. Instead of using these repeated encounters with law enforcement as an opportunity to intervene and get him into treatment, the DA’s office allowed him to keep spiraling. I watched the man I loved move closer and closer to death.
By December, he had four active arrest warrants. He was caught shoplifting whiskey, found incapacitated on a sidewalk and admitted to court officers that he was using fentanyl, cocaine and Xanax. The DA’s solution was an offer of a 30-day sentence. They were ready to let him walk out and do it all again.
I repeatedly contacted the DA’s office and pressed them to intervene. Despite the numerous incidents, outstanding warrants and repeated violations of bail conditions, it was only after my persistent efforts that Philip was finally taken into custody. I fought to have him locked up before he killed himself or an innocent driver.
Pip did five months in jail. Inside, he got clean and sober on day one. He was safe and happy. He called to share the smallest joys — an extra pillow or a movie from commissary. Pip swore he would never go back. Behind those walls, away from the chaos, he had found peace. The certainty of consequences was what kept him alive.
When he was released from jail, the DA’s office gave him only brief probation. It wasn’t long before Pip was no longer checking in with anyone. To my knowledge, he wasn’t being drug tested or regularly monitored. He was back to drinking and using drugs, with no one watching or intervening. Pip repeatedly told me: “They aren’t going to do anything to me. The court is a joke.”
His decline was rapid. I found him freezing on the ice, bruised and bleeding. He lost his job for drinking, his phone and the boat he loved. Because he thought it was inexpensive to live and he was facing homelessness, he planned to move to Mexico.
Six days before he died, we were singing together at a “hippie”-themed Halloween party. I was wearing a vintage handmade ’70s dress he had bought me 25 years earlier in Bar Harbor. He had on a flowered shirt and love beads I bought him for the party. We were so happy. I had no idea and was shocked to learn, after his death, someone had seen him using drugs that night. Two days before he died, I took him to lunch and drove him to a dentist appointment. An hour before he passed, we were texting each other that we loved each other.
On Oct. 25, 2025, Pip died of a drug overdose. The toxicology report showed fentanyl, carfentanil, crack cocaine and crystal meth.
When someone is killing themselves with addiction, looking the other way, handing out 30-day wrist slaps and just opening the door to let them spiral isn’t mercy — it is fatal negligence.
Pip needed structure, firm boundaries and a justice system with the backbone to step in before the cemetery did.
I know what real prosecutorial leadership looks like because I know Stephanie Anderson. During her 28 years as district attorney, she founded Maine’s first Drug Court because she understood that true rehabilitation requires both compassion and firm legal boundaries.
I loved Pip for 30 years. I miss him every single day.
We need a DA with the backbone to intervene while there is still time. That is why Cumberland County needs Stephanie Anderson.

title: Too short-staffed to respond: New report shows serious problems facing Maine fire departments
text:
Too short-staffed to respond: New report shows serious problems facing Maine fire departments
Staffing challenges for fire departments in Maine have been a serious issue for years. A new study is providing insight into just how bad the problem is, especially for those that rely on volunteers.
The Maine Fire Marshal's Office and the University of Maine’s Margaret Chase Smith Policy Center have been working for years on a project to study the issue.
The research project
The effort started with a pilot program in Hancock County in 2019 and then in 2025, surveys were sent to fire departments across the state. A total of 219 of the estimated 398 fire departments in Maine responded and UMaine researchers interviewed 25 fire chiefs across 14 counties to take a closer look at the challenges and their effects on local communities.
The findings
The survey found that 47% of fire departments in Maine who responded say they had been too short staffed to respond to some calls in the last three years.
The report also finds that call volumes across the state have increased by 78% in the last decade, with some individual fire departments saying they doubled, if not tripled.
According to the survey, 94% of responding departments rely at least partly on volunteers and 60% are entirely volunteer. Staff and volunteer turnover is a serious problem, with departments pointing to lost wages, retirement, travel distances and trying to balance work and family obligations as the biggest issues when it comes to staffing.
During working hours, many volunteer firefighters are unavailable to respond.
“Being a call company, most work a full-time job, thus no time for training,” an Oxford County fire chief said in the survey. “They offer very little training in Western Maine. You have to drive a long way to get it.”
Firefighters respond to more than just fires and motor vehicle crashes. They also handle floods and storm damage, provide emergency medical services and often serve as planners, educators and communicators for emergency management.
One volunteer fire chief from Washington County interviewed for the study called the number of calls “too much to be a volunteer,” while another from York County called it “too demanding.”
Researchers say it is crucial to find new ways to make being a volunteer firefighter a sustainable path and model in Maine.
“This work will help lawmakers make informed decisions affecting Maine’s fire service for years to come,” said State Fire Marshal Shawn Esler. “It documents the challenges our firefighters face and gives us a clearer understanding of the support they need to continue protecting their communities.”
Most departments in Maine rely on mutual aid from neighboring communities and departments, especially when there are significant calls or multiple calls at the same time, but the study finds that most of the mutual aid partners are also dealing with significant staffing shortages and gaps.
Highlighting the issue, the Hermon Fire Department reported having 21 mutual aid relationships, and the Kennebunk Fire Department reported having 20.
The age of the equipment and the firefighters themselves is also a concern.
Nearly half of the departments surveyed reported having fleets that were more than 20 years old. The average cost of a fire engine doubled between 2020 and 2026, and new engines can take three to four years to build.
“These are incredibly resilient organizations. They are coming up with creative solutions to meet their communities’ needs and often with very limited resources,” said Dominic Piacentini, a research associate with UMaine’s Margaret Chase Smith Policy Center. “In many cases, these local solutions are working, but they just need more support.”
Tracking the issue for years
This is an issue that Maine's Total Coverage has been tracking for years.
In 2021, Lisbon Fire Chief Nate LeClair said he was worried about the day when they would not have enough firefighters to respond to the call. He called the shortage of volunteer firefighters in Maine critical.
In March of 2022, 8 Investigates surveyed more than 30 fire departments in the Oxford Hills area for data on staffing and wages. Our reporting then found serious staffing issues and challenges with pay.
And in March of this year, the Westbrook Professional Firefighters Association and Westbrook fire chief raised concerns about staffing, especially when there are multiple calls at the same time. Chief Steve Sloan said Westbrook had a full-time staff of 47 firefighters, but more were needed to maintain minimum national guidelines.

title: A humble oyster pail turned takeout icon: The American story of the Chinese food carton
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — It’s an icon, that small white receptacle made from a single piece of cardboard folded into a trapezoid-shaped box. Sometimes there’s a wire handle, sometimes a bright red graphic of a Chinese-style pagoda on the side. And inside, deliciousness.
The Chinese takeout container — at least, as it’s commonly seen in the United States — is actually about as American as it gets, with its mix of ingenuity, immigrant cultures becoming homegrown staples, and the desire for convenience (also known as sitting at home in your PJs.)
The idea of what is essentially a paper bucket dates to 1894, when inventor Frederick Weeks Wilcox was granted a patent for what he called “a new and useful improvement” for pails used to carry oysters. A single piece of material would be folded in such a way that it would have structural stability while also limiting the ways it could leak, and also incorporate a lid.
That’s the container. What about the contents we assume are inside it?
Chinese immigrants started coming to the U.S. in the mid-1800s, taking part in the Gold Rush and working to help build the railroads. The communities they created, known as Chinatowns, rose up in places like San Francisco and later around the country. They included eating spots where the foundations of an Americanized style of Chinese food was laid.
After World War II, there was a “real profusion of Chinese restaurants, diversifying away from just chop suey and chow mein … we see this explosion of interest and growth in Chinese food,” says Michelle King, professor of Chinese history at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
Crucially, it was also the start of an association in the public mind of Chinese food with cheaper prices, availability and convenience, she said. And restaurant owners wanted to be considered accessible, for which takeout played a part, she said. “You need to take it home, you have a dinner party you want to cater for, we can do that for you, right?” King says.
At some point in the 1970s, at a packaging company then known as Fold-Pak, the pagoda design was added, sometimes along with words printed in a font used to stereotypically evoke an association with Chinese culture.
“It kind of becomes claimed as a Chinese American food eatery item, like the pizza box or something like that might be for Italian food,” King said.
These days, takeout cartons come in a variety of shapes, and the food landscape has expanded to include a range of cuisines that might show up in the former oyster pail.
Even so, it IS still an icon — quite literally. Check your emojis for “takeout.”
___

title: Maine doesn’t need Jonathan Bush’s interference in local races
text:
Jonathan Bush doesn’t seem to take defeat lying down.
After coming in a distant third in the Republican gubernatorial primary in June, Bush is now angling to win grassroots support around the state in the future, launching “Maine for Keeps,” a new initiative to get Republicans elected in our larger cities.
By doing this, Bush is injecting even more partisan politics into the cities’ municipal campaigns — exposing, once again, how foolish it is for us to go on pretending these races are nonpartisan.
Bush told WVOM radio this week that he’s using $50,000 of his own money to target races in Lewiston, Bangor and Waterville in a bid “to make it easy for the candidates that kind of come from the land of sanity to win and to take back those city councils.”
Translation for those who have yet to master the tricky language of politics: He is promoting GOP candidates to oust officials aligned with the Democrats.
This isn’t a strategy pioneered by Bush. The Maine Republican Party didn’t hesitate, quite openly, to block Democrat Ben Chin from winning Lewiston’s mayoral races in 2015 and 2017. Maine Democrats angle to win municipal races, too, if only by the practice of calling attention to their candidates.
To his credit, Bush isn’t hiding what he’s doing. As he explained, “I’m fighting where I think we’ve got Republicans and unenrolled folks” with enough business sense to overcome opponents aligned with the Democrats.
As far as I can see, Bush backs a GOP agenda that consists mostly of trashing the cities its champions hope to represent. Following the misbegotten lead of the Maine Wire and other agitators, this involves slamming these communities’ safety and cleanliness and insisting that everything has gone downhill for years. What malarkey.
Not that I’m a fan of most city councilors or mayors; it’s at best a mixed bag. Yet for Bush to come in and say that sitting councilors in these cities don’t have “a basic sense of right and wrong” or “basic sanity” is ridiculous.
Perhaps, though, it’s no more silly than the notion that Bush is somehow going to be the savior whose unexpected cash can turn Maine’s municipalities into Republican strongholds. With President Donald Trump at the helm of the party, that’s not about to happen.
What does strike me about Bush’s foray into city politics across the state is that it could become a turning point for the handling of municipal elections. It’s time we dropped the pretense that they are somehow above politics.
I looked at a few sample ballots in Lewiston this week, trying to get it straight in my head who’s running for what, and was appalled to see that beneath each candidate’s name was not his or her party affiliation, which would help the average voter decide. Instead, the ballots listed their home addresses, which seems both useless to voters as well as risky in this bitter age.
Take Lewiston’s mayoral race. The ballot lists the names of five candidates and where each of them lives (three on the same street!). But it provides nothing to help a voter distinguish among them, as party affiliations do in state and federal races.
I don’t believe Bush has any career prospects in Maine politics. The money resulting from his Maine for Keeps effort, though, could perhaps be remembered as the push needed to toss out nonpartisan elections, and stop hiding what’s most important about candidates from voters who lack the information only party insiders possess.
Meanwhile, instead of trying to buy far-flung city councilors, Bush should consider running for municipal office in his own town. There’s a good chance sanity is needed in Cape Elizabeth, too.

title: Patriots try to avoid letdown against Jets
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The New England Patriots are coming off their best performance of the season, doing almost everything they wanted during a 28-point win over the Las Vegas Raiders.
But there are plenty of reasons for New England to be on guard against the Jets this week. And it starts with Geno Smith.
It’s not just that the veteran New York quarterback has not thrown an interception this season in five starts, the longest opening stretch to a season in his career without one. He also has had the Patriots’ number of late, winning in each of his past two trips to Foxborough (with Seattle in 2024 and Las Vegas in 2025).
In last season’s win with the Raiders, Smith completed 70% of his passes for 362 yards and spoiled Mike Vrabel’s coaching debut with the Patriots.
“They’ve got great players, they’re coached by Mike Vrabel, who’s a defensive guy, so we know he wants to have that defense be at the forefront and they want to establish the run as well on offense, so another great opportunity for us,” Smith said.
Smith’s care of the football has allowed the Jets to enter with a plus-3 turnover differential, compared to a Patriots team that has forced a total of six turnovers, ranking 19th in the NFL entering Week 6.
That’s a concern for Vrabel.
“(Smith has) done a fantastic job. And so, if you want to try to create turnovers, you’re going to have to actually go out and force them,” Vrabel said.
The Patriots also enter with a long list of injured players, including left tackle Will Campbell (right knee) and running back TreVeyon Henderson (ankle). That was on top of cornerback Christian Gonzalez missing his second straight game last weekend because of a shoulder injury and Carlton Davis III sitting out because of a neck injury.
The good news is wide receiver A.J. Brown returned to practice for the first time since going on injured reserve after sustaining a high ankle sprain in New England’s season-opening loss at Seattle. He said he’s impressed with how his fellow receivers performed in his absence.
“Whenever I decide to come back, I’m just going to add,” Brown said.
Need to know
New York Jets (2-3) at New England (3-2)
When/where to watch: 1 p.m. Sunday, CBS
Latest odds: Patriots by 7
Against the spread: Jets 3-1-1; Patriots 3-1-1
Last week: Jets beat Browns, 17-12; Patriots beat Raiders, 45-17
Last meeting: Patriots won 42-10 on Dec. 28, 2025, in East Rutherford, NJ.
Series record: Patriots lead, 77-56-1
Matchup to watch
Patriots offensive line vs. Jets defensive line. The Jets have shown an ability to punch the ball out, recovering five fumbles so far. Drake Maye will be playing behind an O-line that may not have Campbell at full strength, creating opportunities to get to Maye, who has lost two of his five fumbles this season.
Stats and stuff
• Rookie edge rusher David Bailey, the No. 2 overall pick in April, was selected the AFC defensive player of the week after he had three sacks. He’s the third player since 2003 to have a three-sack performance in his first five NFL games, joining Detroit’s Aidan Hutchinson (2022) and Denver’s Elvis Dumervil (2006).
• The Jets are tied with the Los Angeles Chargers for second in the NFL with 47 penalties, two behind Cleveland.
• Braelon Allen had a career-high 116 yards rushing and the winning 22-yard touchdown on 24 carries last Sunday while filling in for the second game in a row for the injured Breece Hall.
• New York has held three of its first five opponents under 200 yards after not doing so in any game last season. The Jets are the first NFL team to hold three teams under 200 yards in the first five games since the 1999 Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
• The Jets had eight sacks against the Browns, led by Bailey’s three, tying the franchise high in a single game by the team since sacks became an official NFL statistic in 1982.
• Smith (147 attempts), Detroit’s Jared Goff (191) and Houston’s C.J. Stroud (185) are the only players with no INTs through five starts this season. Smith’s 69.4% completion rate is second highest behind Cincinnati’s Joe Burrow among QBs with at least 100 pass attempts.
• New England has won three straight and 18 of the past 20 against the Jets.
•The Patriots are coming off a season-high 536 yards in last week’s win over Las Vegas. The most recent time they had two games with at least 500 yards in the same season was in 2014.
• The Patriots, 2-0 at Gillette Stadium, haven’t started a season 3-0 at home since 2019, when they won their first five home games.
• Hunter Henry (3,150 receiving yards) needs 8 yards to move past Russ Francis into third place on New England’s all-time receiving yards list among tight ends.

title: Two UMaine projects receive Department of Energy grant funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Two University of Maine studies are receiving grant money from the U.S. Department of Energy.
“It is just a fantastic honor and opportunity for the University of Maine to be partnering with the Department of Energy because it demonstrates the national presence and quality of our researchers,” said University of Maine President, Joan Ferrini-Mundy.
Electronics research project
One of the projects is on the cutting edge of technological advancements, seeking a new material to carry electricity in devices.
“Basically, we use our molecule, the molecule that our students are making at UMaine, to make the metal atoms communicate better in terms of electronics and magnetism,” said Tomas Marangoni, assistant professor of chemistry at UMaine.
Forest regrowth project
The other project is studying how harvesting forests affects the regrowth process. The study will take place at the Howland research forest and compare a recently harvested section to a nearby non-harvested section.
“Just like it is for DOE, it’s equally useful and important information for the forest industry in Maine because they are very much interested in how the harvesting that they do impacts the resources that they have, how it will recover after harvest,” said Daniel Hayes, School of Forest Resources professor at UMaine. “These models that we’re using are going to kind of project that out into the future under different scenarios. So what if we have an insect outbreak or what if we have changes in weather or something and then they can kind of have some scenarios that they can plan for. So it’s really, we have a lot of interest from the forest industry in this project for sure.”
Preparing students for the field
Both projects will prepare UMaine students for their future fields.
“The very first thing that’s going to do is going to train them in STEM and in all those disciplines that make for you possible to engage in this type of research.”
“There’s no other forestry school or even, I don’t even know if there’s any school to be honest with you, that has this capability. This LIDAR machine we have costs $800,000 and we have an airplane and a pilot. It’s a really awesome, I think it’s a really awesome experience for the students.”

title: What to know before buying refurbished electronics
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As the price of new technology climbs, more consumers are turning to refurbished electronics to save money. Nathan Proctor, senior director of the Right to Repair Campaign at US PIRG, tracks those rising prices closely and said buyers do not always need the newest model available.
“Right now, the cost of new electronics has shot up in part because of the demand from the AI data centers buying up a lot of the same kinds of computing equipment, has increased the price of consumer electronics,” Proctor said. “All of the pressure that right now — refurbished technology and repairing devices we already have, that takes that pressure away.”
Proctor said rising prices are pushing more shoppers toward refurbished devices, but not every refurbished item is a good buy.
“You want to make sure you have a good seller with a good reputation, that they’re going to stand by their product for a long time,” Proctor said. “So if you’re looking to save but still want one of those high-quality devices, it’s a great way to go by looking at the refurbished store for those companies.”
Proctor said buying refurbished works well for phones, laptops and gaming consoles. Wearables are a different story. He warned against buying used AirPods or smartwatches, since their small batteries wear out quickly and are often difficult and expensive to replace.
Proctor said shoppers often skip an important step: checking exactly what comes with a refurbished device.
“You should check to see what you’re getting in terms of what they call accessories — so like the charging cable or other kind of peripherals that might accompany the product,” Proctor said. “Depending on who you’re buying from, they may come with those and they may not. You also may need one, and you also may not. You might already have that.”
Experts also recommend checking a seller’s warranty and return policy before buying, so there is time to test a device’s battery and ports before being locked into the purchase.
