title: Former financial officer of Augusta Crisis and Counseling Centers indicted over $200K embezzlement
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The former chief financial officer of the now-defunct Augusta nonprofit Crisis and Counseling Centers allegedly embezzled more than $200,000 from the organization over eight years.
Timothy Floyd, 59, of Augusta, was charged with one count of theft by unauthorized taking and forgery, both Class B crimes, for allegedly forging checks and taking funds from the mental health services nonprofit and was indicted by the Kennebec County grand jury in January. He pleaded not guilty to both charges.
Amber Kruk, then-executive director of Crisis and Counseling Centers, alerted Maine State Police about the matter in August 2024, according to a criminal affidavit filed at court by a detective with the Office of the Maine Attorney General. Kruk had noticed a large sum of money missing from the organization’s accounts.
Kruk had recently been appointed to the role and gained access to the bank accounts that were previously run by Floyd. The organization fired Floyd from his position as CFO earlier that month after first being censured by the board of directors for tardiness in financial reporting and failure to provide Kruk access to financial accounts.
Floyd and Kruk shared the position of executive director for several months after Michael Mitchell, the former executive director and CEO, left the organization.
After Kruk noticed the low account balances, she reviewed past statements and found more than 200 checks from Crisis and Counseling Centers’ main business checking account made out to various vendors but all deposited into the same bank account — the same checking account Floyd’s paycheck was deposited into.
Kruk discovered that many of the invoices, checks and payment records did not follow the usual pattern from the accounts payable clerk, who was normally responsible for generating invoices, marking payments as authorized by Floyd, printing checks and then marking invoices as paid.
Instead, there were several hundred instances where Floyd’s username was associated with creating the invoice, printing the check and recording the payment. The affidavit states these instances would often occur in quick succession and on days other than Thursday, when the clerk would normally complete the invoices.
Kruk also found a folder in Floyd’s former office that contained stubs and invoices related to the checks.
Several individuals authorized to sign checks for Crisis and Counseling Centers, which Floyd was not, also identified many of those checks included forgeries of their signatures.
The value of the 214 checks identified by a financial investigator from the Office of the Attorney General was $269,816 and spanned from 2016 to 2024. The funds were combined with Floyd’s other funds and were used for household expenses, bills and travel, the affidavit states.
According to Crisis and Counseling Centers’ tax filings from 2024, Floyd was paid a salary of $99,673.
From 2018 to 2024, Floyd deposited $700,000 into his primary checking account, including deposits for his salary. Investigators found that Floyd’s main checking account averaged over $100,000 in debits each year and was often overdrawn. Floyd closed all of his TD bank accounts in late 2024.
When investigators from the Office of the Attorney General interviewed Floyd in June 2025 at his new place of work, nonprofit home healthcare organization Andwell Health Partners, Floyd denied having any knowledge of the missing funds and ended the interview.
Andwell Health Partners did not immediately respond to a request to confirm Floyd’s employment status at the organization.
After the contact with investigators, Floyd allegedly fled to Canada but was apprehended while attempting to reenter the country, according to information in an attorney general’s office memorandum that was accidentally sent to an external mailing list that included local media outlets.
In a statement posted to the Crisis and Counseling Centers website after Floyd’s indictment, Kruk wrote that the organization had transitioned all programs and staff to Kennebec Behavioral Health as of December 2024 in order to prevent any disruption in services.
Kruk confirmed in an interview that the alleged embezzlement was a catalyst for the transition to Kennebec Behavioral Health, but was not the only factor.
“I would say that being in the behavioral health space these days and being a size organization we were, we were going through a period of hard years,” Kruk said. “Finding out about the embezzlement was sort of the precipitating factor that pushed us forward quickly in joining with Kennebec Behavioral Health, so to lay it all at (Floyd’s) feet would be not 100% accurate, but … it was not a survivable discovery.”
The former staff of Crisis and Counseling Centers are happy to be with Kennebec Behavioral Health now and are hopeful that justice will come in the case, Kruk said.
“Our staff were saddened and obviously disappointed to learn that somebody who had been with the organization for so many years and was so trusted and valued had done that to what felt like a family,” Kruk said. “It was a wave of emotions and we rode them all together.”
Andrew Emerson, one of Floyd’s lawyers, declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing legal matter.
Floyd’s next court hearing is scheduled in January.

title: Tinnitus affects millions: Why it can be difficult to manage
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — Millions of Americans experience a constant ringing, hissing or humming in their ears, a condition known as tinnitus. For some, the sound never stops.
Ken Seibert has worn hearing aids for about 20 years. The devices amplify his hearing and also help muffle unwanted sounds caused by his tinnitus.
Goutham Gosu, a doctor of audiology, works with patients like Seibert to manage the condition.
“It’s an unwanted sound that they’re perceiving in the ear,” Gosu said.
Gosu said tinnitus is difficult to measure because it relies on a patient’s description.
“It’s really hard to gauge from a medical standpoint, what the person is feeling, perceiving. We just have to go by how they’re explaining it,” Gosu said.
How many people are affected
The American Tinnitus Association says more than 50 million American adults experience tinnitus. The condition is chronic for 5 million of those people.
Seibert described the sound as similar to air being let out of a tire. He said it is constant.
“If you’re listening to music, TV, anything, it can always be in the background of that,” Seibert said.
Seibert said he has had the condition for 30 years and has tried supplements, hearing aids and acupuncture to manage it. He said some methods have helped, but nothing has eliminated it completely.
Identifying the cause
Gosu said determining the right treatment depends on the cause, which can be difficult to identify.
“The tinnitus can come from as simple thing as a wax in the ear,” Gosu said. “Hearing loss too. Blood pressure. TMJ issues, dental issues, all the way to acoustic neuroma.”
Gosu said everyone experiences ringing in the ears at some point but recommended getting checked if it happens frequently.
“If you start noticing it like, you know, two or three times a week or something like that, there might be something going on,” Gosu said.
The cause of tinnitus is unknown, but the condition tends to be more common among people with loud jobs, such as musicians and veterans.
Gosu said in cases like Seibert’s, there is no obvious explanation and treatment focuses on managing the condition.
“I’ve tried everything and I can’t make it go away,” Seibert said. “The hearing aids help me overall to live a more wonderful life, if you will. But I still always have it in the background.”

Residents appeal Gorham's approval of Amazon warehouse
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A group of Gorham residents are appealing a recent decision by the town Planning Board to greenlight a 146,000-square-foot Amazon distribution facility.
The residents filed an appeal with the Cumberland County Superior Court. They argue that the site plan approved last month does not address their longstanding concerns about the project’s environmental and traffic impacts.
“Our reason for getting into this fight is that we care about our community,” said Josh Trombley, an organizer with Gorham United, which filed the appeal. “We think that this project is not a good fit, that it’s going to bring a lot of significant negative impacts.”
The residents are asking the court to overturn the Gorham Planning Board approval. They argue that the site plan does not address town development codes and land use standards on traffic, road capacity, access, stormwater issues, noise and other impacts.
“The town needs to hold every developer to the same standard and hold them to the standards that we’ve set out in our ordinances,” Trombley said.
The town of Gorham did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Amazon has said the facility will bring 170 jobs to Gorham. The online retail giant must still secure environmental and traffic permits from the state in order for the project to proceed.
And Trombley said Gorham United is still collecting signatures for a citizen’s petition to block the project for at least six months.
If enough signatures are collected, Trombley said the Gorham Town Council could approve the moratorium or send the referendum to a special election.
The town of Gorham purchased the 94-acre parcel off Main Street and Shamrock Drive several years ago with the intent of selling it to a developer that could generate industrial business and property tax revenue for the town. Town councilors have previously said that Gorham had fielded a handful of different offers for the parcel over the years, but none have worked out.
Last summer, the town sold the land to Amazon for $4 million.
Maine’s first Amazon facility opened in Caribou last year. Construction is underway on a warehouse in Hermon, and both Waterville and Sidney have given approval to an Amazon distribution warehouse that shares the city-town line.

title: Watch out for deer: Collisions with vehicles are starting to spike in Maine
text:
Watch out for deer: Collisions with vehicles are starting to spike in Maine
Transportation officials in Maine are reminding drivers to watch out for deer in the roadways.
From 2021 to 2025, data from the Maine Department of Transportation (MaineDOT) shows there was a total of 32,650 crashes involving deer on Maine roads. Nearly 19.5% of those crashes happened in November and numbers start to rise sharply in October. November sees, by far, the most crashes involving deer of any month.
Crashes involving deer are slightly less common on weekends that during the week.
According to MaineDOT data, as of Friday, there have been 3,904 crashes involving deer in Maine in 2026, including 219 in the first half of October. With 607, June had the most crashes involving deer of any month so far this year, followed by 597 in January.
The most common times of day this year for a crash involving a deer is between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m. There are also a lot of crashes involving deer between 5 a.m. and 7 a.m.
Date from MaineDOT shows there have been 114 crashes involving moose in Maine this year. The data shows 41 of those crashes were in June. From 2021 to 2025, there were 1,159 crashes involving moose in Maine. June is the most common month for a crash involving a moose, followed by May and July. There is also a spoke in September.

title: FDA-approved blood test offers new hope for Alzheimer’s diagnosis
text:
(Aging Untold) — The FDA’s first-ever approval of a blood test to help diagnose Alzheimer’s disease marks a significant step forward in treating a condition that affects about 7 million Americans, with that number expected to nearly double by 2060, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.
The blood test, known as Lumipulse, was approved by the FDA in May 2025 as a “less invasive option” that “reduces reliance on PET scans and increases diagnosis accessibility.”
Breakthrough in accessibility
Rebecca Edelmayer, vice president of scientific engagement for the Alzheimer’s Association, said getting a diagnosis can be difficult and time-consuming.
“One of the things that we continue to see is that for some patients it could take years,” Edelmayer said. “And we know that having an early and accurate diagnosis is so critical — especially when there’s treatments that have been approved today, to really help slow down the disease process.”
Traditional diagnosis often involves referrals to specialists, expensive PET scans of the brain and lumbar punctures, also known as spinal taps.
“It’s a very, very exciting time in this field,” Edelmayer said.
How the test works
The blood test detects amyloid plaques in the brain, which are considered key markers for Alzheimer’s disease.
Dr. Abhay Moghekar, an associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, helped study and evaluate the test for FDA approval.
“If this test is positive, there’s a greater than 90% chance that you have amyloid plaque in your brain,” Moghekar said.
Moghekar called it “absolutely a breakthrough in the field.”
“Getting a blood test is gonna be far easier, quicker and cheaper,” he said. “It’s going to allow early access to therapy, so it is going to revolutionize care of patients with dementia.”
Current limitations and future potential
The FDA has cleared the blood test for use only in patients 55 and older who are already experiencing memory problems. The agency cautions that this is not intended as a standalone diagnostic tool for Alzheimer’s. Results should be interpreted alongside a patient’s medical history and other assessments, such as cognitive testing.
Moghekar believes blood biomarker tests could eventually predict whether someone is at risk of developing Alzheimer’s before symptoms appear.
“I think we are moving towards a goal of preventing Alzheimer’s disease rather than treating it once you already have the disease,” he said.
Patient success story
Kathi Rigby was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s in 2023 at the age of 68 after experiencing memory problems and difficulty finding words.
After her diagnosis, she entered a clinical trial for a drug that aims to slow cognitive decline by targeting and removing amyloid plaques. The treatment received FDA clearance in 2024.
“It was so wonderful because it did such a difference for me — night and day — it’s a blessing,” Rigby said.
Her husband, Brent, said doctors told them 95% of the plaque was removed.
“The longer you wait, the more damage is done,” Kathi Rigby said about the importance of early diagnosis.

title: Crossing guard hit, killed by driver near elementary school
text:
MERIDEN, Conn. (WFSB/Gray News) — A Connecticut crossing guard was hit and killed by a driver Wednesday morning, police said.
The crash happened near 391 Broad Street, close to Olive Street, just before 9 a.m. Meriden police said the victim was taken to a hospital, where he died from his injuries.
The impact knocked the crossing guard out of a sneaker and sent his glasses flying. His bright yellow reflective vest remained in the road afterward.
Police withheld the victim’s name until next of kin could be notified.
“The Meriden Police Department is devastated by this loss of one of our Crossing Guards,” Meriden police said in a statement. “Our thoughts and prayers go to the victim’s family, friends, and colleagues here within our agency and within the Crossing Guard unit.”
Investigators collect evidence
The driver remained on the scene, police said. The driver’s car had a shattered windshield.
Police said they are investigating how the crash happened.
Broad Street has traffic lights, a crosswalk and signals. A crossing guard is posted there in the morning and afternoon to help children get to nearby Israel Putnam Elementary School.
Investigators photographed the scene for hours.
Community in mourning
Steve Briers said hearing what happened was difficult.
“It’s a tragedy. Thank God there wasn’t a bunch of little kids crossing with him. They could have been wiped out too,” Briers said.
Lisa, who was walking in the area with her son and grandson, said she is always on alert there. She described cars often going faster than the posted 35 mph speed limit.
“My thoughts and prayers to the family. It’s sad. People need to slow down and be more careful,” she said.
The Meriden Public Schools District released a statement on the death.
“This is an awful tragedy. Our condolences go out to our crossing guard’s family and his relatives,” the district said. “Our students and families will miss his friendly smile and positive approach, which was an important and welcome part of keeping them safe every day.”
Meriden Mayor Kevin Scarpati also released a statement.
“This morning, I was shocked to learn of an accident that claimed the life of one of our valued school crossing guards, who helped children gain safe passage to and from Israel Putnam Elementary School each school day. To the best of our knowledge, no children were present at the time of this tragic incident,” Scarpati said.
On Thursday, Meriden Public Schools made counseling available to any students, families or staff who need the services, according to Scarpati.
Scarpati asked the Meriden community to extend their thoughts and prayers to the victim’s family as the investigation remains active.
On Thursday morning, two crossing guards were posted at the intersection where the crash happened to honor the guard and be visible.
The American Federation of State County and Municipal Employees Council 4 Union released a statement: “Our union is heartbroken by the loss of our brother, a dedicated Meriden crossing guard. He went to work to serve his community and protect children. He should have come home to his own family.”
Gwen Samuel of Meriden Kids Walk Safe - Safe Routes to Schools said a vigil is being planned.
“When I got the call, I was just traumatized, I’ve gotten to meet and know so many of the crossing guards. We do presentations annually. We celebrate our crossing guards because we know they’re helping to keep our children safe,” Samuel said. “He’s a first responder too. When they’re keeping our children safe across these dangerous roadways. They are our first responders and we will honor him accordingly.”
Police, along with Connecticut’s Occupational Health and Safety Division, are investigating.

title: Man allegedly shot, killed mother after argument over cats in family home
text:
WOBURN, Mass. (WCVB) — A 22-year-old Massachusetts man has been charged with first-degree murder in the death of his mother.
Ryan Hanafin was returned to Massachusetts by U.S. Marshals and Reading police. Inside the courtroom Thursday, he was charged with first-degree murder and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon in connection with the death of his mother, 49-year-old Andria Hanafin.
Prosecutors say Ryan Hanafin shot his mother inside the family’s home on Oct. 8.
Argument over cats preceded shooting
Investigators said the mother and son had been arguing over the number of cats being kept in the family home.
“Ms. Andria Hanafin was a foster parent to cats as well as worked at an animal vet clinic, and she fostered many, many cats. There were upwards of 80 that were located in the house,” a prosecutor said.
Investigators said Andria Hanafin was afraid of her son’s gun obsession. Police said Ryan Hanafin fired a single shot into his mother’s head.
Weapons found in bedroom
Prosecutors said a short time after investigators arrived, they found an arsenal of weapons inside Ryan Hanafin’s room.
“Ryan Hanafin always carried a firearm on his person. A search of the lower bedroom where Ryan Hanafin was living at the time uncovered that his bedroom was in hoarding conditions and that there were 19 firearms in the room,” a prosecutor said.
After the shooting, investigators say Ryan Hanafin was on his way to Vermont when he was arrested by state police.
Ryan Hanafin pleaded not guilty and is being held without bail. He is due back in court next month.

title: Maine doesn’t need Jonathan Bush’s interference in local races
text:
Jonathan Bush doesn’t seem to take defeat lying down.
After coming in a distant third in the Republican gubernatorial primary in June, Bush is now angling to win grassroots support around the state in the future, launching “Maine for Keeps,” a new initiative to get Republicans elected in our larger cities.
By doing this, Bush is injecting even more partisan politics into the cities’ municipal campaigns — exposing, once again, how foolish it is for us to go on pretending these races are nonpartisan.
Bush told WVOM radio this week that he’s using $50,000 of his own money to target races in Lewiston, Bangor and Waterville in a bid “to make it easy for the candidates that kind of come from the land of sanity to win and to take back those city councils.”
Translation for those who have yet to master the tricky language of politics: He is promoting GOP candidates to oust officials aligned with the Democrats.
This isn’t a strategy pioneered by Bush. The Maine Republican Party didn’t hesitate, quite openly, to block Democrat Ben Chin from winning Lewiston’s mayoral races in 2015 and 2017. Maine Democrats angle to win municipal races, too, if only by the practice of calling attention to their candidates.
To his credit, Bush isn’t hiding what he’s doing. As he explained, “I’m fighting where I think we’ve got Republicans and unenrolled folks” with enough business sense to overcome opponents aligned with the Democrats.
As far as I can see, Bush backs a GOP agenda that consists mostly of trashing the cities its champions hope to represent. Following the misbegotten lead of the Maine Wire and other agitators, this involves slamming these communities’ safety and cleanliness and insisting that everything has gone downhill for years. What malarkey.
Not that I’m a fan of most city councilors or mayors; it’s at best a mixed bag. Yet for Bush to come in and say that sitting councilors in these cities don’t have “a basic sense of right and wrong” or “basic sanity” is ridiculous.
Perhaps, though, it’s no more silly than the notion that Bush is somehow going to be the savior whose unexpected cash can turn Maine’s municipalities into Republican strongholds. With President Donald Trump at the helm of the party, that’s not about to happen.
What does strike me about Bush’s foray into city politics across the state is that it could become a turning point for the handling of municipal elections. It’s time we dropped the pretense that they are somehow above politics.
I looked at a few sample ballots in Lewiston this week, trying to get it straight in my head who’s running for what, and was appalled to see that beneath each candidate’s name was not his or her party affiliation, which would help the average voter decide. Instead, the ballots listed their home addresses, which seems both useless to voters as well as risky in this bitter age.
Take Lewiston’s mayoral race. The ballot lists the names of five candidates and where each of them lives (three on the same street!). But it provides nothing to help a voter distinguish among them, as party affiliations do in state and federal races.
I don’t believe Bush has any career prospects in Maine politics. The money resulting from his Maine for Keeps effort, though, could perhaps be remembered as the push needed to toss out nonpartisan elections, and stop hiding what’s most important about candidates from voters who lack the information only party insiders possess.
Meanwhile, instead of trying to buy far-flung city councilors, Bush should consider running for municipal office in his own town. There’s a good chance sanity is needed in Cape Elizabeth, too.

title: Letter: Troy Jackson is the candidate for needed healthcare reform
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Both Republicans and Democrats agree with consumers, the nation has a health-care crisis with people struggling to afford the accelerating costs of healthcare. According to Julie Rovner on C-SPAN, with insurance profits capped at 15% by the Affordable Care Act, the bulk of costs in the system come from providers and drug costs. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services data indicate corporatization is a major contributor, especially through provider consolidation and reduced competition.
To address the crisis, Troy Jackson supports Medicare for All, and says he will take on big corporations in the system. He has shown his commitment in his record in the Maine Senate and in his promises for when he becomes a U.S. senator.
Susan Collins’ opposes Medicare for All or seemingly any other comprehensive reform of the entire health-care industrial complex that could reduce corporate power and profit. Her voting record on corporate tax cuts and her dependence on pharmaceutical-industry campaign support are evidence to me of her support for increasing corporatization of the system.
With the right design, Medicare for All could simplify the inefficient, fragmented, and multilayered health-care financing that includes Medicare, Medicaid, veterans’ health programs, private insurance, and separate coverage arrangements for services such as prescription drugs, dental care, and vision care. With the right design, universal coverage, cradle to grave, could reduce or eliminate the role of private insurers and lower administrative costs associated with multiple payers.
I believe Troy Jackson has the right priorities to help create and implement the right design.
Alice Bolstridge
Presque Isle

Public comment period on federal permit for proposed Eastport data center ends Monday
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
EASTPORT, Maine — The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s deadline is Monday, Oct. 19, for comments and motions to intervene on a 48-month preliminary permit application for DeepGreen Western Passage SPV, a proposed subsea artificial intelligence data center in Eastport’s coastal waters.
Save Passamaquoddy Bay recently joined the list of groups seeking a voice in the process. Other entities moving to intervene include the city of Eastport, Eastport Community Solar, the Center for Biological Diversity, local residents Carrie Cobb and Gary Fronheiser and the National Marine Fisheries Service – Greater Atlantic Region.
The Eastport City Council denied the Eastport Coalition for Healthy Oceans, or ECHO, a spot on its meeting agenda for the fourth time this week, coalition member Birdy Velveteen said. Velveteen told Monitor Local that the group wants to discuss updates to a previously dismissed voter approval ordinance, but faces resistance.
When ECHO member Joshua Nicholson submitted a written request for an agenda item, Councilor Colleen Dana-Cummings wrote in response, “Can they do that on their own? … I don’t feel like that is something for a City Council meeting.”
However, Councilor Karen Raye posted on Facebook that she will host a community conversation or informal public meeting with ECHO to address residents’ concerns. Raye previously piloted this format in September, inviting constituents to a public forum on downtown revitalization.
Raye told Monitor Local the meeting will happen, “but we need to work on a date and location.”
In August, Eastport’s legal counsel, Bangor law firm Rudman Winchell, called the proposed ordinance “unenforceable and unlawful.” The measure sought to mandate voter approval for any new development larger than existing city structures. Following that determination, the City Council dismissed the ordinance and instead enacted a full ban on large-scale data centers.
The city’s legal counsel cited case law establishing that the city’s charter, which is governed by a legislative process, takes precedence over local ordinances.
Since then, ECHO has gathered signatures for a revised petition for a voter approval ordinance. The group said the measure is necessary — along with the permanent ban on large-scale data centers — to keep projects like DeepGreen Western Passage SPV out of Eastport.
Velveteen told Monitor Local that the voter approval ordinance prevents developers from bypassing broader bans by altering project descriptions. As evidence of a potential semantic loophole, Velveteen cited op-eds in The Quoddy Tides where developer Louis Wolfson, managing member of DeepGreen Holdings LLC, began referring to the project as subsea computing infrastructure.
The voter approval ordinance, Velveteen said, will ensure Eastport residents maintain a say in large development projects, regardless of how they are framed.
Eastport holds a unique position because of its quasi-municipal port authority, which operates under its own charter. That setup raises questions about the effect of citizen initiatives on land and water usage, particularly if case law gives precedence to charters over local ordinances.
Seeking clarity on the legal distinction between charters, policy and enforcement, Velveteen questioned Eastport Port Authority Executive Director Chris Gardner during a September meeting.
“Does the Port Authority’s charter supersede the city charter with regard to citizen initiatives?” Velveteen asked.
Gardner replied: “It does not supersede the city’s charter. They exist on co-equal planes.”
When Velveteen asked what “co-equal planes” meant, Gardner said, “The charter states that all policies and procedures governing the Port Authority are those of the Port Authority board.”
In an attempt to gain further clarity, Velveteen asked: “So, with the ban in place, you still think that the Port Authority charter. … It could happen?”
She also pressed Gardner on whether a legal loophole might allow future board members to pursue a data center partnership despite the citizen initiative.
Gardner reassured her, saying, “Birdy, I don’t think, regardless of the charter, the Port Authority board would even entertain something like that.”
Velveteen said a promise is not policy, telling Monitor Local, “‘Trust me, I wouldn’t’ is very different from ‘yes or no, I do or don’t have that power.’”
DeepGreen Western Passage SPV filed its preliminary permit in February to begin engineering and environmental studies, which FERC accepted for filing in August.
Save Passamaquoddy Bay, an environmental alliance of U.S. and Canadian citizens alongside the Passamaquoddy Tribe, formally joined the list of municipal and local intervenors on the permit.
Following Monday’s deadline, FERC is expected to review the motions and schedule hearings for all parties seeking to intervene.
To read comments and motions that have already been filed, go to elibrary.ferc.gov under docket number P-15424.
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: Road foreman hospitalized after tree limb falls during Hurricane Isaias cleanup
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — A road foreman for the Georgia Department of Transportation is hospitalized after a tree limb fell on him while he was clearing downed trees after Hurricane Isaias.
Rocky Meeks, 53, has undergone multiple surgeries. His family worries he may be unable to return to work.
Meeks was on call 24/7 for the storm, his wife Robin said. He had been out since 3:30 a.m. Saturday cutting trees. The tree he was cutting was his 11th of the day.
“From what the deputies and paramedics say he was cutting a tree, a tree limb out of another tree fell like 40 feet and hit him in the head,” Robin Meeks said.
Robin Meeks was at home waiting when she was told.
“Panic, panic,” she said.
Rocky Meeks was taken to Northeast Georgia Medical Center in Gainesville, where surgery started quickly. Doctors put stents in his aorta and operated on his leg to repair his tibia and fibula.
“They went in and put a rod in his leg there,” Robin Meeks said.
On Tuesday, Rocky Meeks underwent spinal surgery. Before the surgery, he was awake and told his wife not to worry.
She said he worried about bills and was afraid he would have to sell his antique cars to keep afloat.
Robin Meeks said the department told her Meeks will not lose his job, but she worries about making ends meet and has shared a GoFundMe to help.
Meeks was a few years from retirement and is unsure whether he will be able to work again.
“But if you know Rocky, Rocky’s a very hardworking guy. He does not stop for nothing,” Robin Meeks said.
The department was unable to comment.

title: Obituary: Peggy Lou York Weymouth
text:
CLINTON – In loving memory of Peggy Lou York Weymouth who went to be with her Lord and Savior on Oct. 10, 2026. Peggy was born on Jan. 1, 1942, in Skowhegan, to Dwight and Kathleen (Wilcox) York. From an early age, Peggy’s warmth and kindness touched everyone she met, leaving a legacy of love and compassion.
Peggy’s journey began in Clinton, where she attended school. She excelled both academically and athletically, participating in basketball, softball and the drama club. Her dedication and talent led her to graduate as valedictorian, after which she pursued higher education at Barrington College in Rhode Island, earning a teaching degree.
In a love story for the ages, Peggy married her high school sweetheart, Timothy Weymouth on July 25. 1964. Together they built a life filled with love and laughter raising two wonderful sons, Joel and Dennis. Peggy’s nurturing spirit extended beyond her immediate family, as she dedicated her career to educating and inspiring young minds. She returned to her beloved Clinton and taught throughout the state before finding her longterm home at Clinton Christen School, where she remained until her retirement. 
Peggy’s faith was an integral part of her life. A devout Christian, she was a lifelong member of the Clinton Baptist Church. She shared her musical talents with the congregation singing solos and duets with her father, Dwight and serving on the music committee. Her dedication to the church community was evident in her involvement in the children’s vacation Bible school, where she brought joy and wisdom to many young lives with the Sunday School Charlie Stories.
Beyond her professional and spiritual pursuits, Peggy was an avid seamstress who found joy in creating beautiful pieces through crochet and knitting. Her talents were recognized at local fairs where she often brought home blue ribbons. She cherished her time with her sewing friends and delighted in knitting slippers for those she loved. Peggy’s culinary skills were equally celebrated with her baked goods becoming a beloved staple of family gatherings and holiday celebrations.
Peggy’s love for classic cars was shared with her husband, Tim. Together they would often be seen driving their cherished 1961 Chevy Impala convertible to local Dairy Queens or participating in Lion’s Club parades.
Peggy was predeceased by her parents, Dwight and Kathleen York; in-laws, Lindell and Jerry Weymouth; brother in-law, Stephen Weymouth; and lifelong friend Mary Welch.
She is survived by her beloved husband of 62 years, Timothy Weymouth; brother-in-law and wife Terry and Candy Weymouth and Judy Weymouth-Davis; children, Joel Weymouth and wife Mary Jane, Dennis Weymouth and wife Tracy; grandchildren, Nicholas Weymouth and wife Sydney, Aaron Weymouth and wife Brooke, Andrew Weymouth and wife Zaria , Curtis Weymouth and wife Morgan, Jada Boggs, Nicole Savasuk, Zachary Savasuk and Frannie Higgins; and great grandchildren, Natalie, Bellamie, Olivia, Lauren, Mason, Madelynn, Addison, and Isla; nieces and nephews Megan, Evan, Tyler, and Caroline and their spouses and children.
A service to celebrate Peggy’s life will be held on Oct. 19, 2026, with visiting hours starting at 10 a.m., and the service to follow at 11 a.m., at the Clinton Baptist Church, located at 10 Spring Street, Clinton, Maine 04927.
Peggy’s warmth, generosity, and unwavering faith will forever live in in the hearts of those she touched. She will be dearly missed, but her legacy of love will continue to inspire us all.
In lieu of flowers, the family kindly requests that donations be made to the Clinton Baptist Church Missions Program in Peggy’s memory.

title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving the job after a rocky first briefing
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Katie Zacharia is departing as White House press secretary, saying it “was an honor to work for” President Donald Trump after a short and rocky tenure that was defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists.
A person familiar with the matter, granted anonymity to discuss a personnel decision not yet made public, said earlier Friday that Zacharia would be transitioning out of the role. Trump had cast significant doubt on her future, telling reporters that he would have a discussion with her following his weekend travel — and that if he were her, he would reconsider the job.
In a post late Friday on social media, Zacharia appeared to refer to her job in the past tense and called Trump “a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man.”
Zacharia had come under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments. Her 14-minute briefing was followed by criticism that the conservative commentator had long called herself a lawyer when she had not passed a bar exam nor was otherwise credentialed to practice.
Zacharia was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9, as the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump’s inner circle for years. The chaotic nature of Zacharia’s appointment and subsequent downfall evoked some of the personnel messes of the president’s first term, which had largely been absent from his second.
In a lengthy exchange with reporters at the White House on Friday, Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press.
“I told her, ‘I think you’re better off being happy,’” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. “I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.’ I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider.’”
Zacharia had dinner with Vice President JD Vance and his family on Friday evening, according to another person with knowledge of the meal who was granted anonymity to disclose it.
In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, “’Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this,’” and said he wanted “her to have a good life” and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being “brutalized by the media.”
The president was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said there were a lot of people who wanted the job.
Zacharia’s first official day on the job was Monday
In Zacharia’s first and only briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes.
Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand.
She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings.
In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president’s confidence and responded: “I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me.” But she also wouldn’t say when her next press briefing might be.
Questions about why Zacharia called herself a lawyer
Zacharia, a Pepperdine University law graduate, also faced criticism for describing herself as a lawyer when appearing as a commentator on conservative television outlets. Zacharia said the term was a proper one to use when she was offering legal analysis, and said she had worked as a lawyer in China.
That was part of the unusual amount of skepticism that Zacharia faced from those friendly to the administration, including Fox News host Sean Hannity, who pressed the new White House spokeswoman on why she wasn’t forthcoming about her professional background.
Hannity, known to be friendly with Trump, asked Zacharia after she confirmed she did not pass the bar exam in California, “Why not just say, ‘I went to Pepperdine law school and then took a different career path and I took the bar once and didn’t pass it?’”
“Why get into this long, drawn-out definition between the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?” he asked. “Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction. Why didn’t you just say, ‘I never practiced law?’”
Zacharia reiterated to Hannity that she wasn’t acting as a lawyer nor offering legal advice. And she said Friday during that Fox News interview that she wasn’t asked about passing the bar before becoming press secretary. Both she and Trump have said she was hired to work in press and communications, not as an administration lawyer.
Before joining the White House, Zacharia had been working in communications for Trump Media, the company that oversees the president’s social media site, Truth Social. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump administration.
___
Price reported from Dobbins Air Force Base, Georgia.

title: Before Maine Wildness had a name, it was an inspiration
text:
Zoe Durrant waited. Standing dead center, in front of the stage, next to her father, Colin, the 12-year-old was all eager anticipation. This team is potential personified. It can show his daughter and other girls around Maine a pathway to the possible, Colin Durrant said.
This soccer team, the Maine Wildness, is for Zoe.
“I’m really excited,” she said. “I think it will be an inspiration.”
On Thursday evening, the Maine Wildness name was revealed in front of hundreds of fans crammed into Live at Madrid’s for the announcement. The women’s soccer team, which will play in the USL W League beginning next spring, didn’t have a name or a roster, but it already had an enthusiastic fan base.
In June, the team needed just an hour to sell 5,000 season ticket deposits, with 4,400 of those now Wildness season ticket holders.
Jessica Mayhew of Saco is one of those season ticket holders. She arrived at the party early, wearing her Hearts of Pine scarf. As she waited for the announcement, she chatted with Sarah Robble of Kennebunk.
“It’s great to have the ladies represented,” Robble said.
Robble wasn’t able to get in on season tickets. They sold so fast. Don’t worry, Mayhew said. We’ll get you to some games.
“I grew up playing soccer. We’ve got some young girls who play here. This gives them something to strive for,” Mayhew said.
The Maine Wildness is for Mayhew and Robble.
According to data from the National Federation of State High School Associations, close to 3,000 girls played high school soccer in Maine last fall. There are a dozen women’s college soccer teams in Maine, including the University of Maine, which has won three America East titles to advance to the NCAA Division I tournament.
The Maine Wildness is for them.
The Wildness had two supprt groups before it had a name. The Halyard takes its name from the line that raises a ship’s sail so it can catch wind and go. The Lightkeepers strive to illuminate and promote girls and women’s soccer across Maine.
BrynWynne, 13, and her father, Patrick, were among the first in line for Wildness merch when the pop-up store opened shortly after the team name and crest were revealed. Bryn wore a Lightkeepers T-shirt that states succinctly what the group is about.
“Women’s soccer makes Maine better,” the shirt reads. Throughout the crowd at Live at Madrid’s on Thursday, it was a popular wardrobe choice. Bryn doesn’t play soccer, but she has a lot of friends who do. When she supports Maine Wildness, she supports them.
“(Soccer) has really grown on me,” Bryn said.
The Maine Wildness is for Bryn and all her friends who play the game.
Teila Norris-Julien of Biddeford wore a Halyard T-shirt and talked up the new team to everyone she met. This team is something both her daughter, Gabbi, 11, and son, Hayden, 10, can cheer on and draw inspiration from.
“It’s something they can look up to. These people are in our community. Kids can watch them play and think, they did this, maybe I can,” Norris-Julien said.
The Maine Wildness is for Gabbi and Hayden, and their mom.
The Wildness name evokes the underlying hardscrabbleness of Maine. The coast is rocky. The mountains aren’t the highest peaks, but they’re daunting. The name implies fighting for every scrap you can get against an environment not inclined to hand over anything easily.
It doesn’t immediately roll off the tongue, but it fits. Remember, Hearts of Pine had to grow on a lot of fans, too.
When the Maine Wildness plays, it will be in front of a packed Fitzpatrick Stadium, in front of a loyal fan base that knew it was waiting for something, and that something now has a name.
The Maine Wildness is for all of us.

title: Evening showers, wind shifts tonight and turns cold
text:
Cold and blustery Saturday
Cold and blustery Saturday
Spotty showers in the mountains change from rain to snow Friday night and continue into Saturday morning. Elsewhere, clouds give way to sunshine and temperatures run cool.
Highs are in the 30s and 40s Saturday afternoon, but gusty northwest winds keep it feeling like the 20s and 30s for much of the day. Wind gusts of 25 to 35 mph are possible throughout the day.
Saturday night will be the coldest of the season so far, with a hard freeze expected statewide, including along the coast. After a cold start on Sunday, lighter winds and sunshine allow temperatures to climb into the 50s in the afternoon.
A long dry stretch is likely next week with cold mornings and plenty of sunshine. A storm that bears watching develops off the coast of the Carolinas early to midweek. If the storm trends farther north, clouds and showers could spin our way. For now, the chance is extremely low.

title: Crossing guard hit, killed by driver near elementary school
text:
MERIDEN, Conn. (WFSB/Gray News) — A Connecticut crossing guard was hit and killed by a driver Wednesday morning, police said.
The crash happened near 391 Broad Street, close to Olive Street, just before 9 a.m. Meriden police said the victim was taken to a hospital, where he died from his injuries.
The impact knocked the crossing guard out of a sneaker and sent his glasses flying. His bright yellow reflective vest remained in the road afterward.
Police withheld the victim’s name until next of kin could be notified.
“The Meriden Police Department is devastated by this loss of one of our Crossing Guards,” Meriden police said in a statement. “Our thoughts and prayers go to the victim’s family, friends, and colleagues here within our agency and within the Crossing Guard unit.”
Investigators collect evidence
The driver remained on the scene, police said. The driver’s car had a shattered windshield.
Police said they are investigating how the crash happened.
Broad Street has traffic lights, a crosswalk and signals. A crossing guard is posted there in the morning and afternoon to help children get to nearby Israel Putnam Elementary School.
Investigators photographed the scene for hours.
Community in mourning
Steve Briers said hearing what happened was difficult.
“It’s a tragedy. Thank God there wasn’t a bunch of little kids crossing with him. They could have been wiped out too,” Briers said.
Lisa, who was walking in the area with her son and grandson, said she is always on alert there. She described cars often going faster than the posted 35 mph speed limit.
“My thoughts and prayers to the family. It’s sad. People need to slow down and be more careful,” she said.
The Meriden Public Schools District released a statement on the death.
“This is an awful tragedy. Our condolences go out to our crossing guard’s family and his relatives,” the district said. “Our students and families will miss his friendly smile and positive approach, which was an important and welcome part of keeping them safe every day.”
Meriden Mayor Kevin Scarpati also released a statement.
“This morning, I was shocked to learn of an accident that claimed the life of one of our valued school crossing guards, who helped children gain safe passage to and from Israel Putnam Elementary School each school day. To the best of our knowledge, no children were present at the time of this tragic incident,” Scarpati said.
On Thursday, Meriden Public Schools made counseling available to any students, families or staff who need the services, according to Scarpati.
Scarpati asked the Meriden community to extend their thoughts and prayers to the victim’s family as the investigation remains active.
On Thursday morning, two crossing guards were posted at the intersection where the crash happened to honor the guard and be visible.
The American Federation of State County and Municipal Employees Council 4 Union released a statement: “Our union is heartbroken by the loss of our brother, a dedicated Meriden crossing guard. He went to work to serve his community and protect children. He should have come home to his own family.”
Gwen Samuel of Meriden Kids Walk Safe - Safe Routes to Schools said a vigil is being planned.
“When I got the call, I was just traumatized, I’ve gotten to meet and know so many of the crossing guards. We do presentations annually. We celebrate our crossing guards because we know they’re helping to keep our children safe,” Samuel said. “He’s a first responder too. When they’re keeping our children safe across these dangerous roadways. They are our first responders and we will honor him accordingly.”
Police, along with Connecticut’s Occupational Health and Safety Division, are investigating.

title: Fryeburg football edges Mt. Blue in B North battle
text:
FARMINGTON — Fryeburg Academy quarterback Marcus Sutton and his brother, Darryl, acknowledge they have a special connection. It helped the Raiders earn a key victory on Friday night.
Marcus threw two touchdown passes to Darryl, and Fryeburg held on for a 14-13 victory in a Class B North game when Mt. Blue failed on a 2-point conversion attempt with 1:45 left.
“I just trust (Darryl),” said Marcus. “I just put all my faith into him and he’s down there somewhere.”
Added Darryl: “He’s my brother, we got great chemistry. We’ve been playing sports with each other for a long time, so I’m not surprised, and just can’t wait for the rest of the season.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
The Cougars (2-5) made a defensive stop early when Jakob Corey recovered a Fryeburg fumble. Karter Meader also recovered a fumble on the Raiders’ third drive.
Mt. Blue took the lead with just over five minutes left in the second quarter. A long punt return by Cannon Smith and a couple penalties against Fryeburg (3-4) set up a 5-yard touchdown run by Dillon Gray.
The Sutton brothers connected with just over two minutes left in the first half, but the extra point was blocked.
In the third quarter, Darryl Sutton caught a 24-yard TD pass, and Conner Keaten caught a 2-point conversion pass to give the Raiders the lead.
Gray scored on a 2-yard run in the fourth quarter, but the Cougars threw an incomplete pass on the conversion attempt.
Mt. Blue forced Fryeburg to punt, and when the snap went awry, the Cougars had the ball at the Fryeburg 7 with 28 seconds to play, but they were out of timeouts and were unable to score.
UNSUNG HERO
Buk Awe’s rushing was paramount in Fryeburg’s second touchdown drive. He carried the ball seven straight times to start the possession. Two plays later, Darryl Sutton caught his second touchdown pass.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “I think we both tried to give it away. Their team battled, we battled. We both, I think, (have) been struggling in the same (areas) throughout the year, finding ways to lose games, both us and Mt. Blue, and we just were the ones that were lucky enough to win tonight. It wasn’t anything special … we made enough mistakes to lose, but fortunately, we came out with a win.” — Fryeburg coach David Turner
• “What you see is our season. That’s our season. We’ve been in every game besides one, and we just, right now, can’t find the right one … (Fryeburg) played hard. Neither team deserved to lose tonight. I’m sad for my seniors, because they’ve given me everything I ask.” — Mt. Blue coach Craig Collins
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Fryeburg: Marcus Sutton (4 of 9 passing, 75 yards, two touchdowns), Darryl Sutton (two receptions, 53 yards, two touchdowns)
• Mt. Blue: Dillon Gray (two rushing touchdowns)

title: Vote to keep money coming to Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Whether Mainers like Sen. Susan Collins or not, the fact remains that she is the chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee. If voters choose to elect a junior senator (like Troy Jackson), they can kiss hundreds of millions of dollars for Maine goodbye.
Are people really willing to lose this Maine funding, by voting for another candidate, just because they don’t like the president? As the Maine Senate president, Jackson voted for measures that made the cost of living higher in Maine. Why would anyone believe he will do anything differently if he is elected as a U.S. senator?
Let’s vote intentionally, so that we keep as much money coming to Maine as possible. Vote for Maine, not against a person who’s not even running for office.
Alison Jacobs
Auburn

title: House Speaker Johnson campaigns for LePage in Maine's 2nd District race
text:
House Speaker Mike Johnson campaigns for Paul LePage in Maine's 2nd District race
LePage's opponent, State Auditor Matt Dunlap, held a campaign event with Massachusetts Congressman Jim McGovern
House Speaker Mike Johnson campaigns for Paul LePage in Maine's 2nd District race
LePage's opponent, State Auditor Matt Dunlap, held a campaign event with Massachusetts Congressman Jim McGovern
Speaker Mike Johnson made a campaign swing Wednesday through Maine's picturesque 2nd Congressional District, convinced Republicans will defy history and maintain their House majority, as he worked to boost GOP candidate Paul LePage in what is one of the party's best hopes to flip a Democratic-held seat.
The speaker told a small crowd at the Sea Dog Brewing Co. that he disagrees with the polling and the growing sense that Republicans are heading toward defeat on Nov. 3. Instead, he said he believes that the party in power will maintain its narrow grip on the House — thanks in part to candidates like LePage, the two-term former governor.
“I'm telling you, we’re going to surprise them,” Johnson told the few dozen gathered for lunches of burgers, fish and chips and pot pies at the Bangor eatery.
Johnson has been crisscrossing the country in a campaign blitz that will total more than 20 states and 40 districts in October, in a final sprint ahead of the elections that will determine control of Congress for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term in the White House.
Republicans have increasingly been forced to play defense in the final weeks, trying to shore up their candidates in GOP strongholds nationwide as voters reel from high gas prices, Trump’s tariff policies and the war against Iran. Democrats are reaching deep into districts where Trump has had support, trying and preparing a first 100-days agenda if they win back control.
Johnson said what he’s seeing on the campaign trail tells a different story — of crowds turning out to support the party's candidates, including earlier this week in southern Texas, a key battleground region.
“Now we have to defy history to do this,” Johnson said, noting that rarely does the president’s party win in midterm elections.
But he said, echoing LePage’s own message to the room, “voter turnout is critical.”
With a narrow split, every House district matters
While much of the attention in Maine has been on the state's volatile Senate race between incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, the House race for the open seat held by retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden is another key battleground.
LePage and Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap are vying for the sprawling district that encompasses much of the rural northern part of the state.
LePage acknowledged that getting out the vote is what will make the difference.
The district is one Trump carried in the past, but that Golden has held as a leader of the conservative Blue Dog Coalition, a caucus of more centrist Democrats. The retiring congressman has at times bucked House Democratic leadership in voting with Republicans.
It's also one of the few remaining Trump-won districts represented by a Democrat, which makes it a prime opportunity for Republicans as they work to backfill losses elsewhere and keep their majority.
This week, the main House Republican super PAC aligned with Johnson, the Congressional Leadership Fund, canceled spending in four House races, including Iowa and New Jersey, and increased its investment in others from Texas to Pennsylvania.
Democrats, however, are confident they will seize control, as they begin planning an ambitious agenda focused on affordability issues and anti-corruption investigations of Trump and his administration.
Dunlap campaigns with New England congressman
Dunlap was also on the campaign trail Wednesday, holding an event in Lewiston with U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.), the ranking member of the House Rules Committee.
During that campaign event, Dunlap took aim at LePage by saying the former governor cannot be trusted to protect Social Security.
"Unlike Paul LePage, I understand that our seniors have earned a retirement where they do not have to constantly worry about every bill that comes around," Dunlap said. "This is really important because they're not looking for people to take care of them. They're looking to live in dignity based on their life's work."
In a statement shared with Maine's Total Coverage, LePage's campaign called Dunlap's comments false and said LePage has protected Social Security and always will.
LePage's stance on Social Security was a big point of contention during his debate with Dunlap that was hosted by Maine's Total Coverage. You can watch the debate in its entirety in the video player embedded below, or on the WMTW-TV YouTube channel.

title: Trump ally removed from role after report of State Department feud
text:
Trump ally removed from role after report of State Department feud
A political appointee with deep ties to the Trump family has been removed from his special envoy role following a report of a feud with a top State Department official.
Paolo Zampolli, who served as U.S. special envoy for global partnerships, “was notified today that his status as an envoy has been terminated and he is no longer a government employee,” a U.S. official said Thursday. Two other officials confirmed he’d been removed.
The news of his termination comes hours after a Politico report detailing a monthslong dispute between Zampolli and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. According to the report, the feud played out over email on a widespread number of topics, particularly related to chain of command, and messages between the two included personal attacks.
Zampolli is the second Trump administration diplomat who had personal ties to President Donald Trump to be ousted from the administration in recent days, following the forced resignation of Kimberly Guilfoyle who had served as the U.S. ambassador to Greece.
Zampolli, a businessman and former modeling agent, represented Melania Trump. He hosted a party in 1998 where he said he introduced Melania Trump to her would-be husband.
In a statement Thursday, Zampolli noted that his special envoy role, which was only supposed to last a year, had already been extended by Trump for six months.
“Years ago, (Trump) told me I was too good for modeling and brought me into real estate,” he said. “Now he told me: ‘Why do you want to work in government when you can close all these deals?’”
“The President is always right,” Zampolli said, adding that “serving him and the United States has been the greatest honor of my life.”
“I am deeply grateful to President Trump, Vice President (JD) Vance, Secretary (Marco) Rubio and the entire team,” he said. “Now it is time for the next chapter - back to business, building relationships and closing deals.”
“President Trump changed my life once. He just did it again,” Zampolli said.
Trump announced Zampolli as special envoy for global partnerships in March 2025.
“With his extensive experience working with the United Nations, the Kennedy Center, and various International initiatives, Paolo will help us advance America’s Interests on the Global stage,” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.
Zampolli served on the Board of the Kennedy Center during Trump’s first term and was also an ambassador to the UN for the Caribbean island of Dominica.
Zampolli touted securing business deals for the administration while serving as special envoy.
He stirred controversy earlier this year related to the World Cup when he suggested Italy, where he was born, could play in the place of Iran. He told CNN at the time that he believed Iran was no longer participating amid the war with the U.S. Italy had failed to qualify.
“A World Cup without Messi is not a World Cup,” Zampolli said. “Italy has the same merits after winning four times the World Cup.”

title: Orland accepts $265K bid from H.O.M.E. for former fire station
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The months-long effort by the Town of Orland to sell the old fire station at 91 School House Road, and then apply the proceeds against the outstanding loan used for the construction of the town’s new $3.9 million station on Gray’s Meadow Road, has come to a conclusion, pending final closing.
According to Orland Town Clerk Lisa Smith, the town received five sealed bids by the Monday, October 5 deadline. Immediately after the 4:30 p.m. deadline, the town’s select board met in special session to open and review the bids.
“There were five bids total, and the select board accepted the highest bid,” Smith said, “which was a cash bid for $265,000 from H.O.M.E. Co-op.”
Smith said the town has sent the bid to its lawyer to have the sale and transfer documents for closing prepared, with closing expected in the near future.
Orland Select Board Chair Lester Stackpole confirmed that the net proceeds of the sale would be applied against the outstanding balance for the construction of the new fire station, which was opened in 2025.
The town had originally put the old station up for sale this past year, and had gradually reduced the minimum bid from $400,000 to $200,000 before re-offering the building in mid-September with no minimum bid required.
At the September 17 select board meeting, H.O.M.E had made a proposal to assume ownership of the station for $10,000 and a commitment to expand its services to the town by a value of $250,000 over the next five years.
That proposal, and the fact that the town had not offered the building for sale with no minimum bid required, drew vocal opposition from many of those present.
Rosalani Moore, H.O.M.E.’s Executive Director, said, “We’re really happy that our bid was successful. I think it’s a good result for H.O.M.E. and we hope that the community agrees.”
Moore expects that the sale will be concluded within 30 days and expects that there will be no complications because the building is being sold as is and is not subject to additional inspections.
“We understand that our bid was high,” Moore said, “specially in comparison to the tax assessed value, but part of our reason for that was the people in the town wanted to get money to use against the loan for the new fire department station.”
“So we took that into account,” Moore said, “and then, too, that we are a nonprofit and generally don’t generally pay taxes on property, so our higher bid is partly in lieu of that.”
Founded in 1969, H.O.M.E. offers a wide range of community services, including emergency shelters and housing assistance, a soup kitchen and food pantry, community support resources, childcare, and arts and crafts classes.
Moore said that paying to purchase the building, which is across the street from H.O.M.E.’s campus, “does mean it will probably take longer for us to make some of the renovations we want to do, especially for some types of activities and uses we have in mind, but there are things we can do right away that won’t be a problem.”
Funding the purchase of the old fire station, Moore said, was made possible because, “the organization just felt we needed to do this to make the organization whole and for the community.”
“We always welcome donations and funding,” Moore said, “and we are always seeking volunteers and contributions to our thrift store. It all helps.”

title: What if Maine elected a governor who just gets things done?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Erin Cavallaro lives in Westbrook with her husband and two children and serves on the Westbrook School Committee. She works in higher education and nonprofit fundraising.
After watching the first gubernatorial debate, one thing became even clearer to me: Maine needs Hannah Pingree.
Politics has become very good at telling us what divides us. We know which team everyone is on. We know what we’re supposed to be angry about and who we are supposed to blame. Somewhere along the way, though, we seem to have lost sight of what government is actually supposed to do: make people’s lives better.
That’s why I’m supporting Hannah Pingree for governor.
I’m a Democrat, and Hannah and I share many of the same values. But what impresses me about her isn’t simply that she knows what she believes. It’s that she understands governing requires more than being right. It requires getting something done.
I’ve learned that firsthand serving on my local school committee. The decisions that come before us aren’t theoretical. They affect whether kids get to school, whether teachers have the resources they need, how much taxpayers are asked to contribute and whether families can count on the public institutions that serve them.
You quickly learn that accomplishing anything meaningful requires listening to people you disagree with, finding common ground where it exists and remembering that the work matters more than the politics surrounding it.
Hannah has spent her career doing exactly that.
As a legislator and eventually speaker of the Maine House, she worked with people whose political beliefs were fundamentally different from her own. They disagreed — sometimes significantly. But disagreement didn’t prevent them from sitting at the same table and finding ways to move Maine forward. That feels almost radical in politics today.
Former Republican House leader Josh Tardy, who served alongside Hannah, has spoken about that quality. He and Hannah certainly didn’t agree on everything, but he has said that, despite their partisan differences, she believed Republicans and Democrats needed to work together to find common ground.
That isn’t abandoning your principles. That’s governing — and addressing those challenges will require people who disagree with one another to work together.
I don’t expect Hannah to agree with everyone in Augusta, nor would I want her to abandon her values in the name of artificial bipartisanship. But Maine is a small state with some very big challenges. We need more housing that working families can actually afford. We need young people to be able to build lives and careers here instead of being priced out. We need strong schools, thriving downtowns and an economy that works in communities from York County to Aroostook.
In a state where more than 690,000 Mainers live in rural communities, we need to make sure that where someone lives doesn’t determine whether they can find a doctor or access essential services.
I want a governor who understands that sometimes governing is as simple as finding the thing you agree on, rolling up your sleeves and getting it done. Government shouldn’t be about winning the argument or scoring points against the other side. It should be about results.
At a time when so much of our politics is defined by division, Maine has an opportunity to choose a different approach — a governor who knows what she believes, listens to people who see things differently and understands that finding common ground isn’t a weakness. It’s how good government is supposed to work.
That’s why I’m supporting Hannah Pingree.

title: Brewers sweep Dodgers in NLCS, head to first World Series since 1982
text:
Brewers sweep the Dodgers in the NLCS to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982
Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning, Milwaukee's brilliant bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 on Thursday in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to earn their first World Series trip since 1982.
No. 9 hitter David Hamilton's two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave the Brewers a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.
Video above: Brewers fans shocked by high World Series ticket prices
“We got down early tonight and we were like, it’s going to be a great story,” Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. “We’re going to come back and win this. Like, stay together, start chipping away. And that’s exactly what they did.”
Aaron Ashby pitched three scoreless innings for a save as the Brewers erased a four-run deficit to win their first NL pennant and second overall. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise made its only previous World Series appearance 44 years ago, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.
Shohei Ohtani's first home run this postseason helped put the Dodgers ahead 4-0 in the second inning before the Brewers came back to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending World Series champions a year after getting swept by Los Angeles in the NLCS.
“They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers — and the gamers won this week,” Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said.
The Dodgers' goal of a three-peat — not done since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 and never by a National League team — died with their anemic offense and injuries to Ohtani and others on their aging roster.
“I'm not used to those consolation speeches,” manager Dave Roberts said. “The thing about sports that we all love is no matter how much you prepare, you want it, there’s no guarantees.”
Video below: Parents of Brewers icon Jackson Chourio share childhood memories
After topping the majors with 103 wins during the regular season, Milwaukee became the first major league club to finish a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason.
The Brewers also are the first team to sweep a best-of-seven postseason series in which it trailed in every game.
“There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen tonight. We knew we were going to win that game,” said first baseman Jake Bauers, the NLCS MVP.
With the score tied 4-all, Mitchell fell behind 0-2 before reliever Tanner Scott threw three straight balls for a full count. Mitchell’s 409-foot leadoff drive to center field — the first homer of his career on an 0-2 count — put the Brewers ahead for the first time. Mitchell also homered in their 6-2 victory Wednesday.
“It’s absolutely surreal," Mitchell said. "You talk about the battle-tested Brewers. We went down early and the belief in that dugout got stronger and stronger.”
The Brewers’ bullpen coolly turned away multiple threats when the Dodgers had the potential tying run on base.
Winning pitcher JoJo Romero struck out Max Muncy with Kyle Tucker at third to end the sixth.
With one out in the seventh and a runner on third, Ashby struck out Ohtani swinging before Mookie Betts grounded out to end the inning. Will Smith doubled to right with one out in the eighth and was safe at third when the ball got away from Sal Frelick for an error before Ashby got Tucker to fly out and Teoscar Hernández to strike out.
“Playing with that chip on our shoulder,” Ashby said. “You don’t ever know what to expect going into a series like that last year (against the Dodgers). You don’t know how bad it can be, and then it was as bad as it was. And we came out and we survived, and we came back this year, and those guys played their tails off.”
The Brewers tied it in the fifth, when the Dodgers bullpen issued four walks and Milwaukee stole two bases. Hamilton’s single chased starter Tyler Glasnow and scored Frelick, who walked and stole second, to pull Milwaukee to 4-3.
Alex Vesia came in and promptly walked Brice Turang and William Contreras to load the bases. Vesia then walked Bauers with two outs to force in Hamilton with the tying run.
Glasnow retired his first 10 batters — six on strikeouts — before the Brewers got to him in the fourth. Turang walked, Contreras hit a ground-rule double and Bauers followed with another ground-rule double that closed Milwaukee to 4-2.
Ohtani broke out of his postseason slump with a three-run homer after Andy Pages’ RBI single in the second. The four-time MVP released weeks of pent-up frustration by raising his arms and yelling and the crowd of 49,104 joined him in celebration.
But the Brewers wouldn't be denied. And when it was over, owner Mark Attanasio thought of Milwaukee's longtime owner and beloved late broadcaster.
“It’s so important for the community, the entire state of Wisconsin,” Attanasio said. “We’re standing on shoulders of Bud Selig and Bob Uecker.”

title: AOC to take part in Portland town hall next week
text:
Progressive U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will take part in a town hall event in Portland next week, her campaign announced Friday.
The New York Democrat will participate in a “Students vs. Billionaires” town hall Thursday at 2 p.m.
The More Perfect University event comes after Ocasio-Cortez’s recent campaign stops in Michigan to stump for Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
Ocasio-Cortez’s announcement didn’t say whether any Maine Democrats would join her at Thursday’s event, the exact location of which is only available to attendees who RSVP. Spokespeople for Senate candidate Troy Jackson and gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree’s campaigns didn’t immediately respond to inquiries about whether they might join her.
The event is “part of an effort by the Congresswoman to rally and turn out communities across the country ahead of the midterm election,” according to the announcement, and will feature questions from students.
Ocasio-Cortez is the latest in the growing list of national politicians who have made stops in Maine as the nation’s eyes turn to the hotly contested Senate race between Jackson and Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
Vice President JD Vance made two appearances in Maine this year, in Bangor and in Brewer.
Bernie Sanders, a progressive Vermont independent and well-known ally of Ocasio-Cortez’s, rallied with Jackson during his gubernatorial candidacy and then-Senate candidate Graham Platner in May, and joined Jackson again in Lewiston last weekend.
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., was in Bangor on Wednesday to boost former Gov. Paul LePage’s run for Maine’s 2nd House District.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., rallied with Platner in April and is expected to join Jackson and Pingree at Saturday’s No Kings rally in Deering Oaks park.

title: Police officer fired for sharing Flock login with husband, who works for ICE
text:
SAVANNAH, Ga. (WJCL) - Records show a former police officer in Georgia shared her Flock camera login with her husband, who works as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent.
He used the account for nearly 1,000 license plate searches across six states, which mostly involved vehicles registered to Hispanic owners.
Former Savannah police officer Amber Harpe admitted she gave her husband access to the Savannah Police Department’s Flock surveillance system.
“Did you run these flocks?” an investigator asks Harpe in a recording obtained by WJCL.
“I didn’t,” she responded, later confirming it was her husband who did.
Harpe was fired in August, along with five other Savannah Police Department employees, after an internal investigation uncovered Flock misuse.
Four of those employees were later arrested and charged by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation.
Harpe was not among them, and until now, her name had not been publicly identified as one of the employees fired.
Now WJCL has obtained internal records and interviews in which Harpe and her husband, identified in the interviews as Tyler Harpe, acknowledged that her account was used for ICE-related searches.
“Every name that I ever ran was an ICE target,” Tyler Harpe said in an interview.
An internal investigation found that between January and July, Amber Harpe’s account was used to conduct 983 searches involving 97 license plates.
The searches spanned six states, including Florida, Georgia, New Jersey, Maryland, North Carolina and South Carolina, with South Carolina accounting for 788 of those Flock searches.
Investigators found that most of the registered owners of the vehicles searched were Hispanic.
“I asked her if I could have her Flock login, and she asked what I was going to be using it for,” Tyler Harpe said. “And I told her that once we had already developed target packages for people that had arrest warrants, it would be easier while we’re out on the street to be able to locate them.”
Amber Harpe confirmed that her husband, an ICE agent, did not have access to Flock.
“They don’t have flock. That’s surprising. They don’t have access to Flock,” an investigator said.
“No one really wants to work with them, sir,” Amber Harpe responded.
Further records obtained by WJCL show Savannah police share their Flock data with more than 1,700 agencies, but ICE is not listed as one.
“I’m hoping that, you know, nothing too bad comes out on this as far as it just being a policy violation. But, I mean, the tool actually helped our agency, like, get people off the street,” Tyler Harpe said.
Amber Harpe initially appealed her termination, but later apparently withdrew her appeal.
