title: Sharp decline in baby lobster population in Maine’s Midcoast region, new study finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MAINE (WABI) - A new study by the University of Maine is sounding the alarm for Maine’s lobster industry.
Researchers found there was an 80% drop in the Midcoast’s baby lobster population between 2010 and 2022.
The study revealed that since 2015, the adult population of lobster in the same waters has dropped 50%.
Researchers say the sharp decline in baby lobsters had a huge impact on the amount of legal-sized adult lobsters fisherman could catch.
Researchers cite warming temperatures, less food for baby lobsters, as well as lobsters living in deeper habitats which complicates tracking efforts.
Robert Jarrett worked on the study and says the data doesn’t mean the lobsters are going away, but fishing might have to change with the trends.
“Because of the differences in Eastern and Western Maine, we’re probably going to have different habitats that lobsters can continue to use into the future, but that might result in changes in what the fishery looks like. We might have more fishermen fishing offshore or have better success in, say, Western Maine than Eastern Maine as the Gulf of Maine changes,“ Jarrett said.
Despite the new study, nearly 79 million pounds of lobster, totaling $461 million, were caught in 2025, according to the Maine Department of Marine Resources.

title: Patriots try to avoid letdown against Jets
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The New England Patriots are coming off their best performance of the season, doing almost everything they wanted during a 28-point win over the Las Vegas Raiders.
But there are plenty of reasons for New England to be on guard against the Jets this week. And it starts with Geno Smith.
It’s not just that the veteran New York quarterback has not thrown an interception this season in five starts, the longest opening stretch to a season in his career without one. He also has had the Patriots’ number of late, winning in each of his past two trips to Foxborough (with Seattle in 2024 and Las Vegas in 2025).
In last season’s win with the Raiders, Smith completed 70% of his passes for 362 yards and spoiled Mike Vrabel’s coaching debut with the Patriots.
“They’ve got great players, they’re coached by Mike Vrabel, who’s a defensive guy, so we know he wants to have that defense be at the forefront and they want to establish the run as well on offense, so another great opportunity for us,” Smith said.
Smith’s care of the football has allowed the Jets to enter with a plus-3 turnover differential, compared to a Patriots team that has forced a total of six turnovers, ranking 19th in the NFL entering Week 6.
That’s a concern for Vrabel.
“(Smith has) done a fantastic job. And so, if you want to try to create turnovers, you’re going to have to actually go out and force them,” Vrabel said.
The Patriots also enter with a long list of injured players, including left tackle Will Campbell (right knee) and running back TreVeyon Henderson (ankle). That was on top of cornerback Christian Gonzalez missing his second straight game last weekend because of a shoulder injury and Carlton Davis III sitting out because of a neck injury.
The good news is wide receiver A.J. Brown returned to practice for the first time since going on injured reserve after sustaining a high ankle sprain in New England’s season-opening loss at Seattle. He said he’s impressed with how his fellow receivers performed in his absence.
“Whenever I decide to come back, I’m just going to add,” Brown said.
Need to know
New York Jets (2-3) at New England (3-2)
When/where to watch: 1 p.m. Sunday, CBS
Latest odds: Patriots by 7
Against the spread: Jets 3-1-1; Patriots 3-1-1
Last week: Jets beat Browns, 17-12; Patriots beat Raiders, 45-17
Last meeting: Patriots won 42-10 on Dec. 28, 2025, in East Rutherford, NJ.
Series record: Patriots lead, 77-56-1
Matchup to watch
Patriots offensive line vs. Jets defensive line. The Jets have shown an ability to punch the ball out, recovering five fumbles so far. Drake Maye will be playing behind an O-line that may not have Campbell at full strength, creating opportunities to get to Maye, who has lost two of his five fumbles this season.
Stats and stuff
• Rookie edge rusher David Bailey, the No. 2 overall pick in April, was selected the AFC defensive player of the week after he had three sacks. He’s the third player since 2003 to have a three-sack performance in his first five NFL games, joining Detroit’s Aidan Hutchinson (2022) and Denver’s Elvis Dumervil (2006).
• The Jets are tied with the Los Angeles Chargers for second in the NFL with 47 penalties, two behind Cleveland.
• Braelon Allen had a career-high 116 yards rushing and the winning 22-yard touchdown on 24 carries last Sunday while filling in for the second game in a row for the injured Breece Hall.
• New York has held three of its first five opponents under 200 yards after not doing so in any game last season. The Jets are the first NFL team to hold three teams under 200 yards in the first five games since the 1999 Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
• The Jets had eight sacks against the Browns, led by Bailey’s three, tying the franchise high in a single game by the team since sacks became an official NFL statistic in 1982.
• Smith (147 attempts), Detroit’s Jared Goff (191) and Houston’s C.J. Stroud (185) are the only players with no INTs through five starts this season. Smith’s 69.4% completion rate is second highest behind Cincinnati’s Joe Burrow among QBs with at least 100 pass attempts.
• New England has won three straight and 18 of the past 20 against the Jets.
•The Patriots are coming off a season-high 536 yards in last week’s win over Las Vegas. The most recent time they had two games with at least 500 yards in the same season was in 2014.
• The Patriots, 2-0 at Gillette Stadium, haven’t started a season 3-0 at home since 2019, when they won their first five home games.
• Hunter Henry (3,150 receiving yards) needs 8 yards to move past Russ Francis into third place on New England’s all-time receiving yards list among tight ends.

title: Troy Jackson still fighting for Mainers
text:
Serving with Troy Jackson in the Maine Senate, I got to see firsthand his commitment and passion to work on behalf of all Mainers. I watched Troy push and advocate for important programs that would help so many: better healthcare insurance, universal free meals in public schools, paid family leave, affordable childcare and savings plans for those who didn’t have them at their job.
He worked with anyone who could support an effort and never stopped looking for allies. When there was resistance, he would make his case and try to persuade others to join him. He couldn’t convince everyone but he convinced enough to get key bills passed.
Troy started fighting for better deals for Mainers when he was 18 and didn’t go into public service to get rich. A governor or a new legislator, we knew where Troy stood on issues. I’ve already voted for Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate.
Hon. Ned Claxton, MD
Auburn

title: Working waterfront upgrades are the focus of five SEA Maine grants
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
With a goal to strengthen public marine supply chain infrastructure and provide greater resilience to climate-related shocks, five public marine infrastructure projects will receive a total of $1 million for upgrades.
The Seafood Economic Accelerator for Maine, or SEA Maine, awarded the grants through its Seafood Infrastructure Adaptation Fund.
Togue Brawn, owner of Bath scallop dealer Downeast Dayboat and SEA Maine’s co-chair, said she was optimistic that the funding would “result in a stronger, more vibrant future for Maine’s commercially harvested and farmed seafood resources.”
Cold storage and weatherization
The Hancock County town of Tremont received $161,500 to retrofit a 1,200-square-foot town-owned building and create a cold storage facility. The building currently houses a local bait company and the harbormaster office. It will be outfitted with insulation, weather-tight windows and doors, heat pumps and electrical improvements. The goal is to improve energy efficiency, resilience, cold-storage capacity and year-round usability, while continuing to support working waterfront businesses and the seafood industry.
About 10 miles from Tremont’s coast, the town of Swan’s Island was awarded $126,693 to renovate vacant space at its Harbor Road facility, near Burnt Coat Harbor, for dedicated harbormaster and shellfish warden offices, supporting the island’s commercial fishing and working waterfront.
Improvements will include weatherization, a transition from fuel oil to heat pumps and adding solar-powered cold storage for fishermen, clammers and aquaculture operators. The project is expected to strengthen working waterfront operations while adding climate-resilient, shared seafood infrastructure.
Fish piers and floats
The Knox County city of Rockland was awarded $300,000 to upgrade its commercial fish pier. The two-phase project is expected to strengthen seafood supply chain resilience at the pier, which serves approximately 100 commercial fishing and seafood operations.
In collaboration with fish pier users, Phase 1 will assess vulnerabilities, identify adaptation opportunities, develop a site adaptation plan and complete engineering designs. Contingent on those findings, Phase 2 will carry out the priority improvements identified and activate the resulting adaptation plan.
In Cumberland County, the town of Freeport will use $218,400 to replace deteriorating docks and floats at three locations along the Harraseeket River — Cove Road Wharf, the commercial river floats and the town dock.
The infrastructure supports over 60 municipal shellfish license holders, commercial fishermen, lobster and aquaculture gear storage, and offers temporary vessel berthing. Much of the existing infrastructure has deteriorated due to storm surge, sea level rise, age and heavy commercial use. The project will replace the piers, gangway and floats at all three sites.
“Our local fishers and sea farmers create jobs and economic activity on Maine’s docks and piers, but they also provide iconic seafood that elevates Maine’s brand and supports Main Street restaurants and markets up and down the coast,” said Brett Richardson, Freeport’s development director. The grant “provides a critical investment to help sustain and grow Freeport’s working waterfront well into the future.”
Boothbay updates
In Lincoln County, the town of Boothbay Harbor was awarded $193,406 to help a local business, Harbor Bait, modernize its aging bait-salting and ice-making equipment at the Boothbay Harbor Fish Pier. Installation of an automated bait salter and high-capacity flake ice machine will provide vital access to bait and ice for Maine’s commercial fishing industry.
Grantees will contribute a 5% match of the total project cost.
“It is a great example of how investments supporting commercial fishing and aquaculture at the local level can help ensure resilience and drive innovation that will shape the future of Maine’s coast,” said Carl Wilson, commissioner of the Department of Marine Resources.
Maine Development Foundation, a nonprofit in Hallowell, was the program manager for the initiative. A steering committee included over 100 members from industry, associations, nonprofits, academia, and federal and state government.

title: Women have searched for perimenopause relief. Doctors say it’s under-recognized
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Perimenopause is defined as the phase when the ovaries gradually produce less estrogen. It can begin anywhere from eight to 10 years before menopause.
The most common signs of perimenopause, like those of menopause, are hot flashes, weight gain and mood changes, in addition to at least 31 other symptoms, according to doctors.
It remains under-recognized both among the medical community and the women who experience it.
One woman’s search for answers
Sloane Heller is a former TV news reporter. At 46 years old, she began experiencing symptoms including exhaustion, irritability, brain fog and a body she no longer recognized.
“I didn’t even know where to begin,” Heller said. “I absolutely had no idea what perimenopause was until I was thrust into it.”
When Heller brought her questions to a doctor, he dismissed her concerns as stress.
“I was just like, ‘How can you say this? How can you tell me what I’m going through?’” Heller said. “Because I know my body. I know the symptoms that I’m experiencing that I’ve never experienced in my entire life.”
Heller is not alone. A 2022 survey from the United Kingdom found 60% of perimenopausal women were not informed at all on the topic before age 40.
Doctors describe a knowledge gap
Dr. Carrie Wieneke is an obstetrician gynecologist at the University of Kansas Health System. She said perimenopause is poorly understood even among doctors because it is difficult to diagnose.
“As physicians, we love evidence, and so we love something that I can draw your blood with, I can do a scan with and say, you have, and there isn’t [one for] perimenopause,” Wieneke said.
Wieneke said part of the problem starts in medical school. A 2023 assessment of OB-GYN residency programs shows just under one-third offered a menopause curriculum. The University of Kansas Health System is one of them.
Hormone therapy history
Even when women are diagnosed with perimenopause, one of the most effective treatments, hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, has its own complicated history.
“It made the turning point of, I think, of education of OB-GYNs in menopause,” Wieneke said, referring to the 2002 Women’s Health Initiative study that found the risks associated with HRT outweighed the benefits.
That study noted that using HRT could increase your risk of cancer.
“Yeah, that’s what people heard,” Wieneke said. “Because if you actually look at the study and who was chosen and the different groups, there are some flaws in that which set it up for finding what it did. And so I’m personally sad, I think, because I think a lot of patients have been harmed.”
In 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration removed a 23-year-old black box warning label for estrogen, which is used to stabilize fluctuating hormones. The FDA requires a black box warning when substantial clinical data shows a drug can cause severe harm, hospitalization or death.
The removal marked a shift in how medical experts view the treatment.
Finding a treatment that works
For women like Heller, the damage from decades of fear was already done.
After eventually receiving a perimenopause diagnosis, Heller asked her doctor about hormone replacement therapy. “He said the only thing I can do for you is give you a testosterone pellet.”
The treatment involves inserting a pellet about the size of a grain of rice into the skin to deliver hormones to the body over a period of time. Testosterone relieved some of Heller’s symptoms, but she continued exploring other options.
“I knew the testosterone was just one piece of the puzzle,” she said. Four specialists and many months later, Heller found her current OB-GYN.
Three years after her perimenopause diagnosis, she is on a hormone regimen that includes an estradiol patch, progesterone and testosterone, along with complementary medications for symptoms including hair loss and constipation.
“There will be times where you feel really good and the doses that you’re on work really well for you,” Heller said. “And then a few months later, you might have to adjust those doses.”
Speaking out
Heller said she talks openly about her experience because she believes speaking out will help women avoid suffering in silence.
“The more we can destigmatize and get rid of the shame. I mean, there’s nothing to be embarrassed about,” Heller said. “Some will have an easier ride than others. But we all need to talk about it. We all need to be upfront about it.”
Wieneke and other OB-GYNs say hormone replacement therapy is not for everyone.
Treatment largely depends on symptoms, but most often involves anti-depressants and birth control. It is possible to get pregnant during perimenopause, even if periods are irregular, doctors said.
Doctors say there is no single test for perimenopause, so getting help often starts with asking the right questions.

title: $130M refund to Maine customers in limbo as electric utilities appeal order to cut profits
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Electric utility companies’ profits are under close scrutiny from ratepayers, advocacy groups and regulators these days, including in Maine. But utilities are fighting to maintain their higher returns, citing a need to attract investment to maintain reliable infrastructure, especially as climate change puts pressure on the grid.
Because these companies have monopolies over their service areas and don’t face competition, the returns they can make on their investments are regulated. Deciding how much profit is enough, however, can take months or even years of debate and litigation.
Central Maine Power’s latest distribution rate proposal, which includes bumping up the company’s return on equity, has taken center stage this year. As state regulators very publicly review that request, other regulation affecting customers’ electric bills has been happening more quietly in the background.
State and federal agencies have taken steps to try and limit profits on the transmission side. Earlier this year, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ordered New England transmission utilities to refund more than $1.5 billion to customers after finding that the companies’ authorized returns were set too high. The utilities are pushing back, and litigation is ongoing. More recently, Maine officials asked the federal regulator to get rid of an incentive that also boosted potential returns for utilities — and are being sued by some of the companies in response.
High-voltage transmission lines carry electricity, often over long distances, from the power plants and solar and wind farms where it’s produced to local substations. From there, smaller distribution lines carry that power to homes, businesses and wherever else it’s used. The transmission system crosses state lines and is regulated by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, while the distribution system within Maine is regulated by the Maine Public Utilities Commission.
Transmission owners in Maine include Central Maine Power, Versant, and their joint venture, the Maine Electric Power Company. Central Maine Power covers the southern and central parts of the state, while Versant covers eastern and northern Maine. The Maine Electric Power Company connects Maine to New Brunswick, Canada.
Back in 2011, the Maine Office of the Public Advocate and other consumer advocates complained to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission that New England transmission line owners’ authorized return on equity, 11.14%, was unreasonably high. Return on equity is essentially the profit that companies’ shareholders receive for their investments, which allow the utilities to build and maintain their infrastructure.
After years of back and forth, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued its latest opinion this March, reaffirming an earlier decision to lower this allowed return on equity to 9.57%. It ordered the transmission line owners to retroactively refund customers for the difference by May 2027.
Of the $1.5 billion total, approximately $130 million in refunds are due to customers in Maine. The average residential customer might expect roughly $20 per month over 12 months as a result, according to Heather Sanborn, the current Maine public advocate. But she cautioned that more information is needed from the companies themselves for a more precise estimate.
Central Maine Power, Versant and other New England transmission owners appealed the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s decision in June.
But last month, Versant went ahead and proposed a plan for refunds.
“ISO New England is coordinating the refund process, and Versant has submitted a proposed refund plan to FERC that is awaiting approval. We will be able to confirm details once FERC issues its decision. This matter applies only to Versant’s Bangor Hydro District transmission customers and does not affect Maine Public District customers,” Versant spokesperson Marissa McKay wrote in an email.
She did not say how the company’s participation in the appeal would affect the plan for refunds.
“While we’re unable to comment on ongoing legal proceedings, our focus remains on advancing customer refunds, subject to FERC approval of our proposal,” she added.
Central Maine Power also declined to comment on the ongoing litigation.
Regional cooperation
A separate move by state officials to try and lower transmission rates is also pending.
In 2025, the Maine Legislature passed a law requiring utilities to participate in the regional transmission organization ISO New England. By doing so, the companies give up significant control over their transmission infrastructure, allowing ISO New England to plan and operate the regional grid.
The utilities previously participated in ISO New England voluntarily and received a financial incentive to do so, in the form of a 0.5% “adder” to their authorized return on equity.
Last month, the Office of the Public Advocate, the Maine Public Utilities Commission and the Maine Department of Energy Resources filed a complaint asking the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to eliminate this adder, calling it “an outdated financial perk” now that the utilities are required to join ISO New England.
Consumer advocates estimate that Maine ratepayers would save more than $2 million annually.
Versant is not opposing Maine’s request to eliminate the adder. But last week Central Maine Power and the Maine Electric Power Company filed a lawsuit against Sanborn, Philip Bartlett and Celina Cunningham, the heads of the three state agencies that filed the complaint, seeking to have Maine’s new law declared unconstitutional and prohibit state officials from enforcing it.
The companies argue that Maine is interfering with federal oversight of interstate electric transmission, writing in their complaint that the law “was passed for one reason and one reason only”: to force a change to a rate that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has jurisdiction over.
“The economic impact of the regulation is severe, substantially impairing Plaintiffs’ ability to obtain the full return on equity to which it is entitled and upon which it relies for investment capital to maintain and improve transmission infrastructure and ensure system reliability and undermining the economic basis of its contractual relationship with ISO-NE,” they added.
Balancing affordability and reliability
Transmission costs are just one portion of Maine ratepayers’ overall electric bills, which have increased by 72% over the past six years, according to a recent analysis from the Office of the Public Advocate. The average Central Maine Power customer’s monthly bill rose from an average of $91 in October 2020 to $157 in October 2026.
“There’s no single cause,” said Sanborn. “There’s a whole set of reasons why electric rates are rising.”
Transmission rates, driven mostly by utilities replacing aging infrastructure, are actually the smallest of those reasons. Distribution rates, especially costs from storm damage, are a bigger factor. And the energy supply itself, in particular the price of natural gas, is the biggest driver raising electric rates.
As more people switch to electric technologies such as heat pumps and electric vehicles, demand for electricity is expected to rise. At the same time, more extreme weather caused by climate change is threatening the grid’s infrastructure.
Sanborn thinks the best way to balance affordability with having a reliable grid that meets demand is to be smart about when people are using power, so additional demand is distributed throughout the day and year, and not coming during peak hours.
“Both the distribution system, the transmission system and even the supply system have to be built to support those highest use hours,” she said.
As more renewable energy comes online, using more batteries to store that power for when it’s most needed can help, Sanborn added, and prevent the need to “build and build and build in order to keep up.”
She also supports the optional “time of use” rates that both Central Maine Power and Versant offer to help incentivize customers to time their power use for lower-demand hours.
“The goal really is to use more of the system we already have,” Sanborn said, “to use it more efficiently, and to use it over more kilowatt hours of the year so that we can drive down rates.”
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: Man with bloodied face waves down Bangor officer after alleged robbery
text:
Bangor police arrested a man on Wednesday after an alleged robbery and assault.
Shortly before 5 p.m. that day, a Bangor officer was patrolling on Ohio Street when a man with blood on his face, clothing and hands flagged her down, the department said in a news release Friday.
The man said that he had been in an apartment on Ohio Street when Justin Moulton, a 43-year-old man described by police as transient, demanded money then hit him in the face causing his nose to bleed until the victim handed over the money.
The victim told police that Moulton was still in the apartment, where they found and arrested him.
Moulton was charged with Class A robbery and Class D assault.

title: Banana Ball returning to Portland with 2 games at Hadlock Field
text:
Banana Ball will be back in Portland next summer at Delta Dental Park at Hadlock Field when the Indianapolis Clowns and Loco Beach Coconuts face off in a pair of games.
To buy tickets for the games on Aug. 20-21, fans must enter the ticket lottery at bananaball.com/tickets by Oct. 31. Tickets will go on sale approximately two months before the games.

title: Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary less than a week on the job, reports say
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Katie Zacharia is departing as White House press secretary, saying it “was an honor to work for” President Donald Trump after a short and rocky tenure that was defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists.
A person familiar with the matter, granted anonymity to discuss a personnel decision not yet made public, said earlier Friday that Zacharia would be transitioning out of the role. Trump had cast significant doubt on her future, telling reporters that he would have a discussion with her following his weekend travel — and that if he were her, he would reconsider the job.
In a post late Friday on social media, Zacharia appeared to refer to her job in the past tense and called Trump “a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man.”
Zacharia had come under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments. Her 14-minute briefing was followed by criticism that the conservative commentator had long called herself a lawyer when she had not passed a bar exam nor was otherwise credentialed to practice.
Zacharia was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9, as the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump’s inner circle for years. The chaotic nature of Zacharia’s appointment and subsequent downfall evoked some of the personnel messes of the president’s first term, which had largely been absent from his second.
In a lengthy exchange with reporters at the White House on Friday, Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press.
“I told her, ‘I think you’re better off being happy,’” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. “I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.’ I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider.’”
Zacharia had dinner with Vice President JD Vance and his family on Friday evening, according to another person with knowledge of the meal who was granted anonymity to disclose it.
In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, “’Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this,’” and said he wanted “her to have a good life” and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being “brutalized by the media.”
The president was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said there were a lot of people who wanted the job.
Zacharia’s first official day on the job was Monday
In Zacharia’s first and only briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes.
Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand.
She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings.
In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president’s confidence and responded: “I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me.” But she also wouldn’t say when her next press briefing might be.
Questions about why Zacharia called herself a lawyer
Zacharia, a Pepperdine University law graduate, also faced criticism for describing herself as a lawyer when appearing as a commentator on conservative television outlets. Zacharia said the term was a proper one to use when she was offering legal analysis, and said she had worked as a lawyer in China.
That was part of the unusual amount of skepticism that Zacharia faced from those friendly to the administration, including Fox News host Sean Hannity, who pressed the new White House spokeswoman on why she wasn’t forthcoming about her professional background.
Hannity, known to be friendly with Trump, asked Zacharia after she confirmed she did not pass the bar exam in California, “Why not just say, ‘I went to Pepperdine law school and then took a different career path and I took the bar once and didn’t pass it?’”
“Why get into this long, drawn-out definition between the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?” he asked. “Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction. Why didn’t you just say, ‘I never practiced law?’”
Zacharia reiterated to Hannity that she wasn’t acting as a lawyer nor offering legal advice. And she said Friday during that Fox News interview that she wasn’t asked about passing the bar before becoming press secretary. Both she and Trump have said she was hired to work in press and communications, not as an administration lawyer.
Before joining the White House, Zacharia had been working in communications for Trump Media, the company that oversees the president’s social media site, Truth Social. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump administration.
___
Price reported from Dobbins Air Force Base, Georgia.

title: 2027 pay raise for disabled veterans, military retirees announced
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - The annual cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for 2027 has been announced.
Monthly benefits for military retirees and disabled veterans will increase by 3.6%.
The Department of Veterans Affairs matched its COLA to that of the Social Security Administration, which was announced on Wednesday.
Each year, the SSA creates a cost-of-living adjustment based on inflation rates from the third quarter of the previous year.
The 2027 rate is up from 2.8% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2025, Military.com reported.
For retired military members, that will be a $36 increase per $1,000 of retirement pension, according to the American Legion.
The projected raise is said to apply to all benefits earned through the VA.

title: 6 dead, including grandmother and family, in Wisconsin plane crash
text:
SAUK COUNTY, Wis. (WMTV/Gray News/AP) - Six people, including a grandmother and her family members, died in a plane crash in a wooded area of Wisconsin, authorities said.
The Sauk County Sheriff’s Office said the crash happened around 9:30 p.m. Tuesday. Authorities received several reports of a downed aircraft in the area of Park Lane, a residential neighborhood near Mirror Lake State Park.
According to deputies, the plane was a fixed-wing Piper flying on a return trip from Kenosha to Menomonie. Officials confirmed five adults and one child were killed. They said those were the only people aboard the six-passenger plane, and there were no survivors.
Drone footage shows the wreckage from the crash site in a wooded area.
The victims were identified Thursday as Ronald R. Riek, 63, of Woodville; Tyler J. Harvey, 36, of Cadott; Mary K. Brion, 67, of Nelson; Amanda M. Haremza, 45, of Altoona; Rylan Haremza, 13, of Altoona; and Kayla C. Turpin, 39, of Eau Claire.
Riek was a licensed pilot and local business owner. Video shared by WEAU shows he helped organize a fundraiser for plane crash victims in 2025.
Menomonie Airport Commissioner Dane Johnson spoke about Riek’s reach in the community.
“It’s a terrible loss of a man who was a good citizen, an enthusiastic and highly experienced pilot and a respectable man,” Johnson said.
The Associated Press reported that Brion, Turpin, Amanda Haremza and Rylan Haremza were related. Turpin and Amanda Haremza were Brion’s daughters, and Rylan Haremza was Brion’s grandson.
NTSB investigates crash
The National Transportation Safety Board released preliminary information Wednesday, saying the Piper PA 46 was flying Tuesday night near Dellwood at 24,000 feet when the pilot reported icing and asked to descend.
“We know that they had contact with the tower prior to the crash,” Sauk County Sheriff Chip Meister said.
NTSB said air traffic control approved the plane’s descent, and the plane made a right descending turn that increased in rate until its communications and data tracking were lost.
According to the FAA, in-flight icing can distort the flow of air over a plane’s wing, increase drag and impact handling qualities.
Icing can cause an airplane to stall at much higher speeds and lower angles of attack than normal, causing movements that may make it impossible to recover.
Neighbors recall hearing deadly crash
No one on the ground was hurt, and no buildings were damaged in the crash.
Randi Kubek, who lives near the site, said she was meditating in her home with her dogs when she heard an unmistakable sound.
“It was definitely a sound of a plane coming down,” Kubek said. “I heard engines sputtering; it was cutting in and out. I knew this plane was in distress and it was getting so loud so fast. It sounded like the footage that you like see of World War II, Pearl Harbor, you know, planes losing altitude quickly. It was just not like any sound I have ever been personally a part of.”
She also says she saw lots of light in the sky, including lightning.
“The sky lit up, but I wasn’t sure whether that was more in a series of lightning that I had seen out in the sky or whether it was simultaneous with that crunching metal, the very loud crunching metal and an impact that I could feel in my house. I could feel it,” explained Kubek.
Kubek said she learned of the plane crash after a friend texted her about it.
Mark Schmitz works in the area. He says he heard loud sounds when he was outside with friends.
“Terrible. I remember that sound for quite a while now,” said Schmitz.
He says since the crash, the area has had lots of commotion with fire, EMS and law enforcement vehicles.

title: Cat missing 571 days reunited with Connecticut family after epic journey
text:
Cat missing 571 days reunited with Connecticut family after epic journey
A cat named Turtle has been reunited with his family after being missing for 571 days and traveling across two states.
Turtle disappeared in March 2025. Originally a stray from Tennessee, Turtle had been microchipped and had an ear tip indicating he had been neutered. Before his disappearance, he lived in Greenwich with Kelly Moore.
"I love him so much and it was just a comedy of errors," Moore said, describing how the cat ran away through a partially open screen door.
Moore turned to Rocket Lost Pet Rescue for help after Turtle went missing. Founder Rocco Autero set up cameras near the family's home to determine whether the cat was still in the area.
"He was actually, he was showing up. He came by here, you know, every night we caught him on video. He was afraid of cages," Autero said. "So that's one of his fears, cages."
The sightings eventually stopped, leaving Moore fearing the worst.
"I cried and cried so many nights. And I felt responsible because not being aware of the storm door. And we were ... we were really brokenhearted," she said.
The breakthrough came last week when someone posted about finding a cat in Mamaroneck. Autero saw the post and believed the animal might be Turtle.
"It's shocking, you know, that he was found and he traveled a long distance a lot further than we've seen many cats go," Autero said.
The cat's microchip ultimately confirmed his identity. After some effort to get Turtle into a carrier, he made the trip back home to Greenwich.
"If this can happen, anything can happen. It's so wonderful, and I'm so happy to have him back," Moore said.

title: Tesla’s new Roadster ‘flying car’ can thrust itself in the air
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Tesla has unveiled its new Roadster sports car, which can thrust itself in the air, among other engineering bells and whistles. But drivers shouldn’t expect to take it for a spin anytime soon.
Elon Musk’s electric car company rolled out its second-generation Roadster at a Thursday event, showing off a set of cold gas thrusters and a “multi-mode” suction system that can fling the car in the air for short spurts and spin the vehicle mid-flight.
“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk, Tesla’s CEO, wrote on his social media platform X shortly after.
Well, maybe a long, long time in the future, given the regulatory hurdles for flying vehicles and the tangle of state rules that still need to be met.
“I’m not sure every state is going to allow a driver in the middle of traffic to suddenly elevate himself and fly,” said David Vladeck, a Georgetown Law professor and former director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “There is going to be a long process to let anything like that on a road.”
Thursday’s event was hosted at the Texas rocket testing and development center for SpaceX — Musk’s publicly-traded rocket company — and Tesla’s executives noted that they “borrowed” some SpaceX technology to get the new Roadster in the air. Beyond quick jumps and flips, Tesla also said the car can accelerate from zero to 60 miles (96.6 km) an hour in less than a second.
This week’s launch arrived after years of delays and anticipation around the new Roadster — and Tesla shares climbed in morning trading on Friday before falling amid a sell-off in companies tied to artificial intelligence.
The wait isn’t completely over. Musk said production for consumers won’t begin until 2028. Tesla also didn’t immediately set a price tag on its latest EV.
Tesla was taking reservations for Roadster “rocket” car purchases on its website Friday morning, though the fine print said there was no guarantee when the vehicle would be delivered — or whether it would be delivered at all.
Bryant Walker Smith, a former Department of Transportation lawyer, was unimpressed, though he did note Musk’s ability to keep Tesla’s stock high.
“This was a demonstration of a one-off car using a technology around for many years and will not be coming to public roads in 2028,” said Smith, a law professor at the University of South Carolina. “Tesla pretty uniquely has been able to sell itself on a future that is an order of magnitude greater than reality.”
Musk has repeatedly said that the future of driving will be autonomous — and Austin-based Tesla has focused much of its business on building out self-driving features for its vehicles and, more recently, launching its own (still limited) robotaxi business.
But the company maintains that the Roadster will be made to have humans behind the wheel, calling the EV the “best of the last human-driven cars.”
Thursday’s demo was technically autonomous “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Musk noted. But long-term, he said, the new Roadster will be “the only manually driven car that Tesla makes.”
“This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car,” Musk later added, met by laughter from the audience. But “it takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10.”
Tesla’s first Roadster was launched back in 2008. And in 2018, Musk went as far as placing one on a rocket — with a mannequin dubbed “Starman” in the driver’s seat — and launching it into space.
Again, the second-generation Roadster isn’t immediately hitting the market. And whether the ambitious new vehicle boosts the company’s bottom line remains to be seen.
In second-quarter earnings reported over the summer, Tesla’s profits fell as the company spent more on research and development for its robotaxi and robotics businesses — which cut into money made from an otherwise sharp increase in vehicle sales. Net income totaled $1.11 billion for the period, while revenue climbed to $28.24 billion.

title: Fryeburg football edges Mt. Blue in B North battle
text:
FARMINGTON — Fryeburg Academy quarterback Marcus Sutton and his brother, Darryl, acknowledge they have a special connection. It helped the Raiders earn a key victory on Friday night.
Marcus threw two touchdown passes to Darryl, and Fryeburg held on for a 14-13 victory in a Class B North game when Mt. Blue failed on a 2-point conversion attempt with 1:45 left.
“I just trust (Darryl),” said Marcus. “I just put all my faith into him and he’s down there somewhere.”
Added Darryl: “He’s my brother, we got great chemistry. We’ve been playing sports with each other for a long time, so I’m not surprised, and just can’t wait for the rest of the season.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
The Cougars (2-5) made a defensive stop early when Jakob Corey recovered a Fryeburg fumble. Karter Meader also recovered a fumble on the Raiders’ third drive.
Mt. Blue took the lead with just over five minutes left in the second quarter. A long punt return by Cannon Smith and a couple penalties against Fryeburg (3-4) set up a 5-yard touchdown run by Dillon Gray.
The Sutton brothers connected with just over two minutes left in the first half, but the extra point was blocked.
In the third quarter, Darryl Sutton caught a 24-yard TD pass, and Conner Keaten caught a 2-point conversion pass to give the Raiders the lead.
Gray scored on a 2-yard run in the fourth quarter, but the Cougars threw an incomplete pass on the conversion attempt.
Mt. Blue forced Fryeburg to punt, and when the snap went awry, the Cougars had the ball at the Fryeburg 7 with 28 seconds to play, but they were out of timeouts and were unable to score.
UNSUNG HERO
Buk Awe’s rushing was paramount in Fryeburg’s second touchdown drive. He carried the ball seven straight times to start the possession. Two plays later, Darryl Sutton caught his second touchdown pass.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “I think we both tried to give it away. Their team battled, we battled. We both, I think, (have) been struggling in the same (areas) throughout the year, finding ways to lose games, both us and Mt. Blue, and we just were the ones that were lucky enough to win tonight. It wasn’t anything special … we made enough mistakes to lose, but fortunately, we came out with a win.” — Fryeburg coach David Turner
• “What you see is our season. That’s our season. We’ve been in every game besides one, and we just, right now, can’t find the right one … (Fryeburg) played hard. Neither team deserved to lose tonight. I’m sad for my seniors, because they’ve given me everything I ask.” — Mt. Blue coach Craig Collins
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Fryeburg: Marcus Sutton (4 of 9 passing, 75 yards, two touchdowns), Darryl Sutton (two receptions, 53 yards, two touchdowns)
• Mt. Blue: Dillon Gray (two rushing touchdowns)

title: Prime Minister Mark Carney says US is trying to break Canada as Alberta votes on separation path
Aroostook childcare partnerships aim to fill growing niche for parents and job seekers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maeghan Swanson walked through a colorful classroom for young children, duly appointed with comfortable decor, educational toys and tiny chairs, with a smile as big as the room.
“This makes my heart happy,” she said, leading a reporter through the newly opened Northern Maine Community College Childcare Center in Presque Isle.
It’s one of two new facilities operated by Avec Community Action, where Swanson serves as education manager. The other is in Easton, a small town about 7 miles from Presque Isle. Both arose because people saw parents struggling to work or attend school as daycare options kept shrinking.
The ventures come as licensing difficulties, staff shortages and high costs have shut down daycare centers across Maine, including two large ones in Aroostook in recent years. Leaders say the centers will not only provide slots for more than 100 children, but will help build a workforce for an industry that struggles to find qualified staff.
“This is really about trying to invest first and foremost in the children and families we serve, and then in our own human [resources], because another challenge in the childcare environment is finding and attracting qualified personnel,” Avec CEO Jason Parent said.
It’s difficult to make center-based childcare work financially, and many centers have closed in the last few years, he said.
When Miss Jordyn’s Child Development Center in Caribou closed in 2023, affecting more than 100 children, some parents feared they’d have to stop working. Last year, Kelly’s Place Learning Center in Presque Isle, which served 74 children, closed because of financial difficulties with late state subsidy payments. Those and other closures left parents floundering.
Avec took inspiration from projects happening across Maine. Parent pointed to the Hight Family Learning Center, housed in the Margaret Chase Smith School in Skowhegan. There, children from 6 weeks to elementary age are housed in a single early childhood education wing. That’s what the agency tried to emulate in Easton, he said.
Together, the two facilities can serve as many as 115 children, with room for up to 49 in Presque and up to 56 in Easton. Each space has three classrooms and about nine staff members.
The Easton partnership launched two years ago, when parents who couldn’t find childcare pleaded with town and Easton School Department officials to help, Town Manager Cheryl Clark said.
Clark and Select Board members approached Avec, then known as Aroostook County Action Program, and asked if the agency would operate a daycare center if the town provided the building. They considered a community-based model like the one in Skowhegan, Clark said.
Months of discussion and planning followed, and the Easton Elementary School childcare center opened in January. Avec funded the entire project, including building modifications, staff and supplies. Despite some difficulties maintaining staff, so far residents are pleased, Clark said.
“The infant-toddler group has been very well received. The after-school program has built up continuously,” she said. “People are wrapping their heads around there being a daycare opportunity in the building, but it seems to be integrating into the school seamlessly.”
The Easton campus includes infant and toddler childcare services, Head Start and Early Head Start programming and a preschool partnership, along with after-school and school-break childcare.
Retired NMCC President Timothy Crowley thought of a campus childcare center about six years ago, said Angela Buck, vice president and dean of academic and student affairs at the college.
“We have had a lot of students who were not able to complete their program of study because they did not have dependable childcare,” Buck said “He also recognized the relationship with our early childhood education program, [asking] how can we make it a more robust opportunity.”
The college announced plans for the center in 2021, and work started in 2023 to renovate a former dormitory.
The approximately $5.2 million project got its biggest boost from a $2.8 million grant from the Rodney and Mary Barton Smith Foundation. Other contributions included $1 million approved by the Maine Legislature, $500,000 each from the NMCC Foundation and the college itself, and $500,000 from the Maine Community College System, along with private donations, according to campus reports.
Construction finished this summer, and the NMCC Childcare Center opened earlier this week.
Services include Head Start, Early Head Start, private pay and subsidized childcare options. The building also houses part of the college’s early childhood education program and the United Way of Aroostook’s Aroostook County Childcare Resource Center, which Swanson directs.
With three classrooms and separate observation rooms, the center will allow students to complete their practicum work on campus so they’ll be ready to enter the workforce upon graduation, Swanson said.
Grand openings are slated at 10 a.m. on Friday, Oct. 23, in Presque Isle, and at 3 p.m. that day in Easton. The public will hear from partners, have a chance tour the facilities and enjoy light refreshments.
For Avec, the facilities also carry a wider purpose: to provide a one-stop avenue for support such as nutrition, whole family coaching and other services, Chief Program Officer Megan Barnes said.
‘It’s much larger than simply opening another childcare facility. It’s really not just about creating those additional childcare slots,” she said. “That’s very important, but it’s more about those learning environments that are designed to support overall children’s development, strengthen families and help parents achieve whatever goals they choose.”

title: Obituary: William “Bill” J. Murphy
text:
WOOLWICH – William “Bill” J. Murphy, 65, passed away on Monday Oct. 5, 2026.
He was born in Bath on May 3, 1961, a son of John J. and Maureen (Clancy) Murphy. He attended Woolwich Schools and Morse High School. He married Chris E. Bryer and was employed for the City of Bath, Crooker Construction, a sawmill in Woolwich, and owned and operated his construction business. He enjoyed playing in the dirt with his big toys.
He was predeceased by one son, John Murphy; and his parents.
He is survived by his wife, Chris Murphy of Woolwich; one son, James Murphy of Biddeford; three brothers, John Murphy, Ronald Murphy and Pat Murphy, two sisters, Bonnie Morton and Brenda Reed; many nieces and nephews.
There will be no services. Arrangements are by Daigle Funeral Home, 819 High St., Bath. Condolences may be made online at http://www.DaigleFuneralHome.com

title: Brewers sweep Dodgers in NLCS to reach World Series for first time since 1982
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — After 44 years, the Milwaukee Brewers are finally going back to the World Series.
Propelled by a lockdown bullpen and repeated comebacks, the young and fearless Brewers swept the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers out of the playoffs Thursday with a 6-4 victory in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series.
“We weren’t coming in to play patty-cake,” manager Pat Murphy said. “We were hungry, and as long as it’s an even playing field, we’re going to come in and give it our best shot to win. That’s exactly what we did.”
Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning and Milwaukee’s brilliant relievers slammed the door late, giving a vocal contingent of Brewers fans their chance to celebrate in the Dodger Stadium stands.
Now, the Brewers get an opportunity to win their first title after topping the majors with 103 wins during the regular season. Milwaukee has a week off before hosting Cleveland or Tampa Bay in the World Series opener on Oct. 23.
“I’m excited that we’ve got a few more games to play and get to go home with the fans and celebrate there, too,” Mitchell said.
Shohei Ohtani’s first home run this postseason helped put the Dodgers ahead 4-0 in the second inning before the Brewers came back to complete a four-game sweep.
No. 9 hitter David Hamilton’s two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave Milwaukee a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.
“We got down early tonight and we were like, it’s going to be a great story,” Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. “We’re going to come back and win this. Like, stay together, start chipping away. And that’s exactly what they did.”
Aaron Ashby pitched three scoreless innings for a save as the Brewers won their first NL pennant and second overall. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise made its only previous World Series appearance in 1982, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.
The Dodgers’ goal of a three-peat — not done since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 and never by a National League team — died with their anemic offense and injuries to Ohtani and others on their aging roster.
“I’m not used to those consolation speeches,” manager Dave Roberts said. “Those guys played flawless. You’ve got to sometimes tip your cap.”
Milwaukee became the first major league club to finish a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason. Los Angeles took all four NLCS games against the Brewers last year.
“They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers — and the gamers won this week,” Murphy said.
“I think the Dodgers figured out that we came in here with a little different attitude this year.”
The Brewers also are the first team to sweep a best-of-seven postseason series in which it trailed in every game.
“There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen tonight. We knew we were going to win that game,” said first baseman Jake Bauers, the NLCS MVP.
With the score tied 4-all, Mitchell fell behind 0-2 against reliever Tanner Scott leading off the sixth before taking three straight balls to run the count full. Mitchell then launched a 409-foot drive to center field that put the Brewers ahead for the first time. He also homered in their 6-2 victory Wednesday.
“It’s absolutely surreal,” Mitchell said. ”You talk about the battle-tested Brewers. We went down early and the belief in that dugout got stronger and stronger.”
Milwaukee’s bullpen coolly turned away multiple threats when the Dodgers had the potential tying run on base.
Winning pitcher JoJo Romero struck out Max Muncy with Kyle Tucker at third to end the sixth.
With one out in the seventh and a runner on third, Ashby struck out Ohtani swinging before Mookie Betts grounded out to end the inning.
Will Smith doubled to right with one out in the eighth and reached third on Sal Frelick’s fielding error, but Ashby retired Tucker on a shallow flyball and struck out Teoscar Hernández.
“Playing with that chip on our shoulder,” Ashby said. “You don’t ever know what to expect going into a series like that last year (against the Dodgers). You don’t know how bad it can be, and then it was as bad as it was. And we came out and we survived, and we came back this year, and those guys played their tails off.”
The Brewers tied it in the fifth, when the Dodgers bullpen issued four walks and Milwaukee stole two bases. Hamilton’s single chased starter Tyler Glasnow and scored Frelick, who walked and stole second, to pull Milwaukee to 4-3.
Evan Phillips walked two batters with two outs, one intentionally, before Alex Vesia entered and walked Bauers to force in Hamilton with the tying run.
Glasnow retired his first 10 batters — six on strikeouts — before the Brewers got to him in the fourth. Brice Turang walked, William Contreras hit a ground-rule double and Bauers followed with another ground-rule double that closed Milwaukee to 4-2.
Ohtani broke out of his postseason slump with a three-run homer after Andy Pages’ RBI single in the second. The four-time MVP released weeks of pent-up frustration by raising his arms and yelling as the crowd of 49,104 roared.
But the Brewers wouldn’t be denied. And when it was over, owner Mark Attanasio thought of Milwaukee’s longtime owner and beloved late broadcaster.
“It’s so important for the community, the entire state of Wisconsin,” Attanasio said. “We’re standing on shoulders of Bud Selig and Bob Uecker.”

title: Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs moved to a new prison after reports of a luxury lifestyle behind bars
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Sean “Diddy” Combs has been moved to a federal prison in Pennsylvania after reports that the hip-hop mogul was living the high life and was injured in a fight at his New Jersey lockup, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press on Friday.
The federal Bureau of Prisons is transferring Combs, 56, from FCI Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low, a low-security facility south of Williamsport and about 155 miles (250 kilometers) west of New York City, the person said. The person was not authorized to speak publicly and did so on condition of anonymity.
The Bureau of Prisons confirmed the move but provided no further details. The agency said it does not discuss conditions of confinement for anyone in its custody, including reasons for transfer, for privacy, safety, and security reasons.
“Decisions about inmate placement are made by the BOP, and we are not in a position to speak to the circumstances surrounding this transfer,” said Combs’ spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer. “Sean remains focused on moving forward, and we hope that his time at the new facility will be productive and without unnecessary disruption.”
Combs is serving a four-year, two-month sentence for his conviction last year on prostitution-related charges for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters. The case featured harrowing testimony about violence and sex parties he called “freak-offs.” It was a forceful reckoning for one of music and entertainment’s most influential figures.
Last month, NBC News reported that Combs was continuing to enjoy aspects of his millionaire lifestyle at FCI Fort Dix, smuggling in Hennessy, having fellow inmates cook, clean, make his bed and give him massages, and using a contraband cellphone to view social media and an ex-girlfriend’s nude selfies.
On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Combs was injured in a fight with another inmate at Fort Dix and had to be taken out of the prison for treatment. In a rare rebuttal, the Bureau of Prisons refuted TMZ’s report, telling the AP: “The story you are referring to is false and did not happen.”
In the wake of the NBC report, Combs was placed in the prison’s special housing unit, a heavily secured part of the facility away from the general population, for inmates with disciplinary issues or security concerns. He has also been docked 41 days of good-conduct credit, pushing his release date back to March 2, 2028, according to the person familiar with the matter.
In April, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in Combs’ bid to overturn his conviction and sentence, which his lawyers argued was too harsh. The court has yet to rule.

title: Heal points are the standard in Maine, but what do other New England states do?
text:
In the 1949-50 season, Maine high schools turned to a new system invented by a local principal to seed teams not just by their record, but by the quality of the teams they played and beat, in the hopes of more fairly ranking the best teams in a playoff region
More than 70 years later, the Heal points, named after Durward Heal, remain Maine’s weighted formula of choice. But across New England, other states have found their own systems to try to solve the seeding dilemma and create the most fair, accurate matchups.
Here is how other states go about it:
VERMONT
Vermont uses an index system that since the 2015-16 season has reflected strength of schedule. Like in Maine, teams get points based on the level of the opponent they’re defeating, but Vermont schools also get more points for winning on the road. Home and away doesn’t factor into Maine’s Heals.
Teams beating higher division teams get five points for home wins and six points for road wins, four and five for home and road wins against teams in the same division, 3.5 and 4.5 for wins against teams a division below, and two and three against teams two divisions below. Teams get half those points for ties.
The total amount of points, divided by the amount of games played, is the team’s point index.
MASSACHUSETTS
Massachusetts split its state tournaments into sectionals — the equivalent of regions — until 2021, and seeded its teams by winning percentage. This led to numerous instances of lower seeds that played in tougher conferences beating higher seeds, and even reaching state finals.
Since the fall of 2021, however, Massachusetts has ditched sectionals for statewide tournaments, and instituted a weighted formula to seed teams within a division.
Teams are rewarded for margin of victory (capped at a specific amount); their average margin added to their average opponent’s rating results in their overall rating, with teams slotted according to that overall number.
RHODE ISLAND
Rhode Island used win-loss records to seed teams until 2024, when it opened up scheduling to allow teams to play out of division.
The state then instituted a rating percentage index formula similar to the one used in college basketball. A team’s winning percentage (multiplied by 10) makes up 60% of the number, and its opponents’ winning percentage makes up 40%.
CONNECTICUT
Connecticut handles its seeding systems on a sport-by-sport basis.
Soccer just this fall moved to a formula that factors in multipliers for interdivision games, strength of schedule and winning percentage.
Volleyball, meanwhile, gives teams points for every win an opponent has, then divides that total by the number of games for a final point value.
Not all rankings are done in house. Lacrosse, for instance, uses calculations from LaxNumbers.com to put together its playoff fields.
NEW HAMPSHIRE
New Hampshire, which adopted Maine’s Heal points formula on a trial basis in 2009, now uses a modified version that assigns a point figure for each win (more points for beating a team in a higher division).
All points are added up, then divided by the number of games played, and teams are sorted based on those ratings.

title: Domestic violence survivor says the system failed her
text:
SOUTHWEST HARBOR — “I fear for my life,” said Rebecca Long of Mount Desert Island.
Long survived strangulation and abuse at the hands of her ex-husband, Justin Long, 39, in Southwest Harbor in 2023.
He was convicted of domestic violence aggravated assault and is currently incarcerated at the Maine State Prison, serving a sentence of six years with all but three years suspended. That sentence was further reduced on Oct. 1 due to a court error in sentencing. So, an estimated 1,029-day sentence was reduced to 612 days, according to court documents.
Long spoke to the Islander last week about her experience in the hope that it will help other domestic violence survivors.
But it’s not just Rebecca who survived. On Tuesday, Oct. 13, she attended her ex-husband’s Waldo County sentencing for strangling another woman — the crime of domestic violence aggravated assault.
Rebecca recalled the woman’s testimony before Judge Sean Ociepka.
“She [the ex-girlfriend] even said he’s going to kill someone and even that being said, meant nothing. We mean nothing.”
Ociepka sentenced Long to serve nine months on the Class B aggravated assault charge. A Class B felony carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years.
Long’s Waldo County sentence is to be served concurrently to the Hancock County case, meaning no additional time for the felony he committed against another woman while out on bail for strangling Long.
“It’s an absolute slap in the face for the victims,” Rebecca said. “She sustained nerve damage,” speaking of the ex-girlfriend. “She even told the court, ‘She is not a footnote to the Hancock County matter.’”
Waldo County District Attorney Natasha Irving explained that there was a “global” resolution for the two cases, between Hancock and Waldo counties.
“There was an agreement for an overall sentence, taking both cases into account, for six years, all but three years with three years probation,” Irving said.
“There had been an agreement months ago for concurrent time, but due to some issues with the Hancock sentence, we had to put sentencing on hold in our district,” Irving said. “By the time everything was resolved, he had nine months left on his sentence, so this was not a reflection of the seriousness of the charge, but upholding an agreement for concurrent time that had been delayed while he wasn’t getting credit for the case as he was in prison.”
“He had originally been sentenced to six years, all but three years in Hancock, but because of issues where he was not receiving credit for time served as he should have been, and pursuant to the agreement in that case, he had to be resentenced to six years all but 612 days with three years of probation,” Irving said. “The original agreement in our case was for three years straight, but unfortunately [he] wasn’t receiving credit for that time. So he will spend the same amount of time in custody as he would have, but his sentence in this case is shorter due to those issues.”
Long began serving his Maine sentence after serving a Massachusetts prison sentence for assaulting the ex-girlfriend in that state. Rebecca said he was convicted on the following: assault with a dangerous weapon, intimidation of a witness, suffocation/strangulation and threatening to commit a crime.
The judge who handled Justin Long’s sentencing on the Hancock County charge, Judge Terrence Harrigan, had erred in issuing the man’s sentence, which he ordered to run concurrent with the Massachusetts sentence. The Maine Department of Corrections will not run a Maine sentence concurrent with that of another state’s.
This resulted in the reduction of the sentence on Oct. 1 from six years, with all but three years suspended (amounting to 1,029 days), to 612 days.
“The court’s intent was to give him day for day credit on his Massachusetts sentence against his Maine sentence,” the judge stated in the decision. “The plan was for the unsuspended portion of Long’s sentence to run concurrently with the Massachusetts case. In the interim, the court and indeed counsel for the defendant have learned that the Maine Department of Corrections will not run a Maine sentence concurrent with that of another state’s. Accordingly, since this was the mistake of the court, the sentence must be corrected.”
Rebecca said in an interview last week that she was “blindsided” by this decision, which she said had been initially scheduled to occur in open court but was instead done in the judge’s chambers and without notice to her.
“I was aware there was going to be a hearing,” Rebecca said. “I was told someone would let me know” the date and time. Instead, “It was in chambers, it wasn’t public, and a decision was made.”
“Even the three years was already not enough in my opinion,” Rebecca said. “My life is in jeopardy.”
There are two more outstanding strangulation cases involving Long and the ex-girlfriend still pending in two other Maine counties.
Deputy District Attorney Toff Toffolon prosecuted the Hancock County case.
Bangor attorney Baldacci represents Long. The Islander was unable to reach Baldacci for comment before press time.
Rebecca recalled her ex-husband’s statements to the judicial system when he was charged with Class B domestic violence aggravated assault against her.
“At first it was ‘It was my ex-wife, we have history,’” Rebecca said. “But he was not even with his new girlfriend for six months when he strangled her,” she said. “What is his excuse?” to do something “so drastic, so horrific.”
Judge Harrigan read a portion from a letter Long wrote to the court for the Feb. 19 sentencing.
“‘I take full accountability for my part in our toxic relationship,’” the judge read, commenting, “He’s minimizing his role and what he did here. That’s as manipulative as all get out. Basically blaming her for what happened. The other 10 pages are minimizations and excuses.”
Harrigan described details of the crime, including the presence of the couple’s children in the house, and that Rebecca was strangled to the point of passing out.
Defense attorney Joe Baldacci said during sentencing that Long has post-traumatic stress disorder from military service, including a stint in Afghanistan.
Rebecca said the current system forces survivors to advocate for themselves. She spoke during the interview about what survivors go through when finally making a call for help.
“They feel remorse,” she said. “They feel the unknown, but there’s a glimpse of hope that maybe they did the right thing.”
“It’s so important they do quality work,” speaking of the judicial system from the courts to the prosecutor offices.
Rebecca said she had to relay information about the other cases against her ex-husband to all the Maine prosecutor offices, along with the Massachusetts office.
Justin Long was on bail when he was accused of strangling the ex-girlfriend in Massachusetts and in Waldo County. Rebecca wonders why he was not charged with violating conditions of his release.
“We are putting our lives on the line,” she said. “We are putting our children’s lives on the line. We may not have the money to leave. So we’re left again to brainstorm how we are going to survive.”
Next Step Domestic Violence Project has been critical, Rebecca said. “They are such a crucial service in this community.”
“These court systems, DAs’ offices, do not protect victims of domestic violence. And we are sitting ducks,” said Rebecca. “The way these decisions are made, there’s no hope. I hate to say it; it’s going to take another death for them to take action.”
Statistics back up the woman’s fear.
A 2009 PubMed study examined nonfatal strangulation by an intimate partner as a risk factor for homicide or attempted homicide of women: “Prior nonfatal strangulation was associated with greater than six-fold odds of becoming an attempted homicide and over seven-fold odds of becoming a homicide.”

title: Elon Musk settles fraud lawsuits over his $1 million giveaways to 2024 election voters
text:
Elon Musk settles fraud lawsuits over his $1 million giveaways to 2024 election voters
Tech billionaire and Republican megadonor Elon Musk on Thursday settled the two remaining lawsuits stemming from his $1 million giveaways to voters during the 2024 election, according to court filings, bringing a two-year legal saga to an end.
During the final stretch of the 2024 presidential race, Musk’s super PAC started a daily $1 million giveaway to registered voters in battleground states, while Musk was urging voters to support Donald Trump.
After the election, voters in a handful of battleground states filed proposed class-action civil fraud lawsuits against Musk and his political group, America PAC, which both deny wrongdoing. The voters claimed Musk duped them into believing that they’d have a fair shot at the money if they signed up for the sweepstakes — which included turning over their private data to his political organization.
Musk had publicly stated that the payouts would be given away “randomly” to registered voters. But his lawyers later conceded in court that winners were “not chosen by chance” but rather were picked based on whether they would be a strong spokesperson for the pro-Trump super PAC.
In court filings from the two separate cases on Thursday, lawyers for Musk and for the voters said they had settled the litigation. The filings did not describe the terms of the settlements.
This year, Musk has reprised his role as a Republican megadonor — with at least $276 million in donations to GOP candidates for the midterm elections.
The Justice Department warned Musk back in 2024 that the million-dollar giveaways could violate longstanding federal laws against vote-buying.
The Philadelphia District Attorney filed a lawsuit to shut down the sweepstakes while it was still happening, but a state judge ruled on the eve of Election Day that it could proceed.
The bipartisan Wisconsin Election Commission concluded earlier this year that Musk likely broke state law with the cash giveaways.

title: DOJ reaches settlement with Mississippi police department it found routinely violated civil rights
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice announced Friday it reached a settlement forcing reforms in a Mississippi city and its police department, which the DOJ found discriminated against Black people, used excessive force and retaliated against critics.
The settlement comes after a scathing 2024 DOJ report said the Lexington Police Department routinely violated citizens’ civil rights in the rural, poor, majority-Black city located about 65 miles (100 kilometers) north of the state’s capital. Police targeted Black people for arrests, made arrests for low-level offenses to generate money for the police department and locked people up for extended periods of time if they could not afford to pay fines, according to the report.
The out-of-court settlement requires the City of Lexington and its police department to reform practices on a number of issues — from fines and bail to stops, searches and use of force — and bring them into compliance with state and federal law.
The Associated Press called and emailed city and police department officials but did not immediately receive responses.
The agreement bars the Lexington police from continuing to jail people for unpaid fines without first assessing whether they can afford to pay them, a practice that violates the Fourteenth Amendment. The 2024 report found the city court had issued arrest warrants for more than 650 people, roughly half of the city’s population, for unpaid fines.
The city and the Lexington Police Department must also dismiss all existing warrants for unpaid fines and fees that violate the law and move to expunge the records of all unlawful fine-based convictions.
Additionally, the city and the Lexington Police Department are barred from creating and implementing a quota or incentive system for stops, warnings, citations, arrests or related revenue. The DOJ previously found that between 2022 and 2024, the Lexington Police Department made one arrest for every four people in town, more than 10 times the per-capita arrest rate for the state of Mississippi.
The department will also require DOJ-approved trainings on stops, searches, arrests and use of force, in addition to implementing documentation and review systems to ensure such actions are lawful.
“Through these reforms, we seek not only to address the concerns identified in our investigation, but also to strengthen public trust and promote practices that respect the rights and dignity of every person,” U.S. Attorney J.E. Baxter Kruger for the Southern District of Mississippi said in a news release.
The DOJ said it would work with the city and police to “ensure that they remedy the alleged violations.” The agreement lasts for three years, but could be cut short or extended depending on whether the parties mutually determine the city and police department have reached compliance.
The DOJ launched a probe into the Lexington Police Department in 2023, after citizens accused officers of using roadblocks to target Black drivers, engaging in excessive force, committing sexual assault and arresting people without justification, among other claims.

title: Flamingo recovers with custom brace from orthopedist
text:
TYLER, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A Chilean flamingo at Tyler’s Caldwell Zoo is recovering from a soft tissue injury to his ankle joint with the help of a custom-built brace.
Queenie, 9, got spooked and ran while on exhibit, tearing ligaments in his ankle. Bird Department Supervisor Nichole Moore said keepers noticed him lagging behind.
“He sustained this injury on exhibit. We saw him lagging behind his flock. And then we decided since he’s so tactile, we’d be able to get him in hand and really help him,” Moore said.
Injury first appeared years ago
The injury first showed up in 2021. Medicine did not fully fix the problem, so the zoo worked with Ben Guenther, an orthopedist who typically builds braces and prosthetics for people. Guenther designed a brace for Queenie.
“This was the best opportunity for him because we would be able to put a brace on him and work with him and make sure it would really work so he would be able to live a really long life,” Moore said.
Why leg function matters
Flamingos use their legs for more than walking. They also use their feet to stir up food so they can filter through it.
“It is really important for us to be quick when assessing injuries, especially on long-legged birds like this, they utilize their feet quite a bit when they’re moving around,” Moore said. “They also use their feet to kind of stir up the the food, to really like move things around for them to filter through. So it’s just such a really important thing for them to have function in both legs. So yeah, it’s really important for us to really make sure that we’re able to take care of them as quick as we can.”
Chilean flamingos can live into their 60s.
Brace is a lifelong fit
Moore said the brace provides joint support Queenie’s leg cannot provide on its own. He will wear it for life, and it will be checked weekly for swelling or irritation.
“Now that he’s quite used to it, we see such a change in him. He puts full weight on that leg. He’s around with the rest of the flock. He’s taking baths with the flock and running around,” Moore said.
There is no timeline yet for when Queenie will fully rejoin the rest of the flock.
