title: Obituary: Kerrieann Harrison
text:
EAST DIXFIELD – Kerrieann Harrison of East Dixfield, passed away peacefully with her daughter at her side and family present on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. Kerrieann fought fiercely a courageous two-year battle with cancer. Throughout her health journey, Kerrieann displayed unimaginable resilience, grace, and unwavering hope. When faced with her diagnosis, she fought with everything she had, teaching us all what true bravery looks like. She refused to let her illness define her, choosing instead to focus on the joy of everyday moments and the people she loved. Her strength was an inspiration to all.
She was born on Nov. 25, 1969, in Woburn, Massachusetts, to Lucky and Margaret Harrison. In her grade school years, she was known for her strength, musical talent, and character.
She was a competitive athlete and musician at Barnstable High School. She had a deep love for her time in the marching band and in the track and field, specializing in shotput and discus. After high school, her adventurous spirit took her across the road for years before returning to Maine to start a family and to complete her education. She proudly earned her bachelor’s degree in business administration and accounting while raising her three children that she adored above all else.
Kerrieann was known to her family as the “Queen Bee”. She was a passionate beekeeper that found a community of friends with the Western Maine Beekeepers Association. She happily helped grow the organizations web presence for years as their secretary. Her legacy of love, laughter, and courage will live on in the hearts of those that knew her forever.
Kerrieann will be deeply missed but forever remembered by her family whom she loved spending time with. She leaves behind a family who cherished her, including her children, William Gunter, Laura Gunter, and Amanda Gunter; parents, Lucky (Henson) Harrison and Margaret Mary (Finnin, Henson) Harrison; siblings, Laurieann (Henson, Galer) Ormond, Hollieann (Henson) Harrison, Thomas Peter (Henson) Harrison, and Cherieann (Henson) Harrison; grandchildren, and many loving nieces and nephews. She was predeceased by her brother Steven Andrew Henson.
Public visiting hours will be held on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, from 4-7 p.m., at Wiles Remembrance Center, 137 Farmington Falls Road, Farmington. A Memorial Mass for Kerrieann will occur at St. Joseph Catholic Church on Oct. 24, 2026, at 11 a.m. (133 Middle St., Farmington) Interment of her remains will occur at the Harrison family cemetery in Temple at a later date to be determined.
Family and friends are encouraged to visit Kerrieann’s Book of Memories at http://www.wilesrc.com to leave words of comfort, photos or reflections. Honored to be caring for the family of Kerrieann Harrison is Wiles Remembrance Center – Farmington.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Western Maine Beekeepers Association. Checks can be made out to: WMBA c/o Chris Bailey, 473 North Main Street,
Andover, Maine 04216.

title: Journalist hospitalized after Israeli settler attack on Palestinian olive harvest in West Bank
text:
Washington Post journalist hospitalized after Israeli settler attack on Palestinian olive harvest in West Bank
A Washington Post photojournalist was hospitalized after Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank attacked her and a group of Palestinians during the annual olive harvest.
Veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was on assignment for The Washington Post, said the group of Palestinians she was with began to retreat when they saw dozens of settlers running toward them.
In a video statement, Levine said settlers kicked her while she was on the ground. “I had my camera bag and my pouch with my passport, and my telephone was on a rope around my neck and they broke that off me, and they broke my cameras off me, and they broke my bag, and they kept kicking me,” said Levine, who estimated the attack lasted 10 minutes. “Just absolute craziness, and I didn’t see anybody trying to stop it.”
“I don’t know how a parent can raise such a monster. They’re not even humans, and yes, they are Jewish terrorists,” Levine added. “And you know what? Sadly, none of them will be prosecuted. I am sure of it.”
The Washington Post said Levine was wearing “visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist” during the attack. “We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities.”
Video of the attack showed a group of masked settlers, some armed with clubs, hurling stones at a group of Palestinians, some of whom are also throwing stones. In the background, at least five settlers surround Levine and throw her to the ground, beating her as she covers her face with her hands. The settlers appear to rip away Levine’s bag.
The Palestine Red Crescent Society said it was treating two people after they were beaten by settlers: a 63-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man. The assault is part of a wave of settler attacks at the start of the Palestinian olive harvest that residents reported across the area. Last year’s olive harvest saw a surge of such incidents across the West Bank as settlers attacked Palestinians and prevented them from accessing their land.
Levine was rushed to the Ramallah Government Hospital after the attack, where she was in stable condition, according to the Foreign Press Association (FPA). Photos show Levine’s hand and leg wrapped in bandages as she rests in a hospital bed.
The FPA condemned the attack and called on the head of the Israeli military’s Central Command, which governs operations in the West Bank, to “stop making excuses and do its job of protecting civilians from these violent mobs.”
In a statement, the FPA said, “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”
Additional videos from the scene show a man with a bloodied face after the attack, as well as flame pouring out of a burning car with Palestinian license plates. Another video shows Israeli soldiers blocking the road. One soldier films with his phone; a second hurls what appears to be a smoke grenade as a man begs him, “Please don’t do it!”
Israel Police opened an investigation after receiving reports of the attack. In a statement, police said they “view any act of violence with great severity, particularly when it involves members of the media carrying out their work.”
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they would examine “all circumstances” around the incident. “Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area,” the IDF said. “Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable acts.”
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has repeatedly downplayed settler violence as the actions of a rogue group, tried to cast doubt on the attack, saying in a statement on X that “serious questions remain.” He said that Israel “unequivocally condemns violence against anyone,” without issuing any censure of the masked and armed settlers who carried out the attack.
In sharp contrast to Netanyahu, his main rival in the upcoming elections, Gadi Eisenkot, called the attack on Levine “unacceptable” and said these acts “stain an entire nation.”
A U.S. Embassy spokesperson said the U.S. was in regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security in the West Bank.
“We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions of those responsible,” the spokesperson said.
Mustafa Barghouti, head of the Palestinian National Initiative, said on X that “gangs of Israeli terrorist settlers” launched an attack on the village of Abu Falah, where Palestinians were preparing to harvest their olives.
“In full view of the cameras, the settlers set olive trees on fire, pelt Palestinian farmers with stones, and fired live ammunition, resorting to every possible form of terror and intimidation to prevent Palestinians from harvesting their own olive trees,” said Barghouti.

title: Trump administration sues California to block state from counting alleged noncitizen mail-in ballots
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — The Trump administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for next month’s midterm elections from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
The lawsuit comes after the Justice Department said California officials failed to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.
The lawsuit follows a letter sent earlier this week by a top Justice Department official who threatened potential legal action if California didn’t comply.
The federal government didn’t specify where the 20,000 voters were concentrated, but the list was sent directly to Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan on Tuesday, his office confirmed in a statement. His office said the list contained names of voters throughout California, not just Los Angeles, even though Logan is the only county election official named as a defendant in the lawsuit. He doesn’t have jurisdiction over ballots outside Los Angeles County.
In a statement Thursday, Logan said his office can’t withhold ballots or refuse to count them “based solely on unverified allegations.”
Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and there are a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts that could determine which party has control of the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term.
Expert says lawsuit could set stage for false election claims
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a letter to the Justice Department that the federal government hasn’t provided evidence to support its allegation that 20,000 names on the state’s voter rolls are of noncitizens. She referenced an instance in which the federal government initially alleged nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens were listed on Nevada’s voter rolls, but the state determined that all the people flagged were, in fact, U.S. citizens.
She also noted that voting is already underway in the state. Weber, a Democrat, said the Justice Department was “demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide.”
California’s elections are in “full compliance” with federal law, she added.
David Becker, an election law expert who heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research, called the Justice Department’s lawsuit “fairly frivolous.”
“If they were seeking to work in good faith to clean up the voter list that they believed had issues, they would have done this months ago in a much different fashion,” Becker said. “However, it does raise questions as to whether or not the sole purpose of this is to set the stage for false claims about elections.”
List of alleged illegal voters delivered on a thumb drive
Logan said his office received the thumb drive along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device. The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note.”
Becker said most election officials’ cybersecurity protocols would not allow them to comply with the Justice Department’s request as it was sent.
“Election offices do not just stick thumb drives into their technology, for very good reason,” he said.
The Justice Department’s lawsuit says the federal government sought to “work collaboratively” with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, and “California made no serious effort to do so.”
“The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question,” the lawsuit says. “This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined.”
Weber, who is named in the lawsuit, suggested the federal government’s outreach had not been collaborative.
She said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them.
In her letter Thursday, she called the recent demands “an emergency of the DOJ’s creation.”
Letters sent weeks before elections
The letter sent by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter gave the state 48 hours to research the list of the 20,000 people it claims might not be citizens. For those whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their immigration status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received one.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta said at an unrelated press conference Thursday morning that state officials would not carry out the federal government’s requests to withhold ballots for the alleged noncitizen voters. He noted that the administration’s alleged number of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls had dropped from the 190,000 flagged over the summer by the Department of Homeland Security to the 20,000 noted by the Justice Department.
“What happened to those 170,000? They just got those wrong,” Bonta said.
He also said the Trump administration was violating a federal law that prohibits states from changing voter rolls within 90 days of an election.
“They are in unprecedented, baseless, lawless territory,” he said.
The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, defended the Justice Department’s move to take California to court.
“This is not political or controversial,” he wrote in a post on X. “We will not allow California to dilute the votes of American citizens.”
___
Austin reported from Sacramento, Riddle from Los Angeles and Durkin Richer from Washington. Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed.

title: The shocking amount 10 people paid to hunt moose in Maine
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
One hunter bid more than $35,000 for the chance to hunt a moose in Maine this year.
The Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife auctions 10 moose hunting permits annually, giving hunters another way to obtain a permit beyond the state’s public lottery. The sealed-bid auction allows successful bidders to purchase permits, with proceeds supporting youth conservation programs.
The state received 24 bids in its 2026 moose permit auction, with the highest reaching $35,055, according to records obtained by the Bangor Daily News through a Freedom of Access Act request.
The highest bid was $9,132 more than the highest bid five years ago, when a hunter offered $25,923.
Maine’s moose permit auction began in 1995 after the Legislature authorized the program to raise money for youth conservation education.
What hunters paid for Maine moose permits
The 2026 auction received 24 bids, ranging from $2,000 to $35,055. The table below compares the 2026 auction with the previous five years, including the highest bid and combined total of the top 10 bids.
How Maine’s moose permit auction works
Hunters submit bids without knowing what other applicants have offered. After the deadline, the department opens the bids and notifies applicants of the results.
Successful bidders must pay their full bid amount and select an available wildlife management district, hunting week and permit type. Auction permit holders are subject to the same hunting rules and requirements as other moose permit holders.
Hunters can enter both the public moose permit lottery and the auction, but they can receive only one permit. If an auction bidder is selected through the public lottery, the bidder becomes ineligible for the auction and receives a refund of the bid and bidding fee.
Where the money goes
The auction supports youth conservation education in Maine, including scholarships for children to attend conservation camps. The proceeds also help cover the cost of administering the permit issuance process.
In 2025, the auction raised $270,030, according to MDIFW.
The department provided scholarship funding for approximately 450 campers that year. Two organizations received funding: Maine Youth Fish and Game and the University of Maine 4-H Camp and Learning Centers.
The scholarships help Maine children ages 8 to 17 attend conservation camps, where they learn fishing, hunter safety, archery and outdoor survival, along with wildlife and habitat conservation and responsible outdoor recreation.
The department also used $25,000 to coordinate youth outdoor skills events around the state.
MDIFW plans to continue funding camp scholarships in 2026 and use any remaining money for youth outdoor skills events throughout Maine.
The department’s Youth Conservation Camp Grants program provides information about eligibility and curriculum requirements.
What the law requires
Maine law authorizes the auction to fund youth conservation education and directs the revenue, including bidding fees, into a dedicated, nonlapsing account. The money can support youth conservation education programs and the costs of administering the permit issuance process.
The requirements are outlined in Title 12, Section 11154(11) and Title 12, Section 10206(8).

title: First images released of Pope Leo celebrating Mass at hospital after cancer surgery
text:
ROME (AP) — The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Pope Leo XIV since his lung cancer surgery, showing him celebrating Mass, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.
The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him in Gemelli hospital. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.
In his homily, Leo thanked the hospital staff “for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him,” Bruni said.
Bruni also confirmed Leo would make his first public appearance on Sunday to deliver the traditional noontime prayer.
The 71-year-old Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
A signal of all systems go for trip
In the nearer term, Vatican officials were gaming out possible scenarios for Leo to recite the traditional Sunday noontime Angelus prayer. Vatican media personnel were seen at the Gemelli hospital laying cables for a possible live broadcast, as past popes have done when hospitalized. Spokesman Bruni said he would deliver the prayer, but it wasn’t clear where.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said a recitation of the noontime prayer on Sunday from the hospital was a possibility, but would depend on Leo’s recovery. Such appearances have often served as a welcome confirmation of a hospitalized pope’s well-being for the 1.4 billion-strong Catholic faithful and others.
Secretary of state suggests ‘adjustments’
Parolin said he remained concerned about the pope, but indicated that was also a function of his surprise at learning that Leo needed surgery. Parolin, who was considered a leading contender in the conclave that elected Leo and was recently passed over as dean of the College of Cardinals, surprised some by suggesting that the pontificate itself might need to be adjusted.
“We can’t make any type of predictions,” Parolin said Thursday, according to the LaPresse and ANSA news agencies. “The question now is when he will return, under what circumstances he will return, and what the doctors say. And based on all these factors, the pope will then adjust his pontificate, if it needs to be adjusted,” he was quoted as saying.
Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular and genetic makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.
Cancer patients send well-wishing notes to Leo
Meanwhile, the Vatican on Friday released photos of some get-well notes that had been sent to Leo from patients at Gemelli’s pediatric oncology ward, located on the 10th floor, where popes past have often visited during their own hospitalizations.
One, from 7-year-old Angelo, told Leo that he had been on the 10th floor for 36 days. “My mother and I pray for you every night. Get well soon,” he wrote, with little hearts at the bottom.
Giorgia, a university-aged student, wrote to Leo in his native English, saying she had long loved learning and practicing the language.
“When I heard on the news about you and your situation, I felt it a thousand times harder, because in some ways we’re going through the same thing, and it made me feel closer to you,” she wrote. “I pray to God that we both heal and I ask you to pray for me, too.”
___
Associated Press visual journalist Trisha Thomas contributed to this report.

title: Ask 8 Investigates: Why do TV stations continue to run political ads with misleading claims?
text:
Ask 8 Investigates: Why do TV stations continue to run political ads with misleading claims?
'It could be misleading, but it could also be a matter of opinion'
Ask 8 Investigates: Why do TV stations continue to run political ads with misleading claims?
'It could be misleading, but it could also be a matter of opinion'
Viewers have been asking 8 Investigates why TV stations continue to run political ads that include misleading claims.
A nearly 100-year-old law requires stations to air nearly every ad that's purchased by a candidate, regardless of its content.
"I think it would be reassuring to the public that the candidate is speaking their truth as they see it," said Tim Moore, president of the Maine Association of Broadcasters. "It's not always accurate, but that's their viewpoint."
The Communications Act of 1934 requires stations to allow qualified candidates to buy airtime without discrimination or censorship. Ads must meet some requirements, including a disclaimer in which the candidate endorses the message, but otherwise, campaigns have broad creative freedom.
"It could be misleading, but it could also be a matter of opinion," Moore said.
The same rules don’t apply to political issue ads or ads purchased by political action committees. TV stations aren’t required to air them. When Moore ran a radio station, he said, most issue ads were reviewed by the station's attorneys.
"Oftentimes we would have to send it to attorneys to say, 'Is this something that we can run? Is this misleading?' And most of the time we got a green light," Moore said.
Beyond any legal issues, Moore aimed to give advertisers broad access to avoid any appearance of bias.
"I think that stations air on the side of being magnanimous and giving equal access as much as they can to everybody," Moore said.

title: Officials identify teacher, 5-year-old boy among victims in Oregon school shooting
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school, then tackled and fought with him — likely saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said Friday.
City of Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called the teacher’s actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom.
John was once a special needs student at Silver Rail Elementary, authorities said, and he attacked a classroom with special needs students. He fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, Krantz said.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” he said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”
Investigators are trying to determine how the shooter obtained the pump-action shotgun, Krantz added.
A law enforcement official briefed on the shooting told The Associated Press it was bought by his mother. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
The attacker’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told reporters outside her apartment near the school that if she could have done something to prevent the shooting, she would have.
“I miss my boy,” Nickerson said, sobbing and crying, according to The New York Times and CNN. “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
She declined to say how the 16-year-old obtained the pump-action shotgun and didn’t comment further when The Associated Press and other outlets knocked on her apartment door later.
In a 2020 interview with the local news station KTVZ, Nickerson identified the boy, then 10, as a participant in a special needs program run by the school district. It was called NEST, for Nurturing Empathy, Safety and Trust, and aimed at helping students experiencing intensive behavioral and social skill challenges. Nickerson said he struggled trying to learn from home during the pandemic.
Shooter killed minutes after first 911 call
The first 911 call came from the driver of a red pickup truck early Thursday afternoon who saw the boy throw his gun over a fence outside the school and then climb over it, Krantz said. The driver yelled at the boy, who fired at him, striking the truck three times. The driver was not injured.
A second driver, Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old man whose children attend Silver Rail, saw John shooting at the truck and heading toward the school, where he shot through locked doors to get inside. Giamanco pulled into the parking lot, grabbed his .40-caliber pistol and followed the attacker inside. He saw John wrestling with the teacher and shot him several times.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and teacher Megan Lambert, 25, were killed, police said. A 7-year-old child who was injured received lifesaving care at the scene and is now hospitalized, as is 54-year-old teacher Becky Drury, who her family said was shot in the arm and hand and was recovering from surgery.
There were no other children in the classroom, authorities said.
The youngest victim, Rhoam Summer, was a fearless climber and a fast runner who loved reading, his aunt Swan Sheridan said Friday.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” she said.
Man who stopped the shooter a father of 2 at the school
In a statement read to reporters Friday, Giamanco’s mother, Kenda Freeman, identified him as the person who shot the gunman. She said he is the father of two girls at the school.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said.
She said her family was asking for privacy “during this difficult time.”
Silver Rail Elementary has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for schools across Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 that has become a tourism and outdoor recreation hub in central Oregon.
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.
Trump says the shooting could have been much worse
President Donald Trump on Friday praised the man who stopped the gunman, calling him a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy likely would have been much worse.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that someone pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. ”I’m feeling very grateful.”
___
This story has been updated to correct the name of the teacher killed Thursday. She is Megan Lambert, not Meghan Lambert as police originally reported.
___
Associated Press reporters Alanna Durkin Richer, Eric Tucker and Ben Finley in Washington; Jamie Stengle in Dallas; Ed White in Detroit; Philip Marcelo in New York; and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

title: High school QB dismissed from team after calling audible, 12 teammates suspended for supporting him
text:
MESA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A football player in Arizona says his high school playing career is over after being dismissed from the team following a dispute over a play call.
Gunner Brewer, a senior at Desert Ridge High School, said the situation unfolded on the final play of the game two weeks ago when he was quarterbacking the team.
“Basically called the play, trusted my running back behind me who scored a touchdown, definitely was rolling with him,” Brewer said. “The play was originally called for me, but I definitely wanted him to run the ball and get us the first down to basically seal the game.”
Brewer said changing the play at the line was something he had been allowed to do under his previous offensive coordinator, who was fired at the end of September.
The senior quarterback said after the game, head coach Miles Smith asked to speak with him.
Brewer said Smith told him he had disrespected him, and Brewer was cut from the team.
The following Monday, Brewer said 12 other players told coaches they disagreed with the decision. Those players were suspended for the rest of the season, Brewer said.
“They definitely had my back, and I have theirs 100 percent,” Brewer said. “When they did that, I stood right by them.”
Brewer said earlier this season he was late to a meeting because of car trouble and sat out a quarter, but he felt the dismissal was extreme.
“It’s definitely sad,” Brewer said. “Obviously wanted to come off this field with a win on my senior night, but just want to stay humble. And I know that God’s got a plan for me in the future.”
Since his dismissal, Brewer said Smith has only communicated with his mother, except for last week’s game against Ramon, when Brewer said he was told not to be around the team.
“The only word he said to me was when I tried to go help out last week’s game … [he] told me to get out … Don’t go near the field house. Don’t go near the players," Brewer said.
It wasn’t made clear whether there were any other disciplinary issues leading up to the dismissal.
Officials with Desert Ridge High School did not immediately return a request for comment regarding the situation.

Tinnitus affects millions: Why it can be difficult to manage
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — Millions of Americans experience a constant ringing, hissing or humming in their ears, a condition known as tinnitus. For some, the sound never stops.
Ken Seibert has worn hearing aids for about 20 years. The devices amplify his hearing and also help muffle unwanted sounds caused by his tinnitus.
Goutham Gosu, a doctor of audiology, works with patients like Seibert to manage the condition.
“It’s an unwanted sound that they’re perceiving in the ear,” Gosu said.
Gosu said tinnitus is difficult to measure because it relies on a patient’s description.
“It’s really hard to gauge from a medical standpoint, what the person is feeling, perceiving. We just have to go by how they’re explaining it,” Gosu said.
How many people are affected
The American Tinnitus Association says more than 50 million American adults experience tinnitus. The condition is chronic for 5 million of those people.
Seibert described the sound as similar to air being let out of a tire. He said it is constant.
“If you’re listening to music, TV, anything, it can always be in the background of that,” Seibert said.
Seibert said he has had the condition for 30 years and has tried supplements, hearing aids and acupuncture to manage it. He said some methods have helped, but nothing has eliminated it completely.
Identifying the cause
Gosu said determining the right treatment depends on the cause, which can be difficult to identify.
“The tinnitus can come from as simple thing as a wax in the ear,” Gosu said. “Hearing loss too. Blood pressure. TMJ issues, dental issues, all the way to acoustic neuroma.”
Gosu said everyone experiences ringing in the ears at some point but recommended getting checked if it happens frequently.
“If you start noticing it like, you know, two or three times a week or something like that, there might be something going on,” Gosu said.
The cause of tinnitus is unknown, but the condition tends to be more common among people with loud jobs, such as musicians and veterans.
Gosu said in cases like Seibert’s, there is no obvious explanation and treatment focuses on managing the condition.
“I’ve tried everything and I can’t make it go away,” Seibert said. “The hearing aids help me overall to live a more wonderful life, if you will. But I still always have it in the background.”

title: I support Lead Maine’s scrutiny of MaineCare
text:
MaineCare, at its finest, provides vital healthcare services to vulnerable Maine citizens. Or it should. However, disturbing allegations of fraud have made it clear that stricter methods for accountability need to be implemented in our state.
In addition, grossly inadequate living conditions for autistic individuals under MaineCare have been uncovered by the Maine Wire. As a wife, mother and grandmother who raised my family in Maine, I am finding it difficult to understand why our state government does not do more to protect these individuals.
As a concerned Maine citizen, I want to know that my tax dollars are being used responsibly by our elected officials. I want to know that those who truly need help are getting it the best way possible.
That is why the rules Lead Maine is proposing for MaineCare to adopt are essential in protecting the most vulnerable people in our state (“Amid fraud concerns, conservative group pushes for new MaineCare oversight rules,” June 23). These two rules require on-site inspections of MaineCare providers and pausing payment to providers if improper billing for services is detected by onsite inspections.
These rules are not onerous or overreaching. They are a commonsense approach to beginning the task of making MaineCare truly accountable to the people of Maine.

Livermore Falls

title: Affordability, Social Security driving Maine voters 50 and older
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Affordability, Social Security driving Maine voters 50 and older
AARP Maine’s poll shows voters aged 50 and older are highly motivated to vote in November, prioritizing electricity costs, Social Security, and caregiving policies.
Affordability, Social Security driving Maine voters 50 and older
AARP Maine’s poll shows voters aged 50 and older are highly motivated to vote in November, prioritizing electricity costs, Social Security, and caregiving policies.
A new AARP Maine poll reveals that voters aged 50 and older are highly motivated to vote in November, with electricity costs, Social Security, and caregiving policies among their top concerns.
The group remains a powerful voting bloc. According to the poll, 87% of voters aged 50 and older are “extremely motivated” to vote, compared with 73% of voters under 50.
“Older voters have always been the most committed voters,” AARP Maine State Director Noël Bonam said. “And they're most likely to show up.”
Affordability is a pressing issue for older voters, with nearly half of those surveyed saying rising electricity costs have forced them to cut spending on other essentials.
“They're keeping the house darker much longer. They are not turning on all the lights when they go from one room to another. They're being extremely judicious to keep those electric rates low just because they're having to pay so much on a monthly basis,” Bonam said.
Social Security is also a significant factor influencing voters. The poll found that 81% of respondents consider the program important to their vote, and 93% are more likely to support candidates committed to protecting its benefits.
“I think the number one concern that AARP has about when it comes to Social Security is the lack of action,” Bonam said.
Caregiving policies have strong support as well. More than half of older voters identified themselves as current or former family caregivers, and 76% favor assistance for unpaid caregivers. Bonam said measures such as respite care and home accessibility improvements could provide meaningful support.

title: Who was the protester who interrupted the Susan Collins-Troy Jackson debate?
text:
A Bowdoin College student was removed from Thursday’s U.S. Senate debate after he stood and began yelling that data centers “are poisoning our waters.”
The moment came about 15 minutes into the fourth and final televised debate between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democrat Troy Jackson. It led to Collins quipping that it “was obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” to which Jackson replied, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” Thursday’s debate was the only one of the four to feature a live audience.
Henry Elgie, 19, was the protester whom security removed from the Gracie Theatre at Husson University in Bangor, according to a news release from the Sunrise Movement, a national progressive group focused on young people who are “fighting to stop the climate crisis and win a Green New Deal.”
“I’m so sorry to interrupt, but I’m a young person and I’m terrified. AI data centers are destroying our climate,” Elgie, who appeared to be wearing a press badge, shouted as security moved to take him out of the venue. “They are poisoning our waters. You are taking corporate PAC money to an absurd degree.”
Event organizers said the person was not on the pre-registered media list but presented a Bowdoin Orient press badge and was allowed in. In a statement Thursday night, the editor-in-chief of the Orient said the student paper did not send anyone to the debate and that the credential must have been fabricated.
A Sunrise Movement spokesperson said Friday that Elgie lives and is registered to vote in Brunswick, where Bowdoin is located.
The Sunrise Movement news release that came out late Thursday night made clear that Elgie was directing his words at Collins. It included a statement from Elgie that criticized Collins and her campaign for receiving donations from billionaires and executives of artificial intelligence platforms.
“Instead of investing in real climate solutions, Susan Collins continues to prioritize endless war and tax cuts for billionaires. My generation deserves a livable future,” Elgie said in a statement.
Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen responded Friday by sharing a photo the campaign took of pro-Jackson and pro-Collins supporters who were outside of the Oct. 8 debate hosted by WMTW. A person in the photo was holding a fake check in the amount of $150,000 made out to 1820 PAC, a reference to the ProPublica story on pay-to-play allegations surrounding Collins.
The Collins campaign said the person holding the check last week was Elgie.
The Jackson campaign did not respond to a request for comment Friday morning.
Jackson supported the proposed moratorium on large data centers in Maine that Gov. Janet Mills, an outgoing Democrat, vetoed earlier this year. Mills cited concerns that the proposed pause on new centers until November 2027 would have killed a project in the mill town of Jay. (That project went on hold this summer, despite the veto.)
Collins aligned herself with Mills earlier this year, expressing support in August for projects at former mill sites and saying “there is usually hydropower right there, so there’s an energy source built in.” But Collins has also called for federal guardrails on data center development, including regulations on how much water and energy they use.
President Donald Trump has called for more data center development, despite public polling in Maine and nationally showing a majority of Americans from both parties oppose data centers getting built in their communities.

title: Making Something Out of Anything
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - An old television set, a storm door and even vacuum cleaner attachments - all found new purpose in the hands of one resourceful craftsman. It’s the focus of this week’s Throwback Thursday with Brian Bouchard.
Most of us have something around the house we probably ought to throw away. Paul Cote might have asked you to save it for him. In this week’s Throwback Thursday, we dial the time machine back to 1983 as WAGM reporter Frank Graff meets a retired craftsman who could turn just about anything into something useful.
Even the sound of wind chimes will tell you there’s something different about the man who lives in this house. Though they sound like any other wind chimes, look closely, for they are really old electric sweeper attachments. The sign out front is also handmade, as is the wind vane atop the garage. But this is just a few of 71-year-old Paul Cote’s ingenious handiworks. He’s also made a display railing for China plates from clothespins, a China cabinet from an old storm door, headboards from coffee tables, and a bar from an old TV set, just to name a few creations. Why?
“We don’t waste nothing. We can make everything. Make everything go for one thing or another. We make something out of it. If we got something that somebody else say, well, take that to the dump, I would say give it to me. Maybe I can come up with something and do something out of it, you know? So I do things like that.”
Cote is also a model craftsman. He makes scale model sleds and wagons complete with brakes, all in surprisingly accurate detail. But Cote’s biggest prize is the house he built. It’s made of hand-cut wood on a one inch to 1 foot scale. Cote says he got the idea from Popular Mechanics magazine and was going to build the house himself for he and his wife to live in when they moved to northern Maine from Florida. He bought a house instead, but he decided to make it anyway on a smaller scale.
“The idea is to make things to keep you busy. You see after you retire. I’ve always been active all my life and after I retired you can’t just sit down and watch TV. You got to do something. You got to keep moving. If you don’t, but you’re going to cramp and you’re going to stay right there sitting down. You ain’t going to get up again.”
And if hand-making washers and dryers, drapes and furniture weren’t enough, the house is even insulated. Cote says it helps the resale value. Cotte says his handmaking skills were passed down in his family. His ancestors were early settlers in New Brunswick and now even though he’s a retired builder, brick mason and blacksmith, Cote says he still must build. Whether it’s model houses or a new lawnmower because the old one broke, Paul Cote says he isn’t near ready to give in to old age.
Frank Graff, Newsline 8.

title: Customer sues taco chain after finding cow tooth in order
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (KVUE) — A Texas woman is suing a taco restaurant after she said she found an animal tooth in her food.
The company confirmed the item was a cow tooth.
The woman ordered a Democrat taco for takeout from the Torchy’s Tacos location on South Congress in Austin, according to her lawyer, Scott Vasquez.
“Her reaction was disgust. ‘What is this?’ Looking at it, she thought it was a tooth,” Vasquez said.
Vasquez said his client immediately contacted him. He said when he tried to get answers about what was in the food, a manager and a lawyer at Torchy’s Tacos kept passing the blame.
“I thought they’d want to take care of this internally immediately, and apparently not. They just felt, in my view, ‘Let’s blame someone else,’” Vasquez said.
Lawsuit filed Tuesday
In a lawsuit filed Tuesday, Vasquez claims Torchy’s Tacos knew, or should have known, that this could end up in its food and was negligent about safety standards.
“Someone should have caught it somewhere throughout the process. Should not have even made it to the packaging or the packaged goods that they had,” Vasquez said.
Company response
A Torchy’s Tacos spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the company is aware of the situation and takes all concerns about its food seriously.
The spokesperson said Torchy’s Tacos sources the highest-quality food, and the barbacoa meat in the taco comes from natural beef cheek that the company gets from a supplier.
Upon receiving the guest’s complaint, the company said it conducted a thorough review and identified the item as a cow tooth. The spokesperson said this can occasionally happen and that Torchy’s Tacos has partnered with the supplier to reinforce internal procedures to prevent it from happening again.
“It could choke somebody. It really could,” Vasquez said.
Vasquez said Torchy’s Tacos should have been more forthcoming with a solution.
“How would you feel if you found a large, seemingly cow tooth in your Democrat taco in Austin, Texas, and the folks who gave you that don’t want to make it right?” Vasquez said.
The lawsuit is seeking $250,000 or less, as determined by a jury.

title: US Coast Guard rescues at least 16 and is searching for more in the water off Mexico's Baja Coast
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — At least 16 people seen floating in the Pacific Ocean off Mexico’s Baja California coast were rescued in the predawn hours Friday, and authorities were searching for several others in an area frequented by smugglers transporting migrants by boat to the U.S.
Those rescued were being taken to San Diego hospitals. One person was being treated for a suspected shark bite.
The Coast Guard responded to a report of a vessel in distress at around 1 a.m., authorities said.
People were found floating in the water about 140 miles (225 kilometers) west of Ensenada, said Petty Officer Chris Sappey. Several smuggling boats have capsized over the years in fatal accidents in the area.
“There was no sight of a vessel in the water, just straight people in the water,” Sappey said.
One person rescued said as many as 27 people had been on board a boat, Sappey said. It was unclear how the people ended up in the water, and Sappey had no further details on what they were doing.
Three of the people rescued were taken to Scripps Mercy Hospital San Diego including the person with a suspected shark bite and two people treated for cold exposure, said hospital spokesperson Janice Collins.
The Coast Guard and U.S. Navy were assisting Mexican authorities in the search with two helicopters, a fixed-wing plane and a cutter, Sappey said.
Messages seeking information were left for San Diego’s Fire-Rescue Department.
Migrants are increasingly turning to the risky alternative offered by smugglers to travel by sea to avoid heavily guarded land borders. Small boats called pangas leave Baja in the dead of night and sometimes travel hundreds of miles (kilometers) north.
There have been several incidents in recent years of migrant vessels capsizing en route to California.
In May of 2025, at least three people died when a panga flipped off the coast about 35 miles (56 km) north of the U.S.-Mexico border. In 2023, eight people were killed in one of the deadliest maritime smuggling accidents off the U.S. coast, when two boats approached a San Diego beach in heavy fog and one capsized in the surf.
A federal judge sentenced a San Diego man to 18 years in prison in 2022 for piloting a small vessel overloaded with 32 migrants that smashed apart in powerful surf off the coast, killing three people and injuring more than two dozen.
__
Brown reported from Billings, Montana.

title: Teen shooter who killed 4 at Oregon elementary school was a former student, police say
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school, then tackled and fought with him — likely saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said Friday.
City of Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called the teacher’s actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom.
John was once a special needs student at Silver Rail Elementary, authorities said, and he attacked a classroom with special needs students. He fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, Krantz said.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” he said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”
Investigators are trying to determine how the shooter obtained the pump-action shotgun, Krantz added.
A law enforcement official briefed on the shooting told The Associated Press it was bought by his mother. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
The attacker’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told reporters outside her apartment near the school that if she could have done something to prevent the shooting, she would have.
“I miss my boy,” Nickerson said, sobbing and crying, according to The New York Times and CNN. “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
She declined to say how the 16-year-old obtained the pump-action shotgun and didn’t comment further when The Associated Press and other outlets knocked on her apartment door later.
In a 2020 interview with the local news station KTVZ, Nickerson identified the boy, then 10, as a participant in a special needs program run by the school district. It was called NEST, for Nurturing Empathy, Safety and Trust, and aimed at helping students experiencing intensive behavioral and social skill challenges. Nickerson said he struggled trying to learn from home during the pandemic.
Shooter killed minutes after first 911 call
The first 911 call came from the driver of a red pickup truck early Thursday afternoon who saw the boy throw his gun over a fence outside the school and then climb over it, Krantz said. The driver yelled at the boy, who fired at him, striking the truck three times. The driver was not injured.
A second driver, Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old man whose children attend Silver Rail, saw John shooting at the truck and heading toward the school, where he shot through locked doors to get inside. Giamanco pulled into the parking lot, grabbed his .40-caliber pistol and followed the attacker inside. He saw John wrestling with the teacher and shot him several times.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and teacher Megan Lambert, 25, were killed, police said. A 7-year-old child who was injured received lifesaving care at the scene and is now hospitalized, as is 54-year-old teacher Becky Drury, who her family said was shot in the arm and hand and was recovering from surgery.
There were no other children in the classroom, authorities said.
The youngest victim, Rhoam Summer, was a fearless climber and a fast runner who loved reading, his aunt Swan Sheridan said Friday.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” she said.
Man who stopped the shooter a father of 2 at the school
In a statement read to reporters Friday, Giamanco’s mother, Kenda Freeman, identified him as the person who shot the gunman. She said he is the father of two girls at the school.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said.
She said her family was asking for privacy “during this difficult time.”
Silver Rail Elementary has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for schools across Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 that has become a tourism and outdoor recreation hub in central Oregon.
Trump says the shooting could have been much worse
President Donald Trump on Friday praised the man who stopped the gunman, calling him a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy likely would have been much worse.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that someone pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. ”I’m feeling very grateful.”
___
This story has been updated to correct the name of the teacher killed Thursday. She is Megan Lambert, not Meghan Lambert as police originally reported.
___
Associated Press reporters Alanna Durkin Richer, Eric Tucker and Ben Finley in Washington; Jamie Stengle in Dallas; Ed White in Detroit; Philip Marcelo in New York; and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

title: White House Press Secretary leaving role days after first briefing
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Katie Zacharia will be “transitioning out” of her role as White House press secretary, a White House official said Friday, three days after her first briefing.
Her introductory press conference lasted 14 minutes.
Following the briefing, where she took questions from three outlets, Zacharia received scrutiny over her performance and for referring to herself as a lawyer despite failing the bar exam. Her abilities were criticized by multiple conservative members of the media.
President Donald Trump addressed the coverage Friday.
“Generally the media has been very rough. She was on Sean Hannity last night, and Sean was a little bit tough. And she did, I saw FOX and Friends this morning. They were a little tough,” Trump said.
The announcement of Zacharia’s departure came shortly after she spoke with Trump.
“I said Katie, you know, you don’t have to do this if you don’t want. She said this is a lot tougher. I said welcome to the world of Trump,” Trump said.
Zacharia is expected to remain in the administration in some capacity. A successor as White House Press Secretary has not been named.

title: Trump’s Russian diesel deal is disingenuous — at best

text:
On Oct. 11, President Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” deal between Russia and Ukraine, a “deal” that Ukrainian President Zelensky knew nothing about and that was violated by Russia; mere hours later a Ukrainian thermal power plant in Kharkiv was struck.
This was on the heels of Trump shamelessly upbraiding Zelensky for prior targeting of energy plants and refineries in Russia and declaring that fuel targets within the Russian diesel supply chain were off limits — but only for the Ukrainian defenders.
Trump’s recent deal with Putin — to purchase Russian diesel — is a thinly veiled ploy to assuage concern about skyrocketing prices just weeks before the midterm elections. Trump’s claim that the high prices are attributable to the Ukrainians, and not his disastrous Iran invasion debacle, is a pipe dream. It is farcical that the man who so covets a Nobel Peace Prize apparently cares more about ceasefires to protect energy consumption than ceasefires to prevent the wanton killing of civilians.

title: Patriots try to avoid letdown against Jets
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The New England Patriots are coming off their best performance of the season, doing almost everything they wanted during a 28-point win over the Las Vegas Raiders.
But there are plenty of reasons for New England to be on guard against the Jets this week. And it starts with Geno Smith.
It’s not just that the veteran New York quarterback has not thrown an interception this season in five starts, the longest opening stretch to a season in his career without one. He also has had the Patriots’ number of late, winning in each of his past two trips to Foxborough (with Seattle in 2024 and Las Vegas in 2025).
In last season’s win with the Raiders, Smith completed 70% of his passes for 362 yards and spoiled Mike Vrabel’s coaching debut with the Patriots.
“They’ve got great players, they’re coached by Mike Vrabel, who’s a defensive guy, so we know he wants to have that defense be at the forefront and they want to establish the run as well on offense, so another great opportunity for us,” Smith said.
Smith’s care of the football has allowed the Jets to enter with a plus-3 turnover differential, compared to a Patriots team that has forced a total of six turnovers, ranking 19th in the NFL entering Week 6.
That’s a concern for Vrabel.
“(Smith has) done a fantastic job. And so, if you want to try to create turnovers, you’re going to have to actually go out and force them,” Vrabel said.
The Patriots also enter with a long list of injured players, including left tackle Will Campbell (right knee) and running back TreVeyon Henderson (ankle). That was on top of cornerback Christian Gonzalez missing his second straight game last weekend because of a shoulder injury and Carlton Davis III sitting out because of a neck injury.
The good news is wide receiver A.J. Brown returned to practice for the first time since going on injured reserve after sustaining a high ankle sprain in New England’s season-opening loss at Seattle. He said he’s impressed with how his fellow receivers performed in his absence.
“Whenever I decide to come back, I’m just going to add,” Brown said.
Need to know
New York Jets (2-3) at New England (3-2)
When/where to watch: 1 p.m. Sunday, CBS
Latest odds: Patriots by 7
Against the spread: Jets 3-1-1; Patriots 3-1-1
Last week: Jets beat Browns, 17-12; Patriots beat Raiders, 45-17
Last meeting: Patriots won 42-10 on Dec. 28, 2025, in East Rutherford, NJ.
Series record: Patriots lead, 77-56-1
Matchup to watch
Patriots offensive line vs. Jets defensive line. The Jets have shown an ability to punch the ball out, recovering five fumbles so far. Drake Maye will be playing behind an O-line that may not have Campbell at full strength, creating opportunities to get to Maye, who has lost two of his five fumbles this season.
Stats and stuff
• Rookie edge rusher David Bailey, the No. 2 overall pick in April, was selected the AFC defensive player of the week after he had three sacks. He’s the third player since 2003 to have a three-sack performance in his first five NFL games, joining Detroit’s Aidan Hutchinson (2022) and Denver’s Elvis Dumervil (2006).
• The Jets are tied with the Los Angeles Chargers for second in the NFL with 47 penalties, two behind Cleveland.
• Braelon Allen had a career-high 116 yards rushing and the winning 22-yard touchdown on 24 carries last Sunday while filling in for the second game in a row for the injured Breece Hall.
• New York has held three of its first five opponents under 200 yards after not doing so in any game last season. The Jets are the first NFL team to hold three teams under 200 yards in the first five games since the 1999 Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
• The Jets had eight sacks against the Browns, led by Bailey’s three, tying the franchise high in a single game by the team since sacks became an official NFL statistic in 1982.
• Smith (147 attempts), Detroit’s Jared Goff (191) and Houston’s C.J. Stroud (185) are the only players with no INTs through five starts this season. Smith’s 69.4% completion rate is second highest behind Cincinnati’s Joe Burrow among QBs with at least 100 pass attempts.
• New England has won three straight and 18 of the past 20 against the Jets.
•The Patriots are coming off a season-high 536 yards in last week’s win over Las Vegas. The most recent time they had two games with at least 500 yards in the same season was in 2014.
• The Patriots, 2-0 at Gillette Stadium, haven’t started a season 3-0 at home since 2019, when they won their first five home games.
• Hunter Henry (3,150 receiving yards) needs 8 yards to move past Russ Francis into third place on New England’s all-time receiving yards list among tight ends.

title: Letter: Donald Trump’s Ukraine deal is a stain on America
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
President Donald Trump’s betrayal of Ukraine leaves a stain on this country that may never be erased. In a desperate bid to stave off disaster in the midterms, he has arranged to buy fuel from Russia. He blames the high price of oil on Ukraine for its drone attacks on Russian refineries; in fact the main reason oil prices have skyrocketed is his ill-considered war of choice against Iran, resulting in a bottleneck at the Strait of Hormuz. The deal gives Russia much-needed funds to pursue its bombing of Ukraine’s civilians and infrastructure (war crimes).
In August, Congress passed a law that provides for more economic sanctions against Russia. The bill, signed by the president, was named after the late Sen. Lindsay Graham, a strong supporter of Ukraine and a golfing buddy of Trump’s. Will Congress stand up to defend its prerogatives and what’s right? I’m not confident.
In 1994, when world leaders were concerned about nuclear proliferation, Ukraine was persuaded to give up its significant stockpile of nuclear weapons in return for security guarantees from the United States, the United Kingdom and Russia. Russia, quite obviously, has broken that agreement with its attacks on Ukraine, invading and annexing Crimea in 2014 and sending its tanks toward Kiev in 2022. Now the U.S. is abrogating that agreement as well by withholding support from Ukraine.
If laws and international guarantees are now meaningless, where are we?
Christina Diebold
Bangor

title: Sean 'Diddy' Combs moved to a new prison after reports of a luxury lifestyle behind bars
text:
Sean 'Diddy' Combs moved to a new prison after reports of a luxury lifestyle behind bars
Sean “Diddy” Combs has been moved to a federal prison in Pennsylvania after reports that the hip-hop mogul was living the high life and was injured in a fight at his New Jersey lockup, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press on Friday.
The federal Bureau of Prisons is transferring Combs, 56, from FCI Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low, a low-security facility south of Williamsport and about 155 miles west of New York City, the person said.
Related video above | Trump confirms Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs asked him for a pardon
The person was not authorized to speak publicly and did so on condition of anonymity.
The Bureau of Prisons confirmed the move but provided no further details. The agency said it does not discuss conditions of confinement for anyone in its custody, including reasons for transfer, for privacy, safety, and security reasons.
“Decisions about inmate placement are made by the BOP, and we are not in a position to speak to the circumstances surrounding this transfer,” said Combs’ spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer. “Sean remains focused on moving forward, and we hope that his time at the new facility will be productive and without unnecessary disruption.”
Combs is serving a four-year, two-month sentence for his conviction last year on prostitution-related charges for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters. The case featured harrowing testimony about violence and sex parties he called “freak-offs.” It was a forceful reckoning for one of music and entertainment’s most influential figures.
Last month, NBC News reported that Combs was continuing to enjoy aspects of his millionaire lifestyle at FCI Fort Dix, smuggling in Hennessy, having fellow inmates cook, clean, make his bed and give him massages, and using a contraband cellphone to view social media and an ex-girlfriend’s nude selfies.
On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Combs was injured in a fight with another inmate at Fort Dix and had to be taken out of the prison for treatment. In a rare rebuttal, the Bureau of Prisons refuted TMZ’s report, telling the AP: “The story you are referring to is false and did not happen.”
In the wake of the NBC report, Combs was placed in the prison’s special housing unit, a heavily secured part of the facility away from the general population, for inmates with disciplinary issues or security concerns. He has also been docked 41 days of good-conduct credit, pushing his release date back to March 2, 2028, according to the person familiar with the matter.
In April, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in Combs’ bid to overturn his conviction and sentence, which his lawyers argued was too harsh. The court has yet to rule.

title: Community leaders say foiled Illinois mass shooting was result of surge in anti-Hindu hate online
text:
A thwarted mass shooting targeting a large Hindu temple in suburban Chicago was fueled by years of hateful rhetoric on social media against Hindus and Indians, community leaders say.
Authorities on Wednesday arrested Alexandros Paporakis, 19, who they said drove to the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Illinois, on Sunday afternoon, armed with a rifle and body armor. Officials said he remained in the parking lot for several minutes, but left after his weapon jammed. Paporakis was arrested later that day near his home in Palatine, Illinois, after a co-worker at a Taco Bell alerted authorities to his plan to “kill Indian people.”
The temple, the largest in Aurora, was crowded Sunday with thousands observing the first day of Navaratri, a nine-night celebration of Shakti — the divine feminine energy believed to be foundational to all creation.
U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who represents Illinois’ 8th congressional district, said he and his parents were inside the temple Sunday afternoon.
“Little did we know there was an attacker outside with sinister intent,” he said Thursday. “This has really shaken us.”
During a news conference Friday morning in Chicago, Krishnamoorthi stood with several other faith and civic leaders calling for the attempted mass shooting to be investigated as a hate crime. Speakers also called for an organized community response to prevent hate and extremism targeting all communities.
Hindus face online hate and real-world threats
Pushpita Prasad, a spokesperson for the Coalition of Hindus of North America, said attacks against Hindus and Indians have been escalating in recent years. She said the racial slurs are increasingly visible online.
“You see vitriolic posts associating Indians with dirt and creating disgust about their appearance, food and cultural practices,” she said. “Sooner or later, all that online hate is going to migrate to the real world.”
Over the past two years, the rising wave of anti-Hindu hate has included a rash of vandalism and attacks across the country. Most recently, on Oct. 3, vandals hurled bricks at a Hindu temple in Richmond Heights, Ohio, shattering several windows while devotees were praying inside.
In June 2025, a gunman fired bullets into the Sri Sri Radha Krishna Temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, causing thousands of dollars in damage. In Sugar Land, Texas, a 90-foot statue of the deity Hanuman, consecrated in 2024 at a temple complex, continues to draw disparaging comments, including one YouTube personality who recently urged its demolition.
In Frisco, Texas, where people of Indian origin make up about one-third of the population, speakers have used public comment periods during city council meetings to label the Indian community as “invaders,” characterize Hindu temples as a threat and accuse H-1B work visa holders of stealing American jobs or committing fraud.
Leaders call for resources to combat hate and extremism
Temple administrators in Aurora issued a statement Thursday assuring the community that they value the safety of devotees, employees and volunteers, and have implemented additional security measures including an “armed security presence.”
Krishnamoorthi said the temple, situated on 20 acres, is a cultural hub for the community in the Chicago area. It has been his family’s home away from home for about 40 years, he said.
“For people who were newly immigrated, this became their connection to the homeland,” Krishnamoorthi said.
The temple serves as a venue for concerts, dance performances, birthdays and weddings, and the cafeteria that serves South Indian cuisine is popular, he said.
Krishnamoorthi called for the FBI to prosecute this incident as a hate crime, and for social media companies to end the hateful rhetoric online.
“The FBI also needs to redirect resources to combat domestic violent extremism,” he said. “Election fraud and immigration are not the biggest threats facing our country.”
Joel Finkelstein with the New Jersey-based Network Contagion Research Institute, which tracks cyber-social threats, said in 2025, anti-Indian content on X tripled in weekly volume. The administration’s changes in immigration policies, particularly relating to the H1-B visa, corresponded with measurable surges in racial slurs and deportation rhetoric targeting Indians, he said.
Amid the increase in online hate, Finkelstein said the South Asian community in the U.S., despite significant resources, lacks the ability to advocate for itself with strength and unity.
“There is nothing to stop it from getting worse,” he said.
Advocates say xenophobia has fueled hate
Sravya Tadepalli, executive director of Hindus for Human Rights, says her organization has formed strong coalitions with Muslim, Sikh and other organizations whose members also face hate.
“It’s important to understand that rhetoric is not just rhetoric,” she said. “It is harmful and can result in violence.”
Manjusha P. Kulkarni, co-founder of Stop AAPI Hate, said her organization’s research showed that online slurs targeting South Asians rose 109% from 2023 to 2025. Statistics aside, Kulkarni said she was personally shaken by the threat in Illinois.
“It hits all of us who are temple goers,” she said. “Seeing how going to my house of worship can put me and my children at risk is very scary.”
AAPI Hate pointed to “xenophobic policies and rhetoric” that depict Indian people as a demographic threat — including Vice President JD Vance calling H1-B workers “indentured servants” and Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas’ Railroad Commission calling South Asian students at a Longhorns football game “a problem.” French’s post led to a flurry of other posts on social media calling for violence against Indian communities, including desecrating Hindu temples and statues.
Last month, a Sikh truck driver was stabbed in Wyoming, days after the Department of Homeland Security published a derogatory social media post about Sikh truck drivers.
Sikh temple shooting survivor stresses need for meaningful dialogue
Pardeep Kaleka’s father, Satwant Singh Kaleka, was one of six people killed in 2012 in a mass shooting at their gurdwara in Oak Creek, Wisconsin – the deadliest anti-Sikh attack in the U.S. The shooter, Wade Michael Page, was a self-proclaimed white supremacist.
After Paporakis’ arrest in Illinois, authorities said they recovered weapons, ammunition, a gas canister labeled with a slur referring to South Asians and several items depicting Nazi symbols. Officials said Paporakis wrote a manifesto in which he fantasized about mass murder and expressed his desire to kill as many non-white people as he could.
Kaleka, who co-wrote a book with a former white supremacist about his own journey of forgiveness after the Sikh temple shooting, said the young men who perpetrate these attacks don’t pop up suddenly.
“Most people who do this have lost hope, and their motivation is also to have you and society lose hope,” he said. “Their belief is if you can attack people in the space they hold most sacred, it plants a deep terror in communities.”
The solution is to have candid conversations across racial and religious boundaries so people can understand each other at a human level, Kaleka said. “Unless that happens, we’re more likely to see division rather than a collective spirit that joins us together.”

title: This forgotten Hollywood star was Maine’s Elizabeth Taylor
text:
She was a darling of television. Maine’s “girl next door.” A “raving beauty” who could have passed for Elizabeth Taylor’s sister.
Cancer, however, cut her career short, and she’s largely faded into obscurity despite the many credits to her name.
Born on March 12, 1933, Myrna Fahey spent her earliest years in Carmel before her family moved to Bangor and then settled down in Southwest Harbor, where her father, Francis, worked as a shipbuilder.
A young Fahey didn’t always pine for the glamour of Tinseltown.
As a child, she envisioned a life working as a designer, teacher or even a guide, considering herself an expert at canoeing. Fahey worked briefly at Rines Co. on Main Street in downtown Bangor — a storefront that later became home to Rebecca’s Gift Shop and then Out on a Whimsey Toys.
But it wasn’t until her final year at Pemetic High School, in 1950, when the allure of acting became too strong to ignore.
“Then by the time I was 17 I felt life had to provide me with more excitement than merely existing. Acting seemed to be the one career which could do it,” she told legendary gossip columnist Hedda Hopper in 1959.
Fahey’s parents, though, weren’t enthusiastic about their daughter’s career ambitions.
“I guess father learned more about me in the arguments which followed my declaration of intention,” Myrna told Hopper in 1959, “than he’d gathered in all the years that went before. He couldn’t have been more amazed if I’d said I was embarking on a career as tail gunner on a spaceship. It really shook him out of his New England calm. He found out he and I were very much alike and both could be stubborn over an issue; but this time I won.”
She attended the Pasadena College of Theatre Arts and spent time at the Pasadena Playhouse, working under the tutelage of writer John Butler, a family friend.
Like any New Englander, she worked hard to break into the biz, starting out humbly hocking toothpaste and detergent in TV ads before finally getting real roles.
Fahey was prolific in her early years in Hollywood, performing in some 40 television plays, by her own count, in the mid-1950s. Her first big role, although uncredited, came in 1955, when she appeared alongside Jack Palance, Lee Marvin and a young Dennis Hopper in the noir film “I Died a Thousand Times,” promoted earlier under the title “A Handful of Clouds.”
Around this time, Fahey attracted the eye of photographer Paul Hesse, who convinced her to try for the 1956 Miss Rheingold title, eventually becoming one of six finalists in the nationwide beauty contest.
Fahey wasn’t new to the world of beauty competitions; she was crowned the Hancock Poultry Queen in 1951 and was a finalist for Miss Maine in 1952.
Although she didn’t get the Miss Rheingold title, Fahey was now a recognizable face from Bangor to Barstow.
Then, in 1959, she got her biggest role to date, appearing with Rita Hayworth and Tony Franciosa in “The Story on Page One.” Director Clifford Odets saw big potential in the Mainer, telling a reporter, “This girl has a big career ahead of her.”
By this time, Fahey’s mother, Olevia, had come out to California to help maintain her daughter’s home, but the New Englander didn’t take to the Hollywood life like Myrna, often speaking tersely and curtly to studio people on the telephone.
And when that big break came in 1959, the elder Fahey wasn’t impressed, Myrna Fahey told Hopper.
“I breathlessly described every step of the whole thing to Mother without getting a reaction to anything I’d been saying. I said: ‘Oh Mother, aren’t you thrilled? Aren’t you going to say anything?’ She came over to put her hand on my shoulder, said: ‘Yes, dear, of course I’m pleased since you are, but I don’t like to see you get so excited over these things; it isn’t at all like a state-of-Maine girl.’”
Fahey’s biggest role came the next year, when she appeared alongside Mark Damon and Vincent Price in Roger Corman’s adaptation of Edgar Allan Poe’s gothic tale of decadence, isolation and madness, “The Fall of the House of Usher.”
Fahey played Madeline Usher, the sickly sister of Roderick Usher, the anxious, oversensitive and hypochondriatic scion who longs to see his family line extirpated. When she falls into a cataleptic state, Roderick entombs her alive in the family crypt to keep her from marriage. But consumed with a murderous rage, she escapes the tomb to seek revenge.
“House of Usher,” her last film role, was a staple in Greater Bangor theaters throughout 1960.
It was around this time, as Fahey told Los Angeles Times television critic Cecil Smith, that her parents had come around and were “all for” her Hollywood ambitions.
Into the 1960s, Fahey racked up appearances on numerous popular television shows, including “Batman,” “Bonanza,” “Father of the Bride,” “Gunsmoke,” “Maverick” and “Perry Mason,” becoming, as a Bangor Daily News reporter put it, “one of the best known actresses in modern television.”
And she didn’t shy away from far more colorful roles, playing dipsomaniacs and “bad girls” that got her away from the “simpering sweet parts” often written for women.
Despite her success, Fahey didn’t conform to the Hollywood life, preferring to spend her time skiing and boating rather than drinking and schmoozing with actors and other Hollywood types. That’s no surprise given she came from a conservative New England family.
As the ’60s drew to a close, Fahey was diagnosed with cancer. She died May 6, 1973, at St. John’s Hospital in Santa Monica, California.
Fahey once mused to a reporter that she might never return to live full time in Maine. Although the allure of California and Hollywood held her in life, Fahey chose Mount Pleasant Catholic Cemetery in Bangor for her long repose.
