title: I’m showing that anyone can run for Senate, without millions of dollars
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Brent Andrews is an unaffiliated write-in candidate for U.S. Senate in Maine. He lives in Cape Neddick.
You don’t need millions of dollars to run for the U.S. Senate
I’m an engineer, not a politician. I live in Cape Neddick, I have never held office, and I am running for U.S. Senate in Maine as an unaffiliated write-in candidate. I am paying for my campaign myself and taking no donations at all.
That is a choice. Candidates routinely raise millions of dollars and fill your phone with fundraising texts. I think voters can expect more professionalism and integrity than that from the people who ask for their vote.
My purpose for doing this campaign out of pocket, with no donations, is to show that it’s possible. If this works, anybody can do this, and you don’t need millions of dollars.
I did not plan to run this year. I had been thinking about a future Senate run, but a series of conversations with Mainers, and what I saw in the current race, changed my mind. If I felt like I could see a little more clarity in political situations than some of the people in charge, I started to think, well, then why not me? Somebody just kind of has to say this is enough.
I have spent my career building and repairing infrastructure, from public projects in Hawaii to flood-damaged roads in Vermont to Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery. After the 2023 floods, major roads in Vermont stayed out of service for close to a year, and the crews drilling through them found roads built on World War II-era money. It taught me something I carry into every conversation about infrastructure: When you don’t spend the money on infrastructure, you lose the infrastructure to build the infrastructure.
My approach starts from a simple idea. I think we should be supporting humanity. Most, if not all, of my policy positions start from a foundation of human rights. Education, healthcare, transportation and a good job are things people are entitled to, not privileges that depend on income.
Here is how you can support me without giving anything up. Maine uses ranked-choice voting for U.S. Senate, and the state allows a declared write-in candidate to be ranked like any other. I am a declared write-in, on the secretary of state’s official list. So on your ballot, write my name, Brent Andrews, on the write-in line, and rank me alongside your usual choice. You don’t have to not vote for whoever you intend to vote for. You can just add me as a second. Ranking me does not take a vote away from anyone else.
I know it is unusual to ask for a vote this way. But power belongs to the people, not to the parties or the money behind them, and the people’s vote is still the most powerful thing we have.
You can read more about me and where I stand at brentandrewsforsenate.com.

title: Obituary: Charles Henry Swett Jr.
text:
BROOKSVILLE, Fla. – Charles Henry Swett, Jr., 85, passed away unexpectedly at Tampa Bay General Hospital on Oct 2, 2026.
Charlie was born in Lewiston, on Nov. 21, 1940, to Charles Henry Swett Sr. and Barbara Toothaker. He graduated from Norway High School in Norway in 1959. He joined the U.S. Navy in 1960 and stayed in 21 years retiring in 1981. He was a Vietnam Veteran and did several tours overseas including Spain, Italy, Philippines and Hawaii. While in the Navy he obtained a Bachelors Degree in Business Management from St. Leo College in Memphis, Tenn.
Following retirement from the Navy, he worked for Ann’s Beauty Academy in Norfolk, Va., as a Financial Aid Director for 10 years. Then he moved home to Mechanic Falls in 1995 and worked as a Field Revenue Agent with the IRS until his retirement.
In 1960, he married Brenda Kay Morrel and was married for 55 years until her passing in 2015. Charlie was a devoted family man. He was a member of the Flatland Cloggers from Chesapeake, Va., for 10 years and a member of Auburn Baptist Church in Auburn for 23 years.
Charlie married Rosalyn Thompson in 2016 and they moved to The Wesleyan Village in Brooksville, Fla., in 2023. All of his life he was an avid golfer starting at the age of 10 and was even having a round of golf a day before his passing. He was a devoted servant of our Lord Jesus Christ.
He is predeceased by his first wife, Brenda, his parents and three brothers, Sonny, Wally and Paul.
He is survived by his loving wife, Rosie Swett of Danville, Ind., one son David Damon and wife Carol of Lewiston; daughters Anna Smith and husband Tom of Minot, Pamela Bryant and her husband Ryan of Sabattus, and Katherine Swett of North Chesterfield, Va.; stepchildren, Lenore Delamarter and husband Bobby of Danville, Ind., Mark Thompson and wife Dianna of Moncks Corner, S.C.; 10 grandchildren, 27 great-grandchildren and one great great grandchild.
His celebration of life is Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, at 1 p.m., at East Auburn Baptist Church at 560 Park Ave., Auburn. Graveside service with Military Honors will be Monday, Oct. 26, at 2 p.m., at Maine Veterans Cemetery, 163 Mount Vernon Rd, Augusta.

title: A message for young Mainers: Think journalism.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Dave Griffiths of Mechanic Falls is a retired journalist who worked for the Kansas City Star, Tulsa World and Lewiston Sun Journal. He also covered national security for Business Week magazine during the Reagan years.
This is an open letter to young folks wondering how to shape their careers and have an interesting life.
Think journalism. Every day, the nonprofit Maine Trust for Local News keeps the profession thriving here despite competition from cable “news” and social media. Reporters and editors strive to give us a balanced picture of life in Maine and beyond. Like “newshounds” all over America, they honor our Founding Fathers’ constitutional guarantee of a free press, even though broadsheets 250 years ago were fiercely partisan, focused more on scandal than substance.
It’s simple. Without independent voices, our democracy would wither and die. For the sake of argument, let’s say a power-obsessed, dishonest, corrupt political leader rails against “fake news” and calls the press the “enemy of the people.” You could make the case that by discouraging public confidence in the press, he wants to be a de facto dictator.
To a much lesser degree every presidential administration has dealt with reporters questioning the self-serving statements issuing from every White House. And Graham Platner would still be in the Senate race if not for aggressive reporting by, among others, the New York Times. Democracy is messy.
So what’s in it for young Mainers surveying the job landscape?
For one thing, your work day may range from quiet time devoted to “deathless prose” (a tongue-in-cheek remark I’ve heard in many a newsroom) to an often turbulent, always unpredictable life as you take on crime, drug busts, politics, odd “man bites dog” features, petty squabbles among elected officials, lost pets, acts of everyday courage, government overreach and the sparks that fly in our diverse culture.
Afterward, you’ll be jabbering in groups of two or three or more about a particularly memorable “news day,” perhaps in a watering hole just around the corner from the newsroom. In a good news town — and they’re all good news towns — you’ll never run out of ideas.
Many stories will stay with you years later. The point is: You’re involved in your job, not just putting in another eight hours. Count on it. I’ve worked at six newspapers, magazines and newsletters, and not once do I regret moving on. The next job — learning new turf and a new beat — keeps the juices flowing.
What about the writing itself? It’s not always easy, especially up against deadlines. But with the help of seasoned editors, you’ll develop a style that your peers recognize, and you’ll smile inwardly at just the right sentence and that jewel of a word or phrase that says it all. The English language is a vast treasure house of symbols at your command, but only if, according to Stephen King, you “write a lot and read a lot.” Meanwhile, you’ll come to value the connection between brevity and clarity — key to the quick read that makes writing “sing”(another newsroom buzzword).
But what if the weird hours and pressure to get your facts right on a strict time limit don’t suit you? After all, working into the evening may not lend itself to helping raise kids. So a reporter’s ease at the keyboard could lead to better-paying PR jobs for government agencies, the private sector or nonprofits. I’ve taught business writing courses for some 20 government clients all over the U.S. and in the Middle East, Europe and Asia. It was a challenge. I’m afraid people just don’t read much these days. The emails I saw early in those classes made me wonder why people don’t pick up the phone instead or walk down the hall to deliver a message or ask a question.
A life well lived is full of characters, including the scribblers you work with and the people you meet. I interviewed a federal prisoner in Denver who kidnapped women and kept them in coffins, and several drill instructors at the Marine boot camp in San Diego where a recruit had died during over-the-top training. I also interviewed two defense secretaries who were less forthcoming than a Trappist monk.
So you get to tell stories, holding up a mirror that helps explain us to ourselves. How cool is that?

title: Coastal homes burn as hot winds fuel California fires
text:
SANTA ANA, Calif. (AP) — A fast-moving fire fueled by high winds burned at least six homes in Southern California on Friday, engulfing expensive coastal properties and prompting thousands to evacuate.
Black smoke — visible from miles away — billowed over tennis courts and swimming pools while firefighters doused blazing homes in San Juan Capistrano in Orange County. Some homeowners sprayed water on their properties before heeding evacuation orders.
Two firefighters were taken to the hospital with heat-related injuries, officials said. Authorities have not said how the blaze, which was less than a square mile as of Friday evening, started.
“Had these winds been a little bit stronger, a little bit different direction, this could have been a whole lot worse,” said San Clemente Mayor Rick Loeffler.
Howard Hart, a councilmember for San Juan Capistrano, said he and his wife doused their roof with water and moved propane tanks away from their home before they evacuated Friday with a to-go bag.
Laura Hart hasn’t had to evacuate due to fire in the more than five decades she’s lived in the community, she said.
“This doesn’t usually happen to us, we usually see it on the news,” she said. “We always pray to God it’s not us, but yeah, it was today.”
The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente, and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano. An evacuation shelter has opened in each city. By Friday night, about 16,000 residents had been ordered to evacuate, said Fire Chief TJ McGovern, of the Orange County Fire Authority.
It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast. The strongest winds were expected through Friday afternoon, but conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night, with a heat advisory in effect until 8 p.m. Saturday on the Orange County and San Diego County coast, the National Weather Service said.
Tens of thousands of people in the state are without power after their electricity was turned off. A separate fire by the Marine Corps base Camp Pendleton shut down for hours a section of Interstate 5 that is a major artery connecting Orange County to San Diego. That added hours to commutes throughout Southern California.
The coastal cities are surrounded by hillsides. San Juan Capistrano, a city of 35,000, is known for horse trails and the historic Mission San Juan Capistrano. San Clemente, which is home to 62,000 people, is known as a “Spanish village by the sea” and popular with beachgoers and surfers.
“The fire is right up on the city,” said Victor Cabral, a San Clemente Council member. “It’s on the perimeter of our homes on the north end.”
Nine schools were also closed Friday in San Juan Capistrano, the Capistrano Unified School District said.
Nearby residents were also on edge as smoke darkened the sky.
Wyoming resident Shannon Needham was visiting her mother at her assisted living facility in Dana Point just north of San Clemente when she learned about the fire.
The facility director told her that two buses would be on standby in case they needed to evacuate, Needham said.
“You could hear the fire trucks, you could hear the helicopters and everything above. And it was so smoky, it was just dark smoke,” Needham said.
Some of California’s worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power in dry winds. More than 200,000 customers in California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.
The weather service also issued a red flag warning for parts of central and Northern California through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.
___
Rodriguez reported from San Francisco. Associated Press writer Jaimie Ding contributed from Los Angeles.

title: Maine’s Heal points is a time-tested formula, but many coaches want improvements
text:
In 2025, the Bonny Eagle High School boys basketball team caught a break. The Scots were 6-11 and headed for the last playoff spot in Class AA South, until a victory in the regular season finale over Noble High School allowed them to jump from seventh to fourth, and from a road to a home playoff game.
The 16-1 Noble Knights were without four starters for much of the game, but as far as the Heal point standings were concerned, it didn’t matter. In the tournament, Bonny Eagle parlayed its good fortune into a quarterfinal win over Sanford, and then a shocking semifinal win over No. 1 Thornton Academy.
“It was kind of a gift for us,” Scots coach John Trull said. “If I were another coach, I’d probably be upset. … But it motivated us. We had to prove that we deserved to be in that spot.”
The scenario showed both the strengths and flaws of the Heal point formula, the system the Maine Principals’ Association has used to seed most high school sports (football excluded) for postseason play. Developed by Durward Heal, a former principal of Schenck High in East Millinocket, and implemented in the 1949-50 season, Heal points rank teams according to their strength by factoring in not just their record but the quality of their victories.
And for over 75 years, while sometimes challenged, no one has found a better, more fair way to do it.
“It’s as equitable a system as there is,” Cheverus girls hockey coach Scott Rousseau said. “I don’t think it’s the perfect system, but generally speaking, it gets it right.”
MPA executive director Mike Bisson noted the objectivity of the Heal points formula, which separates itself from more opinion-based rankings and polls used in some other states.
“While it’s not a perfect system, it’s a mathematical formula,” he said. “And any type of power ranking based on a mathematical formula is going to have some weird things in it.”
While most of the coaches interviewed approve of the structure, there are dissidents whose arguments include that the system can punish victories over weaker opponents, lead to scheduling difficulties and reward victories over opponents with good records, rather than opponents tested by better competition.
A Varsity Maine email survey sent to more than 200 coaches asking if they think Heal points are an effective system, an effective system that could be improved, or not effective received 55 responses. Twenty said it’s effective as is, while 35 said either that the system should be improved or that it just doesn’t work.
“Heal points are no longer effective as currently constructed,” Rob Sullivan, the girls basketball coach at Kennebunk for 30 years, wrote in an email. “It is an outdated system that could easily be replaced for a much simpler system.”
‘ONE OF THE BEST SYSTEMS YOU CAN HAVE’
Heal points work by awarding a point value to a team based on how often it wins and the quality of the teams that it beats.
Here’s how the formula works:
- A team is assigned a preliminary index based on their wins — everyone gets 40 points for a win over a Class A team, 38 for Class B, 36 for Class C, 34 for Class D and 32 for eight-man or Class S. Classes are determined by enrollment.
- That number is then divided by the number of scheduled games. The preliminary index grows as the season goes on.
- Next, you add up all of the preliminary indices for the teams you defeated, and divide that by the number of scheduled games.
- That number is then multiplied by 10, which gives you a team’s tournament index.
- The teams are then ranked by their tournament index to form the Heal point standings. Teams at the top, are the top teams of the year.
Debate surrounding Heals and their effectiveness has gone on for decades. Proponents of the system like that it goes beyond just win-loss record, paints a more accurate hierarchy by factoring in who teams have beaten, and aim to provide balance in classes where teams don’t all share common opponents.
Lucas McNelly, who runs the Maine Basketball Rankings website, developed his own formula that ranks teams and predicts outcomes based on a variety of factors, including point differential and home and road performance. He said, though, that Heal points are “one of the best methods you can have.”
“I think the bones of Heal points are so good that I built the entire ranking system on them,” he said. “Every game in the state matters, and it’s hard to find a system that does that. … It can swing a seeding in C North on the last day of the season. I think that level of chaos is awesome.”
McNelly said the ideal system would include every team in a region playing each other twice, but Maine’s geography prohibits that.
“Let’s say Caribou and Gardiner are in the same (region). … You can’t do that on a Tuesday night for a game,” he said. “The state’s too big. The state’s never going to not be big.”
South Portland boys basketball coach Kevin Millington said a big strength of Heal points is that they reward strength of victory (beating good teams) rather than strength of schedule (simply playing them). Craig Roberts, Scarborough’s girls soccer coach, said tournament results have validated the formula.
“The system has gotten it right,” he said. “If you look at the last four teams standing in the regional semis and regional finals, typically it’s the teams that are at the top (or) near the top of the Heal points.”
Brunswick girls basketball coach Sam Farrell likes that Heal points can give a team that would otherwise be out of the playoff race something to play for late in the season.
“I like being rewarded for big wins,” he said. “It keeps the kids motivated: ‘Hey, I know what our record is, but this game matters.’ You can shock the world, and now you get to play in the (Augusta) Civic Center.”
HEAL POINT HICCUPS
Opponents, however, say the system often doesn’t churn out the best representation within a region. A frequent criticism from the coaches’ survey was that Heal points favor teams that beat opponents with many wins, without taking into consideration whether those wins came against strong opponents.
Conversely, a team wouldn’t get as many points for beating a good team that plays strong competition, but has an inferior record as a result.
Boothbay boys basketball coach Dan Hallinan’s Class D team, which plays in the Mountain Valley Conference with several Class C schools, missed the tournament last year despite playing 10 Class C teams and beating two, while three of the teams that qualified played a combined two C teams and beat none.
“We have been penalized for playing a much harder schedule,” he said. “We are rewarding teams for playing weaker schedules. The best (or) better teams aren’t being placed appropriately seeding-wise, or not making the tournament at all.”
Freeport field hockey and girls lacrosse coach Marcia Wood said she sees a similar dynamic in lacrosse, where teams that play in tougher conferences get seeded lower because they don’t get the number of wins that teams that play weaker schedules do.
Because of that, she said, the two strongest teams can meet up in earlier rounds of the tournament, and “the game before states is the big game.”
Some conferences allow schools the ability to schedule a fixed number of out-of-conference games, but the process of determining which teams to compete against also becomes complicated under the Heal points system.
“Now you have the decision to make of, ‘OK … (who) makes the most sense to play against?'” Dirigo boys basketball coach Cody St. Germain said. “The team that’s geographically close and also gives you a challenge? Or a lot of teams are saying, ‘I’m going to go play a 16-win team that stinks that I know I’m going to beat because I know I get 16 guaranteed Heal points out of going and beating that team.
“And we’re starting to see now there are teams that are really utilizing that to their advantage, and I can’t really blame them. I’ve considered it myself at times.”
How Heal points factor into scheduling can also raise issues from an administrative perspective.
Leavitt Athletic Director Ryan LaRoche said it can be difficult to find games for different sports, as well as for girls programs versus boys programs, given different classifications and talent levels.
“There are definitely teams in the state where the boys team is not competitive at all and the girls team is in the state championship every year,” he said. “So when the conference is making a schedule and they’re looking at crossovers that are appropriate, they’re trying to keep those the same for the boys and the girls, it’s sometimes a challenge to make that work where you don’t want a team that’s bad to just have to play good teams every week.
“But if you have a team that’s very competitive and historically successful, you want them to be able to play the best teams and have those opportunities for the Heal points.”
Mt. Blue baseball coach Steve Porter and Deering boys soccer coach Joel Costigan shared another qualm with the structure: wins over bad teams in-conference earn too few points, and teams can be passed in the standings despite winning games they are obigated to play.
“The Heal points are a way to address the scheduling disparities, but they also create disparities in the points,” Costigan said. “You (can) have a team with more wins, but those wins don’t matter because they still finished behind a team that had fewer wins. I see that every year.”
NO ‘REAL TRACTION’ FOR CHANGE
Several soccer coaches said they’d like to see a more straightforward system of awarding three points for wins and one for ties, while Sullivan at Kennebunk said he’d like to see Heals eliminated in favor of an open tournament.
Farrell at Brunswick said he’d prefer a return to the former difference of five points for a win in each class, rather than the current two, in order to discourage teams looking for wins against teams in lower classes.
Bisson at the MPA said he hasn’t had people come forward “with any proposals that have gained any real traction to change.”
“We would certainly listen if people had an alternative that they felt was a better option and gained some support from the schools,” Bisson said.
For over 70 years, no one’s developed a better one.

title: Friday’s high school football: Cony’s balanced attack too much for Brunswick

Drew Lindquist passed for five touchdowns, Anderson Noyes and Landen Perry both scored twice, and Cony cruised to a 55-7 win over Brunswick in a Class B football game Friday night in Augusta.

title: Portland’s warming shelter plan is hitting snags as opening date nears
text:
The city of Portland’s plan to host a winter warming shelter at a Preble Street facility in Bayside has become uncertain one month before it’s supposed to open, and staff are now reviewing alternative options.
While a plan to return the city’s winter shelter to a downtown location appeared to be settled last month, new questions over zoning restrictions and neighborhood impacts have officials scrambling to finalize a plan and secure funding.
The City Council held a special workshop this week to discuss its options, but the bulk of the meeting was held behind closed doors in executive session — despite criticism from residents who argued that the public is being left out of the conversation.
“I think it is safe to say that we’re frustrated by the lack of transparency and engagement throughout the process,” said Robert Sylvain, treasurer of the Bayside Neighborhood Association, on Thursday.
Last month, city officials announced that the Biddeford nonprofit Seeds of Hope would operate a nightly warming shelter in the basement level of Elena’s Way on Portland Street from mid-November to April, which reflected a council goal to partner with a social service agency and return the seasonal shelter to downtown.
Earlier this month, city staff told the Portland Press Herald that using the space as a warming shelter would not require council approval because it is a temporary use, and that staff would likely add conditions that the shelter operators would be required to meet.
However, at the workshop this week, officials said the existing conditional use standards in place for the Elena’s Way shelter would make it impossible to get a warming shelter up and running there in a timely manner.
Assistant City Manager Dena Libner said the planning director has the authority to approve a temporary use, but that doing so at Preble Street’s building would contradict zoning requirements already in place there.
“That’s not something staff is able to administratively override,” she said.
City Attorney Michael Goldman said the Elena’s Way location is not necessarily impossible to stand up, but that it would take significantly more process under a tight timeline.
The conditional use standards for Elena’s Way stipulate that the sleeping area be limited to the upper level, and that a maximum of 40 shelter guests would be allowed at one time.
A recent city inspection of Preble Street’s operation also found that the organization is not following parts of its management plan, including its responsibility to monitor safety in the area, which compounded neighbors’ concerns about doubling the nightly capacity.
Councilor Sarah Michniewicz, who represents the neighborhood, said Thursday that she’s not comfortable with the options laid out so far.
“At this late date, I don’t see a timely procedural path to use Elena’s Way that would protect current shelter guests and families next door, or satisfy the public that the council is acting diligently and transparently,” she said.
Michniewicz said some officials have suggested that declaring a limited state of emergency would allow the warming shelter to proceed at Elena’s Way. But she argued the city should be focused on “finding a location that will be successful both for people seeking shelter and the community around them, not navigating around the legal safeguards that were put in place to prevent overcrowding and unsafe situations.”
The council then went into executive session to consider other options and obtain legal guidance.
In a letter to the council, Sylvain said officials should “re-evaluate more appropriate alternative locations,” including the Cumberland County facility behind Union Station or the city’s Homeless Services Center on Riverside Street, where services already exist.
“The idea that Elena’s Way is the only remaining solution is simply untrue. If compromises must be made, safety must not be one of them,” he said.
Councilor Anna Bullett, who chairs the health and human services and public safety committee, said Friday that she’s “deeply committed” to ensuring that a nightly warming shelter on the peninsula moves forward.
“I’m grateful to Seeds of Hope for their flexibility as city staff urgently expand the community partners search,” she said. “Fingers crossed that we will have a plan to announce next week.”
Bullett added that the situation is “a glaring reminder that Portland shoulders the burden of inadequate state and federal funding for therapeutic and low-income housing and of the county government’s general disinterest in helping the unhoused.”
The shelter effort was recently awarded $361,000 in MaineHousing funding, which staff said represents about half the estimated cost.
Maggie McLoughlin, the city’s director of health and human services, said the budget to host 45-50 people per night, along with food and access to services, would be roughly $688,000. That figure includes Seeds of Hope staffing and an expansion of the downtown ambassadors program to support area safety, she said.
The council is slated to take a first reading Monday to allocate $350,000 in opioid settlement funds to make up the gap. A staff memo states that details regarding the warming shelter will be finalized and published before the council votes on the item Nov. 2.
Last winter’s city-run shelter, located at the former shelter for asylum seekers in the Riverside Industrial Park, received $400,000 in state funding and opened based on temperature and precipitation thresholds that were often criticized.

title: New law aims to end TSA confusion over parents traveling with breast milk
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Emily Calandrelli, an author and former host of “Emily’s Wonder Lab” on Netflix, went viral in 2022 after writing on social media about an experience at a TSA security checkpoint.
Calandrelli said she was on a work trip at the time, writing it was her “first time away from my 10-week-old son, who I’m currently breastfeeding,” and that she “brought my pump and two ice packs.”
Calandrelli said two male TSA agents told her she could not bring the ice packs in a carry-on because they were not frozen solid. She said when she asked to speak to a supervisor, she was asked, “Well, where is the baby?” The supervisor then said if her child was with her, “it wouldn’t be an issue,” according to Calandrelli.
She said she was ultimately escorted from the security line and forced to check her ice packs.
“It shouldn’t be nearly impossible to travel if you’re a mom or are breastfeeding your child,” Calandrelli said in an Instagram video.
What TSA policy says
TSA policy, in place since 2016, states that formula, breast milk, toddler drinks, and baby or toddler food in quantities greater than 3.4 ounces are allowed in carry-on baggage because they are considered medically necessary liquids.
The policy is also supposed to apply to breast milk cooling accessories such as ice packs, freezer packs and gel packs, regardless of whether they are melted or frozen. The regulation also states a child does not need to be present or traveling with a parent for the exemption to apply.
“With or without the baby, it is deemed a medical necessity, just like a medicine,” said Dr. Jessica Nash, a pediatrician at Children’s National Hospital in Washington, D.C., and a member of the DC Breastfeeding Coalition.
Breastfeeding can help protect a baby against conditions including asthma, ear infections, stomach bugs and diabetes, according to the CDC. It can also lower a mother’s risk for certain cancers.
Nash said she believes societal barriers, including challenges while traveling, can disrupt a mother’s breastfeeding intentions.
“The body produces only if it’s stimulated. So if a mom is away from a baby or if it’s at the time a baby needs to eat, the mom either needs to pump or she needs to directly breastfeed,” Nash said. “And if you don’t do that, not only will her supply decrease, but she might start to get a backup of milk, which increases her risk for infection.”
Nash has heard from breastfeeding mothers who have encountered problems at TSA checkpoints, including some forced to throw their milk away and others concerned the screening process could contaminate their baby’s source of nutrition.
“Being asked to open their milk and test strips put in their milk, or where the milk is being handled by someone who hasn’t put on another pair of gloves. Real issues, real mothers, all the time, and just clearly not everyone knowing what the rules are,” Nash said.
Vanessa Snyder lives in Wisconsin and has flown with her husband and daughter, documenting their experiences online, including lessons learned navigating airport security with breast milk.
“It just breaks my heart because I know how hard it is to pump on the go,” Snyder said.
She said that every experience is different and was once told that the milk “had to be frozen.”
“So that was a specific instance where I actually had to push back and say, no, this is allowed,” Snyder said.
Calandrelli worked with lawmakers for several years advocating for breastfeeding mothers to get better protections in airports.
New law expands protections
In late 2025, the bipartisan Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening, or BABES, Enhancement Act was signed into law. It expands on the original BABES Act, which a decade ago mandated TSA exempt breast milk from its 3-1-1 liquids rule but lacked clarity on how it should be screened.
Under the new law, TSA will be required to consult with nationally recognized maternal health organizations to establish standardized and hygienic screening guidelines for breast milk, baby formula and related accessories. TSA must also update its guidance every five years and ensure agents nationwide receive consistent training.
“And they have to comply with it,” said Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Illinois, who introduced the bill in the Senate.
Duckworth said another component of the law directs an independent government watchdog to audit TSA’s compliance and report the results to Congress.
“What we were finding is that depending on which airport you went through, the TSA agent may or may not know, so the audit portion is absolutely in there to increase accountability,” Duckworth said.
Nash said she believes that accountability measure is important.
“I definitely think it’s important. There has to be some checks and balances in place, to make sure that these enhancements happen,” Nash said.
Snyder said she views the law as progress. “I think that’s going to be a win for families.”
She advised breastfeeding mothers preparing to fly to have TSA’s policy readily available, whether it be a screenshot or the TSA website itself.
TSA response
TSA and the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees TSA operations, declined to speak on camera for this story.
The agency said it “fully supports” all requirements outlined in the BABES Enhancement Act. A spokesperson said as of February 2026, TSA is in full compliance with the new law and said the workforce has been trained on updated screening protocols.
“TSA officers who do not follow current screening procedures may be taken off screening duties, retrained, or disciplined to ensure screening procedures are followed,” the spokesperson said.
Travelers can file a complaint with TSA if they believe its policies are not being followed. You can do that by clicking here.

When Maine ski resorts are planning to open for the 2026-27 season
High-elevation areas in Maine will be seeing snow on Saturday and ski season will arrive before we know it.
The three biggest ski areas in Maine — Saddleback, Sugarloaf and Sunday River — have shared when they are planning to open up their trails for the first time.
Sunday River is targeting an opening date of Nov. 15 with the Locke Mountain Triple lift spinning first and the Jordan 8 lift right on its heels. The resort in Newry has released an early season guide with the latest on its opening plans and what guests should expect.
In a newsletter sent Thursday, Sugarloaf said: "only 36 more days until opening day." This would put the opening of the Carrabassett Valley resort at Nov. 20.
Finally, Saddleback shared a Facebook post on Wednesday that touted 50 days until the Rangeley resort opens. That would put Saddleback's opening day at Dec. 4.

title: 65 Maine veterans head to Washington, D.C. with Honor Flight Maine
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - 65 Maine veterans will travel to Washington, D.C. this weekend for free with Honor Flight Maine, a nonprofit that has made the trip possible since 2014.
Veterans, along with their guardians for the weekend, packed their bags Friday morning for their flight to the nation’s capital.
Organizers say they work to make the experience possible for as many veterans as possible because they deserve to see how they have been honored for their service and sacrifices.
“I was very hesitant, but we have a group that meets every Tuesday, a Vietnam vet group, and we support each other, and the guys were telling me, ‘it would be good for you to go,’” said Joseph Mattingly, Navy veteran.
“All the veterans who are watching that say, ‘oh, no, I don’t deserve this. Let someone else go,’ you’re wrong, big time. They deserve it. They served our country. They deserve to go,” said Dale Browning, Navy veteran and volunteer.
While in Washington, D.C., they’ll have a packed itinerary — visiting the Vietnam and Korean War memorials, the Military Women’s Memorial, Fort McHenry and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery.

title: Jared Golden’s unspent campaign funds are going across the country
text:
When U.S. Rep. Jared Golden announced he wouldn’t run for reelection this year, he said he planned to use the nearly $2 million in his war chest to support Democrats across the country.
So far, he’s put his money where his mouth is.
In its latest filing with the Federal Election Commission, made public Thursday afternoon, Golden’s campaign committee reported spending nearly $300,000 between July and October. Much of that cash went toward moderate Democrats’ campaigns.
The largest expenditure by far was to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which supports the party’s candidates for U.S. House. Golden gave the organization $150,000 in late September.
Golden has occasionally drawn the ire of his party’s leadership for his moderate stances and willingness to break party ranks on important votes. In September, he and Rep. Marie Glusenkamp Perez, D-Wash., were scorned by Democratic leaders for a “blindside” vote in support of several Republican-led bills.
After the DCCC, Gluesenkamp Perez was the next largest recipient of Golden’s campaign cash over the last three months. Her reelection PAC received a $40,000 contribution from Golden in late September.
Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez are co-chairs of the Blue Dog PAC, a committee that supports conservative-leaning Democrats running for and serving in Congress.
In recent months, Golden gave the maximum $2,000 to six Democrats backed by Blue Dog PAC that are each vying to flip Republican congressional seats in Florida, Kentucky, Minnesota, Montana, Ohio and Wisconsin.
Three other Democrats’ reelection campaigns received $1,000 contributions from Golden: Incumbent U.S. Reps. John Larson in Connecticut, Darren Soto in Florida and Seth Magaziner in Rhode Island.
“As he’s done during his time in office, Congressman Golden will continue to support candidates and causes he believes in,” Golden spokesperson Mario Moretto said in a statement provided after this story was initially published.
The donation to Larson was made on Aug. 7, just days before he lost a primary election that ultimately ended his nearly 30-year congressional tenure.
Those contributions follow the pattern of Golden’s other donations this year, the majority of which have gone to moderate Democrats facing tight campaigns across the country.
In Maine, Golden gave $500 to both Lewiston Democrat Shenna Cox’s state Senate and Auburn Democrat Adam Lee’s state House campaigns.
Golden also contributed $1,050 to Oxford County Sheriff Chris Wainwright’s reelection bid. Wainwright, notably, is the only Republican Golden contributed to this quarter.
The donation, dated Sept. 30, was made just days after several Oxford County deputies’ complaints of retaliation within the office were made public.
Several Maine-based nonprofits also received thousands of dollars from Golden’s campaign funds. Operation Reboot Outdoors, a Turner-based organization that sponsors hunting and fishing trips for law enforcement officers and veterans, got $25,000. The Solidarity Solutions Foundation in Lisbon Falls received $5,000.
Golden made a “charitable contribution” of $25,000 to Moving America Forward, a Utah-based voter outreach organization that focuses on engaging political independents, namely through canvassing and town halls.
Golden’s spending has ramped up as November has neared. His committee spent about $93,000 in the first quarter of 2026 and $65,000 in the second, according to FEC filings.
The nearly $300,000 he spent during the third quarter blows those totals out of the water. And he still has nearly $105,000 on hand, his latest filing shows.

title: Farmington-area school board votes to join national lawsuit against social media companies
text:
FARMINGTON — Regional School Unit 9 has signed an agreement to participate in nationwide litigation against major social media companies accused of harming students and increasing costs for public schools.
The board of directors voted unanimously Oct. 13 to move forward with participation following a recommendation from its Finance Committee. Superintendent Christian Elkington subsequently confirmed that the district has signed a retainer agreement.
The litigation involves allegations that platforms operated by companies including Meta, TikTok, Snap Inc. and Google were designed to encourage addictive use, contributing to student mental health problems and disruptions to learning.
“It’s not going to cost us any money whatsoever,” Elkington told the board.
In a follow-up email, Elkington confirmed that attorneys will receive 30% of any settlement award, with the district receiving the remaining 70%.
“The retainer has been signed,” Elkington said.
Elkington said other Maine school districts are participating in the litigation and RSU 9 could receive compensation if the lawsuits result in a financial recovery.
“It hopefully will mean some funding that will come our way,” he told the board.
The litigation, known as multidistrict litigation No. 3047, was established in October 2022 and is being handled in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. It consolidates related lawsuits for coordinated pretrial proceedings, including evidence gathering and legal motions.
School districts allege that social media platforms were intentionally designed to encourage addictive use among young people, contributing to mental health problems, disrupted learning and additional costs for counseling, disciplinary intervention and other student services.
The allegations remain contested, and participation does not guarantee RSU 9 will receive compensation.
RSU 9 includes Chesterville, Farmington, Industry, New Sharon, New Vineyard, Starks, Temple, Vienna, Weld and Wilton.

title: Special Olympics Athletes Make Waves
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Dozens of athletes from across the region dove into the competition today at the Special Olympics Aquatic Day in Presque Isle. By the end of the day, every athlete walked away a winner.
From floating competitions to relays, swimmers were making a splash during the Special Olympics Aquatic Day. This year the event was held in Gentile Hall at the University of Maine at Presque Isle and when athletes weren’t competing, they were cheering each other on.
Roy Lafrancoise, one Special Olympics athlete said: “The event was very exciting. It’s very wonderful. Very nice, good people to see. Best friends, good family, good fun, and good times. We are having a really blast of the Special Olympics. We are cheering people on, and I was cheering for my friend Bobby, and cheering for other people. Very excellent, wonderful, challenging, and very fun. Cheering people on. Having a good time.”
Bobby McKenzie, another Special Olympics athlete added: “Yeah, I do the same thing. It’s like a whole thing, event, and then cheering, and laughing, and clapping, and smiling.”
Although today’s event was centered around competition, for Roy and Bobby it was about supporting one another. “We were swimming in the first place of going down and back. I had stopped a couple of times and cheered for Bobby a little bit to be fair for Bobby. So, I’m always there for Bobby to let him know that, “Bobby, you can do it.” It’s always good to not think about yourself but it’s always good to share the tournament for everybody. So, you can have a better friendship. Friendship is the best thing to have. Keep it to make sure you’re fair for everybody,” said Roy.
Organizers and teachers said the event highlights inclusion and acceptance. Frances Cote, a Special Ed teacher for MSAD20 in Fort Fairfield said: “Inclusion is a big part of our world. Our school district is very much an inclusion school district, and we want our kids to feel a part of, and to be able to do all these events, and get their own sports recognition, and their own sports awards and trophies. So, it’s really a part of including them and inclusion all together.”
The day was a blast for the athletes and their supporters. “All around the whole event is one of my favorite days of the year. It was a great event to watch. I recommend that anybody get out and attend one of these events. It’s definitely fun,” Cote continued.
The day ended with an awards ceremony where every athlete took home at least one ribbon for their hard work. For Roy, Bobby, and their fellow athletes, it’s already one for the books and they can’t wait to do it all again next year.

title: Creativity Bar offers workers playful reset to spark new ideas
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (Aging Untold) — Just outside Nashville, some working adults say the daily grind can drain energy and ideas. They are finding a refreshing reset at the Creativity Bar, where community and a little play help people feel better, think clearly and leave inspired.
Founder Stephanie Pruitt-Gaines hopes to help shape the future of those drawn to her door.
“I’ve always loved coloring books, and it feels like walking through a coloring book,” Pruitt-Gaines said. “And also in my dreams, I often dream in black and white.”
Part playroom, part art studio, part office
The Creativity Bar is part playroom, part art studio and part office for members to drop in and work toward their next great idea.
“Our members can come drop in anytime and make stuff,” Pruitt-Gaines said. “To come up with the next great idea, you’ve got to have some playfulness and creativity.”
Every inch of the space is outlined in black and designed to unleash imagination and help ideas flow.
“All of these little lines really intentionally play with your eyes and your mind wants to fill them in,” Pruitt-Gaines said. “And so part of what I hope this space does is people walk in and feel a sense of possibility.”
Members say they leave inspired
Members pay a monthly fee or day rate to use the space and attend workshops.
“My work. It’s all about creating something out of nothing. And so this place is just so inspiring. The energy that’s here,” Dawn Cornelius, a founding member, said.
“I just feel better and I am better when I come here,” she said. “I leave inspired.”
“Community and creativity, it doesn’t have to be difficult,” Leigh Patton, another founding member, said. “You can actually just walk in the door and your brain starts working.”

title: Raising your grandkids full-time? Here’s what you should know
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — For many grandparents, the role shifts from spoiling and sleepovers to full-time, day-in, day-out parenting.
It’s a transition that can bring deep love and purpose — but also real stress on time, money and energy.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down what grandparents need to know when they suddenly find themselves raising their grandkids.
“First thing, breathe”
When grandparents suddenly step into a full-time parenting role, gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said the initial instinct should be to slow down and acknowledge the shift.
“First thing, breathe,” Cradduck said. “You’re not a babysitter. You’re now in the role of molding another human being.”
More than 2 million grandparents are raising grandchildren in the United States, according to the U.S. Department of Labor.
Cradduck said whether the circumstances stem from tragedy or something else, grandparents need to be patient with themselves.
“You’ve got to give yourself grace to get through this,” Cradduck said.
Still, Cradduck pointed to a silver lining, noting that many of the most empathetic adults she knows were raised by their grandparents.
“Some of the best people I’ve ever met in my life were raised by their grandparents, and they grew up with such an absolute amount of empathy and honor and respect for other humans,” Cradduck said. “My hats off to any grandparent that does it.”
Get the legal and practical groundwork in place
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said one of the first practical steps grandparents should take is establishing legal guardianship.
“I think I’d want them to get the legal stuff taken care of — like you need to become guardian, you know, get that, so that when you say something, you’ve got some legal strength behind it,” O’Rourke said.
She also emphasized that grandparents don’t have to navigate the process alone, pointing to resources such as ParentsHelpingParents.org.
“Don’t do it alone. Don’t think you can handle this all alone,” O’Rourke said. “Go to the school, see if there’s mentors and support people there. Maybe groups that you can get tips on.”
That extends to everyday parenting challenges too, from discipline to schoolwork.
“Maybe get some help with technology, because they’re in school, using technology, even learning things,” O’Rourke said. “So get some help with how to help them with their homework, even if it’s bringing somebody else in there to help them.”
A chance to learn — and an opportunity, not just a challenge
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said that despite the difficulties, raising grandchildren offers a chance to grow.
“With all the challenges it has, it’s a tremendous opportunity to learn new things and really have your love and connection that you’re providing echo for generations,” Ambrose said.
Ambrose also encourages grandparents not to feel out of place in the role.
“I really want to offer encouragement to grandparents too to not think that you’re a fish out of water, because there’s a lot of people in the same boat,” she said. “You’re perfectly equipped.”
Pace yourself — and lean on experience
O’Rourke said grandparents raising children later in life shouldn’t hold themselves to the same energy standards they had decades earlier.
“Don’t let yourself raise your kids with the idea that you should have the energy level that you had at 30 at 60,” O’Rourke said. “Just kind of accept that you don’t have the energy. So pace yourself so that you’re not completely exhausted when Friday rolls around.”
Cradduck said that experience — not energy — is often a grandparent’s greatest asset.
“I’m a much, much better grandparent than I ever was a parent,” Cradduck said. “My patience level, my understanding, just my own maturity has developed. Things that I thought were catastrophic before — now you don’t cry over spilled milk. You can just clean it up.”
The legacy grandparents leave behind
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the role grandparents play in raising their grandchildren can shape the next generation in lasting ways.
“I think the most important thing that a grandparent gives is you give a good foundation,” Rogers said. “They have love and support and you’ve given them all the ingredients they need for success.”

- Social Security

- Grandchild’s school for mentors and support
- Get help with technology if needed
- Get help with homework
Key takeaways for grandparents raising grandchildren
- Keep the legacy in focus. Your greatest legacy is who you help your grandchildren become.
- It’s not babysitting. Expect high late-life physical, emotional and financial demands driven by family crisis.
- Find support through kinship, Legal Aid and other resources

title: Chipotle's 'Big Ass Bag' Is What Happens When Takeout Goes Haute Couture
text:
Chipotle Is Making a ‘Big Ass’ Fashion Statement — Literally
Chipotle is giving its classic brown takeout bag a serious glow-up, turning an everyday food-delivery staple into a giant statement accessory.
At three feet wide, this thing is hard to miss... And that's the point.
The restaurant chain has introduced the Big Ass Chipotle Bag, a fashionable version of its familiar takeout packaging that's designed to make carrying dinner for the whole crew a little more fun.
Launched Oct. 13, the limited-edition bag is part of Chipotle's latest campaign for its digital-exclusive Family Meals. And yes, it's every bit as extra as it sounds.
Chipotle's Big Ass Bag Is a Whole Lot of Extra
The Big Ass Chipotle Bag measures 36 inches wide, 24 inches tall, and 12 inches deep, with a whopping 170-liter capacity.
Rather than inventing some random fashion accessory, Chipotle took something customers already recognize and supersized it into an over-the-top statement piece.
It's part takeout packaging, part conversation starter, and entirely too big for your average shopping trip.
How Can You Get Chipotle's Big Ass Bag?
Unfortunately, you can't just add this giant accessory to your next Chipotle order. The bag is available through a digital sweepstakes for U.S. Rewards members running Oct. 13 through Nov. 10, 2026.
Eligible Family Meal orders placed through Chipotle's app or website earn automatic entry, and the official rules also include a no-purchase entry method.
"A Big Ass Meal deserves a Big Ass Bag," Chipotle Chief Brand Officer Fernando Machado said in a statement, adding that the company wanted to take a recognizable part of the Chipotle experience and give it an over-the-top upgrade.
Honestly, if you're going to show up with enough burritos to feed the whole friend group, you might as well make an entrance.

title: Weight loss injections or surgery? How each treatment differs
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - Weight is a daily struggle for millions of Americans and for a lot of them it’s not just the health risks, it’s shame and setbacks.
By 2035, it’s estimated that the number of people in the country living with obesity will rise to 19 million and affect nearly 126 million people. In the same study published by JAMA, researchers found that the number of American adults living with obesity has more than double over the past three decades.
More Americans are choosing weight loss injections over bariatric surgery, according to a new study. But some patients face a different reality when it comes to treatment options due to their insurance coverage.
A study in JAMA Network Surgery shows GLP-1 prescriptions rose 24% between 2018 and 2025. Over the same period, national bariatric surgery use in 2025 was slightly less than half of its 2022 peak.
But Dr. Shauna Levy with Tulane Weight Loss Center at Lakeside Hospital said she has not seen the same shift in her practice. Last year, she performed 250 bariatric surgeries, a number she said has held steady despite the rise of GLP-1 drugs.
The difference comes down to insurance coverage, Levy said.
“Right now in the state of Louisiana, you’re more likely to have bariatric surgery coverage than you are to have GLP-1 coverage,” Levy said. “And many people are surprised by this because they think surgery must be so much more expensive than GLP-1s. But actually, GLP-1s are meant to be taken for life. So if you look at the cost for a lifetime, it’s actually much more affordable to get bariatric surgery, even as a cash pay, than it is to take GLP-1s for the rest of your life.”
Levy said expanded coverage could bring more Louisiana residents into treatment.
Emily Showalter, 35, battled her weight for years. She felt like she was missing out on life’s most precious moments and decided to take control.
After little success with dieting and weighing 265 pounds, she turned to GLP-1 injections a year ago. The class of weight loss drugs includes Ozempic and Wegovy.
Showalter said she lost nearly 100 pounds. She said having the injections helped her relearn how to react to food and being around it.
“My kids have noticed my energy levels, you know, mom is way more involved and wanting to go do things,” Showalter added.
Blake Davenport had a different experience.
He spent a year and a half on GLP-1 medications in 2024 without much success. His doctor then recommended bariatric surgery.
Davenport said he started at 308 pounds and now weighs 173 pounds.
“It feels amazing,” Davenport said. “So it just feels great to have no more medication for blood pressure. No more medications for diabetes. My sleep apnea is almost completely resolved.”
Part of what makes the choice difficult is the stigma that still surrounds obesity, Levy said.
“We’ve really looked at weight as an almost character flaw or a personal failure, and in fact—it is a disease that needs to be treated medically, just like any other diseases,” Levy said.
Levy said no single treatment works for everyone.
Despite the rapid rise of GLP-1 drugs, one study by researchers at the University of California San Diego found that obesity is largely undertreated.
The study used health records of nearly 20 million patients with severe obesity and found nearly 95% of those patients received no treatment.

title: Falmouth passes resolution opposing CMP transmission project
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Following public outcry, the Falmouth Town Council passed a resolution opposing a proposed transmission line upgrade project that would run through the town and surrounding communities.
The project, which is under review by a state regulator, has sparked pushback from residents. As the deadline for testimony nears at the end of the month, Falmouth’s action intended to voice the concerns of residents and ask for answers — and neighboring Cumberland looks to follow suit.
“What we’re seeing now is really an united effort for both abutters and property owners from Falmouth and Cumberland,” said Cumberland council Chair Michael Edes. “It’s really a strong united voice from these groups.”
Central Maine Power’s proposed Greater Portland Transmission Upgrades Project would run from Yarmouth into Portland, with a separate section in Westbrook. It would install and rebuild transmission lines and construct and upgrade substations along the route. The first phase of the project in the section north of Portland will cost an estimated $547 million.
The upgrades will strengthen the energy grid in Greater Portland, according to CMP. The company pointed to a recent equipment failure at an aging Yarmouth substation, which caused 28,000 outages from Gray to Falmouth, as one example of why the upgrades are needed.
Residents along the current power corridor, many organizing under the newly formed Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure, say the project would have a negative impact on their property values, municipal planning, health and local environment.
Much of the Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure’s concerns, as well as its extensive website, include misinformation about the project, said a CMP spokesperson.
The Maine Public Utilities Commission is reviewing the project, tasked with determining if it would serve a public need. The review process, which typically takes a year, started in July.
In September, members of the Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure gained intervenor status in the case, meaning the group could submit official testimony and be part of the review process. They then filed a motion asking the PUC to create a threshold merit phase in the review, meaning an independent party would evaluate the need for the project.
The request, supported by the Conservation Law Foundation, the town of Falmouth and the Maine Office of Public Advocate, was rejected by the PUC commissioners on Oct. 9, who said these steps were already included in the standard PUC review.
In the same ruling, the PUC pushed back the deadline for all intervenor testimony by one week to Oct. 30.
At the Falmouth Town Council meeting on Wednesday, residentaired frustration with CMP for not communicating the scope and scale of the upgrades to them more directly, and asked the council to stand with them in their opposition to the proposal.
“Falmouth needs to send a clear, unequivocal message that this proposal is not acceptable as it stands,” said Falmouth resident and Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure member Erin Becker.
The resolution, which passed unanimously, opposed the PUC certifying the project as necessary and urged the regulators to further examine scale and impact of the project, as well as consider alternatives.
The resolution also calls on CMP to provide clear answers on the project’s need and design and requests more time for intervenors to participate in the PUC review process.
Responding to the resolution, a statement from CMP said staff look forward to communicating with residents at an upcoming open house and appreciated the town’s engagement, also remarking on the resolution’s context.
“Unfortunately, misinformation and misleading speculation about the potential impacts of what is proposed continue to circulate,” said the statement.
At the council’s meeting on Sept. 28, the public spoke for hours against the project. The council sent a letter to CMP conveying what it had heard from residents, as well as supporting the filing to establish a threshold merit phase.
In response to the town’s initial letter, CMP met with council leadership to discuss local concerns.
Other towns are considering similar paths. In Cumberland, the council has heard concerns from residents about the impacts of the transmission project and the lack of communication from CMP — though to a lesser extent than Falmouth, which has more of the corridor running through it.
On Wednesday, the council sent a letter to CMP expressing resident questions and frustrations and asking for more information. The same letter is set to be filed with the PUC, and the council will also consider a resolution on the project at its Oct. 26 meeting.
Cumberland Town Manager Matt Sturgis said that while CMP did host an open house last fall about the upgrades and sent mailers to abutters, residents have been asking for more.
“If folks are coming to us saying, ‘We don’t know anything, we haven’t heard anything’ … we do have a responsibility to our residents to say ‘Hey, can you help us understand what’s going on here?’” said Sturgis.
After the intervenor deadline passes, testimony will be reviewed at an intervenor technical conference on Dec. 2, after which PUC commissioners will issue a final order.
In between these two PUC dates, CMP will host a series of open houses about the project in the communities, including on Nov. 5 in Falmouth and Nov. 12 in Cumberland.

title: Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs moved to a new prison after reports of a luxury lifestyle behind bars
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Sean “Diddy” Combs has been moved to a federal prison in Pennsylvania after reports that the hip-hop mogul was living the high life and was injured in a fight at his New Jersey lockup, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press on Friday.
The federal Bureau of Prisons is transferring Combs, 56, from FCI Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low, a low-security facility south of Williamsport and about 155 miles (250 kilometers) west of New York City, the person said. The person was not authorized to speak publicly and did so on condition of anonymity.
The Bureau of Prisons confirmed the move but provided no further details. The agency said it does not discuss conditions of confinement for anyone in its custody, including reasons for transfer, for privacy, safety, and security reasons.
“Decisions about inmate placement are made by the BOP, and we are not in a position to speak to the circumstances surrounding this transfer,” said Combs’ spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer. “Sean remains focused on moving forward, and we hope that his time at the new facility will be productive and without unnecessary disruption.”
Combs is serving a four-year, two-month sentence for his conviction last year on prostitution-related charges for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters. The case featured harrowing testimony about violence and sex parties he called “freak-offs.” It was a forceful reckoning for one of music and entertainment’s most influential figures.
Last month, NBC News reported that Combs was continuing to enjoy aspects of his millionaire lifestyle at FCI Fort Dix, smuggling in Hennessy, having fellow inmates cook, clean, make his bed and give him massages, and using a contraband cellphone to view social media and an ex-girlfriend’s nude selfies.
On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Combs was injured in a fight with another inmate at Fort Dix and had to be taken out of the prison for treatment. In a rare rebuttal, the Bureau of Prisons refuted TMZ’s report, telling the AP: “The story you are referring to is false and did not happen.”
In the wake of the NBC report, Combs was placed in the prison’s special housing unit, a heavily secured part of the facility away from the general population, for inmates with disciplinary issues or security concerns. He has also been docked 41 days of good-conduct credit, pushing his release date back to March 2, 2028, according to the person familiar with the matter.
In April, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in Combs’ bid to overturn his conviction and sentence, which his lawyers argued was too harsh. The court has yet to rule.

title: Lessons from Maine brands: How to create a lasting logo
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
“Design is just moving around colors and shapes,” a former coworker told me one day.
I saw my career flash before my eyes. The late nights, the coffee, the cold, fried Brussels sprouts, the coffee, the head-spinning, the coffee. I was offended that he had reduced my profession to something my three-year-old could execute.
But I quickly realized he wasn’t entirely wrong. He was just missing the core of it.
Arranging colors and shapes in a specific way creates a feeling, and the right feeling can tell people exactly what a business stands for before they’ve read a single word of copy.
That’s the real job of a logo: making a company’s mission legible at a glance. It’s also where many businesses go wrong, opting for a generic template, a cheap solution or a quick shortcut that could belong to almost any business.
A logo as a mission statement
When you look at a logo, you notice the shape, the color, the typography and maybe a clever detail hidden somewhere. But beneath all of that lies something far less tangible and far more critical to its success.
For many Maine businesses, their work and products are intrinsically linked to community, environment and a strong work ethic. Their logo isn’t just a graphic on a business card or a sign; it’s the visual embodiment of their entire vision and mission.
And as designers, it’s critical to bring that to life visually.
When designing a logo, there is an immense responsibility of stewardship. A business is entrusting you with the monumental task of shaping how they show up in the world. That exchange cannot happen in a vacuum. It requires a strong relationship.
It all comes down to trust
Ultimately, a logo’s success comes down to one fundamental factor: trust.
A deep level of trust opens up a far richer journey during the design process. The work transforms from a transactional service into a collaborative partnership.
Building a visual world requires asking hard questions. It forces business owners to articulate who they are, dive into who they’re speaking to and confront aspects of their brand that might feel uncertain or raw. And this can feel uncomfortable.
And in that discomfort is where design magic can happen.
When a business trusts an agency partner enough to lean into that vulnerability, this gives them the freedom to push past safe ideas and explore deeper territories. That trust lets owners open up, share their authentic story and embrace unexpected creative directions they might have otherwise passed by.
Lessons from Maine’s icons
Look at the state’s most iconic logos. You can immediately see the level of thought, care and mutual trust that went into them. And this is precisely why they’ve become iconic:
L.L.Bean’s “Sunrise Over Katahdin” logo, introduced in 1987, distills water, trees and mountains, the defining elements of Maine wilderness, into a single image built around Katahdin, the state’s tallest peak and the northern end of the Appalachian Trail. The brand doesn’t sell boots. It sells the outdoors the boots were built for.
Allagash Brewing Co.’s autumn leaf is a quiet nod to the Allagash Wilderness Waterway the company is named for. It ties a beer made in Portland back to a specific, remote piece of Maine geography and gives customers a sense of place they can hold in their hand.
Old Town Canoe crafted a timeless wordmark with a subtle visual twist, shaping the inner negative space of the “O” to double as a canoe’s bow.
Point of pride
Here’s a wild take: the best logos reflect the strength of the relationship between the agency and the business owner.
The logo is the culmination of an honest partnership. When an agency listens deeply, and a business owner trusts boldly, the logo is no longer void of meaning, it becomes an enduring point of pride.
