title: Fight over evidence in Alex Murdaugh retrial turns to DNA and missing murder weapons
text:
LEXINGTON, S.C. (AP) — Prosecutors and lawyers for Alex Murdaugh returned to court on Friday amid escalating disputes over evidence for his retrial next year on murder charges.
Murdaugh, a once-rich and imposing heir to a Southern legal dynasty, is scheduled to stand trial again in April on two murder charges in the June 2021 shooting deaths of his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, at their home in Colleton County. Murdaugh, 58, was in court Friday in a suit as he serves a lengthy prison sentence after pleading guilty to stealing from clients.
The killings and his six-week trial in 2023 captivated the true crime world with a mix of treachery, corruption, money, power and Southern accents. While admitting he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict, Murdaugh has adamantly denied the killings.
The South Carolina Supreme Court overturned his convictions earlier this year, ruling that a court clerk influenced jurors during his trial. The clerk told jurors to watch Murdaugh’s body language and not be fooled when he testified in his own defense.
Hearing was called after defense lawyers complained about evidence
The judge called Friday’s hearing after Murdaugh’s lawyers filed a flurry of motions saying prosecutors were dragging their feet sharing evidence. They said it threatened to delay the April 5 retrial date that Judge Debra McCaslin is determined to keep. Prosecutors said the disputes were mostly misunderstandings.
Both sides are expected to argue whether defense DNA experts can test the rest of a sample of genetic material found under the fingernails of Murdaugh’s wife. They’re also expected to argue over whether authorities must turn over ballistics and other evidence from shootings in eight surrounding counties involving the same type of gun as one of the weapons used in the killings.
Defense wants to know if prosecutors now think someone else was at the scene
Very little may be said about the most intriguing dispute of all.
Defense lawyers want to know whether prosecutors have called a grand jury to investigate a police officer who was friends with Murdaugh. Defense attorneys said that prosecutors suggested the officer arrived at Murdaugh’s home before other law enforcement officers and could have helped him hide bloody clothes or the weapons used in the killings. Neither the clothes nor the weapons have been found.
Murdaugh’s lawyers said the evidence is critical because prosecutors argued during his first trial that he acted alone. Prosecutors said no one else was at the home between the killings and Murdaugh’s return from visiting his mother, when he called 911 to report the shootings.
The defense says another person’s involvement would cast doubt on testimony from witnesses who said at Murdaugh’s first murder trial that he acted alone. Murdaugh’s lawyers also demanded any evidence prosecutors have of possible accomplices or a grand jury investigation into them.
In response, prosecutors declined to say whether any evidence exists, citing legal restrictions on disclosing whether a grand jury is meeting.
Both sides get cranky in court filings
Prosecutors and the defense have been getting crankier in their court filings.
After Murdaugh’s lawyers accused the state of not sharing cellphone data, prosecutors wrote, “It’s hard to understand the inexplicably brazen and highly prejudicial falsehoods the defense puts in its public filings (or, as previously seen, on the record in open court). It is stunning, really. Facts matter.”
And when prosecutors offered all the data from a computerized scan of the crime scene before the hearing, Murdaugh’s lawyers wrote in their response, “The defense is glad to hear it. It wishes only that the State had said so a month ago.”
While pretrial hearings are being held in Lexington County, the retrial has been moved to Sumter County, east of Columbia and about 80 miles (129 kilometers) from Colleton County. The judge determined that extensive publicity surrounding the case in Murdaugh’s home county could prevent a fair retrial.
Regardless of what happens in his next murder trial, Murdaugh will remain in prison. He pleaded guilty to stealing around $12 million from his clients and is currently serving a 40-year federal sentence concurrently with a 27-year state sentence for his financial crimes.

title: Proposed Amazon warehouse in Gorham clears key hurdle with environmental approval
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection on Friday issued Amazon a permit to build its proposed warehouse and distribution facility off Main Street in Gorham, clearing one of the few remaining hurdles for the controversial project.
Addressing topics such as noise, visual and scenic character, wildlife and endangered species, soil, water quality and wetlands, the permit states that the DEP found Amazon’s 146,280-square-foot facility would not have unreasonable effects on the environment and complies with all standards.
“The applicant has made adequate provision for fitting the development harmoniously into the existing natural environment and the development will not adversely affect existing uses, scenic character, air quality, water quality or other natural resources in the municipality or in neighboring municipalities,” the permit states.
The DEP held a public meeting focused on the project in July, where several residents asked the agency to deny Amazon’s application over concerns that the project on the undeveloped land in the town’s industrial park would damage wetlands, pollute the area and harm wildlife Over 100 people submitted public comments to the department expressing similar worries, the permit states.
DEP Licensing Division Director Jessica Damon said in July that the department would review the project’s impacts to protected natural resources under the Natural Resources Protection Act, and its efforts to compensate for those impacts. If built, the facility would affect about 34,918 square feet of freshwater wetlands.
The department initially said it would make a decision on Amazon’s application by Sept. 21, but requested two extensions as it waited for the applicant to update wetland impacts. Engineering firm Sebago Technics, developer Bluewater Property Group and consulting firm Flycatcher represented Amazon in the application process.
The permit includes a number of conditions Amazon must follow going forward. The company still needs permits from the Maine Department of Transportation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers before starting construction.
The DEP’s decision comes about a month after Amazon’s project was approved at the town level. Citizens group Gorham United earlier this week appealed that decision in court on the basis that the town did not properly apply local environmental and traffic standards in that decision.

title: Beers Criteria: The medication list every senior should know about
text:
(Aging Untold) — As we age, our bodies process medicine differently — and a drug that felt fine at 40 can cause problems at 70. Even small details, like whether a pill can be cut, chewed or dissolved, can carry serious consequences for older adults.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down the Beers List, or “Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults,” a tool every family should know about before the next doctor’s visit.
What is the Beers List?
“We’re talking about the geriatric list of medications and their adverse effects on our aging population,” “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “It doesn’t mean that just because that medication’s on there that you can’t take it — it means that it could affect you differently because of the way you metabolize after you age.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said the list, published by the American Geriatrics Society, includes about 100 medications and is updated every three years to reflect new research.
The danger of cutting, crushing or chewing pills
One of the biggest risks families overlook has nothing to do with the medication itself — it’s how it’s taken.
“Can’t tell you how many times I’ve heard, ‘We’ll just crush it and put it in applesauce, it’s easier,’” Cradduck said. “Well, you just gave them a lethal dose of a blood pressure med because that was a time release.”
Cradduck offered a simple rule of thumb: “If a pill is scored, it usually means that you can cut it. But if it’s not scored, I don’t care how good that pill cutter is — you shouldn’t be cutting it, because it’s not distributed equally.”
Even physicians can be caught off guard
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said that this information isn’t always top of mind for doctors outside of geriatric specialties.
“I think that information is not known to a lot of physicians,” Rogers said. “As a surgeon, and seeing people in the office, I really did not know that.”
So ongoing education is essential, she said.
“So when we’re doing all this continuing education, these are some basic things that we need to know, especially since we’re taking care of people of all ages,” she said.
Rogers added that time-release medications deserve extra scrutiny as patients get older.
“Understanding as the aging process, the same way that we treat everybody as they’re aging, we look at all their metabolism — that they do metabolize different,” she said. “And then we haven’t even begun to look at their own genetics, what’s going on there to interfere. So it could be a lot of risk for falling and memory and everything else.”
Don’t let social media cause fear over the Beers List
Cradduck warned that misinformation about the list is causing some older adults to stop taking medications they actually need.
“Don’t listen to the fearmongers that are on social media,” Cradduck said. “They’ll start reading from this and say if your loved one, age 65 or older, is on this medication, they can’t take it. This is causing harm, because we’re seeing a lot of people that aren’t taking the medications that they need.”
Cradduck pointed out that the list isn’t new.
“It’s been out there forever,” she said, and it’s revamped every three years.
Rogers said that the fact that a medication is on the list does not mean you can’t take it.
“It just means it’s a higher risk associated with a certain age,” she said.
How to use the Beers List with your doctor
O’Rourke said lifestyle changes are a good reason to revisit the list with a doctor.
“If you’ve changed your lifestyle, you’re more active, or something’s changed, you really want to make sure that that doctor’s looking at your medicine, looking at the Beers List and adjusting it as you grow older,” she said.
O’Rourke recommends bringing a copy of the list straight to an appointment.
“I like to tell people to make a copy of the list and bring it in to your doctor and just ask your doctor, do you know about this list? Is there anything on here? Look at my medicine and compare the two and see how I’m doing,” she said. “Be a really proactive patient with the list with your physician, especially when you’re older.”
Resource
Key takeaways
- Older bodies process meds more slowly: Bodies change with age and process medications more slowly, so drugs stay in the system longer.
- Ask your doctor. Ask your doctor if they use the Beers List of high-risk medications for seniors to help prevent falls and confusion.
- Review and simplify. Advocate for regular reviews of your medications.

title: Obituary: Jeannette T. Saucier
text:
BRUNSWICK – Jeannette T. Saucier, affectionately known as “Nettie” or “Jan”, 88, of Scarborough, Maine, passed away peacefully on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026.
Nettie will be remembered with immense love by her family and all those whose lives she touched. Above all, she cherished her family and the memories they created together. Perhaps her greatest gift was her ability to make people feel loved without ever having to say a word. Her warm smile, infectious laughter, and quiet, unconditional love will be dearly missed by everyone who knew her.
Nettie loved reading, going for rides, and traveling with her children. Whether enjoying a quiet moment with a book or setting off on another adventure, she found happiness in life’s simple pleasures and in the company of those closest to her.
Born on Jan. 2, 1938, in Rochester, N.H., to Alice Soucy Bolduc and Antonio Bolduc, Nettie grew up in Somersworth, N.H., and graduated from Holy Cross High School in 1956. She continued her education at secretarial school, which led to a position at a local shoe factory. It was there that she met her first husband, Bill. They married on July 1, 1957, and together raised six wonderful children.
Nettie’s unwavering dedication to her family was evident in everything she did, including the years she spent working alongside Bill to make the Falcon Restaurant a success. Following their divorce in 1975, she married Richard Saucier in 1979. They shared many loving years together until his passing in 2015.
During the early years of their marriage, Nettie and Richard became active members of the Maine Dairy Goat Association. From the early 1980s through the mid-1990s, they maintained a herd of dairy goats and eventually became involved in showing goats at agricultural fairs. Their adventures took them throughout Maine, as far north as Blue Hill, and out of state for conventions and events.
Nettie was predeceased by her beloved husband, Richard; her sons Mark and Jimmy; and her grandson, Bill.
She is survived by her children, Nola Ormsby, Jon Ormsby and his wife, Donna, Claire Levesque, Celeste Tamburello and her husband, Joe. She also leaves behind her grandchildren, Tenaj Ormsby, Renee Ormsby, Joshua Ormsby, Kaylin Knox, Sasha Crawford, Sal Tamburello, and Gianna Tamburello.
She is also survived by her sister, Cecile Toussaint, and her husband, Charles; her niece, Nicole, her nephews Danny, David, and Mark; and her stepchildren and step-grandchildren.
A special and heartfelt thank you goes to Monica, Rusty, Jade, and Tara, who remained an important part of Nettie’s life following the passing of their father and grandfather. Nettie loved each of you as her own.
The family would also like to express their deepest gratitude to the staff at the Maine Veterans’ Home in Scarborough for the exceptional care, kindness, and love they showed Nettie during her time there. She truly loved you all, and your compassion meant so much to her and her family.
Visiting hours celebrating Jeannette’s life will be held on Monday, Oct. 19, from 9:30 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. at Stetson’s Funeral Home & Cremation Care, 12 Federal St., Brunswick. A Mass of Christian Burial will follow at 11 a.m. at St. Charles Boromeo Catholic Church, McKeen Street, Brunswick. Burial will be in St. John’s Cemetery, Pine Street, Brunswick. Condolences, memories and photos may be shared with the family by visiting Stetson’s Funeral Home website http://www.StetsonsFuneralHome.com

Recreational Therapy Department at the

title: 4 candidates vying for 2 Orono Town Council seats
text:
Four candidates are running for two Orono Town Council seats this November.
The candidates, Devon Biggie, Dan Demeritt, Daniel LaPointe and Colleen Marzilli, have various experience serving on or previously running for the Town Council.
Demeritt is running for reelection. The other council seat up for election is held by Vice Chair Sarah Marx, who announced earlier this year that she would not be seeking reelection after a three and a half year term.
This November’s election will add at least one newcomer to Orono’s seven-member Town Council. In the past year, the council has voted on funding for major town projects, approved a 10-year comprehensive plan and created a committee to revitalize its downtown.
The candidates appear in alphabetical order.
Devon Biggie
Biggie, a University of Maine alumnus and engineer, said during a candidate forum on Oct. 7 he’s running for council to make the town better for his children. Biggie focused on economic development and affordability during the forum.
This is his first time running for council.
The “growth opportunity” that Orono has for housing and businesses gives the town opportunities to expand that he would want to act on as a council member, Biggie said. With those opportunities, Biggie said he would take a “30,000-foot” approach to looking at how current initiatives are being run to learn more about how everything works.
“I want to make this a home for my family, and I want to work toward that,” Biggie said at the forum.
To keep Orono affordable for residents, Biggie said he’d look at proposals for projects and developments to see if they are wants or needs. If the town needs to fund a project, every source for funding should be researched to lower the impact it would have on the town’s tax rate, he said.
Dan Demeritt
Demeritt has served on the Town Council for three and a half years and has been chair during the council’s vote on bond issues and the creation of a noise ordinance.
He’s running for re-election because there’s “more to do” in the town, he said at the forum. Initiatives to bring community members together and create policy from public comments have been successful, but there’s still a chance to bring in new economic and policy opportunities to the town, he said.
“No is not the last word in Orono, even though it’s spelled that way,” Demeritt said.
In response to a question about affordability, he said the town should talk with UMaine about an updated payment in lieu of taxes agreement to help offset costs created by Orono’s services. The amount UMaine pays Orono, $650,000 a year, has not changed in more than a decade, he said.
Daniel LaPointe
LaPointe, who has previously unsuccessfully run for the Orono council, said he’s “really concerned about the abuse of authority and the violations of people’s civil rights” in the town and would focus on these issues if elected. During the forum, he pointed to human trafficking and delayed court dates as problems affecting Orono residents but did not say how he would attempt to change these issues if elected.
Orono used to be a booming community but “paperwork and obstructionism” in the form of administrative oversight and costs have gotten in the way of it being able to welcome businesses or expand services, LaPointe said
“Services are paramount,” LaPointe said, adding that Orono’s emergency services should be kept at their current levels but other costs, including administrative, should be cut to lower the town’s tax rate.
Colleen Marzilli
Marzilli is a professor of nursing at the University of Maine and a nurse practitioner. She ran for a council seat in 2025, and earned the third most votes.
If elected, she said she would work to connect Orono’s “natural beauty and capacity for innovation” with residents’ needs. She would do this through listening, learning and asking questions about any decisions up to vote, she said at the Oct. 7 forum.
Marzilli wants to be fiscally responsible while maintaining essential services and infrastructure, she said. It’s important to review how services are delivered, keep Orono affordable for residents, and invest in future housing and business, she said.
Orono residents can vote in person at the New Balance Field House and Memorial Gym on UMaine’s campus from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.

title: Floaties can build confidence in the water. Swim experts say they can hide a skill many kids never learn
text:
HOUSTON (InvestigateTV) — A flotation device can give a child confidence in the water, but swim experts say it can also hide a dangerous gap in a skill most kids never learn: how to tell the difference between floating and sinking.
They say without it, that same device can quietly set a child up for danger the moment it comes off.
Jenny Bennett’s son, Jackson, was the sweetest, most loving little boy. She told us that in his short 18 months “I truly thought that he was going to change the world someday.”
“I just never thought that we would lose him like we did,” she said.
He often wore a flotation device, or “floatie,” while in the pool. That changed one summer night in 2016.
“One evening, when we thought he was upstairs playing with his older sisters, he had actually wandered out our dog door and found our pool alone where he had jumped in and it was about five minutes that had gone by,” she recalled. “We realized that he wasn’t upstairs with his sisters. And my biggest fear was that he would get to the pool. And I ran outside and found him floating face down in the pool.”
After his death, Bennett learned other parents who lost children to drowning had something in common. Each of their toddlers also used flotation devices. She said she bought a floatie for Jackson three months before he died.
“It said, ‘learn to swim.’ I grabbed it and thought, this is amazing! We can put this on him. It heads above water. He can swim and float around with his sisters. And then I thought that it was keeping him safe,” Bennett said.
“I believe our culture has set children up to drown. I call it the ‘water baby culture’ where we make it so fun for these kids. We encourage them to jump in. We clap for them when they put their face in the water. And we make it so fun that they don’t realize it’s dangerous,” Bennett said.
Bennett said drowning prevention should come first and marketing for floaties should be revised. “It’s really important to teach children how to float on their backs.”
Floating vs. sinking
Genevieve Blasius, a swimming school owner and research scientist, said floating is a foundational skill that many swim schools do not prioritize.
“You’d be shocked about how many people are coming to me from other swim schools and that is not the primary thing that they’re really teaching,” Blasius said.
Blasius said flotation devices can train kids into a head up, hips down, vertical “bicycle kick” posture that does not translate to self-rescue swimming.
“One of the most important things on all every single one of my students: ‘Are you in the floating position? Are you in the sinking position?’ And all of them can answer that question. And that is not a standard practice for most of the schools in the area,” Blasius said.
Blasius said kids and parents can both develop a false sense of security, believing a child can swim, when the child can sink as soon as they stop moving because the device removes the body feedback that teaches what floating versus sinking feels like.
Calls for warning labels
Blasius said warning labels and better education from manufacturers and federal agencies are needed.
“If you go in the water and you go in a completely vertical position and you don’t move anything unless you’re very aware of your body and you tilt your head back and you can float if you feel your lungs inflate your lungs with air. Children are not aware of any of that,” Blasius said.
Blasius said that if the devices are “not doing anything” to give the child a sense of what position they should be in while floating, “it’s completely ignoring science.”
“We’re not even getting into the psychology of it. We’re just talking about physics,” Blasius said.
“There’s warning about everything. And there’s not a warning about this? I mean, how many — we’re talking about the number one cause of death in children. You kind of need to look at all aspects of it.”
A mother turns to advocacy
Bennett started a local chapter of Swim Safe Forever in Houston to provide drowning prevention education, survival swim lessons and scholarships to people in need.
She doesn’t believe the products should be banned and are good for boats and at the beach.
“The problem is when the children repeatedly wear them and their brain changes to think that, first of all, the water is a fun, safe place to be. And second of all, that they’re just going to pop right back up and they can swim in an upright position. But that position is just not obtainable unless they’re wearing the device on their chest, in their arms,” Bennett said.
Bennett said it’s important to teach children how to float on their backs so their heads are far enough out of the water that their nose and mouth are able to breathe.
She said these products should not be marketed as a learn-to-swim device.
“You leave them somewhere for a moment, and you think that they’re safe, and you turn around and they’re gone. And they could be doing something like getting into the pantry and spilling the cereal. They could be doing all of these things in a few seconds of time,” Bennett said of watching your child. “But they could also be wandering outside to your pool or to a neighbor’s pool or a lake, a pond nearby, finding the water and remembering how much fun they had in the water, and then jumping in. And by that point it’s too late. It only takes maybe 30 seconds for a child under 30 pounds to drown.”
One of the leading manufacturers of wearable floaties is Bestway, which licenses the Puddle Jumper brand.
Bestway spokesman Brannon Smith said its products meets standards set by ANSI, a voluntary standards-making group in the U.S.; CAN, which sets standards in Canada; UL, which is the Coast Guard’s third-party testing laboratory; and ISO, the international standards organization.
“While the Coast Guard approval program is not a pool-specific certification program, the underlying ANSI/CAN/UL 12402 requirements establish in-water performance requirements for buoyancy aids used in sheltered waters. Neither ISO 12402 nor ANSI/CAN/UL 12402 states that such products are prohibited from use in swimming pools or are unsuitable for pool environments,” Smith wrote in an email in response to InvestigateTV questions.
Products used in pools generally fall under the CPSC jurisdiction as aquatic toys. Currently, there are no mandatory safety standards for these specific types of wearable floaties.

title: MoMA at MDES: Art teacher brings bite of the Big Apple back to Mount Desert
text:
NORTHEAST HARBOR – After a fruitful summer of learning in New York City, Mount Desert Elementary School art teacher Shannon Westphal brought some of her weeklong art workshop back to her classroom.
Westphal received the Astor Incentive Award from the Maine Community Foundation, a grant intended to allow teachers and library staff from MDES and MDI High School to broaden their experience and education. She saw the opportunity to participate in a course called “Connecting Collections."
This summer, she spent a week in New York City, partaking in the course studying art at the Museum of Modern Art, The Guggenheim Museum and The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
"Every day we would go to a different museum and the curators at the museum would lead us through a series of artwork — similar to how I led the students through — that were all based on a theme,” said Westphal. “But then we would also expand our understanding of each individual artwork based on their connection of that theme, which is something I had never really thought of before.”
The class was hands-on and allowed Westphal and her fellow classmates to more deeply understand the pieces of art they were interacting with.
“Usually if I teach Claude Monet, I’m teaching Claude Monet, but really thinking about place through the lens of a variety of artists through a variety of time periods, just really made me understand Claude Monet a little bit better.”
Exercises integrated throughout the course forced Westphal and her classmates to represent the art they were studying through different physical activities. She brought many of those activities to her students when the school year started back up in the fall.
Typically, Westphal says the start of the school year follows a steady, routine-building approach to encourage students to settle in. This year, she wanted to jump right in with the students, and was met with a positive response.
“I think kids really appreciated it because they’re in their other rooms hearing the rules, building routines,” said Westphal. “And then they come in here and get to get messy. But also I think they really all got to express themselves in such an important way.”
She set out to create a project that included every grade in the school and would eventually transform the school into a modern art gallery, and so MoMA at MDES came to be.
Each grade was tasked with recreating a famous work of art, which sounds straightforward. But she challenged students to sink their teeth into each artwork, teaching them about the artist, the time and place the artwork was created in, and what the artist might have been trying to convey.
The artwork each grade recreated was carefully picked to be appropriate for the age group and align with other lessons the students were learning in other subjects.
Kindergarten recreated Wassily Kandinsky’s “Several Circles” using colored felt. Before jumping into the work, Westphal had students read “The Dot” by Peter Reynolds. “The Dot” is a children’s book about a girl who doesn’t see herself as an artist but learns to after drawing a dot and receiving encouragement from her art teacher.
The Kindergarteners created their own dot artwork before studying Kandinsky’s work closely to recreate it. Using the colored felt, students identified different colors that Kandinsky used and where to place them on the artwork.
First graders took on Jackson Pollock, one of his so-called “drip paintings” a nod to his process of dripping and flinging paint onto a canvas laid out on the floor. Before handing over the paint, Westphal asked the class to sketch or draw the painting, to recreate splatters with their crayons.
She explained to the students that Pollock’s work was performance-based and that his process was a part of the spectacle of the art. After setting up a canvas outside, students took turns splattering paint, but Westphal had them carefully identify the colors and shapes Pollock used and decide what order the colors should be utilized before they started.
The second-grade class tackled Claude Monet’s impressionist painting, “Water Lilies,” a three-panel oil painting currently on display at MoMA in New York City. Westphal had the students think about place and provided paint sample chips for students to pick from that represented one color used in the painting. Once they picked a color that they could identify in the painting, students had to explain how Monet used that color in the painting.
Then they got to work using sponges to achieve an impressionistic look to the painting to dapple paint on the canvas. Each student had a sponge and the opportunity to contribute to the artwork. What resulted was a two-panel painting that stretches to fill the auditorium space in the lower level of the elementary school.
The third-grade class dove into pop art and recreated Claes Oldenburg’s “The Store,” a collection of sculptures of items that might make up a storefront. Before they started sculpting, students had to think about what makes something art and they agreed with fellow pop artist Andy Warhol’s take, “art is what you can get away with.”
Each student recreated an item from “The Store” using clay and then priced the item with a paper tag. The collection is displayed in a glass case at the entrance of the school, much like a pastry case at a coffee shop or diner.
Next to the menu of clay foods is the fourth and fifth grade’s recreation of Louise Nevelson’s “Sky Cathedral.” Nevelson, who grew up in Rockland, Maine, used pieces of scrap wood arranged in boxes and painted black to create the piece.
Students were each given a box to arrange and glue any of the provided scraps in. Their final products were stacked and painted black to create one cohesive piece reflecting Nevelson’s work.
Six and seventh graders pulled inspiration from their favorite snacks and convenience store purchases to recreate “De Todo Un Poco.” Lucia Hierro’s artwork, meaning “a little bit of everything” is a love letter to New York City bodegas, ubiquitous corner stores that are an integral part of the city’s culture. The piece is an oversized clear plastic bag suspended from the ceiling that contains many items commonly found in bodegas across the city.
Westphal asked the students to think about what their go-to’s are at their own corner store and recreate the items in sculpture form. She arranged the finished pieces together to appear as if they were spilling out of a plastic bag onto a table in the art classroom.
The eighth-grade class learns about the Holocaust in social studies, so Pablo Picasso’s “Guernica” was a fitting connection for Westphal to draw. Picasso painted “Guernica” in response to the German arial bombing of the Basque town of the same name.
Students were grouped together and assigned a portion of the painting to recreate using carboard that would then be pieced together to form the finished product. As they worked on the piece, they learned about how artwork can be used to communicate information about an event in real time and relay emotions like the anguish of war.
Together, the collective artworks created MoMA at MDES in time for the school’s open house last week. The school transformed into a mini art gallery with a map created by Westphal to guide attendees through the school to each individual art installation.
“This school has like a culture of really putting a lot of importance on being an artist and I really don’t have to like drag kids through their projects,” said Westphal. “They’re really excited to express themselves already.”
Having the art displayed around the school allowed each class to appreciate each other’s artwork, which Westphal said can also help bolster students’ creativity and confidence. Ultimately, she hopes art can be a beacon for students who may have difficulty in other topics.
“I had a hard time in school and my teachers let me use art to show my learning and I really feel like that’s my purpose in life is to help students learn about the world in a fun way, hands on, learning about art,” said Westphal. “A lot of students just gravitate towards art, especially students who might struggle in other subjects.
“What the purpose of art is, is to show you something in a way that you never imagined it, and to remind you of your like creative being, no other animal on this earth has that ability.”

title: Obituary: Retired U.S. Navy Master Chief Richard Gray
text:
BRUNSWICK – Retired U.S. Navy Master Chief Richard “Dick” Gray passed away at home on Oct. 6, 2026, surrounded by his family.
Dick was born in Deblois, Maine Oct. 25, 1936, the eldest of Jennie and Clyde Gray’s five sons. He attended Calais High School and married Delia “Dee” right after returning from Navy Boot Camp. They were married 70 years.
Dick was predeceased by his parents; and brother, Ronald Gray.
He is survived by his wife, Delia; and his children, daughter, Cindy and husband Leon Dudley of Vassalboro, his son, Michael and wife Beverly Gray of Topsham, daughter, Jo Anne and husband Bruce Dempsey of Wayland, Mich., and daughter, Dianne Gray of Brunswick. He is survived by 10 grandchildren; and 11 great-grandchildren. He is also survived by three of his brothers, Robert, Royce “Jack” and Randy Gray.
Dick went into the Navy directly from high school, he spent 32 years in service to his country with tours around the world. Dick served in the U.S. Navy as a P-2 aircrewman and a P-3 Flight Engineer in VP squadrons 21, 45, 30, and 10, amassing over 20,000 flight hours. He then served as the maintenance master chief at VP-26. He retired in 1976 and spent five years as the service manager at Dow Motors in Ellsworth. He was then voluntarily recalled to active duty and spent 12 years as a command master chief at VP-23, NAS Sigonella, VP-11, NAS Brunswick, and VQ-2 in Rota Spain before retiring again from the Navy in 1992.
After retiring Dick served on the Ellsworth School Board for 20 years, was president of the Maine State School Board, worked as service manager at Darlings in Ellsworth and Northeast Ambulance.
Dick was the patriarch of the family, always with a helping hand, a quick wit and ready smile. He started his mechanical career taking apart everything he could reach as a child, including the kitchen appliances. He was an incredible husband, son, big brother, uncle, cousin, Father and Pop-Pop.
The family would like to thank CHANS Hospice staff for their exceptional care at the end of Dick’s life.
There will be no service. Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.
“Fair winds and following seas, shipmate, we have the watch, you stand relieved.”
In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Brunswick Naval Aviation Museum in Richard’s name.

title: Woman killed in Maine collision has been identified
text:
The woman killed in a Sunday collision in Poland has been identified.
Melinda Parker, 40, of Auburn was driving a 2026 Toyota Camry north on Route 11, also known as Bakerstown Road, where she crossed into the path of a 2019 Ram pickup truck towing a camper, according to the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office.
Parker succumbed to her injuries at the scene, and her passenger, Tony Parker, was taken to Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston with minor injuries, the sheriff’s office said.
The Ram’s driver, 63-year-old George Cole of Akron, Ohio, was treated at the scene for minor injuries. His passenger, Kimberly Cole, wasn’t injured.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Trump’s Russian diesel deal is disingenuous — at best
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Oct. 11, President Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” deal between Russia and Ukraine, a “deal” that Ukrainian President Zelensky knew nothing about and that was violated by Russia; mere hours later a Ukrainian thermal power plant in Kharkiv was struck.
This was on the heels of Trump shamelessly upbraiding Zelensky for prior targeting of energy plants and refineries in Russia and declaring that fuel targets within the Russian diesel supply chain were off limits — but only for the Ukrainian defenders.
Trump’s recent deal with Putin — to purchase Russian diesel — is a thinly veiled ploy to assuage concern about skyrocketing prices just weeks before the midterm elections. Trump’s claim that the high prices are attributable to the Ukrainians, and not his disastrous Iran invasion debacle, is a pipe dream. It is farcical that the man who so covets a Nobel Peace Prize apparently cares more about ceasefires to protect energy consumption than ceasefires to prevent the wanton killing of civilians.
Jon St. Laurent
Windham

title: First images released of Pope Leo at hospital after cancer surgery
text:
First images released of Pope Leo celebrating Mass at hospital after cancer surgery
The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Pope Leo XIV since his lung cancer surgery, showing him celebrating Mass, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.
The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him in Gemelli hospital. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.
In his homily, Leo thanked the hospital staff “for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him,” Bruni said.
Bruni also confirmed Leo would make his first public appearance on Sunday to deliver the traditional noontime prayer.
“His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own,” said a medical update signed by Leo’s personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone and the head of thoracic surgery at the Gemelli hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The 71-year-old Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
A signal of all systems go for trip
Even as questions swirled about what his cancer means for the future of his young pontificate, there were signs Friday that it was all systems go. The Vatican on Friday published the names of journalists accredited to fly on Leo’s plane with him during his Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Video below: Pope Leo's cancer diagnosis sparks push for more screenings
Leo’s ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis, and the Vatican can change plans at any time. But the posting of the media list signaled that at least on an organizational level, the trip was going ahead.
In the nearer term, Vatican officials were gaming out possible scenarios for Leo to recite the traditional Sunday noontime Angelus prayer. Vatican media personnel were seen at the Gemelli hospital laying cables for a possible live broadcast, as past popes have done when hospitalized. Spokesman Bruni said he would deliver the prayer, but it wasn't clear where.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said a recitation of the noontime prayer on Sunday from the hospital was a possibility, but would depend on Leo’s recovery. Such appearances have often served as a welcome confirmation of a hospitalized pope's well-being for the 1.4 billion-strong Catholic faithful and others.

title: ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky says family member died unexpectedly
text:
ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky says family member died unexpectedly
Dan Orlovsky, an ESPN analyst and former NFL player, announced the death of his brother-in-law in a social media post on Thursday.
Orlovsky said his sister's husband, Federico "Fed" Lascano, "passed away unexpectedly." He did not reveal any other details on Lascano's cause of death.
"Our family experienced an unimaginable tragedy," Orlovsky wrote in a post on X.
Lascano is survived by his wife, Christine, and their three sons: Brayden, 18, Cameron, 16, and Colton, 11.
"There are no words to describe the heartbreak of losing a husband, a partner, and a father so suddenly," he said. "In the midst of trying to process this devastating loss, my sister is now facing the overwhelming reality of navigating life as a solo parent and a single-income household, all while helping her boys cope with the loss of their dad."
In the post, Orlovsky went on to ask the public for monetary donations to "help ease some of the financial burden."
Orlovsky was drafted as a quarterback by the Detroit Lions in the fifth round in 2005. He retired from the NFL in 2017 before becoming an ESPN analyst in 2018.

title: Friday’s high school football: Biddeford knocks off Marshwood
text:
Biddeford erased a 14-point deficit with two touchdowns late in the first half, then dominated the second half en route to a 37-14 win over previously undefeated Marshwood in a Class B South football game Friday night in South Berwick.
Marshwood (6-1), ranked No. 4 in the Varsity Maine Top 10, put together two long touchdown drives in the first half. Parker Ferrer’s 9-yard run in the first quarter made it 6-0, and the Hawks held the ball for nearly nine minutes in the second quarter, as a 5-yard run by Greg Castoras capped an 89-yard drive.
Biddeford (5-2), though, quickly drove down the field and cut into its deficit when Stanley Richerson scored on a 10-yard run. Moments later, Alexander Gosselin intercepted a pass and returned it 43 yards for a touchdown. Estevao Lembissa’s conversion rush gave the Tigers a 15-14 halftime lead.
Lembissa broke it open with two long TDs in the third quarter — a 71-yard pass from Ernest Dore and a 49-yard run.
Richerson added a 78-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter.
KENNEBUNK 20, WESTBROOK 14: Peter Landenberger scored the go-ahead touchdown on a 3-yard run midway through the second quarter, and the Rams (6-1) held Westbrook (2-5) scoreless over the final three quarters as they secured a Class B South victory in Kennebunk.
Ethan White had two touchdown runs for the Rams, including a 52-yarder just 48 seconds into the game.
Westbrook, though, led 14-6 after one quarter. Andre Hicks III returned a short punt 39 yards for a TD, and Cole Tanner scored on a 4-yard run.
White’s second touchdown — a 23-yard run — cut the margin to 14-12 early in the second quarter.
The Blue Blazes drove deep into Kennebunk territory late in the game, but the Rams held on downs.
NOBLE 21, SOUTH PORTLAND 7: Mark LaPointe threw two touchdown passes and the Knights (3-4) kept their playoff hopes alive with a Class A South win over the Red Riots (4-3) in North Berwick.
LaPointe tossed a 30-yard scoring pass to Bryson McCormack in the first quarter as Noble took a 14-0 lead. In the fourth quarter, Alec Hale caught a screen pass and went 14 yards for a touchdown.
Noble’s Tristan Miniutti scored on a 3-yard run in the first quarter.
Christopher Salamone scored on a 3-yard run with 20 seconds left in the second quarter for South Portland, the No. 8 team in the Varsity Maine poll.
THORNTON ACADEMY 61, SANFORD 0: The Trojans (7-0) scored on six of their seven possessions in the first half and cruised to a win over the Spartans (1-6) in Saco.
Brennan Tabor scored on runs of 8 and 22 yards in the first quarter to give Thornton, the top-ranked team in the Varsity Maine poll, a 14-0 lead just 2:07 into the first quarter. Noah Fullerton then threw a 23-yard TD pass to Logan O’Keefe, and Chase Paquette scored on a 3-yard run to make it 26-0.
Paquette scored again on a 3-yard run in the second quarter, followed by a pair of rushing touchdowns by Caleb Parenteau (12 and 6 yards).
Owen Morin scored on a 27-yard run in the third quarter and Kendrick Booker added a 6-yard touchdown run in the fourth.
CHEVERUS 27, DEERING 6: Colton Jewett passed for a touchdown and ran for another, and the Stags (2-5) built a 21-0 lead in the first 10 minutes against the Rams (1-6) at Memorial Field in Portland.
Igor Bitencourt scored on a 35-yard run, James Dillon recovered a fumble in the end zone, and Kevin True caught a pass from Jewett for a 24-yard touchdown.
Jewett added a 9-yard TD run in the fourth quarter.
Matt Ciampi scored on a 3-yard run for Deering.
GRAY-NEW GLOUCESTER 25, MT. ARARAT 6: Liam Joyce recorded a rushing touchdown and a receiving touchdown in the first half to help the Patriots (5-1) cruise past the Eagles (0-7) in an eight-man Large School South game in Gray.
Wide receiver Carter Corson gave Gray-New Gloucester a 6-0 lead in the first quarter, scoring on a 3-yard jet sweep.
Joyce scored on a 5-yard run later in the first. In the second quarter, he was left open near the end zone and quarterback Cole Prescott found him for a 15-yard touchdown, extending the lead to 18-0.
Running Grealish scampered 14 yards in the fourth quarter for the Patriots’ final TD.
Mt. Ararat got a 70-yard touchdown run from Ethan Fournier late in the fourth.
CONY 55, BRUNSWICK 7: Drew Lindquist passed for five touchdowns, Anderson Noyes and Landen Perry both scored twice, and the Rams (6-1) cruised to a Class B win over the Dragons (1-6) in Augusta.
Lindquist’s first TD pass, an 18-yarder to Ian Lasselle, gave the Rams an early lead. Brunswick struck back immediately, as Jacob Austin returned the ensuing kickoff 83 yards to the end zone.
Noyes then put Cony ahead for good with the first of his two 3-yard touchdown runs. In the second quarter, a blocked punt set up a 17-yard TD pass to Perry, who later caught a 2-yard pass on fourth-and-goal with 4.9 seconds remaining in the half.
After another TD run by Noyes in the third quarter, Lindquist connected with Jacob Fifield (11 yards) and Brady Noftall (6 yards).
Nolan Noyes capped the scoring with a 60-yard touchdown run in the fourth.

title: ‘A great hero’: Trump praises father who stopped Oregon elementary school shooting
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — President Donald Trump praised the father who helped stop the shooting at an Oregon elementary school.
“Well, I’ll tell you what. There was a great hero, and it could have been — as bad as it was — we had a great hero that went in and did the business. He took care of business,” Trump told reporters Friday at the White House.
Kaylub Giamanco was identified as the man who stopped the 16-year-old shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday.
Giamanco, a Bend-area resident with two daughters who attend the school, according to his mother, Kenda Freeman.
Police said Giamanco saw the 16-year-old go into the school and he followed him inside before shooting and killing him.
“Thank God we had him; otherwise it would have been much worse. It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump added.
Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and one teacher were killed in the shooting. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were also taken to an area hospital in critical condition.
Authorities said the first 911 call came at just before 1 p.m. local time from a driver who said someone with a gun had shot at him multiple times while he was in his car.
Bend Police Chief Chris Carney said callers then reported a person with a gun inside the school on Stone Creek Lane, and the school was put on lockdown.
Officers arrived just a couple of minutes later and reported finding the 16-year-old dead.
A law enforcement official briefed on the case told The Associated Press the 16-year-old used a pump-action shotgun bought by his mother. Police did not immediately release the teen’s name.
Investigators searched the shooter’s home Thursday night and took computers and other electronics. His parents told investigators their son had attended Silver Rail Elementary, according to a senior law enforcement official who spoke to CNN.

title: Obituary: Richard Irving Powell
text:
RUMFORD – Richard Irving Powell of Peru passed away on Oct. 5, 2026, at the age of 73. Richard was born on Oct. 12, 1952, to Richard and Beverly Powell in Rumford. Widely known as “Monkey the Junkie”, he started his salvage business Eastern Metals in 1971.
Richard was an accomplished trapper, hunter, fisherman and was a lifetime member of the National Trapper’s Association. He enthusiastically served as a selectman for the town of Peru. He was happiest with his grandchildren and sharing his many stories.
He will be deeply missed by his loved ones including, his wife Carol Powell (married since 1983); son Richard Powell and his wife Rebecca and their children Sierra and Breanna; son Lucas Powell and his wife Callie and their children Bruce and Henry; his brother Thomas Powell of Rumford and his sister Rebecca Powell of Sebring, Florida.
Richard’s graveside service will be held on Saturday, October 24 at 11 a.m., at Knox Cemetery, Peru. His celebration of life will follow immediately after at the King Hiram Lodge, 795 River Road, Mexico. Relatives and friends are respectfully invited.
Arrangements are in the care of Thibault Remembrance Center, 250 Penobscot Street, Rumford.

title: I support Lead Maine’s scrutiny of MaineCare
text:
MaineCare, at its finest, provides vital healthcare services to vulnerable Maine citizens. Or it should. However, disturbing allegations of fraud have made it clear that stricter methods for accountability need to be implemented in our state.
In addition, grossly inadequate living conditions for autistic individuals under MaineCare have been uncovered by the Maine Wire. As a wife, mother and grandmother who raised my family in Maine, I am finding it difficult to understand why our state government does not do more to protect these individuals.
As a concerned Maine citizen, I want to know that my tax dollars are being used responsibly by our elected officials. I want to know that those who truly need help are getting it the best way possible.
That is why the rules Lead Maine is proposing for MaineCare to adopt are essential in protecting the most vulnerable people in our state (“Amid fraud concerns, conservative group pushes for new MaineCare oversight rules,” June 23). These two rules require on-site inspections of MaineCare providers and pausing payment to providers if improper billing for services is detected by onsite inspections.
These rules are not onerous or overreaching. They are a commonsense approach to beginning the task of making MaineCare truly accountable to the people of Maine.
Wendy Munsell
Livermore Falls

title: Heal points are the standard in Maine, but what do other New England states do?
text:
In the 1949-50 season, Maine high schools turned to a new system invented by a local principal to seed teams not just by their record, but by the quality of the teams they played and beat, in the hopes of more fairly ranking the best teams in a playoff region
More than 70 years later, the Heal points, named after Durward Heal, remain Maine’s weighted formula of choice. But across New England, other states have found their own systems to try to solve the seeding dilemma and create the most fair, accurate matchups.
Here is how other states go about it:
VERMONT
Vermont uses an index system that since the 2015-16 season has reflected strength of schedule. Like in Maine, teams get points based on the level of the opponent they’re defeating, but Vermont schools also get more points for winning on the road. Home and away doesn’t factor into Maine’s Heals.
Teams beating higher division teams get five points for home wins and six points for road wins, four and five for home and road wins against teams in the same division, 3.5 and 4.5 for wins against teams a division below, and two and three against teams two divisions below. Teams get half those points for ties.
The total amount of points, divided by the amount of games played, is the team’s point index.
MASSACHUSETTS
Massachusetts split its state tournaments into sectionals — the equivalent of regions — until 2021, and seeded its teams by winning percentage. This led to numerous instances of lower seeds that played in tougher conferences beating higher seeds, and even reaching state finals.
Since the fall of 2021, however, Massachusetts has ditched sectionals for statewide tournaments, and instituted a weighted formula to seed teams within a division.
Teams are rewarded for margin of victory (capped at a specific amount); their average margin added to their average opponent’s rating results in their overall rating, with teams slotted according to that overall number.
RHODE ISLAND
Rhode Island used win-loss records to seed teams until 2024, when it opened up scheduling to allow teams to play out of division.
The state then instituted a rating percentage index formula similar to the one used in college basketball. A team’s winning percentage (multiplied by 10) makes up 60% of the number, and its opponents’ winning percentage makes up 40%.
CONNECTICUT
Connecticut handles its seeding systems on a sport-by-sport basis.
Soccer just this fall moved to a formula that factors in multipliers for interdivision games, strength of schedule and winning percentage.
Volleyball, meanwhile, gives teams points for every win an opponent has, then divides that total by the number of games for a final point value.
Not all rankings are done in house. Lacrosse, for instance, uses calculations from LaxNumbers.com to put together its playoff fields.
NEW HAMPSHIRE
New Hampshire, which adopted Maine’s Heal points formula on a trial basis in 2009, now uses a modified version that assigns a point figure for each win (more points for beating a team in a higher division).
All points are added up, then divided by the number of games played, and teams are sorted based on those ratings.

Troy Jackson tells Susan Collins to ‘shut up’ during heated Maine Senate debate
text:
Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson told Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during a heated final Maine U.S. Senate debate that also included an interruption from a data center protester.
Thursday night’s debate in a Bangor theater was the last of four meetings between Collins and Jackson, who are running for a seat that’s considered crucial in the fight for a Senate majority. The debate, like those that preceded it, included several testy exchanges over issues including the national debt, Collins’ relationship with President Donald Trump’s administration, and the candidates’ respective roles in worsening partisan divisions.
The scene became briefly chaotic when a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. As moderators asked for the protester to be removed, Collins said the shouting demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”
Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
Maine GOP said in a social media post after the debate that Jackson’s “shut up” comment was “unacceptable behavior.” Jackson’s campaign declined to comment on the exchange.
The issue of party loyalty came up during the debate, with one question posed to Collins asking her to cite a time she has defied the Republican Party. She referenced her push to oppose Pete Hegseth’s nomination as defense secretary, saying she organized Republicans to vote no. But Collins acknowledged he was confirmed despite her effort.
Collins accused Jackson of being a guaranteed vote for the Democratic Party while she has a track record of independence. Jackson disputed that characterization and said Collins is loyal to Trump when he needs key votes.
“What I know is that 100% of the time when Donald Trump goes to Susan Collins for a vote, he gets it,” Jackson said.
Collins, who is seeking her sixth term, has sought to distance herself from Trump during the debates, including using the phrase “Gulf of Mexico” instead of Trump’s preferred “Gulf of America.” Jackson described Collins’ votes against Trump as “managed votes” when she already knows the outcome is decided.
Jackson’s campaign also said Thursday that it raised $20.4 million in the third quarter as it seeks to close a funding gap with Collins. Jackson was a late entry into the race and the third quarter was his first quarter of fundraising.
Collins’ campaign said she raised $5.2 million in the same time period. Collins began the race with a considerable fundraising advantage over Jackson, as she had raised more than $18 million by the end of June and Jackson did not become the Democrats’ nominee until late July.
Story by Patrick Whittle.

title: Out-of-state police agency searched a university’s Flock camera network more than 183K times in 3 months
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - Records obtained from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte show that out-of-state police departments are searching the college’s network of Automatic License Plate Recognition cameras far more than local law enforcement.
The agency that searched the UNC Charlotte network the most between March and May 2026 was the Houston Police Department. The law enforcement agency conducted searches that included the UNC Charlotte network more than 183,000 times from March through May 2026.
Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police ranked 30th in total searches of the UNC Charlotte network. UNC Charlotte Police Department ranked 1,491st, with 229 searches over the three-month period.
Cameras feed a nationwide database
As cars drive by the Flock cameras on the UNC Charlotte campus, the cameras capture license plate numbers and add them to a nationwide database that law enforcement agencies across the country can search. Searching the data and the license plates they capture is limited to law enforcement, but there are also cameras owned by private companies and HOA’s that are included in the network.
Records from UNC Charlotte show that when Houston officers searched a license plate in the Flock system, they often searched more than 6,000 networks across the country, while many other departments appeared to limit their searches to fewer networks.
Students approached on campus were unable to guess which agencies searched the network most.
“Houston, Texas?!? Wow. OK. Interesting!!” said Verity Morgan, a student who recently hosted a campus debate on Flock cameras.
“Houston??? Why is Houston looking at Charlotte?” said Radhika Chaudha, a student.
“I mean what rights do people have now? You’re losing your right to privacy and you don’t have a choice,” Chaudha said.
“In my personal opinion, I don’t see why they’re necessary for our campus,” Morgan said.
“Money could definitely go to different things, I would say. And then it’s kind of creepy that people in Houston are trying to figure out what we got going on over here,” said Peyton Marshall, a student.
In an email statement sent to WBTV, the Houston Police Department said, “The use of automated license plate recognition systems by Houston Police Department personnel is regularly reviewed. The department has identified usage that is being investigated further.”
Attorney tracking flock camera use statewide
Mark Williams, an attorney in Wilmington, North Carolina, runs a website dedicated to opposing Flock cameras and other license plate reading technology. His records requests have helped reveal which police agencies are searching Flock networks on college campuses across the state.
“This is a mass government surveillance system that has been built throughout the state of North Carolina,” Williams said.
Williams warned that while there are rules in North Carolina limiting what law enforcement can use the data for, other agencies in other states lack some of the same guidelines. Meaning UNC Charlotte can’t control how the data their cameras capture is used.
“Under North Carolina law, you can’t sell the data. Texas has no guardrails. Most of those places don’t have rules against selling the data, how it’s used, and who has access to it. That’s a problem,” Williams said.
University responds
UNC Charlotte denied WBTV’s request for an interview with Police Chief Jeffrey Baker.
The university’s Director of Media Relations wrote in an email: “UNC Charlotte participates in a shared law enforcement network that includes approximately 1,600 agencies. When a law enforcement agency searches the network for a specific license plate, UNC Charlotte cameras may be included in that query. If the plate has been detected, the system returns the location, date and time of the detection.”
The university said the technology has helped University police in a wide variety of cases, including the arrest of a suspect in a larceny investigation involving more than $100,000 in equipment stolen from an on-campus construction site. The university has not provided the arrest record nearly a month after it was first requested by WBTV.
UNC Charlotte said it does not share network access with non-law enforcement entities such as homeowner associations and private businesses. Records show some other police agencies that searched the network include CSX railroad police and the parks department in Toledo, Ohio.
UNC Charlotte is not required to share its network with other law enforcement agencies. Appalachian State University turned off national sharing of its Flock network, and UNC Chapel Hill made the same decision last week.
There have been no accusations of misuse of the Flock network at UNC Charlotte. The university says it regularly reviews the system, and officers are required to use specific case numbers any time they search the network.
North Carolina does not require reporting of misuse of the Flock system. Past cases of misuse have come to light when officers were arrested for misusing the system, including at the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department and Mooresville Police Department, or when a department voluntarily reported misuse.

title: A little more sunshine: how to brighten a dark room
text:
Do you have a dark room in your home? I’m not talking about a place to develop film.
It’s the room that somehow feels a little darker, a little dreary and, occasionally, like it belongs in a very chic cave. Maybe it doesn’t get much natural light, faces the wrong direction or has a tree outside that has decided to hog every last ray of sunshine.
While adding clerestory windows and skylights might be a surefire way to dial up the vitamin D, undergoing a massive renovation isn’t compatible with everyone’s bandwidth or budget. A few thoughtful design choices can completely change how a space feels.
Start with the windows
Before changing anything inside, look outside. Are trees, shrubs, awnings or porches blocking valuable natural light? Trimming back landscaping, removing awnings or simply giving the windows a good cleaning can make a surprising difference in how much light makes it inside.
When choosing window treatments, think about how much light you want to let in. Linen, woven shades or sheer drapes can provide privacy without making the room feel closed off. Consider positioning the drapes or Roman shades so they sit just outside the window when open. This keeps the glass clear and lets in more natural light.
Don’t be afraid of color
Painting a dark room white seems like the obvious answer, but it isn’t always the best one. Without enough natural light to bounce around, white can sometimes feel flat or even a little dingy.
Instead, consider a soft, warm neutral or a mid-tone color that gives the room some personality. And don’t automatically leave the ceiling white. Painting the ceiling a similar shade can make the room feel more enveloping and intentional rather than chopping the space into separate planes.
Let there be (more) light
If natural light is limited, you’ll need to create your own.
The secret is layering. Combine overhead lighting with table lamps, floor lamps, sconces and even picture lights. Different sources at different heights help eliminate dark corners and create a softer, more inviting glow.
And please, don’t underestimate the light bulb. Warm, consistent light can make a room feel cozy rather than cold and harsh. Dimmers are another easy upgrade that allow you to change the mood throughout the day.
Reflecting light through mirrors is a classic trick for a reason. Try placing a mirror across from a window or doorway and add smaller reflective touches through glass, metal or polished wood. You don’t need to turn your living room into a disco ball. A few intentional moments are plenty.
Give the room some life
Finally, don’t assume that a dark room needs to be filled with pale furniture and beige everything. A little color, pattern, greenery and texture can actually make the room feel more alive.
The goal isn’t necessarily to make the room look bright. It’s to make it feel bright. Because a room doesn’t have to be naturally sunny to have a little sunshine of its own.

title: Obituary: Linda Pelletier

title: Jason’s Pizza campaign signs removed from Bangor city property
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Over the past 10 years, Jason’s Pizza has brought a some levity to the area during election season.
But in an October surprise, they may need to switch up their political strategy.
You may have seen “Elect Jason’s Pizza for Dinner” signs around town, bringing cheese to roadsides cluttered with campaign signs.
This year, they took the campaign a step further with political-ad style videos on social media.
The silliness came to a stop Thursday when Bangor Public Works came by the shop to say the signs had to go—from city property, anyway.
Their signs across the Queen City have been taken down by workers.
Zachary Black’s family has owned and operated the business since they opened in 1997, growing from one store to four. Black now serves as Chief Experience Officer for Jason’s.
He said while those from the business are disappointed they weren’t able to collect the signs themselves for future use, they say there are no hard feelings.
“I have no idea how many were thrown away. We know where they were all put so when we go to collect them all, we know how many were tossed, hopefully,” Black said. “Customers were like vultures when they heard they were getting picked up. We were getting DMs of customers in their cars with signs, like ‘I got one! It’s going in my yard!’“
We reached out to the city for a response and have not heard back.
Jason’s has a special promotion Friday. If you use the code PUBLICWORKS, on their website or app, you can get a free order of mozzarella breadsticks.

title: Large study finds no link between ultra-processed food and colorectal cancer
text:
Large study finds no link between ultra-processed food and colorectal cancer
A new study offers a surprising twist in the debate over ultra-processed foods and cancer.
A study of more than 461,000 U.S. adults found no overall association between eating ultra-processed foods and developing colorectal cancer.
Researchers followed adults, ages 50 to 71, for a median of nearly 19 years and recorded 10,075 cases of the cancer.
The findings were published Thursday in the journal PLOS Medicine.
Participants who reported the highest intake of ultra-processed foods had about the same rate of colorectal cancer as those who reported the lowest intake, according to the study. The pattern also held for cancers of the colon and rectum.
But the results varied by food type: processed meat was linked to higher incidence, while whole grains and dairy were linked to lower incidence.
The study’s authors said the broad category of ultra-processed foods includes products with different nutritional profiles, so processing alone may not predict cancer risk.
The study relied on participants’ reports of what they ate at the start of the research, which may not reflect their diets over time. And because it tracked associations, it cannot show that a particular food caused or prevented cancer, researchers said.
The authors said the findings support looking at specific foods and overall diet quality, rather than relying only on how processed a food is. To read the study in its entirety, click here.

title: Man who stopped Oregon elementary school shooter is the father of 2 daughters at the school, his mother says
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — The man who stopped a deadly elementary school attack in Oregon by shooting the gunman inside the building is the father of two girls at the school, his mother said Friday.
In a statement read to reporters Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, intervened in Thursday’s attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend and shot the teenage shooter.
Three students and a teacher were killed in the attack, and a fourth student and another teacher were critically injured.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said, noting that her son is a lifelong resident of Bend.
Police have not yet identified who shot the gunman, only saying that the suspect was found dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported. They also haven’t named the gunman.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
Officials are lauding the actions of a local who they say chased down and shot a teenage gunman who killed three children and a teacher at an Oregon elementary school.
A day after the mass shooting that also critically wounded a fourth student and another teacher, well-wishers laid flowers Friday against the sign outside of Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, an outdoorsy city of about 100,000 in central Oregon that is ringed by mountains.
At a news conference hours after Thursday’s attack, Gov. Tina Kotek praised the person who followed the gunman into the school, saying they helped end the rampage as police began arriving on the scene and likely saved lives.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” said Kotek.
Like police, the Democratic governor didn’t provide any details about the person who intervened, including whether they have a link to the school and whether it was a shot they fired that killed the attacker.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartener at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that a member of the public pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. ”I’m feeling very grateful.”
The shooter used a gun bought by his mom
The 16-year-old suspect, identified only as a Bend resident, was found dead inside the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Mike Krantz said. Police said he got into the school by shooting through locked doors.
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Authorities didn’t give details about the teacher who was killed. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded in the attack and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Police said they didn’t know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended it.
Police respond within minutes
The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education.
Children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home.
A community grieves
Shaken residents held a vigil Thursday night, where children drew hearts in chalk on the sidewalk and held candles side-by-side with adults.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for the area’s 32 schools.
Bend, which has about 100,000 residents, is the biggest city in central Oregon. Ringed by mountains, it has ballooned in population over the past three decades and is a tourism and outdoor recreation hub, about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland.
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.
Just four years ago in Bend, a grocery store employee who had served in the U.S. Army attacked a gunman who was spraying shots inside the supermarket. Both the employee, whom police hailed as a hero, and a customer were killed, and the gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

title: Police have no new info 6 months after midcoast death
text:
Detectives with the Maine State Police Major Crimes Unit continue to investigate the circumstances surrounding the death of Darryl Sanborn Sr. in Waldoboro this past spring.
“The investigation remains active and ongoing,” Maine Department of Public Safety spokesperson Shannon Moss said Oct. 15 in response to an inquiry from the Midcoast Villager.
On April 17, a person walking on a dirt road off Wagner Bridge Road in Waldoboro discovered the body of an adult male. The deceased was taken to the Office of Chief Medical Examiner in Augusta, where an autopsy was performed and confirmed as the 64-year-old Sanborn who lived in Thomaston.
The Maine Department of Public Safety said Sanborn was last seen in Waldoboro in the early hours of April 5. On April 7, the Waldoboro Police Department requested assistance from the Maine State Police Major Crimes Unit Central regarding Sanborn’s disappearance.
The Public Safety office stated there was no known danger to the public. Police said no additional information is being released at this time.
The body was found near the location where a man was held against his will at a Reef Road home for a week. The victim in that case said he was beaten and threatened with death.
Police have not said whether the two cases are connected.
Born in Camden, Sanborn was the son of David and Joan Smith Sanborn. He attended school in Warren as a young child and later moved to Thomaston, where he continued his education and graduated from Georges Valley High School.
He worked for many years for MBNA and then Bank of America, including time at the Rockland, Camden and Belfast branches. He retired from Bank of America in 2012 to co-own and operate Dorman’s Dairy Dream. Throughout his life, he served on the school boards of Pen Bay Christian School and Regional School Unit 13 (elected in 2011), taught Sunday School, and was a deacon at Littlefield Memorial Baptist Church. He always spoke with pride about his time in those roles, according to his obituary.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Savannah Bananas release 2027 schedule; games include stops in Canada and Mexico
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — The Savannah Bananas are going to need passports as Banana Ball goes international for the first time in 2027.
The Savannah Bananas and five other teams in their barnstorming style of rollicking baseball entertainment have scheduled stops in Canada and Mexico next year. Banana Ball will also be played in 23 Major League Baseball stadiums and 10 football stadiums in 2027, owner Jessie Cole announced Thursday.
Cole told The Associated Press he couldn’t have imagined the popularity of Banana Ball when he launched the Savannah Bananas in 2016. He added five teams for the 2026 schedule.
The original idea was to generate fan interest for baseball at historic Grayson Stadium in Savannah, Georgia.
“We were just starting to sell tickets and trying to get off the air bed we were sleeping on,” Cole said.
The 2027 schedule announced Thursday night on ESPN2 includes stops in Monterrey, Mexico, on Feb. 5-6, and Tijuana, Mexico, on Feb. 12-13.
The Banana Ball schedule also includes Aug. 14-15 dates at Rogers Centre in Toronto and two visits to Winnipeg — Aug. 26 and Aug. 28.
“This was 10 years in the making,” Cole said of the international dates.
In 2023, the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, New York, opened an exhibit for the Savannah Bananas. The exhibit was recognition of Cole’s success in attracting younger fans who enjoy such shenanigans as a pitcher throwing the ball while on stilts and outs being counted when a fan catches a foul ball in the stands.
On June 26, Banana Ball will add another tweak at Notre Dame Stadium when two baseball fields will be positioned on opposite corners of the football facility, with teams switching fields every inning. The goal is to allow every fan to have a close view of the action.
Cole also announced Disney has produced a film documenting the growth of the Savannah Bananas and Banana Ball. The film will debut at Atlanta’s Truist Park on June 12.
Including minor league stadiums, the 2027 Banana Ball Championship League tour will visit 79 stadiums across 74 cities. Cole expects the tour to draw an estimated 4.3 million fans.
