title: What if Maine elected a governor who just gets things done?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Erin Cavallaro lives in Westbrook with her husband and two children and serves on the Westbrook School Committee. She works in higher education and nonprofit fundraising.
After watching the first gubernatorial debate, one thing became even clearer to me: Maine needs Hannah Pingree.
Politics has become very good at telling us what divides us. We know which team everyone is on. We know what we’re supposed to be angry about and who we are supposed to blame. Somewhere along the way, though, we seem to have lost sight of what government is actually supposed to do: make people’s lives better.
That’s why I’m supporting Hannah Pingree for governor.
I’m a Democrat, and Hannah and I share many of the same values. But what impresses me about her isn’t simply that she knows what she believes. It’s that she understands governing requires more than being right. It requires getting something done.
I’ve learned that firsthand serving on my local school committee. The decisions that come before us aren’t theoretical. They affect whether kids get to school, whether teachers have the resources they need, how much taxpayers are asked to contribute and whether families can count on the public institutions that serve them.
You quickly learn that accomplishing anything meaningful requires listening to people you disagree with, finding common ground where it exists and remembering that the work matters more than the politics surrounding it.
Hannah has spent her career doing exactly that.
As a legislator and eventually speaker of the Maine House, she worked with people whose political beliefs were fundamentally different from her own. They disagreed — sometimes significantly. But disagreement didn’t prevent them from sitting at the same table and finding ways to move Maine forward. That feels almost radical in politics today.
Former Republican House leader Josh Tardy, who served alongside Hannah, has spoken about that quality. He and Hannah certainly didn’t agree on everything, but he has said that, despite their partisan differences, she believed Republicans and Democrats needed to work together to find common ground.
That isn’t abandoning your principles. That’s governing — and addressing those challenges will require people who disagree with one another to work together.
I don’t expect Hannah to agree with everyone in Augusta, nor would I want her to abandon her values in the name of artificial bipartisanship. But Maine is a small state with some very big challenges. We need more housing that working families can actually afford. We need young people to be able to build lives and careers here instead of being priced out. We need strong schools, thriving downtowns and an economy that works in communities from York County to Aroostook.
In a state where more than 690,000 Mainers live in rural communities, we need to make sure that where someone lives doesn’t determine whether they can find a doctor or access essential services.
I want a governor who understands that sometimes governing is as simple as finding the thing you agree on, rolling up your sleeves and getting it done. Government shouldn’t be about winning the argument or scoring points against the other side. It should be about results.
At a time when so much of our politics is defined by division, Maine has an opportunity to choose a different approach — a governor who knows what she believes, listens to people who see things differently and understands that finding common ground isn’t a weakness. It’s how good government is supposed to work.
That’s why I’m supporting Hannah Pingree.

title: Susan Collins’ Portland office receives letter containing ‘unknown substance’
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ office in Portland received a letter containing an “unknown substance” on Friday as the FBI investigates a slew of such incidents reported across the country.
A spokesperson for the Republican confirmed in an email that the letter at the Portland office was intercepted and no injuries were reported. She also said Collins’ Washington, D.C., office received such a letter Thursday.
“Thank you to the Portland police, the Portland fire department, the hazmat team, and the FBI (for) their quick and courageous response,” Katie Brown, Collins’ chief of staff, said in a written statement.
Last month, Collins’ Biddeford office was vandalized by someone who spray-painted a vulgar message on the office’s outer doors.
The FBI has been investigating “a series of suspicious mailings” across the country, including to secretary of state and election offices.
“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the FBI said in a written statement.
A spokesperson for the FBI’s Boston field office said the agency is “not confirming specific instances of letters” when asked about the incident in Portland on Friday.
A spokesperson for the Portland Fire Department did not immediately respond to a request for information on the department’s involvement in the response at Collins’ office. A Portland police spokesperson deferred inquiries on the incident to the FBI.
Collins is currently seeking her sixth term in the U.S. Senate, facing Democrat Troy Jackson.

title: Viral foster kitten with custom-made wheelchair gets adopted
text:
Viral foster kitten with custom-made wheelchair gets adopted
An Ohio animal shelter has shared a new development regarding a foster kitten who captured the hearts of thousands across the country.
Gelato, a kitten who went viral for his homemade wheelchair, now has a forever home. He was adopted earlier this week, officials said, after spending months at Cincinnati Animal Care.
Gelato’s story made national headlines.
The kitten suffered a spinal injury that left his back legs weak and unable to support his weight.
His first mobility aid came courtesy of one of the shelter’s lead veterinary technicians, who assembled his first wheelchair with the use of cardboard, rulers, Hot Wheels and tape.
"Sometimes, all it takes is a little creativity, a lot of heart, and someone who refuses to give up," the shelter said when it first shared Gelato's story.
His next big upgrade came in the form of a custom 3D-printed wheelchair to help strengthen his back legs.
The shelter wrote a big thank-you to Gelato’s adoring public on social media, saying in part, "Your shares truly make a difference and help us reach the people who can help animals like Gelato.”

title: Georgia amusement park to reopen as scheduled days after roller coaster death
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Six Flags Over Georgia is set to open its gates Friday for the first time since a man fell to his death from one of the amusement park’s towering roller coasters.
Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, was thrown from the Goliath coaster on Monday, and authorities are investigating what happened. The park was already scheduled to be closed Tuesday through Thursday and is reopening as scheduled Friday evening, though Goliath is not expected to be running.
Witnesses described seeing Kariem ejected from the coaster, and some people who rode the Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints. At least 11 roller coasters in the U.S. and Canada were temporarily closed after his death, nine of which were manufactured by the company that built Goliath and with similar restraints.
Online photos and videos of most of the closed coasters show each equipped with clamshell restraints, which are mounted in front of each seat on a vertical bar that sits between the rider’s knees. The bar locks the padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.
It’s unclear from the images whether any of those coasters also have seat belts or other secondary restraints. Goliath in Georgia has no such backup restraints.
Bollinger & Mabillard, the company that manufactured Goliath, said in an email it would have no further comment until it had a “better understanding of what transpired” on Monday.
Kariem was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Goliath, one of Six Flags Over Georgia’s headline attractions, towers above the park’s entrance. It opened in 2006 and features a series of hills and turns. It doesn’t take riders upside down, but its first hill rises to 200 feet (61 meters) and it has a top speed of 70 miles per hour (112 kilometers).

title: Maine veterans file FEC complaint against Sen. Collins
text:
Maine veterans file FEC complaint against Sen. Susan Collins over donor funds
A group of U.S. military veterans from Maine has filed a formal complaint with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) against Sen. Susan Collins.
The group detailed the filing against Collins, her authorized campaign committee, the 1820 PAC and convicted defense contractor Martin Kao during a news conference held at Bangor's Davenport Park on Thursday.
Complainant Jason Tkacs and fellow veterans allege that Kao made campaign contributions to Collins and an allied super PAC in connection with earmark-style naval research funding. The filing further alleges Kao privately admitted to law enforcement that the naval project funded by the appropriations was neither sought nor deployed by the U.S. Navy.
The allegations were laid out in a ProPublica report that Collins and her campaign have vehemently denied.
The complaint also alleges the Collins campaign failed to surrender the funds to the U.S. Treasury, as required under federal campaign finance rules and precedents. Instead, the campaign has said it donated the money to help rebuild a school in Frenchville, Maine, following a fire.
"Maine veterans like us put everything on the line to defend our country. Our national defense budget, which Sen. Collins plays a key role in setting, should protect the people who serve, not be used as an ATM for her political donors," said U.S. Navy veteran Melinda Swayne. "I feel deeply betrayed by our current commander in chief, who derailed the FBI’s investigation into whether or not our senator sold us out, and now I want answers from Sen. Collins. Maine veterans deserve a senator who will fight for them."
In a statement shared with WMTW media partner WABI, the Collins campaign once again rejected the allegations.
"These Troy Jackson supporters are reaching a new low," the Collins campaign said in a statement. "They are now criticizing a legal and proper donation to a school that burnt down in Frenchville, Maine. They have displayed absolutely no understanding of the law, they don’t know the facts, and are today filing a complaint with the FEC, which fully cleared Senator Collins and her staff almost five years ago."
The Collins campaign also pointed to a statement from former FEC Commissioner Sean Cooksey, who served when the FEC investigated Navatek in 2021.
"At no time did the FEC have any evidence that 1820 PAC or Senator Collins' campaign knew or did anything wrong. We dismissed or took no action on every potential violation against the PAC, and pursued significant civil penalties against the company," the senator's campaign said. "Those are the facts. Any suggestion otherwise is hackery."

title: Bridge of Hope Cancer Walk marks 21st year in Houlton
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WAGM) - The Bridge of Hope Cancer Walk takes place at Riverfront on Saturday in Houlton, marking its 21st year.
From 9 a.m. on, Bridge to Hope Board of Directors member Kim Folsom plans to be at Riverfront Park with other supporters, through rain or snow, just as they have done in past years.
“And that’s why we’re out in the rain today, because that is a symbolism when you’re going through cancer, no matter the weather, you have to continue your fight. So we do not cancel our walk, we don’t reschedule it. We’ve walked in the snow, we’ve walked in the rain. Tomorrow’s supposed to, I think, be dry. It’s going to be cool, but dry, but that’s okay,” Folsom said.
Walk to honor those affected by cancer
For some, Saturday’s walk will be about celebrating their own fight. For others, it will be about showing up for someone who can’t.
“We’ve got a lot of people that are really struggling this year, some tough diagnosis just recently, people that typically would be with us that are not able to attend. So we’re just thinking about all of those people and everybody that comes tomorrow has also got those on their minds,” Folsom said.
The walk covers about a mile and a half along the riverfront, but Folsom said people can participate at their own pace. The organization isn’t setting a fundraising goal this year. Instead, Folsom said the hope is for a strong turnout to show support for everyone affected by cancer.

title: Weight loss injections or surgery? How each treatment differs
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - Weight is a daily struggle for millions of Americans and for a lot of them it’s not just the health risks, it’s shame and setbacks.
By 2035, it’s estimated that the number of people in the country living with obesity will rise to 19 million and affect nearly 126 million people. In the same study published by JAMA, researchers found that the number of American adults living with obesity has more than double over the past three decades.
More Americans are choosing weight loss injections over bariatric surgery, according to a new study. But some patients face a different reality when it comes to treatment options due to their insurance coverage.
A study in JAMA Network Surgery shows GLP-1 prescriptions rose 24% between 2018 and 2025. Over the same period, national bariatric surgery use in 2025 was slightly less than half of its 2022 peak.
But Dr. Shauna Levy with Tulane Weight Loss Center at Lakeside Hospital said she has not seen the same shift in her practice. Last year, she performed 250 bariatric surgeries, a number she said has held steady despite the rise of GLP-1 drugs.
The difference comes down to insurance coverage, Levy said.
“Right now in the state of Louisiana, you’re more likely to have bariatric surgery coverage than you are to have GLP-1 coverage,” Levy said. “And many people are surprised by this because they think surgery must be so much more expensive than GLP-1s. But actually, GLP-1s are meant to be taken for life. So if you look at the cost for a lifetime, it’s actually much more affordable to get bariatric surgery, even as a cash pay, than it is to take GLP-1s for the rest of your life.”
Levy said expanded coverage could bring more Louisiana residents into treatment.
Emily Showalter, 35, battled her weight for years. She felt like she was missing out on life’s most precious moments and decided to take control.
After little success with dieting and weighing 265 pounds, she turned to GLP-1 injections a year ago. The class of weight loss drugs includes Ozempic and Wegovy.
Showalter said she lost nearly 100 pounds. She said having the injections helped her relearn how to react to food and being around it.
“My kids have noticed my energy levels, you know, mom is way more involved and wanting to go do things,” Showalter added.
Blake Davenport had a different experience.
He spent a year and a half on GLP-1 medications in 2024 without much success. His doctor then recommended bariatric surgery.
Davenport said he started at 308 pounds and now weighs 173 pounds.
“It feels amazing,” Davenport said. “So it just feels great to have no more medication for blood pressure. No more medications for diabetes. My sleep apnea is almost completely resolved.”
Part of what makes the choice difficult is the stigma that still surrounds obesity, Levy said.
“We’ve really looked at weight as an almost character flaw or a personal failure, and in fact—it is a disease that needs to be treated medically, just like any other diseases,” Levy said.
Levy said no single treatment works for everyone.
Despite the rapid rise of GLP-1 drugs, one study by researchers at the University of California San Diego found that obesity is largely undertreated.
The study used health records of nearly 20 million patients with severe obesity and found nearly 95% of those patients received no treatment.

title: Creativity Bar offers workers playful reset to spark new ideas
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (Aging Untold) — Just outside Nashville, some working adults say the daily grind can drain energy and ideas. They are finding a refreshing reset at the Creativity Bar, where community and a little play help people feel better, think clearly and leave inspired.
Founder Stephanie Pruitt-Gaines hopes to help shape the future of those drawn to her door.
“I’ve always loved coloring books, and it feels like walking through a coloring book,” Pruitt-Gaines said. “And also in my dreams, I often dream in black and white.”
Part playroom, part art studio, part office
The Creativity Bar is part playroom, part art studio and part office for members to drop in and work toward their next great idea.
“Our members can come drop in anytime and make stuff,” Pruitt-Gaines said. “To come up with the next great idea, you’ve got to have some playfulness and creativity.”
Every inch of the space is outlined in black and designed to unleash imagination and help ideas flow.
“All of these little lines really intentionally play with your eyes and your mind wants to fill them in,” Pruitt-Gaines said. “And so part of what I hope this space does is people walk in and feel a sense of possibility.”
Members say they leave inspired
Members pay a monthly fee or day rate to use the space and attend workshops.
“My work. It’s all about creating something out of nothing. And so this place is just so inspiring. The energy that’s here,” Dawn Cornelius, a founding member, said.
“I just feel better and I am better when I come here,” she said. “I leave inspired.”
“Community and creativity, it doesn’t have to be difficult,” Leigh Patton, another founding member, said. “You can actually just walk in the door and your brain starts working.”

title: Maine’s most frustrating fish might be its most addictive
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
In 2016, I decided I wanted to catch a musky on a fly rod. I had never done it before and really didn’t know where to start.
A friend introduced me to an angler from northern Maine who had fished for musky a few times. He told me orange and yellow flies worked well, so I went home and started watching YouTube videos about tying musky flies. Using what I learned, I came up with an articulated fly of my own. I had no idea if it would work, but it did.
For my first musky trip, I took my son, Jax, who was 14 at the time. We spent two days exploring the St. John River, armed with little more than a vague idea of where to fish. Over those two days, we had 18 follows. Jax accounted for 15 of them and even landed a 40-inch musky.
That trip hooked me on musky fishing.
Since then, I’ve spent countless days chasing musky and guiding clients who want to catch their first. I guide only fly anglers for musky, which limits the number of people I can take. The fishing is demanding, both physically and mentally.
You need to be comfortable casting a 10- to 12-weight fly rod with a heavy line and flies ranging from 4 to 12 inches long. You cast repeatedly, strip the fly aggressively toward the boat and work it in a figure eight beside the boat before casting again.
Then you do it all over.
You can spend hours casting without a bite. Even getting a fish to follow your fly is an accomplishment.
Recently, one of my longtime clients, Mark, decided it was time to try musky fishing. We had been planning the trip for more than a year. He had previously fished with a guide in Virginia but had never seen a musky, so his expectations were probably pretty low.
A few days before the trip, he started asking questions about flies and leaders. I told him my goal was to get a follow first, then an eat, then a fish in the net. After that, we could work on finding a bigger one.
Mark drove up from Massachusetts on Friday, and we left at 5 a.m. Saturday. During the three- to four-hour drive, he mentioned that he hadn’t seen a moose in years.
Along the way, I spotted a car pulled over on the side of the road.
“They’re either peeing or they see a moose,” I said.
I was wrong. There wasn’t just one moose. There were four.
Mark got his wish before we even reached the river.
We had three days of fishing ahead of us, and the first day brought winds around 20 mph. The wind made casting difficult and controlling the boat a challenge. I had to work to keep Mark in position to cast effectively.
We hadn’t been fishing for more than 30 minutes when he had his first follow.
The wind forced me to try some new spots, and by the end of the day, Mark had seen 11 musky and landed his first one. It measured 22 inches, not a giant by musky standards but a special fish nonetheless.
We had accomplished the first two goals: getting follows and landing a fish.
Day two brought better conditions, with little wind and cloudy skies. Although we were fishing the same general stretch of river, I moved to different spots. The day before, most of our follows had come on black flies, but Mark had caught his fish on yellow.
I decided to start with a larger yellow fly in hopes of finding a bigger fish.
About 30 minutes into the morning, I looked away for a second. When I looked back, Mark was hooked up.
I could tell he didn’t think it was a particularly big fish.
“It’s bigger than you think,” I told him.
Just then, the musky took off. Mark moved to the back of the boat as the fish made a powerful run. Because we were fishing deep water, the musky headed down and put up a tough fight.
Mark brought it close to the net several times, but each time we thought we had it, the fish took off again.
On our final attempt, the musky jumped and the hook came free. Fortunately, I managed to scoop it into the net before it could swim away.
Mark had landed a 30-inch musky.
The day continued to get better. He finished with nine eats, four follows and three landed fish, including another musky measuring 25 inches.
We also found a bigger fish, one I estimated to be in the high 30-inch range. It followed the fly right to the boat and appeared to be chewing on it, but it wouldn’t commit.
We changed flies four times and got the fish to follow five times without an eat. Twice, it followed a small pink fly, a color I had never tried for musky.
We decided to stick with pink for the rest of the day. Mark had three more follows, and the final one turned out to be his biggest fish of the trip.
It was a 34-inch musky with a much heavier body than the 30-inch fish he had caught earlier.
As I brought it to the net, Mark asked, “Now can I be done?”
He was exhausted.
Day three was even tougher, with high winds and rain. We moved only three fish, including one I estimated to be around 40 inches. We tried several flies to get it to follow again, but it never showed itself.
Around noon, I suggested we eat lunch and let the boat drift. After eating about half my sandwich, I decided to make a few casts. Catching a musky during a lunch break isn’t something you count on, but it was worth a try.
On one cast, I hooked the bottom in about 2 feet of water. After freeing the fly, I cast toward the middle of the river.
The fly hit something almost immediately.
At first, I thought I had hooked the bottom again. Then it moved.
I had caught my lunch-break musky, a 25-inch fish.
We didn’t move another fish that day, but the trip had already given us plenty to remember.
Over three days, we had seen more than 20 musky and landed five. Mark had experienced nearly every aspect of musky fishing, from the excitement of a follow to the frustration of a fish refusing a fly and the satisfaction of bringing several fish to the net.
Chasing them has also taught me that success isn’t always measured by the size or number of fish you catch. Sometimes, just seeing one follow your fly is enough to keep you coming back.
But when you finally get an eat, set the hook and feel a big musky pulling against your line, you understand why people become obsessed with these fish.

title: Forever chemicals found in most waterways, drinking water
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A new report from Environment America found that 83% of water samples collected across the United States tested positive for PFAS, also known as forever chemicals.
A U.S. Geological Survey study found nearly half of tap water in the country contains forever chemicals. Bottled water also contains the chemicals.
Trey Sherard, Anacostia Riverkeeper, said, “Their solution? Bottled water may be just a different toxin.”
Where the chemicals come from
PFAS are used in many everyday products. The chemicals are what make non-stick cookware non-stick. Products branded as waterproof or stain-resistant are also likely to contain PFAS.
The chemicals are known carcinogens, specifically linked to ovarian and testicular cancer. They can also cause infertility, and in children, developmental delays.
The biggest sources of PFAS entering water supplies are industrial runoff and firefighting foam.
Calls for regulation
Environment America is calling attention to the issue.
Lisa Frank, who heads Environment America said, “When we allow the use of toxic chemicals and we allow those chemicals to get into our environment without considering the downstream consequences, the problem can get out of hand very quickly,” adding “Removing all those parts from our environment is going to be a very tall order. But stopping new people’s contamination can start right now.”
The organization is calling on lawmakers to take action. U.S. Rep. Paul Tonko, D-New York, is calling for an overhaul of the Safe Drinking Water Act to include forever chemicals.
Tonko said, “Americans deserve to have confidence and peace of mind that when they turn on the tap, they’re being delivered safe, safe drinking water.”
Some of the worst contamination can be found in the Northeast and along the northern Mississippi River.

title: Billy Joel gives health update after recent brain surgery
text:
'I can't do performances': Billy Joel gives health update after recent brain surgery
"Piano Man" singer Billy Joel, 77, may be itching to get back on stage, but his doctors have an important message for him:
"Slow down, you're doin' fine."
Joel is still recovering from a recent brain surgery to treat a neurological condition called normal pressure hydrocephalus. It's a condition previously known as water on the brain.
Related video above: Billy Joel opens up about his recent brain surgery
The "Vienna" singer opened up in a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter, saying, "Well, my health is good. I have this thing called hydrocephalus. It used to be called water on the brain, so it affects your balance, it affects your memory, it affects your vision, your hearing. But I'm OK. They call it a brain disorder, but it's not that serious. It's just something that affects your balance mostly."
Joel canceled a series of tour dates in 2025 before eventually cutting the tour altogether due to his ongoing memory and balance issues. His latest song, "Turn the Lights Back On," was released in 2024. It marked his first pop single in almost 20 years.
When asked if he'd be able to perform again, the singer said it was still uncertain.
"I don't know. I have to take a series of tests before I know, but I can't drive right now. I'm not allowed to drive," Joel said. "And I can't do performances because what the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it's like you're getting a concussion."
Previously, Joel said doctors discussed getting a shunt placed in his brain to improve his memory and balance issues. He said he was hesitant about the procedure at first.
"I didn't want to do that, but then I read up on it, and I realized it can help improve your balance and can help your memory. You know, I don't want to lose my marbles," Joel said.
The singer went on to describe why his doctors are hesitant to give him the all-clear to hit the stage again.
"The volume. Rock and roll is loud, man. Rock and roll made me deaf already. So it's the lighting, the sound, the stress of the show, the audience, the energy of the performance. There's a lot going on when you're onstage," he said.
While he may be sidelined for now, the singer has expressed his desire to get back to performing soon.
"They have to test me further to see if I can go back and do performing again, which I would like to be able to do," Joel said.

title: Astronomers say they’ve discovered the first green star
text:
Astronomers say they’ve discovered the first green star
Astronomers analyzing white dwarf stars have for the first time found a star that would appear green to human eyes, according to a new study.
Related video above: New images of the sun show its surface in the finest detail yet
While for most stars, color is temperature-dependent and limited to a few hues, white dwarfs, which are the dense remnants of sun-like stars that have died, can glow in an incredible range of colors, said lead study author Mark Hollands, an astrophysicist at the University of Warwick, England, on Thursday.
"The colors that normal stars can have are pretty much only orange, white or blue," Hollands told CNN.
"What we found is, for most white dwarfs, that’s the same as well. But there are some special cases where the physics in the outer layers of these stars are sufficiently strange that it causes actually quite big deviations in terms of their spectrum," he said.
These deviations are due to the interaction between the helium in their atmosphere and traces of other elements, which vary between white dwarfs, depending on what material has interacted with the star over the course of its lifetime.
For instance, iron, magnesium and sodium, elements commonly found in rocks, can be found on the surface — potential evidence of a nearby former planetary system, or from "something like an asteroid that ventures too close to the white dwarf," Hollands explained.
"It gets shredded up into dust, and then those rocky bits of dust and debris fall onto the white dwarf," he said.
"And then that gets mixed into the outer layers, and then you can actually use that to measure what the rocky stuff was made of," said Hollands.
"So we can actually use the white dwarf as a sort of diagnostic tool to actually measure the chemistry of planetary material," he added.
"The white dwarf is taking apart the planets, and we’re able to see what was actually inside that planet — the proportion of the different elements — and that gives us clues in how these planets were formed," said Adam Burgasser, a professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of California San Diego. "It is a crime scene, and we’re kind of piecing through the evidence that we have left available to us, and that’s allowing us to kind of piece the story of what the planet was and how it was made way, way, way back in history."
Human connection
For this study, Hollands looked at the 151 known white dwarf stars that are within 20 parsecs, or around 65 light-years, of Earth.
As for the green star, the main elements present are calcium, sodium and lithium, Hollands said. The star is identified as WD J13306435, nestled in the constellation Draco.
"It kind of stimulated interest in me in looking more at that object and why it has so much material being accreted onto it," said Burgasser, who was not involved in the study. "It can excite the public as well as the scientists in learning more about some of the more, I would say, extreme objects in this sample."
Another notable star was "almost like a salmon pink," due to the presence of a high density of carbon molecules, Hollands added.
While no white dwarf stars can be seen directly from Earth, Hollands was able to calculate their color using star spectrum data, which a statement from the researchers defines as "the 'fingerprint' produced when starlight is split apart by wavelength, much like a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow."
Hollands explained that the research has also brought these space objects much closer to home.
"It gives you a nice human connection to these very distant things that are so far away that sometimes even as a researcher you feel quite disconnected from these objects that you study," he said. "But then you can sort of add a human element into it, and it feels a lot more tangible."
The observations about green stars are based on existing data and may not shed new understandings about white dwarfs, but the study does offer an intriguing approach and view of these celestial bodies, said Agnès Kim, an astrophysicist and professor of physics at Penn State Scranton, who was not involved in the work.
"Doing a study that goes from spectrum to what the human eye would see is a cool intersection of physics and biology to me," Kim wrote in an email. "I love that some would look green to us if they were close enough for us to see them, and even more fun that some would look pink."
Burgasser added that the study’s categorization scheme using temperatures and atmospheric properties can be useful for the field moving forward.
"Some things are kind of purplish pink, and some other things were greenish and blue — and that kind of classification, which, by the way, we do all the time in astronomy, is classify things, allows us to focus on: why are these types of objects these colors, and are they related to each other based on their composition?" Burgasser said. "We have that information in other forms, but I think this is maybe a simplified way of organizing that data."
Next, Hollands is planning to keep analyzing more white dwarf star spectra, with advances in scientific techniques meaning that researchers will be able to look at a new tranche of stars that are even farther away from Earth.
"We know of white dwarfs that we don’t have spectra for," he said. "But that’s all about to change because there’s quite a few spectroscopic surveys" that are going to start delivering data.
"We’ll be getting a tenfold increase in the number of white dwarfs that have spectra," Hollands said. "And so maybe if we’re lucky, we’ll go from one or maybe two green white dwarfs to 10 or 20."
The study was published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, or RASTI.

title: Graham Platner had millions of dollars on hand when he dropped out. Where has it gone?
text:
Graham Platner’s U.S. Senate campaign fell apart in a matter of days. His campaign is still dishing out payments to pick up the pieces.
The then-unknown oyster farmer launched what was initially a longshot campaign in August last year. Platner’s slick online presence, military background and passionate speaking style powered him to an overwhelming primary victory over Gov. Janet Mills — a feat that seemed impossible when he jumped into the race.
The campaign galvanized support from small-dollar donors in Maine and around the country. But after Platner abruptly ended his campaign in July following a credible allegation of sexual assault from one of his former partners, which Platner vehemently denied, the campaign was left with around $1.7 million on hand.
New filings with the Federal Election Commission submitted Thursday show where that money has gone since his bid ended.
The campaign has spent over $2.3 million since July, the data shows. Much of that was used to reimburse those who powered Platner’s ascent.
Over $70,000 in small-dollar donations were refunded after Platner dropped out, the FEC filing shows, while campaign staffers cumulatively got just over $350,000 in severance pay following his withdrawal.
The largest single severance payout was just over $20,000, given to Amy Gertner: Platner’s wife. Gertner also received about $980 as a “win bonus” following the primary, as did about 30 other campaign staffers.
The severance pay was stipulated in the Platner staff’s union contract, according to a former campaign source not authorized to speak publicly. The amount given to each staffer was determined based on their tenure with the campaign. Gertner had been there since the beginning.
Neither Platner nor several other former campaign employees responded to requests for comment on the post-withdrawal expenditures.
The campaign cumulatively spent around $350,000 on consulting firms specializing in communications, fundraising, research and other areas between July and October.
About a third of the consulting spending came after Platner’s withdrawal in early July. Those payouts were the result of contracts the campaign had signed with consulting firms through Election Day, the campaign source said — though some were for a “postmortem” winding down of the campaign’s operations.
None of Platner’s leftover campaign funds have gone to his replacement in the Senate race, Troy Jackson, or any other campaigns around the country. Asked in July if he would accept an endorsement from Platner, Jackson said “It’s unfortunate, but I just don’t want it.”
Other Maine politicians with cash remaining from now-dormant campaigns have put tens of thousands of dollars toward other candidates in Maine and around the country.
U.S. Rep. Jared Golden has given contributions to about 10 other moderate Democrats in recent months after announcing he wouldn’t seek reelection this year. Sara Gideon, who still has some $2 million on hand from her failed campaign against Sen. Susan Collins in 2020, has chipped in over $375,000 to Democrats in Maine, New Hampshire and elsewhere, per her most recent FEC filing.
Platner has largely stayed out of the public eye since dropping out. He was initially slated to speak and lead a veterans’ march at a Labor Day event in Ellsworth, which would have been his first public appearance post-campaign. But Platner ultimately didn’t speak following widespread backlash.
Platner’s FEC filing indicates he still has just under $100,000 on hand.

title: Maine’s fire and EMS services are in increasingly dire straits, researchers find
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA — When John Smith decided to shut down the local fire department in Burlington six years ago, he didn’t feel like he had much choice. His kids, who had volunteered there, moved away, and so did another multi-generation firefighting family in town.
That left Smith, who was in his mid-60s, and just one other volunteer.
“I was really afraid for myself and for him, and the fact that people thought they were getting something that they weren’t,” Smith said in an interview this month. “We were not a good service at that point.”
Fire departments across Maine have felt the same sorts of pressures for decades but haven’t known just how bad the problem was or how to express it, said state Fire Marshal Shawn Esler. On Friday, his office and the University of Maine released findings of a two-year study that shows fire and EMS services across the state are in increasingly dire straits.
“They finally documented the freight train that we’ve seen coming for the last 20 years,” said Roger Hooper, chief of the York County Fire Academy and director of the regional training center.
Esler and the researchers say 94% of fire departments that responded to the survey rely on volunteerism to some extent, yet fewer people are available and a significant portion of those who remain are aging and can no longer do all aspects of the work. Forty-seven percent of fire departments that responded to the survey said they were too short-staffed to respond to at least one call in the last three years.
The survey also found big gaps in training, and at the same time, a huge increase in calls to fire and EMS departments. Fire service leaders said gone are the days when a boot drive could generate sufficient funds for departments to be able to provide what their communities expect.
Discussing the study’s findings at the Maine Municipal Association conference in Augusta earlier this month, Esler said: “I think the general public has an expectation that when they dial 911 they’re going to receive a response.”
Augusta Fire Chief David Groder finished Elser’s thought. “You just go up the road 15 miles,” he said, “and there’s a town that may not respond because nobody’s in town that day.”
Maine cities that employ career firefighters are hurting, too, Esler said, because they have long hired people who already have experience as volunteers. He said urban departments have fewer applicants and have to seek mutual aid from smaller cities and towns more often.
Overall calls to fire departments were up 78% from 2014 to 2024, according to the study’s findings, and some departments reported even higher increases, in part because they are filling gaps in healthcare access. Fire departments have become “the backbone of the community,” said research associate Alexander Rezk.
“Without reform, if things continue as they are, we’ll be coming to a point of dysfunction,” he said. Rezk‘s team at UMaine’s Margaret Chase Smith Policy Center surveyed 219 fire departments, along with code enforcement officers and municipal administrators, and interviewed 25 fire chiefs to better understand the challenges and their effects on local communities.
Fire departments have historically received far less public funding than police, Rezk said, and the research findings should challenge Mainers to consider whether that’s still appropriate. While some fire departments have added incentives to recruit and retain volunteers, he said, more will be needed in the future.
Providing fire and EMS services will inevitably get more expensive for Mainers, according to interviews with several people involved in firefighting around the state. They say volunteerism will still be a crucial part of the service, but it is already becoming more regionalized and requires more paid members.
Esler and others pointed to what has happened in Burlington. After Smith was forced to shut down the department, he helped partner with neighboring towns to create the Central Maine Highlands fire district in 2024, the first of its kind in the state. It has a roster of paid firefighters and paramedics.
“I think we’re at a turning point in the fire service,” Esler said. It’s up to state legislators, local governments and residents to make changes and provide funds, he said, “before it continues in decay.”
TRAINING GAP
Just about half of the people on department rosters are trained to fight indoor fires in Oxford, Franklin, Hancock and Waldo counties, according to the survey. It’s not much higher in Washington, Knox and Sagadahoc counties. Training sites can be hours away from a fire department, particularly Down East, along the Midcoast and along the state’s western border.
“It’s not uncommon for a department to be able to respond to a call but lack the number of certified firefighters to do anything,” Rezk said. “Imagine, they scramble to a call but they stand around outside.”
There are more types of industrial and energy infrastructure hazards, like factories, mills, landfills, solar farms, natural gas pipelines, battery storage facilities and data centers, that require more specialized training, said Groder, the chief in Augusta.
“We’re asking our firefighters to understand it, know it, and don’t make mistakes. That’s a big responsibility,” he said.
What happened in Searsmont in May, when a sealed silo at Robbins Lumber exploded, is an apt example, he acknowledged. Firefighters from dozens of departments arrived with no way of knowing the specific hazard the silo presented or what kind of response it required, an assessment by the National Institute for Occupational Health and Safety later found. It said water poured on the initial silo fire likely contributed to the explosion. Three people, including two firefighters, died from their injuries.
As new hazards come into communities, there’s no funding to train firefighters on how to deal with them, Esler said.
“Fires are growing exponentially faster than they did in the past, and burning hotter, and they’re way more toxic than they were in the past,” said Todd Zsiga, the fire chief in Kennebunkport.
The challenges he and others face — to find new people who can stick with training — reflect the ways Maine is changing even beyond the fire service. They’re related to the higher costs of nearly everything in the state (including firefighting equipment); the demographics of aging; and cultural shifts toward online life and away from community volunteerism.
GENERATIONAL CHANGE
Jennifer LaHaye started with the Southwest Harbor Fire Department when she was 18, more than 20 years ago. She said despite the department leadership’s best efforts, “There’ll be times when we have an alarm and one person is going in the middle of the night.” recommends 15 people respond to a house fire.
High housing costs are part of the reason
Rezk, the university researcher, said people are having to work more hours and more jobs to afford to live in many places in Maine and that affects their ability to volunteer.
Three quarters of departments that rely solely on volunteers without compensation that responded to the University of Maine survey said they’re understaffed on weekdays. The number is nearly as high — 67% — for departments that pay their volunteers for calls.
Southwest Harbor adapted by establishing two career positions to provide basic staffing on weekdays. Even the volunteers now get paid during their shifts, LaHaye said. The per diem payments are meant to make it more worthwhile to run into a burning building, she said.
“It’s kind of crazy to think that we expected that they do that and not get compensated for so many years.”
As it is at so many other departments, LaHaye said, there aren’t a lot of young people hanging around the fire station as when she was a teenager. The survey found that at least three of every 10 firefighters in Maine are over 50 years old. Esler said it’s increasingly unlikely those men and women will be able to fight fires inside buildings.
Esler has seen the generational change in his own family. When he joined his community’s fire department, “that’s what every young man in the town of Albion did,” he said.
It was expected that volunteer firefighters would devote their free time to the service and pay their own way for training, Esler said.
“The culture has been prideful,” he said. “It’s been, ‘I’m going to take care of my own fires and my own community.’”
These days, he said, “Our younger generation doesn’t have that same expectation.” He understands why his son, who he said already works 60 hours a week, doesn’t plan to join the fire service.
A REGIONAL APPROACH
In Burlington, Smith said he’d watched volunteerism and participation drop at events and organizations across town — at the historical society, the Independence Day parade, the snowmobile club and the local Veterans of Foreign Wars post.
“We all communicate on Facebook but never look each other in the eye,” he said. “There’s not the community spirit that there was.”
Smith said that with declining help at the fire department,
Smith helped steer Burlington toward the regionalized district and he serves on its board of directors. The costs are distributed among the participating towns. As a taxpayer, Smith was charged $268 this year for fire and EMS.
“The quality of service and abilities these men and women have is like night and day from a small volunteer fire department,” he said. He and the other volunteers “did the best we could with what we had,” he said, but the paid full-timers get the experience of answering many more calls and have access to better equipment.
“They might be 10 minutes further away, but when they get here they make such a difference,” Smith said.
Esler said, “Ten years ago, regionalization was a swear word,” but that is changing, and there’s no prescription for exactly what it has to mean.
Smith said some towns will not want to give up part of their identity and local control. “But I think it’s going to have to happen,” he said.
In York County, Hooper directs a new regional training center that opened this year — a county-level investment that Esler said is rare but welcome. Hooper said having even a few staff to handle routine calls can in turn make it easier to recruit volunteers, “because you’re not wasting their time,” he said.
Rome partnered with Belgrade about five years ago to pay for someone who covers calls during the day, fire Chief Gary Foss said. Without that paid position, many more calls would have gone unanswered, he said, though he’s still nervous it won’t be enough.
“I’ve been telling our townspeople we’ll have to consider having someone here five days a week,” he said.
The decline in volunteers, “is going to end up costing our small towns lots of money,” he said. But if communities choose not to fund fire and EMS services, then home insurance costs will rise, he predicted.
Regionalizing won’t save money up front, according to those who have done it or studied the fire service. The University of Maine researchers said it should eventually, though, by creating a centralized capacity to raise funds, no longer duplicating the costs of equipment, and creating the ability to buy it in bulk. Hooper and others said the state could help provide funds or other incentives to get regionalization started.
The researchers also recommend that Maine increase access to firefighting training, and encourage employers to work with fire departments to make volunteers available.
According to the Maine Office of State Fire Marshal, a comprehensive report will be published next year.
Mainers should feel uneasy about the survey’s findings, Rezk said.
“This isn’t going away,” he said.

title: Troy Jackson still fighting for Mainers
text:
Serving with Troy Jackson in the Maine Senate, I got to see firsthand his commitment and passion to work on behalf of all Mainers. I watched Troy push and advocate for important programs that would help so many: better healthcare insurance, universal free meals in public schools, paid family leave, affordable childcare and savings plans for those who didn’t have them at their job.
He worked with anyone who could support an effort and never stopped looking for allies. When there was resistance, he would make his case and try to persuade others to join him. He couldn’t convince everyone but he convinced enough to get key bills passed.
Troy started fighting for better deals for Mainers when he was 18 and didn’t go into public service to get rich. A governor or a new legislator, we knew where Troy stood on issues. I’ve already voted for Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate.
Hon. Ned Claxton, MD
Auburn

title: BH selectmen receive BHML invitation, explore internships
text:
Boothbay Harbor Memorial Library (BHML) has proposed a capital project and, on Oct.13, Executive Director Johanna Breen invited the selectboard to tour the facilities.
Renovations will add an elevator, additional public restrooms, an accessible community room, a dedicated teen space, and updated HVAC and electrical systems, among other improvements. The Hyde House Used Bookstore will be replaced and incorporated into the library building. However, the beloved porch will be maintained with added courtyard seating.
Drawing inspiration from Lincoln County Regional Planning Commission, the town is exploring requesting one or two interns interested in municipal government for a 12-week, grant-funded program. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) now requires GPS coordinates for all town culverts, data needed for reimbursement purposes, so Town Manager Julia Latter floated having an intern complete the undertaking. Digitizing town files for the website was also identified as a priority.
Chair Mike Tomko suggested an intern take stock of the shorter, accessory utility poles whose wires have yet to be fully moved over to the larger replacements. "Just being able to have a database of those, so we could then try and work on some type of plan to have all the utilities moved over onto the larger poles, I think that would be helpful," he said.
In other business, the board adopted the new annual Maine Municipal General Assistance Ordinances for October through next September. The board also approved the sale of town-owned property, primarily unused pieces of equipment in storage.
Harbor Master Jeff Lowell reported a successful season with few major complaints, highlighting great assistant support, smooth pump-out operations and well-used town floats and docks. However, he did find this year's big boats and transient dockage to be a bit slow.
There was a brief discussion on the Oct. 7 comprehensive plan meeting with VHB, Inc., where the selectboard floated next steps before sending the plan to the state for approval, and how to encourage implementation efforts.
Updates to the town website are ongoing with hopes to unveil the final product before spring. One new feature includes digitized tax maps. It will cost $2,900 a year to maintain.
The town is seeking applications for a new code enforcement officer/licensed plumbing inspector, as well as alternate members for the planning board, appeals board and port committee.
The deadline to request an absentee ballot is Oct. 29. Early voting is also available at the town office.

title: Maine group aims for 100 mph lobster boat record
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Belfast boat building group aims for 100 mph lobster boat record
A Maine boat building company is working on a lobster boat designed to exceed 100 miles per hour.
Holland Custom Boats, which is based in Belfast, is building the vessel with the goal of breaking lobster boat racing speed records.
“The first thing I’d like to do is scare the competition a little bit,” Gavin Holland told WMTW media partner WABI.
The Holland family has a history of exceeding lobster boat speed expectations.
“I can remember back, they said if we ever made 40 miles an hour, we're doing good. And the guy that was a naval architect that told me that, by the time he told us, we were already pushing 50," said Glenn Holland, Gavin's grandfather. "He said we’d never get by 40. I said, 'We’ve passed that a while back.'"
The Hollands are seeking to double that 40 mph mark with the new boat.
"There have been rumors of people hitting 80 mph. Never seen it in a race, though. Seventies have been achieved," Gavin Holland said.
Gavin Holland said one of the family's boats, the Red Baron, hit 60 mph and noted that the vessel was not built for the specific purpose of racing.
"But she was a work boat," he said. "It would lobster during the week and race on the weekends."
Gavin Holland said setting the record would continue the family’s legacy of fast boats.
"It's an important thing to me. I don’t want to see it die," he said. "From my great-grandfather starting out lobstering and my grandfather designing these and building the reputation that we have, the whole family’s been involved in it forever. I mean, everyone has had a hand in it at some point in my family, so to keep that going is pretty important to me."
"It's something I’ve been wanting to do for a long time," Glenn Holland said. "I’m finally getting around to doing it, but (Gavin is) going to do it instead of me, which is alright with me."
Gavin Holland said the new boat might create a new class for lobster boat racing if the project goes according to plan.
The Holland Custom Boats team is working on prepping the molds for the new boat, and the process will be documented on its website.

title: Graham Platner had millions of dollars on hand when he dropped out. Where has it gone?
text:
Graham Platner’s U.S. Senate campaign fell apart in a matter of days. His campaign is still dishing out payments to pick up the pieces.
The then-unknown oyster farmer launched what was initially a longshot campaign in August last year. Platner’s slick online presence, military background and passionate speaking style powered him to an overwhelming primary victory over Gov. Janet Mills — a feat that seemed impossible when he jumped into the race.
The campaign galvanized support from small-dollar donors in Maine and around the country. But after Platner abruptly ended his campaign in July following a credible allegation of sexual assault from one of his former partners, which Platner vehemently denied, the campaign was left with around $1.7 million on hand.
New filings with the Federal Election Commission submitted Thursday show where that money has gone since his bid ended.
The campaign has spent over $2.3 million since July, the data shows. Much of that was used to reimburse those who powered Platner’s ascent.
Over $70,000 in small-dollar donations were refunded after Platner dropped out, the FEC filing shows, while campaign staffers cumulatively got just over $350,000 in severance pay following his withdrawal.
The largest single severance payout was just over $20,000, given to Amy Gertner: Platner’s wife. Gertner also received about $980 as a “win bonus” following the primary, as did about 30 other campaign staffers.
The severance pay was stipulated in the Platner staff’s union contract, according to a former campaign source not authorized to speak publicly. The amount given to each staffer was determined based on their tenure with the campaign. Gertner had been there since the beginning.
Neither Platner nor several other former campaign employees responded to requests for comment on the post-withdrawal expenditures.
The campaign cumulatively spent around $350,000 on consulting firms specializing in communications, fundraising, research and other areas between July and October.
About a third of the consulting spending came after Platner’s withdrawal in early July. Those payouts were the result of contracts the campaign had signed with consulting firms through Election Day, the campaign source said — though some were for a “postmortem” winding down of the campaign’s operations.
None of Platner’s leftover campaign funds have gone to his replacement in the Senate race, Troy Jackson, or any other campaigns around the country. Asked in July if he would accept an endorsement from Platner, Jackson said “It’s unfortunate, but I just don’t want it.”
Other Maine politicians with cash remaining from now-dormant campaigns have put tens of thousands of dollars toward other candidates in Maine and around the country.
U.S. Rep. Jared Golden has given contributions to about 10 other moderate Democrats in recent months after announcing he wouldn’t seek reelection this year. Sara Gideon, who still has some $2 million on hand from her failed campaign against Sen. Susan Collins in 2020, has chipped in over $375,000 to Democrats in Maine, New Hampshire and elsewhere, per her most recent FEC filing.
Platner has largely stayed out of the public eye since dropping out. He was initially slated to speak and lead a veterans’ march at a Labor Day event in Ellsworth, which would have been his first public appearance post-campaign. But Platner ultimately didn’t speak following widespread backlash.
Platner’s FEC filing indicates he still has just under $100,000 on hand.

title: Woman charged after she allegedly shot at her neighbor during fence dispute, police say
text:
ST. CHARLES COUNTY, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - A woman in Missouri was charged after police said she shot at a neighbor during a fight about a fence.
Paula Kohensky, 60, faces charges of first-degree assault/attempted assault and armed criminal action after an incident Sunday night stemming from a property dispute with a neighbor, according to court documents.
St. Charles County police began an investigation after the neighbor reported that someone shot at her husband, according to the probable cause statement.
Kohensky refused to leave her home to talk with police until she eventually came out 30 minutes later.
In the statement, the husband told police he had been working on a fence through Sunday evening after a property-line dispute between him, Kohensky and her husband. He had brought out an electric grinder to cut a fence post after he misaligned it.
The husband heard yelling while the grinder was running, then a countdown from three, followed by a gunshot. He ran back inside and asked his wife to call the police.
Kohensky told police she had a “history of harassment and stalking issues” involving the neighbors.
Kohensky told police that she decided to walk her dog in the backyard that night and left the home with a handgun. She then heard loud metal scraping and saw sparks coming from under a tarp covering the fence.
Kohensky said she saw her neighbor’s shadow and yelled at him to get away from the fence. She claimed that the gun accidentally went off while she was holding it.
The statement said video surveillance footage from the neighbors’ home showed Kohensky and her husband standing side by side while Kohensky was pointing a gun at the fence.
The gun then appeared to fire before Kohensky’s husband took the gun, and both went back into their home.
Kohensky is held on a $500,000 bond and is scheduled for a preliminary hearing on Dec. 2, according to court records.
