title: Fight over evidence in Alex Murdaugh retrial turns to DNA and missing murder weapons
text:
Fight over evidence in Alex Murdaugh retrial turns to DNA and missing murder weapons
Alex Murdaugh’s defense lawyers can do their own tests of unknown DNA found under his wife’s fingernails after she and her son were shot to death in 2021, a judge said Friday, part of an increasingly bitter battle over what evidence can be used in his retrial next year on murder charges.
The DNA belonged to a male who was not a member of the Murdaugh family, and investigators haven't found a match. Although this piece of DNA evidence didn't feature prominently in the first trial in 2023, the defense lawyers wants to test it themselves at a private lab. The judge called Friday’s hearing after Murdaugh’s lawyers filed a flurry of motions saying prosecutors were dragging their feet sharing evidence.
Murdaugh, a once-rich and imposing heir to a Southern legal dynasty, is scheduled to face another jury in April over the killings of his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the rural lowcountry region of South Carolina. While admitting he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict, the 58-year-old Murdaugh has adamantly denied the killings.
The state Supreme Court overturned his convictions earlier this year, ruling that a court clerk influenced jurors during his trial. The case has captivated the true crime world with its mix of treachery, corruption, power and Southern accents.
Judge says Murdaugh's lawyers can't go on a ‘fishing expedition’
Judge Debra McCaslin refused to let the defense test every casing and bullet found in shootings for the past five years in eight surrounding counties involving the same type of gun as one of the weapons used in the killings. The judge called it a fishing expedition.
“If there’s any casings that come through that’s going to match this crime, red flags are going up,” McCaslin said of testing the state has done on all the evidence. “Bells are going to ring and you’re going to know something is going on, and none of that has happened.”
The judge ended her hearing admonishing both sides to be professional and not turn the trial into a circus after a flurry of motions with barbed comments like “facts matter” and “glad to hear it.”
“Y’all need to stop this, OK?” McCaslin told the lawyers at Friday’s hearing. “I don’t want this tit for tat between y’all. Y’all are lawyers — you’re professionals. This is a court. This isn’t a sound bite.”
Murdaugh prepares for another trial after clerk's misconduct
Murdaugh is currently serving a lengthy prison sentence after pleading guilty to stealing from clients. He wore a suit in court on Friday because the judge ruled that wearing his prison jumpsuit during pretrial hearings could influence future jurors into thinking he's guilty.
Prosecutors said he killed his wife and son because his law firm was close to discovering that he was stealing money, and Murdaugh thought the sympathy generated by the killings would buy him time to fix things.
The judge has moved the trial to another county, saying extensive publicity surrounding the case in Murdaugh’s home county could prevent a fair retrial.
Defense wants to know if prosecutors think someone else was at the scene
Nothing was said Friday about the most intriguing dispute of all.
Defense lawyers want to know whether prosecutors have called a grand jury to investigate a police officer who was friends with Murdaugh. Defense attorneys said that prosecutors suggested the officer arrived at Murdaugh’s home before other law enforcement officers and could have helped him hide bloody clothes or weapons. Neither clothing nor the guns have been found.
Murdaugh’s lawyers said the evidence is critical because prosecutors argued during his first trial that he acted alone. Prosecutors said no one else was at the home between the killings and Murdaugh’s return from visiting his mother, when he called 911 to report the shootings.
The defense says another person’s involvement would cast doubt on testimony from witnesses who said at Murdaugh’s first murder trial that he acted alone. Murdaugh’s lawyers also demanded any evidence prosecutors have of possible accomplices or a grand jury investigation into them.
In response, prosecutors declined to say whether any evidence exists, citing legal restrictions on disclosing whether a grand jury is meeting. Because of that, the motion was not argued Friday.

title: Maine’s Heal points is a time-tested formula, but many coaches want improvements
text:
In 2025, the Bonny Eagle High School boys basketball team caught a break. The Scots were 6-11 and headed for the last playoff spot in Class AA South, until a victory in the regular season finale over Noble High School allowed them to jump from seventh to fourth, and from a road to a home playoff game.
The 16-1 Noble Knights were without four starters for much of the game, but as far as the Heal point standings were concerned, it didn’t matter. In the tournament, Bonny Eagle parlayed its good fortune into a quarterfinal win over Sanford, and then a shocking semifinal win over No. 1 Thornton Academy.
“It was kind of a gift for us,” Scots coach John Trull said. “If I were another coach, I’d probably be upset. … But it motivated us. We had to prove that we deserved to be in that spot.”
The scenario showed both the strengths and flaws of the Heal point formula, the system the Maine Principals’ Association has used to seed most high school sports (football excluded) for postseason play. Developed by Durward Heal, a former principal of Schenck High in East Millinocket, and implemented in the 1949-50 season, Heal points rank teams according to their strength by factoring in not just their record but the quality of their victories.
And for over 75 years, while sometimes challenged, no one has found a better, more fair way to do it.
“It’s as equitable a system as there is,” Cheverus girls hockey coach Scott Rousseau said. “I don’t think it’s the perfect system, but generally speaking, it gets it right.”
MPA executive director Mike Bisson noted the objectivity of the Heal points formula, which separates itself from more opinion-based rankings and polls used in some other states.
“While it’s not a perfect system, it’s a mathematical formula,” he said. “And any type of power ranking based on a mathematical formula is going to have some weird things in it.”
While most of the coaches interviewed approve of the structure, there are dissidents whose arguments include that the system can punish victories over weaker opponents, lead to scheduling difficulties and reward victories over opponents with good records, rather than opponents tested by better competition.
A Varsity Maine email survey sent to more than 200 coaches asking if they think Heal points are an effective system, an effective system that could be improved, or not effective received 55 responses. Twenty said it’s effective as is, while 35 said either that the system should be improved or that it just doesn’t work.
“Heal points are no longer effective as currently constructed,” Rob Sullivan, the girls basketball coach at Kennebunk for 30 years, wrote in an email. “It is an outdated system that could easily be replaced for a much simpler system.”
‘ONE OF THE BEST SYSTEMS YOU CAN HAVE’
Heal points work by awarding a point value to a team based on how often it wins and the quality of the teams that it beats.
Here’s how the formula works:
- A team is assigned a preliminary index based on their wins — everyone gets 40 points for a win over a Class A team, 38 for Class B, 36 for Class C, 34 for Class D and 32 for eight-man or Class S. Classes are determined by enrollment.
- That number is then divided by the number of scheduled games. The preliminary index grows as the season goes on.
- Next, you add up all of the preliminary indices for the teams you defeated, and divide that by the number of scheduled games.
- That number is then multiplied by 10, which gives you a team’s tournament index.
- The teams are then ranked by their tournament index to form the Heal point standings. Teams at the top, are the top teams of the year.
Debate surrounding Heals and their effectiveness has gone on for decades. Proponents of the system like that it goes beyond just win-loss record, paints a more accurate hierarchy by factoring in who teams have beaten, and aim to provide balance in classes where teams don’t all share common opponents.
Lucas McNelly, who runs the Maine Basketball Rankings website, developed his own formula that ranks teams and predicts outcomes based on a variety of factors, including point differential and home and road performance. He said, though, that Heal points are “one of the best methods you can have.”
“I think the bones of Heal points are so good that I built the entire ranking system on them,” he said. “Every game in the state matters, and it’s hard to find a system that does that. … It can swing a seeding in C North on the last day of the season. I think that level of chaos is awesome.”
McNelly said the ideal system would include every team in a region playing each other twice, but Maine’s geography prohibits that.
“Let’s say Caribou and Gardiner are in the same (region). … You can’t do that on a Tuesday night for a game,” he said. “The state’s too big. The state’s never going to not be big.”
South Portland boys basketball coach Kevin Millington said a big strength of Heal points is that they reward strength of victory (beating good teams) rather than strength of schedule (simply playing them). Craig Roberts, Scarborough’s girls soccer coach, said tournament results have validated the formula.
“The system has gotten it right,” he said. “If you look at the last four teams standing in the regional semis and regional finals, typically it’s the teams that are at the top (or) near the top of the Heal points.”
Brunswick girls basketball coach Sam Farrell likes that Heal points can give a team that would otherwise be out of the playoff race something to play for late in the season.
“I like being rewarded for big wins,” he said. “It keeps the kids motivated: ‘Hey, I know what our record is, but this game matters.’ You can shock the world, and now you get to play in the (Augusta) Civic Center.”
HEAL POINT HICCUPS
Opponents, however, say the system often doesn’t churn out the best representation within a region. A frequent criticism from the coaches’ survey was that Heal points favor teams that beat opponents with many wins, without taking into consideration whether those wins came against strong opponents.
Conversely, a team wouldn’t get as many points for beating a good team that plays strong competition, but has an inferior record as a result.
Boothbay boys basketball coach Dan Hallinan’s Class D team, which plays in the Mountain Valley Conference with several Class C schools, missed the tournament last year despite playing 10 Class C teams and beating two, while three of the teams that qualified played a combined two C teams and beat none.
“We have been penalized for playing a much harder schedule,” he said. “We are rewarding teams for playing weaker schedules. The best (or) better teams aren’t being placed appropriately seeding-wise, or not making the tournament at all.”
Freeport field hockey and girls lacrosse coach Marcia Wood said she sees a similar dynamic in lacrosse, where teams that play in tougher conferences get seeded lower because they don’t get the number of wins that teams that play weaker schedules do.
Because of that, she said, the two strongest teams can meet up in earlier rounds of the tournament, and “the game before states is the big game.”
Some conferences allow schools the ability to schedule a fixed number of out-of-conference games, but the process of determining which teams to compete against also becomes complicated under the Heal points system.
“Now you have the decision to make of, ‘OK … (who) makes the most sense to play against?'” Dirigo boys basketball coach Cody St. Germain said. “The team that’s geographically close and also gives you a challenge? Or a lot of teams are saying, ‘I’m going to go play a 16-win team that stinks that I know I’m going to beat because I know I get 16 guaranteed Heal points out of going and beating that team.
“And we’re starting to see now there are teams that are really utilizing that to their advantage, and I can’t really blame them. I’ve considered it myself at times.”
How Heal points factor into scheduling can also raise issues from an administrative perspective.
Leavitt Athletic Director Ryan LaRoche said it can be difficult to find games for different sports, as well as for girls programs versus boys programs, given different classifications and talent levels.
“There are definitely teams in the state where the boys team is not competitive at all and the girls team is in the state championship every year,” he said. “So when the conference is making a schedule and they’re looking at crossovers that are appropriate, they’re trying to keep those the same for the boys and the girls, it’s sometimes a challenge to make that work where you don’t want a team that’s bad to just have to play good teams every week.
“But if you have a team that’s very competitive and historically successful, you want them to be able to play the best teams and have those opportunities for the Heal points.”
Mt. Blue baseball coach Steve Porter and Deering boys soccer coach Joel Costigan shared another qualm with the structure: wins over bad teams in-conference earn too few points, and teams can be passed in the standings despite winning games they are obigated to play.
“The Heal points are a way to address the scheduling disparities, but they also create disparities in the points,” Costigan said. “You (can) have a team with more wins, but those wins don’t matter because they still finished behind a team that had fewer wins. I see that every year.”
NO ‘REAL TRACTION’ FOR CHANGE
Several soccer coaches said they’d like to see a more straightforward system of awarding three points for wins and one for ties, while Sullivan at Kennebunk said he’d like to see Heals eliminated in favor of an open tournament.
Farrell at Brunswick said he’d prefer a return to the former difference of five points for a win in each class, rather than the current two, in order to discourage teams looking for wins against teams in lower classes.
Bisson at the MPA said he hasn’t had people come forward “with any proposals that have gained any real traction to change.”
“We would certainly listen if people had an alternative that they felt was a better option and gained some support from the schools,” Bisson said.
For over 70 years, no one’s developed a better one.

title: Expanding weight loss care across Maine
text:
BANGOR — A new name for a program that has widely expanded its offerings as well as its reach. Northern Light Comprehensive Weight Loss program (formerly Surgical Weight Loss) offers a multidisciplinary approach that includes nutritional education, physical therapy, behavioral counseling and peer support groups. The program’s care team is made up of bariatric surgeons, obesity certified registered dietitians, nurse practitioners and psychologists.
The name change is important, as it reflects the program growth and evolution, bringing more services to patients across the state of Maine.
“We know the need for comprehensive weight management care is evolving. We have the ability to meet with patients using telehealth technology, expanding access to areas like Blue Hill, Presque Isle, and across the state,” Program Director, Dr. Matthew Sharbaugh, DO said. “We want people to know; they don’t need to live here in the Bangor area in order to find specialized weight management care.”
Even those patients selecting a path that includes surgery (in Bangor) can participate in nutritional therapy, behavioral counseling, and other elements of the program, from home.
The Comprehensive Weight Loss program is accredited by the Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery Accreditation and Quality Improvement Program. The team met rigorous national standards for patient safety and quality of care, with a focus on minimizing complications and improving surgical outcomes through continuous self-improvement and are leaders in weight loss surgery.
To learn more about the Comprehensive Weight Loss program, visit northernlighthealth.org/EMMCWeightLoss or to talk to your primary care provider about a referral today.

title: Maine’s fire and EMS services are in increasingly dire straits, researchers find
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA — When John Smith decided to shut down the local fire department in Burlington six years ago, he didn’t feel like he had much choice. His kids, who had volunteered there, moved away, and so did another multi-generation firefighting family in town.
That left Smith, who was in his mid-60s, and just one other volunteer.
“I was really afraid for myself and for him, and the fact that people thought they were getting something that they weren’t,” Smith said in an interview this month. “We were not a good service at that point.”
Fire departments across Maine have felt the same sorts of pressures for decades but haven’t known just how bad the problem was or how to express it, said state Fire Marshal Shawn Esler. On Friday, his office and the University of Maine released findings of a two-year study that shows fire and EMS services across the state are in increasingly dire straits.
“They finally documented the freight train that we’ve seen coming for the last 20 years,” said Roger Hooper, chief of the York County Fire Academy and director of the regional training center.
Esler and the researchers say 94% of fire departments that responded to the survey rely on volunteerism to some extent, yet fewer people are available and a significant portion of those who remain are aging and can no longer do all aspects of the work. Forty-seven percent of fire departments that responded to the survey said they were too short-staffed to respond to at least one call in the last three years.
The survey also found big gaps in training, and at the same time, a huge increase in calls to fire and EMS departments. Fire service leaders said gone are the days when a boot drive could generate sufficient funds for departments to be able to provide what their communities expect.
Discussing the study’s findings at the Maine Municipal Association conference in Augusta earlier this month, Esler said: “I think the general public has an expectation that when they dial 911 they’re going to receive a response.”
Augusta Fire Chief David Groder finished Elser’s thought. “You just go up the road 15 miles,” he said, “and there’s a town that may not respond because nobody’s in town that day.”
Maine cities that employ career firefighters are hurting, too, Esler said, because they have long hired people who already have experience as volunteers. He said urban departments have fewer applicants and have to seek mutual aid from smaller cities and towns more often.
Overall calls to fire departments were up 78% from 2014 to 2024, according to the study’s findings, and some departments reported even higher increases, in part because they are filling gaps in healthcare access. Fire departments have become “the backbone of the community,” said research associate Alexander Rezk.
“Without reform, if things continue as they are, we’ll be coming to a point of dysfunction,” he said. Rezk‘s team at UMaine’s Margaret Chase Smith Policy Center surveyed 219 fire departments, along with code enforcement officers and municipal administrators, and interviewed 25 fire chiefs to better understand the challenges and their effects on local communities.
Fire departments have historically received far less public funding than police, Rezk said, and the research findings should challenge Mainers to consider whether that’s still appropriate. While some fire departments have added incentives to recruit and retain volunteers, he said, more will be needed in the future.
Providing fire and EMS services will inevitably get more expensive for Mainers, according to interviews with several people involved in firefighting around the state. They say volunteerism will still be a crucial part of the service, but it is already becoming more regionalized and requires more paid members.
Esler and others pointed to what has happened in Burlington. After Smith was forced to shut down the department, he helped partner with neighboring towns to create the Central Maine Highlands fire district in 2024, the first of its kind in the state. It has a roster of paid firefighters and paramedics.
“I think we’re at a turning point in the fire service,” Esler said. It’s up to state legislators, local governments and residents to make changes and provide funds, he said, “before it continues in decay.”
TRAINING GAP
Just about half of the people on department rosters are trained to fight indoor fires in Oxford, Franklin, Hancock and Waldo counties, according to the survey. It’s not much higher in Washington, Knox and Sagadahoc counties. Training sites can be hours away from a fire department, particularly Down East, along the Midcoast and along the state’s western border.
“It’s not uncommon for a department to be able to respond to a call but lack the number of certified firefighters to do anything,” Rezk said. “Imagine, they scramble to a call but they stand around outside.”
There are more types of industrial and energy infrastructure hazards, like factories, mills, landfills, solar farms, natural gas pipelines, battery storage facilities and data centers, that require more specialized training, said Groder, the chief in Augusta.
“We’re asking our firefighters to understand it, know it, and don’t make mistakes. That’s a big responsibility,” he said.
What happened in Searsmont in May, when a sealed silo at Robbins Lumber exploded, is an apt example, he acknowledged. Firefighters from dozens of departments arrived with no way of knowing the specific hazard the silo presented or what kind of response it required, an assessment by the National Institute for Occupational Health and Safety later found. It said water poured on the initial silo fire likely contributed to the explosion. Three people, including two firefighters, died from their injuries.
As new hazards come into communities, there’s no funding to train firefighters on how to deal with them, Esler said.
“Fires are growing exponentially faster than they did in the past, and burning hotter, and they’re way more toxic than they were in the past,” said Todd Zsiga, the fire chief in Kennebunkport.
The challenges he and others face — to find new people who can stick with training — reflect the ways Maine is changing even beyond the fire service. They’re related to the higher costs of nearly everything in the state (including firefighting equipment); the demographics of aging; and cultural shifts toward online life and away from community volunteerism.
GENERATIONAL CHANGE
Jennifer LaHaye started with the Southwest Harbor Fire Department when she was 18, more than 20 years ago. She said despite the department leadership’s best efforts, “There’ll be times when we have an alarm and one person is going in the middle of the night.” recommends 15 people respond to a house fire.
High housing costs are part of the reason
Rezk, the university researcher, said people are having to work more hours and more jobs to afford to live in many places in Maine and that affects their ability to volunteer.
Three quarters of departments that rely solely on volunteers without compensation that responded to the University of Maine survey said they’re understaffed on weekdays. The number is nearly as high — 67% — for departments that pay their volunteers for calls.
Southwest Harbor adapted by establishing two career positions to provide basic staffing on weekdays. Even the volunteers now get paid during their shifts, LaHaye said. The per diem payments are meant to make it more worthwhile to run into a burning building, she said.
“It’s kind of crazy to think that we expected that they do that and not get compensated for so many years.”
As it is at so many other departments, LaHaye said, there aren’t a lot of young people hanging around the fire station as when she was a teenager. The survey found that at least three of every 10 firefighters in Maine are over 50 years old. Esler said it’s increasingly unlikely those men and women will be able to fight fires inside buildings.
Esler has seen the generational change in his own family. When he joined his community’s fire department, “that’s what every young man in the town of Albion did,” he said.
It was expected that volunteer firefighters would devote their free time to the service and pay their own way for training, Esler said.
“The culture has been prideful,” he said. “It’s been, ‘I’m going to take care of my own fires and my own community.’”
These days, he said, “Our younger generation doesn’t have that same expectation.” He understands why his son, who he said already works 60 hours a week, doesn’t plan to join the fire service.
A REGIONAL APPROACH
In Burlington, Smith said he’d watched volunteerism and participation drop at events and organizations across town — at the historical society, the Independence Day parade, the snowmobile club and the local Veterans of Foreign Wars post.
“We all communicate on Facebook but never look each other in the eye,” he said. “There’s not the community spirit that there was.”
Smith said that with declining help at the fire department,
Smith helped steer Burlington toward the regionalized district and he serves on its board of directors. The costs are distributed among the participating towns. As a taxpayer, Smith was charged $268 this year for fire and EMS.
“The quality of service and abilities these men and women have is like night and day from a small volunteer fire department,” he said. He and the other volunteers “did the best we could with what we had,” he said, but the paid full-timers get the experience of answering many more calls and have access to better equipment.
“They might be 10 minutes further away, but when they get here they make such a difference,” Smith said.
Esler said, “Ten years ago, regionalization was a swear word,” but that is changing, and there’s no prescription for exactly what it has to mean.
Smith said some towns will not want to give up part of their identity and local control. “But I think it’s going to have to happen,” he said.
In York County, Hooper directs a new regional training center that opened this year — a county-level investment that Esler said is rare but welcome. Hooper said having even a few staff to handle routine calls can in turn make it easier to recruit volunteers, “because you’re not wasting their time,” he said.
Rome partnered with Belgrade about five years ago to pay for someone who covers calls during the day, fire Chief Gary Foss said. Without that paid position, many more calls would have gone unanswered, he said, though he’s still nervous it won’t be enough.
“I’ve been telling our townspeople we’ll have to consider having someone here five days a week,” he said.
The decline in volunteers, “is going to end up costing our small towns lots of money,” he said. But if communities choose not to fund fire and EMS services, then home insurance costs will rise, he predicted.
Regionalizing won’t save money up front, according to those who have done it or studied the fire service. The University of Maine researchers said it should eventually, though, by creating a centralized capacity to raise funds, no longer duplicating the costs of equipment, and creating the ability to buy it in bulk. Hooper and others said the state could help provide funds or other incentives to get regionalization started.
The researchers also recommend that Maine increase access to firefighting training, and encourage employers to work with fire departments to make volunteers available.
According to the Maine Office of State Fire Marshal, a comprehensive report will be published next year.
Mainers should feel uneasy about the survey’s findings, Rezk said.
“This isn’t going away,” he said.

title: ‘A great hero’: Trump praises father who stopped Oregon elementary school shooting
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — President Donald Trump praised the father who helped stop the shooting at an Oregon elementary school.
“Well, I’ll tell you what. There was a great hero, and it could have been — as bad as it was — we had a great hero that went in and did the business. He took care of business,” Trump told reporters Friday at the White House.
Kaylub Giamanco was identified as the man who stopped the 16-year-old shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday.
Giamanco, a Bend-area resident with two daughters who attend the school, according to his mother, Kenda Freeman.
Police said Giamanco saw the 16-year-old go into the school and he followed him inside before shooting and killing him.
“Thank God we had him; otherwise it would have been much worse. It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump added.
Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and one teacher were killed in the shooting. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were also taken to an area hospital in critical condition.
Authorities said the first 911 call came at just before 1 p.m. local time from a driver who said someone with a gun had shot at him multiple times while he was in his car.
Bend Police Chief Chris Carney said callers then reported a person with a gun inside the school on Stone Creek Lane, and the school was put on lockdown.
Officers arrived just a couple of minutes later and reported finding the 16-year-old dead.
A law enforcement official briefed on the case told The Associated Press the 16-year-old used a pump-action shotgun bought by his mother. Police did not immediately release the teen’s name.
Investigators searched the shooter’s home Thursday night and took computers and other electronics. His parents told investigators their son had attended Silver Rail Elementary, according to a senior law enforcement official who spoke to CNN.

title: Trump’s Russian diesel deal is disingenuous — at best
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Oct. 11, President Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” deal between Russia and Ukraine, a “deal” that Ukrainian President Zelensky knew nothing about and that was violated by Russia; mere hours later a Ukrainian thermal power plant in Kharkiv was struck.
This was on the heels of Trump shamelessly upbraiding Zelensky for prior targeting of energy plants and refineries in Russia and declaring that fuel targets within the Russian diesel supply chain were off limits — but only for the Ukrainian defenders.
Trump’s recent deal with Putin — to purchase Russian diesel — is a thinly veiled ploy to assuage concern about skyrocketing prices just weeks before the midterm elections. Trump’s claim that the high prices are attributable to the Ukrainians, and not his disastrous Iran invasion debacle, is a pipe dream. It is farcical that the man who so covets a Nobel Peace Prize apparently cares more about ceasefires to protect energy consumption than ceasefires to prevent the wanton killing of civilians.
Jon St. Laurent
Windham

title: Belfast councilor questioned over lease with city manager’s parents
text:
This post was originally published by The Belfast, Maine Conversation. To receive regular coverage from the Belfast, Maine Conversation, sign up for a free subscription here.
There have been ongoing attempts to dismiss this publication as something other than journalism whenever the reporting becomes uncomfortable.
The Midcoast Villager covered the Harkness tenancy story too, and linked to this publication. The Villager didn’t treat it as gossip or drama. It did what newspapers do when another outlet breaks a legitimate story: it followed it.
There’s now a pattern. The Bangor Daily News has also republished articles from this publication, so any suggestion that this isn’t journalism has two problems: it follows a long-established journalistic style that predates modern newspaper conventions (and never disappeared), and established news organizations are associating with it.
Before getting into Councilor Neal Harkness’s response to reporting that he rents his home from City Manager Erin Herbig’s parents, it’s worth explaining that I didn’t know about this relationship until recently. I had been covering the Belfast City Council for two years. Someone tipped me off, and I started checking records.
I checked election records, nomination papers, then property records. I established the family relationship to City Manager Erin Herbig, searched Council records for a disclosure or abstention, checked Maine law, checked Belfast’s own ethics policy and only then published.
Councilor Dan Miller mocked the reporting and minimized the relationship. Harkness had said nothing publicly at that point, so Miller was effectively making the defense for him: this was “drama,” the relationship was insignificant, move along. I specifically suggested asking the Maine Municipal Association (MMA) for advice. Miller had been at MMA training for councilors only a few days before the Harkness article came out — but appeared to bring none of that seriousness about ethics compliance back with him.
Mockery would have been a familiar response from Harkness himself. Silence would have been even more familiar. This publication has been trying to get him to answer questions for a couple of years. My outbox contains many emails that went unanswered, some going back to 2017. In more than a decade of being an engaged citizen, I’ve never received a response to an email from him or his colleague Councilor Mary Mortier. That’s not hyperbole — not one single response from either of them, ever.
This time, Harkness spoke to someone else. He offered a smorgasbord of explanations seemingly aimed at explaining the issue away. And then, among all of that, he said this:
“I can understand why someone might perceive a conflict of interest, but it did not occur to me at the time.”
Harkness confirmed that he rents from Leslie and Cindy Herbig and that the relationship began while he was serving on the Council, and Erin Herbig was city manager. He gave a date, May 2021. He acknowledged that someone could perceive the relationship as a conflict of interest. And when given the opportunity to identify a disclosure, Harkness told the Villager: “I don’t recall making any specific ‘disclosure’ of the arrangement.”
He didn’t say he received advice from the City Attorney before renting the house, nor did he mention that he asked the MMA whether becoming the city manager’s parents’ tenant was appropriate. He didn’t call the law invalid.
Harkness was first elected in 2014. He voted in favor of Herbig’s hiring. She started in March 2020. On February 16, 2021, Harkness and the rest of the Council formally adopted Belfast’s Core Value Statement. It applies to elected officials and directs them to:
“Avoid interest or activity that may be in conflict with or lends to a perception of being in conflict with official City responsibilities.”
Sometime after Herbig was hired, Harkness needed housing that would allow him to remain in Ward 2. He learned a house owned by the city manager’s parents was available, and he rented it. Per his stated date, he did this three months after adopting Belfast’s ethics statement.
Harkness told the Villager that he pays market-rate rent. My October 2 article explicitly said: “I do not know Harkness’s rent, and I’m not claiming he receives a discount.”
I explained why it didn’t matter whether he paid market rent, because the rent doesn’t change who Harkness’s landlords are. It doesn’t negate that finding affordable housing in Ward 2 is a tall order for anyone.
Consider a thought exercise to show why market rent is irrelevant to the ethics issue. Imagine if Herbig’s family owned numerous rentals in town, rentals were hard to come by, and all five councilors lived in them at market rents. Would that be a problem? If you don’t think so, explain why in the comments.
If one councilor is “no big deal,” then what changed between one and five councilors? How does councilor number three or four’s identical rental arrangement become a problem when councilor number one’s wasn’t?
“The fact that we rent from the Herbigs is no secret,” he told the Villager. “My address can be found on the city website, as can the ownership of the property.”
His residential address is not on Belfast’s Mayor and City Council page, or anywhere on the website that I could find. The City publishes his name, ward, term expiration, telephone number and City email address.
Councilor addresses are not on the City website
Maybe Harkness has some other particular City webpage in mind. He didn’t provide a link. At the candidates forum, Harkness got a couple straightforward facts wrong, like claiming the City wasn’t spending money on a second city hall, even though $2 million has already been spent or appropriated. That one was a secret — I had to demand documents the public had never seen, to figure it out.
Let’s follow Harkness’s argument through. A member of the public would need to locate his correct residential address somewhere. Search the property records. Identify Leslie and Cindy Herbig as the owners. Know or independently establish that they’re Erin Herbig’s parents. And determine that Harkness was actually renting the house from them.
Harkness appeared on the fall 2022 ballot as a Pearl Street resident. If Harkness was already renting on Miller Street in late 2022, more than a year after he claims his tenancy began, why did his election paperwork not identify Miller Street as his residence?
If the public could find out by looking up his address and then checking property ownership, which address were Belfast voters supposed to look up in 2022?
More than 4,200 Belfast voters cast municipal ballots in 2024. Quite a few of them told me after this story ran that they had no idea Harkness rented from the city manager’s parents. So how exactly were all of those people supposed to find out about something he never disclosed? By gossip?
An “insiders knew” defense has its own ethical problem. Belfast has a City Attorney on a $60,000-per-year retainer and belongs to MMA.
If this arrangement was no secret among the people involved, did it seriously never occur to any of them — Herbig, another councilor, any staff at City Hall or any supporter who thinks this is “no big deal” — to seek legal advice before a sitting councilor made the city manager’s immediate family his landlords?
Harkness also told the Villager that he has known the Herbigs “since before my time on the council.”
That doesn’t explain how he learned about this specific rental, how the arrangement came together, or even whether that prior acquaintance amounted to anything more than having met them a few times.
Erin Herbig was well situated to clarify that. Harkness made his prior familiarity with her parents part of his explanation. She could say whether she had anything to do with the rental and whether she knew about it when it began. She usually has an explanation for everything.
The Villager asked her for comment. She didn’t respond.
Harkness also told the Villager: “I would think that any counselor [sic] who has a mortgage or does business with a local bank would have a similar conflict.”
Having a mortgage or checking account at Camden National Bank creates “a similar conflict”?
Simon Griffiths is the president of Camden National Bank. A Belfast city councilor doesn’t appoint Simon, set Simon’s compensation, supervise Simon or possess governmental authority to suspend or remove Simon.
Neal does have those powers over the city manager.
On March 1, 2022, Harkness joined a unanimous Council vote approving Herbig’s three-year employment contract. That contract automatically renewed in 2025 without another affirmative Council vote. Harkness was already renting from her parents when he exercised one of the clearest powers the Council has over her employment.
Harkness made a campaign argument that experienced councilors provide an independent check on staff. In reviewing Council records, I still have not found a single administrative proposal Harkness voted against. Readers haven’t pointed to any. He didn’t offer one in his response either.
This publication has reported on numerous instances of Belfast’s Charter, laws, rules and regulations being ignored by Harkness, Herbig and the entire Council. title: Bar Harbor in limbo as legal disputes over cruise ships continue
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bar Harbor recently took new enforcement action against a business that brings passengers ashore from cruise ships — the latest flashpoint in a lengthy legal battle over the number of tourists disembarking in the popular destination.
The town on Mount Desert Island is embroiled in state and federal lawsuits stemming from an ordinance that aimed to dramatically cut back on cruise ship visitation. Officials, businesses and residents are waiting for a federal court order that could determine the scale of the industry going forward.
“We’d like to hope it’s relatively sooner rather than later,” said Everal Eaton, executive director of the Bar Harbor Chamber of Commerce. “That certainty is better for the business community and better for the residents as well to know going into next year what it’s going to look like.”
Since the early 2000s, Bar Harbor has become an increasingly popular destination for cruise ships. In 2022, 143 vessels called on the port, according to the town.
That growth brought concerns about congestion and safety. In 2022, voters approved an ordinance that limited disembarkations from cruise ships to 1,000 passengers a day. The citizen initiative passed with 58% of the vote. In 2024, an effort to repeal that ordinance failed by an even closer margin.
A group of businesses filed a federal lawsuit against the town in 2022 to challenge the ordinance. Nearly four years, a bench trial and a trip to the appeals court later, the case is still unresolved.
In May, Chief U.S. District Judge Lance Walker ruled that the 1,000-passenger cap is only constitutional and enforceable in July and August. Charles Sidman, a Bar Harbor resident who has championed the ordinance and intervened in the case, filed a motion asking the judge to reconsider and amend that order. Walker has not yet issued a ruling.
In the meantime, the parties have also become entrenched in disputes in state court over enforcement of the ordinance. Bar Harbor sent a notice of violation this month to a private pier owner for disembarking cruise ship passengers without a permit, which could add to the quagmire.
“The majority of people that I actually speak to in my day-to-day life are like, ‘When is this going to end?’ ” said Maya Caines, chair of the Bar Harbor Town Council.
ONGOING DISPUTE
Bar Harbor does not have a pier big enough for cruise ships. Instead, the vessels anchor nearby, and smaller tender boats transport passengers to and from the shore.
Eben Salvatore, director of operations for Bar Harbor Resorts, as well as two private piers and the primary tender boats in town, said that the ordinance that limited disembarkations prompted “hundreds of cancellations.”
“Every time the phone rang, it was another massive amount of revenue for a business owner out the window,” Salvatore said. “It was a very painful shock, and it still is.”
In 2024, the Bar Harbor Town Council created a regulatory framework with two separate permits required to enforce the ordinance.
“It’s really just there to ensure we understand and know the level of visitation,” Town Manager James Smith said.
The private piers, overseen by Salvatore, have never applied for the permits.
That summer, the town sent a notice of violation to one of the piers for disembarking passengers from a cruise ship. That action set off a flurry of additional litigation in state court. The parties are waiting for the Maine Supreme Judicial Court to address two separate appeals. If the violation stands, the pier owner could have to pay steep fines.
The town and the business disagree on whether the permitting system is constitutional, based on the latest order from Walker in the federal case.
This month, Bar Harbor issued a second notice of violation to the pier, known as Golden Anchor LC in court records.
“It’s troubling that we seem to have been triggered without our own willingness into another round of litigation,” said Timothy Woodcock, the lawyer representing Golden Anchor and other businesses.
BUSINESSES UNCERTAIN
Sidman, a retired scientist who operates a Bar Harbor gallery with his wife, fought to get the ordinance in front of voters in 2022 and has since defended it in court as an intervenor in the federal lawsuit.
“It was worse than bumper cars at a circus,” Sidman said of the peak traffic from cruise ships. “It was aesthetically unpleasant, it was dangerous and it was detrimental to business.”
He said he would pursue another citizen initiative if the federal court ultimately overturns the ordinance.
“If we have to, we will relegislate it even stronger and more clearly,” Sidman said. “We want our town. We don’t want it submerged by cruise ships and big hotels.”
With lawsuits pending, many say the town is in limbo. Vessels continue to call on Bar Harbor, but not in the same numbers as in the past, according to the town. A dozen or so cruises with a capacity of 3,000-plus visited this year because they made reservations in 2020 and weren’t subject to the newer rules, according to the town.
The town also reached an agreement with American Cruise Lines and got the required permits to regularly disembark its passengers at a public pier this year. Those vessels have a capacity of 250 or less, Smith said.
Eaton, from the local chamber of commerce, said some businesses are uncertain how to staff or order inventory for next year because they don’t know how many cruise ship passengers will be allowed. Kevin DesVeaux, who owns West Street Cafe, said the restaurant has not been profitable since 2022, and lunch sales are down 30% in that time.
He said he is draining his savings to keep the restaurant open.
“We have no more to give,” DesVeaux wrote in an email. “This winter we will decide if we are going to go on the market or hold on for one more year for the cruise ship traffic to return.”
Salvatore and Woodcock said town officials should be making plans to welcome visitors from cruise ships in 2027, especially in the shoulder seasons when the 1,000-passenger cap is not currently enforceable.
“Let’s sit down in a room and work this out,” Salvatore said. “It can’t be hard. Staying in litigation is the worst thing to do.”
Town officials said it’s hard to proceed when so many lawsuits are active.
“We’re trying to be respectful and honoring the citizens’ initiative while being mindful of the legal rights and interests of other parties,” Smith said. “We believe that there is a need for local regulations for disembarking cruise ship passengers, and we want to be able to do that in a way that will meet the test of the court.”
Caines, the town council chair, said she and others want to focus on compromise instead of reacting to court proceedings.
“It’s really dependent quite a lot on the other parties that have been initiating these lawsuits,” she said.

title: Maine Music Society to hold online auction
text:
DEAR SUN SPOTS: Expect the unexpected when you join Maine Music Society (MMS) for the 9th Annual Maine Music Society Online Auction. Check out the website above for the performances coming up over the coming months at the Franco Center. You’ll be delighted by the offerings and appreciate these opportunities to have something special to look forward to.
DEAR SUN SPOTS: I’m a novice at writing and my friends keep telling me that my poetry should be published. Can you please point me in the direction of how to go about this? I’m looking for organizations that would be interested in publishing my late grandfather’s poetry along with my poetry in one volume. My father had hopes to have both generations’ poetry together in one book. — James, no town
ANSWER: Check out Maine Writers & Publishers Alliance in Portland at https://www.mainewriters.org/ to be directed to information on publishing and more. Membership costs $55 per year and is well worth it. They offer workshops, events, and all types of tools to help with the writing and publishing process. Through this membership, you’ll have access to lists of professionals, including editors and publishers who can help you move forward with your goal of having a beautiful book of poetry in your hands, with your and your grandfather’s names on the cover.
Maine Authors Publishing (https://maineauthorspublishing.com/) in Thomaston supports local, independent authors throughout the publishing process with affordable editing, design, printing, distribution, and marketing services. You can choose whatever amount of hand-holding you need as you go through the process. To see other books of poetry published by this organization, go to https://maineauthorspublishing.com/poetry/ .
Another option is Amazon. Review their free self-publishing tools at https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/.
I highly recommend that you have an editor, or at the very least, a proofreader before publishing. Readers, if you have recommendations for James, fire away!

title: ‘Presumably a space object’: 11-foot metallic object found in Minnesota cornfield
text:

The sheriff’s office said the Minnesota Duty Officer was notified. State and federal agencies are working to identify the object’s owner and plan for its removal from the field.

title: What if Maine elected a governor who just gets things done?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Erin Cavallaro lives in Westbrook with her husband and two children and serves on the Westbrook School Committee. She works in higher education and nonprofit fundraising.
After watching the first gubernatorial debate, one thing became even clearer to me: Maine needs Hannah Pingree.
Politics has become very good at telling us what divides us. We know which team everyone is on. We know what we’re supposed to be angry about and who we are supposed to blame. Somewhere along the way, though, we seem to have lost sight of what government is actually supposed to do: make people’s lives better.
That’s why I’m supporting Hannah Pingree for governor.
I’m a Democrat, and Hannah and I share many of the same values. But what impresses me about her isn’t simply that she knows what she believes. It’s that she understands governing requires more than being right. It requires getting something done.
I’ve learned that firsthand serving on my local school committee. The decisions that come before us aren’t theoretical. They affect whether kids get to school, whether teachers have the resources they need, how much taxpayers are asked to contribute and whether families can count on the public institutions that serve them.
You quickly learn that accomplishing anything meaningful requires listening to people you disagree with, finding common ground where it exists and remembering that the work matters more than the politics surrounding it.
Hannah has spent her career doing exactly that.
As a legislator and eventually speaker of the Maine House, she worked with people whose political beliefs were fundamentally different from her own. They disagreed — sometimes significantly. But disagreement didn’t prevent them from sitting at the same table and finding ways to move Maine forward. That feels almost radical in politics today.
Former Republican House leader Josh Tardy, who served alongside Hannah, has spoken about that quality. He and Hannah certainly didn’t agree on everything, but he has said that, despite their partisan differences, she believed Republicans and Democrats needed to work together to find common ground.
That isn’t abandoning your principles. That’s governing — and addressing those challenges will require people who disagree with one another to work together.
I don’t expect Hannah to agree with everyone in Augusta, nor would I want her to abandon her values in the name of artificial bipartisanship. But Maine is a small state with some very big challenges. We need more housing that working families can actually afford. We need young people to be able to build lives and careers here instead of being priced out. We need strong schools, thriving downtowns and an economy that works in communities from York County to Aroostook.
In a state where more than 690,000 Mainers live in rural communities, we need to make sure that where someone lives doesn’t determine whether they can find a doctor or access essential services.
I want a governor who understands that sometimes governing is as simple as finding the thing you agree on, rolling up your sleeves and getting it done. Government shouldn’t be about winning the argument or scoring points against the other side. It should be about results.
At a time when so much of our politics is defined by division, Maine has an opportunity to choose a different approach — a governor who knows what she believes, listens to people who see things differently and understands that finding common ground isn’t a weakness. It’s how good government is supposed to work.
That’s why I’m supporting Hannah Pingree.

title: Governor praises local who 'heroically' helped end the mass shooting at an Oregon elementary school
text:
Governor praises local who 'heroically' helped end the mass shooting at an Oregon elementary school
Officials are lauding the actions of a local who they say chased down and shot a teenage gunman who killed three children and a teacher at an Oregon elementary school.
At a news conference hours after Thursday's attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Gov. Tina Kotek praised the person's response as police arrived at the scene, saying they helped end the rampage and likely saved lives.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” Kotek said.
Related video above: Gov. Tina Kotek speaks at news conference after Thursday's attack at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Like police, the Democratic governor didn't provide any details about the person who intervened, including whether they have a link to the school and whether it was a shot they fired that killed the attacker.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartener at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that a member of the public pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening," Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. "I’m feeling very grateful.”
The shooter used a gun bought by his mom
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Authorities didn’t give details about the teacher who was killed. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded in the attack and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said.
Police said they didn't know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended it.
Police respond within minutes
The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
Children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home.
A community grieves
Shaken residents held a vigil Thursday night, where children drew hearts in chalk on the sidewalk and held candles with other community members.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for the area’s 32 schools.
Bend, which has about 100,000 residents, is the biggest city in central Oregon. Ringed by mountains, it has ballooned in population over the past three decades and is a tourism and outdoor recreation hub, about 125 miles southeast of Portland.
Just four years ago in Bend, a grocery store employee who had served in the U.S. Army attacked a gunman who was spraying shots inside the supermarket. Both the employee, whom police hailed as a hero, and a customer were killed, and the gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

title: Bar Harbor Mount Desert PD pushes single-employer plan ahead of FY28
text:
BAR HARBOR — Leaders of the Bar Harbor and Mount Desert Police Department, along with the managers for each of the towns, presented the latest developments in the police force consolidation plan to members of Mount Desert Select Board and Bar Harbor Town Council at a joint workshop on Thursday, Oct. 15.
The changes presented to both governing bodies dealt with the financial and administrative needs of a joint force based on some of the redundancies observed by Chief Dave Kerns and Captain Chris Wharff over the last three years of Kerns's tenure running both departments. The department has asked both towns to consider a shift to a unified employer for police personnel, with Bar Harbor incorporating the entire organization into its municipal budget and Mount Desert contributing revenue towards the operating costs.

title: College football player dies days after suffering injury during game
text:
(Gray News) – A college football player from Southern Nazarene University in Oklahoma died five days after sustaining a traumatic injury during a game against Ouachita Baptist Saturday.
The university announced the death of sophomore safety Tyler Ulrich on Instagram Thursday but did not go into detail about his injury.
He was 21.
SNU President Dr. Keith Newman said Ulrich was surrounded by the “love, prayers and presence of his family, teammates and dear friends” when he died.
“This loss is deeply felt across our campus. Our hearts are with his family, friends, teammates, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing him. We ask that you join us in lifting them up in prayer during this incredibly difficult time,” the university wrote in its post on Instagram.
“Man of God, ultimate example of quiet strength, loyal, worker, joyous. That’s who Tyler was,” coach Dustin Hada said about Ulrich in a post on X.
SNU held a campuswide prayer in honor of Ulrich Tuesday and has grief counseling support available to anyone in need.
Ulrich was in his third season with the SNU football team and had 16 starts in 20 games.
The team has canceled its game Saturday against Southwestern Oklahoma State University.

title: Letter to the Editor: Maine’s water is being taken, treated and contaminated — and nobody is keeping the books
Vote to keep money coming to Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Whether Mainers like Sen. Susan Collins or not, the fact remains that she is the chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee. If voters choose to elect a junior senator (like Troy Jackson), they can kiss hundreds of millions of dollars for Maine goodbye.
Are people really willing to lose this Maine funding, by voting for another candidate, just because they don’t like the president? As the Maine Senate president, Jackson voted for measures that made the cost of living higher in Maine. Why would anyone believe he will do anything differently if he is elected as a U.S. senator?
Let’s vote intentionally, so that we keep as much money coming to Maine as possible. Vote for Maine, not against a person who’s not even running for office.
Alison Jacobs
Auburn

title: NCAA sues Ohio governor over his executive order allowing schools to ignore new eligibility rule
text:
NCAA sues Ohio governor over his executive order allowing schools to ignore new eligibility rule
The NCAA sued the governor of Ohio on Friday, three days after he signed an executive order giving the state’s universities the option of allowing athletes who graduated from high school in 2022 to play a fifth year of college ball in defiance of the NCAA’s new eligibility rule.
Video above: Pat Kelsey testifies at NCAA eligibility hearing 
NCAA President Charlie Baker called the lawsuit, filed in federal court in Ohio, an “extraordinary step” designed to prevent Gov. Mike DeWine from making it “impossible for all schools to compete on a level playing field.”
The lawsuit itself claimed DeWine was trying to give players in his state “a hall pass” from following the rules.
DeWine's executive order and the NCAA's lawsuit in reaction to it marks the latest tit-for-tat in a torrent of legal maneuverings that are creating new rules on a state-by-state basis.
“This whole thing has become comical,” Danny White, the athletic director at Tennessee, said on social media in reaction to the NCAA announcement.
Under DeWine's order, public and private universities in Ohio would be able to allow the Class of ’22 athletes to play, even though the NCAA’s new guidance excludes those who have already played four seasons. The rule, passed in June, is the subject of multiple court fights.
DeWine's office did not immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press seeking comment. The NCAA suing a governor is rare but not unprecedented. It won a case in the early 1990s against then-Nevada Gov. Bob Miller over a law there that would have required the NCAA to provide more due process protections in enforcement proceedings.
In its court filing challenging DeWine, the NCAA said it was trying "to halt a misguided attempt to give Ohio colleges and universities an unfair, unprecedented and unwarranted competitive advantage in stadiums and arenas throughout the country.”
“College sports, like all sports, depend on participants following the rules. (DeWine) is attempting to give Ohio institutions a hall pass to break the rules," the lawsuit said.
In reaction to the governor's move, the Ohio Supreme Court said it would step in and determine the legality of the executive order. As part of that, it paused an appeals court ruling in a case there that had declared the ’22 athletes ineligible. The court asked both sides to file briefs in the case, in which basketball player Filip Borovićanin is the lead plaintiff, by next Monday.
Baker said the NCAA did not believe the Supreme Court's order did, in fact, declare those players immediately eligible to compete and said it would submit arguments in that case.
That case, like others around the country, is becoming more urgent by the day, as it involves football players, along with a handful of basketball players whose status for the upcoming season is in jeopardy. Among them: Gonzaga transfer Javon Bennett, Cincinnati's MJ Collins and Borovićanin himself, who played in an exhibition against Tennessee on Thursday night after DeWine's order put him back on the eligible list.
Another case in Louisiana involves basketball player RJ Luis, who has been granted eligibility by the court but not placed on the roster by LSU. The Southeastern Conference is suing the school in an attempt to make it conform to its own policy, which would not allow Luis to play.
The NCAA has long explained that it knew excluding the Class of '22 from the five-year rule would cause those athletes hardship, but the decision was between them and the new class of high school recruits coming into college this year, many of whom would be displaced if the veterans were allowed another year.
Ultimately, the NCAA has argued it made its decision based on which move harmed fewer people.
The NCAA lawsuit goes through the history of the rule and the flood of legal actions that have come since. One of the original cases, a federal lawsuit involving basketball player Brock Wisne, is leaning in the NCAA's direction, though victories there have only spawned more lawsuits in state court.
“The results of this second wave of lawsuits were mixed, with the NCAA winning some and losing others,” the lawsuit said. “But the lawsuits unquestionably destabilized college sports, with ever-more disruptive lawsuits challenging foundational rules at the heart of organized sport.”
During testimony in a similar case in Kentucky earlier this week, an NCAA attorney asked Louisville basketball coach Pat Kelsey why he was among those looking for Class of '22 athletes when the NCAA rules forbid that.
“From a coach's standpoint, every time the NCAA says something, we all shrug our shoulders and say, ‘Is that going to stand up? Is that a rule?’” Kelsey said. “We don't think there are rules right now. That's why we want guardrails, we want Congress to act, we want the chaos to end. Because nobody knows what the crap is going on. No one.”
The NCAA has long called for a federal law to tamp down on the lawsuits undermining its rules for hundreds of thousands of athletes across the country. The Senate has sent a bill with that protection — the Protect College Sports Act — to the House, where its fate is uncertain in this election year.

Maine Wildness merchandise goes on sale after team name, logo reveal

Fans can now show their support for Maine’s new professional women’s soccer team, Maine Wildness, with merchandise available following the unveiling of the team’s name and logo Thursday night.
The team, the women’s side of Portland Hearts of Pine, is selling merchandise featuring its new crest at the team store on Marginal Way and online.
The crest incorporates Mount Katahdin, Maine’s highest peak, along with the Dirigo Heart featured in the Portland Hearts of Pine crest.
Fans who stopped by the team store Friday afternoon said they were excited to check out the new gear and offered positive reactions to the team’s branding.
“It’s great. I really like the logo. It’s very similar, but it’s got the twist to it, which I think is very cool,” said Brian Knierim, a Hearts of Pine season ticket holder.
“The name tripped me up at first. I first saw it and I thought it said wilderness, and then I was like, ‘Wait, no, it doesn’t say that.’ So it took me a second, but I think I do like it,” Knierim said.
Maine Wildness is preparing for its inaugural season, which is scheduled to begin in May.

title: Obituary: Eric Paul Poulin
text:
WATERVILLE – Eric Paul Poulin, 67, of Waterville, passed away Sunday Oct. 4, 2026, after an extended period of poor health. Eric was born on Nov. 15, 1958, at Sister’s Hospital in Waterville. He was the son of David J. Poulin (Fairfield/Warren), and Virginia T. Poulin (Waterville).
Eric was a happy sweet little boy, and he carried his kind and tender heart throughout his life. As a boy, he would share anything he had, and he never took the last cookie, he’d always ask if someone else wanted it. He spent some of his early childhood in California where his family lived for several years. The family returned to Maine in the early 1970’s and Eric completed his primary education in Waterville. He was especially bright, and loved to read. He graduated from Waterville High school and then went on to trade school. He attended Job Corps at Husson College and graduated with a degree in Machine Tooling. After graduating from Job Corps Eric worked as a machinist at Fisher Plow in Rockland for several years before returning to live and work in Waterville.
Eric worked a variety of jobs, and eventually became employed at Harris Bakery. He would work at Harris for several years up until they closed. It was at Harris that Eric met his “sweetie,” Linda Fairburn. They fell in love, and shared the next 30-plus years together. After Harris closed, Eric began working for McDonald’s as part of their maintenance crew. The favorite part of his time at McD’s was taking his morning break and having breakfast with some of the weekday morning regulars. Eric loved to tell stories, and hear stories from others. He retired from McDonald’s after having a heart attack in 2016.
He especially loved quick wit and sarcasm, and he took every chance he had to make a wise-crack. He would strike up friendly conversation with anyone. He was a big, loud guy with a tender heart. He was hard to stay in touch with because he wasn’t good at reaching out and even worse at calling back.
Eric was an avid reader until his vision made it difficult. He loved Science Fiction/Dystopian Literature; Douglas Adams, Isaac Asimove, Ray Bradbury. He loved Star Trek, Star Wars, he loved comics – DC not Marvel. He loved Bugs Bunny, the Beatles, the Green Bay Packers and George Carlin. He was a dreamer, with a big imagination.
Eric had the special quality of being able to connect with any animal he met. He loved animals, and enjoyed watching many of the amazing animal videos on YouTube.
He was a loving son, and called his mother every day. He was a kind big brother. He was loved and will be deeply missed.
Eric was predeceased by both of his parents. He is survived by fiancé Linda Fairburn of Waterville; his sister Lauren (Poulin) Ross and brother-in-law Rick Ross, also of Waterville; and longtime friend Paul Cinq-Mars of Las Vegas. The family plans a spring 2027 interment and will notify friends and family once plans are finalized.

title: 2027 pay raise for disabled veterans, military retirees announced
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - The annual cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for 2027 has been announced.
Monthly benefits for military retirees and disabled veterans will increase by 3.6%.
The Department of Veterans Affairs matched its COLA to that of the Social Security Administration, which was announced on Wednesday.
Each year, the SSA creates a cost-of-living adjustment based on inflation rates from the third quarter of the previous year.
The 2027 rate is up from 2.8% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2025, Military.com reported.
For retired military members, that will be a $36 increase per $1,000 of retirement pension, according to the American Legion.
The projected raise is said to apply to all benefits earned through the VA.

title: What to know before buying refurbished electronics
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As the price of new technology climbs, more consumers are turning to refurbished electronics to save money. Nathan Proctor, senior director of the Right to Repair Campaign at US PIRG, tracks those rising prices closely and said buyers do not always need the newest model available.
“Right now, the cost of new electronics has shot up in part because of the demand from the AI data centers buying up a lot of the same kinds of computing equipment, has increased the price of consumer electronics,” Proctor said. “All of the pressure that right now — refurbished technology and repairing devices we already have, that takes that pressure away.”
Proctor said rising prices are pushing more shoppers toward refurbished devices, but not every refurbished item is a good buy.
“You want to make sure you have a good seller with a good reputation, that they’re going to stand by their product for a long time,” Proctor said. “So if you’re looking to save but still want one of those high-quality devices, it’s a great way to go by looking at the refurbished store for those companies.”
Proctor said buying refurbished works well for phones, laptops and gaming consoles. Wearables are a different story. He warned against buying used AirPods or smartwatches, since their small batteries wear out quickly and are often difficult and expensive to replace.
Proctor said shoppers often skip an important step: checking exactly what comes with a refurbished device.
“You should check to see what you’re getting in terms of what they call accessories — so like the charging cable or other kind of peripherals that might accompany the product,” Proctor said. “Depending on who you’re buying from, they may come with those and they may not. You also may need one, and you also may not. You might already have that.”
Experts also recommend checking a seller’s warranty and return policy before buying, so there is time to test a device’s battery and ports before being locked into the purchase.

title: Is Maine’s foliage peaking later as falls get warmer?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
While satellite models show New England’s foliage arriving a week later than it did 70 years ago, Maine’s weekly forest ranger maps reveal a climate system in flux, with peak dates swung wildly between early drought-induced leaf drops and warm, delayed autumns.
This shifting schedule is watched closely by Maine residents, for whom the vibrant crimson and gold canopy is cherished, and by leaf peepers who pump nearly a half-billion dollars in economic activity into Maine’s tourism economy each fall.
How leaves change color every autumn is dictated by plant biology.
As the days grow shorter and cool temperatures arrive, deciduous trees stop pumping out green chlorophyll, allowing underlying yellow, gold and red pigments to finally be revealed. However, chlorophyll breakdown is slowed by rising fall temperatures, keeping leaves green into October.
But ecologists say temperature is only one piece of the puzzle. Seasonal foliage timing and color brilliance are also heavily influenced by rainfall, soil moisture and pest outbreaks, which is why year-to-year ranger reports can mask the long-term trends in Maine’s changing foliage.
Comparing weather and climate is akin to mood versus personality. Daily moods can be easily swayed by immediate events, much like short-term weather anomalies. In contrast, a person’s underlying personality is formed gradually over decades, much like long-term climate baselines.
A review of the state forest rangers’ weekly foliage progression reports underscores the year-to-year variability. In 2020, after a severe summer drought, more than half the state’s seven foliage zones peaked in late September. It would be another six years before any zone peaked so early.
Tree stress caused by severe summer droughts often triggers premature browning and leaf drop, creating the appearance of an early peak. Conversely, fungal blights promoted by heavy fall rain and sudden windstorms can denude entire canopies before peak vibrancy.
How can the long-term delay in fall color be confirmed when the ranger reports look so chaotic?
The underlying shift was uncovered by geographer Stephanie Spera through research at Acadia National Park. She used decades of satellite imagery alongside historical diaries and park photos to strip away annual weather noise.
She identified a distinct pattern: Peak foliage at Acadia, which would fall into Maine’s Zone 2 in the statewide fall foliage map, was arriving nine to 10 days later than it did in the 1950s, or about one day later with each passing decade.
Acadia has warmed by 3.4 degrees Fahrenheit over the last century. One out of five plant species documented in the park a century ago are gone. Seven of the park’s 10 most common tree species are expected to decline or possibly even disappear by 2100.
Climate change is driving not just rising temperatures, but several of the other variables that play a role in Maine’s annual foliage show. The future climate will likely see more more droughts and deluges play out in the same calendar year, according to the Maine Climate Council.
Because fall nights are warming across Maine, trees are staying active later in the season. Thus, while year-to-year peak foliage dates remain at the mercy of the fickle weather moods, Maine’s climate personality is predicted to push peak colors deeper into the calendar over time.
Maine’s modern foliage tracking traces back to 1959, when then Forestry Commissioner Austin Wilkins ordered weekly foliage updates from state forest rangers. These early assessments were radioed to state headquarters and manually distributed to local reporters by phone.
In 1996, Maine became the first state to post weekly leaf conditions on the web. Over time, these reports have established a baseline for seasonal environmental tracking and created a marketing tool for the state’s growing leaf-peeping economy.
