Six Flags Over Georgia to reopen as scheduled days after roller coaster death
text:
Six Flags Over Georgia reopens as scheduled days after roller coaster death
Six Flags Over Georgia opened its gates Friday evening for the first time since a man fell to his death from one of the amusement park's towering roller coasters.
A steady trickle of vehicles drove into the park, some of which had lined up outside about an hour before opening. Most of the visitors said they had not thought about canceling their plans after Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, was thrown from the Goliath coaster on Monday.
“We didn’t plan on riding that specific ride," said Alayna Bruce, who was visiting the park with family. “Hopefully, we can enjoy all the other stuff they have.”
Eleanor Adcock of Griffin, Georgia, said she had second thoughts after hearing about what happened and said she probably would not be riding any roller coasters. But she said she still looked forward to the park’s Halloween-themed Fright Fest attractions of haunted houses and mazes.
“Honestly, I wouldn’t let an incident like this, like, scare everybody out of just going out and enjoying yourself,” she said. “But it’s still very alarming.”
Authorities are investigating what led to Kariem's fall. The park was already scheduled to be closed Tuesday through Thursday. It reopened as scheduled Friday evening, though Goliath was not expected to be running.
Witnesses described seeing Kariem ejected from the coaster, and some people who rode the Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints.
Six Flags Over Georgia's park president, Richard Pretlow, issued a statement Friday afternoon thanking patrons for their support, offering condolences to Kariem's family and reiterating the park's commitment to safety.
“While serious incidents of this nature are exceedingly rare, we never take responsibility to our guests for granted and remain committed to continuously strengthening our operations and safety practices,” Pretlow said.
Local officials in Cobb County, where Six Flags is located, declined to discuss any investigative findings during a news conference Friday. Assistant Police Chief Damon Ballard said county police plan to wait for state investigators to determine what went wrong before deciding whether criminal charges are warranted.
Cobb County's elected commission chairperson, Lisa Cupid, was asked what she might say to reassure patrons that Six Flags is safe. She said people should “use their judgment.”
Documents indicate no safety violations related to restraints
The Georgia coaster passed its latest annual state inspection in March with no safety violations found, according to an Associated Press review of documents obtained from the Georgia agency that inspects amusement park rides.
Inspections from 2016 to 2021 found a total of 18 safety violations related to the ride that included corrosion on welds, loose handrails in the waiting area and maintenance needed on grout and padding around the ride’s support structure. Inspectors said Six Flags corrected each violation within days. None of the problems appeared to involve the ride's restraints.
At least 11 roller coasters in the U.S. and Canada — including the ride on which Kariem died — have been temporarily closed. They were all manufactured by the same company and equipped with similar restraints.
Online photos and videos of the coasters show each equipped with clamshell restraints, which are mounted in front of each seat on a vertical bar that sits between the rider’s knees. The bar locks the padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.
It’s unclear from the images whether any of those coasters also have seat belts or other secondary restraints. Goliath in Georgia has no such backup restraints.
Manufacturer confident of restraint's safety and comfort
Goliath’s manufacturer, the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, was granted a U.S. patent for its clamshell restraint system in September 2001.
In the patent document, the company states that most roller coasters bind riders in “very tight retention devices” that “detract from their comfort.” It says the company's clamshell restraints give each rider a sensation “that he is seated on a flying carpet or that he is at the controls of a kind of flying scooter, while still guaranteeing optimum security.”
Bolliger & Mabillard has said by email that it will not comment on the Georgia death until it has a “better understanding of what transpired.”
Kariem was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Goliath, one of Six Flags Over Georgia’s headline attractions, towers above the park’s entrance. It opened in 2006 and features a series of hills and turns. It does not take riders upside down, but its first hill rises to 200 feet (61 meters), and it has a top speed of 70 miles per hour (112 kilometers).
___
This story has been corrected to show that all 11 roller coasters shut down in the U.S. and Canada were created by the same manufacturer and have similar restraint systems, instead of nine of the 11 rides. It has also been updated to correct a misspelling of one reference to the company Bolliger & Mabillard.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia.

title: A Rainy Friday... Then Blustery & Colder Saturday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Periods of rain will continue through the afternoon and evening as low pressure approaches. The rain could be moderate to heavy at times. The rain is expected to taper off later this evening/early tonight as the low pulls a cold front through the state. Overall rainfall totals will average .25″ to .75″ by later this evening. As the rain exits early tonight... skies will be partly to mostly cloudy for the remainder of the night with low temperatures dropping to the mid-30s to around 40° north and low to mid-40s elsewhere. The wind will shift out of the northwest and increase after midnight with gusts to 30-40 MPH possible.
A few scattered snow showers will be possible Saturday morning.... mainly across the north and in the mountains otherwise expect morning clouds to give way to clearing skies as the day progresses. The pressure gradient will tighten up again on the backside of our departing storm leading to a strong northwest wind Saturday with gusts to 30-40 MPH possible. This will usher colder air into the region too with highs on Saturday only reaching the upper 30s to low 40s north and low to mid-40s elsewhere but will feel colder of course with the wind factored in. The wind will begin to diminish Saturday night as high pressure builds towards the area... allowing the pressure gradient to relax. The diminishing wind combined with clear skies and a colder air mass in place will lead to a cold night with lows dropping to the 20s to near 30° for most spots. High pressure will continue to build into the area for the second half of the weekend giving us lots of sunshine Sunday. As high pressure builds in on Sunday... it will allow the pressure gradient to relax... leading to a much lighter wind for the day. After a cold start to the day... temperatures will be a bit better with highs in the mid-40s to near 50° north and low to mid-50s elsewhere. High pressure will provide us with a nice start to the work week with sunshine and seasonable temps Monday. Monday’s high temperatures will reach the 50s to near 60°. The nice weather continues Tuesday with a mix of sun and clouds and highs in the mid-50s to low 60s.
Rest of Today: Periods of rain. Highs in the mid-40s to around 50° north and 50s elsewhere. Southeast wind 10-20 MPH with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible.
Tonight: Showers ending early then partly to mostly cloudy. Lows in the mid-30s to around 40° north and low to mid-40s elsewhere. Winds will become northwest 10-20 MPH with gusts to 30-40 MPH possible after midnight.
Saturday: Morning clouds giving way to increasing sunshine. Breezy and colder. Highs in the upper 30s to low 40s north and low to mid-40s elsewhere. Northwest winds 10-20 MPH with gusts to 30-40 MPH possible.
Sunday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the mid-40s to near 50° north and low to mid-50s elsewhere.
Monday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the mid-50s to low 60s.
Tuesday: Mix of sun and clouds. Highs in the mid-50s to low 60s.

title: First images released of Pope Leo celebrating Mass at hospital after cancer surgery
text:
ROME (AP) — The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Pope Leo XIV since his lung cancer surgery, showing him celebrating Mass, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.
The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him in Gemelli hospital. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.
In his homily, Leo thanked the hospital staff “for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him,” Bruni said.
Bruni also confirmed Leo would make his first public appearance on Sunday to deliver the traditional noontime prayer.
“His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own,” said a medical update signed by Leo’s personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone and the head of thoracic surgery at the Gemelli hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The 71-year-old Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
A signal of all systems go for trip
Even as questions swirled about what his cancer means for the future of his young pontificate, there were signs Friday that it was all systems go. The Vatican on Friday published the names of journalists accredited to fly on Leo’s plane with him during his Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Leo’s ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis, and the Vatican can change plans at any time. But the posting of the media list signaled that at least on an organizational level, the trip was going ahead.
In the nearer term, Vatican officials were gaming out possible scenarios for Leo to recite the traditional Sunday noontime Angelus prayer. Vatican media personnel were seen at the Gemelli hospital laying cables for a possible live broadcast, as past popes have done when hospitalized. Spokesman Bruni said he would deliver the prayer, but it wasn’t clear where.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said a recitation of the noontime prayer on Sunday from the hospital was a possibility, but would depend on Leo’s recovery. Such appearances have often served as a welcome confirmation of a hospitalized pope’s well-being for the 1.4 billion-strong Catholic faithful and others.
Secretary of state suggests ‘adjustments’
Parolin said he remained concerned about the pope, but indicated that was also a function of his surprise at learning that Leo needed surgery. Parolin, who was considered a leading contender in the conclave that elected Leo and was recently passed over as dean of the College of Cardinals, surprised some by suggesting that the pontificate itself might need to be adjusted.
“We can’t make any type of predictions,” Parolin said Thursday, according to the LaPresse and ANSA news agencies. “The question now is when he will return, under what circumstances he will return, and what the doctors say. And based on all these factors, the pope will then adjust his pontificate, if it needs to be adjusted,” he was quoted as saying.
Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular and genetic makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.
Cancer patients send well-wishing notes to Leo
Meanwhile, the Vatican on Friday released photos of some get-well notes that had been sent to Leo from patients at Gemelli’s pediatric oncology ward, located on the 10th floor, where popes past have often visited during their own hospitalizations.
One, from 7-year-old Angelo, told Leo that he had been on the 10th floor for 36 days. “My mother and I pray for you every night. Get well soon,” he wrote, with little hearts at the bottom.
Giorgia, a university-aged student, wrote to Leo in his native English, saying she had long loved learning and practicing the language.
“When I heard on the news about you and your situation, I felt it a thousand times harder, because in some ways we’re going through the same thing, and it made me feel closer to you,” she wrote. “I pray to God that we both heal and I ask you to pray for me, too.”
___
Associated Press visual journalist Trisha Thomas contributed to this report.

10 Beloved Stores Mainers Wish Were Still Around
Shopping in Maine used to be an adventure!
Remember when the Bangor Mall and the Maine Mall were packed with stores you couldn’t wait to check out? Or places like Borders with stacks of books everywhere, Circuit City with all the gadgets, or Blockbuster where picking a Friday night movie was a ritual? Those spots are gone now, and it feels a little emptier without them, but that is the one constant in life, things change.
Shopping habits shifted, online stores boomed, and trends moved faster than anyone could keep up with. Some of those beloved stores are still around online, but it’s just not the same as roaming the aisles and stumbling on something you didn’t even know you wanted.
For anyone who grew up wandering Maine’s malls, or driving down Stillwater Avenue in Bangor, just remember, those memories are forever!

title: Inflation drives up family expenses by hundreds per month since Jan. 2025
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Family expenses are up hundreds of dollars a month since 2025. See how inflation is affecting your budget
A sample family budget shows monthly costs have risen by $275 since January 2025, as inflation continues to outpace wage growth and voters express dissatisfaction with President Trump's economic policies.
Family expenses are up hundreds of dollars a month since 2025. See how inflation is affecting your budget
A sample family budget shows monthly costs have risen by $275 since January 2025, as inflation continues to outpace wage growth and voters express dissatisfaction with President Trump's economic policies.
A family of four with two children in daycare and a pet could be paying about $275 more each month for everyday expenses than when President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, according to an analysis by our Get the Facts Data Team.
This week, the Consumer Price Index showed prices were up 3.7% over the past year, while the Producer Price Index showed prices paid by businesses were up 6.3%.
During his 2024 campaign, Trump promised to bring prices down.
"Starting on day one, we will drive down prices and make America affordable again. We have to make it affordable. It's not affordable. People can't live like this," Trump said at the Republican National Convention in 2024.
With the midterm elections approaching, our Get the Facts Data Team looked at what has happened to some of the everyday costs families pay. The team built an interactive tool that lets you enter what you spend each month on groceries, gasoline, electricity, childcare and pet food. The tool then uses Consumer Price Index data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics to estimate how those costs have changed since Trump took office.
To show how those changes can add up, we built a family-of-four example using national spending benchmarks from several different sources.
For groceries, we used about $1,150 a month, based on the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Moderate-Cost Food Plan for a family of four with two young children.
For gasoline, we used about $220 a month based on household spending data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
For electricity, we used about $150 a month based on national residential electricity data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
For childcare, we used about $2,350 a month. That is based on Child Care Aware of America's national average prices for center-based care for an infant and a 4-year-old.
For pet food, we used about $60 a month, an estimate based on American Pet Products Association data on nationwide spending on pet food and treats and the number of U.S. households that own pets.
We then entered each of those monthly amounts into the Get the Facts tool.
The tool does not simply apply the overall inflation rate to the entire budget. Instead, it looks at how prices have changed in each individual category since January 2025 and applies those changes to the amount entered for that expense.
Those changes vary significantly. Since Trump took office, the Consumer Price Index for groceries has risen about 3.5%, electricity about 10% and gasoline nearly 40%.
When the changes across all five categories are added together, the tool estimates those expenses now cost our family-of-four example about $275 more each month than they did in January 2025.
The example is meant to show how higher prices can add up. Your number will be different depending on what your household spends, where you live, your childcare needs and other factors. You can enter your own monthly expenses into the Get the Facts tool to see an estimate for your budget.
"People are spending, but they're being very, very careful how they spend. They're looking to stretch their dollar," said Mark Mathews, chief economist and executive director of research at the National Retail Federation.
Mathews recommends shopping around, using retailer apps and promotions and even using artificial intelligence tools to compare prices.
NerdWallet recommends looking at some of the biggest bills that hit each month. That can include canceling subscriptions you no longer use and shopping around or trying to negotiate recurring expenses such as phone, internet and insurance.
At the grocery store, NerdWallet also recommends comparing the price per ounce or pound instead of looking only at the sticker price.
Republicans argue their tax cuts are leaving families with more money in their pockets. But higher prices have been eating into paychecks, with inflation outpacing average hourly wage growth over the past year.
The latest AP-NORC poll, conducted Oct. 8-12, found 25% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's handling of the economy and 19% approve of his handling of the cost of living.
A separate AP-NORC poll conducted in late September found 65% of adults said higher-than-usual prices were the result of Trump's policies, while 34% attributed them more to factors beyond the president's control.

title: President Trump ramps up campaign efforts with 18 days left until the midterms
text:
President Trump ramps up campaign efforts with 18 days left until the midterm elections
President Donald Trump is intensifying his campaign schedule with rallies in multiple states as the midterm elections approach, amid challenging poll numbers.
President Trump ramps up campaign efforts with 18 days left until the midterm elections
President Donald Trump is intensifying his campaign schedule with rallies in multiple states as the midterm elections approach, amid challenging poll numbers.
With 18 days until the midterm elections, President Donald Trump is ramping up his campaign efforts, traveling to key states and holding rallies as part of a 32-day campaign blitz.
The president is scheduled to attend a rally in northern Kentucky on Saturday in support of Republican Senate candidate Andy Barr. He's running against Democrat Charles Booker. Both are looking to replace Sen. Mitch McConnell, who is stepping down at the end of his term.
Trump has also endorsed Ed Gallrein, who defeated Rep. Thomas Massie in the GOP primary. Gallrein now faces Democrat Melissa Strange in the fourth congressional district. 
According to multiple reports, Trump will hold a rally in Wichita, Kansas, on Monday, followed by an event in Greenville, North Carolina, on Tuesday. The Greenville rally comes as the state faces an open Senate seat following Republican Thom Tillis' retirement. Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper is facing former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley in the race for the seat.
A new Fox News poll reveals that 70% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, while 77% disapprove of his approach to inflation. On border security, voters appear divided.
Todd Belt, a political analyst, said, "It's going to be difficult for Donald Trump to find an issue because the midterm elections are always a referendum on the president's handling of his job, and of course, job number one is the economy, and Donald Trump's not doing well on that in the polls."
On Thursday, Trump floated the idea of returning to Texas before Nov. 3 if necessary, which would mark his fourth campaign visit to the state in about a month.

title: Sanford's Police Chief gives his version of the ICE operation
text:
Sanford police chief answers questions about ICE operation that ended with man in custody, toddler in hospital
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conducted an enforcement operation Thursday in Sanford, after which, the Department of Homeland Security shared the following message with Maine's Total Coverage: "If you are here illegally, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you."
That appeared to be the case on Brook Street just after 9 a.m., as two ICE vehicles stopped Manucho Nseka, an immigrant from Angola who had his 1-year-old child in the backseat of his SUV.
"The baby was in a car seat in the backseat of the car, but the car seat wasn't properly installed," said Sanford Police Chief Eric Small.
Small was on the scene Thursday morning, as Sanford police officers responded because Nseka had backed into an ICE vehicle that approached his SUV from behind.
The toddler was taken to a local hospital as a precaution and was not injured, Small said.
Social workers and others assisting the family said the mother of the child was working and that Nseka took the 1-year-old with him to run an errand while two other children, ages 2 and 11, were left home alone. Police had said members of the Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) responded to the home to ensure the children's safety and welfare.
"The children have returned home to their mother," Small said.
Small also addressed questions about the Maine law that states local authorities should not cooperate with ICE in regard to immigration issues. The police chief said his department uses common sense.
"We follow the state law. We don't participate in any searches for people, for immigration violations. We don't provide ICE with any non-public information," Small said.
Small said when it comes down to public safety, in this case, a crash with a child involved, Sanford police can and will respond, as well as cooperate.
"If something happens in Sanford that we become aware of, the officers are going to go there and make sure that our public, the people that live on the street, the people who live in the city, are safe," Small said.
Homeland Security said ICE initiated the targeted enforcement operation because Nseka failed to show up for a mandatory immigration proceeding. It is unclear where Nseka is being held.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security said Nseka will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the United States.

title: Man who stopped Oregon elementary school shooter is the father of 2 daughters at the school, his mother says
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — The man who stopped a deadly elementary school attack in Oregon by shooting the gunman inside the building is the father of two girls at the school, his mother said Friday.
In a statement read to reporters Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, intervened in Thursday’s attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend and shot the teenage shooter.
Three students and a teacher were killed in the attack, and a fourth student and another teacher were critically injured.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said, noting that her son is a lifelong resident of Bend.
Police have not yet identified who shot the gunman, only saying that the suspect was found dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported. They also haven’t named the gunman.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
Officials are lauding the actions of a local who they say chased down and shot a teenage gunman who killed three children and a teacher at an Oregon elementary school.
A day after the mass shooting that also critically wounded a fourth student and another teacher, well-wishers laid flowers Friday against the sign outside of Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, an outdoorsy city of about 100,000 in central Oregon that is ringed by mountains.
At a news conference hours after Thursday’s attack, Gov. Tina Kotek praised the person who followed the gunman into the school, saying they helped end the rampage as police began arriving on the scene and likely saved lives.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” said Kotek.
Like police, the Democratic governor didn’t provide any details about the person who intervened, including whether they have a link to the school and whether it was a shot they fired that killed the attacker.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartener at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that a member of the public pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. ”I’m feeling very grateful.”
The shooter used a gun bought by his mom
The 16-year-old suspect, identified only as a Bend resident, was found dead inside the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Mike Krantz said. Police said he got into the school by shooting through locked doors.
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Authorities didn’t give details about the teacher who was killed. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded in the attack and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Police said they didn’t know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended it.
Police respond within minutes
The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education.
Children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home.
A community grieves
Shaken residents held a vigil Thursday night, where children drew hearts in chalk on the sidewalk and held candles side-by-side with adults.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for the area’s 32 schools.
Bend, which has about 100,000 residents, is the biggest city in central Oregon. Ringed by mountains, it has ballooned in population over the past three decades and is a tourism and outdoor recreation hub, about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland.
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.
Just four years ago in Bend, a grocery store employee who had served in the U.S. Army attacked a gunman who was spraying shots inside the supermarket. Both the employee, whom police hailed as a hero, and a customer were killed, and the gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

title: Savannah Bananas release 2027 schedule; games include stops in Canada and Mexico
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — The Savannah Bananas are going to need passports as Banana Ball goes international for the first time in 2027.
The Savannah Bananas and five other teams in their barnstorming style of rollicking baseball entertainment have scheduled stops in Canada and Mexico next year. Banana Ball will also be played in 23 Major League Baseball stadiums and 10 football stadiums in 2027, owner Jessie Cole announced Thursday.
Cole told The Associated Press he couldn’t have imagined the popularity of Banana Ball when he launched the Savannah Bananas in 2016. He added five teams for the 2026 schedule.
The original idea was to generate fan interest for baseball at historic Grayson Stadium in Savannah, Georgia.
“We were just starting to sell tickets and trying to get off the air bed we were sleeping on,” Cole said.
The 2027 schedule announced Thursday night on ESPN2 includes stops in Monterrey, Mexico, on Feb. 5-6, and Tijuana, Mexico, on Feb. 12-13.
The Banana Ball schedule also includes Aug. 14-15 dates at Rogers Centre in Toronto and two visits to Winnipeg — Aug. 26 and Aug. 28.
“This was 10 years in the making,” Cole said of the international dates.
In 2023, the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, New York, opened an exhibit for the Savannah Bananas. The exhibit was recognition of Cole’s success in attracting younger fans who enjoy such shenanigans as a pitcher throwing the ball while on stilts and outs being counted when a fan catches a foul ball in the stands.
On June 26, Banana Ball will add another tweak at Notre Dame Stadium when two baseball fields will be positioned on opposite corners of the football facility, with teams switching fields every inning. The goal is to allow every fan to have a close view of the action.
Cole also announced Disney has produced a film documenting the growth of the Savannah Bananas and Banana Ball. The film will debut at Atlanta’s Truist Park on June 12.
Including minor league stadiums, the 2027 Banana Ball Championship League tour will visit 79 stadiums across 74 cities. Cole expects the tour to draw an estimated 4.3 million fans.

title: Obituary: Robyn Butler
text:
PHIPPSBURG – Robyn Butler died peacefully surrounded by her loving family after a courageous eight-year battle with cancer. She was a devoted wife, mother, and grandmother.
Robyn loved education. Her own education included high school in Delaware where she was a proud cheerleader. She studied education at the University of Maryland and University of North Florida. She earned her master’s degree in Literacy at the University of Maine.
Robyn met her husband Tom, a midshipman, on a blind date in 1969. They were married in 1970 at the Naval Academy Chapel. Robyn found great purpose in her 28 years as a Navy wife. Robyn and Tom were married for 56 years; their marriage filled with love, respect and admiration. They were best friends.
Tom and Robyn first fell in love with Maine when the Navy brought them to Bath in 1985. It was then they joined Grace Episcopal Church and put down roots in the Bath community. When their time with the military ended, they returned to Maine, a place they loved.
Robyn’s passion and profession was teaching. She was an elementary school teacher in Virginia and a literacy specialist in Maine. She proudly served her community as a board member of Family Focus and as a member of the vestry of Grace Episcopal Church. She would also have loved to tell you about her time as a tour guide while living at the Naval Academy.
Her life was filled with her children, grandchildren, friends, gardening, church, teaching, boating and travel.
Robyn is survived by her husband, Tom; her daughter, Wendy, her husband, Graham, and their children Bennett and Lindsay; her son, Todd, his wife Florencia, and their children, Lucas, Sebastian, Julian, and Mia; her brothers Mark and his wife Helen, David and his wife Maria, and sister, Dianne
A memorial service will be held at Grace Episcopal Church on Saturday, Oct. 24, at noon. A gathering of family and friends will be at the Church Fellowship Hall.
There will be a celebration of life at the United States Navel Academy in the spring.
Condolences can be made online at http://www.DaigleFuneralHome.com.

title: Bar Harbor in limbo as legal disputes over cruise ships continue
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bar Harbor recently took new enforcement action against a business that brings passengers ashore from cruise ships — the latest flashpoint in a lengthy legal battle over the number of tourists disembarking in the popular destination.
The town on Mount Desert Island is embroiled in state and federal lawsuits stemming from an ordinance that aimed to dramatically cut back on cruise ship visitation. Officials, businesses and residents are waiting for a federal court order that could determine the scale of the industry going forward.
“We’d like to hope it’s relatively sooner rather than later,” said Everal Eaton, executive director of the Bar Harbor Chamber of Commerce. “That certainty is better for the business community and better for the residents as well to know going into next year what it’s going to look like.”
Since the early 2000s, Bar Harbor has become an increasingly popular destination for cruise ships. In 2022, 143 vessels called on the port, according to the town.
That growth brought concerns about congestion and safety. In 2022, voters approved an ordinance that limited disembarkations from cruise ships to 1,000 passengers a day. The citizen initiative passed with 58% of the vote. In 2024, an effort to repeal that ordinance failed by an even closer margin.
A group of businesses filed a federal lawsuit against the town in 2022 to challenge the ordinance. Nearly four years, a bench trial and a trip to the appeals court later, the case is still unresolved.
In May, Chief U.S. District Judge Lance Walker ruled that the 1,000-passenger cap is only constitutional and enforceable in July and August. Charles Sidman, a Bar Harbor resident who has championed the ordinance and intervened in the case, filed a motion asking the judge to reconsider and amend that order. Walker has not yet issued a ruling.
In the meantime, the parties have also become entrenched in disputes in state court over enforcement of the ordinance. Bar Harbor sent a notice of violation this month to a private pier owner for disembarking cruise ship passengers without a permit, which could add to the quagmire.
“The majority of people that I actually speak to in my day-to-day life are like, ‘When is this going to end?’ ” said Maya Caines, chair of the Bar Harbor Town Council.
ONGOING DISPUTE
Bar Harbor does not have a pier big enough for cruise ships. Instead, the vessels anchor nearby, and smaller tender boats transport passengers to and from the shore.
Eben Salvatore, director of operations for Bar Harbor Resorts, as well as two private piers and the primary tender boats in town, said that the ordinance that limited disembarkations prompted “hundreds of cancellations.”
“Every time the phone rang, it was another massive amount of revenue for a business owner out the window,” Salvatore said. “It was a very painful shock, and it still is.”
In 2024, the Bar Harbor Town Council created a regulatory framework with two separate permits required to enforce the ordinance.
“It’s really just there to ensure we understand and know the level of visitation,” Town Manager James Smith said.
The private piers, overseen by Salvatore, have never applied for the permits.
That summer, the town sent a notice of violation to one of the piers for disembarking passengers from a cruise ship. That action set off a flurry of additional litigation in state court. The parties are waiting for the Maine Supreme Judicial Court to address two separate appeals. If the violation stands, the pier owner could have to pay steep fines.
The town and the business disagree on whether the permitting system is constitutional, based on the latest order from Walker in the federal case.
This month, Bar Harbor issued a second notice of violation to the pier, known as Golden Anchor LC in court records.
“It’s troubling that we seem to have been triggered without our own willingness into another round of litigation,” said Timothy Woodcock, the lawyer representing Golden Anchor and other businesses.
BUSINESSES UNCERTAIN
Sidman, a retired scientist who operates a Bar Harbor gallery with his wife, fought to get the ordinance in front of voters in 2022 and has since defended it in court as an intervenor in the federal lawsuit.
“It was worse than bumper cars at a circus,” Sidman said of the peak traffic from cruise ships. “It was aesthetically unpleasant, it was dangerous and it was detrimental to business.”
He said he would pursue another citizen initiative if the federal court ultimately overturns the ordinance.
“If we have to, we will relegislate it even stronger and more clearly,” Sidman said. “We want our town. We don’t want it submerged by cruise ships and big hotels.”
With lawsuits pending, many say the town is in limbo. Vessels continue to call on Bar Harbor, but not in the same numbers as in the past, according to the town. A dozen or so cruises with a capacity of 3,000-plus visited this year because they made reservations in 2020 and weren’t subject to the newer rules, according to the town.
The town also reached an agreement with American Cruise Lines and got the required permits to regularly disembark its passengers at a public pier this year. Those vessels have a capacity of 250 or less, Smith said.
Eaton, from the local chamber of commerce, said some businesses are uncertain how to staff or order inventory for next year because they don’t know how many cruise ship passengers will be allowed. Kevin DesVeaux, who owns West Street Cafe, said the restaurant has not been profitable since 2022, and lunch sales are down 30% in that time.
He said he is draining his savings to keep the restaurant open.
“We have no more to give,” DesVeaux wrote in an email. “This winter we will decide if we are going to go on the market or hold on for one more year for the cruise ship traffic to return.”
Salvatore and Woodcock said town officials should be making plans to welcome visitors from cruise ships in 2027, especially in the shoulder seasons when the 1,000-passenger cap is not currently enforceable.
“Let’s sit down in a room and work this out,” Salvatore said. “It can’t be hard. Staying in litigation is the worst thing to do.”
Town officials said it’s hard to proceed when so many lawsuits are active.
“We’re trying to be respectful and honoring the citizens’ initiative while being mindful of the legal rights and interests of other parties,” Smith said. “We believe that there is a need for local regulations for disembarking cruise ship passengers, and we want to be able to do that in a way that will meet the test of the court.”
Caines, the town council chair, said she and others want to focus on compromise instead of reacting to court proceedings.
“It’s really dependent quite a lot on the other parties that have been initiating these lawsuits,” she said.

title: Events center at Shaw Cherry Hill Farm in Gorham nears completion
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GORHAM — Driving into Gorham on Route 25, it is difficult to miss the large stone building that has been rising by the entrance of Shaw Cherry Hill Farm for over a year.
Called Cherry Hill Place, the New England post-and-beam barn, 5,917-square-foot structure will serve as an events center. It is in its final stages of construction and will open for its first weekly indoor makers market on Nov. 1.
Shaw Brothers Family Foundation, the nonprofit run by Jon and Dan Shaw, of Shaw Brothers Construction, is building the venue and leasing it to neighboring Sebago Brewing Co., which will administer and cater weddings, work gatherings, birthday parties, reunions and other events. It can hold up to 350 people.
“The owners want to get back to their agricultural roots,” said Lee Pratt, general manager of Shaw Brothers Construction. “This is a legacy building for them. It’s something that’s going to outlive all of us.”
The building features an open floor for gatherings and the 40-vendor market, a bar, industrial kitchen, and a silo with a spiral staircase leading to a second-floor mezzanine, where there are six bridal suite changing rooms. The owners of Gorham-based restaurant, MK Kitchen, will run a new ice cream shop, Milk Ice Cream, from a designated window and space in the back of the building come spring.
Large windows in the event space overlook the farm, which Pratt said are intended to provide bucolic views. There is also a projector and space for bands to play inside, as well as lighting that can change to custom colors.
The large wooden beams that give the interior its historic barn feel are made of Douglas fir timbers brought in from Washington state because there are no trees large enough in Maine, Pratt said. The biggest are 62 feet and weigh 2,800 pounds.
Pratt declined to provide a cost of construction.
The indoor makers market — a winter version of the farmers market held outside the center in the warmer months — will see food trucks, drinks sold at the bar and the projector streaming football games on Sundays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. through the end of the year, said Samantha Dyer, director of venue and event operations. Starting Nov. 27, Westbrook-Gorham Rotary Club will sell Christmas trees every day through December.
Dyer said some events are already booked for the months after the opening and she has many ideas for the future of the building, including hosting a summer camp, adding an outdoor wedding ceremony space, and holding Oktoberfest celebrations.

title: Friday’s high school football: Gray-New Gloucester rolls past Mt. Ararat
text:
Liam Joyce recorded a rushing touchdown and a receiving touchdown in the first half to help Gray-New Gloucester cruise to a 25-6 win over Mt. Ararat in an eight-man Large School South game in Gray.
Wide receiver Carter Corson gave Gray-New Gloucester (5-1) a 6-0 lead in the first quarter, scoring on a 3-yard jet sweep.
Joyce scored on a 5-yard run later in the first. In the second quarter, he was left open near the end zone and quarterback Cole Prescott found him for a 15-yard touchdown, extending the lead to 18-0.
Running Grealish scampered 14 yards in the fourth quarter for the Patriots’ final TD.
Mt. Ararat (0-7) got a 70-yard touchdown run from Ethan Fournier late in the fourth.
BANGOR 35, EDWARD LITTLE 14: Gavin Hughes returned the opening kickoff 87 yards for a touchdown and added three 2-yard touchdown runs as the Rams (3-3) took down the Red Eddies (2-4) in Bangor.
The victory bolsters Bangor’s postseason chances and delivers a blow to Edward Little’s. The top four teams in Class A North advance to the playoffs, and the Rams are now solidly in fourth place and the Red Eddies are stuck in fifth.
Edward Little responded quickly to Hughes’ kickoff return. The Red Eddies were without starting quarterback Logan Stout and used a rotating cast of players under center. A few plays into their opening drive, Ashton Sullivan, listed as a tight end, threw over the defense to Logan Averill for a 63-yard touchdown to tie the game at 7-7.
Bangor went ahead for good on a 21-yard run by QB Alex Tennett. On Edward Little’s next drive, a low snap resulted in punter Logan Billings being tackled near the goal line. A few plays later, Hughes ran in his first 2-yard TD to put the Rams up 21-7 with 1:35 left in the first quarter.
Edward Little’s Evan Madigan cut the deficit to 21-14 with a 21-yard touchdown run midway through the second quarter. That came one play after he ran for a first down on fourth-and-9. Madigan, one of the many players who played QB for the Eddies, had a 39-yard TD run called back by a penalty in the fourth quarter. He finished with 99 yards rushing on 18 carries.
Hughes scored twice more in the third quarter.
Will Houghton recovered to fumbles and Hayden Summerlin intercepted a pass for Bangor. Elijah Odunlami blocked an extra point for Edward Little.

title: Bath Rotary grants available
text:
The Rotary Club of Bath is once again encouraging nonprofit charitable organizations to submit applications for Community Service Grants. It’s often a juggling act for nonprofits to direct limited funds in a way that benefits those who need it most. Many times a few thousand dollars can be enough to expand a critically needed service. For that reason, the club distributes money every year to several nonprofit organizations who reach out to make lives better for people who need a helping hand.
Up to $10,000 has been designated for grants this year. Beginning in 1919, the Bath Rotary Club in its earliest days raised money for basic needs like food, clothing, and education. While continuing to meet those needs, the club continued to expand its mission over the next 100-plus years to meet new challenges from Bath and surrounding communities. In the last few years Rotary members have awarded volunteer time and grants to the Backpack Program, Best Buddies at Morse High School, the Midcoast Youth Center, Bath Parks & Recreation, the Bath Area YMCA, Woolwich Odyssey of the Mind, and Salvation Army Bell Ringing.
The deadline for submitting applications is Dec. 31, 2027. Application forms are available on the Bath Rotary website, bathrotary.org. For more information, email bathrotary@gmail.com.

A brief rumble of thunder cannot be ruled out in far southwestern Maine.

title: European grocery store hack raises concerns about supermarket cybersecurity
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Cyberattack disrupts refrigeration in European supermarkets
A cyberattack over the weekend disrupted refrigeration systems in hundreds of European supermarkets, causing millions of dollars in food spoilage and raising concerns about similar incidents in the U.S.
Hackers affected about 700 grocery stores in France, Spain, Portugal, Poland and Germany by turning on the defrost cycles in display cases, forcing all food in those cases to be discarded. No group or individual has claimed responsibility for the attack or demanded a ransom.
Supermarket refrigeration systems are operated by controllers that can be accessed online.
"These refrigeration units are mechanical devices that monitor performance, temperature and utilization," cybersecurity expert Nick Paulukow said. "It's connected to the internet to allow controllers to kind of monitor these systems."
Video below: Massachusetts water systems monitored as cyberattacks target other states
Paulukow said this type of hack could also happen in American supermarkets and even to modern appliances in homes that are connected to the internet.
"When we access the internet and put something on the internet, such as a TV or another device, we really have invited someone in and opened the door to allowing them to be part of our household," he said.

title: A message for young Mainers: Think journalism.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Dave Griffiths of Mechanic Falls is a retired journalist who worked for the Kansas City Star, Tulsa World and Lewiston Sun Journal. He also covered national security for Business Week magazine during the Reagan years.
This is an open letter to young folks wondering how to shape their careers and have an interesting life.
Think journalism. Every day, the nonprofit Maine Trust for Local News keeps the profession thriving here despite competition from cable “news” and social media. Reporters and editors strive to give us a balanced picture of life in Maine and beyond. Like “newshounds” all over America, they honor our Founding Fathers’ constitutional guarantee of a free press, even though broadsheets 250 years ago were fiercely partisan, focused more on scandal than substance.
It’s simple. Without independent voices, our democracy would wither and die. For the sake of argument, let’s say a power-obsessed, dishonest, corrupt political leader rails against “fake news” and calls the press the “enemy of the people.” You could make the case that by discouraging public confidence in the press, he wants to be a de facto dictator.
To a much lesser degree every presidential administration has dealt with reporters questioning the self-serving statements issuing from every White House. And Graham Platner would still be in the Senate race if not for aggressive reporting by, among others, the New York Times. Democracy is messy.
So what’s in it for young Mainers surveying the job landscape?
For one thing, your work day may range from quiet time devoted to “deathless prose” (a tongue-in-cheek remark I’ve heard in many a newsroom) to an often turbulent, always unpredictable life as you take on crime, drug busts, politics, odd “man bites dog” features, petty squabbles among elected officials, lost pets, acts of everyday courage, government overreach and the sparks that fly in our diverse culture.
Afterward, you’ll be jabbering in groups of two or three or more about a particularly memorable “news day,” perhaps in a watering hole just around the corner from the newsroom. In a good news town — and they’re all good news towns — you’ll never run out of ideas.
Many stories will stay with you years later. The point is: You’re involved in your job, not just putting in another eight hours. Count on it. I’ve worked at six newspapers, magazines and newsletters, and not once do I regret moving on. The next job — learning new turf and a new beat — keeps the juices flowing.
What about the writing itself? It’s not always easy, especially up against deadlines. But with the help of seasoned editors, you’ll develop a style that your peers recognize, and you’ll smile inwardly at just the right sentence and that jewel of a word or phrase that says it all. The English language is a vast treasure house of symbols at your command, but only if, according to Stephen King, you “write a lot and read a lot.” Meanwhile, you’ll come to value the connection between brevity and clarity — key to the quick read that makes writing “sing”(another newsroom buzzword).
But what if the weird hours and pressure to get your facts right on a strict time limit don’t suit you? After all, working into the evening may not lend itself to helping raise kids. So a reporter’s ease at the keyboard could lead to better-paying PR jobs for government agencies, the private sector or nonprofits. I’ve taught business writing courses for some 20 government clients all over the U.S. and in the Middle East, Europe and Asia. It was a challenge. I’m afraid people just don’t read much these days. The emails I saw early in those classes made me wonder why people don’t pick up the phone instead or walk down the hall to deliver a message or ask a question.
A life well lived is full of characters, including the scribblers you work with and the people you meet. I interviewed a federal prisoner in Denver who kidnapped women and kept them in coffins, and several drill instructors at the Marine boot camp in San Diego where a recruit had died during over-the-top training. I also interviewed two defense secretaries who were less forthcoming than a Trappist monk.
So you get to tell stories, holding up a mirror that helps explain us to ourselves. How cool is that?

title: Norway backs mobile home lot rent stabilization ordinance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Norway residents at a special town meeting Oct. 15 backed a new mobile home park lot rent stabilization ordinance in about five minutes, limiting how corporations can raise rents.
It took moderator Terry Hayes longer to explain the process for voting than it did for residents to move the main article and overwhelmingly pass it.
The ordinance went into effect immediately.
The Norway Mobile Home Lot Rent Stabilization Ordinance states that a mobile home park owner may not increase lot rents and fees more than once during a 12-month period. It limits increases to the Consumer Price Index, plus 1%, and cannot exceed 5% calculated against each resident’s existing rent or fee.
Sun Communities, a Michigan-based real estate investment trust corporation owning more than 500 manufactured home and RV parks, purchased the 55-plus mobile home park Norway Commons four years ago. Since then it has raised rents on tenants and new homes.
It announced early this year that it would again increase lot rents starting April 1.
Sun Communities based the hike on a figure it said was the average lot rent for mobile home parks in the area, $741. The average in the Oxford Hills area at the time was 80% less than that.
Exempted from the ordinance are: resident-owned cooperative or membership parks; lots subject to agreements more restrictive than the ordinance; and mobile home parks where all lots are subject to an aggregate lot rent and fee at or below the affordability threshold, defined as 20% of current fair market rent for existing housing in Oxford County, as determined by the Maine State Housing Authority.
Timothy Stevens, a Norway resident who does not reside in a mobile home park, took to the mic first in Oxford Hills Comprehensive High School’s Forum in support of taking local action to protect low-income housing while keeping people’s incomes close to home and out of corporate pockets.
Norway Commons resident Betty Jones was second to speak. “I am 88 years old,” she said, addressing Norway officials. “I live on Social Security and a pension — not a huge pension. If they raise rent the way they want to, I’m out of the park with nowhere to go.
“And I’ll have to leave my home there, because I can’t afford to move it anywhere else.”
Norway is the latest community to address what many say are predatory practices by out-of-state companies that buy mobile home parks and hike lot rents on residents through a loophole in Maine state law.
The law, meant to prevent excessive rent and fee increases, passed in 2025 as LD 1723, created the opposite effect, allowing park owners to raise rents as often as every three months using formulas with vague, inflated data and no geographic basis.
The town previously adopted a moratorium on lot rent increases last March at a special town meeting attended by 160 voters.
The meeting started late due a line of residents waiting to register to vote.

title: Susan Collins’ Portland office receives letter containing ‘unknown substance’
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ office in Portland received a letter containing an “unknown substance” on Friday as the FBI investigates a slew of such incidents reported across the country.
A spokesperson for the Republican confirmed in an email that the letter at the Portland office was intercepted and no injuries were reported. She also said Collins’ Washington, D.C., office received such a letter Thursday.
“Thank you to the Portland police, the Portland fire department, the hazmat team, and the FBI (for) their quick and courageous response,” Katie Brown, Collins’ chief of staff, said in a written statement.
Last month, Collins’ Biddeford office was vandalized by someone who spray-painted a vulgar message on the office’s outer doors.
The FBI has been investigating “a series of suspicious mailings” across the country, including to secretary of state and election offices.
“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the FBI said in a written statement.
A spokesperson for the FBI’s Boston field office said the agency is “not confirming specific instances of letters” when asked about the incident in Portland on Friday.
A spokesperson for the Portland Fire Department did not immediately respond to a request for information on the department’s involvement in the response at Collins’ office. A Portland police spokesperson deferred inquiries on the incident to the FBI.
Collins is currently seeking her sixth term in the U.S. Senate, facing Democrat Troy Jackson.

title: Man who stopped the Oregon school shooter is the father of 2 daughters at the school
text:
Teen shooter who killed 4 at Oregon elementary school was a former student, police say
A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school, then tackled and fought with him — likely saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said Friday.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called the teacher's actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom.
Authorities said John had been a special needs student at the school and had attacked a classroom with special needs students. He fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, Krantz said.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” he said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”
The police chief added that police are also still trying to determine how the shooter obtained the gun.
The attacker’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told reporters outside her apartment near the school that if she could have done something to prevent the shooting, she would have.
“I miss my boy,” Nickerson said, sobbing and crying, according to The New York Times and CNN. “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
She declined to say how the 16-year-old obtained the pump-action shotgun and didn’t comment further when The Associated Press and other outlets knocked on her apartment door later.
In a 2020 interview with the local news station KTVZ, Nickerson identified the boy, then 10, as a participant in a special needs program run by the school district. It was called NEST, for Nurturing Empathy, Safety and Trust, and aimed at helping students experiencing intensive behavioral and social skill challenges. Nickerson said he struggled trying to learn from home during the pandemic.
Man who stopped the shooter a father of 2 at the school
In a statement read to reporters Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, shot the gunman in Thursday’s attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend. She said he is the father of two girls at the school.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said, noting that her son is a lifelong resident of Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon.
She said her family was asking for privacy “during this difficult time.”
The youngest victim, just 5 years old, was a fast runner and fearless climber who loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said Friday.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said his aunt, Swan Sheridan, who described him as “a little ball of energy from the moment he was born.”
Trump says the shooting could have been much worse
President Donald Trump on Friday praised the actions of a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy likely would have been much worse.
At a news conference hours after Thursday’s attack, Gov. Tina Kotek — without naming Giamanco — said he had followed the gunman into the school and helped end the rampage as police began arriving.
“Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” said Kotek.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that someone pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening," Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. "I’m feeling very grateful.”
The shooter was found dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Krantz said. He shot through locked doors to get inside, police said.
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said Thursday.
The wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun bought by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
Police respond within minutes
The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for schools across Bend, a tourism and outdoor recreation hub that has ballooned in population and sits about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland.

title: Police officer crashes patrol car into school bus stopped picking up children; 4 sent to hospital
text:
OCALA, Fla. (WCJB/Gray News) - A police officer in Florida has been sent to the hospital after crashing his patrol car into a Marion County school bus Friday morning.
According to the Florida Highway Patrol, troopers responded to a reported crash on Southwest 49th Avenue involving a Gainesville police officer in a marked patrol car that collided with the school bus.
Troopers investigating the crash say the bus was stopped in the southbound lane with lights flashing and the stop sign extended as it prepared to pick up children at a bus stop.
The off-duty officer driving behind the bus failed to stop and crashed into the back of it, authorities said.
Thirteen children were on the bus, and one student was taken to the hospital as a precaution. The bus driver and the bus aide were also taken to the hospital as a precaution.
The Gainesville police officer was taken to the hospital, and troopers say his injuries were “very serious,” but not life-threatening.

title: Who was the protester who interrupted the Susan Collins-Troy Jackson debate?
text:
A Bowdoin College student was removed from Thursday’s U.S. Senate debate after he stood and began yelling that data centers “are poisoning our waters.”
The moment came about 15 minutes into the fourth and final televised debate between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democrat Troy Jackson. It led to Collins quipping that it “was obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” to which Jackson replied, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” Thursday’s debate was the only one of the four to feature a live audience.
Henry Elgie, 19, was the protester whom security removed from the Gracie Theatre at Husson University in Bangor, according to a news release from the Sunrise Movement, a national progressive group focused on young people who are “fighting to stop the climate crisis and win a Green New Deal.”
“I’m so sorry to interrupt, but I’m a young person and I’m terrified. AI data centers are destroying our climate,” Elgie, who appeared to be wearing a press badge, shouted as security moved to take him out of the venue. “They are poisoning our waters. You are taking corporate PAC money to an absurd degree.”
Event organizers said the person was not on the pre-registered media list but presented a Bowdoin Orient press badge and was allowed in. In a statement Thursday night, the editor-in-chief of the Orient said the student paper did not send anyone to the debate and that the credential must have been fabricated.
A Sunrise Movement spokesperson said Friday that Elgie lives and is registered to vote in Brunswick, where Bowdoin is located.
The Sunrise Movement news release that came out late Thursday night made clear that Elgie was directing his words at Collins. It included a statement from Elgie that criticized Collins and her campaign for receiving donations from billionaires and executives of artificial intelligence platforms.
“Instead of investing in real climate solutions, Susan Collins continues to prioritize endless war and tax cuts for billionaires. My generation deserves a livable future,” Elgie said in a statement.
Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen responded Friday by sharing a photo the campaign took of pro-Jackson and pro-Collins supporters who were outside of the Oct. 8 debate hosted by WMTW. A person in the photo was holding a fake check in the amount of $150,000 made out to 1820 PAC, a reference to the ProPublica story on pay-to-play allegations surrounding Collins.
The Collins campaign said the person holding the check last week was Elgie.
The Jackson campaign did not respond to a request for comment Friday morning.
Jackson supported the proposed moratorium on large data centers in Maine that Gov. Janet Mills, an outgoing Democrat, vetoed earlier this year. Mills cited concerns that the proposed pause on new centers until November 2027 would have killed a project in the mill town of Jay. (That project went on hold this summer, despite the veto.)
Collins aligned herself with Mills earlier this year, expressing support in August for projects at former mill sites and saying “there is usually hydropower right there, so there’s an energy source built in.” But Collins has also called for federal guardrails on data center development, including regulations on how much water and energy they use.
President Donald Trump has called for more data center development, despite public polling in Maine and nationally showing a majority of Americans from both parties oppose data centers getting built in their communities.
