title: Maine’s fire and EMS services are in increasingly dire straits, researchers find
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA — When John Smith decided to shut down the local fire department in Burlington six years ago, he didn’t feel like he had much choice. His kids, who had volunteered there, moved away, and so did another multi-generation firefighting family in town.
That left Smith, who was in his mid-60s, and just one other volunteer.
“I was really afraid for myself and for him, and the fact that people thought they were getting something that they weren’t,” Smith said in an interview this month. “We were not a good service at that point.”
Fire departments across Maine have felt the same sorts of pressures for decades but haven’t known just how bad the problem was or how to express it, said state Fire Marshal Shawn Esler. On Friday, his office and the University of Maine released findings of a two-year study that shows fire and EMS services across the state are in increasingly dire straits.
“They finally documented the freight train that we’ve seen coming for the last 20 years,” said Roger Hooper, chief of the York County Fire Academy and director of the regional training center.
Esler and the researchers say 94% of fire departments that responded to the survey rely on volunteerism to some extent, yet fewer people are available and a significant portion of those who remain are aging and can no longer do all aspects of the work. Forty-seven percent of fire departments that responded to the survey said they were too short-staffed to respond to at least one call in the last three years.
The survey also found big gaps in training, and at the same time, a huge increase in calls to fire and EMS departments. Fire service leaders said gone are the days when a boot drive could generate sufficient funds for departments to be able to provide what their communities expect.
Discussing the study’s findings at the Maine Municipal Association conference in Augusta earlier this month, Esler said: “I think the general public has an expectation that when they dial 911 they’re going to receive a response.”
Augusta Fire Chief David Groder finished Elser’s thought. “You just go up the road 15 miles,” he said, “and there’s a town that may not respond because nobody’s in town that day.”
Maine cities that employ career firefighters are hurting, too, Esler said, because they have long hired people who already have experience as volunteers. He said urban departments have fewer applicants and have to seek mutual aid from smaller cities and towns more often.
Overall calls to fire departments were up 78% from 2014 to 2024, according to the study’s findings, and some departments reported even higher increases, in part because they are filling gaps in healthcare access. Fire departments have become “the backbone of the community,” said research associate Alexander Rezk.
“Without reform, if things continue as they are, we’ll be coming to a point of dysfunction,” he said. Rezk‘s team at UMaine’s Margaret Chase Smith Policy Center surveyed 219 fire departments, along with code enforcement officers and municipal administrators, and interviewed 25 fire chiefs to better understand the challenges and their effects on local communities.
Fire departments have historically received far less public funding than police, Rezk said, and the research findings should challenge Mainers to consider whether that’s still appropriate. While some fire departments have added incentives to recruit and retain volunteers, he said, more will be needed in the future.
Providing fire and EMS services will inevitably get more expensive for Mainers, according to interviews with several people involved in firefighting around the state. They say volunteerism will still be a crucial part of the service, but it is already becoming more regionalized and requires more paid members.
Esler and others pointed to what has happened in Burlington. After Smith was forced to shut down the department, he helped partner with neighboring towns to create the Central Maine Highlands fire district in 2024, the first of its kind in the state. It has a roster of paid firefighters and paramedics.
“I think we’re at a turning point in the fire service,” Esler said. It’s up to state legislators, local governments and residents to make changes and provide funds, he said, “before it continues in decay.”
TRAINING GAP
Just about half of the people on department rosters are trained to fight indoor fires in Oxford, Franklin, Hancock and Waldo counties, according to the survey. It’s not much higher in Washington, Knox and Sagadahoc counties. Training sites can be hours away from a fire department, particularly Down East, along the Midcoast and along the state’s western border.
“It’s not uncommon for a department to be able to respond to a call but lack the number of certified firefighters to do anything,” Rezk said. “Imagine, they scramble to a call but they stand around outside.”
There are more types of industrial and energy infrastructure hazards, like factories, mills, landfills, solar farms, natural gas pipelines, battery storage facilities and data centers, that require more specialized training, said Groder, the chief in Augusta.
“We’re asking our firefighters to understand it, know it, and don’t make mistakes. That’s a big responsibility,” he said.
What happened in Searsmont in May, when a sealed silo at Robbins Lumber exploded, is an apt example, he acknowledged. Firefighters from dozens of departments arrived with no way of knowing the specific hazard the silo presented or what kind of response it required, an assessment by the National Institute for Occupational Health and Safety later found. It said water poured on the initial silo fire likely contributed to the explosion. Three people, including two firefighters, died from their injuries.
As new hazards come into communities, there’s no funding to train firefighters on how to deal with them, Esler said.
“Fires are growing exponentially faster than they did in the past, and burning hotter, and they’re way more toxic than they were in the past,” said Todd Zsiga, the fire chief in Kennebunkport.
The challenges he and others face — to find new people who can stick with training — reflect the ways Maine is changing even beyond the fire service. They’re related to the higher costs of nearly everything in the state (including firefighting equipment); the demographics of aging; and cultural shifts toward online life and away from community volunteerism.
GENERATIONAL CHANGE
Jennifer LaHaye started with the Southwest Harbor Fire Department when she was 18, more than 20 years ago. She said despite the department leadership’s best efforts, “There’ll be times when we have an alarm and one person is going in the middle of the night.” recommends 15 people respond to a house fire.
High housing costs are part of the reason
Rezk, the university researcher, said people are having to work more hours and more jobs to afford to live in many places in Maine and that affects their ability to volunteer.
Three quarters of departments that rely solely on volunteers without compensation that responded to the University of Maine survey said they’re understaffed on weekdays. The number is nearly as high — 67% — for departments that pay their volunteers for calls.
Southwest Harbor adapted by establishing two career positions to provide basic staffing on weekdays. Even the volunteers now get paid during their shifts, LaHaye said. The per diem payments are meant to make it more worthwhile to run into a burning building, she said.
“It’s kind of crazy to think that we expected that they do that and not get compensated for so many years.”
As it is at so many other departments, LaHaye said, there aren’t a lot of young people hanging around the fire station as when she was a teenager. The survey found that at least three of every 10 firefighters in Maine are over 50 years old. Esler said it’s increasingly unlikely those men and women will be able to fight fires inside buildings.
Esler has seen the generational change in his own family. When he joined his community’s fire department, “that’s what every young man in the town of Albion did,” he said.
It was expected that volunteer firefighters would devote their free time to the service and pay their own way for training, Esler said.
“The culture has been prideful,” he said. “It’s been, ‘I’m going to take care of my own fires and my own community.’”
These days, he said, “Our younger generation doesn’t have that same expectation.” He understands why his son, who he said already works 60 hours a week, doesn’t plan to join the fire service.
A REGIONAL APPROACH
In Burlington, Smith said he’d watched volunteerism and participation drop at events and organizations across town — at the historical society, the Independence Day parade, the snowmobile club and the local Veterans of Foreign Wars post.
“We all communicate on Facebook but never look each other in the eye,” he said. “There’s not the community spirit that there was.”
Smith said that with declining help at the fire department,
Smith helped steer Burlington toward the regionalized district and he serves on its board of directors. The costs are distributed among the participating towns. As a taxpayer, Smith was charged $268 this year for fire and EMS.
“The quality of service and abilities these men and women have is like night and day from a small volunteer fire department,” he said. He and the other volunteers “did the best we could with what we had,” he said, but the paid full-timers get the experience of answering many more calls and have access to better equipment.
“They might be 10 minutes further away, but when they get here they make such a difference,” Smith said.
Esler said, “Ten years ago, regionalization was a swear word,” but that is changing, and there’s no prescription for exactly what it has to mean.
Smith said some towns will not want to give up part of their identity and local control. “But I think it’s going to have to happen,” he said.
In York County, Hooper directs a new regional training center that opened this year — a county-level investment that Esler said is rare but welcome. Hooper said having even a few staff to handle routine calls can in turn make it easier to recruit volunteers, “because you’re not wasting their time,” he said.
Rome partnered with Belgrade about five years ago to pay for someone who covers calls during the day, fire Chief Gary Foss said. Without that paid position, many more calls would have gone unanswered, he said, though he’s still nervous it won’t be enough.
“I’ve been telling our townspeople we’ll have to consider having someone here five days a week,” he said.
The decline in volunteers, “is going to end up costing our small towns lots of money,” he said. But if communities choose not to fund fire and EMS services, then home insurance costs will rise, he predicted.
Regionalizing won’t save money up front, according to those who have done it or studied the fire service. The University of Maine researchers said it should eventually, though, by creating a centralized capacity to raise funds, no longer duplicating the costs of equipment, and creating the ability to buy it in bulk. Hooper and others said the state could help provide funds or other incentives to get regionalization started.
The researchers also recommend that Maine increase access to firefighting training, and encourage employers to work with fire departments to make volunteers available.
According to the Maine Office of State Fire Marshal, a comprehensive report will be published next year.
Mainers should feel uneasy about the survey’s findings, Rezk said.
“This isn’t going away,” he said.

title: 10 Bad (On Purpose) Movies That Are Actually Great
text:
10 Bad-on-Purpose Movies That Are Actually Great
Good movies are good. Bad movies are bad. We all know this. However, some bad movies are so bad that their sheer badness horseshoes back around to somehow being good. Yes, we’re talking so-bad-they’re-good movies, a subgenre we particularly enjoy celebrating and one that doesn’t seem to be running out of steam anytime soon. For every generation-defining masterpiece, there’s at least one total dud that nonetheless gets popular because of how dumb it is. Bad-good movies are special experiences whose appeal is difficult to describe, but always appreciated.
Most so-bad-they’re-good movies don’t set out to be bad, and are often made with an earnestness that can only come from a group of artists who genuinely believe they’re making something profound. And then there are the bad movies that are bad on purpose, whose creators definitely did not set out to make the next Citizen Kane. A lot of these movies are just annoyingly terrible low-budget slop designed to parody whatever’s popular at the time, but some of them are so charmingly stupid we can’t help but love them.
Some of these bad-on-purpose movies are so much fun they’re genuinely popular, and distributors like the Asylum and Troma Entertainment have become household names simply through releasing terrible films. Whatever the genre and no matter how small the budget, these movies have a few key things in common: The acting is terrible, the effects are terrible, and the plot is so dumb you wonder how a human being could have thought it up.

title: A widow sold her home to care for her husband with Alzheimer’s. She’s not alone.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (InvestigateTV) - Family caregivers are considered the backbone of America’s long-term care system and experts say that backbone is breaking.
About one in four adults in the country provide ongoing care for a loved one, sometimes at the expense of their own well-being.
Caregiving costs can add up fast, forcing caregivers to take on debt and in some cases making it hard to cover basic necessities. This is often driven by fixed budgets, high out of pocket medical costs, and the immense time constraints of caregiving.
When police in Floyd County, Georgia arrived to search for a missing 74-year-old man last year, they found him army crawling through the woods, believing he was back in Vietnam.
Lamar Jones had escaped his memory care facility. His wife, Sue Jones, described the scene.
“They found him belly crawling, just like army crawling through the woods,” Sue Jones said. “He crawled under a log, just like you would if you were in the war and at some point in time, he found a pipe in the woods. He was pretending like it was a gun.”
Lamar Jones’ behavior — a symptom of his Alzheimer’s disease — repeated itself for years. He would wander away from facilities, and staff would call police. The facilities would refuse to take him back.
Then Sue Jones would search for another care home, pay another entry fee, pay monthly bills, and begin the cycle again.
“The part that was not manageable was probably the last three years,” Sue Jones said.
Months after the police incident in the woods, Lamar Jones died peacefully. Sue Jones held onto his memory and the life they built together: 44 years of marriage. He was a father and grandfather.
“Sometimes the grief that I have is because I loved him so much,” Sue Jones said. “That’s the price for paying for love: it’s a very long hard grief.”
An Atlanta News First investigation found memory care facilities in Georgia average $3,849 per month. Georgia State University (GSU) recently conducted the research which shows based on that monthly payment, in one year alone a family would spend more than $46,000 for bed at a specialized memory facility.
According to the GSU study, dementia patients in Georgia spent nearly 83% of their monthly income on long-term care.
To afford her husband’s care, Sue Jones sold everything she owned, including her home. She moved into her daughter’s basement.
“We had dementia,” Sue Jones said when asked about the burden. “My husband did not have dementia; he and I had dementia, because it takes over your life.”
Data from the Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reveals unpaid caregivers across the country like Sue Jones provide the equivalent of nearly $470 billion a year in free care.
But the greatest cost, Sue Jones argued, is isolation. Without enough support groups, she navigated the emotional toll, insurance decisions and facility placements alone.
“I just kept trying to find a solution,” she said. “I just wanted to fix it. I was never able to fix it.”
That isolation is why the Georgia chapter of the Alzheimer’s Association went to the state capitol for advocacy day during the current legislative session. They were urging lawmakers to appropriate an extra $2 million in the state’s dementia support program for respite care, which is short-term relief and services for overwhelmed primary caregivers.
Nancy Pitra, the association’s director of government affairs, said such services are needed “so that caregivers don’t get burnt out or have their own crisis. If you are caring for someone, chances are, you’re not taking care of your own health.”
The $2 million appropriation passed through the Georgia legislature, but was removed from the budget by Governor Brian Kemp.
The Alzheimer’s Association called the veto a “setback” and said: “...we are deeply encouraged by the strong, bipartisan support this initiative received in both the Georgia House and Senate. This widespread legislative alignment highlights a growing, shared recognition of the essential role caregivers play in our communities.”
In the room where Lamar Jones spent his final months, Sue Jones showed a whiteboard where her husband — a man whose memory had largely faded — wrote a message that never wavered: “I love you.”
Sue Jones has since started her own support group in Cobb County for other dementia caregivers.

- Alzheimer’s Foundation of America - helpline: 866-232-8484
- Family Caregiver Alliance
- National Institute on Aging

title: So many scams: Criminals are targeting Mainers with a wide range of schemes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
So many scams: Criminals are targeting Mainers with a wide range of schemes
There are a lot of ways that criminals try to scam people out of money, and the schemes are getting more and more elaborate all the time. There are similarities between many of the tactics, but there are always a lot of scams circulating at the same time.
On Thursday, the Sanford Police Department shared the scams that had been reported just to them by people from Sanford/Springvale in just the month of September, including threats, fake emergencies, and demands for quick payments.
September scams in Sanford/Springvale
- Online dating scam: Someone on Plenty of Fish claimed to have been arrested in Turkey and asked a resident for money and banking information. The resident provided neither, blocked the person, and reported the account.
- Threats to share explicit images: A resident reported being threatened with having explicit images sent to their social media contacts unless they paid. The resident said the pictures were images from Google, not personal photos. No money was sent, and the number was blocked.
- Gift card extortion: A resident reported losing nearly $3,000 in gift cards after scammers accused them of purchasing illegal material and demanded payment. The scam occurred in August and was reported to police in September.
- Identity theft: A resident reported that someone had attempted to obtain a loan in their name in Maryland. The resident had already contacted a credit bureau and came to police for a report requested by their bank.
- Suspicious links and fake technical support: One resident received repeated demands for money after clicking a suspicious link. Another encountered a phone warning with loud sirens and called a displayed number claiming to be Microsoft support. The person answering made claims about hacking and felony charges. The first resident reported no financial loss; the second reported providing no information.
- CMP impersonation: A caller claiming to represent CMP threatened to shut off a resident’s power within an hour unless they paid $2,000 in cash. The resident contacted CMP directly and confirmed the account was in good standing. No money was paid
- Suspected rental scam: A resident searching for an apartment reported concerns about someone offering a rental. The information available did not establish whether the offer was fraudulent.
"Give yourself time to pause, ask questions, and verify who you’re dealing with," police said. "Please look out for one another. If something feels wrong, reach out. There’s no shame in asking for help or reporting what happened—these scams are designed to catch people off guard."
Other scams
A scam that targets people who have submitted building plans to their local planning and zoning boards has been spreading all year with numerous communities reporting incidents and issuing warnings this year.
Over the summer, the Cumberland County Sheriff's Office and several other law enforcement agencies, including the Portland Police Department, received reports of an ongoing jury duty scam.
According to officials, a scammer posing as a lieutenant with the Cumberland County Sheriff's Office is contacting people and telling them that they have either missed jury duty or have been requested to report for jury duty.
The Cumberland County Sheriff's Office said it is not responsible for the selection, scheduling or appearances for those selected for jury duty, nor are other law enforcement agencies.
8 Investigates reported earlier this year that older Mainers are less likely than younger people to fall victim to scams, but when they do, the financial losses are often much greater.
According to the FBI, 608 Mainers age 60 and older reported losing money to scams in 2024. Together, they lost $12,980,616 — and officials say the true number is likely higher because many cases go unreported.
American consumers lost a total of $2.1 billion to scams on social media last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission’s latest Consumer Sentinel Network report.
That’s eight times more than what consumers lost in 2020. Social media is becoming a preferred contact method for scammers, according to the FTC. Nearly 30% of individuals who reported losing money to scams said it began on social media.
How to stay safe
What the FTC recommends:
- Limit who can see your posts and contacts on social media.
- Never let someone you meet on social media guide your investment decisions, and learn how to spot investment scams.
- Before buying an item from an ad, check whether the company is actually offering that deal and whether anyone has filed a complaint about the deal being a scam.
Learn more about how to spot, avoid, and report scams by visiting ftc.gov/scams.

title: 'I'm not a chicken': Senior citizens bare nearly all for charity calendar
text:
'I'm not a chicken': Senior citizens bare nearly all for charity calendar
A group of Michigan men is proving that age is no barrier to having fun for a good cause.
The Monroe Center for Healthy Aging has unveiled its 2027 fundraiser calendar, titled "Naturally, The Other Half," featuring male volunteers who posed in playful, tasteful photographs to help raise money for the center.
The project follows last year's successful calendar featuring women from the center, which was inspired by the movie "Calendar Girls."
According to center Director Sandie Pierce, the men wanted their turn after seeing the enthusiasm surrounding the original effort.
The calendar features local men ranging in age and background, including 91-year-old Danny Richardville, who said the experience gave participants something new and exciting to focus on.
"Nothing new happens to me," Richardville said. "So she gives us something to think about besides growing old."
Some participants admitted they needed time to decide whether they would take part. Others jumped at the opportunity.
For Antonio Terry, the center's cook and one of the youngest participants at age 40, the photo shoot was easy.
"I'm not camera shy or anything," Terry said.
Most of the men kept their boxer shorts on during the shoot, using props and creative photography to preserve modesty while embracing the fundraiser's lighthearted spirit.
The women featured in the previous calendar jokingly suggested the men were not quite as daring as they had been.
"I think they weren't brave enough," Pierce said.
The photographs were taken by Amy Fuller, whose creative approach helped participants feel comfortable throughout the process.
Organizers hope to match last year's success, when sales of 250 calendars generated about $3,000 for the Monroe Center for Healthy Aging. Proceeds help cover daily operating expenses and programs at the center.
The center is also hosting a calendar-signing event to help promote sales and celebrate the volunteers who participated.
"I’m not a chicken," Richardville joked.

title: Boothbay has plans for a dog park
text:
There may be a new dog park coming to a location near you. On Oct. 14, Boothbay Town Manager Dan Bryer announced negotiations with Boothbay Region Land Trust had begun for a dog park. The proposed location is at Cross River Preserve. "It came together pretty quickly and we are really excited about this," Bryer said during the selectboard meeting.
The proposed location would be penned in and not require any tree removal, said Bryer. The proximity of seasonal water was also a factor in selecting the location.
Bryer reported there are no confirmed details about the project such as when it would open and how large it would be. "Those are all part of the negotiations. Legal liability is being worked out. What happens if it doesn't work out? Is this a lease or would the town own the land? These are the questions being discussed," Bryer said.
In other action, selectmen renewed a self-sponsored events liquor license for Boothbay Playhouse Events, LLC. Selectmen also adopted the new Maine Municipal Association general assistance ordinance and appendices for Oct. 1, 2026 to Sept. 30, 2027.
In his report, Bryer told selectmen that absentee voting was happening at a high rate. "Ballots are flying right out of here," he said. Bryer added, early voting was so prevalent that "lines may not be that long on Election Day."
Selectmen tabled a proposed Interlocal Agreement with Boothbay Region Ambulance Service.
Selectmen meet next at 6 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 28 in the conference room.

title: Who was the protester who interrupted the Susan Collins-Troy Jackson debate?
text:
A Bowdoin College student was removed from Thursday’s U.S. Senate debate after he stood and began yelling that data centers “are poisoning our waters.”
The moment came about 15 minutes into the fourth and final televised debate between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democrat Troy Jackson. It led to Collins quipping that it “was obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” to which Jackson replied, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” Thursday’s debate was the only one of the four to feature a live audience.
Henry Elgie, 19, was the protester whom security removed from the Gracie Theatre at Husson University in Bangor, according to a news release from the Sunrise Movement, a national progressive group focused on young people who are “fighting to stop the climate crisis and win a Green New Deal.”
“I’m so sorry to interrupt, but I’m a young person and I’m terrified. AI data centers are destroying our climate,” Elgie, who appeared to be wearing a press badge, shouted as security moved to take him out of the venue. “They are poisoning our waters. You are taking corporate PAC money to an absurd degree.”
Event organizers said the person was not on the pre-registered media list but presented a Bowdoin Orient press badge and was allowed in. In a statement Thursday night, the editor-in-chief of the Orient said the student paper did not send anyone to the debate and that the credential must have been fabricated.
A Sunrise Movement spokesperson said Friday that Elgie lives and is registered to vote in Brunswick, where Bowdoin is located.
The Sunrise Movement news release that came out late Thursday night made clear that Elgie was directing his words at Collins. It included a statement from Elgie that criticized Collins and her campaign for receiving donations from billionaires and executives of artificial intelligence platforms.
“Instead of investing in real climate solutions, Susan Collins continues to prioritize endless war and tax cuts for billionaires. My generation deserves a livable future,” Elgie said in a statement.
Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen responded Friday by sharing a photo the campaign took of pro-Jackson and pro-Collins supporters who were outside of the Oct. 8 debate hosted by WMTW. A person in the photo was holding a fake check in the amount of $150,000 made out to 1820 PAC, a reference to the ProPublica story on pay-to-play allegations surrounding Collins.
The Collins campaign said the person holding the check last week was Elgie.
The Jackson campaign did not respond to a request for comment Friday morning.
Jackson supported the proposed moratorium on large data centers in Maine that Gov. Janet Mills, an outgoing Democrat, vetoed earlier this year. Mills cited concerns that the proposed pause on new centers until November 2027 would have killed a project in the mill town of Jay. (That project went on hold this summer, despite the veto.)
Collins aligned herself with Mills earlier this year, expressing support in August for projects at former mill sites and saying “there is usually hydropower right there, so there’s an energy source built in.” But Collins has also called for federal guardrails on data center development, including regulations on how much water and energy they use.
President Donald Trump has called for more data center development, despite public polling in Maine and nationally showing a majority of Americans from both parties oppose data centers getting built in their communities.

title: Spruce Mountain classrooms face recurring technology failures
text:
JAY — Teachers in Regional School Unit 73 are complaining that consistent failures with the interactive classroom displays purchased with pandemic-era grant funding are creating challenges for daily instruction.
Chris Hollingsworth, the district’s curriculum and technology coordinator, told the board of directors Oct. 8 that Promethean interactive displays have experienced recurring problems, particularly with internal power boards that prevent the equipment from turning on.
“That’s the one thing they say they can’t do without, but yet they’re the ones that keep breaking,” Hollingsworth said, referring to teachers’ reliance on the displays.
The boards were purchased with grant funding during the COVID-19 pandemic. Hollingsworth suggested that manufacturing conditions during that period may have contributed to the reliability problems.
He said similar failures occurred last school year, when the manufacturer provided repairs at relatively low cost. However, obtaining repair estimates and scheduling technicians has taken considerable time.
“Every year we come back and all of a sudden teachers go to use their Promethean board and it doesn’t turn on,” Hollingsworth said.
He explained that the problem involves an internal computer power board rather than a conventional power supply, complicating repairs.
While the district waits for service, Hollingsworth said he is working with school principals and technology staff to identify alternative equipment and instructional options for affected teachers.
The district has not provided figures on the number of displays affected or the total cost of repairs and could not be reached for further comment.

title: Honor Flight Maine departs on its last trip to Washington this year
Franklin Towers residents forced to move after renovations reveal hazardous chemicals
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Residents of the first few floors of Portland’s beleaguered high rise, Franklin Towers, were preparing to move. They wouldn’t be going far, just to the top of the 16-story building on Cumberland Avenue.
The building, run by the Portland Housing Authority, is poised for a sorely needed multimillion dollar overhaul and upgrade, and as part of the process, residents were told they would be shuffled around while work was done in chunks.
At least one resident said on social media that he had already received the keys to his new unit and had begun moving his belongings to the top floor.
But then, crews found toxic chemicals in the building, the soil and the air, and the roughly 150 low-income residents, many of whom are older or have disabilities, were told this month that they couldn’t stay in the building.
They don’t know where they’ll go next.
“We have to find another place to live, that’s all there is to it,” said David Caston Sr., who has lived in the building for 17 years. “I’m not happy about it all, but there’s nothing I can do about it.”
Caston said in a phone interview that he didn’t know when he’ll have to move or where he’ll end up but added that the Portland Housing Authority told residents in a meeting Thursday that they would not have to foot the bill.
AN EMPTY BUILDING
In a letter dated Oct. 6., the housing authority told residents that testing in some parts of the building revealed polychlorinated biphenyls — toxic chemicals that were once used in building materials and are common in older buildings like Franklin Towers.
The housing authority said it plans to address the areas identified and do follow-up testing after the work is done.
“To do this work safely and efficiently, it will be best to have the building unoccupied, as this is a large and significant renovation,” the agency said. “We understand that Franklin Towers is your home, and we recognize how difficult a temporary move can be. We are working to minimize the impact on residents to the extent possible.”
The process to find homes for all the residents could take up to six months, according to Jay Waterman, the housing authority’s director of real estate development.
“It all depends on finding the right temporary homes to accommodate all our Franklin Towers residents and their diverse needs,” he said in an email, adding that the agency is committed to ensuring no one is displaced without a personalized housing plan.
Portland Housing Authority is working with other local affordable housing organizations to find temporary homes for tower residents.
Residents will keep their housing subsidy and continue to pay just 30% of their income on rent, no matter where they end up, Waterman said. All residents will have their moving costs covered by the housing authority and will have the right to return to the building once the work is done.
PLAGUED BY PROBLEMS
The discovery of toxic chemicals is the latest in a litany of problems that have plagued the 57-year-old building in recent years.
Residents have, among other issues, dealt with bug infestations, plumbing issues and a weekslong electrical outage in 2022.
The housing authority is undertaking a large-scale redevelopment that is expected to cost about $50 million, Waterman said.
The 200-unit building is home to about 150 low-income older adults and people with disabilities. In preparation for the renovation, the housing authority has not been leasing newly vacant units as residents have left.
In public housing, tenants pay 30% of their income toward rent. At the time, the current average monthly rent payment was about $385. Waterman said he did not have an updated estimate.
In 2024, the complex was added to the National Register of Historic Places, which gave the housing authority access to tax credits that could shave off up to $14 million from the cost of renovations.
At the time, then-executive director Brian Frost said that money would make all the difference — Portland Housing Authority has barely been able to keep the building’s major systems running, let alone the “deep renovations” the building needs.
Renovations are expected to improve the tower’s energy efficiency with new windows, upgraded ventilation and heating, and an overall facelift that officials said should make residents more comfortable.
Construction is running at least a year behind schedule, with original plans eyeing a 2025 start and completion sometime next year.
Franklin Towers was built in 1969 as a joint venture between the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Portland Housing Authority. It was the first and largest local example of a federal subsidy for low-income senior housing, according to the national register.

title: College football player dies days after suffering injury during game
text:
(Gray News) – A college football player from Southern Nazarene University in Oklahoma died five days after sustaining a traumatic injury during a game against Ouachita Baptist Saturday.
The university announced the death of sophomore safety Tyler Ulrich on Instagram Thursday but did not go into detail about his injury.
He was 21.
SNU President Dr. Keith Newman said Ulrich was surrounded by the “love, prayers and presence of his family, teammates and dear friends” when he died.
“This loss is deeply felt across our campus. Our hearts are with his family, friends, teammates, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing him. We ask that you join us in lifting them up in prayer during this incredibly difficult time,” the university wrote in its post on Instagram.
“Man of God, ultimate example of quiet strength, loyal, worker, joyous. That’s who Tyler was,” coach Dustin Hada said about Ulrich in a post on X.
SNU held a campuswide prayer in honor of Ulrich Tuesday and has grief counseling support available to anyone in need.
Ulrich was in his third season with the SNU football team and had 16 starts in 20 games.
The team has canceled its game Saturday against Southwestern Oklahoma State University.

title: Billy Joel says he can no longer perform or drive due to health condition
text:
(Gray News) — Billy Joel said his health is keeping him from being able to perform or drive, he revealed in a new interview with The Hollywood Reporter.
Joel, 77, said he has a condition called hydrocephalus that has affected his balance.
He wants nothing more than to get back onstage, but he said he must take a series of tests before he knows if he can.
“I can’t do performances because what the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion,” Joel told The Hollywood Reporter.
He said the extremely loud volume, lighting, stress and energy it takes to perform are all concerns and stressors on his health.
Joel also said he is not allowed to drive.
Joel said hydrocephalus affects his balance, memory, vision and hearing.
“But I’m OK. They call it a brain disorder, but it’s not that serious. It’s just something that affects your balance mostly,” he said.
According to The Mayo Clinic, hydrocephalus is the buildup of cerebrospinal fluid in spaces called ventricles deep within the brain. This buildup can make the ventricles larger and put pressure on the brain.
Symptoms can vary by age group. Among adults 60 and older, common symptoms of hydrocephalus include memory loss, trouble walking, poor coordination or balance and progressive loss of other reasoning skills.

title: Brewers sweep Dodgers in NLCS to reach World Series for first time since 1982
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — After 44 years, the Milwaukee Brewers are finally going back to the World Series.
Propelled by a lockdown bullpen and repeated comebacks, the young and fearless Brewers swept the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers out of the playoffs Thursday with a 6-4 victory in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series.
“We weren’t coming in to play patty-cake,” manager Pat Murphy said. “We were hungry, and as long as it’s an even playing field, we’re going to come in and give it our best shot to win. That’s exactly what we did.”
Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning and Milwaukee’s brilliant relievers slammed the door late, giving a vocal contingent of Brewers fans their chance to celebrate in the Dodger Stadium stands.
Now, the Brewers get an opportunity to win their first title after topping the majors with 103 wins during the regular season. Milwaukee has a week off before hosting Cleveland or Tampa Bay in the World Series opener on Oct. 23.
“I’m excited that we’ve got a few more games to play and get to go home with the fans and celebrate there, too,” Mitchell said.
Shohei Ohtani’s first home run this postseason helped put the Dodgers ahead 4-0 in the second inning before the Brewers came back to complete a four-game sweep.
No. 9 hitter David Hamilton’s two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave Milwaukee a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.
“We got down early tonight and we were like, it’s going to be a great story,” Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. “We’re going to come back and win this. Like, stay together, start chipping away. And that’s exactly what they did.”
Aaron Ashby pitched three scoreless innings for a save as the Brewers won their first NL pennant and second overall. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise made its only previous World Series appearance in 1982, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.
The Dodgers’ goal of a three-peat — not done since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 and never by a National League team — died with their anemic offense and injuries to Ohtani and others on their aging roster.
“I’m not used to those consolation speeches,” manager Dave Roberts said. “Those guys played flawless. You’ve got to sometimes tip your cap.”
Milwaukee became the first major league club to finish a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason. Los Angeles took all four NLCS games against the Brewers last year.
“They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers — and the gamers won this week,” Murphy said.
“I think the Dodgers figured out that we came in here with a little different attitude this year.”
The Brewers also are the first team to sweep a best-of-seven postseason series in which it trailed in every game.
“There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen tonight. We knew we were going to win that game,” said first baseman Jake Bauers, the NLCS MVP.
With the score tied 4-all, Mitchell fell behind 0-2 against reliever Tanner Scott leading off the sixth before taking three straight balls to run the count full. Mitchell then launched a 409-foot drive to center field that put the Brewers ahead for the first time. He also homered in their 6-2 victory Wednesday.
“It’s absolutely surreal,” Mitchell said. ”You talk about the battle-tested Brewers. We went down early and the belief in that dugout got stronger and stronger.”
Milwaukee’s bullpen coolly turned away multiple threats when the Dodgers had the potential tying run on base.
Winning pitcher JoJo Romero struck out Max Muncy with Kyle Tucker at third to end the sixth.
With one out in the seventh and a runner on third, Ashby struck out Ohtani swinging before Mookie Betts grounded out to end the inning.
Will Smith doubled to right with one out in the eighth and reached third on Sal Frelick’s fielding error, but Ashby retired Tucker on a shallow flyball and struck out Teoscar Hernández.
“Playing with that chip on our shoulder,” Ashby said. “You don’t ever know what to expect going into a series like that last year (against the Dodgers). You don’t know how bad it can be, and then it was as bad as it was. And we came out and we survived, and we came back this year, and those guys played their tails off.”
The Brewers tied it in the fifth, when the Dodgers bullpen issued four walks and Milwaukee stole two bases. Hamilton’s single chased starter Tyler Glasnow and scored Frelick, who walked and stole second, to pull Milwaukee to 4-3.
Evan Phillips walked two batters with two outs, one intentionally, before Alex Vesia entered and walked Bauers to force in Hamilton with the tying run.
Glasnow retired his first 10 batters — six on strikeouts — before the Brewers got to him in the fourth. Brice Turang walked, William Contreras hit a ground-rule double and Bauers followed with another ground-rule double that closed Milwaukee to 4-2.
Ohtani broke out of his postseason slump with a three-run homer after Andy Pages’ RBI single in the second. The four-time MVP released weeks of pent-up frustration by raising his arms and yelling as the crowd of 49,104 roared.
But the Brewers wouldn’t be denied. And when it was over, owner Mark Attanasio thought of Milwaukee’s longtime owner and beloved late broadcaster.
“It’s so important for the community, the entire state of Wisconsin,” Attanasio said. “We’re standing on shoulders of Bud Selig and Bob Uecker.”
___
A previous version of this story was corrected to fix the sequence of Dodgers pitchers and Brewers walks in the top of the fifth inning.

title: Bangor man arrested for allegedly threatening woman with knife, police say
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor man was taken into custody after police say he threatened a woman with a knife and said he would kill any law enforcement that intervened.

title: Bangor and Edward Little football square off with playoff berth at stake
text:
Friday night’s high school football game between Bangor and visiting Edward Little of Auburn at Cameron Stadium is much more than a regular season affair.
It has serious post-season implications because the teams are tied for the fourth and final playoff berth in Class A North.
The winner is all but assured a playoff spot, although Bangor still has a point-worthy game remaining with Class A North leader Oxford Hills/Buckfield in the regular season finale.
Bangor and Edward Little are both 2-3 heading into Friday night’s 7:00 p.m. kickoff and each will have two games remaining after Friday. Bangor will travel to play Class A South team Sanford, currently 1-5, before hosting 4-1 Oxford Hills/Buckfield while Edward Little will host 2-4 Class B North team Mt. Blue of Farmington and 0-5 Lewiston.
Bangor is coming off a 28-21 road loss to 5-1 Portland, a game decided by a late touchdown run by Alex Martin. Portland is the defending two-time Class A North champ.
Bangor’s three losses have all come by one score or less.
“I was definitely proud of how the kids played,” said Bangor first-year head coach Jack Hersom. “It’s never okay to lose but we showed ourselves we can play with one of the top teams in the north.”
He compared Edward Little to season-opening opponent Massabesic of Waterboro, which beat the Rams 22-18.
“Edward Little will try to control the ball and control the clock to limit our possessions,” Hersom said. “They’re going to want to keep the ball on the ground. We know how important it will be for us to get some early stops and get them in situations where they aren’t comfortable.”
The Rams are led by the combination of quarterback Alex Tennett and dynamic receiver-running back Gavin Hughes, both juniors.
Tennett threw for 336 yards and three touchdowns and Hughes caught all three TD passes, including a 73-yarder. Hughes accounted for more than 200 of Tennett’s passing yards, Hersom said.
It is the second time in three games Tennett has thrown for more than 300 yards, according to Hersom. He also threw for 300-plus yards in a 32-13 victory over Deering of Portland.
Defensive back Hughes and linebacker Will Houghton each had 10-plus tackles against Portland. Hersom said he also received impressive performances from defensive ends Lucian Matzilevich and Owen Glanville-True.
Glanville-True is doubtful for the Edward Little game due to an injury, according to Hersom.
Sophomore Logan Stout had a four-touchdown game in a double-overtime win over Scarborough earlier this season as he rushed for three TDs and threw for another.
“He’s shifty when he has the ball in space. We’re going to have to bracket him and get 11 guys to the football,” Hersom said.
Defensive end Kohlson Alexander and linemen Joe Barriault and Elijah Odunlami are among other solid performers for the Eddies, who are coming off a 34-9 loss to Windham.
In other interesting matchups, the 6-0 Hermon Hawks will travel to take on defending state C champ 5-1 Greely High of Cumberland Center, 5-1, on Friday night at 7 p.m. in an important statewide Class C matchup.
The Hawks, led by slot back Sam Hopkins and quarterback Ethan Curtis, have outscored their opponents by an average of just over 40 points per game.
Greely has won all of its games by at least 20 points and its only loss has come to Leavitt of Turner. Leavitt lost to Greely in the state title game a year ago.
Among other 7 p.m. games on Friday, defending state Eight-Player Small champ Stearns/Schenck, 6-0, entertains 4-2 Ellsworth/Sumner, which is in the Eight-Player North Large School division; 2-3 Bucksport and 3-2 Washington Academy square off in East Machias in a battle of Eight-Player North Small playoff contenders and Class D North teams John Bapst of Bangor, 3-3, and 2-4 Mattanawcook Academy of Lincoln will meet in Lincoln.

title: Forever chemicals found in most waterways, drinking water
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A new report from Environment America found that 83% of water samples collected across the United States tested positive for PFAS, also known as forever chemicals.
A U.S. Geological Survey study found nearly half of tap water in the country contains forever chemicals. Bottled water also contains the chemicals.
Trey Sherard, Anacostia Riverkeeper, said, “Their solution? Bottled water may be just a different toxin.”
Where the chemicals come from
PFAS are used in many everyday products. The chemicals are what make non-stick cookware non-stick. Products branded as waterproof or stain-resistant are also likely to contain PFAS.
The chemicals are known carcinogens, specifically linked to ovarian and testicular cancer. They can also cause infertility, and in children, developmental delays.
The biggest sources of PFAS entering water supplies are industrial runoff and firefighting foam.
Calls for regulation
Environment America is calling attention to the issue.
Lisa Frank, who heads Environment America said, “When we allow the use of toxic chemicals and we allow those chemicals to get into our environment without considering the downstream consequences, the problem can get out of hand very quickly,” adding “Removing all those parts from our environment is going to be a very tall order. But stopping new people’s contamination can start right now.”
The organization is calling on lawmakers to take action. U.S. Rep. Paul Tonko, D-New York, is calling for an overhaul of the Safe Drinking Water Act to include forever chemicals.
Tonko said, “Americans deserve to have confidence and peace of mind that when they turn on the tap, they’re being delivered safe, safe drinking water.”
Some of the worst contamination can be found in the Northeast and along the northern Mississippi River.

title: Couple accused of waiting hours to call for help after toddlers ate 20 hemp gummies, authorities say
text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (Gray News) - A Kentucky couple is accused of waiting hours to call for help after toddlers ate 20 hemp gummies, according to authorities.
Courtney Johnson, 30, was arrested in July after her 3-year-old and her 4-year-old children were hospitalized for allegedly eating hemp-infused gummies, police said.
A special victims investigator spoke with Johnson, who said she had opened a new container of 25 “hemp-infused gummies” and took one before going to sleep, WDKY reported.
Authorities said the two children were taken to a hospital where they were unconscious.
An arrest citation alleged that, instead of putting the gummies back where the children couldn’t reach, Johnson said she “likely left [them] on my bathroom sink,” where the children allegedly found and ate about 20 of them.
Since her arrest, Johnson has made multiple accusations that her husband, 33-year-old Sean East, was the one who left the gummies in an unsecured location.
East was arrested on July 26 for an unrelated warrant, and this led to the confiscation of his phone and Johnson’s.
Authorities said they obtained a search warrant for both phones and discovered East accepting fault for the incident with the gummies.
Officials said the search found that Johnson at least knew about the children ingesting the gummies.
Johnson allegedly found the empty container on a bedroom floor where the toddlers were found. Around noon that day, the toddlers still hadn’t woken up and had to be taken to the emergency room by first responders.
East’s arrest does not negate the criminal abuse charges that Johnson is facing after she allegedly “took a substantial and unreasonable amount of time” to request medical care for the children, authorities said.
East is facing charges in relation to child abuse following the investigation.

title: Birth mother urged to come forward after dead infant found at waste facility
text:
UTICA, N.Y. (WKTV) — Police in New York are searching for answers after a worker found a deceased baby girl in the recycling sorting area at a solid waste authority Wednesday.
The girl is estimated to be about 2 weeks old.
The mother is not being called a suspect, and police are not saying a crime has been committed.
Utica Police Chief Mark Williams made a plea Thursday to the mother to come forward and tell authorities how the baby girl ended up there.
“So, I would make a plea to the birth mother of this child, please come forward,” Williams said. “She may have a story to tell, but we need to know it. This baby girl deserves proper burial and an identity.”
Police officers involved in the investigation are being offered counseling.

title: Trump administration sues California to block state from counting alleged noncitizen mail-in ballots
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — The Trump administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for next month’s midterm elections from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
The lawsuit comes after the Justice Department said California officials failed to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.
The lawsuit follows a letter sent earlier this week by a top Justice Department official who threatened potential legal action if California didn’t comply.
The federal government didn’t specify where the 20,000 voters were concentrated, but the list was sent directly to Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan on Tuesday, his office confirmed in a statement. His office said the list contained names of voters throughout California, not just Los Angeles, even though Logan is the only county election official named as a defendant in the lawsuit. He doesn’t have jurisdiction over ballots outside Los Angeles County.
In a statement Thursday, Logan said his office can’t withhold ballots or refuse to count them “based solely on unverified allegations.”
Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and there are a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts that could determine which party has control of the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term.
Expert says lawsuit could set stage for false election claims
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a letter to the Justice Department that the federal government hasn’t provided evidence to support its allegation that 20,000 names on the state’s voter rolls are of noncitizens. She referenced an instance in which the federal government initially alleged nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens were listed on Nevada’s voter rolls, but the state determined that all the people flagged were, in fact, U.S. citizens.
She also noted that voting is already underway in the state. Weber, a Democrat, said the Justice Department was “demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide.”
California’s elections are in “full compliance” with federal law, she added.
David Becker, an election law expert who heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research, called the Justice Department’s lawsuit “fairly frivolous.”
“If they were seeking to work in good faith to clean up the voter list that they believed had issues, they would have done this months ago in a much different fashion,” Becker said. “However, it does raise questions as to whether or not the sole purpose of this is to set the stage for false claims about elections.”
List of alleged illegal voters delivered on a thumb drive
Logan said his office received the thumb drive along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device. The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note.”
Becker said most election officials’ cybersecurity protocols would not allow them to comply with the Justice Department’s request as it was sent.
“Election offices do not just stick thumb drives into their technology, for very good reason,” he said.
The Justice Department’s lawsuit says the federal government sought to “work collaboratively” with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, and “California made no serious effort to do so.”
“The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question,” the lawsuit says. “This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined.”
Weber, who is named in the lawsuit, suggested the federal government’s outreach had not been collaborative.
She said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them.
In her letter Thursday, she called the recent demands “an emergency of the DOJ’s creation.”
Letters sent weeks before elections
The letter sent by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter gave the state 48 hours to research the list of the 20,000 people it claims might not be citizens. For those whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their immigration status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received one.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta said at an unrelated press conference Thursday morning that state officials would not carry out the federal government’s requests to withhold ballots for the alleged noncitizen voters. He noted that the administration’s alleged number of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls had dropped from the 190,000 flagged over the summer by the Department of Homeland Security to the 20,000 noted by the Justice Department.
“What happened to those 170,000? They just got those wrong,” Bonta said.
He also said the Trump administration was violating a federal law that prohibits states from changing voter rolls within 90 days of an election.
“They are in unprecedented, baseless, lawless territory,” he said.
The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, defended the Justice Department’s move to take California to court.
“This is not political or controversial,” he wrote in a post on X. “We will not allow California to dilute the votes of American citizens.”
___
Austin reported from Sacramento, Riddle from Los Angeles and Durkin Richer from Washington. Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed.

title: Old Orchard Beach park removes more than 500 trees to fight invasive insect
text:
OLD ORCHARD BEACH — Guild Park looks jarringly bare from the road, a noticeable clearing catching the eye. Until recently, the park was chock full of trees, with a vast canopy that gave way to little sunlight.
But in the past few years, an invasive insect moved in, and more than 500 trees were recently removed in an effort to keep its impact on the forest at bay.
And now, the tree removal is paving the way for a brighter future at the park.
Mark Lauritano, a member of the Ocean Park Association Environment and Natural Resources Committee, said the hemlock woolly adelgid has likely been plaguing the trees for years, attacking the sap and needles of a tree until it dies.
“They can kill a mature tree in a couple of years,” Lauritano said. “They’re very prolific in terms of the population. They can reproduce very quickly.”
The tiny, invasive insects native to East Asia are becoming more prevalent in New England as the winters get warmer. A cold snap with temperatures below zero can kill the insect, Lauritano said, but those stretches of weather are becoming increasingly rare.
“And it’s not just in Ocean Park,” he said. “They’re up and down the coast.”
A PROBLEM REIMAGINED
At first, when the Maine Forest Service recommended removing 578 trees as part of a Guild Park Forest Management Plan, the news was shocking.
“It was very emotional,” Lauritano said. “A lot of people use the park. People get emotional when you remove trees.”
But as the diseased and dying trees came down and a clearing began to emerge, so did silver linings.
Guild Park, which sits on 20 acres of land close to businesses and restaurants, was originally intended to be developed. Instead, it was designated as a conservation easement and has been acting as a park since the late 1800s.
“It was also pretty much untouched since the late 1800s,” Lauritano said.
That meant the land was overgrown, with nearly 4,000 trees creating a canopy that let in very little sunlight. A less dense forest with an open canopy will allow native flora and fauna to thrive, Lauritano said.
The new open space will also make room for a visitors’ center geared toward education about the native plants and animals that inhabit the park. The project, which is led by the Ocean Park Association Environment and Natural Resources Committee, will be funded through a mix of grants and private donations.
“We’re viewing (the tree clearing) as an opportunity,” Lauritano said.
WHAT COMES NEXT
There’s a lot going on at Guild Park, Lauritano said. Visitors will notice various markings on the trees: bright orange bands, reddish trail markings and even little white flags sticking out of the ground. (They’re easy to miss if a hiker isn’t careful.)
The orange bands signify hemlock trees, each of which will need to be monitored for woolly adelgid activity and treated with a specific pesticide geared toward eliminating the insect.
The little white flags indicate one of the 500 saplings that were planted this spring — and with additional sunlight filtering through a thinner canopy, the saplings will continue to grow and thrive.
Lauritano and other members of the Environment and Natural Resources Committee, along with help from professional foresters, will continue to monitor the forest for any new growth from invasive species, like shrub honeysuckles and Japanese knotweed.
In the spring, volunteers will release predator beetles that feed on the woolly adelgid, further diminishing the invasive population. At $3 a beetle, they’re not cheap, Lauritano said, but they’re worth the price.
“We hope for the best with them,” he said.
Planning for the visitors’ center is also at the forefront of Lauritano’s mind. Although the project is still in the very early stages, he hopes it will be beneficial for the many hikers, educational camps and student groups who come through the forest.
“This project is for the good of the park and for safety,” Lauritano said. “It’ll be good for wildlife as well.”

title: Woman says ‘something felt off’ during first date with man accused of posing as 49ers player
text:
PORTLAND (KPTV/Gray News) - An Oregon woman said she went on a date with a man accused of posing as an NFL player to defraud at least 26 women of more than $1 million.
Daejon Labrayae Delenar Love, 35, appeared in federal court Tuesday before a U.S. magistrate judge.
He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Portland on one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
News of his indictment shocked many people, including Rachel Anderson, who briefly went on a date with Love.
In 2024, Anderson said she met Love on the dating app Bumble. He told her his name was John Prince and that he was a Swiss real estate developer.
But during their first date, Anderson said something felt off.
“He said I’m very intentional and efficient when it comes to dating, and if I pursue you, you will be the only one I pursue you I need someone who has been around money, who understands these things aren’t luxuries to me this is just my normal life,” Anderson said. “Within five minutes I knew I wasn’t going to see him again.”
Investigators said he also worked with alleged accomplice Taylor Chan, 18. Both are charged with wire fraud and conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
The indictment also alleges Love used online dating and social media profiles with false personal and financial information, built romantic relationships with victims and showed signs of wealth to persuade them to send cash or wire money. Instead of investing the money, Love is accused of spending it on travel, hotels, luxury cars, clothes, jewelry and other buys.
“When I saw that, I almost fell out of bed, I could not believe it,” Anderson said. “It’s just awful, I can’t imagine how those women feel, I really can’t.”
Anderson said that, although her time with Love was brief, he falsely portrayed himself to be wealthy and having close friendships with celebrities and NFL players.
“He did say I have $5 million sitting in this account, and he said the home that I just mentioned in Vancouver was $3 million the entire time it was just that, this cost this, this cost this, I had never seen or heard anything like it before and I was just totally blown away,” Anderson said.
Recently, Netflix announced a new documentary titled “Untold: Wide Deceiver” about Love.
Netflix didn’t reveal when the documentary will be released.
Love was arraigned, pleaded not guilty and was ordered held in jail pending a jury trial set to start Dec. 15, 2026.

title: Bangor, Maine Man Accused of Making Knife Threats Following Family Altercation
text:
Bangor, Maine Man Accused of Threatening a Woman With a Knife
A Maine man faces multiple charges after an incident in which he allegedly threatened a woman with a knife.
Bangor, Maine Man Arrested For Allegedly Threatening a Woman With a Knife
Jacob Auer, 32, of Bangor, was taken into custody on Thursday, October 16, 2026, after police responded to a report of a family fight at a home on Ohio Street.
Auer left the residence before law enforcement arrived.
When police officers interviewed the victim, at approximately 10:10 Thursday night, she said Auer had gone to the residence to pick up his belongings.
During his time at the residence, she said he allegedly threatened her with a knife and allegedly planned to kill any law enforcement personnel who responded to the call.
Auer allegedly stabbed an inflatable lawn decoration and crashed his vehicle into the victim's before leaving.
Bangor, Maine Man Faces Multiple Charges After Family Fight and Car Crash
Police located the suspect and arrested him on the following charges:
- Domestic violence criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon
- Domestic violence criminal mischief
- Theft by unauthorized taking
- Leaving the scene of an accident
- Violation of a protection order
Auer was transported to the Penobscot County Jail.
Maine Resources are Available to Victims of Domestic Abuse
Anyone experiencing domestic violence or who is concerned about someone who may be is encouraged to seek help immediately.
In Maine, they can call the Statewide Domestic Abuse Helpline at 1-866-834-HELP (1-866-834-4357) for confidential support, safety planning, and connections to local resources 24/7.
Partners for Peace offers 24/7 assistance to residents of Penobscot and Piscataquis counties. 1-800-863-9909.
The National Domestic Violence Hotline is also available 24/7 at 1-800-799-SAFE (1-800-799-7233), or by texting START to 88788.
If you feel you are in danger, call 911 immediately.
We'll update this story as more details become available.

title: Man raises awareness about rare cancer with soccer-themed prosthetic eye
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (Aging Untold) — Ryan Gibson faced an unexpected choice after losing his right eye to ocular melanoma: blend in with a normal-looking prosthetic or make a statement.
Gibson chose to make a statement.
After getting official clearance from the professional soccer team Bayern Munich, Gibson unveiled a prosthetic eye featuring his favorite team’s logo.
“I could go back to normality and get the same eye, nobody will really know — or I can go big or go home,” Gibson said.
Extremely rare diagnosis
Ocular melanoma affects only five or six out of every million people each year. The cancer starts in specialized cells that make melanin, the pigment that gives color to eyes and skin.
Most eye melanomas form in parts of the eye that cannot be seen when looking in a mirror.
The cancer may not cause symptoms, but when they occur, signs can include flashes of light that look like specks of dust, a growing dark spot in the colored part of the eye, poor or blurry vision in one eye and loss of peripheral vision.
“In 2016, I started seeing spots everywhere,” Gibson said.
After weeks of blurry vision and spots in his right eye, Gibson went to a doctor and received a rare diagnosis.
“The 30 years she’s been an eye doctor she’s never seen that before,” Gibson said. “It was like the yeti or bigfoot. Heard of it, never seen it.”
Treatment and recovery
Treatment for large ocular melanomas typically leads to vision loss, and in some cases, loss of the entire eye. Gibson faced a choice of radiation treatment or amputation.
“I went ahead and made the decision, pop it out,” Gibson said.
Gibson, who lives outside Charlotte, said his love of Bayern Munich has been a family tradition that has remained constant through his most difficult chapter.
“Family tradition-type thing. Over the years it’s just gotten more ingrained and more personal for me,” Gibson said. “It’s always there, it’s the constant.”
Raising awareness
Gibson uses his prosthetic eye as a conversation starter to raise awareness about ocular melanoma.
“I want to use it as a tool, not just an eye,” Gibson said. “At some point in that conversation, they’ll get up the nerve to go ‘What happened?’ And when they get to that point, then you have the opening for awareness for ocular melanoma.”
His love of Bayern Munich has taken him to games around the world.
“I have to sit extremely close so I can at least see what’s going on,” Gibson said. “For some people it’s not just a game. Some people don’t quite grasp that.”
Gibson encourages anyone having issues with their eyes to get regular dilated eye exams to catch any potential cancer early.

title: Red Shop building in Lewiston deserves careful consideration
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I’m a resident of Auburn, raised in Lewiston, who attended the community conversation about the future of the Red Shop building in Simard-Payne Memorial Park.
The sunny description of the event by Mark LaFlamme (“‘Diamond in the rough’: Plans for Lewiston’s Red Shop discussed,” Oct. 5) prompted me to share a few thoughts.
The Red Shop building is one of a kind and a part of Lewiston’s history. But is its best use to serve primarily as a concession stand for a concert venue like Thompson’s Point in Portland — notorious for its $60 parking fees?
Aside from the question of the desirability, feasibility and financial benefits of devoting that section of the park to an expensive date-night venue, the potential sale of this property to a developer should entail serious consideration of the effects on the abutting properties and other users of the park.
The Red Shop potentially offers the community a space for many activities that may not be moneymakers but are still vital, especially for our youth. These benefits should not depend on the goodwill of a developer, but be controlled by the city and the community stakeholders.
To my mind, the best piece of news was a throwaway line about an independent consultant being hired to review any sale or lease of the building. A truly independent evaluation of the entire picture would ease fears of a sweetheart deal that takes a community asset out of the hands of the community.
Renee Cote
Auburn

title: Lawyer who lost everything to addiction reclaims law license
text:
LANSING, Mich. (InvestigateTV) - Jarrod Barron stood before an Ingham County courtroom, surrounded by friends, family and supporters who helped him rebuild his life after addiction cost him his career and left him homeless.
“I was painfully aware of how far I’d fallen,” Barron said in an earlier interview.
Climbing back took years. He met his wife, Carrie, while he was in recovery. A relapse led to an ultimatum.
“These two, this one, probably wouldn’t have been here at all if things had gone differently,” Carrie Barron said, standing between her two young sons. “I was pregnant with Andrew when we kind of came to a head and said, like, we need to get things straightened out. We need a life together, and that cannot include this addiction.”
With a focus on family, Barron worked day by day to stay sober.
“I had a ton of people who helped me with that process, from sponsors to recovery coaches to organizations, friends, family, all kinds of people, became part of my community of support,” Barron said.
That support filled the courtroom as Barron met another milestone. He lost his license to practice law during his addiction. He returned to court to reclaim it.
Attorney Michael Marutiak spoke on Barron’s behalf.
“I will risk my entire license to practice law myself on what I’m about to say. I believe he will be a credit to the profession, demonstrate moral turpitude. He will do nothing to bring any dishonor to the legal profession if he’s given the oath of office today,” Marutiak said.
Attorney John Jafiszewski also testified.
“Jarrod has been there for me in some of my darkest times. I’m always willing to pick up the phone to meet. He is an amazing asset to the recovery community,” Jafiszewski said.
Barron addressed the court.
“Over time and with a lot of help, I’ve rebuilt my entire life brick by brick. Today, I see the resulting life and community represented in this very courtroom,” Barron said. “I count every person in this room as my friend because everyone present and many others who could not be here have actively contributed and continue to contribute to my life in meaningful ways. In essence, jointly and severally, they have saved my life and continue to do so on a daily basis. And I love them all dearly.”
Ingham County Judge Clinton Canady administered the oath of office.
“I, Jared Barron,” Barron repeated after the judge. “Do you solemnly swear or affirm that you will support the Constitution of the United States and the Constitution of the State of Michigan.”
“I do,” Barron said.
“Well, let me come down and shake. Let’s give him a hand,” Canady said.
The courtroom erupted in applause.
Carrie Barron brought their sons to the ceremony, pulling them out of school for the occasion.
“He made the right choices. And, you know, every day was another right choice, and another right choice, and another right choice, and now we have, you know, this great family,” Carrie Barron said. “They watched Dad study for the bar exam, and, you know, they know that he’s gone to all kinds of meetings and leads meetings every Friday night just to help others. And so they are part of the whole journey.”
Barron said his sons have been a guide.
“They’ve been a sort of a north star that gives me a daily means of guidance,” Barron said. “I couldn’t imagine doing any of this without them.”
Barron serves on the board of Face Addiction Now. Along with his dedication to his family, he is dedicated to helping others struggling through addiction.
“There is hope and there is help. It is hard, but you don’t have to do any of this alone. There are tons of people out there willing to go to bat for you,” Barron said.
Substance use disorder is a treatable illness, but the decision to seek help isn’t always easy for the person battling addiction or their loved ones.
An expert we spoke to said once someone admits they have a problem, recovery is not a quick fix and even people with years of sobriety have to make the daily decision not to use.
“Relapse is a part of recovery,” said Kellie Ross, a clinical addiction specialist. “I think on average it takes people seven times to kick the habit.”
For more information on substance use disorder, you can call SAMHSA’s national helpline at 1-800-622-HELP (4357) or online at findtreatment.gov to find help in your area.
