Groundwater levels hit record lows in Maine as drought continues
text:
Groundwater levels hit record lows in Maine as drought continues
MEMA has received 156 reports of dry wells in 2026.
Groundwater levels hit record lows in Maine as drought continues
MEMA has received 156 reports of dry wells in 2026.
Groundwater levels in parts of Maine have dropped to their lowest levels on record, surpassing those seen during the historic drought of the early 2000s.
According to the Maine Drought Task Force, monitoring wells in Oxford and Clayton Lake reached record lows this month, following 16 months of below-normal precipitation across the state.
“We are seeing low groundwater records being set,” said Nick Stasulis, Task Force co-chair with the U.S. Geological Survey. “Wells in Oxford and at Clayton Lake, with decades of data, hit their lowest levels on record this month - lower than the early 2000s drought that most people consider the benchmark.”
During an October 16 meeting, state and federal officials reported that Maine is experiencing a multi-year water resources drought that will likely continue into 2027.
Precipitation deficits have climbed to as much as 12 inches in northern Maine and between one and two feet across central and southern portions of the state.
While recent rainfall has helped improve surface conditions, including lawns and streams, it has done little to replenish groundwater supplies.
The National Weather Service offices in Gray and Caribou estimate Maine would need up to 200% of its normal precipitation over the next two months to significantly improve drought conditions before the ground freezes.
The impacts are becoming increasingly noticeable for residents who rely on private wells.
As of October 15, the Maine Emergency Management Agency had received 156 reports of dry wells in 2026, compared to just 39 reports at the Task Force’s September 3 meeting.
Some households have reported using laundromats and gyms for access to water, while others are waiting until December or next spring for well drilling services. Several residents have also experienced well problems for multiple consecutive years.
Water storage levels also remain below long-term averages in several river basins, including the Androscoggin, Penobscot and Union.
Looking ahead, a strengthening El Niño could influence Maine’s winter weather patterns. The seasonal outlook favors warmer-than-normal temperatures, near- to above-normal precipitation and below-normal snowfall.
Despite the possibility of additional precipitation, officials say groundwater levels are unlikely to recover before the ground freezes, raising concerns that the drought will extend into another year.
Residents are encouraged to conserve water, monitor local conditions and report dry wells through MEMA’s dry-well survey as Maine continues to deal with the impacts of its prolonged drought.
As drought conditions continue across Maine, there are several steps residents can take to protect their water supplies and stay informed.
Residents are encouraged to conserve water by following local water-use restrictions and finding simple ways to reduce unnecessary use. Water-saving tips can help households make the most of their available supply.
Those who rely on private wells should keep an eye on their water levels and report dry wells through the state’s dry well survey.
Public water systems experiencing drought-related problems should notify the Maine CDC’s Drinking Water Program to help officials track impacts on drinking water supplies.
Farmers should monitor water availability and explore drought assistance and other resources offered through state agricultural programs.
Because drought conditions can vary widely across Maine, residents are also encouraged to follow updates from the Maine Emergency Management Agency (MEMA), local emergency management agencies, and other state officials.

title: InvestigateTV+: The hidden cost of care
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ uncovers the hidden cost of care; how families facing complex medical needs can be pushed into financial and emotional crisis, and why caregivers say support still falls short.
Plus, one man shares his powerful journey from substance use disorder to recovery and redemption.
Then, stressed nursing students find comfort through the healing power of dogs.
Hidden cost of care
Family caregivers are considered the backbone of America’s long-term care system and experts say that backbone is breaking.
About one in four adults in the country provide ongoing care for a loved one, sometimes at the expense of their own well-being.
Caregiving costs can add up fast, forcing caregivers to take on debt and in some cases making it hard to cover basic necessities. This is often driven by fixed budgets, high out of pocket medical costs, and the immense time constraints of caregiving.
Held up by hope
Jarrod Barron stood before an Ingham County courtroom, surrounded by friends, family and supporters who helped him rebuild his life after addiction cost him his career and left him homeless.
Two years ago, Barron shared his story as part of a mental health series. At that time, he was 10 years into recovery and helping others in their journey. He had been a successful lawyer before addiction led him to live under the Oakland Avenue Bridge in Lansing.
Depending on blood donations
Emily Rodgers is 12. She loves tumbling, the color pink and her best friend.
This seventh grader measures time in 21-day increments.
Emily has beta thalassemia major, a rare blood disorder that prevents her body from making hemoglobin. Since she was an infant, doctors at Vanderbilt University Medical Center (VUMC) have given her transfusions.
Dogs give a chance to relax
Between exams, clinicals and sleepless nights, nursing students face a lot of pressure. At Galen College of Nursing in Louisville, some students find relief from two lovable dogs.
Henry and Maisy, two English Cream Golden Retrievers, have become unofficial therapy dogs for students struggling with the demands of nursing school.

title: Mainers who import prescription drugs face new customs rule
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine residents who import prescription drugs face new customs rule
A new Customs and Border Protection (CBP) rule would make it nearly impossible for personal prescription shipments from pharmacies outside the United States to enter the country, affecting Maine residents who rely on lower-cost prescriptions from Canada and elsewhere.
The change was supposed to start next week on Thursday, Oct. 22, but CBP decided Wednesday to delay the deadline 90 days to Jan. 20, 2027.
The group Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation told WMTW media partner WABI that the reprieve came after its members sent more than 107,000 letters to Congress. The group says it is seeking a permanent solution.
Ken Hunter, executive director of the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation, said some patients may not be able to afford their drugs under the new rule.
"Some patients are going to be in the situation of not being able to afford their drugs. We're not talking about a $10 or $15 price increase. This is hundreds of dollars per month. Then you multiply that across multiple prescriptions that, for instance, a senior might take, you can see that can be a couple of thousand dollars," Hunter said. "It's going to be very important that we get personal pharmaceuticals carved out and set aside from this new rule, because it's really a matter of life and death."
Hunter said a number of U.S. senators, including Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), signed a letter to CBP demanding personal prescriptions be exempted, arguing the rule will not help with tariffs or stopping fentanyl, its intended purpose. Hunter said Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) was not among the senators who signed on to the letter, but added that he would welcome her support.
Hunter is urging people to keep pressuring Congress at personalimportation.org.

title: New law aims to end TSA confusion over parents traveling with breast milk
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Emily Calandrelli, an author and former host of “Emily’s Wonder Lab” on Netflix, went viral in 2022 after writing on social media about an experience at a TSA security checkpoint.
Calandrelli said she was on a work trip at the time, writing it was her “first time away from my 10-week-old son, who I’m currently breastfeeding,” and that she “brought my pump and two ice packs.”
Calandrelli said two male TSA agents told her she could not bring the ice packs in a carry-on because they were not frozen solid. She said when she asked to speak to a supervisor, she was asked, “Well, where is the baby?” The supervisor then said if her child was with her, “it wouldn’t be an issue,” according to Calandrelli.
She said she was ultimately escorted from the security line and forced to check her ice packs.
“It shouldn’t be nearly impossible to travel if you’re a mom or are breastfeeding your child,” Calandrelli said in an Instagram video.
What TSA policy says
TSA policy, in place since 2016, states that formula, breast milk, toddler drinks, and baby or toddler food in quantities greater than 3.4 ounces are allowed in carry-on baggage because they are considered medically necessary liquids.
The policy is also supposed to apply to breast milk cooling accessories such as ice packs, freezer packs and gel packs, regardless of whether they are melted or frozen. The regulation also states a child does not need to be present or traveling with a parent for the exemption to apply.
“With or without the baby, it is deemed a medical necessity, just like a medicine,” said Dr. Jessica Nash, a pediatrician at Children’s National Hospital in Washington, D.C., and a member of the DC Breastfeeding Coalition.
Breastfeeding can help protect a baby against conditions including asthma, ear infections, stomach bugs and diabetes, according to the CDC. It can also lower a mother’s risk for certain cancers.
Nash said she believes societal barriers, including challenges while traveling, can disrupt a mother’s breastfeeding intentions.
“The body produces only if it’s stimulated. So if a mom is away from a baby or if it’s at the time a baby needs to eat, the mom either needs to pump or she needs to directly breastfeed,” Nash said. “And if you don’t do that, not only will her supply decrease, but she might start to get a backup of milk, which increases her risk for infection.”
Nash has heard from breastfeeding mothers who have encountered problems at TSA checkpoints, including some forced to throw their milk away and others concerned the screening process could contaminate their baby’s source of nutrition.
“Being asked to open their milk and test strips put in their milk, or where the milk is being handled by someone who hasn’t put on another pair of gloves. Real issues, real mothers, all the time, and just clearly not everyone knowing what the rules are,” Nash said.
Vanessa Snyder lives in Wisconsin and has flown with her husband and daughter, documenting their experiences online, including lessons learned navigating airport security with breast milk.
“It just breaks my heart because I know how hard it is to pump on the go,” Snyder said.
She said that every experience is different and was once told that the milk “had to be frozen.”
“So that was a specific instance where I actually had to push back and say, no, this is allowed,” Snyder said.
Calandrelli worked with lawmakers for several years advocating for breastfeeding mothers to get better protections in airports.
New law expands protections
In late 2025, the bipartisan Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening, or BABES, Enhancement Act was signed into law. It expands on the original BABES Act, which a decade ago mandated TSA exempt breast milk from its 3-1-1 liquids rule but lacked clarity on how it should be screened.
Under the new law, TSA will be required to consult with nationally recognized maternal health organizations to establish standardized and hygienic screening guidelines for breast milk, baby formula and related accessories. TSA must also update its guidance every five years and ensure agents nationwide receive consistent training.
“And they have to comply with it,” said Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Illinois, who introduced the bill in the Senate.
Duckworth said another component of the law directs an independent government watchdog to audit TSA’s compliance and report the results to Congress.
“What we were finding is that depending on which airport you went through, the TSA agent may or may not know, so the audit portion is absolutely in there to increase accountability,” Duckworth said.
Nash said she believes that accountability measure is important.
“I definitely think it’s important. There has to be some checks and balances in place, to make sure that these enhancements happen,” Nash said.
Snyder said she views the law as progress. “I think that’s going to be a win for families.”
She advised breastfeeding mothers preparing to fly to have TSA’s policy readily available, whether it be a screenshot or the TSA website itself.
TSA response
TSA and the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees TSA operations, declined to speak on camera for this story.
The agency said it “fully supports” all requirements outlined in the BABES Enhancement Act. A spokesperson said as of February 2026, TSA is in full compliance with the new law and said the workforce has been trained on updated screening protocols.
“TSA officers who do not follow current screening procedures may be taken off screening duties, retrained, or disciplined to ensure screening procedures are followed,” the spokesperson said.
Travelers can file a complaint with TSA if they believe its policies are not being followed. You can do that by clicking here.

title: Portland Museum of Art, Portland schools partner on Black history lessons
text:
PORTLAND — Approximately 23 seventh-graders from Portland’s Lyman Moore Middle School sat in the front rows of the Portland Museum of Art’s auditorium on Thursday as Jonathan Tunstall, assistant professor of education at Bowdoin College, took kids through a presentation on Black music, spanning spirituals to hip-hop.
“Black music is a living archive of Black history,” Tunstall said.
As the musical journey took the kids from spirituals to the blues and then to funk, they gradually became more energized and engaged. By the time Tunstall arrived at hip-hop, they were pointing at the screen, moving along to the music snippets and yelling out the names of celebrities they recognized.
“That’s Cardi B,” yelled one seventh-grader.
A few minutes earlier, a group of 10 students was on the second floor of the museum’s gallery, standing around a display of sugar bowls when their tour guide, museum educator Beth Walker, asked a question: “Did anyone have sugar this morning?”
After a few children raised their hands, Walker explained the connection between the sugar trade of the 19th century, which relied on slave labor, and the way in which Portland economically benefited from that system. She wanted students to understand the brutal history behind what looked like just a beautiful piece of art.
Since Oct. 1, nearly 425 seventh-graders from Portland schools have visited the PMA to learn about Black history through a gallery walk, an interactive music history presentation and a printmaking activity with local artist Jordan Parks. The partnership is part of Portland Public Schools’ new Black history curriculum, which was created to comply with a 2021 law requiring all K-12 schools in Maine to teach African American studies.
For the last three years, the Portland Museum of Art has hosted similar sessions in January centered around teaching fifth-graders about Wabanaki history.
“We wanted them to understand the contemporary connections about what they’re learning in the 19th century and how that is playing out in various kinds of artwork today,” said Fiona Hopper, social studies projects coordinator for Portland Public Schools.
Hopper said the work that students have done inside and outside the classroom, including their visit to the PMA, has prepared them to walk Portland’s Freedom Trail, which documents the city’s Black history, next week.
“This is a very, very long time coming, and it’s a super important moment for Maine to finally be acknowledging and teaching about its African American history,” said Hopper.
Students visiting the museum were exposed to many pieces of art spanning the 19th century to the Civil Rights Era and the present day, including two pieces by Portland-based artist Daniel Minter; a video installation by Adama Delphine Fawunda that highlights the history of Malaga Island, where a mixed-race community off Phippsburg was evicted and destroyed in 1912; and a painting by David Driskell titled “Ghetto Wall #2.”
Sarah Timm, the Peggy L. Osher Head of Education at the PMA, said the museum wanted the program to center around finding creative expression through history lessons.
“Kids don’t often have opportunities to express themselves, so how can we use our collection to really inspire learning, but also just let kids have a moment and permission to be creative?” said Timm.
Tunstall hopes that the kids’ excitement over the hip-hop music will translate into better learning and engagement with Black history.
“(I’m hoping) that I can play a small part in undoing the erasure of Black histories that is happening right now,” said Tunstall. “And hopefully get them excited so when they do the curriculum with their teachers, they have something concrete to grab onto.”

title: Obituary: Dolores “Del” MacLean
text:
NAPLES, Fla. – Dolores “Del” Cecile (Fraser) MacLean, 86, of Naples, Fla., passed away peacefully on Oct. 9, 2026.
Dolores was born in Madawaska, Maine on Oct. 26, 1939 to Hermanegilde and Isabel (Michaud) Fraser, (both born and raised on L’Isle Vert, Quebec, Canada). She, her parents, and seven siblings relocated to Lewiston, Maine where she attended locals parochial schools (speaking little English until the age of 10), was a finalist in the Miss Lewiston-Auburn Pageant in 1958, and graduated from St. Dominic Academy the same year. She was the school page reporter for the Lewiston Evening Journal in 1955-’56, worked at The Poland Spring House in Poland, and at Pirate’s Cove Restaurant on Bailey Island, where she met her husband, David Peter MacLean, of Brunswick. They were married on Dec. 6, 1958 in Brunswick and resided near the end of Pinkham’s Point where they remained until 1965.
In 1965, David and Del purchased and renovated an old farmhouse with some land on outer McKeen Street in Brunswick. As their four children grew, Del worked part time as an Avon representative, a waitress at Howard Johnson’s, and as a Tupperware hostess. Between babies four and five, she started her own business, “Ye Yarn Barn” in a small room at the front of the house. The business soon outgrew the space, so David renovated the bottom floor of the barn and they moved her shop in. She enjoyed and excelled at this business, where customers could purchase yarn and other fiber arts materials and take lessons in knitting and crocheting. She was the proprietor of “Ye Yarn Barn” for over a decade, (until the home was sold). Del was also great with accounting and kept the books for David’s foundation business in addition to her own.
David and Del separated in 1978 and divorced. In 1981, Del closed the yarn shop, sold the house on McKeen Street, and moved to Marietta, Ga. where she worked for “Bernat”, a France-based yarn company she had done business with, and was very useful to because of her French-speaking background. A year later she moved to Naples, Fla., where she obtained her real estate license and was part of the opening team for both “Lely Resort Golf & Country Club” in Naples, Fla. and then“Windstar” on Naples Bay. After some years there, Del then worked at and purchased a home near “Grey Oaks”, a lovely golf community in central Naples, Fla. where she excelled in selling real estate and thoroughly enjoyed her work there. Del was their top sales person and was recognized for her achievements at Grey Oaks and within the greater Naples real estate market several times with awards and accolades until she retired.
After retiring, Del traveled the U.S., Europe, plus several trips to L’Isle Vert, a small island in the St. Lawrence River in Quebec, and to Quebec City, where she had extended family and enjoyed many summers. She was very proud of her French-Canadian heritage. Del loved her family and often hosted special gatherings for them and friends at her home of 25 years in the “Walden Oaks” community of Naples, Fla., where she remained until 2023. From 2023 until her death, she resided at “Aston Gardens”, a retirement community in North Naples, Fla.
Del is survived by her five children, Stephen MacLean of Brunswick, Tracey MacLean of St. Augustine, Fla., Mary MacLean of Bozeman, Mont., Allyson MacLean and Amanda MacLean of Naples, Fla.; and her five grandchildren, Joshua MacLean, Savannah MacLean, Zev Bliss, Frankie Bliss, and Carli Bliss; plus several nieces, nephews; and cousins in the U.S. and Canada.
A funeral service will be held on Monday, Oct. 19, at 1:30 p.m., at Hodges Funeral Home, 525 – 111th Avenue North, Naples, FL 34108.
In lieu of flowers, please send donations to

title: UMaine professors receive $2M in federal funding for forestry and microchip projects
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Projects for mapping forests before and after harvesting and researching quantum materials used in electronics at the University of Maine are being funded by the federal government, the U.S. Department of Energy announced Friday.
Each of the two projects, both led by UMaine professors, will receive roughly $1 million in increments over multiple years. Funding will be used to pay for equipment and employ researchers and graduate students.
Friday’s announcement is a stark difference from last spring, when President Donald Trump withheld millions of dollars in funding for UMaine. Although there are still uncertainties surrounding federal funding, UMaine President Joan Ferrini-Mundy said the grant reinforces the university’s research and relationship with the federal government.
“We have a very successful funding record with federal agencies right now, and we do hope that our work in these new areas will help us broaden that even further,” Ferrini-Mundy said.
While forestry and quantum materials used in processing chips are two different fields, both professors leading the projects said their research is poised to be used in the future.
Funding will be used for data collection at the Howland Research Forest, which has been used for atmosphere and ecosystem research since the 1990s, said Daniel Hayes, a professor of geospatial analysis and remote sensing. The land has been preserved for years, but the adjacent lot has been privately managed and logged, he said.
Before the adjacent lot, which is owned by American Forest Management, was harvested this summer, Hayes asked to use lidar — light detection and ranging — technology to scan above-grown growth. Through laser imaging, data about the tree growth, ecosystem and gas emissions were collected, he said.
By scanning the area again after the harvest, Hayes and other researchers could see how forest management — and how the wood is used after it’s harvested — changes emissions and future growth.
Hayes has already been conducting this research, but the Department of Energy funding will allow for more data collection with a UMaine plane and drones, and, in a partnership with the Oak Ridge Laboratory in Tennessee, that data will be used for a model of earth that tracks energy and water cycles, Hayes said.
Currently, those models don’t take into account how forest management changes those cycles, he said.
“They kind of consider currently that the trees are all just sitting there doing whatever, and they don’t actually have a realistic representation of the fact that, especially in a place like Maine, these forests are intensively managed and they’re harvested,” Hayes said.
Although the research will be used on a global level, Hayes said it could also be used by Maine- based land and forest management companies to better understand how harvesting and logging change growth and carbon storage.
Away from the woods and in the labs on UMaine’s campus, Tomas Marangoni, a chemistry professor, is leading research attempting to find new ways to build quantum materials used in electronics. The materials are often used in microchips found in phones and computers, he said.
Science is reaching “a bit of a limit” on how small these chips can be, but chemistry could be used to create a new material that could make them smaller, Marangoni said.
“What we do is basically we use our molecule, the molecule that our students are making at UMaine, to make the metal atoms communicate better in terms of electronics and magnetism,” Marangoni said.
While the project is focused on miniaturization and how microchip technology can be improved, Marangoni said it also focuses on expanding future technologies. Discovering how a new material can be used or how atoms interact with electricity could lead to more advancements, he said.
“This is not a project that is interested in making a microchip tomorrow. It’s a project that is interested in seeing what comes after that,” Marangoni said.

Troy Jackson tells Susan Collins to ‘shut up’ during heated Maine Senate debate
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson told Republican Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during a heated final Maine U.S. Senate debate that also included an interruption from a data center protester.
Thursday night’s debate in a Bangor theater was the last of four meetings between Collins and Jackson, who are running for a seat that’s considered crucial in the fight for a Senate majority. The debate, like those that preceded it, included several testy exchanges over issues including the national debt, Collins’ relationship with President Donald Trump’s administration, and the candidates’ respective roles in worsening partisan divisions.
The scene became briefly chaotic when a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. As moderators asked for the protester to be removed, Collins said the shouting demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”
Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
Maine GOP said in a social media post after the debate that Jackson’s “shut up” comment was “unacceptable behavior.” Jackson’s campaign declined to comment on the exchange.
The issue of party loyalty came up during the debate, with one question posed to Collins asking her to cite a time she has defied the Republican Party. She referenced her push to oppose Pete Hegseth’s nomination as defense secretary, saying she organized Republicans to vote no. But Collins acknowledged he was confirmed despite her effort.
Collins accused Jackson of being a guaranteed vote for the Democratic Party while she has a track record of independence. Jackson disputed that characterization and said Collins is loyal to Trump when he needs key votes.
“What I know is that 100% of the time when Donald Trump goes to Susan Collins for a vote, he gets it,” Jackson said.
Collins, who is seeking her sixth term, has sought to distance herself from Trump during the debates, including using the phrase “Gulf of Mexico” instead of Trump’s preferred “Gulf of America.” Jackson described Collins’ votes against Trump as “managed votes” when she already knows the outcome is decided.
Jackson’s campaign also said Thursday that it raised $20.4 million in the third quarter as it seeks to close a funding gap with Collins. Jackson was a late entry into the race and the third quarter was his first quarter of fundraising.
Collins’ campaign said she raised $5.2 million in the same time period. Collins began the race with a considerable fundraising advantage over Jackson, as she had raised more than $18 million by the end of June and Jackson did not become the Democrats’ nominee until late July.

Man allegedly shot, killed mother after argument over cats in family home
text:
WOBURN, Mass. (WCVB) — A 22-year-old Massachusetts man has been charged with first-degree murder in the death of his mother.
Ryan Hanafin was returned to Massachusetts by U.S. Marshals and Reading police. Inside the courtroom Thursday, he was charged with first-degree murder and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon in connection with the death of his mother, 49-year-old Andria Hanafin.
Prosecutors say Ryan Hanafin shot his mother inside the family’s home on Oct. 8.
Argument over cats preceded shooting
Investigators said the mother and son had been arguing over the number of cats being kept in the family home.
“Ms. Andria Hanafin was a foster parent to cats as well as worked at an animal vet clinic, and she fostered many, many cats. There were upwards of 80 that were located in the house,” a prosecutor said.
Investigators said Andria Hanafin was afraid of her son’s gun obsession. Police said Ryan Hanafin fired a single shot into his mother’s head.
Weapons found in bedroom
Prosecutors said a short time after investigators arrived, they found an arsenal of weapons inside Ryan Hanafin’s room.
“Ryan Hanafin always carried a firearm on his person. A search of the lower bedroom where Ryan Hanafin was living at the time uncovered that his bedroom was in hoarding conditions and that there were 19 firearms in the room,” a prosecutor said.
After the shooting, investigators say Ryan Hanafin was on his way to Vermont when he was arrested by state police.
Ryan Hanafin pleaded not guilty and is being held without bail. He is due back in court next month.

title: Hughes scores 4 touchdowns as Bangor High football tops Edward Little
text:
BANGOR, Maine — Dynamic Bangor High School junior slotback-wide receiver Gavin Hughes scored four touchdowns and the Rams took a giant step forward in clinching a Class A North playoff berth with a 35-14 victory over undermanned and turnover-prone Edward Little High School of Auburn at Cameron Stadium on Friday night.
The teams were tied for the fourth and final playoff berth entering the game.
Bangor is now 3-3 while the Eddies fell to 2-4.
Edward Little only had 26 players due to injuries and disciplinary action.
Bangor was holding a 21-14 lead early in the third period when linebacker Will Houghton recovered a fumble at the Bangor 41-yard line.
Bangor strung together an 11-play, 59-yard drive capped by Hughes’ two-yard TD run with 3:53 left in the period.
On the next drive, a pass from Ashton Sullivan went through the hands of his receiver and Bangor’s Hayden Summerlin intercepted it and returned it to the EL-25.
“(Summerlin) has great ball skills. It was one of those situations where it was right place, right time. He has been making big plays like that for us all year,” said Bangor head coach Jack Hersom.
Sullivan is a tight end who was filling in at quarterback for the injured Logan Stout.
Junior quarterback Alex Tennett found Summerlin for an 18-yard completion and, two plays later, Hughes dashed into the end zone from the three.
Hughes’ touchdown was his seventh over the last two games.
He returned the game’s opening kickoff 87 yards for a touchdown.
“I’m trying to do the best I can but as long as Bangor is on top at the end of the day, it doesn’t matter what I do. It takes all of us. Everybody on that field works hard,” said the 5-foot-9½, 170-pound Hughes, who was utilized more in the second half with five carries for 18 yards and a pass reception for 15 after having just two carries for eight yards in the first half.
“I just take advantage of the touches I get,” said Hughes. “The coaches are going to do what is right for the team whether it’s giving the ball to me or giving it to my teammates. Whenever I get the ball, I try to make the most out of it. As long as the Bangor side of the scoreboard has higher numbers than the other team, that’s all that matters.”
“It’s a fine balance,” said Hersom. “We don’t want to wear him out but he’s an explosive player so we’re trying to find that balance of getting him the ball and not letting the defense sell out on him a little bit because we do have other guys who are capable.”
Hughes said he told his teammates before the game he was going to return the opening kickoff for a touchdown.
“Just coming out of the gate, Coach (Hersom) got me fired up. I was ready to go. I told everyone before it, I was going to take it back (for a touchdown). We were going to get this started off with a bang and then we’re going to play tough all game and get the win.”
Summerlin finished with five catches for 68 yards.
EL lost another fumble on its next possession.
Bangor took a 21-14 lead into the intermission.
Hughes was untouched on his 87-yard kickoff return but the Red Eddies answered with a nice 64-yard touchdown pass from Sullivan to Logan Averill, who got behind the Ram defensive back.
Bangor responded with a nine-play, 72-yard drive capped by Tennett’s 21-yard keeper. He had rattled off a 16-yard run earlier in the drive and tossed a 32-yard pass to Summerlin while he was being chased toward the sidelines.
Bangor expanded the lead with 1:29 left in the first quarter when a low snap went through punter Logan Billings’ legs and was recovered by Bangor’s Lucas Matzilevich at the EL-2 yard line.
Two plays later, Hughes sprinted into the end zone from the one yard line.
But EL used a little trickery to cut the lead to 21-14 in the second period as Evan Madigan extended a drive by dashing 21 yards to pick up a first down on a fake punt while lined up in front of the punter.
The hard-running and elusive Madigan finished off the drive with runs of 13 and 22 yards.
Senior Madigan wound up with 115 rushing yards on 17 carries and had another touchdown run of 25 yards negated by a penalty.
Tennett completed 8 of 13 passes for 89 yards.
“We told our kids coming in we were going to have to play for four quarters,” said Hersom. “I thought the kids did a good job coming in at the half staying composed with it being just a one-touchdown game at that point.
“Our goal in the second half was shut them out, defensively, and we did that,” said Hersom.
He said getting the three turnovers in the second half was “huge.
“Field position-wise, that was helpful. We had some short fields for our offense and we capitalized. That was good to see,” he added.
The Bangor defense was led by Houghton, linebacker Obi Okafor, defensive end Matzilevich and defensive backs Hughes and Summerlin.
Defensive back Madigan, defensive end Kohlson Alexander and linebacker Cameron Davis were among EL’s defensive standouts. Davis had a sack.
Bangor will travel to Sanford for a Friday night game at 7 while Edward Little will entertain Mt. Blue of Farmington the same night at 7.

title: Hollywood Casino hosts inaugural Maine Science Awards
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Hollywood Casino in Bangor hosted the inaugural Maine Science Awards Thursday night.
The formal evening included cocktails, dinner and recognition honoring scientists, researchers and advocates making Maine a better and smarter place.
Honorees were recognized in five categories: Lifetime Achievement, Innovation, Impact, Surprising Science, and Advancing Trust in Science.
Organizers say that while the Maine Science Festival is a great gathering every year, they needed something more to shine a spotlight on Maine’s brightest science innovators.
“We realized we have a gap of we’re not actually really leaning into a few people in Maine that we can hold up in a spotlight and celebrate the work that they’ve done for Maine explicitly,” said Kate Dickerson, Executive Director of the Maine Discovery Museum.
“So that’s what this is about. Tons of nominations came in, like actually way more than we expected, so our committee had a lot of work to do. And that just shows me that people were both really interested in this and that we do have really great things happening here, and we had a lot to work with,” she said.
Dickerson also mentioned that she hopes to make the award ceremony an annual tradition celebrating excellence in Maine science.

title: Bar Harbor in limbo as legal disputes over cruise ships continue
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bar Harbor recently took new enforcement action against a business that brings passengers ashore from cruise ships — the latest flashpoint in a lengthy legal battle over the number of tourists disembarking in the popular destination.
The town on Mount Desert Island is embroiled in state and federal lawsuits stemming from an ordinance that aimed to dramatically cut back on cruise ship visitation. Officials, businesses and residents are waiting for a federal court order that could determine the scale of the industry going forward.
“We’d like to hope it’s relatively sooner rather than later,” said Everal Eaton, executive director of the Bar Harbor Chamber of Commerce. “That certainty is better for the business community and better for the residents as well to know going into next year what it’s going to look like.”
Since the early 2000s, Bar Harbor has become an increasingly popular destination for cruise ships. In 2022, 143 vessels called on the port, according to the town.
That growth brought concerns about congestion and safety. In 2022, voters approved an ordinance that limited disembarkations from cruise ships to 1,000 passengers a day. The citizen initiative passed with 58% of the vote. In 2024, an effort to repeal that ordinance failed by an even closer margin.
A group of businesses filed a federal lawsuit against the town in 2022 to challenge the ordinance. Nearly four years, a bench trial and a trip to the appeals court later, the case is still unresolved.
In May, Chief U.S. District Judge Lance Walker ruled that the 1,000-passenger cap is only constitutional and enforceable in July and August. Charles Sidman, a Bar Harbor resident who has championed the ordinance and intervened in the case, filed a motion asking the judge to reconsider and amend that order. Walker has not yet issued a ruling.
In the meantime, the parties have also become entrenched in disputes in state court over enforcement of the ordinance. Bar Harbor sent a notice of violation this month to a private pier owner for disembarking cruise ship passengers without a permit, which could add to the quagmire.
“The majority of people that I actually speak to in my day-to-day life are like, ‘When is this going to end?’ ” said Maya Caines, chair of the Bar Harbor Town Council.
ONGOING DISPUTE
Bar Harbor does not have a pier big enough for cruise ships. Instead, the vessels anchor nearby, and smaller tender boats transport passengers to and from the shore.
Eben Salvatore, director of operations for Bar Harbor Resorts, as well as two private piers and the primary tender boats in town, said that the ordinance that limited disembarkations prompted “hundreds of cancellations.”
“Every time the phone rang, it was another massive amount of revenue for a business owner out the window,” Salvatore said. “It was a very painful shock, and it still is.”
In 2024, the Bar Harbor Town Council created a regulatory framework with two separate permits required to enforce the ordinance.
“It’s really just there to ensure we understand and know the level of visitation,” Town Manager James Smith said.
The private piers, overseen by Salvatore, have never applied for the permits.
That summer, the town sent a notice of violation to one of the piers for disembarking passengers from a cruise ship. That action set off a flurry of additional litigation in state court. The parties are waiting for the Maine Supreme Judicial Court to address two separate appeals. If the violation stands, the pier owner could have to pay steep fines.
The town and the business disagree on whether the permitting system is constitutional, based on the latest order from Walker in the federal case.
This month, Bar Harbor issued a second notice of violation to the pier, known as Golden Anchor LC in court records.
“It’s troubling that we seem to have been triggered without our own willingness into another round of litigation,” said Timothy Woodcock, the lawyer representing Golden Anchor and other businesses.
BUSINESSES UNCERTAIN
Sidman, a retired scientist who operates a Bar Harbor gallery with his wife, fought to get the ordinance in front of voters in 2022 and has since defended it in court as an intervenor in the federal lawsuit.
“It was worse than bumper cars at a circus,” Sidman said of the peak traffic from cruise ships. “It was aesthetically unpleasant, it was dangerous and it was detrimental to business.”
He said he would pursue another citizen initiative if the federal court ultimately overturns the ordinance.
“If we have to, we will relegislate it even stronger and more clearly,” Sidman said. “We want our town. We don’t want it submerged by cruise ships and big hotels.”
With lawsuits pending, many say the town is in limbo. Vessels continue to call on Bar Harbor, but not in the same numbers as in the past, according to the town. A dozen or so cruises with a capacity of 3,000-plus visited this year because they made reservations in 2020 and weren’t subject to the newer rules, according to the town.
The town also reached an agreement with American Cruise Lines and got the required permits to regularly disembark its passengers at a public pier this year. Those vessels have a capacity of 250 or less, Smith said.
Eaton, from the local chamber of commerce, said some businesses are uncertain how to staff or order inventory for next year because they don’t know how many cruise ship passengers will be allowed. Kevin DesVeaux, who owns West Street Cafe, said the restaurant has not been profitable since 2022, and lunch sales are down 30% in that time.
He said he is draining his savings to keep the restaurant open.
“We have no more to give,” DesVeaux wrote in an email. “This winter we will decide if we are going to go on the market or hold on for one more year for the cruise ship traffic to return.”
Salvatore and Woodcock said town officials should be making plans to welcome visitors from cruise ships in 2027, especially in the shoulder seasons when the 1,000-passenger cap is not currently enforceable.
“Let’s sit down in a room and work this out,” Salvatore said. “It can’t be hard. Staying in litigation is the worst thing to do.”
Town officials said it’s hard to proceed when so many lawsuits are active.
“We’re trying to be respectful and honoring the citizens’ initiative while being mindful of the legal rights and interests of other parties,” Smith said. “We believe that there is a need for local regulations for disembarking cruise ship passengers, and we want to be able to do that in a way that will meet the test of the court.”
Caines, the town council chair, said she and others want to focus on compromise instead of reacting to court proceedings.
“It’s really dependent quite a lot on the other parties that have been initiating these lawsuits,” she said.

Jared Golden’s unspent campaign funds are going across the country
text:
When U.S. Rep. Jared Golden announced he wouldn’t run for reelection this year, he said he planned to use the nearly $2 million in his war chest to support Democrats across the country.
So far, he’s put his money where his mouth is.
In its latest filing with the Federal Election Commission, made public Thursday afternoon, Golden’s campaign committee reported spending nearly $300,000 between July and October. Much of that cash went toward moderate Democrats’ campaigns.
The largest expenditure by far was to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which supports the party’s candidates for U.S. House. Golden gave the organization $150,000 in late September.
Golden has occasionally drawn the ire of his party’s leadership for his moderate stances and willingness to break party ranks on important votes. In September, he and Rep. Marie Glusenkamp Perez, D-Wash., were scorned by Democratic leaders for a “blindside” vote in support of several Republican-led bills.
After the DCCC, Gluesenkamp Perez was the next largest recipient of Golden’s campaign cash over the last three months. Her reelection PAC received a $40,000 contribution from Golden in late September.
Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez are co-chairs of the Blue Dog PAC, a committee that supports conservative-leaning Democrats running for and serving in Congress.
In recent months, Golden gave the maximum $2,000 to six Democrats backed by Blue Dog PAC that are each vying to flip Republican congressional seats in Florida, Kentucky, Minnesota, Montana, Ohio and Wisconsin.
Three other Democrats’ reelection campaigns received $1,000 contributions from Golden: Incumbent U.S. Reps. John Larson in Connecticut, Darren Soto in Florida and Seth Magaziner in Rhode Island.
“As he’s done during his time in office, Congressman Golden will continue to support candidates and causes he believes in,” Golden spokesperson Mario Moretto said in a statement provided after this story was initially published.
The donation to Larson was made on Aug. 7, just days before he lost a primary election that ultimately ended his nearly 30-year congressional tenure.
Those contributions follow the pattern of Golden’s other donations this year, the majority of which have gone to moderate Democrats facing tight campaigns across the country.
In Maine, Golden gave $500 to both Lewiston Democrat Shenna Cox’s state Senate and Auburn Democrat Adam Lee’s state House campaigns.
Golden also contributed $1,050 to Oxford County Sheriff Chris Wainwright’s reelection bid. Wainwright, notably, is the only Republican Golden contributed to this quarter.
The donation, dated Sept. 30, was made just days after several Oxford County deputies’ complaints of retaliation within the office were made public.
Several Maine-based nonprofits also received thousands of dollars from Golden’s campaign funds. Operation Reboot Outdoors, a Turner-based organization that sponsors hunting and fishing trips for law enforcement officers and veterans, got $25,000. The Solidarity Solutions Foundation in Lisbon Falls received $5,000.
Golden made a “charitable contribution” of $25,000 to Moving America Forward, a Utah-based voter outreach organization that focuses on engaging political independents, namely through canvassing and town halls.
Golden’s spending has ramped up as November has neared. His committee spent about $93,000 in the first quarter of 2026 and $65,000 in the second, according to FEC filings.
The nearly $300,000 he spent during the third quarter blows those totals out of the water. And he still has nearly $105,000 on hand, his latest filing shows.

title: New York Democrats want parking lot owners to ban ICE from their properties
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Mayor Zohran Mamdani and top New York Democrats are calling on the owners of private parking lots to block federal immigration officers from using their properties as staging areas, days after immigration officers shot a man in the city.
In a Friday letter, Mamdani, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and dozens of state and local lawmakers told lot and garage owners that the city needs their “help at a critical juncture.”
“In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend, or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations,” the letter reads. “Make it known to ICE that it is not authorized to use your garages and lots.”
The plea came after immigration officers shot 28-year-old Dominican national Oscar Belgal during an arrest last week as he rode in a car with his young son. The shooting sparked protests and drew renewed attention to the federal government’s immigration crackdown.
The federal officers had been using a nearby private parking lot as a staging area before the shooting, according to Friday’s letter.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security slammed the letter in a statement that read: “Mayor Mamdani should be grateful to our brave law enforcement officers for cleaning up the streets of NYC since he won’t. Luckily, no terminated parking will stop ICE from deporting criminal illegal aliens to make New York safe again.”
Federal officials maintain the immigration officers believed their lives were in danger and opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and accelerated toward them.
New York City has previously barred outside law enforcement agencies such as DHS from setting up staging areas on city property unless they have a judicial warrant or qualify for certain “limited legal exceptions,” according to the letter. “But these laws govern City property, not the private lots and garages that you operate,” it adds.
Private businesses have at times found themselves in the middle of tense political fights over President Donald Trump’s administration’s immigration enforcement push.
In one instance, a Minnesota hotel that refused to let immigration officers stay there in January apologized after public criticism from DHS, saying the decision violated its internal policies. In another, protesters occupied the lobby of a Manhattan hotel they said was housing some immigration officers.

title: Hargrove, Goodwin Win Week Six Athlete of the Week
text:
Wisdom’s Hargrove and Houlton’s Goodwin named Fall Week Six Athletes of the Week
The votes are in, and Cayden Hargrove of Wisdom and Presley Goodwin of Houlton are the Fall Week Six Aroostook County Athletes of the Week.
Hargrove earned the boys honor after a huge offensive stretch for the Wisdom boys soccer team, while Goodwin takes the girls award following a top-three finish at the Class C State Golf Championships.
They emerged from a Week Six field featuring 15 nominees and standout performances in soccer, cross country and golf from across Aroostook County.
Boys Athlete of the Week: Cayden Hargrove, Wisdom
Hargrove put together one of the most productive offensive weeks of the fall.
Across three reported games, the Wisdom standout totaled 4 goals and 3 assists, consistently creating scoring opportunities for the Pioneers.
That seven-point stretch helped Hargrove earn his place on a loaded Week Six boys ballot and ultimately the most support from County voters.
Girls Athlete of the Week: Presley Goodwin, Houlton
Goodwin delivered when the stakes were highest.
Representing Houlton at the Class C State Golf Championships, Goodwin shot a 92 to finish third in the state.
The postseason performance earned her a spot on the Week Six ballot and, after the votes were counted, the girls Athlete of the Week honor.
Fall Week Six Boys Nominees
Hunter Anderson, Southern Aroostook, Soccer
The freshman scored an unassisted hat trick and added an assist in Southern Aroostook's 4-1 victory over Washburn, accounting for all four Warrior goals in just their second win of the season.
Malachi Witmer, Houlton/GHCA, Cross Country
Witmer won the Red Riot Challenge, crossing the finish line in 13:22.20.
Finn Gardiner, Hodgdon, Soccer
Gardiner recorded 1 goal and 4 assists during Hodgdon's win over MSSM.
Aiden Carleglio, Hodgdon, Soccer
Carleglio made 22 saves in Hodgdon's 1-1 double-overtime tie with Fort Fairfield before adding another 18 saves against MSSM, giving him 40 saves across two games.
Conor Schmidt, Katahdin, Soccer
Schmidt continued his strong season with 3 goals and 1 assist during Katahdin's Week Six action.
Cayden Hargrove, Wisdom, Soccer
Hargrove totaled 4 goals and 3 assists across three reported games for the Pioneers.
Beckett Peabody, Houlton, Golf
Peabody shot a 76 to tie for third place in Class C at the State Golf Championships.
Fall Week Six Girls Nominees
Trinity Lane, Katahdin, Soccer
Lane recorded the shutout in Katahdin's 4-0 victory over Piscataquis Community and followed it by helping keep the Cougars tied with Shead through regulation and into double overtime in a 2-1 loss.
Clara St. Pierre, Van Buren, Soccer
St. Pierre contributed 2 goals and 1 assist during Van Buren's victory over MSSM.
Stevi Pierce, Central Aroostook, Soccer
Pierce scored 2 goals in Central Aroostook's 4-0 victory over Ashland.
Sadie Trams, Ashland, Soccer
Trams exploded for 7 goals across two reported games, scoring five in one contest and two in another.
Reece Doucette, Fort Kent, Soccer
Doucette scored 6 goals across two games, including a four-goal performance.
Ellie Cyr, Wisdom, Soccer
Cyr continued her high-scoring season with 4 goals and 1 assist during Week Six.
Presley Goodwin, Houlton, Golf
Goodwin shot a 92 to finish third at the Class C State Golf Championships.
Ava Toussaint, Madawaska, Soccer
Toussaint earned her nomination after recording a hat trick for Madawaska.
Another Big Week Across The County
Week Six brought together everything Athlete of the Week is designed to recognize: state championship performances, race victories, huge scoring totals, goalkeeper heroics and players stepping up in important moments for their teams.
Congratulations to Cayden Hargrove and Presley Goodwin, and to all 15 athletes who earned nominations.
Thank you to everyone who submitted nominations and voted throughout the week.

title: Showers Ending Early, Cold & Windy Saturday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A cold front moving from northwest to southeast will continue to bring light showers through the early evening. Most spots will see less than a tenth of an inch of additional rainfall.
Low pressure departs Friday night, high pressure will build in behind it, tightening the pressure gradient. Northwest winds will increase Friday night, gusting at times to 30 mph.
Lows will fall into the 30s and low 40s, but the wind will make it FEEL sub-freezing into early Saturday.
There will be a chance for minor icing on raised surfaces, including bridges, overpasses and decks, across northern areas early Saturday if wet surfaces remain. Use caution on elevated roadways.
Saturday: Cold and Windy
Saturday will be cold and windy. Expect clouds in the morning Saturday that will give way to sunshine by the afternoon.
Highs Saturday will range from the upper 30s to the mid 40s, but it will FEEL at or below freezing thanks to a strong northwest wind gusting to 35 mph.
Wrap-around precipitation will be possible in the Mountains Saturday, where light snow is possible with little, if any, accumulation.
It will get cold Saturday night into Sunday morning, with overnight lows down into the 20s. This could be one of the coldest nights so far this season. The good news: winds will weaken Saturday night, so wind chill values will not play a big role.
Sunday: Pick Of The Weekend
Sunday will feature mostly sunny skies with highs in the 40s and low 50s. West winds will be much weaker Sunday, with gusts to 20 mph.
Next Week: Dry and Milder
High pressure will remain parked over the Northeast for most of next week. This will keep conditions dry with mostly clear skies through the week. Highs will climb into the 50s and 60s.
First Alert 7-Day Forecast
TONIGHT: Cloudy with rain showers ending early. Lows will range from 32° to 42°. Winds out of the northwest will pick up with gusts to 30 mph possible.
SATURDAY: Mostly sunny skies with snow showers in the mountains. Highs in the 30s & 40s and will FEEL colder. NW gusts to 35 mph.
SUNDAY: Cold morning. Mostly sunny skies with highs in the 40s and low to mid 50s. NW gusts to 20 mph.
MONDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s and low 60s.
TUESDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s and low to mid 60s.
WEDNESDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s and low to mid 60s.
THURSDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s.

title: Looking back week of Oct. 22
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Southwest Harbor
Pemetic Elementary School has begun a small-scale solar energy project that could expand and help cut the school’s electric bill. School board member Prentice “Skip” Strong said the project was in response to an increase in electric rates. “Last year, around March, our electric bill jumped from $5,000 to $8,000 a month,” Mr. Strong said. Two years ago, Mr. Strong purchased three small photovoltaic panels for use at his home. The units convert sunlight into electricity. Although each panel produces only 160 watts of electricity, Mr. Strong was impressed with their performance. Because the system connects with the Bangor Hydro-Electric power grid, the excess electricity generated by the panels was fed back into the company’s system. “It was really cool to see that [electric] meter run backwards,” Mr. Strong said. If the panels could reduce his own electric bill, why couldn’t they do the same thing at the school, Mr. Strong thought. He decided to loan his panels to the school, to be used both as an educational tool and to study the feasibility of generating electricity for the school on a larger scale.

title: More roller coasters shut down as authorities investigate fatal fall at Georgia amusement park
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — A growing number of amusement parks have shut down roller coasters as police and state regulators investigate what caused a man to fall out of his seat and plummet to his death at a Georgia park.
SeaWorld Orlando in Florida and La Ronde theme park in Montreal, Canada, confirmed on Thursday they had temporarily closed rides, bringing the total number of roller coasters halted to 11.
Police and a state regulatory agency are investigating what caused Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, to fall from the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. Witnesses described seeing him ejected from the coaster; some people who rode the Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints.
Nine of the roller coasters taken out of service have the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system as the Goliath at Six Flags.
Mom says her son’s restraint didn’t work properly
Erica Billups said her son and daughter rode Goliath about an hour before Kariem’s death and encountered a problem with the restraint on one seat. Her son initially sat in that seat and tried to lock it, but then moved when it repeatedly became unlocked. The roller coaster embarked with the seat empty and the harness up, she said in a post on X.
She confirmed the post in a text message to The Associated Press on Thursday.
She said staff did not tell her kids there was a problem.
Summer Bates, who was at the Georgia park with her husband and three children and saw Kariem fall, told the AP previously that her older two children kept trying to push their restraints down tighter while on the ride. She understood why they were doing that later when she was on the coaster, she said, because the restraints didn’t feel secure.
Six Flags did not immediately respond to an email for comment on any issues with restraints.
At least one of the other closures is for safety
La Ronde in Montreal said one of its coasters — also named Goliath — is offline “while we conduct a thorough safety review in collaboration with the ride’s manufacturer.” Sea World Orlando said that it closed its Mako roller coaster with no set date to reopen.
Neither La Ronde nor SeaWorld Orlando said why those specific rides were closed. Both were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, which also built the Goliath ride in Georgia and eight of the other coasters that Six Flags closed. Bolliger & Mabillard declined Thursday to answer questions about the shutdowns.
In an updated list of ride closures provided Thursday, Six Flags no longer included the Goliath coaster at its Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California. The coaster has a different manufacturer and restraint system from the others. Six Flags had listed it as closed earlier in the week.
Online photos and videos of most of the closed coasters show each equipped with so-called “clamshell” restraints, mounted in front of each seat on a vertical bar that sits between the rider’s knees. The bar locks the padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.
It’s unclear from the images whether any of those coasters also have seat belts or other secondary restraints. Goliath in Georgia has no such backup restraints.
Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group, said the similar restraint systems are almost certainly why most of the coasters were closed.
Speigel said they’re likely to remain shut down until investigators have determined what went wrong on the Georgia coaster, but he said that “obviously it was something with the restraint.”
Roller coaster manufacturers decide what type of restraints to use after considering speed, force and the track’s transitions, said Brian D. Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert.
He advocates the use of a backup restraint for riders, but there is a long-running debate in the industry over whether that would increase wait times, Avery said.
Bolliger & Mabillard says it is investigating
The company said in an email it would have no further comment until it had a “better understanding of what transpired” on Monday.
Kariem was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Goliath, one of Six Flags Over Georgia’s headline attractions, towers above the park’s entrance. It opened in 2006 and features a series of hills and turns. It doesn’t take riders upside down, but its first hill rises to 200 feet (61 meters) and it has a top speed of 70 miles per hour (112 kilometers).
Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars passing overhead, said it looked like Kariem was hovering because the car was moving underneath him. He fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mendenhall said, and then was ejected from the ride on its final turn.
Six Flags has faced legal trouble before
A class-action lawsuit filed by investors in 2025 alleges that Six Flags concealed the poor state of its amusement parks — including long-neglected maintenance — ahead of its merger with major amusement park operator Cedar Fair.
“Prior to the Merger, Legacy Six Flags had for years deferred or foregone basic park maintenance, operational improvements, infrastructure repairs, and ride design and development updates,” the complaint said. The company also cut staffing to reduce costs, it alleges.
Timothy Loranger, a California attorney who sued Six Flags in a fatal case, said it’s a positive step that the theme park chain closed down rides at other parks as a precaution. Loranger represented the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 roller coaster in 2022 at Six Flags Magic Mountain.
“In all instances, X2 had many reports of injury in the past, and instead of doing a deep dive investigation into the ride, they did things like blame the passengers, the injured person for not sitting properly or holding their head against the headrest or they blamed an imaginary pre-existing condition,” Loranger said.
Six Flags permanently closed the X2 ride last month.
Georgia park to reopen
Six Flags Over Georgia is set to reopen on Friday. The Goliath, however, is not expected to be running.
The park, which has about a dozen roller coasters, is in Mableton, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta.

title: Graham Platner had millions of dollars on hand when he dropped out. Where has it gone?
text:
Graham Platner’s U.S. Senate campaign fell apart in a matter of days. His campaign is still dishing out payments to pick up the pieces.
The then-unknown oyster farmer launched what was initially a longshot campaign in August last year. Platner’s slick online presence, military background and passionate speaking style powered him to an overwhelming primary victory over Gov. Janet Mills — a feat that seemed impossible when he jumped into the race.
The campaign galvanized support from small-dollar donors in Maine and around the country. But after Platner abruptly ended his campaign in July following a credible allegation of sexual assault from one of his former partners, which Platner vehemently denied, the campaign was left with around $1.7 million on hand.
New filings with the Federal Election Commission submitted Thursday show where that money has gone since his bid ended.
The campaign has spent over $2.3 million since July, the data shows. Much of that was used to reimburse those who powered Platner’s ascent.
Over $70,000 in small-dollar donations were refunded after Platner dropped out, the FEC filing shows, while campaign staffers cumulatively got just over $350,000 in severance pay following his withdrawal.
The largest single severance payout was just over $20,000, given to Amy Gertner: Platner’s wife. Gertner also received about $980 as a “win bonus” following the primary, as did about 30 other campaign staffers.
The severance pay was stipulated in the Platner staff’s union contract, according to a former campaign source not authorized to speak publicly. The amount given to each staffer was determined based on their tenure with the campaign. Gertner had been there since the beginning.
Neither Platner nor several other former campaign employees responded to requests for comment on the post-withdrawal expenditures.
The campaign cumulatively spent around $350,000 on consulting firms specializing in communications, fundraising, research and other areas between July and October.
About a third of the consulting spending came after Platner’s withdrawal in early July. Those payouts were the result of contracts the campaign had signed with consulting firms through Election Day, the campaign source said — though some were for a “postmortem” winding down of the campaign’s operations.
None of Platner’s leftover campaign funds have gone to his replacement in the Senate race, Troy Jackson, or any other campaigns around the country. Asked in July if he would accept an endorsement from Platner, Jackson said “It’s unfortunate, but I just don’t want it.”
Other Maine politicians with cash remaining from now-dormant campaigns have put tens of thousands of dollars toward other candidates in Maine and around the country.
U.S. Rep. Jared Golden has given contributions to about 10 other moderate Democrats in recent months after announcing he wouldn’t seek reelection this year. Sara Gideon, who still has some $2 million on hand from her failed campaign against Sen. Susan Collins in 2020, has chipped in over $375,000 to Democrats in Maine, New Hampshire and elsewhere, per her most recent FEC filing.
Platner has largely stayed out of the public eye since dropping out. He was initially slated to speak and lead a veterans’ march at a Labor Day event in Ellsworth, which would have been his first public appearance post-campaign. But Platner ultimately didn’t speak following widespread backlash.
Platner’s FEC filing indicates he still has just under $100,000 on hand.

title: Teacher says she thought she was ‘going to die saving my kids’ in deadly elementary school shooting
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — A teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Oregon said she was prepared to die to save her students during a mass shooting that left multiple people dead.
From her classroom window, Kathy Smith said she witnessed the 16-year-old shooter walking into the elementary school with a long gun.
“I just figured today, OK, today is the day that I’m sure every teacher at the school thought, today is the day that I’m going to die saving my kids,” Smith said.
Smith said she immediately called the main office to warn them an active shooter was on school grounds, then hid her students in a corner, hoping the shooter wouldn’t come inside.
“They were so afraid, the looks on their faces, it was really hard to see. I was just trying to calm them down. Some kids were praying, some kids were consoling other kids, but they were doing it quietly because they know you don’t make any noise,” she said.
Bend police said the shooter shot at a person in a vehicle before forcing his way into the school by shooting at locked doors.
The shooting killed a 5-year-old, an 8-year-old, an 11-year-old and one teacher. Another child and a teacher were wounded and taken to a hospital in critical condition.
The 16-year-old shooter was killed by a bystander who police said followed the gunman into the building.
Smith said that person saved countless lives, including her own.
“That person saw something, they did something, and that took its own courage,” Smith said.
Smith said the tragedy is constantly replaying in her head, and she can’t imagine how the close-knit school family will ever be the same.
“I don’t see how, but also in my head I refuse to let somebody tear apart our family even more, because if we don’t return and if we don’t come together, then that person wins,” she said.

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: The fight for water product safety changes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A mother’s fight for water product safety changes a decade after losing her son.
Plus, “learn to swim” – that’s what one floatie label promised. But critics are concerned some devices actually may teach a false sense of safety.
Fight for water product safety changes
Wearable floaties are often marketed as learn-to-swim aids for toddlers. Some even carry “Coast Guard approved” language—but parents and researchers worry they can create a false sense of safety.
National Investigative Reporter Caresse Jackman examines drowning-prevention concerns, including stories from families who say tragedy struck after taking the floaty off - and she investigates potential gaps in federal oversight as advocates push for clearer warnings and stronger standards.
Discount deception
Prices and affordability are a major concern to Americans everywhere, and many may not realize some stores are taking advantage of them—with deceptive pricing tactics.
Our investigation looks at examples of some retailers inflating original prices before sales, creating fake discounts, and running constant promotions that make deals seem urgent when they’re not real at all.
Even though these tactics are against FTC regulations, the federal government rarely steps in. We find out why, show you the signs of deceptive pricing, and walk the viewer through what they can do to fight back.
Claiming Social Security
When you claim Social Security could mean tens of thousands of dollars over the course of your retirement.
In this Watching Your Wallet, Consumer Investigator Rachel DePompa digs into when it makes sense to claim early, when to hold off, and the special strategies married couples should consider so they don’t leave money on the table.

title: ‘Presumably a space object’: 11-foot metallic object found in Minnesota cornfield
text:
STEVENS COUNTY, Minn. (Valley News Live/Gray News) — State and federal authorities are working to identify a large metallic object found in a cornfield in Minnesota.
The Stevens County Sheriff’s Office received a call around 3:30 p.m. on Oct. 14 reporting foreign debris in a Scott Township field.
Deputies responded and confirmed a large metallic object, approximately 11 feet in diameter, which the sheriff’s office said is “presumably a space object.”
The sheriff’s office said the Minnesota Duty Officer was notified. State and federal agencies are working to identify the object’s owner and plan for its removal from the field.
There is no danger to the public, the Stevens County Sheriff’s Office said.

title: The Latest: 16-year-old kills 3 children and a teacher at Oregon elementary school
text:
A 16-year-old opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before he was shot by a person at the scene who pursued him into the school, according to the chief of police.
The three children killed were aged 5, 8 and 11. Another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, were injured and taken to the hospital in critical condition, authorities say.
Police said they did not know if the shooter, a Bend resident, knew anyone at the school or whether he had attended.
The Latest:
Police responded within minutes
Some 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education.
Children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their childrens’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home.
Man who stopped the shooter has 2 daughters at the school
The man who shot and killed the school shooter in Bend, Oregon has been identified by his mother.
Kenda Freeman said Kyle Giamanco is a lifelong Bend resident and a father with two young daughters at Silver Rail Elementary School.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” she said, reading from a prepared statement to reporters outside her son’s residence near the school.
Freeman said the family is asking for privacy “during this difficult time” and is not giving interviews.
Trump praises ‘great hero’ who helped after Oregon school shooting
President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House he had been briefed on the shooting and praised the actions of a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump said, saying the tragedy otherwise likely would have been much worse.
The shooter used a gun bought by his mom
The 16-year-old suspect, identified only as a Bend resident, was found dead inside the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Mike Krantz said. Police said he got into the school by shooting through locked doors.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Police said they didn’t know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended it.
—- By Haven Daley, Alanna Durkin Richer and Eric Tucker
A parent says she was amazed a member of the public pursued the shooter
Brooke Olsen’s daughter is a kindergartener at Silver Rail.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. “I’m feeling very grateful.”
Officials will provide an update on the shooting
Officials plan to hold a news conference at 2 p.m. PDT Friday at the Bend Municipal Court about the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary. They say they will provide the latest information and share resources that are available for community members.

title: Officials say investigation into Six Flags roller coaster death continues as the park prepares to reopen
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — Six Flags Over Georgia reopens on Friday, less than a week after a man died falling off a roller coaster at the park.
The park will be open from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m. for Fright Fest, a Halloween-themed event, as originally scheduled. Goliath, the roller coaster on which the accident happened, will remain closed.
On Monday, 42-year-old Hassan Kariem was ejected from the ride, hitting and injuring several other patrons before the fall, according to Cobb County police. His body was found underneath the roller coaster, and the park was evacuated.
Kariem’s niece was on the ride next to him, according to his brother-in-law, Joshua Nelson. Nelson said that Kariem’s restraint came undone as the ride dropped.
Cobb County and police officials on Friday said no new investigative findings were going to be announced but said the investigation into what happened is ongoing.
Cobb County Commission Chairwoman Lisa Cupid said the investigation into the accident is a priority for the county.
“Right now, our attention belongs to the people who were hurt,” Cupid said.
Cobb County police said they are assisting the state in its investigation. Police reported that the state is looking into the maintenance of the roller coaster. Cobb County police said if there are no criminal charges, the department’s case will close when the state finishes its investigation.
As the park prepares to reopen, park management called safety its highest priority.
In a statement released on Friday, Six Flags Over Georgia Park President Richard Pretlow said the park is “deeply saddened” by the death.
“As efforts to understand the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident continue, we remain focused on supporting those affected and maintaining the safe operation of our park and attractions,” he said. “All other rides and attractions that were scheduled to operate will be available to guests, subject to normal operating conditions and availability.”
He added that millions of people safely enjoy rides and other attractions at Six Flags parks every year.
“While serious incidents of this nature are exceedingly rare, we never take responsibility to our guests for granted and remain committed to continuous learning and improvement,” Pretlow said.
Documents from the Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire show the Goliath roller coaster passed its inspections from 2016 to 2026, with its most recent inspection in March noting only that “bushings” needed replacing. Ride manufacturers describe bushings as equipment that reduces friction and absorbs shock between the ride’s metal parts.
Earlier reports in 2016 and 2019 noted some corrosion and rust on parts of the ride, which records show were addressed.
Six Flags has also temporarily shut down nine rides across six parks that are similar to Goliath, which uses a lap restraint.
As park officials plan to reopen, some park-goers have overarching concerns about safety in the park.

Not even just that family, everyone else in the Atlanta area who might be considering going to the park or who have even said I’m not going to the park at all,” he told ANF. “To see it open, I think that’s probably a bad look.”
