title: Tesla’s new Roadster ‘flying car’ can thrust itself in the air
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Tesla has unveiled its new Roadster sports car, which can thrust itself in the air, among other engineering bells and whistles. But drivers shouldn’t expect to take it for a spin anytime soon.
Elon Musk’s electric car company rolled out its second-generation Roadster at a Thursday event, showing off a set of cold gas thrusters and a “multi-mode” suction system that can fling the car in the air for short spurts and spin the vehicle mid-flight.
“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk, Tesla’s CEO, wrote on his social media platform X shortly after.
Well, maybe a long, long time in the future, given the regulatory hurdles for flying vehicles and the tangle of state rules that still need to be met.
“I’m not sure every state is going to allow a driver in the middle of traffic to suddenly elevate himself and fly,” said David Vladeck, a Georgetown Law professor and former director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “There is going to be a long process to let anything like that on a road.”
Thursday’s event was hosted at the Texas rocket testing and development center for SpaceX — Musk’s publicly-traded rocket company — and Tesla’s executives noted that they “borrowed” some SpaceX technology to get the new Roadster in the air. Beyond quick jumps and flips, Tesla also said the car can accelerate from zero to 60 miles (96.6 km) an hour in less than a second.
This week’s launch arrived after years of delays and anticipation around the new Roadster — and Tesla shares climbed in morning trading on Friday before falling amid a sell-off in companies tied to artificial intelligence.
The wait isn’t completely over. Musk said production for consumers won’t begin until 2028. Tesla also didn’t immediately set a price tag on its latest EV.
Tesla was taking reservations for Roadster “rocket” car purchases on its website Friday morning, though the fine print said there was no guarantee when the vehicle would be delivered — or whether it would be delivered at all.
Bryant Walker Smith, a former Department of Transportation lawyer, was unimpressed, though he did note Musk’s ability to keep Tesla’s stock high.
“This was a demonstration of a one-off car using a technology around for many years and will not be coming to public roads in 2028,” said Smith, a law professor at the University of South Carolina. “Tesla pretty uniquely has been able to sell itself on a future that is an order of magnitude greater than reality.”
Musk has repeatedly said that the future of driving will be autonomous — and Austin-based Tesla has focused much of its business on building out self-driving features for its vehicles and, more recently, launching its own (still limited) robotaxi business.
But the company maintains that the Roadster will be made to have humans behind the wheel, calling the EV the “best of the last human-driven cars.”
Thursday’s demo was technically autonomous “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Musk noted. But long-term, he said, the new Roadster will be “the only manually driven car that Tesla makes.”
“This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car,” Musk later added, met by laughter from the audience. But “it takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10.”
Tesla’s first Roadster was launched back in 2008. And in 2018, Musk went as far as placing one on a rocket — with a mannequin dubbed “Starman” in the driver’s seat — and launching it into space.
Again, the second-generation Roadster isn’t immediately hitting the market. And whether the ambitious new vehicle boosts the company’s bottom line remains to be seen.
In second-quarter earnings reported over the summer, Tesla’s profits fell as the company spent more on research and development for its robotaxi and robotics businesses — which cut into money made from an otherwise sharp increase in vehicle sales. Net income totaled $1.11 billion for the period, while revenue climbed to $28.24 billion.

Seahawks roll past Bulldogs
text:
The Boothbay Region High School field hockey team got its eighth win of the season by defeating the Hall-Dale Bulldogs for the second time this season, 3-1, at Perkins Field Thursday afternoon.
Junior Moriah Smith, the team’s leading scorer, gave Boothbay a 1-0 lead with a goal at 2:06 of the first quarter.
Both teams picked up their offense in the second quarter with the Seahawks and Bulldogs each getting three penalty corner opportunities.
Boothbay extended its lead to 2-0 with 4:12 to play in the second quarter when sophomore Olivia Hardwick pushed the ball into an open goal after an assist from freshman Emma Doucette.
But just before the halftime horn sounded, the Bulldogs scored with 21 seconds to play on a goal by Avery Croll.
The Seahawks had several chances to score early in the third quarter but Bulldog goalie Haylie Stevens made some nice saves.
Junior Zuri Smith gave Boothbay its final goal pushing the ball into the left corner of the goal with 4:07 to play in the third.
Boothbay’s defense didn’t allow another shot on goal in the fourth quarter as the team improved to 8-4 and, as of Friday morning, moved into fourth place in Class C South.
The team’s final two games of the regular season will be at home against Oak Hill (rescheduled twice due to rain) on Saturday, Oct. 17 at 2 p.m. and Monday, Oct. 19 at 3:30 p.m. against Telstar. Oak Hill is 4-8 and Telstar is 1-12.

title: Woman charged after she allegedly shot at her neighbor during fence dispute, police say
text:
ST. CHARLES COUNTY, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - A woman in Missouri was charged after police said she shot at a neighbor during a fight about a fence.
Paula Kohensky, 60, faces charges of first-degree assault/attempted assault and armed criminal action after an incident Sunday night stemming from a property dispute with a neighbor, according to court documents.
St. Charles County police began an investigation after the neighbor reported that someone shot at her husband, according to the probable cause statement.
Kohensky refused to leave her home to talk with police until she eventually came out 30 minutes later.
In the statement, the husband told police he had been working on a fence through Sunday evening after a property-line dispute between him, Kohensky and her husband. He had brought out an electric grinder to cut a fence post after he misaligned it.
The husband heard yelling while the grinder was running, then a countdown from three, followed by a gunshot. He ran back inside and asked his wife to call the police.
Kohensky told police she had a “history of harassment and stalking issues” involving the neighbors.
Kohensky told police that she decided to walk her dog in the backyard that night and left the home with a handgun. She then heard loud metal scraping and saw sparks coming from under a tarp covering the fence.
Kohensky said she saw her neighbor’s shadow and yelled at him to get away from the fence. She claimed that the gun accidentally went off while she was holding it.
The statement said video surveillance footage from the neighbors’ home showed Kohensky and her husband standing side by side while Kohensky was pointing a gun at the fence.
The gun then appeared to fire before Kohensky’s husband took the gun, and both went back into their home.
Kohensky is held on a $500,000 bond and is scheduled for a preliminary hearing on Dec. 2, according to court records.

title: Officials give update on Six Flags roller coaster death as the park prepares to reopen
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — Six Flags Over Georgia reopens on Friday, less than a week after a man died falling off a roller coaster at the park.
The park will be open from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m. for Fright Fest, a Halloween-themed event, as originally scheduled. Goliath, the roller coaster on which the accident happened, will remain closed.
On Monday, 42-year-old Hassan Kariem was ejected from the ride, hitting and injuring several other patrons before the fall, according to Cobb County police. His body was found underneath the roller coaster, and the park was evacuated.
Kariem’s niece was on the ride next to him, according to his brother-in-law, Joshua Nelson. Nelson said that Kariem’s restraint came undone as the ride dropped.
Cobb County and police officials on Friday said no new investigative findings were going to be announced but said the investigation into what happened is ongoing.
Cobb County Commission Chairwoman Lisa Cupid said the investigation into the accident is a priority for the county.
“Right now, our attention belongs to the people who were hurt,” Cupid said.
Cobb County police said they are assisting the state in its investigation. Police reported that the state is looking into the maintenance of the roller coaster. Cobb County police said if there are no criminal charges, the department’s case will close when the state finishes its investigation.
As the park prepares to reopen, park management called safety its highest priority.
In a statement released on Friday, Six Flags Over Georgia Park President Richard Pretlow said the park is “deeply saddened” by the death.
“As efforts to understand the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident continue, we remain focused on supporting those affected and maintaining the safe operation of our park and attractions,” he said. “All other rides and attractions that were scheduled to operate will be available to guests, subject to normal operating conditions and availability.”
He added that millions of people safely enjoy rides and other attractions at Six Flags parks every year.
“While serious incidents of this nature are exceedingly rare, we never take responsibility to our guests for granted and remain committed to continuous learning and improvement,” Pretlow said.
Documents from the Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire show the Goliath roller coaster passed its inspections from 2016 to 2026, with its most recent inspection in March noting only that “bushings” needed replacing. Ride manufacturers describe bushings as equipment that reduces friction and absorbs shock between the ride’s metal parts.
Earlier reports in 2016 and 2019 noted some corrosion and rust on parts of the ride, which records show were addressed.
Six Flags has also temporarily shut down nine rides across six parks that are similar to Goliath, which uses a lap restraint.
As park officials plan to reopen, some park-goers have overarching concerns about safety in the park.
Billy Giles said resuming operations so soon after a fatal incident leaves him questioning whether profits are taking priority over guest safety.
“I think it’s very inconsiderate. I don’t think they’re taking into account the family’s feelings. Not even just that family, everyone else in the Atlanta area who might be considering going to the park or who have even said I’m not going to the park at all,” he told ANF. “To see it open, I think that’s probably a bad look.”
Georgia Insurance and Fire Safety Commissioner John King said his office is investigating the death. Inspectors have been on the ground looking at “every nook and cranny,” he added.

title: Hot, windy weather stoke brush fires spark in Southern California, power turned off for many
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Several brush fires were burning in Southern California on Friday, stoked by hot, windy weather that’s led to some evacuations and tens of thousands of people in the state waking up in the dark after their electricity was turned off.
A rapidly spreading blaze in Malibu, a coastal town west of Los Angeles, prompted evacuation orders and warnings for a large swathe of the Santa Monica Mountains. A large cloud of black smoke over the hilltops could be seen on nearby cameras and miles away. Wind gusts of up to 30 mph (48 kph) were reported early Friday and were forecast to increase, the National Weather Service said.
With humidity levels dropping, “this will favor a critical fire weather threat,” the service said early Friday.
More than 285 firefighters battled the Bryson Fire overnight, which grew to about 200 acres (81 hectares) and threatened a Los Angeles County juvenile detention and rehabilitative facility, which was evacuated Thursday night. Fire officials planned to give an update Friday morning.
Firefighters worked to contain two other fires that had sparked Thursday afternoon and triggered evacuation orders in the city of Azusa, north of LA, and Camp Pendleton, near San Diego.
More than 150,000 customers in northern, central and southern California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.
Some of California’s worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power during dry, windy weather in an effort to prevent blazes.
Weather conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday.
Santa Ana winds hit Southern California
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who faced criticism for her city’s response to deadly fires in 2025, directed the fire department to deploy personnel and equipment ahead of the winds. The fire department also requested assistance from the state’s office of emergency services.
“It’s a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
Dry, warm and gusty northeast winds known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior of Southern California toward the coast and offshore, were forecast, with the strongest winds expected through Friday afternoon.
The winds could reach 20 to 40 mph (32 to 64 kph), with gusts from 50 to 70 mph (80 to 113 kph), in the San Gabriel mountains in Los Angeles County and the Santa Susana mountains, which are mostly in Ventura County, Schoenfeld said. Elevated, though brief, critical fire weather conditions were also forecast for portions of the Santa Lucia mountains in San Luis Obispo County.
A wind-driven fire in Azusa burned over 40 acres (16 hectares) on Thursday and briefly prompted evacuation orders for a neighborhood in the foothills of the San Gabriel mountains. Forward progress on the blaze had been stopped by midafternoon.
Farther south, a fire at Camp Pendleton threatened buildings. Evacuation orders were issued in the Las Flores area of the military base and lifted by evening, military officials said in a statement.
Power cuts are widespread in Northern California
In Northern California, some communities in the Sierra Nevada and its foothills began experiencing strong winds, high temperatures and low humidity Wednesday night.
The weather service issued a red flag warning for parts of central and Northern California through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly. Such warnings are issued when weather conditions create an increased risk of wildfires.
The potential interruption in electricity to customers from the Central Coast to the upper corners of the Sierra Nevada could last through Saturday afternoon, Pacific Gas and Electric Company said.
Hot and windy conditions are expected through the weekend
In Southern California, the Red Flag Warning for the mountainous areas in Ventura and Los Angeles counties was in effect through Friday night.
In January 2025, the Palisades Fire — fanned by Santa Ana winds — ripped through a hillside Los Angeles neighborhood, killing 12 people and destroying mansions with spectacular ocean views. Authorities determined the Palisades Fire was a carryover from another fire that authorities alleged was started intentionally by a 29-year-old man.
Another fire that burned at the same time in the city of Altadena, in Los Angeles County, killed 19 people and destroyed more than 9,400 homes and businesses. That fire was caused by sparks from an idle transmission tower owned by Southern California Edison, officials said.
Schoenfeld said the Santa Ana winds are not going to be as strong as during those fires, when they were gusting 60 to 100 mph (96 to 160 kph).
___
Jaimie Ding reported from Los Angeles.

title: US to revive shuttered nuclear plants to power data centers, meet electricity demand
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
US to revive shuttered nuclear plants to power data centers and meet electricity demand
The United States is making an unprecedented attempt to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet rising energy demand, including from large-scale data centers.
Related video above: Senate blocks bill aimed at keeping data center costs off electric bills
No commercial nuclear reactor is known to have resumed generating electricity after beginning the decommissioning process that takes one out of service, though some reactors have restarted after long outages.
The Department of Energy is lending as much as $4.4 billion to restart the Palisades Power Plant in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center on Pennsylvania's Three Mile Island and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa to restore a combined 2.25 gigawatts of electricity, which can power roughly 2 million homes and businesses. All three of the plants closed before their licenses expired, largely because the electricity they produced was considered too expensive.
Not anymore. Two of the plants have contracts with Big Tech companies that will pay a premium to get large amounts of carbon-free energy for data centers. The Trump administration is pushing hard to deploy nuclear power for artificial intelligence and manufacturing. It's also lending billions of dollars for upgrades to produce more electricity from currently operating nuclear plants.
Restarting a reactor is a fairly quick way to get a lot of electricity, and it's cheaper than building a new, large reactor, said nuclear engineering expert Todd Allen.
"There's a demand in the country for more power," he said. "You have these assets that were previously hooked up. They were previously operable, and you can relatively quickly get them generating electricity again, compared to your other possibilities. For anyone who wants zero carbon, nuclear provides that. For the Trump administration, which really wants nuclear, this fits that story also."
Restarting a reactor is kind of like restoring a car
Allen compared restarting a decommissioned nuclear plant to restarting a car that sat idle for a few years. The driver still needs a valid license and all the parts need to be working correctly.
"That’s what they’re trying to do with these nuclear plants, but it’s a much bigger, complicated system," said Allen, associate dean for research at the University of Michigan's College of Engineering.
With a nuclear plant, the owner has to bring nuclear workers back and ensure their training is current, make sure everything is working and that maintenance is up to date, ensure they have enough fuel and ask regulators to restore their operating license, he added.
Allen said it's a lot to keep track of, but it's relatively straightforward.
Expert says restarts are risky
Edwin Lyman, at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the taxpayer money being used should go toward addressing safety risks. For example, most U.S. plants were built between 1970 and 1990 and were designed to withstand natural disasters of that era, said Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at UCS. But climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe.
"It’s possible, if they set the right level of safety and spend the necessary funds to meet that, they could restore these plants to operable condition," he said. "That's not happening at this point."
Iowa’s only nuclear facility, Duane Arnold, began operating in 1975. It was scheduled to permanently close in October 2020. Replacing it with cheaper energy sources, including wind, was projected to save Iowa customers $300 million in energy costs. The plant shut down early, in August 2020, when it was damaged during a powerful storm known as a derecho.
NextEra Energy owns Duane Arnold. Looking at its condition, CEO John Ketchum said company officials "felt really good about the ability to bring it back."
Palisades plant is the furthest along
The Palisades plant operated from 1971 until 2022, when its owner, Entergy, left the nuclear power business. The plant's operating license lasted until 2031.
Holtec International bought it and began dismantling it, though none of the steps were irreversible. Michigan officials, not wanting to lose nuclear jobs or energy, encouraged Holtec to pursue reopening the plant and provided state funding. The Biden administration in 2024 approved a $1.5 billion loan to restart the facility, and the Trump administration continued the payments.
In August, Holtec began loading nuclear fuel, one of the final major phases before a reactor can restart. The company paused the process after a fuel assembly tilted from its upright position and Holtec determined it needed to figure out why. Its power purchase agreements require Palisades to be in service by March 2027.
Holtec says its efforts will restore baseload power, strengthen energy security and demonstrate the role of nuclear energy in meeting the nation's growing electricity demands.
Big Tech will purchase power for data centers
NextEra Energy and Google are collaborating to restart Duane Arnold by early 2029.
"This is a perfect example of data centers paying their own way," Ketchum said in an interview. "We’re able to sign a long-term contract with a hyperscaler for that project. So none of the costs are being paid by residential customers in Iowa."
Microsoft has a contract with the Crane Clean Energy Center on Three Mile Island just outside Harrisburg. The plant was the site of the nation’s worst commercial nuclear power accident in 1979. The accident destroyed one reactor, leaving the plant with one functioning reactor. In 2019, Constellation Energy’s then-parent company Exelon shut down the functioning reactor, saying it was losing money and that Pennsylvania lawmakers had refused to subsidize it.
Constellation Energy announced in 2024 that it would spend $1.6 billion to restart the reactor under a 20-year agreement with Microsoft. It hopes to bring the plant back online in 2027. The Energy Department provided a $1 billion loan, and Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly took a tour last week.
Jack Spencer at The Heritage Foundation said he cannot think of a worse use of taxpayer money than using it to restart reactors. These are low-risk projects where there is a massive demand for the energy, so there is no reason to funnel federal dollars to these companies, said Spencer, director of the foundation's Center for Energy, Climate and Environment.
Conversely, Jennifer Gordon at the Atlantic Council said she thinks it's a terrific way of leveraging federal financing to get needed electricity. Gordon directs the council's Nuclear Energy Policy Initiative.
Industry group says reactors shouldn't close early
The World Nuclear Association said restarting nuclear reactors should be celebrated, but preventing them from closing prematurely would be the best option.
Palisades is expected to be the first nuclear plant in the world to resume generating power after beginning the decommissioning process, but other countries have restarted or refurbished reactors after long-term shutdowns, the association said. That includes Canada, Armenia, Belgium, Japan, India and South Korea. Others are considering or in the process of restarting reactors.
___
Associated Press writer Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia, contributed to this report.

title: ‘Paranormal Activity’ on Broadway Is Scarier Than Most ‘Paranormal Activity’ Movies
text:
‘Paranormal Activity’ on Broadway Is Better Than Most of the ‘Paranormal Activity’ Movies
At first glance, Paranormal Activity seems ripe for adaptation to the stage. The cast is small; primarily just a troubled young woman and her loving boyfriend. The original Paranormal film takes almost entirely place in one location; the couple’s simple suburban home. And its scares are mostly built out of suggestion and imagination, rather than elaborate and explicit special effects. A woman creepily sleepwalks. Something off-camera goes bump in the night.
But then you think about Paranormal Activity’s specifics, or you look back at the original film (which is currently streaming on Paramount+) and you realize: It’s actually a horrible candidate for a stage play. First and foremost it’s a found-footage movie, which means the entire story is organized around scenes that could plausibly be captured by an amateur photographer and his home-video camera. A lot of the movie consists of time-lapse video of the couple sleeping, punctuated by brief glimpses of vague spookiness. Imagine a play that faithfully recreated that on stage. It would be unbearable.
So first and foremost Broadway’s Paranormal Activity is a canny act of transformation. While the show contains the basic elements of the famous movie — a troubled young woman, a skeptical man, a single setting, dark secrets of the past coming to light — it possesses few of its formal qualities. The couple never records their home or what transpires in their bedroom while they’re asleep. Instead, their descent into paranoia and terror builds to multiple crescendos of supernatural dread as their rickety old home (beautifully replicated on stage by scenic and costume designer Fly Davis) fills with inexplicable shadows and smoke and unexplainable happenings. This Paranormal Activity is closer to Grand Guignol than found footage — and it’s a hell of a lot of fun.
READ MORE: The Differences Between Wicked the Film and Wicked the Show
The victims of its supernatural shenanigans are Jimmy (Travis A. Knight) and Lou (Cher Álvarez), recent transplants to London from Chicago. Playwright Levi Holloway’s script teases out murky trouble in their past; Jimmy asks Lou about her medication, and some sort of incident in their home that sparked their voyage across the Atlantic.
Jimmy loves and cares for Lou, but he may not necessarily believe everything she says. (She claims to experience gaps in her memory, where she wakes up in a place with no memory where she went or what she did, and occasionally senses some sort of spiritual presence floating around them.) But gradually the evidence begins to pile up Jimmy (and the audience) — flickering lights, home electronics suddenly turning off and on, knocks on doors and windows when no one is there — that becomes impossible to ignore.
Knight and Álvarez make a very credible couple, and they do a convincing job depicting their happy home’s bout of unearthly madness — and, without spoiling too much, of performing some of Holloway’s spooky plot twists. (They also get ghoulishly effective support from Shannon Cochran as Jimmy’s mother Carolanne.) But the real stars here are ultimately the staging and the scares which, through careful use of lighting (designed by Anna Watson) and sound effects (Greath Fry), generate an enormous amount of suspense across Paranormal Activity’s two-ish hours (including one intermission).
The set is a two-story cross-section of a London home, with a large kitchen and living room on the ground level, and an upstairs containing a bedroom, a bathroom, and a mostly unseen guest room whose door can open ominously on its own when required. Part of what made the original Paranormal Activity film such a phenomenon was the way it used low-fi digital photography to create a highly plausible simulacrum of reality. It was easy to get caught up in the film’s haunting because it was so simple and small.
A play can’t rely on judicious edits or careful camera placement to conjure such a specter of danger; there are no edits or cameras. Instead, Holloway and director Felix Barrett control the audience’s attention with blocking, movement, and very sneaky sleight of hand and misdirection. (The Playbill credits Chris Fisher as “Illusion Designer.”) Sometimes the action unfolds simultaneously on multiple levels; tracking it all at once suggests that Carrie director Brian De Palma and his famous split-screens might have been as much of an inspiration on Paranormal Activity as the movies that gave the show its title.
By pure coincidence, the same day I saw Paranormal Activity at New York’s August Wilson Theatre I finished reading a history of illusions and stage magic called Hiding the Elephant by Jim Steinmeyer. The book reveals the origins of some of the most famous magic tricks in history; making objects or animals disappear, sawing beautiful women in half.
The timing couldn’t have been more fortuitous; Barrett deploys some of the same 100-year-old illusions detailed in the book to bring Jimmy and Lou’s paranormal activity to life (or, uh, afterlife). All these decades later, they will work chillingly well. The result is like a modern fable set inside a haunted house, and a play that’s not only worthy of the movies that inspired it, it’s far more effective than a lot of them. I’m not sure you’ll find a more satisfyingly scary fright fest this Halloween season.

title: ‘Stranger photo sessions’ are bringing singles looking for love to Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine has long been a magnet for its romantic edge — fiancees, newlyweds and elopers come to enjoy the state’s dramatic coastlines, charming fishing villages and serene pine forests — but a new service being offered in the state is also luring a new demographic: singles.
On a windy Saturday morning in early October, along a wooded sideroad in Dover-Foxcroft, a Maine photographer captured intimate photos of a Minnesota flight attendant and a Kennebec County medical secretary.
The couple posed in various positions before a canopy of autumn leaves — with their hands clasped together, their noses nearly touching and, for the final shot, their lips locked in a soft kiss.
It was their first kiss. It was also their first time meeting.
Before the roughly hourlong shoot, the couple were strangers. But after more than a dozen photographed poses and light small talk, the couple left holding hands — well after the photographer and her camera had retired.
The pair, Adam Roemer and Casey Spencer, participated in a social media-driven trend that has gained traction across the country. Coined “stranger photo sessions,” the fad is marketed as a unique way to meet a potential romantic partner outside of the endless swiping synonymous with modern online dating.
It’s also the latest example of people making romantic visits to Maine. The state has long been a tourism destination for extravagant weddings, dramatic proposals and private elopements. Now, visitors are coming to Maine for a new romantic reason: to find love.
Roemer, 35, and Spencer, 41, knew nothing of the other — they didn’t know the other’s name, occupation or where they lived. They put their trust in photographer Tyla Racila of Farmhouse Frames Photography and her “hype woman,” assistant and sister-in-law Brittany Brewer, whom they’d also never met.
“They know absolutely nothing,” Brewer said. “There was one guy who said ‘I know I’m not supposed to know anything about my match, but does she have any kids? If she does, do you know the gender and approximately how old?’ He wanted to buy the kid a present because he’s buying her a present.”
Most of the men have gifted their partners a bouquet of flowers upon meeting, Brewer said.
Roemer and Spencer were among more than 300 singles who applied for the family duo’s stranger sessions. The sister-in-laws have scheduled roughly 35 photo shoots in just a few months, they said.
“I just thought I’d give it a shot,” said Roemer, who is stationed in Boston but requested a day off from Republic Airlines, a regional air carrier, for the trip north. “I don’t love traveling so much: I have a hard time meeting people, so I thought I’d give something different a try.”
Brewer said an overwhelming majority of applicants are women. When she receives an inquiry from a man, they’re matched fairly quickly, she said, adding she charges a $10 application fee that does not guarantee a match. The shoot itself costs $75 per participant.
Brewer has fielded hundreds of applications and is responsible for matching singles together based on their answers to a 25-question survey. She said she’s received inquiries from applicants throughout and beyond New England.
“There’s people from Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Kentucky, Connecticut, Vermont and Minnesota,” Brewer said. “We have somebody flying from Minnesota to one of our sessions.”
The questionnaire asks participants about themselves and for qualities they’re looking for in a romantic partner. It inquires about the applicant’s hobbies and music preferences, and what kind of personality traits they want in a significant other.
The survey also asks about potential dealbreakers — like tattoos or drug use — and their comfort level in showing affection on their first date, including holding hands, hugging and kissing.
The couple arrived separately. Roemer drove from Bangor, where he’s a regular at Paddy Murphy’s whenever he visits Maine. Spencer arrived from Benton, a small rural town near Waterville, roughly an hour from where the shoot was held.
Both were, understandably, nervous. Brewer and Racila — whose photo business prior to the stranger sessions focused on weddings, high school senior shoots, maternity sessions, and other celebrations — placed blindfolds on the pair before arranging them back-to-back prior to the big reveal.
Racila feverishly clicked photos as the couple was instructed to remove the blindfolds, turn around and meet one another for the first time. The reveal managed to calm both of their nerves: They introduced themselves before Roemer handed Spencer a gift for their first date: a bag of M&Ms.
Following the shoot, the couple chatted for roughly 20 minutes before Roemer walked Spencer to her car, hand in hand. They parted ways, but only for a handful of hours, after which Roemer asked Spencer to dinner. They sent Brewer a picture of themselves on their second date.
Racila and Brewer have received applications for singles from 18 to 70 years old, they said, adding that roughly half of their applicants are between 18 and 25.
Once Brewer pairs clients together, she helps them ease into the shoots, cracking jokes to lighten an otherwise anxiety-provoking and often awkward situation.
The photographers also separate each participant near the end of the shoot, under the guise of taking solo shots, to confirm a single is still comfortable with kissing their match. Roemer and Spencer said they were game for a kiss.
“I think it went well, it was really great,” Spencer said. “I think we will exchange numbers: He seems genuine.”
Racila and Brewer had two more stranger photo shoots that day, each of which ended with the couples exchanging contact information. One of the matches shared a drink after their session, Brewer said.
“I’ve had a lot of people say that in 2026 their goal was to do something that put them outside of their comfort zone,” Brewer said. “They want to be able to meet new people in a more natural way, rather than [through] social media. [Other] people say they’ve had bad luck with dating apps, and they’d rather meet somebody in person and see how it goes.”

title: K-9 officer seen jumping off highway overpass, survives fall
text:
PARK CITY, Utah (CNN) - A Utah police dog is on the mend after a terrifying fall from an overpass that was caught on camera.
Newly released video shows the moment a police K-9 jumped off a highway overpass, seriously injuring itself.
It happened when Park City police officers responded to a suspicious object spotted on a highway overpass.
As the officer and his K-9, Bruno, began investigating, Bruno suddenly leaped over the edge and fell to the roadway below.
His handler hurries back to his patrol unit and quickly drives down to find Bruno seriously injured on the road below.
The handler then lays down to comfort the injured K-9 and to prevent it from trying to stand.
The department said Bruno later underwent surgery for serious injuries to his front legs and jaw and is now recovering at home.
The department later posted on Facebook that Bruno is more than a police K-9; he’s a partner, a companion and part of the police family.

title: Tesla unveils what it says is a flying car
text:
Tesla unveils what it says is a flying car
Tesla unveils what it says is a flying car
Tesla CEO Elon Musk Thursday unveiled a car that he said will be able to fly.
See video of the flying car demonstration in the player above.
At a product reveal at a Texas test facility belonging to SpaceX, Musk’s other public company, he showed off Tesla’s new Roadster, a two-person sports car that not only could go from 0 to 60 mph in record time of less than a second, but he said used suction underneath the car to climb up a steep ramp and hang upside down before spinning off the ramp, flipping in the air and using air jets to land.
The car did not have an actual driver during the demonstration, which was done “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Musk told the crowd.
“Success is not guaranteed,” he said. “I mean that. It’ll probably work, but if it doesn’t work, we’re at a safe distance.”
Later in Thursday’s demonstration, the Roadster used the same jets to leap over a line of Tesla’s existing models parked side-by-side, and then used the jets off the back of the car to accelerate to 60 mph in that record time.
But even with the success of the staged event, whether the car will actually be able to live up to the promise and provide owners with the ability to both fly rather than just hop, while also being able to drive very fast on roads, remains to be proven.
The car uses 10 nozzles and what Musk described as “ultra high-pressure air tanks” to propel itself, both in the air, and to accelerate quickly when on the ground. He described the technology as “the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company.”
He said the car will go into production in 2028.
Musk told an enthusiastic crowd of Tesla fans “we need an audience to prove that it’s not AI or SI. So you guys can tell people you saw it with your eyes, because what you see with your eyes, you will not believe.”
In recent years, there have been many advancements in electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, known as eVTOL’s. While there are some working models, there are still many engineering roadblocks to road-worthy cars that can truly fly.
One car that is in development, made by California start-up Alef, has been able to get airborne using eight propellers, four in the front and four in the back. But the vehicle weighs 254 pounds, a small fraction of the weight of a Tesla Roadster. It can also only carry one person which must weigh less than the vehicle itself.

Obituary: Thomas Guy McDorr
text:
WEST BATH – Thomas Guy McDorr, 91, of Brunswick, Maine, passed away peacefully, following a brief illness on Thursday Oct. 8, 2026, at home surrounded by his children. Born on Dec. 9, 1934 in Bath, he was the loving husband of Dorothy MacGillivary, formerly of Five Islands Maine, for 68 years.
He formed his life around duty and sacrifice, for his family and country. He left Morse High School at 17 to voluntarily enlist in the Army Airforce during the Korean War and again at 33 in 1967 during the Vietnam War. Following 20 years in the Airforce he worked at Naval Station Brunswick, as a federal contractor managing the maintenance shop for an additional 20 years. Outside of work, he was known for a quite unassuming nature, he found joy in being with and assisting his extended family, friends and community working as fire chief and as an EMT in the Georgetown Fire Department for many years. He will be greatly missed and forever remembered for his charm and kind nature. Although we mourn his loss, we also celebrate the love and benevolence that were the essence of Tom’s being.
He is survived by his five children, Guy McDorr and Gary McDorr of Bath, Karen McDorr of West Bath, Tom McDorr of Tiverton, R.I. and Shawn McDorr of Evans, Ga.; and a host of loving grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
His was preceded in death by his loving wife, Dorothy by six years; his son, Terry McDorr by 46 years.
A private memorial service for family will be held later to honor Tom’s life and legacy.

title: Hargrove, Goodwin Win Week Six Athlete of the Week
text:
Wisdom’s Hargrove and Houlton’s Goodwin named Fall Week Six Athletes of the Week
The votes are in, and Cayden Hargrove of Wisdom and Presley Goodwin of Houlton are the Fall Week Six Aroostook County Athletes of the Week.
Hargrove earned the boys honor after a huge offensive stretch for the Wisdom boys soccer team, while Goodwin takes the girls award following a top-three finish at the Class C State Golf Championships.
They emerged from a Week Six field featuring 15 nominees and standout performances in soccer, cross country and golf from across Aroostook County.

Hargrove put together one of the most productive offensive weeks of the fall.

title: A message for young Mainers: Think journalism.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Dave Griffiths of Mechanic Falls is a retired journalist who worked for the Kansas City Star, Tulsa World and Lewiston Sun Journal. He also covered national security for Business Week magazine during the Reagan years.
This is an open letter to young folks wondering how to shape their careers and have an interesting life.
Think journalism. Every day, the nonprofit Maine Trust for Local News keeps the profession thriving here despite competition from cable “news” and social media. Reporters and editors strive to give us a balanced picture of life in Maine and beyond. Like “newshounds” all over America, they honor our Founding Fathers’ constitutional guarantee of a free press, even though broadsheets 250 years ago were fiercely partisan, focused more on scandal than substance.
It’s simple. Without independent voices, our democracy would wither and die. For the sake of argument, let’s say a power-obsessed, dishonest, corrupt political leader rails against “fake news” and calls the press the “enemy of the people.” You could make the case that by discouraging public confidence in the press, he wants to be a de facto dictator.
To a much lesser degree every presidential administration has dealt with reporters questioning the self-serving statements issuing from every White House. And Graham Platner would still be in the Senate race if not for aggressive reporting by, among others, the New York Times. Democracy is messy.
So what’s in it for young Mainers surveying the job landscape?
For one thing, your work day may range from quiet time devoted to “deathless prose” (a tongue-in-cheek remark I’ve heard in many a newsroom) to an often turbulent, always unpredictable life as you take on crime, drug busts, politics, odd “man bites dog” features, petty squabbles among elected officials, lost pets, acts of everyday courage, government overreach and the sparks that fly in our diverse culture.
Afterward, you’ll be jabbering in groups of two or three or more about a particularly memorable “news day,” perhaps in a watering hole just around the corner from the newsroom. In a good news town — and they’re all good news towns — you’ll never run out of ideas.
Many stories will stay with you years later. The point is: You’re involved in your job, not just putting in another eight hours. Count on it. I’ve worked at six newspapers, magazines and newsletters, and not once do I regret moving on. The next job — learning new turf and a new beat — keeps the juices flowing.
What about the writing itself? It’s not always easy, especially up against deadlines. But with the help of seasoned editors, you’ll develop a style that your peers recognize, and you’ll smile inwardly at just the right sentence and that jewel of a word or phrase that says it all. The English language is a vast treasure house of symbols at your command, but only if, according to Stephen King, you “write a lot and read a lot.” Meanwhile, you’ll come to value the connection between brevity and clarity — key to the quick read that makes writing “sing”(another newsroom buzzword).
But what if the weird hours and pressure to get your facts right on a strict time limit don’t suit you? After all, working into the evening may not lend itself to helping raise kids. So a reporter’s ease at the keyboard could lead to better-paying PR jobs for government agencies, the private sector or nonprofits. I’ve taught business writing courses for some 20 government clients all over the U.S. and in the Middle East, Europe and Asia. It was a challenge. I’m afraid people just don’t read much these days. The emails I saw early in those classes made me wonder why people don’t pick up the phone instead or walk down the hall to deliver a message or ask a question.
A life well lived is full of characters, including the scribblers you work with and the people you meet. I interviewed a federal prisoner in Denver who kidnapped women and kept them in coffins, and several drill instructors at the Marine boot camp in San Diego where a recruit had died during over-the-top training. I also interviewed two defense secretaries who were less forthcoming than a Trappist monk.
So you get to tell stories, holding up a mirror that helps explain us to ourselves. How cool is that?

title: White House Press Secretary leaving role days after first briefing
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Katie Zacharia will be “transitioning out” of her role as White House press secretary, a White House official said Friday, three days after her first briefing.
Her introductory press conference lasted 14 minutes.
Following the briefing, where she took questions from three outlets, Zacharia received scrutiny over her performance and for referring to herself as a lawyer despite failing the bar exam. Her abilities were criticized by multiple conservative members of the media.
President Donald Trump addressed the coverage Friday.
“Generally the media has been very rough. She was on Sean Hannity last night, and Sean was a little bit tough. And she did, I saw FOX and Friends this morning. They were a little tough,” Trump said.
The announcement of Zacharia’s departure came shortly after she spoke with Trump.
“I said Katie, you know, you don’t have to do this if you don’t want. She said this is a lot tougher. I said welcome to the world of Trump,” Trump said.
Zacharia is expected to remain in the administration in some capacity. A successor as White House Press Secretary has not been named.

title: New public sculpture unveiled at Blaine House
text:
New public sculpture unveiled at Maine governor's residence
A new public sculpture by a Maine artist was unveiled at the Blaine House in Augusta on Thursday.
Gov. Janet Mills, the Friends of the Blaine House, the Blaine House Commission and the Maine Arts Commission celebrated the unveiling of "Pinecone Pair with Tassel," which was sculpted by Patrick Plourde.
Plourde made the sculpture out of reclaimed hand tools once used by Maine farmers, builders and communities. The Maine Arts Commission said the sculpture celebrates the state's natural landscape and working industry.
"To be chosen for this is a really, really special thing," Plourde said. "To have it mounted in this manner and shown professionally like this, a really, really super job."
The sculpture was selected through a statewide artist selection process led by the Maine Arts Commission. The artwork was also acquired entirely through private fundraising conducted by the Friends of the Blaine House.
The commission said Plourde's sculpture stood out, in part, because of its compatibility with the Blaine House grounds and how it reflects Maine's forests and fields. The white pinecone and tassel was designated as Maine's state flower in 1895.

title: Couple accused of waiting hours to call for help after toddlers ate 20 hemp gummies, authorities say
text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (Gray News) - A Kentucky couple is accused of waiting hours to call for help after toddlers ate 20 hemp gummies, according to authorities.
Courtney Johnson, 30, was arrested in July after her 3-year-old and her 4-year-old children were hospitalized for allegedly eating hemp-infused gummies, police said.
A special victims investigator spoke with Johnson, who said she had opened a new container of 25 “hemp-infused gummies” and took one before going to sleep, WDKY reported.
Authorities said the two children were taken to a hospital where they were unconscious.
An arrest citation alleged that, instead of putting the gummies back where the children couldn’t reach, Johnson said she “likely left [them] on my bathroom sink,” where the children allegedly found and ate about 20 of them.
Since her arrest, Johnson has made multiple accusations that her husband, 33-year-old Sean East, was the one who left the gummies in an unsecured location.
East was arrested on July 26 for an unrelated warrant, and this led to the confiscation of his phone and Johnson’s.
Authorities said they obtained a search warrant for both phones and discovered East accepting fault for the incident with the gummies.
Officials said the search found that Johnson at least knew about the children ingesting the gummies.
Johnson allegedly found the empty container on a bedroom floor where the toddlers were found. Around noon that day, the toddlers still hadn’t woken up and had to be taken to the emergency room by first responders.
East’s arrest does not negate the criminal abuse charges that Johnson is facing after she allegedly “took a substantial and unreasonable amount of time” to request medical care for the children, authorities said.
East is facing charges in relation to child abuse following the investigation.

title: Death Notice: Kerrieann Harrison
ICE pursuit in Houston that broke a man's leg targeted a suspect who died years ago, family says
text:
HOUSTON (AP) — A federal immigration vehicle slammed into a Houston construction worker and broke his leg while pursuing a man who apparently died years ago, his family said Friday, raising questions about why the operation took place at all.
The worker, 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez of Mexico, remains hospitalized with multiple leg fractures and needs reconstructive ankle surgery, according to the Houston-based immigration advocacy group FIEL. At a news conference Friday, the group said the alleged suspect’s family had shared documentation proving his death.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to a request for comment.
“ICE is lying,” said Cesar Espinosa, FIEL’s executive director. “Either somebody is not telling the truth or all of a sudden these two ICE agents have developed a sixth sense and are able to see dead people.”
ICE said its officers spotted Parra Hernandez with a man it identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, the target of the operation, and tried to detain them both.
However, the man in a photo released by ICE was actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died years ago, according to FIEL. The group said the man’s daughter provided documents confirming his death, which have been turned over to the district attorney.
Criminal charges against the ICE officer who drove the vehicle are being considered by the Harris County District Attorney’s Office, after surveillance footage contradicted ICE’s claim that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the vehicle.
The video shows a black SUV speeding over a median and driving toward a man who is running away. The video does not show the car hitting him — that view is blocked by another vehicle — but it shows the SUV inches from the fleeing man. The video then shows him on the ground.
The man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes was not in Parra Hernandez’s vehicle, Harris County District Attorney’s Office spokesperson Rafael Lemaitre told The Associated Press.
Jimenez’s daughter, Jamie Jimenez, did not respond to requests for comment from the AP. Her husband, Andres Rendon, confirmed to the AP that Jose Hector Jimenez was his wife’s deceased father.
He died while being pursued by federal immigration authorities as he was trying to reenter the U.S., according to FIEL.
Parra Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, told reporters that her client is suffering from depression in federal custody, especially after learning that he was not the target of the operation.
“This never should have happened in the first place,” Bruno said.
His brother, Roberto Parra, said they would work construction all day together and he just wants his brother treated with humanity. He said Parra Hernandez has a family to support, and his only crime was coming to a country out of necessity.
FIEL is seeking Parra Hernandez’s release before he is moved from a hospital to a federal detention center.
Nidia Delfín, the sister of Luis Enrique Delfín, who was detained in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra Hernandez, called for her brother’s release from federal custody so he could serve as a witness.
“He’s still very concerned, still very afraid,” she said. “He’s not the same guy that was out last week.”

title: FDA-approved blood test offers new hope for Alzheimer’s diagnosis
text:
(Aging Untold) — The FDA’s first-ever approval of a blood test to help diagnose Alzheimer’s disease marks a significant step forward in treating a condition that affects about 7 million Americans, with that number expected to nearly double by 2060, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.
The blood test, known as Lumipulse, was approved by the FDA in May 2025 as a “less invasive option” that “reduces reliance on PET scans and increases diagnosis accessibility.”
Breakthrough in accessibility
Rebecca Edelmayer, vice president of scientific engagement for the Alzheimer’s Association, said getting a diagnosis can be difficult and time-consuming.
“One of the things that we continue to see is that for some patients it could take years,” Edelmayer said. “And we know that having an early and accurate diagnosis is so critical — especially when there’s treatments that have been approved today, to really help slow down the disease process.”
Traditional diagnosis often involves referrals to specialists, expensive PET scans of the brain and lumbar punctures, also known as spinal taps.
“It’s a very, very exciting time in this field,” Edelmayer said.
How the test works
The blood test detects amyloid plaques in the brain, which are considered key markers for Alzheimer’s disease.
Dr. Abhay Moghekar, an associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, helped study and evaluate the test for FDA approval.
“If this test is positive, there’s a greater than 90% chance that you have amyloid plaque in your brain,” Moghekar said.
Moghekar called it “absolutely a breakthrough in the field.”
“Getting a blood test is gonna be far easier, quicker and cheaper,” he said. “It’s going to allow early access to therapy, so it is going to revolutionize care of patients with dementia.”
Current limitations and future potential
The FDA has cleared the blood test for use only in patients 55 and older who are already experiencing memory problems. The agency cautions that this is not intended as a standalone diagnostic tool for Alzheimer’s. Results should be interpreted alongside a patient’s medical history and other assessments, such as cognitive testing.
Moghekar believes blood biomarker tests could eventually predict whether someone is at risk of developing Alzheimer’s before symptoms appear.
“I think we are moving towards a goal of preventing Alzheimer’s disease rather than treating it once you already have the disease,” he said.
Patient success story
Kathi Rigby was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s in 2023 at the age of 68 after experiencing memory problems and difficulty finding words.
After her diagnosis, she entered a clinical trial for a drug that aims to slow cognitive decline by targeting and removing amyloid plaques. The treatment received FDA clearance in 2024.
“It was so wonderful because it did such a difference for me — night and day — it’s a blessing,” Rigby said.
Her husband, Brent, said doctors told them 95% of the plaque was removed.
“The longer you wait, the more damage is done,” Kathi Rigby said about the importance of early diagnosis.

title: Waterfront Concerts generated $600M in economic impact over 15 years in Bangor, report finds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Waterfront Concerts, one of Bangor’s biggest seasonal attractions, generated $601 million in economic impact between 2010 and 2025.
That’s according to a new report by Professor Todd Gabe, the director of the University of Maine School of Economics, who studies the economics of arts and culture and provided his research to the city pro bono.
The research quantifies the significant economic activity generated by the venue, which has brought more than a million people to the Queen City since its inception. It also points to the possibility of future development that could help the city better accommodate the many visitors who travel here for concerts.
Gabe used several data sources, including revenue, employment and payroll information provided by Waterfront Concerts, concert attendance data and taxable retail sales from the area reported to Maine Revenue Services, to measure the economic impact of the summer concert venue.
This year’s study is an update to work Gabe started more than a decade ago, when the venue first opened. It’s changed a lot since then, transforming from a temporary setup beside the river to a fully developed venue now known as Maine Savings Amphitheater.
Bangor’s Waterfront Concerts venue hosted its first show, featuring Celtic Woman, in July 2010. It held about 245 concerts between then and 2025, drawing a total attendance of about 1.6 million people, according to the study. The best-attended show was Imagine Dragons in 2018.
Gabe’s study measures the concerts’ economic contribution, which comes in the form of jobs, labor income and economic output. That work incorporates ticket sales, minus the share given to artists, but it also factors in other spending that occurs in the area because of the concerts, since concertgoers often travel to Bangor and spend money at restaurants, hotels and other businesses.
The estimated $601 million economic output and $158 million labor income generated by the concerts includes a multiplier effect, which represents indirect economic impacts in Penobscot County. That includes benefits to businesses that supply goods and services to the concerts or that serve concertgoers, or the household spending of workers who are paid by Waterfront Concerts.
Just in 2025, the concerts generated about $67 million in economic output and about $15 million in labor income, which is about on par with the previous two years, according to the study.
“It’s amazing, the number of people that flock in,” Anne Krieg, Bangor’s economic development director, said. She noted the venue’s proximity to downtown, adding that the city becomes so busy on concert nights that it can be hard to get a hotel room or a table at a restaurant.
Much of what drives the venue’s economic impact is the lineup of artists set to play there, according to Gabe.
“The more shows and the better known the artists, the more people they’re going to draw,” he said.
Gabe reviewed ticket data from 2025 and found that about a third of ticket sales came from counties at least 200 miles from the venue, meaning a significant number of people travel great distances to attend shows in Bangor.
He also noted that economic impacts on the hospitality sector are some of the most visible. In some summer months, 10% or more of sales at restaurants and hotels are attributed to the concerts, he said. He’s working on doing more research to determine the impact of concerts on hotel room rates and availability.
Alex Gray, who owns Waterfront Concerts, said the report checked out with his company’s own estimates.
In terms of potential future development, Gray noted that the venue’s original plans included an additional building that is still in the works.
He also thinks adding more upscale hotel options in the city would help raise the concerts’ economic impact in the future.
“We’re missing that premium component,” he said.
Another hotel would be the most important piece of building up the concerts and the waterfront area as an economic boon, Krieg said.
The city’s economic development team is looking at city properties that could possibly be used for hotel development, she said. No particular location has been identified yet, although Krieg said another downtown hotel would be ideal.
She noted that local hotels fill up, especially when Waterfront Concerts hosts an event at the same time as the Cross Insurance Center across the street.
“And the good news is, we have a lot of people that want to be here,” she said. “We want to be able to accommodate that.”

title: Collins challenges Jackson over campaign ads, calling his promise to reject billionaire and corporate funding hypocritical
Susan Collins’ offices among targets of suspicious mailings to political figures
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ offices in Portland and Washington were among those that got suspicious letters under investigation by federal authorities.
The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service said Thursday that they are investigating “a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide,” including state election officials and congressional offices. Some of the letters contained an unknown powdery substance, the agencies said.
A Collins spokesperson said the senator’s Portland office received such a letter Friday. The letter was addressed directly to the five-term Republican, who is just three weeks away from Election Day in her reelection bid against Democrat Troy Jackson.
The letter was intercepted and there were no injuries. A separate suspicious letter sent to Collins’ Washington office was also intercepted, a spokesperson said.
“Despite escalating political rhetoric and harassment, we will continue our work for the people of Maine,” Katie Brown, Collins’ chief of staff, said in a statement.
U.S. Capitol Police, which has cited an continued increase in threats against members of Congress, their staffs and families, have been coordinating with the FBI and Postal Inspection Service on the investigation. The letters have so far tested negative for hazardous substances, The New York Times reported.
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the FBI said Thursday. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
Collins’ Biddeford office was vandalized with a vulgar message last month, coming just over a week after her Bangor home was egged. Nobody has been charged in connection with either incident.
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors condemned the mailings, saying in a joint statement that “those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties.”

title: Lawyer who lost everything to addiction reclaims law license
text:
LANSING, Mich. (InvestigateTV) - Jarrod Barron stood before an Ingham County courtroom, surrounded by friends, family and supporters who helped him rebuild his life after addiction cost him his career and left him homeless.
Two years ago, Barron shared his story as part of a mental health series. At that time, he was 10 years into recovery and helping others in their journey. He had been a successful lawyer before addiction led him to live under the Oakland Avenue Bridge in Lansing.
“I was painfully aware of how far I’d fallen,” Barron said in an earlier interview.
Climbing back took years. He met his wife, Carrie, while he was in recovery. A relapse led to an ultimatum.
“These two, this one, probably wouldn’t have been here at all if things had gone differently,” Carrie Barron said, standing between her two young sons. “I was pregnant with Andrew when we kind of came to a head and said, like, we need to get things straightened out. We need a life together, and that cannot include this addiction.”
With a focus on family, Barron worked day by day to stay sober.
“I had a ton of people who helped me with that process, from sponsors to recovery coaches to organizations, friends, family, all kinds of people, became part of my community of support,” Barron said.
That support filled the courtroom as Barron met another milestone. He lost his license to practice law during his addiction. He returned to court to reclaim it.
Attorney Michael Marutiak spoke on Barron’s behalf.
“I will risk my entire license to practice law myself on what I’m about to say. I believe he will be a credit to the profession, demonstrate moral turpitude. He will do nothing to bring any dishonor to the legal profession if he’s given the oath of office today,” Marutiak said.
Attorney John Jafiszewski also testified.
“Jarrod has been there for me in some of my darkest times. I’m always willing to pick up the phone to meet. He is an amazing asset to the recovery community,” Jafiszewski said.
Barron addressed the court.
“Over time and with a lot of help, I’ve rebuilt my entire life brick by brick. Today, I see the resulting life and community represented in this very courtroom,” Barron said. “I count every person in this room as my friend because everyone present and many others who could not be here have actively contributed and continue to contribute to my life in meaningful ways. In essence, jointly and severally, they have saved my life and continue to do so on a daily basis. And I love them all dearly.”
Ingham County Judge Clinton Canady administered the oath of office.
“I, Jared Barron,” Barron repeated after the judge. “Do you solemnly swear or affirm that you will support the Constitution of the United States and the Constitution of the State of Michigan.”
“I do,” Barron said.
“Well, let me come down and shake. Let’s give him a hand,” Canady said.
The courtroom erupted in applause.
Carrie Barron brought their sons to the ceremony, pulling them out of school for the occasion.
“He made the right choices. And, you know, every day was another right choice, and another right choice, and another right choice, and now we have, you know, this great family,” Carrie Barron said. “They watched Dad study for the bar exam, and, you know, they know that he’s gone to all kinds of meetings and leads meetings every Friday night just to help others. And so they are part of the whole journey.”
Barron said his sons have been a guide.
“They’ve been a sort of a north star that gives me a daily means of guidance,” Barron said. “I couldn’t imagine doing any of this without them.”
Barron serves on the board of Face Addiction Now. Along with his dedication to his family, he is dedicated to helping others struggling through addiction.
“There is hope and there is help. It is hard, but you don’t have to do any of this alone. There are tons of people out there willing to go to bat for you,” Barron said.
Substance use disorder is a treatable illness, but the decision to seek help isn’t always easy for the person battling addiction or their loved ones.
An expert we spoke to said once someone admits they have a problem, recovery is not a quick fix and even people with years of sobriety have to make the daily decision not to use.
“Relapse is a part of recovery,” said Kellie Ross, a clinical addiction specialist. “I think on average it takes people seven times to kick the habit.”
For more information on substance use disorder, you can call SAMHSA’s national helpline at 1-800-622-HELP (4357) or online at findtreatment.gov to find help in your area.

title: Vote to keep money coming to Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Whether Mainers like Sen. Susan Collins or not, the fact remains that she is the chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee. If voters choose to elect a junior senator (like Troy Jackson), they can kiss hundreds of millions of dollars for Maine goodbye.
Are people really willing to lose this Maine funding, by voting for another candidate, just because they don’t like the president? Alison Jacobs
Auburn

title: Hallowell considering temporary ban on data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HALLOWELL — Hallowell could become the latest Maine community to temporarily block data center development as city officials are considering a 180-day moratorium on the facilities.
City councilors voted unanimously Tuesday to move forward the proposed ordinance that would prohibit new applications and development for six months while officials consider how to regulate the facilities.
After Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a bill that would enact a statewide data center moratorium in May, numerous towns across the state have passed or are considering data center moratoriums on the local level.
The Hallowell Conservation Commission urged the City Council to adopt a moratorium at the September meeting, citing the need for proper safeguards to protect residents and the environment before moving forward.
In a letter to the council, Conservation Commission Chair Hilary Neckles raised concerns about data centers’ significant use of electricity, water, land and local infrastructure in addition to questions about pollution, noise, emergency response, tax agreements and high electricity prices.
Neckles said Mills’ veto “left municipalities to fend for themselves” and said she still hopes to see statewide regulations in the future.
The moratorium would give city officials time to hear more public feedback, evaluate concerns and develop a permanent ordinance regulating, or even restricting, potential data center developments.
Members of the public can weigh in on the proposed moratorium during a public hearing at the Nov. 9 council meeting. Councilors could waive the need for a third reading of the ordinance at that meeting, thereby enacting the moratorium. If not, the third reading would take place at the December meeting.

title: Jared Golden’s unspent campaign funds are going across the country
text:
When U.S. Rep. Jared Golden announced he wouldn’t run for reelection this year, he said he planned to use the nearly $2 million in his war chest to support Democrats across the country.
So far, he’s put his money where his mouth is.
In its latest filing with the Federal Election Commission, made public Thursday afternoon, Golden’s campaign committee reported spending nearly $300,000 between July and October. Much of that cash went toward moderate Democrats’ campaigns.
The largest expenditure by far was to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which supports the party’s candidates for U.S. House. Golden gave the organization $150,000 in late September.
Golden has occasionally drawn the ire of his party’s leadership for his moderate stances and willingness to break party ranks on important votes. In September, he and Rep. Marie Glusenkamp Perez, D-Wash., were scorned by Democratic leaders for a “blindside” vote in support of several Republican-led bills.
After the DCCC, Gluesenkamp Perez was the next largest recipient of Golden’s campaign cash over the last three months. Her reelection PAC received a $40,000 contribution from Golden in late September.
Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez are co-chairs of the Blue Dog PAC, a committee that supports conservative-leaning Democrats running for and serving in Congress.
In recent months, Golden gave the maximum $2,000 to six Democrats backed by Blue Dog PAC that are each vying to flip Republican congressional seats in Florida, Kentucky, Minnesota, Montana, Ohio and Wisconsin.
Three other Democrats’ reelection campaigns received $1,000 contributions from Golden: Incumbent U.S. Reps. John Larson in Connecticut, Darren Soto in Florida and Seth Magaziner in Rhode Island.
“As he’s done during his time in office, Congressman Golden will continue to support candidates and causes he believes in,” Golden spokesperson Mario Moretto said in a statement provided after this story was initially published.
The donation to Larson was made on Aug. 7, just days before he lost a primary election that ultimately ended his nearly 30-year congressional tenure.
Those contributions follow the pattern of Golden’s other donations this year, the majority of which have gone to moderate Democrats facing tight campaigns across the country.
In Maine, Golden gave $500 to both Lewiston Democrat Shenna Cox’s state Senate and Auburn Democrat Adam Lee’s state House campaigns.
Golden also contributed $1,050 to Oxford County Sheriff Chris Wainwright’s reelection bid. Wainwright, notably, is the only Republican Golden contributed to this quarter.
The donation, dated Sept. 30, was made just days after several Oxford County deputies’ complaints of retaliation within the office were made public.
Several Maine-based nonprofits also received thousands of dollars from Golden’s campaign funds. Operation Reboot Outdoors, a Turner-based organization that sponsors hunting and fishing trips for law enforcement officers and veterans, got $25,000. The Solidarity Solutions Foundation in Lisbon Falls received $5,000.
Golden made a “charitable contribution” of $25,000 to Moving America Forward, a Utah-based voter outreach organization that focuses on engaging political independents, namely through canvassing and town halls.
Golden’s spending has ramped up as November has neared. His committee spent about $93,000 in the first quarter of 2026 and $65,000 in the second, according to FEC filings.
The nearly $300,000 he spent during the third quarter blows those totals out of the water. And he still has nearly $105,000 on hand, his latest filing shows.

title: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson are still sparring over his ‘shut up’ remark
text:
When a young man jumped from his seat to shout at U.S. Sen. Susan Collins about the perils of data centers during her final debate with Democrat Troy Jackson on Thursday, some in the crowd loudly told him to “sit down and shut up.”
But the moment that drove headlines came next. Collins suggested the protester was one of Jackson’s backers, and the Democrat lightly shot back, “Oh, shut up.”
The exchange, in the first 15 minutes of the high-stakes race’s last debate, captured a trait the candidates have shared across four debates in two weeks: Neither shies away from a fight. Republicans tied it to Jackson’s well-documented temper dating back to confrontations as Maine Senate president. The Democrat’s allies called it an overblown distraction from issues like health care costs, the war with Iran and Collins’ record with President Donald Trump.
The candidates shook hands before and after the debate. But they’re characteristically still divided on how the “shut up” moment played out.
Maggie Amjad, Jackson’s campaign spokesperson, said the episode came after Collins had run “a campaign based on personal attacks against Troy and his family,” including echoing stories in conservative media about how his long-term partner, Lana Pelletier, is his second cousin.
The Sunrise Movement, a progressive group, later claimed the protester as a member in an Instagram post, saying 19-year-old Bowdoin College student Henry Elgie. A photo shared with the BDN shows him holding an anti-AI sign near Jackson allies outside a previous debate. He had a fake press badge and was not among the supporters Jackson invited Thursday.
“Senator Collins falsely accused him of planting a protester during the debate, and he responded,” she said. “Her campaign’s attempt to turn that exchange into anything else is baseless.”
Collins’ team linked it to other episodes that have aired during the campaign, including confrontations in the Maine Legislature and a 1988 police report documenting an assault when he was 19 years old. The report alleged he “pushed around” Pelletier, which both of them denied.
“This is yet another example of Troy Jackson’s angry outbursts with female colleagues,” Blake Kernen, Collins’ campaign spokesperson, said. “It raises a serious question about how he handles women who disagree with him.”
The moment highlighted vulnerabilities in both candidates, voters said. Beth Clark, a longtime Democratic voter from Troy who supports Collins, said Friday that Jackson had been “entirely disrespectful” to the senator.
“Maybe the rules have changed in debating since I was in high school,” she said. “But you have to be in full control of your faculties and think about what you’re saying.”
Jackson supporters argued even if his word choice on the fly wasn’t wise, his tone leaned toward lighthearted. They said it was Collins’ who veered into rudeness by seizing on the chaotic moment as security led out the heckler and saying he was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”
Some said it reminded them of a moment captured on audio after the end of the first debate, when Collins needled Jackson for being a lifelong Pittsburgh Steelers fan.
“It was a very Maine response … more like, ‘Oh, come on,’” a Jackson supporter granted anonymity because the organization she works for doesn’t allow her to speak on the race, said Friday. “As a woman, I was not offended. If [Republicans] want to take the woman angle, taking reproductive rights away from women is more offensive.”
When Republicans shared the clip on social media, accusing Jackson of lashing out at the senator, many on the left responded by pointing to Trump’s widely reported vulgar comments about women, including telling a reporter last year, “Quiet, piggy.”
Jackson’s remark didn’t spark immediate signs of offense from the senator herself, as she showed during several points of contention on her record in the three previous debates.
Instead, she stuck to the point she argued, retorting sarcastically, “Yeah, right.”

title: Trump heads to Kansas to stump for Sen. Marshall ahead of midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is campaigning across the country ahead of the midterms, with stops planned in several states, including one notable visit to a longtime Republican stronghold.
Trump will travel to Wichita, Kan., on Monday. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and Trump won the state in three previous elections.
Trump is campaigning on behalf of incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.). Polling shows Marshall trailing Democrat Adam Hamilton. A recent YouGov poll shows Hamilton leading by three points.
Democrats need to flip four seats to regain control of the Senate. According to CIVIQS polling, Kansas is one of only 10 states where Trump’s approval rating remains above water, at 46%.
