title: How laughter can help improve your mental health
text:
How laughter can help improve your mental health
How laughter can help improve your mental health
They say laughter is the best medicine, but can adding a dose of humor to your life actually improve your mental well-being? According to the Journal of Psychiatric Research, the answer is yes.
Sweetser spokesperson Justin Chenette joined Maine's Total Coverage on Friday to discuss the benefits of laughter.
Chenette said laughter uplifts your mood, reduces stress and anxiety, provides a temporary escape from negative thoughts and worries, and fosters social connection. He noted that laughter is not a replacement for treatment, but it is a free tool that works right alongside it.
How can people get their daily dose of laughter?
- Practice Self-Humor: Don’t take yourself too seriously, and learn to laugh at your own mistakes and imperfections.
- Find the Funny in the Mundane: A small shift in mindset can help you spot the humor in everyday moments.
- Make It a Habit: Just like exercise, a little bit on a regular basis adds up.
- Seek Out the Laughs: Put on a funny show, call the friend who always cracks you up, or share a silly moment with your kids.
Does it make a difference if we laugh with other people instead of on our own?
Chenette said we are about 30 times more likely to laugh when we are with other people, and laughing together is what helps strengthen our social bonds.
That reason is exactly why Sweetser is bringing back its Smiles for Sweetser Comedy Show, which is happening Friday, Oct. 23, from 7 to 9:30 p.m. at the Italian Heritage Center in Portland.
The following four comedians are set to perform:
- Jody Sloane, who has a knack for finding humor in the darkest corners of life, including stories from her own childhood.
- Leonard Kimble, a Chicago native now living in Auburn who works in IT by day and jokes about family life, raising two kids, and a cat he never wanted.
- Jolanda Logan, who performs across New England with upbeat, observational humor about marriage, motherhood, and everyday absurdities.
- Mark Turcotte, a lifelong New Englander, founder of Maine Event Comedy and the Bricks & Bridges Comedy Fest, and a finalist for Funniest Comic on the East Coast.
People can get tickets at ComedyTickets.org. Consider it your dose of laughter for a great cause, with every ticket helping fuel mental health treatment for those who need it most.

title: US is reviving shuttered nuclear plants to meet growing electricity demand and to power data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The United States is making an unprecedented attempt to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet rising energy demand, including from large-scale data centers.
No commercial nuclear reactor is known to have resumed generating electricity after beginning the decommissioning process that takes one out of service, though some reactors have restarted after long outages.
The Department of Energy is lending as much as $4.4 billion to restart the Palisades Power Plant in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center on Pennsylvania’s Three Mile Island and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa to restore a combined 2.25 gigawatts of electricity, which can power roughly 2 million homes and businesses. All three of the plants closed before their licenses expired, largely because the electricity they produced was considered too expensive.
Not anymore. Two of the plants have contracts with Big Tech companies that will pay a premium to get large amounts of carbon-free energy for data centers. The Trump administration is pushing hard to deploy nuclear power for artificial intelligence and manufacturing. It’s also lending billions of dollars for upgrades to produce more electricity from currently operating nuclear plants.
Restarting a reactor is a fairly quick way to get a lot of electricity, and it’s cheaper than building a new, large reactor, said nuclear engineering expert Todd Allen.
“There’s a demand in the country for more power,” he said. “You have these assets that were previously hooked up. They were previously operable, and you can relatively quickly get them generating electricity again, compared to your other possibilities. For anyone who wants zero carbon, nuclear provides that. For the Trump administration, which really wants nuclear, this fits that story also.”
Restarting a reactor is kind of like restoring a car
Allen compared restarting a decommissioned nuclear plant to restarting a car that sat idle for a few years. The driver still needs a valid license and all the parts need to be working correctly.
“That’s what they’re trying to do with these nuclear plants, but it’s a much bigger, complicated system,” said Allen, associate dean for research at the University of Michigan’s College of Engineering.
With a nuclear plant, the owner has to bring nuclear workers back and ensure their training is current, make sure everything is working and that maintenance is up to date, ensure they have enough fuel and ask regulators to restore their operating license, he added.
Allen said it’s a lot to keep track of, but it’s relatively straightforward.
Expert says restarts are risky
Edwin Lyman, at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the taxpayer money being used should go toward addressing safety risks. For example, most U.S. plants were built between 1970 and 1990 and were designed to withstand natural disasters of that era, said Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at UCS. But climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe.
“It’s possible, if they set the right level of safety and spend the necessary funds to meet that, they could restore these plants to operable condition,” he said. “That’s not happening at this point.”
Iowa’s only nuclear facility, Duane Arnold, began operating in 1975. It was scheduled to permanently close in October 2020. Replacing it with cheaper energy sources, including wind, was projected to save Iowa customers $300 million in energy costs. The plant shut down early, in August 2020, when it was damaged during a powerful storm known as a derecho.
NextEra Energy owns Duane Arnold. Looking at its condition, CEO John Ketchum said company officials “felt really good about the ability to bring it back.”
Palisades plant is the furthest along
The Palisades plant operated from 1971 until 2022, when its owner, Entergy, left the nuclear power business. The plant’s operating license lasted until 2031.
Holtec International bought it and began dismantling it, though none of the steps were irreversible. Michigan officials, not wanting to lose nuclear jobs or energy, encouraged Holtec to pursue reopening the plant and provided state funding. The Biden administration in 2024 approved a $1.5 billion loan to restart the facility, and the Trump administration continued the payments.
In August, Holtec began loading nuclear fuel, one of the final major phases before a reactor can restart. The company paused the process after a fuel assembly tilted from its upright position and Holtec determined it needed to figure out why. Its power purchase agreements require Palisades to be in service by March 2027.
Holtec says its efforts will restore baseload power, strengthen energy security and demonstrate the role of nuclear energy in meeting the nation’s growing electricity demands.
Big Tech will purchase power for data centers
NextEra Energy and Google are collaborating to restart Duane Arnold by early 2029.
“This is a perfect example of data centers paying their own way,” Ketchum said in an interview. “We’re able to sign a long-term contract with a hyperscaler for that project. So none of the costs are being paid by residential customers in Iowa.”
Microsoft has a contract with the Crane Clean Energy Center on Three Mile Island just outside Harrisburg. The plant was the site of the nation’s worst commercial nuclear power accident in 1979. The accident destroyed one reactor, leaving the plant with one functioning. In 2019, Constellation Energy’s then-parent company Exelon shut down the functioning reactor, saying it was losing money and that Pennsylvania lawmakers had refused to subsidize it.
Constellation Energy announced in 2024 that it would spend $1.6 billion to restart the reactor under a 20-year agreement with Microsoft. It hopes to bring the plant back online in 2027. The Energy Department provided a $1 billion loan, and Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly took a tour last week.
Jack Spencer at The Heritage Foundation said he can’t think of a worse use of taxpayer money than using it to restart reactors. These are low-risk projects where there is a massive demand for the energy, so there is no reason to funnel federal dollars to these companies, said Spencer, director of the foundation’s Center for Energy, Climate and Environment.
Conversely, Jennifer Gordon at the Atlantic Council said she thinks it’s a terrific way of leveraging federal financing to get needed electricity. Gordon directs the council’s Nuclear Energy Policy Initiative.
Industry group says reactors shouldn’t close early
The World Nuclear Association said restarting nuclear reactors should be celebrated, but preventing them from closing prematurely would be the best option.
Palisades is expected to be the first nuclear plant in the world to resume generating power after beginning the decommissioning process, but other countries have restarted or refurbished reactors after long-term shutdowns, the association said. That includes Canada, Armenia, Belgium, Japan, India and South Korea. Others are considering or in the process of restarting reactors.
___

title: These golden retrievers help nursing students cope with academic pressure
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (InvestigateTV) - Between exams, clinicals and sleepless nights, nursing students face a lot of pressure. At Galen College of Nursing in Louisville, some students find relief from two lovable dogs.
Henry and Maisy, two English Cream Golden Retrievers, have become unofficial therapy dogs for students struggling with the demands of nursing school.
The dogs belong to Jim Hack, senior facilities manager at Galen College. His main job is maintaining the building, but he discovered his pets had a different calling.
“Henry is just a big love bug,” Hack said. “Maisy is younger and is needy.”
Hack brought the dogs to work one day and noticed how students reacted.
“They all ran over they put their books down they just start petting them and that’s when I went... this is kinda cool. That wasn’t the initial intention, it’s kind of evolved to that,” Hack said.
The dogs now have official ID badges and know their way around campus. Students say the animals provide crucial emotional support during stressful moments.
“They are amazing. Especially when you come and you are really scared. Today, we have sim lab it’s so stressful you go in and people watch you and the dogs are here and you are ...ah! It’s okay. They make everything better for a little,” said Savannah Price, a nursing student said.
For Hack, providing comfort to future nurses is personal. His wife is a nurse, and when their daughter was young, nurses supported his family during a difficult time.
“My daughter when she was 14 was diagnosed with Ewing’s Sarcoma. It was a pretty hard diagnosis we mostly lived with her at Kosair Hospital for almost 3 years and while you are there and for extended periods the nurses become your family you laugh together, you cry together, and you get very attached to them,” Hack said.
Sharing Maisy and Henry is his way of saying thank you to the nursing profession.
“If you are having a rough day they can just tell you don’t have to express it and they are just there. I think it’s the best thing,” Hack said.
The dogs do leave behind some evidence of their visits.
“I buy the lint rollers by the case,” Hack said. “We call it golden glitter!”
Students and staff don’t mind the extra hair. The dogs provide a reminder that compassion matters for both patients and caregivers.
“They are just as happy to see us as we are to see them,” Price said.
Hack said the dogs have such busy days at work that they sleep well when they get home.

title: Windham combines conservation areas to create Windham Community Forest
text:
A naming and ribbon-cutting ceremony for the combined Windham Community Forest is scheduled for 9 a.m. on Saturday, Oct. 17. The ceremony is the culmination of a yearlong project to unify Lowell Preserve and the East Windham Conservation Area and will take place at the Atherton Trailhead.
The two preserves were opened in 2021 and 2023, respectively, and were jointly managed by the town of Windham and Presumpscot Regional Land Trust. The town owns the combined properties, while the land trust holds a conservation easement.
Windham Community Forest consists of 1,104 acres of hardwood forest, and is notable for a scenic view of the White Mountains. The property is part of a 2,000-acre scenic corridor, which also includes North Falmouth Community Forest.
The town established a steering committee in January to unify the preserves under one name and establish a plan for further development and management of the property. The committee was composed of 11 members, and staffed by Parks and Recreation Director Linda Brooks and Will Sedlack, executive director of Presumpscot Regional Land Trust.
Several potential names for the property were chosen by the committee based on input received at a community forum, said Brooks. From there, two finalists were chosen via FlashVote, and the Town Council voted in favor of Windham Community Forest on Sept. 8.
Emily Southard, director of development and marketing at the land trust, said the idea of combining the two properties was a natural move, as the trail systems are interconnected, and many visitors, particularly bikers, enter the area through one preserve and spend quite a bit of time in the other.
In addition to the renaming of the preserve, a ribbon-cutting for the new Universal Access Trail will be held. The trail stretches 1 mile from the parking lot of the former East Windham Conservation Area to the White Mountain overlook. If weather permits, a guided walk will follow.
The ceremony will feature speakers from the town and land trust. The speakers are expected to discuss the history of the properties, the process undertaken to unite them under one name, and future goals.
The previous preserves will be recognized via the renaming of the entrances, with the former entrance to East Windham Conservation Area being renamed Atherton Hill Trailhead, while the Lowell Preserve entrance will be renamed Lowell Farm Trailhead.
When asked about how upcoming collaborations between Presumpscot Regional Land Trust and the town, Southard said Amanda Lessard, assistant town manager for Windham and a member of the land trust’s board of directors, will have a station to solicit public feedback on potential improvements to the project at the land trust’s annual meeting on Sunday, Oct. 18. On Nov. 5, the trust and the town will host a joint open house at Windham Town Hall to talk with property owners about land conservation.

title: Floaties can build confidence in the water. Swim experts say they can hide a skill many kids never learn
text:
HOUSTON (InvestigateTV) — A flotation device can give a child confidence in the water, but swim experts say it can also hide a dangerous gap in a skill most kids never learn: how to tell the difference between floating and sinking.
They say without it, that same device can quietly set a child up for danger the moment it comes off.
Jenny Bennett’s son, Jackson, was the sweetest, most loving little boy. She told us that in his short 18 months “I truly thought that he was going to change the world someday.”
“I just never thought that we would lose him like we did,” she said.
He often wore a flotation device, or “floatie,” while in the pool. That changed one summer night in 2016.
“One evening, when we thought he was upstairs playing with his older sisters, he had actually wandered out our dog door and found our pool alone where he had jumped in and it was about five minutes that had gone by,” she recalled. “We realized that he wasn’t upstairs with his sisters. And my biggest fear was that he would get to the pool. And I ran outside and found him floating face down in the pool.”
After his death, Bennett learned other parents who lost children to drowning had something in common. Each of their toddlers also used flotation devices. She said she bought a floatie for Jackson three months before he died.
“It said, ‘learn to swim.’ I grabbed it and thought, this is amazing! We can put this on him. It heads above water. He can swim and float around with his sisters. And then I thought that it was keeping him safe,” Bennett said.
“I believe our culture has set children up to drown. I call it the ‘water baby culture’ where we make it so fun for these kids. We encourage them to jump in. We clap for them when they put their face in the water. And we make it so fun that they don’t realize it’s dangerous,” Bennett said.
Bennett said drowning prevention should come first and marketing for floaties should be revised. “It’s really important to teach children how to float on their backs.”
Floating vs. sinking
Genevieve Blasius, a swimming school owner and research scientist, said floating is a foundational skill that many swim schools do not prioritize.
“You’d be shocked about how many people are coming to me from other swim schools and that is not the primary thing that they’re really teaching,” Blasius said.
Blasius said flotation devices can train kids into a head up, hips down, vertical “bicycle kick” posture that does not translate to self-rescue swimming.
“One of the most important things on all every single one of my students: ‘Are you in the floating position? Are you in the sinking position?’ And all of them can answer that question. And that is not a standard practice for most of the schools in the area,” Blasius said.
Blasius said kids and parents can both develop a false sense of security, believing a child can swim, when the child can sink as soon as they stop moving because the device removes the body feedback that teaches what floating versus sinking feels like.
Calls for warning labels
Blasius said warning labels and better education from manufacturers and federal agencies are needed.
“If you go in the water and you go in a completely vertical position and you don’t move anything unless you’re very aware of your body and you tilt your head back and you can float if you feel your lungs inflate your lungs with air. Children are not aware of any of that,” Blasius said.
Blasius said that if the devices are “not doing anything” to give the child a sense of what position they should be in while floating, “it’s completely ignoring science.”
“We’re not even getting into the psychology of it. We’re just talking about physics,” Blasius said.
“There’s warning about everything. And there’s not a warning about this? I mean, how many — we’re talking about the number one cause of death in children. You kind of need to look at all aspects of it.”
A mother turns to advocacy
Bennett started a local chapter of Swim Safe Forever in Houston to provide drowning prevention education, survival swim lessons and scholarships to people in need.
She doesn’t believe the products should be banned and are good for boats and at the beach.
“The problem is when the children repeatedly wear them and their brain changes to think that, first of all, the water is a fun, safe place to be. And second of all, that they’re just going to pop right back up and they can swim in an upright position. But that position is just not obtainable unless they’re wearing the device on their chest, in their arms,” Bennett said.
Bennett said it’s important to teach children how to float on their backs so their heads are far enough out of the water that their nose and mouth are able to breathe.
She said these products should not be marketed as a learn-to-swim device.
“You leave them somewhere for a moment, and you think that they’re safe, and you turn around and they’re gone. And they could be doing something like getting into the pantry and spilling the cereal. They could be doing all of these things in a few seconds of time,” Bennett said of watching your child. “But they could also be wandering outside to your pool or to a neighbor’s pool or a lake, a pond nearby, finding the water and remembering how much fun they had in the water, and then jumping in. And by that point it’s too late. It only takes maybe 30 seconds for a child under 30 pounds to drown.”
One of the leading manufacturers of wearable floaties is Bestway, which licenses the Puddle Jumper brand.
Bestway spokesman Brannon Smith said its products meets standards set by ANSI, a voluntary standards-making group in the U.S.; CAN, which sets standards in Canada; UL, which is the Coast Guard’s third-party testing laboratory; and ISO, the international standards organization.
“While the Coast Guard approval program is not a pool-specific certification program, the underlying ANSI/CAN/UL 12402 requirements establish in-water performance requirements for buoyancy aids used in sheltered waters. Neither ISO 12402 nor ANSI/CAN/UL 12402 states that such products are prohibited from use in swimming pools or are unsuitable for pool environments,” Smith wrote in an email in response to InvestigateTV questions.
Products used in pools generally fall under the CPSC jurisdiction as aquatic toys. Currently, there are no mandatory safety standards for these specific types of wearable floaties.

title: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia defends her legal background and short first briefing
text:
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia defends her legal background and short first briefing
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia on Thursday defended her legal background and justified her truncated inaugural briefing as she navigates a rocky first week as the president's chief spokeswoman.
Zacharia sat down for an interviews with conservative media. She told the conservative Human Events outlet that she did not have time to get fully prepared ahead of her first briefing on Tuesday and that it was always the plan to keep it short because President Donald Trump would field questions from journalists later that morning.
"It was absolutely my goal to keep it short, considering he is his own best spokesperson, and he would love -- and does love -- gaggling with the media as he goes to Marine One," Zacharia said. "So I wanted to give ample deference and not barge into his time."
The initial briefing materials were given to Zacharia on Monday evening, then completed Tuesday at 8 a.m., less than two hours before she would appear before the White House press corps. She had been up since 3 a.m. preparing, Zacharia said.
"I never had a full briefing beforehand, and I went out and I effectuated the briefing," she said.
Later, speaking to Fox News commentator Sean Hannity, she said she "probably should have stepped aside" instead of taking questions from the press corps without having time to prepare.
"I could have just given a brief intro and said, 'I'm only here to introduce myself, and I want to engage with the press corps,'" she said.
Zacharia calls failure to pass bar exam 'inconsequential'
As for her legal background, Zacharia said she was preparing to take the bar exam in California at a time that she had just gotten married and was readying a move to China to join her new husband, who had been working in private equity in Beijing.
"I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I'd been long distance from for at least a year," Zacharia said.
She said the results of the bar exam, which she did not pass, were "somewhat inconsequential" because she would not need to be a barred attorney while living in China.
Zacharia, who has been under scrutiny for calling herself a "lawyer," said she consulted several legal experts to ensure that title was accurate when offering legal analysis.
"It's unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp. The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law."
She will not weigh in on legal matters in her White House capacity, Zacharia said.
She says she didn't lobby for the job
She also divulged details of how she went about securing the White House press secretary job. Zacharia stressed that she did not want to be seen as lobbying for the position, left vacant when Karoline Leavitt announced she would depart the administration to spend more time with her family.
Zacharia, who was a communications adviser for the company that runs Truth Social, said she closely monitored the president's social media posts to determine what was top of mind for him, then would go on air to talk about those topics.
"My philosophy is, I'm on TV enough where if he sees me and he likes me, then I will be recruited for the job. I do not believe that lobbying for that job would have been successful, and I wanted to work for it. I wanted to audition for it."
Then on Oct. 7, as Zacharia was preparing to take one of her children to a pumpkin patch, she received a phone call from Trump about the press secretary position.
She promptly flew out the next day from her home in California to Washington, met with the president about the job on Friday and formally accepted the position later that day.
___
Associated Press writer Jonathan J. Cooper in Phoenix contributed.

title: Road foreman hospitalized after tree limb falls during Hurricane Isaias cleanup
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — A road foreman for the Georgia Department of Transportation is hospitalized after a tree limb fell on him while he was clearing downed trees after Hurricane Isaias.
Rocky Meeks, 53, has undergone multiple surgeries. His family worries he may be unable to return to work.
Meeks was on call 24/7 for the storm, his wife Robin said. He had been out since 3:30 a.m. Saturday cutting trees. The tree he was cutting was his 11th of the day.
“From what the deputies and paramedics say he was cutting a tree, a tree limb out of another tree fell like 40 feet and hit him in the head,” Robin Meeks said.
Robin Meeks was at home waiting when she was told.
“Panic, panic,” she said.
Rocky Meeks was taken to Northeast Georgia Medical Center in Gainesville, where surgery started quickly. Doctors put stents in his aorta and operated on his leg to repair his tibia and fibula.
“They went in and put a rod in his leg there,” Robin Meeks said.
On Tuesday, Rocky Meeks underwent spinal surgery. Before the surgery, he was awake and told his wife not to worry.
She said he worried about bills and was afraid he would have to sell his antique cars to keep afloat.
Robin Meeks said the department told her Meeks will not lose his job, but she worries about making ends meet and has shared a GoFundMe to help.
Meeks was a few years from retirement and is unsure whether he will be able to work again.
“But if you know Rocky, Rocky’s a very hardworking guy. He does not stop for nothing,” Robin Meeks said.
The department was unable to comment.

title: ‘Street Fighter’: All the Best Video Game Easter Eggs in the Movie
text:
All the Video Game Easter Eggs in ‘Street Fighter’
If you spent any appreciable amount of time in an arcade in the early 1990s, if you know what it means when someone places a quarter in the corner of a game cabinet’s screen, then you will recognize that the new Street Fighter movie is not just loosely based on the Capcom fighting series. This movie is practically up to its black belt in Easter eggs, callbacks, and little references to the games, especially its iconic 1991 sequel, Street Fighter II.
Below, let’s take a look at some of the more fun shoutouts to the button-mashing glory days of yesteryear. And we’re not even counting the obvious ones, like the massive cast of Street Fighter characters, like E. Honda, Dhalsim, Balrog, and more.
The World Warrior
M. Bison’s contest to determine the greatest fighter on the planet is called “The World Warrior Tournament.” Although most gamers then and now just called it Street Fighter II, the game’s full title (visible on the arcade cabinet’s title screen) was Street Fighter II: The World Warrior.
Beating Up a Car
An early montage shows Ken (Noah Centineo) making ends meet by taking a variety of embarrassing gigs — including, at one point, kicking the crap out of a car. Pretty silly! But 100 percent accurate to Street Fighter II, where kicking the crap out of a car was one of the game’s bonus stages.
Mike Haggar
Pay close attention to the magazine covers shown in Street Fighter. One mentions “Mayor Mike Haggar” — a character from another Capcom game series, Final Fight. Although Haggar didn’t appear in Street Fighter II, he has made cameos in some of its sequels and did become a playable character in later Capcom spinoffs, like Marvel vs. Capcom: Infinite.
“My Best Friend Charlie”
During the big scene in M. Bison’s bar, Cody Rhodes’ Guile makes a passing reference to “my best friend Charlie.” In fact, Charlie’s murder, and Guile’s desire to bring M. Bison to justice for the crime, was supposedly his motivation for entering the tournament in Street Fighter II. Charlie later became a playable character in the prequel game Street Fighter Alpha.
Joe
Most of the characters in Street Fighter are the iconic fighters from the Street Fighter II arcade game: Ryu, Ken, Bison, Chun-Li, Guile, Vega, and so on. But one of the fighters in the movie’s tournament is a blonde dude named Joe. Who is Joe? He’s actually one of the opponents from the far more obscure first title in the series, 1987’s Street Fighter. Unlike most of the other characters from that original game, Joe’s made very few subsequent appearances in the series, making him one of the deeper cuts of Street Fighter lore in the movie.
“It was Tuesday.”
READ MORE: All the Classic Nintendo Easter Eggs in The Super Mario Bros. Movie
In the first live-action Street Fighter movie from 1994, there’s a very surreal scene between Chun-Li (Ming-Na Wen). and M. Bison (Raul Julia). She lays out her tragic backstory; he shrugs. His cruelty ruined her life! He has no memory of his actions. “You don’t remember any of it?” she cries. “For you, the day Bison graced your village was the most important day of your life! But for me, it was Tuesday,” he replies. Street Fighter (2026) recreates this scene — right down to David Dastmalchian saying “It was Tuesday.”
That Amazing M. Bison Painting
Speaking of that scene: Bison’s compound is decorated with a glorious painting of Julia in character, riding a horse like he’s Napoleon or something. Once again, the new Street Fighter imports this detail almost exactly; Dastmalchian’s Bison has a similar taste for interior decorating and has a painting of himself hanging proudly on the wall of his office.
Random Dudes Punching Each Other In Front of a Skyscraper
The establishing shot of Metrolao, M. Bison’s base of operations, shows two random dudes beating each other up in front of Bison’s personal skyscraper. Here, director Kitao Sakurai is paying homage to the opening titles of the Street Fighter II arcade game, here a dude knocks another guy’s block off and then the camera pans up a skyscraper in the background.

title: Steep roads, runoff concerns surface at Coplin Plantation development hearing
text:
STRATTON — Residents of Coplin Plantation expressed concerns about the land proposed for a high-density residential development at a Land Use Planning Commission public hearing Oct. 13.
Twelve lots are plotted for development, each with a single-family home. The subdivision, proposed by Loaf Land Development LLC, would create two 14-foot-wide gravel roads, Mountain Village Road and Courtney Lane, with a hammerhead turnaround at the end of both.
The 24.5-acre parcel is on a steep hill, with a subdivision sitting at the base. New development would abut property on Hedgehog Trail and Mountain Road. Included in the plan is a 3.7-acre natural space.
Comments ranged from residents who supported the development if concerns were taken into account, to others who expressed opposition.
Homeowners from the downhill subdivision overwhelmingly cited the steep hill as the primary reason they opposed the development, particularly during icy conditions.
Mike Dansky, a resident who lives at the intersection of Mountain Road and Hedgehog Trail, told the commission that drivers already have a tough time making the slope, and adding to the traffic would mean more accidents and stuck vehicles.
“In the winter time, cars and trucks rev up and come up the road as fast as they can because they got to be able to make the hill,” Dansky said. “We have an endless flow of cars sliding down the road, not being able to make the road, parking down at the bottom and walking up.”
Peter Collins, who lives on Mountain Road and plows for the plantation, reiterated Dansky’s points, adding that “not only do I think it’s a problem in the winter going up, I think it’s even worse going down.”
He, as did other speakers, recounted an instance of his truck going out of control on the hill, which also has a curve, obstructing the intersection at the base.
“If I didn’t have a plow on, I would have went right into the trees,” he said.
Four filter ponds are proposed for the subdivision. Homeowners highlighted fears about water runoff, which has caused damage to nearby lots in the past. Robert Ferrar, a member of the plantation’s board of assessors, questioned whether the ponds would adequately handle the amount of water and who would be responsible for maintaining them.
A representative of the Eustis Fire Department, Connor Dolan, cited multiple points with the development that worried the department in the event of an emergency.
He said the proposed 14-foot gravel roadways are below the 20 foot width recommended by the National Fire Protection Agency. The size of the proposed roadways, and the dead ends would be difficult for multiple engines to work with in the event of a fire.
Paired with the road size, the nearest hydrant is a mile away, requiring tankers to maneuver past each other to refill.
Dolan recommended that the roads be widened to account for fire protection, underground water tanks be installed to make up for the lack of a hydrant and household sprinklers be encouraged for all the houses in the development.
The commission will hold a session on Nov. 12 in Brewer to review technical evidence for the subdivision.

title: Ballot question to appoint Franklin County treasurer raises debate in Jay
Austin Lancaster runs wild as Skowhegan football tops Messalonskee
text:
SKOWHEGAN — A week after beating Biddeford by four scores, the Skowhegan football team made another impressive statement.
The River Hawks won their fourth consecutive game Friday, breezing to a 40-8 win over shorthanded Messalonskee at Reginald Clark Memorial Field. Quarterback Austin Lancaster rushed for 176 yards and five touchdowns.
“It’s (all thanks to) the offensive line; their blocking was incredible,” Lancaster said. “I just found the gaps, and I got to the end zone.”
HOW THEY DID IT
• Lancaster ran wild: Running the power read all night long, the junior shredded Messalonskee’s defense. He had touchdown runs of 4, 23, 1 and 51 yards in the first half as the River Hawks (5-2) took a 32-0 lead into the break. Lancaster added a 43-yard score in the third quarter.
“Power read is something we’ve done for a long time; going back to the state (championship) team (in 2022), that was one of our more successful plays,” said Skowhegan coach Brad Cyr. “When we have a QB we believe in, we’re excited to do it. It puts pressure on a defense because, if you go the wrong way, you’re in trouble.”
• Skowhegan’s defense completely shut down Messalonskee’s passing game. Eagles quarterback Fin Minkel had 856 yards passing and 12 touchdowns entering Friday, and receiver Malachi Cusano led Class B North in receiving yards (545) and touchdowns (eight).
Against Skowhegan, those Messalonskee standouts were completely neutralized. Cusano had one catch, an 8-yarder late in the first half. That was the only completion for Minkel, who threw an interception to Matthew Keister early in the second quarter.
“Our guys were very sticky in coverage,” Cyr said. “When you’re facing a guy like Cusano, you know they’re going to try and get him the ball, so it’s about not letting that happen. We held him to one catch, and I don’t think you can say that about any other game he’s played in.”
WHAT IT MEANS
• Skowhegan is assured a top-three seed in Class B North, which would mean a home playoff game in the first round if the River Hawks don’t move up higher. Following a win over Biddeford, which beat previously undefeated Marshwood 37-14 on Friday, the River Hawks look like one of the most dangerous teams in Class B.
• Injuries took a toll on Messalonskee (4-3), which was missing 12 players. The Eagles had to cancel their junior varsity season because of injuries, and they were without Andrew Witham and a bevy of other key players on the line against a Skowhegan team that’s been tough in the trenches.
“I would have liked to see less mental mistakes in the first half, but we’re (battling),” said Messalonskee coach Blair Doucette. “Skowhegan was physical, and they’re a really good football team. That’s probably the best we’ve seen them in the four years (I’ve been head coach).”
UNSUNG HERO
The River Hawks controlled the game up front, and Cyr specifically shouted out Cael Hamilton, a junior who moved to left guard after starting the season at left tackle.
“He’s got good feet, and even though he doesn’t look like the quickest kid, he gets where he’s going on his pull and has some power behind him,” Cyr said. “It won’t show up on any box score, but he’s definitely the leader of that unit.”
A WIN FOR COACH CYR
After coaching practice on Monday, Cyr was away from his team until Friday as his mother, Lorene, was hospitalized with pneumonia. Lancaster dedicated the win to Cyr, who was emotional following the game as he praised his team’s poise and execution.
“It was a great job by my kids and a great job by my staff,” Cyr said. “That’s why I have that staff — I can trust those guys to put the plan together and execute. When the kids are playing that well, it’s pretty easy.”
NOTABLE QUOTABLE

title: A year after St. Dom’s closes, Auburn schools see big uptick in enrollment
text:
Enrollment in the Auburn School Department is up by nearly 100 students, school officials said.
Superintendent Susan Dorris shared the news with the School Committee at last week’s meeting.
In total, the school department has 92 new students, compared to 34 last year.
Dorris believes it could be in part because of the closure of St. Dominic Academy in Auburn, which officially closed its high school at the end of the 2024-25 school year. The Catholic Diocese maintained the program for prekindergarten through eighth grade.
“We do know St. Dom’s closed. We don’t have all the facts lined up, but it may be one of the reasons why we are seeing an increase in students enrolled at middle and high school,” she said.
St. Dominic Academy was a popular prekindergarten through 12th grade program in the Lewiston and Auburn area. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Portland abruptly closed the high school and a group of supporters attempted to bring the school back through fundraising efforts.
At the time of its closure in spring 2025, St. Dom’s had around 137 students enrolled at the high school. Some students re-enrolled for the 2026 school year, but fundraising efforts to open a new high school in Lewiston did not pan out.
In total, the Auburn School Department has 3,396 students, including the new students.
Of the 92 new students, the Auburn Middle School has the largest increase with 33, Dorris said.
The state requires school departments to submit their enrollments yearly on Oct. 1. Those figures are what determines the amount of subsidy the state will grant the district during budget season.
“It’s good news for us with state funding,” Dorris told the committee, though specifics about how much more Auburn could receive because of the enrollment increase are unclear.

title: Maine utility sues five companies over PFAS contamination claims
text:
Augusta utility sues five companies over PFAS contamination claims
The Greater Augusta Utility District is suing five companies tied to four paper mills over claims that the companies' operations resulted in per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contaminating the utility's riverside wells.
The complaint against Sappi North America, the Kimberly-Clark Corporation, Huhtamaki, American Tissue Mills of Maine and the American Tissue Corporation was filed earlier this month in U.S. District Court.
In the lawsuit, the Greater Augusta Utility District said that its two Riverside Wells, which are hydraulically connected to the Kennebec River, have been contaminated by PFAS.
The water utility said that by November 2024, PFAS levels in the Riverside Wells had risen to approximately 23.3 nanograms per liter, exceeding Maine's then-applicable drinking water standard of 20.
According to the utility, it was forced to remove one of the Riverside Wells from service and undertake substantial action, including an investigation, an engineering evaluation, pilot testing and building the treatment infrastructure necessary to bring the well back online.
The lawsuit states that the companies owned and operated paper, paperboard, tissue, packaging and related manufacturing facilities within the Kennebec River watershed. The Greater Augusta Utility District said the companies' facilities used PFAS-containing materials and generated PFAS-containing wastewater, sludge, landfill leachate, stormwater and other waste streams. According to the utility, PFAS released from one or more of the facilities entered the Kennebec River watershed, migrated downstream through surface water and hydrologically connected groundwater, and contributed to the PFAS contamination of the Riverside Wells.
The Greater Augusta Utility District is seeking recovery of the necessary costs incurred in response to the releases and threatened releases of PFAS under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA). The utility also seeks damages and other relief under Maine law.
PFAS are also known as "forever chemicals" because they resist breaking down, which means they stay around in the environment and can be hazardous to people.

title: Raising your grandkids full-time? Here’s what you should know
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — For many grandparents, the role shifts from spoiling and sleepovers to full-time, day-in, day-out parenting.
It’s a transition that can bring deep love and purpose — but also real stress on time, money and energy.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down what grandparents need to know when they suddenly find themselves raising their grandkids.
“First thing, breathe”
When grandparents suddenly step into a full-time parenting role, gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said the initial instinct should be to slow down and acknowledge the shift.
“First thing, breathe,” Cradduck said. “You’re not a babysitter. You’re now in the role of molding another human being.”
More than 2 million grandparents are raising grandchildren in the United States, according to the U.S. Department of Labor.
Cradduck said whether the circumstances stem from tragedy or something else, grandparents need to be patient with themselves.
“You’ve got to give yourself grace to get through this,” Cradduck said.
Still, Cradduck pointed to a silver lining, noting that many of the most empathetic adults she knows were raised by their grandparents.
“Some of the best people I’ve ever met in my life were raised by their grandparents, and they grew up with such an absolute amount of empathy and honor and respect for other humans,” Cradduck said. “My hats off to any grandparent that does it.”
Get the legal and practical groundwork in place
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said one of the first practical steps grandparents should take is establishing legal guardianship.
“I think I’d want them to get the legal stuff taken care of — like you need to become guardian, you know, get that, so that when you say something, you’ve got some legal strength behind it,” O’Rourke said.
She also emphasized that grandparents don’t have to navigate the process alone, pointing to resources such as ParentsHelpingParents.org.
“Don’t do it alone. Don’t think you can handle this all alone,” O’Rourke said. “Go to the school, see if there’s mentors and support people there. Maybe groups that you can get tips on.”
That extends to everyday parenting challenges too, from discipline to schoolwork.
“Maybe get some help with technology, because they’re in school, using technology, even learning things,” O’Rourke said. “So get some help with how to help them with their homework, even if it’s bringing somebody else in there to help them.”
A chance to learn — and an opportunity, not just a challenge
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said that despite the difficulties, raising grandchildren offers a chance to grow.
“With all the challenges it has, it’s a tremendous opportunity to learn new things and really have your love and connection that you’re providing echo for generations,” Ambrose said.
Ambrose also encourages grandparents not to feel out of place in the role.
“I really want to offer encouragement to grandparents too to not think that you’re a fish out of water, because there’s a lot of people in the same boat,” she said. “You’re perfectly equipped.”
Pace yourself — and lean on experience
O’Rourke said grandparents raising children later in life shouldn’t hold themselves to the same energy standards they had decades earlier.
“Don’t let yourself raise your kids with the idea that you should have the energy level that you had at 30 at 60,” O’Rourke said. “Just kind of accept that you don’t have the energy. So pace yourself so that you’re not completely exhausted when Friday rolls around.”
Cradduck said that experience — not energy — is often a grandparent’s greatest asset.
“I’m a much, much better grandparent than I ever was a parent,” Cradduck said. “My patience level, my understanding, just my own maturity has developed. Things that I thought were catastrophic before — now you don’t cry over spilled milk. You can just clean it up.”
The legacy grandparents leave behind
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the role grandparents play in raising their grandchildren can shape the next generation in lasting ways.
“I think the most important thing that a grandparent gives is you give a good foundation,” Rogers said. “They have love and support and you’ve given them all the ingredients they need for success.”
Resources
- Parents Helping Parents
- Social Security
- Foster care system
- Legal Aid
- Grandchild’s school for mentors and support
- Get help with technology if needed
- Get help with homework
Key takeaways for grandparents raising grandchildren
- Keep the legacy in focus. Your greatest legacy is who you help your grandchildren become.
- It’s not babysitting. Expect high late-life physical, emotional and financial demands driven by family crisis.
- Find support through kinship, Legal Aid and other resources

title: Women have searched for perimenopause relief. Doctors say it’s under-recognized
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Perimenopause is defined as the phase when the ovaries gradually produce less estrogen. It can begin anywhere from eight to 10 years before menopause.
The most common signs of perimenopause, like those of menopause, are hot flashes, weight gain and mood changes, in addition to at least 31 other symptoms, according to doctors.
It remains under-recognized both among the medical community and the women who experience it.
One woman’s search for answers
Sloane Heller is a former TV news reporter. At 46 years old, she began experiencing symptoms including exhaustion, irritability, brain fog and a body she no longer recognized.
“I didn’t even know where to begin,” Heller said. “I absolutely had no idea what perimenopause was until I was thrust into it.”
When Heller brought her questions to a doctor, he dismissed her concerns as stress.
“I was just like, ‘How can you say this? How can you tell me what I’m going through?’” Heller said. “Because I know my body. I know the symptoms that I’m experiencing that I’ve never experienced in my entire life.”
Heller is not alone. A 2022 survey from the United Kingdom found 60% of perimenopausal women were not informed at all on the topic before age 40.
Doctors describe a knowledge gap
Dr. Carrie Wieneke is an obstetrician gynecologist at the University of Kansas Health System. She said perimenopause is poorly understood even among doctors because it is difficult to diagnose.
“As physicians, we love evidence, and so we love something that I can draw your blood with, I can do a scan with and say, you have, and there isn’t [one for] perimenopause,” Wieneke said.
Wieneke said part of the problem starts in medical school. A 2023 assessment of OB-GYN residency programs shows just under one-third offered a menopause curriculum. The University of Kansas Health System is one of them.
Hormone therapy history
Even when women are diagnosed with perimenopause, one of the most effective treatments, hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, has its own complicated history.
“It made the turning point of, I think, of education of OB-GYNs in menopause,” Wieneke said, referring to the 2002 Women’s Health Initiative study that found the risks associated with HRT outweighed the benefits.
That study noted that using HRT could increase your risk of cancer.
“Yeah, that’s what people heard,” Wieneke said. “Because if you actually look at the study and who was chosen and the different groups, there are some flaws in that which set it up for finding what it did. And so I’m personally sad, I think, because I think a lot of patients have been harmed.”
In 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration removed a 23-year-old black box warning label for estrogen, which is used to stabilize fluctuating hormones. The FDA requires a black box warning when substantial clinical data shows a drug can cause severe harm, hospitalization or death.
The removal marked a shift in how medical experts view the treatment.
Finding a treatment that works
For women like Heller, the damage from decades of fear was already done.
After eventually receiving a perimenopause diagnosis, Heller asked her doctor about hormone replacement therapy. “He said the only thing I can do for you is give you a testosterone pellet.”
The treatment involves inserting a pellet about the size of a grain of rice into the skin to deliver hormones to the body over a period of time. Testosterone relieved some of Heller’s symptoms, but she continued exploring other options.
“I knew the testosterone was just one piece of the puzzle,” she said. Four specialists and many months later, Heller found her current OB-GYN.
Three years after her perimenopause diagnosis, she is on a hormone regimen that includes an estradiol patch, progesterone and testosterone, along with complementary medications for symptoms including hair loss and constipation.
“There will be times where you feel really good and the doses that you’re on work really well for you,” Heller said. “And then a few months later, you might have to adjust those doses.”
Speaking out
Heller said she talks openly about her experience because she believes speaking out will help women avoid suffering in silence.
“The more we can destigmatize and get rid of the shame. I mean, there’s nothing to be embarrassed about,” Heller said. “Some will have an easier ride than others. But we all need to talk about it. We all need to be upfront about it.”
Wieneke and other OB-GYNs say hormone replacement therapy is not for everyone.
Treatment largely depends on symptoms, but most often involves anti-depressants and birth control. It is possible to get pregnant during perimenopause, even if periods are irregular, doctors said.
Doctors say there is no single test for perimenopause, so getting help often starts with asking the right questions.

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: The fight for water product safety changes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A mother’s fight for water product safety changes a decade after losing her son.
Plus, “learn to swim” – that’s what one floatie label promised. But critics are concerned some devices actually may teach a false sense of safety.
Fight for water product safety changes
Wearable floaties are often marketed as learn-to-swim aids for toddlers. Some even carry “Coast Guard approved” language—but parents and researchers worry they can create a false sense of safety.
National Investigative Reporter Caresse Jackman examines drowning-prevention concerns, including stories from families who say tragedy struck after taking the floaty off - and she investigates potential gaps in federal oversight as advocates push for clearer warnings and stronger standards.
Discount deception
Prices and affordability are a major concern to Americans everywhere, and many may not realize some stores are taking advantage of them—with deceptive pricing tactics.
Our investigation looks at examples of some retailers inflating original prices before sales, creating fake discounts, and running constant promotions that make deals seem urgent when they’re not real at all.
Even though these tactics are against FTC regulations, the federal government rarely steps in. We find out why, show you the signs of deceptive pricing, and walk the viewer through what they can do to fight back.
Claiming Social Security
When you claim Social Security could mean tens of thousands of dollars over the course of your retirement.
In this Watching Your Wallet, Consumer Investigator Rachel DePompa digs into when it makes sense to claim early, when to hold off, and the special strategies married couples should consider so they don’t leave money on the table.
